# PART ONE — THE HISTORY OF THE FRANKS
## Gregorii Turonensis Historiarum libri X


---

# BOOK ONE

## The Scene

Gregory of Tours was born about 538 into a Gallo-Roman senatorial family with close episcopal connections. Raised principally in the Auvergne, he became a
deacon and was consecrated bishop of Tours in 573. He wrote from personal acquaintance with many of the rulers, bishops, and other figures in his narrative,
while also drawing on Scripture, chronicles, earlier histories, written records, oral testimony, and his own observation. He died in 594.

The ten Books of the Histories move from creation to 591. Book One is a chronological and theological prologue extending from Adam to the death of Saint Martin
in 397; the later books carry the account through the Frankish kingdoms and into Gregory’s own episcopate. Gregory’s chronological totals and synchronisms are
retained as transmitted and flagged where needed, not silently corrected. His reports of miracles, visions, and divine judgments remain part of the history he
wrote: they express his understanding of sanctity, justice, and God’s action in human affairs.

## ENGLISH TRANSLATION

### Gregory’s First Preface

**[001]** As the cultivation of liberal letters was declining—or rather perishing—in the cities of Gaul, while many deeds were being done, both righteous and
wicked, the savagery of the peoples was raging, the fury of kings was growing sharper, churches were being attacked by heretics and defended by catholics, faith
in Christ was burning in many and growing lukewarm in some, and churches themselves were being enriched by the devout or stripped by the faithless, no
grammarian skilled in the art of dialectic could be found to depict these things either in prose or in metrical verse. Many therefore kept lamenting: “Woe to
our days, for the study of letters has perished among us, and no orator is found among the peoples who can publish present deeds upon the page.” As I
continually heard these and similar complaints, I could not conceal, for the remembrance of the past and the knowledge of those to come, either the struggles of
the wicked or the life of those who lived rightly, even in uncultivated speech. I was especially impelled by the fact that I have often heard my own people say
with wonder: “Few understand the philosophizing orator; many understand the rustic speaker.” I also wished the beginning of the first book to be devoted to a
calculation of the years from the very beginning of the world, and I have set down its chapters below.

### The Author’s Profession of Faith and Purpose

**[002]** As I am about to write of the wars of kings with hostile peoples, of martyrs with pagans, and of churches with heretics, I wish first to set forth my
faith, so that whoever reads me may not doubt that I am catholic. I have also thought fit, for the sake of those who despair as the end of the world approaches,
to gather the sum of earlier years from the chronicles and histories and explain openly how many years there have been since the world’s beginning. But first I
beg the reader’s pardon if in letters or syllables I transgress the art of grammar, with which I am not fully imbued. My one concern is to retain without
pretence or hesitation of heart what is preached as worthy of belief in the church, for I know that one who is subject to sin can obtain pardon before God
through pure faith.

I believe in God the Father almighty. I believe in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord, born of the Father, not made, not after time, but always with the
Father before all time. For the Father could not be called Father unless He had a Son, nor would the Son be a Son if He did not have a Father. Those who say,
“There was a time when He was not,” I abominate and declare separated from the church. I believe that this Christ is the Word of the Father, through whom all
things were made. I believe that this Word was made flesh, that the world was redeemed by His passion, and that His humanity, not His deity, underwent the
passion. I believe that He rose on the third day, freed lost humanity, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come to judge the
living and the dead.

I believe that the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father and the Son, not inferior as though He had not existed before, but equal, always God coeternal with the
Father and the Son, of one substance in nature, equal in omnipotence, coeternal in essence; He was never without the Father or the Son, and is not inferior to
the Father or the Son. I believe that this holy Trinity subsists in the distinction of persons: one person of the Father, another of the Son, another of the
Holy Spirit. In this Trinity I confess one deity, one power, one essence. I believe that blessed Mary was a virgin before the birth and remained a virgin after
the birth. I believe that the soul is immortal, yet has no share in the divine essence. I faithfully believe all things instituted by the 318 bishops at Nicaea.

Concerning the end of the world, I hold what I learned from earlier writers: first the Antichrist will come. The Antichrist will first introduce circumcision,
declaring himself Christ; then he will place his statue in the temple at Jerusalem to be adored, as we read that the Lord said: “You will see the abomination of
desolation standing in the holy place.” But the Lord Himself makes that day known to the eyes of all, saying: “Of that day and hour no one knows, neither the
angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone.” Here we may also answer the heretics who attack us by asserting that the Son is inferior to the Father
because He does not know that day. Let them understand that it is the Christian people, called the son, of whom God foretells: “I will be their father, and they
shall be my sons.” For if He had foretold this of the only-begotten Son, He would never have placed the angels before Him. Thus He says: “Neither the angels of
heaven nor the sons,” showing that He said this not of the only-begotten but of the adopted people. Our end is Christ Himself, who in generous kindness will
grant us eternal life if we turn to Him.

The chronicles of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and of the priest Jerome speak plainly concerning the calculation of this world’s years and unfold the reckoning
of the whole sequence. Orosius too, investigating most diligently, gathered the entire number of years from the world’s beginning to his own time. Victorius
likewise did this when he investigated the order of the paschal solemnities. Following the copies of these writers, I wish, if the Lord deigns to lend His aid,
to compute the whole accumulation of years from the formation of the first man to my own time. I shall accomplish this more readily if I begin with Adam
himself.

### 1. Adam and Eve

**[003]** In the beginning the Lord formed heaven and earth in His Christ, who is the beginning of all things—that is, in His Son. After creating the elements
of the whole world, He took a clod of fragile clay and formed man in His image and likeness; He breathed into his face the breath of life, and he became a
living soul. While he slept, a rib was taken from him and the woman Eve was created. There is no doubt that this first man Adam bore the type of the Redeemer
before he sinned. For the Redeemer, sleeping in the sleep of His passion, produced water and blood from His side and presented to Himself the virgin and
immaculate church, redeemed by blood and cleansed by water, having neither spot nor wrinkle: washed by water because of the spot, stretched upon the cross
because of the wrinkle. These first human beings lived blessed amid the delights of paradise, but, beguiled by the serpent’s cunning, they transgressed the
divine commandments; cast out from the angelic dwelling, they were assigned to the labors of the world.

### 2. Cain and Abel

**[004]** The woman knew the attendant and conceived and bore two sons. But while God graciously accepted the sacrifice of one, the other swelled with kindled
envy and, rising as a new parricide to shed his brother’s blood, overpowered, defeated, and killed his brother.

### 3. Enoch the Righteous

**[005]** Thereafter the whole race rushed into abominable crime except righteous Enoch, who walked in the ways of God and was taken up by the Lord Himself
because of his righteousness, thus being removed from amid a sinful people. For we read: “Enoch walked with God, and he did not appear, because God took him.”

### 4. The Flood

**[006]** The Lord, moved against the iniquities of a people not walking in His paths, sent the Flood, and with its inundation destroyed every living soul from
the face of the earth. Only Noah, most faithful and especially His own, bearing in himself the type of the Redeemer, did He preserve in the ark, together with
his wife and the wives of his three sons, for the restoration of posterity. Here heretics object to us: why did Holy Scripture say that the Lord was angry? Let
them understand that our God is not angry as a man is. He is moved to terrify, drives away to recall, and is angry to correct. Nor do I doubt that the form of
the ark bore the type of mother church. Passing among the waves and rocks of this age, she carries us in her maternal bosom, defending us from threatening evils
with loving embrace and protection. From Adam to Noah there are ten generations: Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah. In
these ten generations 2,242 years are found. **[FLAG — Gregory’s received chronology.]** The book of Joshua plainly explains that Adam was buried in the land of
Enacim, formerly called Hebron.

### 5. Cush, the Inventor of the Idol

**[007]** After the Flood Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Nations issued from Japheth, and likewise from Ham and Shem; as the ancient history says,
the human race was dispersed by them beneath the whole heaven. Ham’s firstborn was Cush. He possessed the whole magical art through the devil’s instruction and
was the first inventor of idolatry. At the devil’s instigation he was the first to set up an idol for adoration; he also showed men stars and fire falling from
heaven by false power. He crossed into Persia. The Persians called him Zoroaster, that is, “living star.” From him they also learned to adore fire; they worship
as a god the man who was himself consumed by divine fire.

### 6. Babylon

**[008]** When multiplied humanity was dispersing through every land, they came from the east and found a grassy plain at Shinar. There they built a city and
strove to construct a tower that would reach the heavens. God, confounding their vain thought and their language at once, scattered them over the whole
wide-extending earth. The city was called Babel, that is, confusion, because there God confounded their languages. This is Babylon, built by the giant Nimrod,
son of Cush. As Orosius’s history relates, it was laid out as a square on the wondrous level of the plain. Its wall, made of baked brick set in bitumen, was
fifty cubits broad and two hundred cubits high, with a circuit of 470 stades. One stade contains five arpents. Fifty gates stood on each side, making one
hundred. **[FLAG — the transmitted figures say “quinae,” fifty on each side, but give one hundred as the total.]** The doors of these gates were formed of cast
bronze in wondrous size. The same historian relates many other things about this city, adding: “And although the building possessed such magnificence,
nevertheless it was conquered and overthrown.”

### 7. Abraham and Ninus

**[009]** Noah’s first son was Shem; in the tenth generation from him Abraham was born: Noah, Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, and Terah, who
begot Abraham. In these ten generations—from Noah to Abraham—942 years are found. **[FLAG — Gregory’s received chronology.]** At that time Ninus reigned; he
built the city Ninus, which they call Nineveh, whose extent Jonah the prophet defined as a three days’ journey. Abraham was born in the forty-third year of his
reign. This Abraham is the beginning of our faith. He received the promise. Christ our Lord revealed to him that He would be born and suffer for us in exchange
for the victim, saying in the Gospels: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad.” Severus relates in his chronicle that this burnt
offering was offered on Mount Calvary, where the Lord was crucified, just as is famously reported in Jerusalem to this day. On this mountain stood the holy
cross to which the Redeemer was fixed, and from which His blessed blood flowed. Abraham received the sign of circumcision, showing that what he bore in the body
we should bear in the heart, as the prophet says: “Circumcise yourselves for your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart; and do not follow strange
gods”; and again: “No one uncircumcised in heart shall enter my holy places.” After adding a syllable to his name, God called this Abraham the father of many
nations.

### 8. Isaac, Esau, Job, and Jacob

**[010]** When Abraham was one hundred years old, he begot Isaac. In the sixtieth year of Isaac’s life twin sons were born to Rebecca. The first was Esau, that
is Edom, meaning earthly, who sold his birthright because of gluttony. He is the father of the Idumeans. In the fourth generation from him Jobab was born: Esau,
Reuel, Zerah, Jobab, who is also Job. He lived 249 years; in the eighty-ninth year he was delivered from his affliction. After the affliction he lived 170
years, with all his possessions restored twofold, and rejoiced in as many sons as he had lost. **[FLAG — Gregory’s transmitted chronology and figures.]**

### 9. Joseph in Egypt

**[011]** The second son was Jacob. Jacob was beloved of God, as He says through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” After wrestling with the angel
he was called Israel, from whom come the Israelites. He begot the twelve patriarchs, whose names are Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan,
Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. After these he begot Joseph by Rachel in the ninety-second year of his life. He loved him more than his other sons. He also had
Benjamin by her, the last of all. When Joseph was in the sixteenth year of his life, bearing the type of the Redeemer, he saw dreams which he related to his
brothers: as though he were binding sheaves and his brothers’ sheaves adored his; and again, as though the sun, moon, and eleven stars came before him. This
bred great hatred toward him among his brothers. Inflamed with envy, they sold him for thirty pieces of silver to Ishmaelites passing into Egypt. When famine
threatened and his brothers went down into Egypt, they were recognized by Joseph, but they did not recognize Joseph. After subjecting them to many trials and
bringing Benjamin there, he revealed himself to them; Benjamin too had been born of his mother Rachel. Afterward all the Israelites went down into Egypt and
through Joseph enjoyed Pharaoh’s favor. Jacob blessed his sons and died in Egypt; Joseph buried him in his father’s tomb in the land of Canaan. After Joseph and
Pharaoh died, the whole race was subjected to servitude. Through Moses it was freed after the ten plagues of Egypt, when Pharaoh was drowned in the Red Sea.

### 10. The Crossing of the Red Sea

**[012]** Since many have said much about this crossing of the sea, I have thought fit to insert something here about the situation of the place and the
crossing itself. The Nile runs through Egypt, as you well know, and irrigates it by its flood; hence the Egyptians are called Nilicolae, dwellers by the Nile.
Many who have explored the region say that its banks are now filled with sacred monasteries. On its bank stands not the Babylon mentioned above, but the city of
Babylon in Egypt, where Joseph built granaries of squared stone and cement with wondrous workmanship. They were broader at the bottom and narrowed toward the
top, so that grain could be poured in through a small opening; these granaries are still seen today. The king set out from this city with armies of chariots and
a great force of infantry to pursue the Hebrews. The river just mentioned comes from the east, turns toward the west, and goes to the Red Sea. From the west a
lake or arm of the Red Sea advances eastward, about fifty miles long and eighteen broad. At the head of this lake the city Clysma was built, not for the
fertility of the place—nothing is more barren—but for its harbor, because ships coming from India rest there for the harbor’s convenience; goods brought there
are carried through all Egypt. The Hebrews came through the desert toward this lake as far as the sea itself, found fresh water, and pitched camp. They were
hemmed into this narrow place by both desert and sea, as it is written: “Pharaoh, hearing that the sea and desert had shut them in and that there was no way by
which they could proceed, set out to pursue them.” When the people cried to Moses as the enemy approached, the rod was cast over the sea at the Divine command
and the sea was divided. They proceeded through the dry bed, walled on every side by water, as Scripture says; unharmed, they reached the shore opposite Mount
Sinai, and crossed under Moses’ leadership while the Egyptians were drowned.

Many things are told about this crossing, as I have said, but I have taken care to include in this page what I learned from wise men, and certainly from those
men who had approached that very place. They also say that the ruts made by the chariot wheels remain to this day and can be seen in the depths as far as the
eye’s sight reaches. If a slight disturbance of the sea covers them, when it grows still they are divinely renewed as they had been. Others say that, making a
small circuit by sea, they returned to the same shore from which they had entered. Others assert that there was one entrance for all; some, that a separate way
lay open to each tribe, using the testimony of the psalm: “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions.” I must understand these divisions spiritually, not
literally. For in this world too, figuratively called a sea, there are many divisions; not all can pass to life equally or by one road. Some cross at the first
hour: those reborn through baptism who can remain immaculate from every carnal defilement until the end of their present life. Others at the third hour: those
converted at a greater age. Others at the sixth: those restrained by the ardor of wantonness. As the evangelist records, they are hired for work in the Lord’s
vineyard at each of these hours according to their own faith. These are the divisions by which this sea is crossed.

As for those who came from the sea and returned along the shore of the lake, this is what the Lord says to Moses: “Let them return and pitch camp opposite
Pi-hahiroth, which is between Migdol and the sea opposite Baal-zephon.” There is no doubt that the crossing of the sea and the pillar of cloud bore the type of
my baptism, as blessed Paul the apostle says: “I would not have you ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all were baptized into
Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” The pillar of fire bore the type of the Holy Spirit. From the birth of Abraham to the departure of the children of Israel
from Egypt and the crossing of the Red Sea—which was Moses’ eightieth year—462 years are computed. **[FLAG — Gregory’s received chronology.]**

### 11. The People in the Desert, and Joshua

**[013]** Then for forty years the Israelites dwelt in the desert, were instructed in the laws, were tested, and were fed with angelic food. After receiving the
Law and crossing the Jordan with Joshua, they obtained the land of promise.

### 12. The Captivity of the Israelite People, and the Generations down to David

**[014]** After this crossing, because they neglected the divine commandments, they were often subjected to the service of foreigners. But when they turned back
and groaned, the Lord delivered them by the arm of strong men. Afterward they asked the Lord through Samuel for a king, as other nations had; they received
first Saul and then David. From Abraham to David there are fourteen generations: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon,
Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David. David begot Solomon by Bathsheba. Solomon was raised to the kingdom through Nathan the prophet, his brother, and his mother.

### 13. Solomon and the Building of the Temple

**[015]** When David died and his son began to reign, the Lord appeared to him and promised to grant what he asked. Setting earthly riches aside, he sought
wisdom instead. This pleased the Lord, so that he heard from Him: “Because you did not seek the kingdoms of the world or their riches, but asked for wisdom,
therefore receive it. Before you no one was so wise, and after you there will be none.” He later proved this by the judgment he gave between two women disputing
over one infant. This Solomon built the temple in the Lord’s name with wondrous workmanship, bringing into it much gold, silver, bronze, and iron, so that some
said no building like it had ever been made in the world. From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt to the building of the temple—which was in the
seventh year of Solomon’s reign—480 years are found, as the history of Kings testifies. **[FLAG — Gregory’s transmitted chronology.]**

### 14. The Division of the Israelite Kingdom

**[016]** After Solomon’s death the kingdom was divided into two parts through Rehoboam’s harshness. Two tribes remained with Rehoboam and were called Judah;
ten tribes went to Jeroboam and were called Israel. Thereafter they turned aside to idolatry, and neither the prophecies of the prophets, nor the prophets’
deaths, nor the ruin of their country, nor even the destruction of their own kings subdued them.

### 15. The Captivity in Babylon

**[017]** At last the Lord, angered against them, raised up Nebuchadnezzar, who carried them captive into Babylon with all the ornaments of the temple. In this
captivity the distinguished prophet Daniel went unharmed among hungry lions, and the three boys went dewy into the midst of the fire as captives. Ezekiel also
prophesied in this captivity, and Ezra the prophet was born. From David to the desolation of the temple and the removal into Babylon there are fourteen
generations: David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah. In these fourteen generations
390 years are found. **[FLAG — Gregory’s received chronology and genealogy.]** They were freed from this captivity through Zerubbabel, who afterward restored
both temple and city.

But I think this captivity bears the type of that captivity into which the sinful soul is led away and from which, unless Zerubbabel—that is, Christ—frees it,
it will suffer a dreadful exile. The Lord Himself says in the Gospel: “If the Son frees you, you will be free indeed.” May He establish in us a temple in which
He deigns to dwell, in which faith shines like gold, the eloquence of preaching gleams like silver, and all the ornaments of that visible temple become bright
in the honor of our senses. May He also grant a saving effect to our good will, because “unless He builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.” This
captivity is said to have lasted seventy years.

### 16. The Birth of Christ

**[018]** After they returned through Zerubbabel, as I have said, they were now murmuring against God, now rushing after idols or imitating the abominations
practiced by the nations; despising God’s prophets, they were delivered to the nations, subjugated, and slaughtered. At last the Lord Himself, promised by the
voices of patriarchs and prophets, entered the womb of the Virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit and deigned to be born for the redemption both of that nation and
of all nations. From the removal into captivity to the birth of Christ there are fourteen generations: Jechoniah, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Abiud, Eliakim, Azor,
Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, and Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom our Lord Jesus Christ was born; Joseph is counted as the fourteenth.

### 17. The Various Kingdoms of the Nations

**[019]** Lest I appear to know only the history of the Hebrew people, I record the other kingdoms and the times at which they existed in relation to the
Israelites. In Abraham’s time Ninus reigned over the Assyrians, Europs over the Sicyonians, and the sixteenth ruling power—which in their language they called a
dynasty—was over the Egyptians. In Moses’ time the seventh Tropas reigned among the Argives; Cecrops was the first in Attica; the twelfth Cenchris was among the
Egyptians and was drowned in the Red Sea; the sixteenth Agatadis was among the Assyrians; and Maratis was among the Sicyonians. In Solomon’s time, when he
reigned over Israel, the fifth Silvius reigned among the Latins, Fistus among the Lacedaemonians, the second Oxion among the Corinthians; it was the 126th year
of the Egyptian Thebes; Eutropes ruled the Assyrians and the second Agasastus the Athenians. When Amon reigned over Judea and the people went into captivity in
Babylon, Argeus ruled the Macedonians, Cyces the Laedi, Vaphres the Egyptians, Nebuchadnezzar—who carried them away captive—the Babylonians, and the sixth
Servius the Romans. **[FLAG — Gregory reproduces a received synchronistic scheme; its names, ordinals, and chronology are not silently modernized.]**

### 18. When Lyon Was Founded

**[020]** After these rulers, Julius Caesar was the first emperor and obtained sole rule of the empire. The second was Octavian, Julius Caesar’s descendant,
whom they call Augustus and after whom the month August is named. I find it most clearly recorded that Lyon in Gaul was founded in the nineteenth year of his
rule. Later, illustrious with the blood of martyrs, it was called most noble.

### 19. The Gifts of the Magi and the Killing of the Infants

**[021]** In the forty-third year of Augustus’s rule our Lord Jesus Christ, as I have said, was born according to the flesh of the Virgin Mary at Bethlehem, the
town of David. The Magi from the east saw His immense star and came with gifts; offering their humble presents, they adored the child. Herod, out of zeal for
his kingdom, killed the little infants while striving to persecute Christ the God. He himself was afterward struck by divine judgment. **[FLAG — Gregory’s
regnal chronology.]**

### 20. The Miracles and Passion of Christ

**[022]** While our Lord God Jesus Christ preached repentance, granted the grace of baptism, promised the heavenly kingdom to all nations, and worked prodigies
and signs among the peoples—bringing wine from water, extinguishing fevers, giving light to the blind, restoring life to the buried, freeing those possessed by
unclean spirits, and restoring the wretched lepers’ disfigured skin—by these and many other signs He most plainly declared to the peoples that He was God. Among
the Jews anger was kindled, envy stirred, and a mind fed on the blood of the prophets plotted unjustly to kill the just one. So that the oracles of the ancient
prophets might be fulfilled, He was betrayed by a disciple, condemned by the chief priests, mocked by the Jews, crucified with the wicked, and, after giving up
His spirit, guarded by soldiers. When these things had been done, darkness came over the whole world, and many, turning and groaning, confessed Jesus to be the
Son of God.

### 21. Joseph, Who Buried Him

**[023]** Joseph, who laid Him in his own tomb after treating Him with spices, was also arrested, shut in a little cell, and guarded by the chief priests
themselves. As the Acts of Pilate sent to the emperor Tiberius relate, they showed greater cruelty toward him than toward the Lord Himself: the Lord was guarded
by soldiers, Joseph by the priests. But when the Lord rose, the guards were terrified by an angelic vision and He was not found in the tomb. At night the walls
of the cell in which Joseph was held were lifted high; an angel released him from custody, and the walls were restored to their place. When the chief priests
reproached the guards and urgently demanded the holy body from them, the soldiers said: “You return Joseph, and we will return Christ; but, as we recognize the
truth, neither can you now return God’s benefactor nor we God’s Son.” The priests were confounded, and the soldiers were released under this excuse.

### 22. James the Apostle

**[024]** It is related that when the apostle James saw that the Lord had died upon the cross, he abjured and swore that he would never eat bread unless he saw
the Lord risen. On the third day the Lord returned in triumph after despoiling hell and, appearing to James, said: “Arise, James, and eat, for I have now risen
from the dead.” This is James the Just, whom they call the brother of the Lord because he was a son born to Joseph by another wife.

### 23. The Day of the Lord’s Resurrection

**[025]** I believe that the Lord’s resurrection occurred on the first day, not the seventh, as many think. This is the day of the resurrection of our Lord
Jesus Christ, which I properly call the Lord’s Day because of His holy resurrection. It first saw light at the beginning, and it first merited to behold the
Lord rising from the tomb. From the captivity of Jerusalem and the desolation of the temple to the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, to the seventeenth
year of Tiberius—668 years are computed. **[FLAG — Gregory’s received chronology.]**

### 24. The Ascension of the Lord, and the Deaths of Pilate and Herod

**[026]** After rising, the Lord disputed with His disciples about the kingdom of God for forty days; then, as they watched, He was taken up in a cloud, carried
into heaven, and sat gloriously at the Father’s right hand. Pilate sent an account of these events to Tiberius Caesar and informed him of Christ’s powers as
well as His passion and resurrection. These Acts are still preserved among us in writing today. Tiberius read the account to the Senate, which angrily rejected
it because the report had not first come to them. From this the first seeds of hatred against Christians sprouted. Pilate did not remain unpunished: because of
the crime of his malice—that is, the killing which he carried out against our Lord Jesus Christ—he killed himself with his own hands. Many think he was a
Manichee because of what is read in the Gospel: “Some Galileans came, reporting to Him those whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.” King Herod
likewise, while raging against the Lord’s apostles, was divinely struck for such great crimes; swelling and swarming with worms, he took a knife to purge the
evil and released himself by a blow of his own hand.

### 25. The Passion of the Apostles, and Nero

**[027]** The blessed apostle Peter came to Rome under the emperor Claudius, fourth from Augustus, and by preaching there with many miracles proved most plainly
that Christ is the Son of God. From those days Christians began to be found in the city of Rome. As the name of Christ spread more and more among the peoples,
the ancient serpent’s envy arose against it, and savage malice entered the emperor’s whole heart. For the dissolute, vain, and proud Nero—submissive to men and
in turn desiring men, the foulest violator of his mother, sisters, and nearest women relatives—was the first, to complete the mass of his wickedness, to stir
persecution against those believing in the worship of Christ. He kept with him Simon Magus, a man of utter malice and master of every device of the magical art.
When Simon had been cast down by the Lord’s apostles Peter and Paul, Nero was moved against them because they preached Christ, the Son of God, and refused to
adore idols. He ordered Peter to be killed by the cross and Paul by the sword. Nero himself, attempting to escape the sedition stirred against him, killed
himself with his own hand at the fourth milestone from the city.

### 26. James, Mark, and John the Evangelist

**[028]** Then James, the brother of the Lord, and Mark the evangelist were crowned with glorious martyrdom for Christ’s name. Stephen the deacon and martyr had
been the first of all to enter this path. A great calamity for the Jews followed the killing of the apostle James. At Vespasian’s coming the temple was burned,
and 600,000 Jews perished by sword and famine in that war. **[FLAG — Gregory’s transmitted figure.]** Domitian, the second after Nero to rage against
Christians, sent the apostle John into exile on the island of Patmos and inflicted various cruelties upon the people. After Domitian’s death the blessed apostle
and evangelist John returned from exile. Old, full of days, and living a life perfected in God, he laid himself in the tomb. It is said that he will not taste
death until the Lord comes again to judge, as He Himself says in the Gospel: “Thus I wish him to remain until I come.”

### 27. The Persecution under Trajan

**[029]** Trajan, third after Nero, stirred a persecution against Christians. Under him blessed Clement—who was the third bishop of the Roman church—suffered;
Saint Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem and son of Cleophas, is said to have been crucified for Christ’s name; and Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was led to Rome and
assigned to the beasts. These things occurred in Trajan’s time.

### 28. Hadrian, the Heresies, Justin, and Polycarp

**[030]** After him Aelius Hadrian, Domitian’s successor, was made emperor. Jerusalem is called Aelia after Aelius Hadrian because he rebuilt it. After these
passions of the saints, it was not enough for the adversary to have stirred unbelieving nations against the worshippers of Christ without also stirring schisms
among Christians themselves. He provoked heresies, and divided catholic faith was expounded in conflicting ways. Under Antoninus’s rule the insane Marcionite
and Valentinian heresies arose. The philosopher Justin, after writing books for the catholic church, was crowned with martyrdom for Christ’s name. In Asia, when
persecution arose, the most blessed Polycarp, disciple of the apostle and evangelist John, was consecrated to the Lord by fire like a most pure burnt offering
in the eightieth year of his life. Many in Gaul too were crowned with heavenly gems through martyrdom for Christ’s name; faithful histories of their passions
are preserved among us to this day.

### 29. Saint Photinus, Irenaeus, and the Other Martyrs of Lyon

**[031]** Among these was Photinus, the first bishop of the church of Lyon, who, full of days and afflicted with various torments, suffered for Christ’s name.
The most blessed Irenaeus, successor to this martyr, had been sent to this city by blessed Polycarp and shone with admirable virtue; in a short time he
especially restored the city wholly to Christianity by his preaching. But when persecution came, the devil waged such war there through the tyrant, and so great
a multitude of Christians was slaughtered for confessing the Lord’s name, that rivers of Christian blood ran through the streets. I could not gather either
their number or their names, for the Lord inscribed them in the book of life. His executioner afflicted blessed Irenaeus with various torments in his own
presence and consecrated him to Christ the Lord through martyrdom. After him forty-eight martyrs suffered, of whom I read that the first was Vettius Epagatus.

### 30. The Seven Men Sent to Preach in Gaul

**[032]** Under the emperor Decius many wars arose against the Christian name, and there was such slaughter of believers that they could not be numbered.
Babylas, bishop of Antioch, with three little boys—Urban, Prilidan, and Epolon—and Sixtus, bishop of the Roman church, the archdeacon Lawrence, and Hippolytus
were consummated through martyrdom for confessing the Lord’s name. Valentinian and Novatian, the chief heretics of that time, raged against our faith at the
enemy’s prompting.

At this time seven men were ordained bishops and sent to preach in the Gauls, as the history of the passion of the holy martyr Saturninus relates. It says: “In
the consulship of Decius and Gratus, as is retained in faithful memory, the city of Toulouse first had the holy Saturninus as its foremost and highest priest.”
These were sent: Catianus as bishop to the people of Tours, Trophimus to those of Arles, Paul to Narbonne, Saturninus to Toulouse, Dionysius to Paris,
Stremonius to Clermont, and Martial was appointed bishop to Limoges. Of these, blessed Dionysius, bishop of Paris, afflicted with various torments for Christ’s
name, ended his present life with the sword threatening. Saturninus, already assured of martyrdom, said to his two priests: “Behold, I am now offered, and the
time of my release is at hand. I ask that you not abandon me altogether until I complete the debt of my end.” When he was seized and led to the Capitol,
abandoned by them, he was dragged alone. Seeing himself deserted by them, he is said to have prayed: “Lord Jesus Christ, hear me from Your holy heaven, that
this church may never deserve to have a bishop from among these citizens forever.” I know that it has happened in that city to this very day. He was bound to
the feet of a raging bull, hurled from the Capitol, and ended his life. Catianus, Trophimus, Stremonius, Paul, and Martial, living in the highest holiness,
acquired peoples for the church and extended Christ’s faith among all; they departed in blessed confession. Thus those who left the earth through martyrdom and
these through confession were joined together equally in heaven.

### 31. The Church at Bourges

**[033]** One of the disciples of these men came to the city of Bourges and announced Christ the Lord, the salvation of all, to the people. A few of them
believed; clerics were ordained, received the rite of psalmody, and were instructed how to build a church and celebrate solemn rites to almighty God. Since they
still had little means for building, they asked a certain citizen for a house from which they might make a church. The senators and other leading men of the
place were then bound to pagan cults; those who had believed were among the poor, according to the Lord’s reproach to the Jews: “Prostitutes and tax collectors
go before you into the kingdom of God.”

Unable to obtain the house from the man they asked, they found a certain Leocadius, a leading senator of Gaul, who was of the stock of Vettius Epagatus, whom I
mentioned above as having suffered for Christ’s name at Lyon. When they made their petition and faith known to him together, he answered: “If my house, which I
have in the city of Bourges, were worthy of this work, I would not refuse to provide it.” Hearing this, they prostrated themselves at his feet, offered three
hundred gold pieces with a silver dish, and said that it was fitting for this ministry. He accepted three of the gold pieces as a blessing and graciously waived
the rest. Though still entangled in the error of idolatry, he became a Christian and made his house a church. This is now the first church in the city of
Bourges, constructed with wondrous workmanship and illustrious with the relics of the first martyr Stephen.

### 32. Chrocus and the Temple of the Auvergne

**[034]** In the twenty-seventh place Valerian and Gallienus obtained the Roman empire and stirred a grievous persecution against Christians in their time. Then
Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage made the churches illustrious with their blessed blood. In their time Chrocus, king of the Alamans, set his army in
motion and ranged through the Gauls. This Chrocus is said to have been exceedingly arrogant. Having committed many iniquities, he gathered the nation of the
Alamans, as I have said, by the counsel of his wicked mother, ranged through all the Gauls, and overthrew from their foundations all buildings constructed in
antiquity. Coming into the Auvergne, he burned, demolished, and overthrew the temple which in the Gallic tongue they call Vasso Galate. It had been made and
fortified with wondrous workmanship. Its wall was double: inside it was constructed of small stone, outside of carved squared stones. The wall was thirty feet
thick. Within it was adorned with marble and mosaic; the pavement of the building was laid with marble, and above it was covered with lead.

### 33. The Martyrs Who Suffered near the Auvergne

**[035]** Near this city the martyrs Liminius and Antolianus rest. There Cassius and Victorinus, joined in the love of Christ with brotherly affection, obtained
the kingdoms of heaven together through the shedding of their own blood. Antiquity reports that Victorinus was a slave of the priest of the temple just named.
While he often went to the village called the Christians’ village to persecute Christians, he found Cassius, a Christian. Moved by his preaching and miracles,
he believed in Christ; leaving the filth of pagan rites and consecrated in baptism, he became great in the working of miracles. Not long afterward, joined on
earth through martyrdom, as I have said, they came together equally to the heavenly kingdoms.

### 34. Saint Privatus the Martyr

**[036]** When the Alamans burst into the Gauls, Saint Privatus, bishop of the city of Javols, was found in a cave of Mount Memmate, where he devoted himself to
fastings and prayers, while the people of the fortress of Grèdo had been shut in by his warning. But while the good shepherd refused to hand his sheep over to
wolves, he was compelled to sacrifice to demons. Abhorring and rejecting that filth alike, he was beaten with clubs until he was thought lifeless. After a few
days he breathed out his spirit from that very battering. Chrocus himself was captured at Arles, a city of Gaul, afflicted with various torments, and died by
the sword, not undeservedly paying the penalties he had inflicted on the saints of God.

### 35. Quirinus, Bishop and Martyr

**[037]** Under Diocletian, who ruled the Roman empire in the thirty-third place, a grievous persecution against Christians raged for four years, so that on one
occasion, on the most sacred day of Easter itself, a great multitude of Christian people was killed for worshipping the true God. At that time Quirinus, priest
of the church of Siscia, bore a glorious martyrdom for Christ’s name. The pagans’ savagery tied a millstone to his neck and drove him into the whirlpool of a
river. When he fell into the depths, he was borne upon the waters for a long time by divine power; the waters did not swallow him whom no weight of sin pressed
down. The surrounding multitude, marveling at what had happened, set aside their gentile fury and hastened to free the priest. Seeing this, he would not allow
himself to be withdrawn from martyrdom. Raising his eyes to heaven, he said: “Lord Jesus, who sit gloriously at the Father’s right hand, do not allow me to be
removed from this course, but receive my soul and deign to join me to Your martyrs in eternal rest.” With these words he gave up his spirit. His body was taken
up by the Christians and committed to burial with veneration.

### 36. The Birth of Saint Martin and the Finding of the Cross

**[038]** Constantine obtained the Roman empire in the thirty-fourth place and reigned prosperously for thirty years. In the eleventh year of his rule, when
peace had been restored to the churches after Diocletian’s departure, the most blessed bishop Martin was born at Sabaria, a city of Pannonia, to parents who
were pagan but not of the lowest rank. In the twentieth year of his own rule this Constantine killed his son Crispus by poison and his wife Fausta in a heated
bath, because they were said to have wished to betray his kingdom. In his time the venerable wood of the Lord’s cross was found through the diligence of his
mother Helena, the Hebrew Judas pointing it out; after baptism Judas was called Quiriacus. The historian Eusebius wrote his chronicle down to this time. From
the twenty-first year of Constantine’s rule the priest Jerome continued it, recording that the priest Juvencus composed the Gospels in verse at the aforesaid
emperor’s request.

### 37. James, Bishop of Nisibis

**[039]** Under the rule of Constans lived James of Nisibis. The ears of divine clemency, inclined toward his prayers, repelled many dangers from his city.
Maximinus, bishop of Trier, is also found to have been powerful in all holiness.

### 38. The Death of Anthony the Monk

**[040]** In the nineteenth year of Constantine the Younger, Anthony the monk died in the 105th year of his life. The most blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers,
was sentenced to exile at the persuasion of heretics. Writing books there for the catholic faith, he sent them to Constantius, who in the fourth year of his
exile ordered him released and permitted him to return home.

### 39. The Coming of Saint Martin

**[041]** Then my light arose, and Gaul was illuminated by new rays of lamps: at that time the most blessed Martin began to preach in the Gauls. Declaring
Christ, the Son of God, to be true God among the peoples through many miracles, he turned away the incredulity of the gentiles. He destroyed temples, suppressed
heresy, and built churches; while he shone with many other virtues, he restored three dead persons to life to complete the record of his praise. In the fourth
year of Valentinian and Valens, Saint Hilary died at Poitiers and went to heaven, full of holiness and faith and endowed with many virtues; it is also read that
he raised the dead.

### 40. The Matron Melania

**[042]** The noble matron Melania, an inhabitant of the city of Rome, went to Jerusalem out of devotion, leaving her son Urban in Rome. She showed herself to
everyone in such complete goodness and holiness that the inhabitants called her Thecla.

### 41. The Death of the Emperor Valens

**[043]** After Valentinian’s death, Valens succeeded to the whole empire. He ordered monks to be compelled into military service and commanded those who
refused to be beaten with clubs. Afterward the Romans waged a most savage war in Thrace, in which the slaughter was so great that the Romans, deprived of the
protection of their horses, fled on foot. While they were being cut down by the Goths in a very great massacre and Valens, wounded by an arrow, was fleeing, he
entered a small hut. The enemy approached and set the little house on fire above him, and he was deprived even of the burial he desired. Thus divine vengeance
for the shed blood of the saints, long delayed, at last came forth. Thus far Jerome; from this time forward the priest Orosius wrote further.

### 42. The Rule of Theodosius

**[044]** When the emperor Gratian saw that the republic was destitute, he made Theodosius his colleague in the empire. This Theodosius placed all his hope and
trust in God’s mercy. He subdued many nations not so much by the sword as by vigils and prayers, strengthened the republic, and entered the city of
Constantinople as a victor.

### 43. The Death of Maximus the Tyrant

**[045]** Maximus, having gained a victory through tyranny by subduing the Britons, was made emperor by the soldiers. Establishing his seat in the city of
Trier, he killed the emperor Gratian after ensnaring him by deceit. To this Maximus the blessed Martin came when he was already bishop. Theodosius, who had
placed all his hope in God, took over the whole empire in Gratian’s place. Thereafter, relying on divine utterances, he deprived Maximus of the empire and
killed him.

### 44. Urbicus, Bishop of the Auvergne

**[046]** Among the people of the Auvergne, the first bishop after the bishop and preacher Stremonius was Urbicus, a convert from the senators. He had a wife
who, according to ecclesiastical custom, lived religiously apart from the priest’s company. Both devoted themselves to prayer, almsgiving, and good works. While
they were doing these things, the enemy’s malice, always jealous of holiness, was stirred in the woman; inflaming her with desire for her husband, it made her a
new Eve. Burning with lust and covered by the darkness of sin, the woman went through the darkness of night to the church house. Finding everything barred, she
began to beat upon the doors of the ecclesiastical house and cried out: “How long, priest, will you sleep? How long will you not unbar the closed door? Why do
you reject your attendant? Why do you not hear Paul’s precepts with hardened ears? For he wrote: ‘Return to one another, lest Satan tempt you.’ Behold, I return
to you; I do not run to a stranger, but return to my own vessel.”

As she long proclaimed these and similar words, the priest’s religious resolve at last grew lukewarm. He ordered her admitted to his chamber, used intercourse
with her, and then ordered her to leave. Coming to himself too late and grieving over the crime committed, he sought a monastery in his diocese to perform
penance. There, washing away with groans and tears what he had committed, he returned to his own city. When the course of his life was complete, he departed
from the world. A daughter was born from this union and remained in religion. The priest himself was buried with his wife and daughter in the crypt of Chantoin
beside the public embankment. Legonus was appointed bishop in his place.

### 45. Saint Illidius the Bishop

**[047]** When Legonus died, Saint Illidius succeeded, a man of exceptional holiness and illustrious virtue. He was so eminent in holiness that his fame reached
even foreign territories. Thus it happened that he was sought out and healed the daughter of the emperor of Trier who was afflicted by an unclean spirit, as I
recorded in the book I wrote about his life. As fame reports, he was very old, full of days and full of good works. Completing the course of this life with a
blessed end, he went to Christ and was buried in a crypt outside that city. He had an archdeacon named Justus, who was just in merit as well as name. He too
completed the course of his life in good works and was placed beside his master’s tomb. After the passing of the blessed confessor Illidius, such great virtues
appeared at his glorious tomb that they can neither be written in full nor retained in memory. Saint Nepotianus succeeded him.

### 46. Nepotianus and Artemius, Bishops

**[048]** Saint Nepotianus was regarded as the fourth bishop among the people of the Auvergne. Envoys were sent from Trier into Spain, among them a certain
Artemius, admirable in wisdom and beauty and flourishing in early life, who was seized by the force of fevers. While the others went ahead, he was left sick in
the Auvergne; at that time he was bound by a betrothal at Trier. Visited by Saint Nepotianus and anointed with holy oil, he was restored to health by the Lord’s
gift. When he had received the word of preaching from the saint, he forgot both his earthly betrothed and his own possessions and was joined to the holy church.
Made a cleric, he excelled in such holiness that at blessed Nepotianus’s death he became his successor in ruling the folds of the Lord’s flock.

### 47. The Chastity of the Two Lovers

**[049]** At the same time a certain Injuriosus, one of the senators of the Auvergne and a man of great wealth, sought in marriage a girl like himself; the
betrothal gift was given, and the wedding day appointed. Each was their father’s only child. When the day came and the wedding solemnity had been celebrated,
they were placed in one bed according to custom. But the girl, deeply distressed, turned toward the wall and wept most bitterly. He said: “Why are you troubled?
Tell me, I ask.” She remained silent, and he added: “I implore you by Jesus Christ, the Son of God, that you wisely explain to me what grieves you.” Then she
turned to him and said:

“If I lament all the days of my life, will there ever be tears enough to wash away so immense a sorrow in my breast? I had resolved to keep my little body
immaculate for Christ, untouched by a man. But woe to me, who have been so abandoned by Him that I could not accomplish what I desired, and on this last day,
which I ought never to have seen, I have lost what I had preserved from the beginning of my life. Behold, abandoned by the immortal Christ, who promised me
paradise as a dowry, I have obtained the companionship of a mortal man. Instead of unfading roses, the spoil of withering roses does not adorn but disfigures
me. When I ought to have put on the robe of purity above the fourfold river of the Lamb, this garment presents a burden, not an honor. But why do I prolong my
words further? Unhappy I, who ought to have merited heaven by lot, am plunged today into the abyss. Oh, if these things were to happen to me, why was not the
day that was the beginning of my life also its end? Oh, if only I had entered death’s gate before receiving the nourishment of milk! Oh, if only the kisses of
my sweet nurses had been expended at my funeral! Earthly forms horrify me, because in place of worldly life I look upon the Redeemer’s pierced hands. I do not
see diadems shining resplendent with gems, when I contemplate in my mind that crown of thorns. I reject the spaces of your earth spread far and wide, because I
desire the loveliness of paradise. Your halls horrify me when I look upon the Lord seated above the stars.”

The young man, moved with compassion as she uttered these things with great weeping, said: “My most noble parents had us as their only children in the Auvergne
and wished to join us to propagate their line, lest an outside heir succeed them when they departed the world.” She replied: “The world is nothing, riches are
nothing, the pomp of this age is nothing, and the very life we enjoy is nothing. Rather, that life must be sought which is not closed by the termination of
death, is not dissolved by any stain, and is not ended by any setting; where man remains in eternal beatitude, lives with a light that does not set and, what is
greater than all these, enjoys the Lord’s own presence in perpetual contemplation and, translated into an angelic state, rejoices in indissoluble gladness.”

He said: “Your sweetest words have shone eternal life upon me like a great radiance. Therefore, if you wish to abstain from carnal desire, I will become a
sharer in your purpose.” She answered: “It is difficult for the male sex to grant this to women. Nevertheless, if you act so that we remain immaculate in the
world, I will give you a share in the dowry promised to me by my spouse and Lord Jesus Christ, to whom I have devoted myself as both handmaid and bride.” Then,
armed with the standard of the cross, he said: “I will do what you urge.” They joined right hands and rested. For many years afterward they lay in one bed, but
with praiseworthy chastity, as was later revealed at their deaths.

When the girl’s contest was complete and she was departing to Christ, the man performed the funeral office. As he placed the girl in the tomb, he said: “I thank
You, Lord Jesus Christ, eternal Lord and my God, because I return this treasure immaculate to Your mercy, just as I received it committed by You.” At this she
smiled and said: “Why do you speak without being asked?” He himself followed her not long after she was buried. Although their tombs had been placed on
different walls, a new miracle appeared to manifest their chastity. When morning came and the people approached the place, they found together the tombs which
they had left far apart: those whom heaven holds as companions, the monument does not separate here in their buried bodies. To this day the inhabitants of the
place have wished to call them the Two Lovers. I have mentioned them in the Book of Miracles.

### 48. The Death of Saint Martin

**[050]** In the second year of the rule of Arcadius and Honorius, Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, full of virtues and holiness, bestowing many benefits upon the
sick, departed from the world at the village of Candes in his own diocese, in the eighty-first year of his life and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate, and
passed blessedly to Christ. He died in the middle of the night, which was a Sunday, in the consulship of Atticus and Caesarius. Many heard singers in heaven at
his passing, as I explained more fully in the first book of his Virtues.

When the holy man of God first began to fall sick at the village of Candes, as I have said, the people of Poitiers assembled for his death just as the people of
Tours did. When he died, a great dispute arose between the two peoples. The people of Poitiers said: “He is our monk; he was our abbot; we shall reclaim him as
one committed to us. Let it suffice you that, while he was a bishop in the world, you enjoyed his conversation, shared his table, were strengthened by his
blessings, and moreover delighted in his miracles. Let all these things suffice you, and permit us to carry away at least his lifeless corpse.”

The people of Tours answered: “If you say that the miracles done for you suffice, know that while he was with you he worked more than here. To pass over most of
them, he raised two dead persons for you and one for us; and, as he himself often said, his power was greater before his episcopate than after it. Therefore
what he did not complete while living with us, let him fulfill when dead. He was taken from you, but given to us by God. If the custom instituted of old is
preserved, a man shall have his tomb, by God’s command, in the city where he was ordained. Certainly, if you wish to vindicate him by the privilege of the
monastery, know that his first monastery was among the people of Milan.”

While they disputed thus, night closed as the sun sank. The body was placed in the middle, the doors were barred, and it was guarded by both peoples; when
morning came, the people of Poitiers intended to carry it away by force. But almighty God would not let the city of Tours be deprived of its own patron. At
midnight the whole company of Poitiers was overcome by sleep, and none of that multitude remained to watch. When the people of Tours saw them asleep, some
lifted the most sacred body and passed it through the window while others received it from outside. They placed it in a boat and went down the river Vienne with
all their people; entering the bed of the Loire, they made their way to the city of Tours with abundant psalmody and great praises. The people of Poitiers,
awakened by their voices and no longer possessing the treasure they had guarded, returned home in great confusion.

If anyone asks why only one bishop, Litorius, held office between the passing of Bishop Catianus and Saint Martin, let him know that the city of Tours was long
without priestly blessing because pagans prevented it. Those who appeared to be Christians at that time celebrated the divine office secretly and in hiding. If
any Christians were discovered by pagans, they were afflicted with blows or cut down by the sword. From the Lord’s passion to the passing of Saint Martin, 412
years are computed. **[FLAG — Gregory’s received chronology.]**

Here ends the first book, containing 5,596 years computed from the beginning to the passing of the blessed bishop Martin. **[FLAG — Gregory’s total for the book.]**
