Aetius was coming; he had previously gone to him at Arles because he suspected what was to happen. They looked from the wall but saw no one. He said: “Pray
faithfully, for the Lord will deliver you today!” While they prayed, he said: “Look again!” They looked but saw no one bringing help. He told them a third time:
“If you ask faithfully, the Lord will quickly be at hand.” With weeping and great wailing they implored the Lord’s mercy. When the prayer was finished, they
looked from the wall a third time at the old man’s command and saw in the distance something like a cloud rising from the earth. When they reported this, the
priest said: “It is the Lord’s help.”

Meanwhile the walls were already shaking under the rams’ blows and were about to fall, when Aetius, Theodoric king of the Goths, and his son Thorismud came
running to the city with their armies and drove out and repelled the enemy. The city was liberated through the blessed bishop’s intercession, and they put
Attila to flight. Attila went to the Mauriac plain and prepared for battle. When Aetius and his allies heard this, they prepared themselves bravely against him.

In those days a report reached Rome that Aetius was struggling in the greatest danger amid the enemy’s ranks. His wife, anxious and sorrowful at the news, went
continually to the basilicas of the holy apostles and prayed to receive her husband back safe from this campaign. While she did this day and night, a poor man,
drunk with wine, fell asleep one night in a corner of the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. The doors were closed according to custom, and the guards did
not find him. Rising in the night, with lamps shining throughout the building, he was terrified and looked for a way out. But when he tried the doors, first one
and then another, and found everything barred, he lay down on the floor and waited anxiously until the people assembled for morning hymns and he could leave
freely.

Meanwhile he saw two figures greeting each other with veneration and asking solicitously about one another’s welfare. The elder began: “I can no longer endure
the tears of Aetius’s wife. She continually asks me to bring her husband back safe from the Gauls, although something different had been determined by divine
judgment. Nevertheless, I have obtained boundless mercy for his life, and now I am hurrying to bring him back from there alive. But I adjure you: let whoever
hears this keep silent and not dare to make God’s secret known, lest he quickly perish from the earth.”

The man who heard this could not keep silent. As soon as daylight came, he disclosed everything he had heard to the wife. When he finished speaking, he lost the
sight of his eyes. Aetius then joined the Goths and Franks in battle against Attila. Seeing his army being destroyed, Attila escaped in flight. Theodoric, king
of the Goths, fell in this struggle. No one should doubt that the Hunnish army was put to flight through the intercession of the bishop already mentioned.
Aetius the patrician and Thorismod obtained the victory and destroyed the enemy.

When the battle was over, Aetius said to Thorismod: “Hurry back quickly to your homeland, lest your brother press on and you be deprived of your father’s
kingdom.” Hearing this, Thorismod departed swiftly, as though to anticipate his brother and obtain his father’s throne first. Aetius drove away the king of the
Franks by a similar trick. After they had withdrawn, Aetius stripped the battlefield and returned victoriously to his own country with great spoils. Attila
returned with only a few men. Not long afterward Aquileia was captured, burned, and razed by the Huns, and Italy was overrun and devastated. Thorismod, whom I
mentioned above, subdued the Alans in war; afterward, following many quarrels and battles, he was overcome by his brothers and died by slaughter.

### 8. What the historians wrote of Aetius

**[009]** Now that these events have been related and completed in order, I have thought it wrong to pass over in silence what the history of Renatus Frigeridus
records about the Aetius mentioned above. In the twelfth book of his Histories he relates that after the death of the divine Honorius, the little boy
Valentinian, only five years old, was made emperor by his cousin Theodosius; that the tyrant John rose to imperial power in the city of Rome; and that his
envoys were treated with contempt by the Caesar. Renatus adds:

“While these things were happening, the envoys returned to the tyrant bearing harsh instructions. Moved by them, John sent Aetius, then keeper of the palace, to
the Huns with an immense weight of gold. Aetius had been known to them and bound to them in close friendship since the time of his own service as a hostage.
John sent instructions that, as soon as the opposing forces entered Italy, Aetius should attack them from the rear while John advanced against their front.
Because many things about this man must be related in sequence, it is fitting to begin with his family and character. His father Gaudentius, a man of leading
rank in the province of Scythia, began his military service among the domestics and advanced to the highest office of master of the cavalry. His mother was an
Italian, a noble and wealthy woman. Their son Aetius belonged to the praetorians from boyhood; he was a hostage for three years with Alaric and then with the
Huns. Afterward he became Carpilio’s son-in-law, having served as count of the domestics and John’s keeper of the palace. He was of medium height and manly
build, handsomely formed so as to be neither weak nor heavy, alert in mind and vigorous in limb, a most ready horseman, skilled in shooting arrows, and tireless
with the spear. He was most suited to war and renowned for the arts of peace. He had no avarice and very little cupidity; he was endowed with good qualities of
mind and did not turn from his purpose even under evil persuasion. He was most patient of injuries, eager for labor, fearless amid dangers, and most enduring of
hunger, thirst, and sleeplessness. It is clear that from his earliest years it was foretold how great a power he was destined by fate to attain, to be
celebrated in his own times and places.”

This is what the aforesaid historian relates about Aetius. When Valentinian grew up, he feared that Aetius would overthrow him by usurpation and killed him
although no charges existed. Afterward, while the emperor Augustus himself was seated on a tribunal in the Campus Martius addressing the people, Occila,
Aetius’s bodyguard, came from the opposite direction and ran him through with a sword. Such was the end of both men.

### 9. What the same writers say of the Franks

**[010]** Many people do not know who was the first king of the Franks. Although Sulpicius Alexander’s history says much about them, it nowhere names their
first king, but says that they had dukes. It seems right to record what he relates about them. After saying that Maximus remained inside Aquileia, having lost
all hope of empire and as though out of his mind, he adds:

“At that time the Franks, led by the dukes Genobaudes, Marcomer, and Sunno, burst into Germany. They broke through the border, killed many people, devastated
especially the fertile districts, and struck fear even into Colonia Agrippina. When this news reached Trier, the military commanders Nanninus and Quintinus, to
whom Maximus had committed his son’s infancy and the defense of the Gauls, assembled an army and met at Agrippina. But the enemy, laden with plunder after
stripping the richest parts of the provinces, crossed the Rhine. They left many of their men on Roman soil, prepared to renew the devastation. An engagement
with these men proved advantageous to the Romans, and many Franks were killed by the sword at Carbonaria. When the angry soldiers debated whether they ought to
cross into Francia, Nanninus refused, because he knew that the Franks would not be unprepared and would undoubtedly be stronger in their own territory. Since
this displeased Quintinus and the other military men, Nanninus returned to Mainz, while Quintinus crossed the Rhine with the army near the fortress of Neuss.
After two days’ march from the river, he found huts empty of inhabitants and great villages deserted. The Franks had feigned fear and withdrawn into the remoter
woodlands, constructing barricades of felled trees at the forests’ edges. The soldiers burned every house; their cowardly certainty of victory made them think
that raging against buildings completed their triumph, and they passed an anxious night under the burden of their arms. At first light they entered the woods
with Quintinus as commander in the battle. Entangling themselves in the errors of the paths, they wandered through the whole area almost until midday. At last
they found everything enclosed by enormous solid barricades. As they tried to break out into the marshy fields adjoining the woods, a few of the enemy appeared.
Standing together on tree trunks or on the felled trees, they poured down arrows as though from the tops of towers, in the manner of artillery. The arrows were
smeared with poisonous herbs, so that wounds inflicted only on the surface of the skin and not in lethal places were followed by an uncertain death. Then a
greater multitude of the enemy surrounded the army, which poured eagerly into the open fields that the Franks had left free. The first cavalry were swallowed in
the abysses; the bodies of men and beasts mingled, and the falling men crushed their own comrades. The infantry too, though not trampled by the weight of
horses, became entangled in the mud and could scarcely free their steps; those who had barely emerged a little earlier hid themselves again, trembling, in the
woods. The ranks were thrown into confusion and the legions slaughtered. Heraclius, tribune of the Jovinians, and nearly all who commanded the soldiers were
killed; for only a few did night and the hiding places of the forests provide a complete escape.”

Sulpicius related this in the third book of his History. In the fourth book, while describing the killing of Victor, son of the tyrant Maximus, he says: “At
that time Carietto and Syrus, appointed in Nanninus’s place, were staying in Germany with an army stationed opposite the Franks.” A little later, when the
Franks had taken plunder from Germany, he adds: “Arbogastes, unwilling to delay, warned the Caesar that he must exact the penalties owed by the Franks unless
they immediately restored everything they had seized in the previous year when the legions were slaughtered, and surrendered the authors of the war, on whom
would rest the perfidy of having violated the peace.” Sulpicius related that these things happened while they were dukes. He then says: “After a few days he
held a hurried conference with Marcomer and Sunno, the regales of the Franks and, having received hostages according to custom, withdrew to Trier to spend the
winter.” Since Sulpicius calls them regales, I do not know whether they were kings or held the royal power in turn.

The same writer, when recording the difficulties of the emperor Valentinian, adds: “While various events were occurring in the East throughout Thrace, the
condition of the state in Gaul was disturbed. The emperor Valentinian was shut within the palace buildings at Vienne and reduced almost below the condition of a
private person; the conduct of military affairs was entrusted to Frankish retainers, and civil offices also passed into Arbogastes’s conspiracy. None of those
bound by military oaths was found who dared obey the emperor’s private speech or commands.” He then relates: “In the same year Arbogastes, pursuing Sunno and
Marcomer, the petty kings of the Franks, with hereditary hatred, attacked Agrippina at the height of winter. He knew that every recess of all Francia could now
be penetrated and burned, since with the leaves fallen the bare and dry forests could not conceal ambushers. He assembled an army, crossed the Rhine, and
devastated the Bructeri nearest the bank and also the district inhabited by the Chamavi. No one ever opposed him, except that a few of the Ampsivarii and Chatti
appeared with Marcomer as their leader on the ridges of the more distant hills.”

Again, after this passage in which he has abandoned the terms “dukes” and “regales,” Sulpicius plainly indicates that the Franks had a king. Omitting the king’s
name, he says: “Afterward the tyrant Eugenius undertook a military expedition and sought the Rhine frontier, so that, after renewing ancient treaties with the
kings of the Alamanni and Franks according to custom, he might display an immense army to the savage nations at that time.” This is what the historian mentioned
above wrote about the Franks.

Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus, whom I have already mentioned, says in relating the capture and destruction of Rome by the Goths: “Meanwhile Respendial, king of
the Alans, after Goar had gone over to the Romans, turned his army away from the Rhine. The Vandals were struggling in war against the Franks: their king
Godigisel had been destroyed and nearly twenty thousand of their army killed by the sword, and all the Vandals would have been annihilated if the force of the
Alans had not come to their aid in time.” This passage troubles me: since he names the kings of other nations, why does he not also name the king of the Franks?

When Renatus says that Constantine, having assumed the tyranny, ordered his son Constans to come to him from the Spains, he writes: “The tyrant Constantine
summoned from the Spains his son Constans, likewise a tyrant, so that they might consult together in person about the highest affairs. Constans therefore left
the apparatus of the court and his wife at Caesaraugusta, entrusted everything within the Spains to Gerontius, and hastened without interruption to his father.
After they met and many days had passed, with no danger arising from Italy, Constantine, devoted to gluttony and his belly, advised his son to return to the
Spains. Constans sent his columns ahead and remained with his father, but messengers arrived from Spain reporting that Gerontius had invested Maximus, one of
his clients, with imperial power and had prepared him by surrounding him with an escort of barbarian nations. Terrified by this, they sent Edobec ahead to the
German nations. Constans and Decimius Rusticus, formerly master of offices and now prefect, made for the Gauls, intending to return immediately to Constantine
with the Franks, Alamanni, and the entire body of soldiers.”

Likewise, when Renatus describes the siege of Constantine, he says: “The fourth month of Constantine’s siege had scarcely begun when messengers suddenly arrived
from farther Gaul reporting that Jovinus had assumed royal ornaments and, with the Burgundians, Alamanni, Franks, Alans, and the whole army, was threatening the
besiegers. The customary measures were hastened; the city was opened and Constantine surrendered. He was at once sent toward Italy, but executioners dispatched
by the emperor met him, and he was beheaded above the river Mincius.” A little later the same writer relates: “In those same days Decimius Rusticus, prefect of
the tyrants, Agroetius, formerly chief of Jovinus’s notaries, and many nobles were captured in the Auvergne by Honorius’s commanders and cruelly killed. The
city of Trier was plundered and burned by the Franks in a second invasion.” When Asterius had received the patriciate by imperial letters, Renatus adds: “At the
same time Castinus, count of the domestics, was sent into the Gauls after undertaking an expedition against the Franks.” These writers said this about the
Franks.

The historian Orosius likewise records in the seventh book of his work: “Stilicho assembled the nations, crushed the Franks, crossed the Rhine, traversed the
Gauls, and went as far as the Pyrenees.” This is the information about the Franks which these historians have left me, without naming their kings. Many people
relate that the Franks set out from Pannonia and first inhabited the banks of the river Rhine; afterward they crossed the Rhine and passed through Thuringia.
There, in each district and city, they established over themselves long-haired kings drawn from their first and, so to speak, nobler family. Clovis’s later
victories proved this, as I shall explain in what follows.

I also read in the Consular Lists that Theudomer, king of the Franks and son of the late Richimer, was killed by the sword together with his mother Ascyla. They
further say that Clodio was then an able king of the Franks and the most noble among his people. He lived at the fortress of Dispargum, which is on the border
of the Thuringians. In these regions—that is, toward the south—the Romans lived as far as the river Loire. Beyond the Loire the Goths ruled. The Burgundians
too, following the Arian sect, lived across the Rhône, which adjoins the city of Lyon. Clodio sent scouts to the city of Cambrai and explored everything; he
then followed, crushed the Romans, and captured the city. After remaining there for a short time, he occupied the country as far as the river Somme. Some assert
that King Merovech was of this man’s stock, and that Childeric was Merovech’s son.

### 10. What the prophets of the Lord wrote of the idols of the nations

**[011]** But this nation always seemed to have devoted itself to pagan cults and knew nothing of God. They fashioned images for themselves of woods and waters,
birds and beasts and other elements, and were accustomed to worship these as God and offer sacrifices to them. Oh, if only that terrible voice which spoke to
the people through Moses had touched the fibres of their hearts, saying: “You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself a graven
image, nor worship any likeness of the things in heaven, on earth, or moving in the waters; you shall not make them or serve them.” And again: “You shall adore
the Lord your God, serve him alone, and swear by his name.” What if they could have understood what vengeance overtook and crushed the people of Israel for
worshipping the molten calf, when after feasting and singing, after wantonness and dancing, they proclaimed with unclean mouths concerning that image: “These
are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”? Twenty-four thousand of them fell. What of those initiated into the worship of Baal-peor who
committed fornication with the Moabites and were slaughtered and laid low by their nearest kin? In that plague Phinehas the priest killed the adulterers,
appeased God’s fury, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. What if those words which the Lord thunders through David had reached their ears: “All the
gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens”? And: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. Let those who make
them become like them, and all who trust in them.” Or this: “Let all who adore graven images and glory in their idols be confounded.” And again what the prophet
Habakkuk testifies: “What use is the graven image they have carved? They have made it a molten image, a false phantom. It is a casting of silver and gold, and
there is no breath in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.” Another prophet says: “Let the gods who did not make
heaven and earth perish from the earth and from beneath the heavens.” And again: “Thus says the Lord, who created the heavens, the very God who formed the earth
and all that is in it. He is its maker; he did not create it in vain but formed it to be inhabited. I am the Lord; that is my name. I shall not give my glory to
another or my power to graven images, which have passed away from the beginning.” And elsewhere: “Are there any among the idols of the nations who can send
rain?” Through Isaiah he says again: “I am the first and the last, and besides me there is no god formed whom I do not know. All makers of idols are nothing,
and their most beloved works shall profit them nothing. They themselves are witnesses that they neither see nor understand, and they shall be confounded.
Behold, all who share in them shall be confounded, for their makers are only men. He shaped it with burning coals and hammers and worked it with the strength of
his arm. Likewise the carpenter turned it with a compass and made the image of a man like a handsome human being dwelling in a house. He cut down wood, worked
it, made an idol, and adored it as god; he fastened it with nails and hammers so that it would not fall apart. When carried, idols must be lifted because they
cannot walk. The rest of the wood men make into a fire and warm themselves. From another piece he makes a god and an idol for himself. He bows before it, adores
it, and prays: ‘Deliver me, for you are my god. I burned half of it in the fire and baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and ate, and shall I make an idol
of what remains? Shall I adore a block of wood? Part of it is ashes.’ A foolish heart adored it and did not deliver its soul. Nor does it say: ‘Perhaps there is
a lie in my right hand.’” This nation of the Franks did not understand at first, but afterwards they understood, as the following history relates.

### 11. Of the emperor Avitus

**[012]** Avitus was one of the senators and, as is very well known, a citizen of the Auvergne. After seeking the Roman empire, he wished to live dissolutely
and was cast out by the senators; he was then ordained bishop in the city of Piacenza. Learning that the Senate, still indignant, wished to deprive him of life,
he sought the basilica of Saint Julian, martyr of the Auvergne, bringing many gifts. But the course of his life was completed on the journey, and he died. He
was carried to the village of Brioude and buried at the feet of the aforesaid martyr. Marcian succeeded him. In the Gauls, Aegidius, a Roman, was appointed
master of the soldiers.

### 12. Of King Childeric and Egidius

**[013]** Childeric ruled over the nation of the Franks but was excessively dissolved in wantonness and began to dishonor their daughters by seduction.
Indignant at this, the Franks drove him from the kingdom. Learning that they also intended to kill him, he went to Thuringia. He left behind a man dear to him
who could soften the minds of angry men with smooth words, and gave him a sign for when he could return to his homeland. Together they divided a gold solidus:
Childeric took one part with him, while his friend kept the other and said: “When I send you this part and the joined pieces make one whole solidus, then return
to your homeland with a secure mind.” Going into Thuringia, Childeric hid with King Bisinus and his wife Basina.

After expelling Childeric, the Franks unanimously chose as their king Aegidius, whom I mentioned above as having been sent by the state as master of the
soldiers. When Aegidius had ruled over them for eight years, that faithful friend secretly pacified the Franks and sent a messenger to Childeric with the part
of the divided solidus which he had kept. Recognizing the sure token that the Franks desired his return, Childeric came back from Thuringia at their request and
was restored to his kingdom.

While these men were ruling, that same Basina whom I mentioned above left her husband and came to Childeric. When he asked carefully why she had come to him
from so distant a region, she is said to have answered: “I know your ability and that you are very energetic; therefore I have come to live with you. Know that
if I had known anyone beyond the sea more capable than you, I would certainly have sought to live with him.” Rejoicing, he joined her to himself in marriage.
She conceived and bore a son, whom she named Clovis. He was a great man and an outstanding warrior.

### 13. Of the bishops Venerandus and Rusticus of the Auvergne

**[014]** In the Auvergne, after Saint Artemius’s death, Venerandus, a member of the senatorial order, was ordained bishop. Paulinus bears witness to his
character: “If today you would see priests worthy of the Lord—Exsuperius of Toulouse, Simplicius of Vienne, Amandus of Bordeaux, Diogenianus of Albi, Dinamius
of Ecolisna, Venerandus of the Auvergne, Alithius of Cahors, and now Pegasius of Périgueux—you will see, whatever evils the age brings, men most worthy to guard
the whole faith and religion.” Venerandus is said to have died on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity itself; when morning came, the procession formed the solemn
service of his funeral.

After his death, a shameful dispute over the bishopric agitated the citizens. The parties divided, each wishing to elevate a different man, and the people
clashed violently. While the bishops were seated on the Lord’s day, a veiled woman devoted to God boldly entered and said: “Hear me, priests of the Lord! Know
that God is not pleased with those whom these men have chosen for the priesthood. Today the Lord Himself will provide a bishop. Do not disturb or crush the
people, but be patient for a little while; the Lord will now send the man who is to govern this church.” While they were marveling at her words, a priest named
Rusticus, from the diocese of the city of Clermont itself, suddenly arrived. He had already been indicated to the woman in a vision. Seeing him, she said: “Here
is the man whom the Lord has chosen! This is the bishop He has appointed for you! Let him be ordained!” As she spoke, all the people set aside their disputes
and cried out that this was right and just. He was placed in the episcopal chair and, amid the people’s rejoicing, received the honor of the pontificate as the
seventh bishop of that see.

### 14. Of Eustochius of Tours and Perpetuus, and of the basilica of Saint Martin

**[015]** At Tours, Bishop Eustochius died in the seventeenth year of his priesthood, and Perpetuus was ordained as the fifth bishop after blessed Martin.
Perpetuus saw that miracles occurred continually at Martin’s tomb and judged the little cell built over it too small and unworthy of such wonders. He removed it
and built on the site the great basilica which remains to this day, 550 paces from the city. It is 160 feet long, 60 feet wide, and 45 feet high up to the
vault. It has 32 windows in the sanctuary, 20 in the nave, and 41 columns; in the entire building there are 52 windows, 120 columns, and eight doors—three in
the sanctuary and five in the nave.

The basilica’s solemnity is distinguished by a threefold significance: the dedication of the church, the translation of the saint’s body, and his ordination as
bishop. You will keep it on the fourth day before the Nones of July; know that his deposition is on the third day before the Ides of November. If you celebrate
these faithfully, you will merit the blessed bishop’s patronage both in the present world and in the world to come.

Because the vault of the earlier cell had been made with elegant workmanship, the bishop considered it wrong for that work to perish. He therefore built another
basilica in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and installed the vault there. He built many other basilicas as well, which stand to this day in
Christ’s name.

### 15. Of the Basilica of Saint Symphorian

**[016]** At the same time the priest Eufronius built the basilica of blessed Symphorian, martyr of Autun. Eufronius himself later obtained the episcopate of
Tours. With great devotion he also sent the marble which is placed over Saint Martin’s holy tomb.

### 16. Of Namatius the bishop and the church of the Auvergne

**[017]** After Bishop Rusticus’s death, Saint Namatius was the eighth bishop of the Auvergne in those days. Through his own efforts he built the church which
now stands and is regarded as the oldest within the city walls. It is 150 feet long, 60 feet wide within the nave, and 50 feet high up to the vault. It has a
rounded apse at the front and side chambers constructed with elegant workmanship on either side; the whole building is laid out in the form of a cross. It has
42 windows, 70 columns, and eight doors. A great fear of God and a great splendor are perceived there, and religious people often truly sense a most sweet
fragrance, as of spices, arising within it. The walls around the altar are adorned with inlaid work made from many kinds of marble.

When the blessed bishop had completed the building in the twelfth year, he sent priests to the city of Bologna in Italy to obtain for him relics of Saints
Agricola and Vitalis, whom I know were plainly crucified for the name of Christ our God.

### 17. Of his wife and the basilica of Saint Stephen

**[018]** Namatius’s wife built the basilica of Saint Stephen outside the city walls. Wishing to adorn it with colored pigments, she held a book in her lap and
read the histories of ancient deeds, indicating to the painters what they should depict on the walls. One day, while she sat reading in the basilica, a poor man
came to pray. Seeing that she wore black clothing and was already advanced in age, he thought she was one of the needy. He drew out a quarter-loaf of bread,
placed it in her lap, and departed. She did not disdain the gift of a poor man who did not recognize her. She accepted it with thanks and set it aside,
preferring it to her own meals and receiving a blessing from it each day until it was consumed.

### 18. How Childeric came to Orléans and Angers, and Odoacer

**[019]** Childeric fought battles at Orléans, while Odoacer came with the Saxons to Angers. A great plague then devastated the population. Aegidius died,
leaving a son named Syagrius. After Aegidius’s death, Odoacer received hostages from Angers and other places. The Goths drove the Britons from Bourges, and many
were killed at the village of Déols. Count Paul, with Romans and Franks, waged war against the Goths and took plunder. When Odoacer came to Angers, King
Childeric arrived on the following day; Count Paul was killed, and Childeric took possession of the city. On that day the great church building was consumed by
fire.

### 19. Of the war between the Saxons and the Romans

**[020]** After these events war was waged between the Saxons and the Romans. The Saxons turned their backs and, as the Romans pursued, left many of their own
men to the sword. The Franks captured and destroyed their islands, killing a great many people. In the ninth month of that year there was an earthquake. Odoacer
made a treaty with Childeric, and together they subdued the Alamanni who had overrun part of Italy.

### 20. Of the duke Victorius

**[021]** In the fourteenth year of his reign, Euric, king of the Goths, placed Duke Victorius over seven cities. Victorius came immediately to the Auvergne and
wished to extend the city; the crypts from that work remain to this day. He ordered columns to be supplied for the basilica of Saint Julian, and they are set in
the building. He also ordered the construction of the basilica of Saint Lawrence and that of Saint Germanus in the village of Licaniacum. He remained in the
Auvergne for nine years.

He brought false charges against the senator Eucherius. After imprisoning him, Victorius ordered him to be brought out at night and bound beside an old wall,
and then ordered the wall itself to be thrown down upon him. Victorius was excessively dissolute in his love of women. Fearing that the people of the Auvergne
would kill him, he fled to Rome; there he tried to practice similar wantonness and was stoned to death. After Victorius’s departure Euric reigned for four more
years and died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign. There was also a great earthquake at that time.

### 21. Of Eparchius the bishop

**[022]** When Bishop Namatius died in the Auvergne, Eparchius succeeded him, a most holy and religious man. Because the church possessed only a small property
within the city walls at that time, the bishop’s residence was in the building now called the Salutatorium, and he would rise during the night to give thanks to
God at the church’s altar.

One night he entered and found the church full of demons, with their prince seated on the chair of his throne in the likeness of an adorned woman. The bishop
said: “Accursed prostitute, is it not enough for you to infect every place with your various pollutions? Must you also defile the chair consecrated to the Lord
with the foul approach of your sitting? Depart from God’s house, so that it may no longer be polluted by you.” The demon answered: “Because you call me a
prostitute, I shall prepare many snares for you through the desire of women.” Saying this, it vanished like smoke. The priest was indeed tempted by bodily
stirrings of concupiscence, but protected by the sign of the holy cross, he could not be harmed by the enemy.

People also relate that Eparchius established a monastery on the height of Mount Chantoin, where an oratory now stands, and that he shut himself in there during
the days of holy Lent. On the day of the Lord’s Supper he would return to his church with great psalmody, accompanied by clergy and citizens. When he died,
Sidonius, a former prefect, was appointed in his place. Sidonius was most noble in worldly rank and one of the leading senators of the Gauls; he had married a
daughter of the emperor Avitus.

In Sidonius’s time, while Victorius, whom I mentioned above, was still staying in the city of Clermont, an abbot named Abraham lived in the monastery of Saint
Cyricus in that city. He shone with the grace of the earlier Abraham in faith and works, as I have written in the book of his Life.

### 22. Of the bishop Sidonius

**[023]** Saint Sidonius possessed such eloquence that he could often compose extemporaneously, with the greatest brilliance and without any halting delay,
whatever he wished to say. One day he came by invitation to a festival at the basilica of the monastery mentioned above. His booklet, from which he customarily
conducted the most sacred rites, had been maliciously taken from him; yet, prepared by the occasion, he performed the whole service of the festival so well that
everyone marveled, and those present thought that an angel, rather than a man, had spoken there. I explained this more fully in the preface to the book in which
I collected the masses he composed.

He was of magnificent holiness and, as I have said, one of the leading senators. Without his wife’s knowledge, he often carried silver vessels away from the
house and gave them to the poor. When she discovered this, she was angry with him; he then paid the needy the price and restored the vessels to the house.

### 23. Of the holiness of Sidonius

**[024]** After Sidonius had been consecrated to the Lord’s service and was living a holy life in the world, two priests rose against him. They took away all
his authority over the church’s property, left him only a scanty and meager diet, and reduced him to the deepest humiliation. But divine mercy would not allow
the injury done to him to remain unavenged for long.

One of these most wicked men, unworthy to be called a priest, had threatened during the previous night to drive Sidonius out of the church. When he heard the
signal for matins, he rose, boiling with gall against God’s holy man and intending to carry out the wicked plan he had discussed on the preceding day. He
entered his privy and, while trying to empty his bowels, breathed his last. His servant waited outside with a candle for his master to come out. Daylight had
already arrived, and his accomplice—that is, the other priest—sent a message: “Come without delay, so that we may together carry out what we agreed yesterday.”
When the dead man gave no answer, the servant lifted the curtain over the door and found his master dead on the privy seat. There can be no doubt that he was
guilty of no less a crime than Arius, whose bowels likewise poured out through his lower parts in a privy. Nor can it be accepted without heresy that a priest
of God to whom the sheep have been committed for feeding should be disobeyed in the church, while another intrudes into an authority committed to him neither by
God nor by men.

Afterward the blessed bishop was restored to his authority, although one enemy still remained. Later Sidonius fell ill with a fever and asked his people to
carry him into the church. When he had been brought there, a multitude of men and women and even infants gathered, weeping and saying: “Why do you abandon us,
good shepherd? To whom do you leave us as orphans? Shall we have life after your departure? Will anyone afterward season us so with the salt of wisdom or
instruct us in the fear of the Lord’s name with such prudent reasoning?” As the people said these and similar things with loud weeping, the bishop at last
answered under the influence of the Holy Spirit within him: “Do not be afraid, my people. Behold, my brother Aprunculus is alive, and he shall be your bishop.”
They did not understand and thought he was speaking in ecstasy.

When Sidonius died, the other wicked priest who remained immediately seized all the church’s property with greedy desire, as though he were already bishop,
saying: “At last God has looked upon me, recognized that I am more righteous than Sidonius, and granted me this authority.” He went proudly through the whole
city. On the Lord’s day following the holy man’s death, he prepared a banquet and ordered all the citizens to be invited to the church house. Disregarding the
elders, he reclined first on the couch.

The cupbearer offered him a cup and said: “My lord, I have seen a dream which I will relate if you permit. I saw this night that it was the Lord’s day, and
there was a great house. In the house stood a throne, on which someone like a judge was seated, greater in power than all others. Many priests in white garments
stood beside him, and also an exceedingly great and innumerable mixed multitude of peoples. As I contemplated these things in fear, I saw blessed Sidonius
standing among them at a distance, earnestly disputing with that priest who was most dear to you and who departed from this world a few days ago. When the
priest had been defeated, the king ordered him to be thrust back into the deepest confines of prison. After that man had been removed, Sidonius brought another
charge against you, saying that you had shared in the crime for which the earlier man had been condemned. When the judge began to inquire carefully whom he
should send to you, I tried to hide among the others and stood at the back, reasoning to myself that I, whom the man knows, might be sent. While I silently
turned this over in my mind, everyone else was removed, and I remained alone in the open. Called by the judge, I approached closer. Looking upon his power and
splendor, I became faint and began to stagger with fear. He said: ‘Do not be afraid, boy, but go and tell that priest: Come to answer the charge, because
Sidonius has prayed that you be summoned. Do not delay in going, for that king commanded me to say this to you under a solemn warning, saying: If you remain
silent, you will die a most wretched death.’”

As the cupbearer spoke, the terrified priest dropped the cup from his hand and gave up his spirit. He was carried dead from his couch and committed to burial,
to possess hell together with his accomplice. The Lord executed such judgment upon obstinate clerics in this world that one received the death of Arius, while
the other, like Simon Magus at the holy apostle’s prayer, was hurled headlong from the lofty height of pride and crushed. Those who acted wickedly together
against their holy bishop are undoubtedly in possession of hell together.

Meanwhile the terror of the Franks was already resounding in these regions, and everyone desired with longing love that they should rule. Saint Aprunculus,
bishop of the city of Langres, therefore began to be regarded with suspicion among the Burgundians. As hatred grew from day to day, an order was given that he
should be struck down with the sword. When this news reached him, he was lowered over the wall of the fortress of Dijon by night and came to the Auvergne.
There, according to the word which the Lord had placed in Saint Sidonius’s mouth, he was appointed the eleventh bishop.

### 24. Of the famine in Burgundy and of Ecdicius

**[025]** In Bishop Sidonius’s time a severe famine oppressed Burgundy. The people scattered through different regions, and there was no one to give alms to the
poor. A certain senator named Ecdicius, a kinsman of Sidonius, is said then to have done a great deed in trust in God. As the famine intensified, he sent his
servants with horses and wagons through the neighboring cities to bring to him those afflicted by want. They went and brought to his house all the poor they
could find. Feeding them there throughout the whole period of barrenness, he saved them from death by famine. Many say that there were more than four thousand
persons of both sexes. When abundance returned, he again arranged transport and restored each person to his own place.

After they had departed, a voice descended from heaven to him: “Ecdicius, Ecdicius, because you have done this, bread shall never be lacking to you and your
seed, for you have obeyed my words and satisfied my hunger by feeding the poor.” Many record that Ecdicius was remarkably swift: on one occasion he is described
as having put a multitude of Goths to flight with only ten men. Saint Patiens, bishop of Lyon, is said to have shown the people a similar kindness in the same
famine. A letter of blessed Bishop Sidonius on this subject survives among me to this day, in which he praised him in a declamation.

### 25. Of the persecutor Euric

**[026]** At this time Euric, king of the Goths, crossed the Spanish frontier and inflicted a severe persecution upon the Christians in Gaul. In his perversity
he mutilated those who did not agree with him, imprisoned clergy, exiled some bishops, and slaughtered others with the sword. He even ordered the entrances to
the sacred temples to be blocked with thorns, intending that infrequent access should cause the faith to be forgotten. At that time especially the cities of
Novempopulania and the two Germanies were devastated by this storm. A letter of the noble Bishop Sidonius himself concerning this matter, addressed to Bishop
Basilius, survives to this day and speaks of it. But not long afterward the persecutor was struck by divine vengeance and died.

### 26. Of the death of the holy Perpetuus

**[027]** After this blessed Perpetuus, bishop of the city of Tours, rested in peace after completing thirty years in the episcopate. Volusianus, one of the
senators, was appointed in his place. Because the Goths regarded him with suspicion, he was taken to the Spains like a captive in the seventh year of his
episcopate and immediately ended his life. Verus succeeded him and was ordained bishop, the seventh after blessed Martin.

### 27. How Clovis received the kingdom, and of Syagrius

**[028]** After these events Childeric died, and his son Clovis reigned in his place. In the fifth year of Clovis’s reign, Syagrius, king of the Romans and son
of Egidius, had his seat at Soissons, the city which the aforementioned Egidius had once held. Clovis came against him with his kinsman Ragnachar, who also held
a kingdom, and demanded that a field of battle be prepared. Syagrius did not delay and did not fear to resist. As the two sides fought, Syagrius saw his army
crushed, turned in flight, and fled swiftly to King Alaric at Toulouse. Clovis sent to Alaric demanding that he surrender Syagrius, otherwise he should know
that war would be made upon him for harbouring him. Fearing that he would incur the Franks’ anger on Syagrius’s account, as the Goths are easily terrified,
Alaric handed him over in chains to the envoys. Clovis ordered him to be imprisoned and, having taken his kingdom, commanded that he be secretly struck with the
sword.

At that time Clovis’s army plundered many churches, because he was still entangled in pagan errors. The enemy had taken from one church a ewer of remarkable
size and beauty together with the other ornaments of the church’s ministry. The bishop of that church sent a messenger to the king, asking that, if he could not
recover any other sacred vessel, his church might at least receive back the ewer. Hearing this, the king told the messenger: “Follow me to Soissons, where all
the captured goods are to be divided. If the lot gives me that vessel, I shall fulfil what the bishop asks.” When he came to Soissons and the whole mass of
plunder had been placed in the centre, the king said: “I ask you, bravest warriors, not to refuse to grant me this vessel in addition to my share”—he meant the
ewer mentioned above. Those of sounder mind answered: “Glorious king, everything I see is yours, and I myself am subject to your dominion. Do now whatever seems
good to you, for no one can resist your power.” But one frivolous, envious, and impulsive man raised his axe and with a loud cry struck the ewer, saying: “You
shall receive nothing from this except what the true lot grants you.” All were astonished. The king restrained his resentment with patient gentleness, returned
the ewer to the church messenger, and kept the wound hidden in his breast.

A year later he ordered the whole army to assemble with its equipment and display the brightness of its arms on the March field. While reviewing everyone, he
came to the man who had struck the ewer and said: “No one has kept his arms as neglected as you; your spear, sword, and axe are all unfit for use.” He seized
the man’s axe and threw it to the ground. When the man bent down to pick it up, the king raised his own axe and buried it in his head, saying: “Thus did you
treat that ewer at Soissons.” He then ordered the others to depart, having established great fear of himself by this deed. He fought many wars and won many
victories. In the tenth year of his reign he made war upon the Thuringians and subjected them to his authority.

### 28. How Clovis took Chrodigildis

**[029]** Gundevech, king of the Burgundians, belonged to the family of the persecuting King Athanaric, whom I mentioned above. He had four sons: Gundobad,
Godigisel, Chilperic, and Godomar. Gundobad killed his brother Chilperic with the sword and drowned Chilperic’s wife by tying a stone to her neck and casting
her into the water. He condemned Chilperic’s two daughters to exile. The elder, who had changed her clothing for the religious habit, was called Crona; the
younger was named Chrotchildis.

While Clovis was frequently sending embassies into Burgundy, his envoys discovered the girl Chrotchildis. They saw that she was elegant and wise and learned
that she was of royal birth, and they reported this to King Clovis. Without delay he sent an embassy to Gundobad, requesting her in marriage. Not daring to
refuse, Gundobad handed her over to the men. They received the girl and presented her to the king with all speed. Clovis rejoiced greatly at seeing her and
joined her to himself in marriage. He already had a son named Theuderic by a concubine.

### 29. Of their first son

**[030]** Queen Clotilde bore Clovis his firstborn son. When she wished to consecrate him by baptism, she continually exhorted her husband, saying: “The gods
you worship are nothing; they can help neither themselves nor others. They are carved from stone, wood, or some metal. The names you have given them belonged to
men, not gods: Saturn, who is said to have fled to avoid being driven from his kingdom by his son; and Jupiter himself, the foulest perpetrator of every
debauchery, a defiler of men and a mocker of his relatives, who could not even refrain from intercourse with his own sister, as the verse says: ‘Jupiter’s
sister and wife.’ What power did Mars and Mercury have? They were endowed with magical arts rather than with the power of the divine name. He alone ought to be
worshipped who by his word created heaven and earth, the sea and everything in them out of nothing; who made the sun shine and adorned the heaven with stars;
who filled the waters with creeping things, the earth with animals, and the air with flying creatures; at whose command the earth is adorned with crops, the
trees with fruit, and the vines with grapes; by whose hand the human race was created; and by whose bounty all creation serves the man he created, both in
obedience and in benefit.” Although the queen said these things, the king’s mind was in no way moved to belief. He said: “Everything is created and comes forth
by the command of our gods. Your God is shown to have no power and, what is more, is proved not even to belong to the race of gods.”

Meanwhile the faithful queen presented her son for baptism. She ordered the church to be adorned with hangings and curtains, hoping that the man who could not
be moved by preaching might at least be led to belief by this mystery. The boy was baptized and named Ingomer, but died in the white robes in which he had been
regenerated. Enraged by this, the king rebuked the queen severely: “If the boy had been dedicated in the name of my gods, he would surely have lived. But
because he was baptized in the name of your God, he could not live at all.” The queen answered: “I give thanks to almighty God, the Creator of all, who did not
judge me altogether unworthy but deigned to receive into his kingdom the child born of my womb. My heart is not touched by grief over this, because I know that
one called from this world in white robes will be nourished in God’s sight.” Afterwards she bore another son, whom she named Chlodomer at his baptism. When he
fell ill, the king said: “Nothing else can happen to him than happened to his brother: now that he has been baptized in the name of your Christ, he will die
immediately.” But at his mother’s prayer and by the Lord’s command he recovered.

### 30. The war against the Alamanni

**[031]** The queen did not cease exhorting him to acknowledge the true God and abandon idols. But he could in no way be moved to believe these things, until at
last war against the Alamanni arose, in which he was compelled by necessity to confess what he had previously refused by choice. When the two armies engaged,
they slaughtered one another violently, and Clovis’s army began to rush toward utter destruction. Seeing this, he raised his eyes to heaven; stricken in heart
and moved to tears, he said: “Jesus Christ, whom Chrotchildis proclaims to be the Son of the living God, and who is said to give help to those in trouble and
grant victory to those who hope in You, I devoutly implore the glory of Your aid. If You grant me victory over these enemies, and I experience that power which
the people dedicated to Your name claim to have proved in You, I will believe in You and be baptized in Your name. For I have invoked my gods, but, as I now
experience, they have withdrawn from helping me. I therefore believe that they possess no power, since they do not come to the aid of those who obey them. Now I
invoke You; I desire to believe in You; only let me be delivered from my adversaries.”

While he was saying this, the Alamanni turned their backs and began to flee. Seeing that their king had been killed, they submitted to Clovis’s rule, saying: “I
beg you, let the people perish no further; we are now yours.” Clovis stopped the battle, exhorted the people, and returned in peace. He told the queen how he
had merited victory by invoking Christ’s name. **[This occurred in the fifteenth year of his reign.]**

### 31. Of the baptism of Clovis

**[032]** The queen then secretly ordered Saint Remigius, bishop of the city of Reims, to be summoned, begging him to impart the word of salvation to the king.
When the bishop had come, he began privately to urge the king to believe in the true God, the maker of heaven and earth, and to abandon idols, which could
benefit neither themselves nor others. Clovis answered: “Most holy father, I would gladly hear you; but one difficulty remains: the people who follow me will
not consent to abandon their gods. I will go and speak to them according to your word.” When he met with his men, before he could speak, God’s power went before
him, and all the people cried out together: “We reject the mortal gods, pious king, and we are ready to follow the immortal God whom Remigius preaches.”

When this was reported to the bishop, he was filled with great joy and ordered the baptismal bath to be prepared. The streets were shaded with decorated
awnings; the churches were adorned with white curtains; the baptistery was set in order; balsam was spread about; gleaming candles gave forth fragrance; and the
whole baptistery was sprinkled with a divine odor. God bestowed such grace on those present that they imagined themselves situated amid the fragrances of
paradise.

The king asked to be baptized by the bishop before anyone else. Like a new Constantine, he advanced to the bath, to wash away the disease of his ancient leprosy
and remove with fresh water the filthy stains he had borne from of old. As he entered the baptismal water, God’s saint addressed him with eloquent speech:
“Gently bow your neck, Sicambrian; adore what you have burned, and burn what you have adored.” Saint Bishop Remigius was a man of outstanding learning and
thoroughly trained in rhetorical studies; he was also so eminent in holiness that he equaled Sylvester in miracles. A book of his Life now exists which relates
that he raised a dead man.

The king confessed almighty God in the Trinity, was baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and was anointed with sacred
chrism bearing the seal of Christ’s cross. More than three thousand of his army were baptized. His sister Albofled was also baptized and not long afterward
departed to the Lord. When the king grieved for her, Saint Remigius sent a letter of consolation, which began: “The cause of your sadness distresses me, and
distresses me greatly: your sister Albofled of good memory has died. But I can be consoled, because she has departed from this world in such a condition that
she ought rather to be looked up to than mourned.” His other sister, named Lanthechild, who had fallen into the Arian heresy, was also converted; she confessed
the Son equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, and received the chrism.

### 32. The war against Gundobad

**[033]** At that time the brothers Gundobad and Godegisel held the kingdom around the Rhône and Saône together with the province of Marseille. Both they and
their people belonged to the Arian sect. When they began attacking each other, Godegisel heard of King Clovis’s victories and secretly sent an embassy to him,
saying: “If you give me help against my brother so that I can kill him in battle or drive him from the region, I shall pay you every year whatever tribute you
wish to impose.” Clovis gladly accepted and promised help whenever necessity required. At the appointed time he moved his army against Gundobad. Hearing this
and unaware of his brother’s treachery, Gundobad sent to Godegisel: “Come to my aid, for the Franks are moving against me and approaching my region to capture
it. Let me be of one mind against this hostile people, lest, separated, I suffer what other nations have suffered.” Godegisel answered: “I shall come with my
army and give you help.” The three armies moved: Clovis against Gundobad, and Godegisel with his whole war equipment. They reached the fortress called Dijon.
When battle was joined on the river Ouche, Godegisel joined Clovis, and together their armies destroyed Gundobad’s people. Gundobad then perceived his brother’s
unsuspected treachery, turned in flight, hurried along the banks of the Rhône, and entered Avignon. Godegisel, having obtained victory, departed in peace after
promising Clovis part of his kingdom. He entered Vienne in triumph as though he already possessed the whole kingdom.

King Clovis increased his forces and pursued Gundobad, intending to drag him from the city and kill him. Hearing this, Gundobad was terrified and feared sudden
death. He had with him an illustrious man named Aridius, shrewd and wise. Summoning him, Gundobad said: “Difficulties surround me on every side, and I do not
know what to do. These barbarians have come upon me to kill me and overthrow the whole region.” Aridius answered: “You must soothe this man’s ferocity so that
you do not perish. If it pleases you, I shall pretend to flee from you and go over to him. When I reach him, I shall arrange matters so that they harm neither
you nor this region. Only be careful to fulfil whatever he demands through my counsel until the Lord in his mercy deigns to make your cause prosper.” Gundobad
said: “I shall do whatever you command.” Aridius took leave, departed, and went to King Clovis, saying: “Behold, most pious king, I humbly come to your power,
abandoning that most miserable Gundobad. If your kindness deigns to receive me, you and your posterity will have in me a whole and faithful servant.” Clovis
received him readily and kept him with him, for Aridius was agreeable in conversation, shrewd in counsel, just in judgment, and faithful in what was entrusted
to him.

When Clovis had settled with his whole army around the city walls, Aridius said: “If the glory of your highness would graciously deign, king, to hear a few
words of my humility, I shall offer counsel with complete faithfulness, although you do not need it. It will benefit both you and the cities through which you
intend to pass. Why do you keep your army here while your enemy sits in an impregnable place? You devastate the fields, graze the meadows, cut down the vines,
fell the olive groves, and destroy all the fruits of the region, while you cannot harm him at all. Instead send an embassy and impose a tribute for him to pay
each year, so that the region may be preserved and you may rule for ever over the tribute-payer. If he refuses, then do as you please.” The king accepted this
counsel and ordered the army to return home. He sent an embassy to Gundobad commanding him to pay the imposed tribute every year. Gundobad paid it for the
present and promised to pay thereafter.

### 33. Of the death of Godigisil

**[034]** Afterward Gundobad recovered his strength and, now disdaining to pay King Clovis the promised tribute, moved his army against his brother Godigisel
and besieged him inside the city of Vienne. When food began to fail the common people, Godigisel feared that the famine would reach even him and ordered the
common people to be expelled from the city. Among the others expelled was the workman responsible for the care of the aqueduct. Indignant at having been cast
out of the city with the rest, he went furiously to Gundobad and showed him how to break into the city and take vengeance on his brother. The army was then led
through the aqueduct with him as guide, many men going ahead with iron bars. The outlet was closed by a great stone, but this was driven back with the bars
under the workman’s direction, and they entered the city. While the defenders shot arrows from the wall, these attackers took them from behind. A trumpet
sounded from the middle of the city; the besiegers captured the gates, which were opened, and both forces entered together. As the people of the city were
slaughtered between the two armies, Godigisel fled to a church of the heretics and was killed there together with the Arian bishop.

The Franks who had been with Godigisel gathered in a single tower. Gundobad ordered that none of them should be harmed; he seized them and sent them into exile
at Toulouse to King Alaric. The senators and Burgundians who had supported Godigisel were killed. Gundobad restored the whole region now called Burgundy to his
own dominion. He also established milder laws for the Burgundians, so that they would not oppress the Romans.

### 34. How Gundobad wished to be converted

**[035]** When Gundobad had learned that the heretics’ assertions were worthless, he confessed to Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, that Christ the Son of God and
the Holy Spirit were equal to the Father, and secretly asked to be chrismated. The bishop said: “If you truly believe, you ought to carry out what the Lord
himself taught me. He says: ‘Whoever confesses me before men, him shall I also confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, him
shall I also deny before my Father who is in heaven.’ When he taught his holy and beloved blessed apostles about the temptations of future persecution, he
likewise said: ‘Beware of men. They will deliver you to councils and scourge you in their synagogues, and you shall stand before kings and governors for my sake
as a testimony to them and to all nations.’ Though you are a king and fear no physical arrest, you dread a popular disturbance and therefore will not confess
the Creator of all in public. Abandon this folly and proclaim before the people with your mouth what you say you believe in your heart. The blessed apostle
says: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’ The prophet likewise says: ‘I shall confess you,
Lord, in the great church; I shall praise you among the mighty people.’ And again: ‘I shall confess you among the peoples, Lord; I shall sing a psalm to your
name among the nations.’ You fear the people, king, not knowing that it is better for the people to follow your faith than for you to indulge popular weakness.
You are the head of the people, not the people your head. When you go to war, you lead the ranks against the enemy, and they follow where you go. It is
therefore better that they learn the truth under your leadership than that they remain in error when you perish. God is not mocked, and he does not love the man
who refuses to confess him before the world for the sake of an earthly kingdom.”

Confounded by this reasoning, Gundobad nevertheless persisted in his madness until the end of his life and would not publicly confess the equality of the
Trinity. Blessed Avitus was a man of great eloquence at that time. When heresy arose at Constantinople—both Eutyches’s heresy and that taught by Sabellius,
namely that my Lord Jesus Christ possessed no divinity—Avitus wrote against them at King Gundobad’s request. Admirable letters of his survive among me today;
just as they suppressed heresy then, so now they build up God’s Church. He wrote one book of homilies, six books in verse on the beginning of the world and
various other creations, and nine books of letters, among which the letters mentioned above are contained.

In one homily on the Rogations he relates that these very Rogations, which I celebrate before the triumph of the Lord’s Ascension, were instituted by Mamertus,
bishop of Vienne, over whom Avitus himself then presided, when that city was terrified by many prodigies. It was shaken by frequent earthquakes, and wild deer
and wolves entered the gates and wandered fearlessly through the whole city, as he wrote. While these things occurred throughout the year and the days of the
Easter solemnity approached, all the people devoutly awaited God’s mercy, hoping that the great feast would end their terror. But during the vigil of that
glorious night, while mass was being celebrated, the royal palace within the walls was suddenly kindled by divine fire. Everyone fled the church in terror,
believing either that the whole city would be consumed by the fire or that it would collapse as the earth split open. The holy bishop prostrated himself before
the altar and implored the Lord’s mercy with groans and tears. What more need I say? The illustrious bishop’s prayer penetrated the heights of heaven, and the
river of flowing tears extinguished the fire in the house. As these things happened and the Ascension of the Lord’s majesty approached, he proclaimed a fast to
the people and instituted a form of prayer, an order of eating, and a cheerful distribution of alms. When the terrors ceased, the report of the deed spread
through every province and prompted all bishops to imitate what the bishop had done in faith. It is celebrated to this day in God’s name in every church with
compunction of heart and contrition of spirit.

### 35. How Clovis and Alaric saw each other

**[036]** When Alaric, king of the Goths, saw King Clovis continually defeating nations, he sent envoys to him, saying: “If my brother is willing, let it be his
desire that we meet together with God’s favour.” Clovis did not refuse and came to him. They met on an island in the Loire near the village of Amboise in the
territory of Tours. They talked, ate, and drank together, pledged friendship, and departed in peace. Many in Gaul even then desired with the deepest longing to
have the Franks as their lords.

### 36. Of the bishop Quintianus

**[037]** Because of this hatred Quintianus, bishop of Rodez, was driven from his city. The citizens told him: “Your desire is for Frankish dominion to possess
this land.” A few days later discord arose between him and the citizens, and suspicion fell upon the Goths living in the city, while the citizens reproached him
for wishing to subject himself to Frankish rule. Taking counsel, the Goths planned to run him through with the sword. When this was reported to the man of God,
he rose at night and left Rodez with his most faithful servants, coming to Clermont. Saint Bishop Eufrasius, who had succeeded Aprunculus of Dijon, received him
kindly, gave him houses, lands, and vineyards, and kept him with him, saying: “This church’s resources are sufficient to support us both; only let the love
which the blessed apostle preaches remain between priests of God.” The bishop of Lyon also gave him part of his church’s property in Auvergne. The other things
concerning Saint Quintianus, both the plots he suffered and the works the Lord deigned to perform through him, are written in the book of his Life.

### 37. The war with Alaric

**[038]** King Clovis said to his men: “It is a great grief to me that these Arians hold part of Gaul. Let me go with God’s help, defeat them, and bring the
land under my authority.” When this speech pleased everyone, he mobilized the army and marched towards Poitiers, where Alaric was then staying. Because part of
his army was passing through the territory of Tours, in reverence for blessed Martin he issued an edict that no one should take anything from that region except
fodder and water. A soldier found a poor man’s hay and said: “Did the king not command that only grass and nothing else be taken? This is grass. I shall not
transgress his command if I take it.” He used violence against the poor man and carried off the hay by force. The deed reached the king, who immediately killed
him with the sword and said: “Where will my hope of victory be if I offend blessed Martin?” It was enough to keep the army from taking anything further from
that region.

The king sent messengers to the blessed church, saying: “Go, and perhaps you will receive some omen of victory from the holy building.” Giving them gifts to
present at the holy place, he said: “If you, Lord, are my helper and have decreed to deliver this unbelieving people, ever hostile to you, into my hands, deign
graciously to reveal it as I enter Saint Martin’s church, so that I may know that you will be favourable to your servant.” The servants hurried and, arriving at
the place by the king’s command, entered the holy church. The precentor unexpectedly began this antiphon: “You have girded me with strength for battle; you have
subdued under me those who rose against me, you have given me the backs of my enemies, and you have destroyed those who hated me.” Hearing the singers, they
thanked God, made vows to the blessed confessor, and joyfully reported to the king.

When Clovis came with his army to the river Vienne, he did not know at all where he ought to cross, for it had swollen with rainwater. That night he prayed to
the Lord to deign to show him a ford. In the morning a doe of wonderful size entered the river before them by God’s command, and as it crossed the people
learned where they could pass. When the king came to Poitiers and was staying in tents at a distance, he saw a fiery beacon come out of Saint Hilary’s church
and seem to approach above him. Aided by the blessed confessor Hilary’s light, he was to defeat more freely the heretical ranks against which that bishop had
often contended for the faith. Clovis charged the whole army not to despoil anyone or seize anyone’s property either there or on the march.

In those days there was a man of praiseworthy holiness, Abbot Maxentius, who for fear of God lived as a recluse in his monastery in the territory of Poitiers. I
have not given the monastery’s name in this account because the place is still called the Cell of Saint Maxentius today. When his monks saw a troop of the enemy
approaching the monastery, they begged the abbot to come out of his cell and console them. When he delayed, they were so terrified that they opened the door and
brought him out. He went intrepidly to meet the enemy as though to ask for peace. One of them drew his sword to strike off Maxentius’s head, but his hand,
raised to his ear, became rigid, and the sword fell backwards. The man prostrated himself at the blessed man’s feet and begged pardon. Seeing this, the others
returned to the army in great fear, afraid that they too would perish. The blessed confessor touched the man’s arm with blessed oil, made the sign of the cross,
and restored it to health. Through his intercession the monastery remained unharmed. Maxentius performed many other miracles; anyone who inquires diligently and
reads the book of his Life will find them all.

Meanwhile, in the twenty-fifth year of Clovis, King Clovis met Alaric, king of the Goths, on the field of Vouillé at the tenth milestone from Poitiers. Clovis’s
men fought at a distance, while the Goths resisted at close quarters. When the Goths turned their backs according to their custom, King Clovis obtained victory
with the Lord’s help. He had as his helper Chloderic, son of Sigibert the Lame. This Sigibert had been wounded in the knee while fighting the Alamanni at
Zülpich and limped. After Clovis had put the Goths to flight and killed King Alaric, two enemies suddenly came up and struck him on both sides with lances, but
the help of his armour and his swift horse saved him from death. A great multitude of Auvergne people who had come with Apollinaris fell there, including the
leading senators. From this battle Alaric’s son Amalaric fled to Spain and skilfully secured his father’s kingdom. Clovis sent his son Theuderic through Albi
and Rodez to Clermont. Going there, Theuderic subjected those cities from the Gothic frontiers to the Burgundian border to his father’s authority. Alaric had
reigned for twenty-two years. Clovis spent the winter at Bordeaux, took all Alaric’s treasures from Toulouse, and came to Angoulême. The Lord granted him such
grace that the walls fell of their own accord at his appearance. He drove out the Goths and subjected the city to his dominion. After winning this victory he
returned to Tours, offering many gifts to the holy church of blessed Martin.

### 38. Of the patriciate of King Clovis

**[039]** Clovis received codicils granting him the consulship from the emperor Anastasius. In the basilica of blessed Martin he put on a purple tunic and a
military cloak and placed a diadem on his head. Then he mounted a horse and, with most generous intent, scattered gold and silver with his own hand among the
people present along the route between the gate of the atrium and the city church. From that day he was addressed as consul or Augustus. He left Tours and came
to Paris, where he established the seat of his kingdom. Theuderic also came to him there.

### 39. Of the bishop Licinius

**[040]** When Eustochius, bishop of Tours, died, Licinius was ordained bishop of Tours, eighth after Saint Martin. The war described above took place in his
time, and King Clovis came to Tours in his time. Licinius is said to have been in the East, visited the places of the saints, gone to Jerusalem itself, and
often seen the places of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection which I read of in the Gospels.

### 40. Of the death of Sigibert the elder, and of his son

**[041]** While King Clovis was staying at Paris, he secretly sent to Sigibert’s son, saying: “Behold, your father has grown old and limps from a lame foot. If
he were to die, his kingdom would rightly be delivered to you together with my friendship.” Seduced by greed, Chloderic plotted to kill his father. When
Sigibert left Cologne, crossed the Rhine, and prepared to travel through the forest of Buchonia, he fell asleep in his tent at noon. Chloderic sent assassins
against him, and they killed him there, intending that Chloderic should possess his kingdom. But by God’s judgment he fell into the pit he had hostilely dug for
his father. He sent messengers to King Clovis to report his father’s death and say: “My father is dead, and I have his treasures and kingdom. Send your men to
me, and I shall willingly send you whatever pleases you from his treasures.” Clovis answered: “I thank you for your goodwill and ask that you show everything to
my men when they come; you yourself shall possess it thereafter.” When they came, Chloderic displayed his father’s treasures. While they examined various
objects, he said: “My father used to heap his gold coins in this little chest.” They said: “Put your hand in to the very bottom and find everything.” When he
did so and was bent far over, one of them raised his hand and struck his brain with a battle-axe. Thus the unworthy son suffered what he had inflicted on his
father.

Hearing that Sigibert and his son had been killed, Clovis came to the same place and summoned all the people, saying: “Hear what has happened. While I was
sailing on the river Scheldt, Chloderic, my kinsman’s son, pursued his father, claiming that I wished to kill him. As Sigibert fled through the forest of
Buchonia, Chloderic sent bandits against him, delivered him to death, and killed him. Chloderic himself was struck by someone unknown while opening his father’s
treasures and died. I have no part in any of this. I cannot shed my kinsmen’s blood, which would be sacrilege. But since these things have happened, I offer you
advice, if it seems acceptable: turn to me and place yourselves under my protection.” Hearing this, they applauded with shields and voices, raised Clovis on a
shield, and established him as king over them. He accepted Sigibert’s kingdom and treasures and brought the people themselves under his authority. For God daily
cast down his enemies beneath his hand and increased his kingdom because he walked with an upright heart before him and did what was pleasing in his sight.

### 41. Of the death of Chararic and his son

**[042]** After this Clovis moved against Chararic. When Clovis had fought Syagrius, Chararic, though summoned to assist him, stood at a distance and aided
neither side. He waited for the outcome, intending to form friendship with whichever side won. Angered by this, Clovis went against him. He trapped Chararic by
deceit and captured him with his son. He bound them and had their hair cut off; he ordered Chararic to be ordained a priest and his son a deacon.

While Chararic lamented and wept over his humiliation, his son is said to have answered: “These leaves have been cut from a green tree, but it has not withered
completely. The branches will quickly spring forth and grow again. Would that the man who did this might perish just as quickly!” These words reached Clovis’s
ears: they were threatening to let their hair grow and to kill him. He therefore ordered both to be struck on the head and killed. After their deaths he
acquired their kingdom, together with its treasures and people.

### 42. Of the death of Ragnachar and his brothers

**[043]** At that time Ragnachar, who ruled at Cambrai, was so unrestrained in debauchery that he scarcely showed indulgence even to his nearest relatives. His
counselor was Farro, a man defiled by similar filth. It is said that whenever food, a gift, or anything else was brought to the king, Farro would say that it
was enough for him and for his Farro. The Franks swelled with the greatest indignation at this.

Clovis therefore gave gold ornaments, armlets, and belts to Ragnachar’s leudes so that they would invite him to attack their king. But all the supposed gold was
counterfeit: the objects were made of gilded bronze by deceit. When Clovis moved his army against Ragnachar, Ragnachar repeatedly sent scouts to learn about the
force. When the messengers returned, he asked how strong the army was. They answered: “It is a very great reinforcement for you and your Farro.” Clovis
approached and drew up his army for battle. Seeing his own army defeated, Ragnachar prepared to escape in flight, but the soldiers captured him, bound his hands
behind his back, and brought him before Clovis together with his brother Richarius.

Clovis said to him: “Why have you humiliated our family by allowing yourself to be bound? It would have been better for you to die.” He raised his axe and
buried it in Ragnachar’s head. Turning to the brother, he said: “If you had given your brother help, he would not have been bound.” He likewise struck Richarius
with the axe and killed him.

After their deaths the traitors discovered that the gold they had received from the king was false. When they told the king, he is said to have answered: “A man
who willingly leads his own lord to death deserves to receive such gold.” He said that it should be enough for them to remain alive, so that they would not
perish under torments in wretched expiation of betraying their lords. Hearing this, they begged to obtain his favor, declaring that it would be enough if they
were permitted to live.

The kings mentioned above were Clovis’s relatives. Their brother, named Rignomer, was killed at the city of Le Mans on Clovis’s orders. After their deaths
Clovis took their whole kingdom and treasures. He also killed many other kings and close relatives whom he feared might take the kingdom from him, and extended
his rule through all the Gauls. Nevertheless, when he had once assembled his men, he is said to have spoken of the relatives whom he himself had destroyed: “Woe
to me, who have remained like a pilgrim among strangers and have no relative who can help me if adversity comes.” He said this not out of grief for their
deaths, but by deceit, hoping to discover whether anyone still remained whom he could kill.

### 43. Of the death of Clovis

**[044]** After these events Clovis died at Paris and was buried in the basilica of the holy apostles which he himself had built with Queen Chrotchildis. He
died in the fifth year after the battle of Vouillé. His whole reign comprised thirty years, and his entire life forty-five years. From Saint Martin’s death to
