ab hominibus. Tradent enim vos in conciliis, et in sinagogis suis flagellabunt vos, et ante regis et praesides stabitis propter me in testimonium illis et
omnibus gentibus. Tu vero cum sis rex et ad nullo adpraehendi formidas, seditionem paviscis populi, ne Creatorem omnium in publico fateares. Relinque hanc
stultitiam, et quod corde te dicis credere, ore profer in plebe. Sic enim et beatus apostolus ait: Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad
salutem. Sic et propheta ait: Confitebor tibi, Domine, in eclesia magna, in populo gram laudabo te. Et iterum: Confitebor tibi in populis, Domine, psalmum dicam
nomini tuo inter gentes. Metuens enim populum, o rex, ignorans, quia satius est, ut populus sequatur fidem tuam, quam tu infirmitate faveas populari. Tu enim es
capud populi, non populus capud tuum. Si enim ad bellum proficiscaris, tu praecedis catervas hostium, et ille quo abieris subsequuntur. Unde melius est, ut te
praecedente cognoscant veritatem, quam pereunte permaneant in errorem. Nam Deus non inriditur, nec enim diligit illum qui propter terrenum regnum eum non
confitetur in saeculum'. Ista ille ratione confusus, usque ad exitum vitae suae in hac insania perduravit, nec publice aequalitatem Trinitatis voluit confiteri.
Magnae enim facundiae erat tunc temporis beatus Avitus; namque insurgente heresim apud urbem Constantinopolitanam tam illam quam Eutices quam quae Sabellius
docuit, id est nihil divinitatis habuisse dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, rogante Gundobado rege, ipse contra eas scripsit. Extant exinde nunc apud nos
epistolae admirabilis, quae sicut tunc heresim oppraesserunt, ita nunc eclesiam Dei aedificant. Scripsit enim humiliarum librum unum, de mundi principio et de
diversis aliis conditionibus libros sex versu conpaginatus, epistolarum libros novem, inter quas supradictae contenentur epistolae. Refert enim in quadam
omilia, quam de rogationibus scripsit, has ipsas rogationes, quas ante ascensionis dominicae triumphum caelebramus, a Mamerto ipsius Viennensis urbis episcopo,
cui et hic eo tempore praeerat, instatutas fuisse, dum urbis illa multis terreretur prodigiis. Nam terrae moto frequenti quatiebatur, sed et cervorum atque
luporum feritas portas ingressa, per totam, ut scripsit, urbem nihil metuens oberrabat. Cumque haec per anni circulum gererentur, advenientibus paschalis
sollemnitatis diebus, expectabat misericordiam Dei plebs tota devote, ut vel hic magnae sollemnitatis dies huic terrori terminum darent. Sed in ipsa gloriosae
noctis vigilia, dum missarum celebrarentur sollemnia, subito palatium regale intramuraneum divino igne succenditur. Pavore omnibus perterritis et eclesiam
egressis, credentibus, ne aut hoc incendio urbs tota consumeretur aut certe disrupta tellore degiscerit, sanctus sacerdus prostratus ante altare, cum gemitu et
lacrimis Domini misericordiam inpraecatur. Quid plura? Penetravit excelsa poli oratio pontefecis incliti, restinxitque domus incendium flumen profluentium
lacrimarum. Cumque haec agerentur, adpropinquante ascensione, ut iam diximus, maiestatis dominicae, indixit populis ieiunium, instituit orandi modum, edendi
seriem, erogandi helarem dispensationem. Cessantebus quoque exinde terroribus, per cunctas provintias dispersa facti fama cunctus sacerdotes imitare conmonuit,
quod sacerdus fecit ex fide. Quae usque nunc in Dei nomine per omnes eclesias in conpunctione cordis et contritione spiritus caelebratur.

## 35. Quod Chlodovechus et Alaricus se viderunt.

**[036]** Igitur Alaricus rex Gothorum cum viderit, Chlodovechum regem gentes assiduae debellare, legatus ad eum dirigit, dicens: 'Si frater meus vellit,
insederat animo, ut nos Deo propitio pariter videremus'. Quod Chlodovechus non respuens, ad eum venit. Coniunctique in insula Ligeris, quae erat iuxta vicum
Ambaciensim terreturium urbis Toronicae, simul locuti, comedentes pariter ac bibentes, promissa sibi amicitia, pacifici discesserunt. Multi iam tunc ex Galleis
habere Francos dominos summo desiderio cupiebant.

## 36. De Quintiano episcopo.

**[037]** Unde factum est, ut Quintianus Rutenorum episcopus per hoc odium ab urbe depelleretur. Dicebant enim ei: 'Quia desiderium tuum est, ut Francorum
dominatio possideat terram hanc'. Post dies autem paucos, orto inter eum et cives scandalum, Gothos, qui in hac urbe morabantur, suspitio attigit,
exprobrantibus civibus, quod velit se Francorum ditionibus subiugare; consilioque accepto, cogitaverunt eum perfodere gladio. Quod cum viro Dei nuntiatum
fuisset, de nocte consurgens, cum fidelissimis ministris suis ab urbe Rutena egrediens, Arvernus advenit. Ibique a sancto Eufrasio episcopo, qui quondam
Aprunculo Divionensi successerat, benigne susceptus est, largitisque ei tam domibus quam agris et vineis, secum retenuit, dicens: 'Sufficit huius facultas
ecclesiae, ut utrumque susteneat: tantum caritas, quam beatus praedicat apostolus, permaneat inter sacerdotes Dei'. Sed et Lugdunensis episcopus largitus est ei
aliqua possessionis ecclesiae suae, quam in Arverno habebat. Reliqua vero de sancto Quintiano, tam insidiae quas pertulit quam illa quae per eum Dominus operare
dignatus est, scripta sunt in libro Vitae eius.

## 37. Bellum cum Alarico.

**[038]** Igitur Chlodovechus rex ait suis: 'Valde molestum fero, quod hi Arriani partem teneant Galliarum. Eamus cum Dei adiutorium, et superatis redegamus
terram in ditione nostra'. Cumque placuisset omnibus hic sermo, conmoto exercitu, Pectavus dirigit. Ibi tunc Alaricus commorabatur. Sed quoniam pars hostium per
territurium Turonicum transiebat, pro reverentia beati Martini dedit edictum, ut nullus de regione illa aliud quam herbarum alimenta aquamque praesumeret.
Quidam autem de exercitu, inventum cuiusdam pauperis faenum, ait: 'Nonne rex herbam tantum praesumi mandavit, nihil aliud? Et hoc, inquid, 'herba est. Non enim
erimus transgressores praecepti eius, si eam praesumimus'. Cumque vim faciens pauperi faenum vertute tulisset, factum pervenit ad regem. Quem dicto citius
gladio peremptum, ait: 'Et ubi erit spes victuriae, si beato Martino offendimus?' Satisque fuit exercitui nihil ulterius ab ac regione praesumere. Ipsi vero rex
direxit nuntius ad beatam basilicam, dicens: 'Ite et forsitan aliquod victuriae auspicium ab aedae sancta suscipitis'. Tunc datis muneribus, quod loco sancto
exhiberent, ait: 'Si tu, Domine, adiutor mihi es et gentem hanc incredulam semperque aemulam tibi meis manibus tradere decrevisti, in ingressu basilicae sancti
Martini dignare propitius revelare, ut cognuscam, quia propitius dignaberis esse famulo tuo'. Maturantibus autem pueris et ad locum accedentibus iuxta imperium
regis, dum sanctam ingrederentur basilicam, hanc antefanam ex inproviso primicirius, qui erat, inposuit: Praecinxisti me, Domine, virtutem ad bellum,
subplantasti insurgentes in me subtus me et inimicorum meorum dedisti mihi dorsum et odientes me disperdedisti. Quod psallentium audientes, Domino gratias
agentes et vota beato confessori promittentes, laeti nuntiaverunt regi. Porro ille cum ad fluvium Vigennam cum exercitu advenisset, in quo loco eum transire
deberit, paenitus ignorabat. Intumuerat enim ab inundationem pluviarum. Cumque illa nocte Dominum depraecatus fuisset, ut ei vadum quo transire possit
dignaretur ostendere, mane facto cerva mirae magnitudinis ante eos nuto Dei flumine ingreditur, illaque vadante, populus quo transire possit agnovit. Veniente
autem rege apud Pictavus, dum eminus in tenturiis commoraret, pharus ignea, de basilica sancti Helari egressa, visa est ei tamquam super se advenire, scilicet
ut, lumine beati confessoris adiutus Helarii, liberius hereticas acies, contra quas saepe idem sacerdos pro fide conflixerat, debellaret. Contestatus est autem
omni exercitu, ut nec ibi quidem aut in via aliquem expoliarent aut res cuiusquam direperent. Erat in his diebus vir laudabilis sanctitatis Maxentius abba,
reclausus in monastyrio suo ob Dei timore infra terminum Pictavensim. Cuius monastyrio nomen lectioni non indidimus, quia locus ille usque hodie Cellula sancti
Maxenti vocatur. Cuius monachi cum unum hostium cuneum ad monastyrium cernerent propinquare, abbatem exorant, ut de cellola sua egrederetur ad consolandum eos.
Illoque demorante, hii timore perculsi, eum aperto ustio de cellola sua producunt. At ille in occursum hostium, quasi pacem rogaturus, perget intrepidus. Unus
autem ex his evaginato gladio, ut capud eius libraret, manus ad aurem erecta diriguit, gladiusque retrursum ruit. Ad ipse ad pedes beati viri veniam deposcens
sternitur. Quod videntes reliqui, cum timore maximo ad exercitum redierunt, timentes, ne et ipse pariter interirent. Huius vero brachium beatus confessor cum
oleo benedicto contrectans, inposito signo crucis, restituit sanum, eiusque obtentu monastyrio permansit inlaesum. Multasque et alias virtutes operatus est,
quas si quis diligenter inquiret, librum Vitae illius legens cuncta repperiet. [Anno 25. Chlodovechi.] Interea Chlodovechus rex cum Alarico rege Gothorum in
campo Vogladense decimo ab urbe Pictava miliario convenit, et confligentibus his eminus, resistunt comminus illi. Cumque secundum consuetudinem Gothi terga
vertissent, ipse rex Chlodovechus victuriam, Domino adiuvante, obtinuit. Habebat autem in adiuturium suum filium Sygiberthi Claudi nomen Chlodericum. Hic
Sygiberthus pugnans contra Alamannos apud Tulbiacensim oppidum percussus in genuculum claudicabat. Porro rex, cum, fugatis Grothis, Alaricum regem
interfecisset, duo ex adverso subito advenientes, cum contis utraque ei latera feriunt. Sed auxilio tam luricae quam velocis equi, ne periret, exemptus est.
Maximus ibi tunc Arvernorum populus, qui cum Apollinare venerat, et primi qui erant ex senatoribus corruerunt. De hac pugna Amalaricus, filius Alarici, in
Spaniam fugit regnumque patris sagaciter occupavit. Chlodovechus vero filium suum Theudoricum per Albigensim ac Rutinam civitatem ad Arvernus dirigit. Qui
abiens, urbes illas a finibus Gothorum usque Burgundionum terminum patris sui dicionibus subiugavit. Regnavit autem Alaricus annos 22. Chlodovechus vero apud
Burdigalinsi urbe hiemem agens, cunctos thesauros Alarici a Tholosa auferens, Ecolisnam venit. Cui tantam Dominus gratiam tribuit, ut in eius contemplatione
muri sponte corruerent. Tunc, exclusis Gothis, urbem suo dominic subiugavit. Post haec, patrata victuria, Turonus est regressus, multa sanctae basilicae beati
Martini munera offerens.

## 38. De patriciato Chlodovechi regis.

**[039]** Igitur ab Anastasio imperatore codecillos de consolato accepit, et in basilica beati Martini tunica blattea indutus et clamide, inponens vertice
diademam. Tunc ascenso equite, aurum argentumque in itinere illo, quod inter portam atrii et eclesiam civitatis est, praesentibus populis manu propria spargens,
voluntate benignissima erogavit, et ab ea die tamquam consul aut augustus est vocitatus. Egressus autem a Turonus Parisius venit ibique cathedram regni
constituit. Ibi et Theudericus ad eum venit.

## 39. De Licinio episcopo.

**[040]** Denique migrante Eustochio Turonorum episcopo, VIII. post sanctum Martinum Licinius Turonicis episcopus ordinatur. Huius tempore bellum superius
scriptum gestum est. Et huius tempore Chlodovechus rex Turonus venit. Hic fertur in Oriente fuisse ac loca visitasse sanctorum ipsamque adisse Hierusolimam et
loca passionis ac resurrectionis dominicae, quae in euangeliis legimus, saepe vidisse.

## 40. De interitu Sigiberthi senioris et fili eius.

**[041]** Cum autem Chlodovechus rex apud Parisius moraretur, misit clam ad filium Sigyberthi, dicens: 'Ecce! pater tuus senuit et pede dibile claudicat. Si
illi', inquid, 'moreretur, recte tibi cum amicitia nostra regnum illius reddebatur'. Qua ille cupiditate seductus, patrem molitur occidere. Cumque ille egressus
de Colonia civitate, transacto Rheno, per Buconiam silvam ambulare disponeret, meridiae in tenturia sua obdormiens, inmissis super eum filius percussoribus eum
ibidem interfecit, tamquam regnum illius possessurus. Sed iuditio Dei in foveam, quam patri hostiliter fodit, incessit. Misit igitur nuntius ad Chlodovechum
regem de patris obito nuntiantes atque dicentes: 'Pater meus mortuos est, et ego thesaurus cum regnum eius paenes me habeo. Dirige tuos ad me, et ea quae tibi
de thesauris illius placent bona voluntate transmittam'. Et illi: 'Gratias', inquid, 'tuae voluntate ago et rogo, at venientibus nostris patefacias, cuncta ipse
deinceps possessurus'. Quibus venientibus iste patris thesauros pandit. Qui dum diversa respicerent, ait: 'In hanc arcellolam solitus erat pater meus numismata
auri congerere'. – 'Inmitte', inquiunt illi, 'manum buam usque ad fundum et cuncta reppereas'. Quod cum fecisset et esset valde declinus, imus elevata manu
bipinnem cerebrum eius inlisit, et sic quae in patre egerat indignus incurrit. Quod audiens Chlodovechus, quod scilicet interfectus esset Sygibertus vel filius
eius, in eodem loco adveniens, convocavit omnem populum illum, dicens: 'Audite, quid contingerit. Dum ego', inquid, 'per Scaldem fluvium navigarem, Chlodericus,
filius parentis mei, patrem suum insequebatur, verbo ferens, quod ego eum interficere vellim. Cumque ille per Buconiam silvam fugiret, inmissis super eum
latruncolis, morti tradidit et occidit. Ipse quoque dum thesaurus eius aperit, a nescio quo percussus interiit. Sed in his ego nequaquam conscius sum. Nec enim
possum sanguinem parentum meorum effundere, quod fieri nefas est. Sed quia haec evenerunt, consilio vobis praebeo, si videtur acceptum: convertimini ad me, ut
sub meam sitis defensionem'. At ille ista audientes, plaudentes tam parmis quam vocibus, eum clypeo evectum super se regem constituunt. Regnumque Sigyberthi
acceptum cum thesauris, ipsos quoque suae ditioni adscivit. Prosternebat enim cotidiae Deus hostes eius sub manu ipsius et augebat regnum eius, eo quod
ambularet recto corde coram eo et facerit quae placita erant in oculis eius.

## 41. De interitu Chararici et fili eius.

**[042]** Post haec ad Chararicum dirigit. Quando autem cum Siagrio pugnavit, hic Chararicus, evocatus ad solatium Chlodovechi, eminus stetit, neutre adiuvans
parti; sed eventum rei expectans, ut cui evenerit victuriam, cum illo et hic amicitia conligaret. Ob hanc causam Chlodovechus indignans, contra eum abiit. Quem
circumventum dolis coepit cum filio vinctusque totondit et Chararicum quidem presbiterum, filio vero eius diaconem ordinari iubet. Cumque Chararicus de
humilitate sua conquireret et fleret, filius eius dixisse fertur: 'In viridi', inquid, 'lignum hae frondis succisae sunt nec omnino ariscunt, sed velociter
emergent, ut crescere queant; utinam tam velociter qui haec fecit intereat!' Quod verbum sonuit in aures Chlodovechi, quod scilicet minarentur sibi caesariem ad
crescendum laxare ipsumque interficere. At ille iussit eos pariter capite plecti. Quibus mortuis, regnum eorum cum thesauris et populis adquesivit.

## 42. De interitu Ragnachari et fratrum eius.

**[043]** Erat autem tunc Ragnacharius rex apud Camaracum tam effrenis in luxoria, ut vix vel propinquis quidem parentibus indulgeret. His habebat Farronem
consiliarium simili spurcitia lutolentum, de quo fertur, cum aliquid aut cibi aut muneris vel cuiuslibet rei regi adlatum fuisset, dicere solitum, hoc sibi
suoque Farroni sufficere. Pro qua re Franci maxima indignatione tumibant. Unde factum est, ut, datis aureis sive armellis vel baltheis, Chlodovechus, sedtotum
adsimilatum auro – erat enim aereum deauratum sub dolo factum–haec dedit leudibus eius, ut super eum invitaretur. Porro cum exercitum contra eum commovisset, et
ille speculatores plerumque ad cognuscendum transmitteret, reversis nuntiis, interrogat, quam valida haec manus foret. Qui responderunt: 'Tibi tuoque Farroni
est maximum supplimentum'. Veniens autem Chlodovechus, bellum contra eum instruit. At ille devictum cernens exercitum suum, fuga labi parat, sed ab exercitum
conpraehensus ac ligatis postergum manibus in conspectu Chlodovechi una cum Richario fratre suo perducetur. Cui ille: 'Cur', inquid, 'humiliasti genus nostrum,
ut te vincere permitteris? Melius enim tibi fuerat mori'. Et elevatam securem capite eius defixit, conversusque ad fratrem eius, ait: 'Si tu solatium fratri
tribuissis, allegatus utique non fuisset'; similiter et hunc secure percussum interfecit. Post quorum mortem cognuscent proditores eorum, aurum, quod a regi
acceperant, esse adulterum. Quod cum rege dixissent, ille respondisse fertur: 'Merito', inquid, 'tale aurum accepit, qui domino suo ad mortem propria voluntate
deducit'; hoc illis quod viverent debere sufficere, ne male proditionem dominorum suorum luituri inter tormenta deficerent. Quod ille audientes, optabant
gratiam adipisci, illud sibi adserentes sufficere, si vivere mererentur. Fuerunt autem supradicti regis propinqui huius; quorum frater Rignomeris nomen apud
Cinomannis civitatem ex iusso Chlodovechi est interfectus. Quibus mortuis, omnem regnum eorum et thesaurus Chlodovechus accepit. Interfectisque et aliis multis
regibus vel parentibus suis primis, de quibus zelum habebat, ne ei regnum auferrent, regnum suum per totas Gallias dilatavit. Tamen, congregatis suis quadam
vice, dixisse fertur de parentibus, quos ipse perdiderat: 'Vae mihi, qui tamquam peregrinus inter extraneus remansi et non habeo de parentibus, qui mihi, si
venerit adversitas, possit aliquid adiuvare'. Sed hoc non de morte horum condolens, sed dolo dicebat, si forte potuisset adhuc aliquem repperire, ut
interficeret.

## 43. De obitu Chlodovechi.

**[044]** His ita transactis, apud Parisius obiit, sepultusque in basilica sanctorum apostolorum, quam cum Chrodechilde regina ipse construxerat. Migravit autem
post Vogladinse bellum anno quinto. Fueruntque omnes dies regni eius anni triginta; [aetas tota XLV anni]. A transitu ergo sancti Martini usque ad transitum
Chlodovechi regis, qui fuit XI. annus episcopatus Licini Toronici sacerdotes, supputantur anni CXII. Chrodechildis autem regina post mortem viri sui Toronus
venit, ibique ad basilica beati Martini deserviens, cum summa pudititia atque benignitate in hoc loco commorata est omnibus diebus vitae suae, raro Parisius
visitans. EXPLICIT LIBER SECUNDUS.

# BOOK THREE

## LIBER TERTIUS

### Preface

**[001]** I should like, if you please, to compare briefly the prosperity that has attended Christians confessing the blessed Trinity and the ruin that has
befallen heretics dividing it. Let me pass over how Abraham venerated it at the oak, Jacob preached it in blessing, Moses knew it in the bush, the people
followed it in the cloud and trembled before it on the mountain; how Aaron bore it on his breastplate, or David prophesied of it in the psalm, praying to be
renewed by the right spirit, that the Holy Spirit not be taken from him, and that he be strengthened by the principal Spirit. Here too I see a great mystery:
the prophetic voice called “principal” Him whom heretics assert to be inferior. But leaving these things, as I said, let me return to my own times. Arius, the
first and wicked inventor of this wicked sect, voided his bowels in a privy and was subjected to infernal fires. Blessed Hilary, defender of the undivided
Trinity, was given over to exile because of it and restored both to his country and to paradise. King Clovis confessed it, overcame the heretics themselves by
its aid, and extended his kingdom through all the Gauls. Alaric denied it and was deprived of kingdom, people, and—what is greater—eternal life. The Lord
restores a hundredfold here to those who truly believe in Him, even if by the enemy’s plotting they lose something; but heretics do not acquire anything better,
and even what they seem to have is taken from them. The deaths of Godigisil, Gundobad, and Godomar, who lost both country and souls together, proved this. I
confess one Lord, invisible, immense, incomprehensible, glorious, everlasting, and perpetual: one in Trinity because of the number of persons, Father, Son, and
Holy Spirit; and threefold in unity because of the equality of substance, deity, omnipotence, and power. He is the one highest and almighty God, reigning
forever and ever.

### 1. Of the sons of Clovis

**[002]** After King Clovis’s death, his four sons—Theuderic, Chlodomer, Childebert, and Chlothar—received his kingdom and divided it among themselves in equal
portions. Theuderic already had a son named Theudebert, a handsome and capable young man. Because the brothers possessed great strength and a vigorous desire
for military action, Amalaric, son of Alaric and king of Spain, asked for their sister in marriage. They graciously granted his request and sent her themselves
into the region of Spain with a great array of ornaments.

### 2. Of the bishops Dinifius, Apollinaris, and Quintianus

**[003]** When Licinius, bishop of the city of Tours, died, Dinifius ascended the episcopal chair. In the Auvergne, after blessed Aprunculus’s death, Saint
Eufrasius was regarded as the twelfth bishop. He lived for four years after Clovis’s death and died in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate.

The people chose Saint Quintianus, who had been expelled from Rodez. Alchima and Placidina, the wife and sister of Apollinaris, came to Saint Quintianus and
said: “Holy lord, let it suffice your old age that you have been ordained a bishop. May your piety permit your servant Apollinaris to obtain the place of this
honor. When he ascends to this height, he will obey whatever pleases you; you will command, and he will submit to your every order. Only lend a kindly ear to
our humble petition.” He answered: “What can I bestow, when nothing is subject to my authority? It is enough that, while I devote myself to prayer, the church
supplies my daily food.”

Hearing this, they sent Apollinaris to the king. He went, offered many gifts, and succeeded to the bishopric. After abusing it for four months, he departed from
the world. When this was reported to Theuderic, he ordered Saint Quintianus to be established there and all authority over the church to be entrusted to him,
saying: “He was expelled from his own city because of his zeal for love of me.” Messengers were dispatched immediately; the bishops and people assembled and
placed him in the chair of the church of the Auvergne. He was the fourteenth bishop set over that church. The rest of his deeds, his miracles, and the time of
his death are written in the book I composed about his Life.

### 3. How the Danes sought the Gauls

**[004]** After these events the Danes, with their king named Chlochilaichus—that is, Hygelac—came by sea in ships against the Gauls. Going ashore, they
devastated one district of Theuderic’s kingdom and took captives. They loaded their ships with captives and other spoils and wished to return to their homeland.
Their king remained on the shore until the ships reached the deep sea, intending to follow afterward. When Theuderic was told that foreigners had devastated his
region, he sent his son Theudebert into those parts with a powerful army and a great array of weapons. Theudebert killed the king, defeated and overwhelmed the
enemy in a naval battle, and restored all the plunder to the land.

### 4. Of the kings of the Thuringians

**[005]** At that time three brothers—Baderic, Hermanfrid, and Berthachar—held the kingdom of the Thuringian people. Hermanfrid overpowered and killed his
brother Berthachar. Dying, Berthachar left an orphaned daughter, Radegund, and also a son; I shall write about them later.

Hermanfrid’s wife, a wicked and cruel woman named Amalaberga, sowed civil war among these brothers. One day her husband came to a banquet and found half the
table uncovered. When he asked his wife what this meant, she answered: “A man despoiled of half his kingdom deserves to have half his table stripped.” Moved by
these and similar words, he rose against his brother and secretly invited King Theuderic by messengers to attack him, saying: “If you kill him, we shall divide
this region in equal shares.” Theuderic rejoiced at the message and directed his army against Baderic. The allies joined together and pledged faith to one
another before going out to war. Engaging Baderic, they destroyed his army and cut him down with the sword. After obtaining the victory, Theuderic returned
home. Hermanfrid immediately forgot his pledge and disdained to give King Theuderic what he had promised. A great enmity arose between them.

### 5. How Sigismund killed his son

**[006]** After Gundobad’s death his son Sigismund obtained the kingdom. With skillful care he built the monastery of Agaune, together with its houses and
basilicas. His first wife, a daughter of Theodoric, king of Italy, had died; by her he had a son named Sigeric. He married another wife, who began, as is the
custom of stepmothers, to malign his son vehemently and stir up trouble.

On a feast day the boy recognized his mother’s garments on her. Moved with bitterness, he said: “You were not worthy to have these garments cover your back, for
they are known to have belonged to your lady—that is, my mother.” Inflamed with fury, she incited her husband with deceitful words: “This wicked boy desires to
possess your kingdom. He intends to kill you and extend his rule as far as Italy, so that he may also possess the kingdom which his grandfather Theodoric held
in Italy. He knows that he cannot accomplish this while you live, and that unless you fall he cannot rise.”

Incited by these and similar words, Sigismund followed his wicked wife’s counsel and became a criminal parricide. He ordered his son, heavy with wine, to sleep
after midday. While the boy slept, a napkin was placed beneath his neck and tied under his chin; two servants pulled its ends in opposite directions and
strangled him. When this had been done, the father repented too late. Falling upon the lifeless corpse, he began to weep most bitterly. An old man is said to
have told him: “Weep now for yourself, who through evil counsel have become a most savage parricide. There is no need to mourn this boy, who was innocent when
he was strangled.”

Nevertheless Sigismund went to the holy place of Agaune and remained for many days in weeping and fasting, begging for pardon. He established continual psalmody
there and returned to Lyon, with divine vengeance following close behind. King Theuderic received Sigismund’s daughter.

### 6. Of the death of Chlodomer

**[007]** Queen Chrotchildis addressed Chlodomer and her other sons: “My dearest sons, let me not regret having nurtured you so tenderly. I beg you, be
indignant at the injury done to me and avenge the deaths of my father and mother with resolute care.” Hearing this, they made for the Burgundies and marched
against Sigismund and his brother Godomar. Their enemies’ army was defeated, and Godomar fled. Sigismund, while trying to escape to the holy place of Agaune,
was captured by Chlodomer and led away captive with his wife and sons. He was placed in custody within the territory of the city of Orléans and held there.

After these kings departed, Godomar recovered his strength, gathered the Burgundians, and regained the kingdom. Chlodomer prepared to march against him again
and resolved to kill Sigismund. Blessed Abbot Avitus, a great priest of that time, told him: “If you look to God and amend your plan so that you do not permit
these people to be killed, God will be with you, and you will go forth and obtain victory. But if you kill them, you yourself will be delivered into your
enemies’ hands and perish by a similar fate. What you do to Sigismund, his wife, and his children will be done to you, your wife, and your sons.”

Disdaining to heed this counsel, Chlodomer said: “I think it foolish counsel to leave enemies at home and march against the others, so that I rush between two
enemy formations, one rising behind me and the other in front. Victory will be achieved more surely and easily if one is separated from the other. Once one has
been killed, the other can easily be marked out for death.” He immediately killed Sigismund together with his wife and sons, ordered them thrown into a well at
the village of Colomna in the territory of Orléans, and made for the Burgundies, calling King Theuderic to his aid. Unwilling to avenge the injury done to his
father-in-law, Theuderic nevertheless promised to go.

They joined forces at Vézeronce, a place near the city of Vienne, and fought Godomar. Godomar and his army turned in flight, and Chlodomer pursued until he was
separated from his own men by a considerable distance. The enemy imitated his signal and called to him: “Turn this way, this way! We are your men.” Believing
them, he went and rushed into the midst of the enemy. They cut off his head, fixed it on a pike, and raised it high. When the Franks saw this and knew that
Chlodomer had been killed, they recovered their strength, put Godomar to flight, overwhelmed the Burgundians, and brought their country under their own power.

Without delay Chlothar married Guntheuca, his brother’s widow. After the days of mourning were completed, Queen Chrotchildis received Chlodomer’s sons and kept
them with her. They were named Theudoald, Gunthar, and Chlodovald. Godomar regained the kingdom.

### 7. The war against the Thuringians

**[008]** After this Theuderic, remembering King Hermanfrid’s perjury, called his brother Chlothar to his aid and prepared to march against him. He promised
King Chlothar a share of the plunder if God granted them the gift of victory. He assembled the Franks and said: “I beg you, be indignant both at my injury and
at the destruction of your kinsmen. Remember that the Thuringians once violently attacked our ancestors and inflicted many evils upon them. Our ancestors gave
hostages and wished to make peace, but the Thuringians destroyed the hostages by various deaths. Rushing upon our ancestors, they took all their substance. They
hung boys from trees by the sinews of their thighs. They cruelly killed more than two hundred girls: they bound their arms over horses’ necks, goaded the horses
into sharp movement in different directions, and tore the women apart. They stretched others over the ruts of the roads, fixed stakes in the ground, and drove
loaded wagons over them. Then, with their bones broken, they gave them to dogs and birds for food. Now Hermanfrid has broken his promise to me and altogether
refuses to fulfill it. I have a clear cause: let us go against them with God’s help!”

Hearing this and indignant at such great crimes, they made for Thuringia with one mind and one resolve. Theuderic took his brother Chlothar and his son
Theudebert as allies and set out with the army. The Thuringians prepared traps for the approaching Franks. They dug ditches in the field where the battle was to
be fought and covered their openings with dense turf, making them resemble level ground. When the fighting began, many Frankish horsemen fell into these pits,
which greatly impeded them; but once they recognized the trick, they began to watch for it.

When the Thuringians saw themselves being slaughtered violently and their king Hermanfrid put to flight, they turned their backs and came as far as the river
Unstrut. Such slaughter of the Thuringians occurred there that the riverbed was filled with heaps of corpses, and the Franks crossed over them to the farther
bank as though over a bridge. Having won the victory, they occupied the region and brought it under their own power.

On his return Chlothar took with him as a captive Radegund, daughter of King Berthachar, and joined her to himself in marriage. Later her brother was unjustly
killed by wicked men. Radegund turned to God, changed her clothing for the religious habit, and built herself a monastery within the city of Poitiers.
Distinguished by prayers, fasts, and almsgiving, she became so eminent that she was regarded as great among the people.

While the aforesaid kings were still in Thuringia, Theuderic wished to kill his brother Chlothar. He secretly prepared armed men and summoned Chlothar as though
to discuss something privately. He stretched a curtain across part of the house from one wall to the other and ordered the armed men to stand behind it. Because
the curtain was too short, the armed men’s feet were visible. Recognizing this, Chlothar entered the house armed and accompanied by his own men. Theuderic
understood that he had discovered the plot, invented a story, and changed from one subject to another. Finally, not knowing how to disguise his treachery, he
gave Chlothar a great silver dish as a token of goodwill. Chlothar took leave, thanked him for the gift, and returned to his camp.

Theuderic then complained to his men that he had lost his dish for no reason and told his son Theudebert: “Go to your uncle and ask him willingly to grant you
the gift I gave him.” Theudebert went and obtained what he asked. Theuderic was exceedingly skilled in such deceptions.

### 8. Of the death of Hermanfrid

**[009]** After Theuderic returned home, he gave Hermanfrid a pledge of safety and ordered him to come to him without fear. He also enriched him with honorable
gifts. One day, while they were talking together on the wall of the city of Zülpich, Hermanfrid was pushed by someone unknown, fell from the height of the wall
to the ground, and there breathed out his spirit. I do not know who threw him down, but many assert that Theuderic’s treachery was plainly revealed in this
deed.

### 9. How Childebert went to the Auvergne

**[010]** While Theuderic was still in Thuringia, a report spread through the Auvergne that he had been killed. Archadius, one of the senators of the Auvergne,
invited Childebert to take possession of the region. Childebert went there without delay. So dense a fog covered that day that nothing could be discerned beyond
two acres. The king used to say: “I wish I could one day see with my own eyes the Limagne in the Auvergne, which is said to shine with such delightful charm.”
But God did not grant it to him. The city gates were barred, and he had no open passage by which to enter. Archadius sawed through the bar of one gate and
admitted him into the city. While these things were happening, news arrived that Theuderic had returned alive from Thuringia.

### 10. Of the death of Amalaric

**[011]** Certain of this, Childebert returned from the Auvergne and made for Spain on account of his sister Chrotchildis. She had suffered many injuries from
her husband Amalaric because of the catholic faith. When she went to the holy church, he often ordered dung and various kinds of filth to be thrown over her.
Finally he is said to have beaten her so cruelly that she sent her brother a handkerchief stained with her own blood. Greatly moved by this, Childebert made for
the Spains.

Hearing of his approach, Amalaric prepared ships for flight. As Childebert drew near and Amalaric was about to board a ship, he remembered that he had left a
multitude of precious stones in his treasury. When he returned to the city to fetch them, the army cut him off from the harbor. Seeing that he could not escape,
he tried to take refuge in a Christian church. Before he could touch the sacred threshold, one man hurled a spear and wounded him with a mortal blow; he fell
there and gave up his spirit.

Childebert then wished to bring his sister back with him, together with great treasures, but by some chance she died on the journey. She was afterward carried
to Paris and buried beside her father Clovis. Among the other treasures Childebert brought back very precious church vessels: sixty chalices, fifteen patens,
and twenty Gospel cases, all made of pure gold and adorned with precious gems. He would not allow them to be broken up, but distributed and delivered them all
to churches and basilicas of the saints.

### 11. How Childebert and Chlothar went to Burgundy

**[012]** After this Chlothar and Childebert resolved to make for Burgundy. Theuderic was summoned to assist them but refused to go. The Franks who followed him
said: “If you disdain to go into Burgundy with your brothers, we shall leave you and prefer to follow them.” Considering the people of the Auvergne disloyal to
him, Theuderic answered: “Follow me, and I shall lead you into a country where you may take as much gold and silver as your greed can desire, and from which you
may carry away cattle, slaves, and clothing in abundance. Only do not follow them!” Enticed by these promises, they undertook to do his will. He prepared to
cross into the Auvergne, repeatedly promising the army permission to carry all the region’s plunder, together with its people, into their own territories.
Meanwhile Chlothar and Childebert made for Burgundy, besieged Autun, put Godomar to flight, and occupied all Burgundy.

### 12. Of the devastation of the Auvergne

**[013]** Theuderic came with his army into the Auvergne, devastated the whole region, and crushed it. Meanwhile Archadius, the author of the crime through
whose cowardice the region was devastated, went to the city of Bourges, which was then in King Childebert’s kingdom. His mother Placidina and his father’s
sister Alchima were seized in the city of Cahors, deprived of their property, and condemned to exile.

King Theuderic advanced as far as the city of Clermont and pitched camp in its suburbs. Blessed Quintianus was bishop in those days. The army ranged through all
that wretched region, destroying and overwhelming everything. Some came to Saint Julian’s basilica, broke the doors, removed the bars, and plundered the poor
people’s property which had been gathered there, committing many evils in that place. But the perpetrators were seized by an unclean spirit and tore themselves
with their own ravenous teeth, crying out: “Why do you torment me so, holy martyr?” I have written about this in the book of Julian’s Virtues.

### 13. Of Lovolautrum and the castle of Meroliacum

**[014]** The enemy stormed the fortress of Lovolautrum and wretchedly killed the priest Proculus at the church altar—the same Proculus who had once injured
Saint Quintianus. I believe that the fortress was delivered into wicked men’s hands on his account, though it had been defended until that day. When the enemy
could not capture it, they prepared to return home. Hearing this, the besieged became joyful and felt secure, but they were deceived, as the apostle says: “When
they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them.” Through the priest Proculus’s own servant, the people, now secure, were delivered
into the enemy’s hands. When the fortress had been devastated and the captives were being led away, an immense rain, which had been withheld for thirty days,
descended.

The besieged in the fortress of Meroliacum paid a ransom and were freed, lest they be led away as captives. Their cowardice caused this, although the fortress
was protected by its own natural position. It is enclosed by a sheer rock face one hundred feet high or more, without any construction of walls. In the middle
is a great pool of very pleasant water, and on another side are most abundant springs, so that a stream of living water flows through the gate. The
fortification extends over so great an area that those living within its enclosures cultivate the land and gather crops in abundance. Elated by this protection,
the besieged went outside to seize some plunder and then hide themselves again within the fortress, but the enemy captured them. They were fifty men. With their
hands bound behind their backs, they were brought forward before their parents’ faces. With the sword already threatening them, the besieged agreed to pay
thirty trientes for each man as his ransom, so that they would not be killed.

When Theuderic departed from the Auvergne, he left his kinsman Sigivald there as a guard. At that time a certain commoner named Litigius was preparing great
snares against Saint Quintianus. Although the holy bishop prostrated himself at Litigius’s feet, he was never moved to submit to him; on one occasion he even
pointed this out as a joke to his wife, who revered the saint. She, moved by better understanding, said: “If he is so cast down today, you will never rise.” On
the third day messengers came from the king’s presence and led Litigius away bound, together with his wife and children. He departed and never returned to the
Auvergne.

### 14. Of the death of Munderic

**[015]** Munderic, who claimed kinship with the royal family, was greatly puffed up with pride and said: “What is there between me and King Theuderic? The
throne of the kingdom is due to me just as it is to him. I shall go out, gather my people, and exact an oath from them, so that Theuderic may know that I am a
king just as he is.” He went out and began to seduce the people, saying: “I am a prince. Follow me, and it will be well with you.” A rustic multitude followed
him, as often happens with human frailty, swearing fidelity and honoring him as king.

When Theuderic learned this, he sent Munderic a command: “Come to me, and if any portion of the rule of my kingdom is due to you, take it.” Theuderic said this
deceitfully, intending to kill him when he came. Munderic refused: “Go and tell your king that I am a king just as he is.” The king then ordered the army to
move so that Munderic could be crushed by force. Realizing that he could not defend himself, Munderic sought the walls of the fortress of Vitry with all his
possessions. Gathering those whom he had seduced, he tried to establish himself there. The army surrounded the fortress and besieged it for seven days. Munderic
and his men resisted, and he said: “Let us stand bravely, fight together even to death, and not submit to the enemy.” The army hurled javelins from every side
but accomplished nothing, and reported this to the king.

Theuderic sent one of his men, named Aregisilus, and told him: “You see how this perfidious man prevails in his obstinacy. Go and swear to him that he may come
out safely. When he has come out, kill him and blot out his memory from my kingdom.” Aregisilus went and did as commanded. First he gave the people a signal:
“When I say such and such, rush in immediately and kill him.” Entering, Aregisilus said to Munderic: “How long will you remain here like a fool? Can you resist
the king for long? Your food has been cut off! When hunger overwhelms you, you will come out of your own accord, be delivered into the enemy’s hands, and die
like a dog. Listen instead to my counsel and submit to the king, so that you and your sons may live.”

Softened by these words, Munderic said: “If I go out, the king will seize and kill me, my sons, and all the friends gathered with me.” Aregisilus answered: “Do
not be afraid. If you wish to go out, receive an oath concerning this offense and stand secure before the king. Do not fear; you will be with him as you were
before.” Munderic replied: “If only I could be certain that I shall not be killed!” Aregisilus placed his hands on the holy altar and swore that he would come
out safely.

After the oath had been given, Munderic went out through the fortress gate holding Aregisilus’s hand, while the people watched from a distance. As the signal,
Aregisilus said: “Why are you staring so intently, my people? Have you never seen Munderic before?” The people immediately rushed at Munderic. Understanding, he
said: “I recognize very plainly that by these words you gave the people the signal to kill me. Nevertheless, because you deceived me by perjury, I tell you that
no one will see you alive again.” He hurled his lance into Aregisilus’s shoulders and pierced him through; Aregisilus fell dead. Munderic then drew his sword
and, with his men, inflicted great slaughter on the people. Until he breathed his last, he did not cease killing everyone he could overtake. When he had been
killed, his property was taken into the royal treasury.

### 15. Of the captivity of Attalus

**[016]** Theuderic and Childebert made a treaty. They swore that neither would move against the other and exchanged hostages to confirm their agreement more
firmly. Many sons of senators were given as hostages at that time. When discord arose between the kings again, these hostages were condemned to public service,
and whoever received one for custody made him his own slave. Many escaped by flight and returned to their homeland, but some were retained in servitude.

Among them was Attalus, nephew of blessed Gregory, bishop of Langres. He was assigned to public service and appointed a keeper of horses, serving a certain
barbarian in the territory of Trier. Blessed Gregory sent servants to find him. When they had found him, they offered the man gifts, but he refused, saying: “A
youth of such a family ought to be redeemed for ten pounds of gold.” When they returned, a certain Leo from his master’s kitchen said: “If only you would permit
me, perhaps I could bring him back from captivity.” His master rejoiced and sent him.

Leo came to the place and tried to withdraw the youth secretly, but could not. He then hired a man and said: “Come with me and sell me into that barbarian’s
household. Let my price be your profit; only let me have freer access to do what I have resolved.” The man accepted an oath, went, sold Leo for twelve gold
pieces, and departed. When the purchaser asked his raw servant what work he knew, Leo answered: “I know very well how to prepare everything that ought to be
served at lords’ tables, and I do not fear that anyone equal to me in this skill can be found. Indeed, even if you wished to prepare a feast for a king, I could
compose royal dishes, and no one could do it better.” The barbarian said: “Sunday is coming”—for barbarians customarily call the Lord’s day the day of the
sun—“and on that day my neighbors and relatives will be invited to my house. I ask you to prepare a meal that will make them marvel and say that they have seen
nothing better in a king’s house.” Leo replied: “Let my master order a great number of chickens to be collected, and I shall do what you command.”

When everything Leo had requested had been prepared, Sunday dawned, and he made a great banquet filled with delicacies. Everyone feasted and praised the meal,
and the relatives departed. The master gave favor to the youth and granted him authority over everything in his store. He loved Leo greatly, and Leo himself
distributed food and dishes to everyone in the household.

After a year, when Attalus’s master was completely confident in him, Leo went with Attalus, the horse keeper, into a meadow near the house. They lay on the
ground at a distance from the others, with their backs turned away, so that no one would know they were speaking together. Leo told the youth: “It is time for
us to think about our homeland. I advise you not to be overcome by sleep tonight when you have brought the horses in to be shut up. As soon as I call you, be
ready, and let us go.”

The barbarian had invited many relatives to a banquet, among them his son-in-law, who had married his daughter. When the guests rose from the feast at midnight
and went to rest, Leo accompanied his master’s son-in-law to his lodging with drink and offered him a cup. The man said jokingly: “Tell me, you who have won my
father-in-law’s confidence, when will you decide to take his horses and go to your own country?” Leo was delighted and asked this as though in jest. The other,
likewise answering the joke in kind, said: “I intend to do it tonight, if it is God’s will.” Leo replied: “I hope my servants will guard me, so that you do not
take any of my property!” They departed laughing.

When everyone was asleep, Leo called Attalus. After saddling the horses, he asked whether Attalus had a sword. Attalus answered: “I have nothing but a small
lance.” Leo entered his master’s chamber and took his shield and spear. When the master asked who he was and what he wanted, Leo answered: “I am your servant
Leo, and I am waking Attalus so that he may rise quickly and take the horses to pasture; he is held down by sleep as though drunk.” The master said: “Do as you
please,” and fell asleep again.

Leo went out, gave the youth the weapons, and found the courtyard doors divinely opened, although at the beginning of the night he had barred them with wedges
struck by a hammer to guard the horses. Giving thanks to God, they took the remaining horses and departed, carrying also one hawk and the clothing. When they
came to the river Moselle to cross and were detained by certain men, they abandoned the horses and clothing. Supporting themselves on their shields, they swam
across the river and came out on the farther bank. They entered the woods in the darkness of night and hid.

It was now the third night of their journey without tasting food. By God’s guidance they found a tree full of the fruit commonly called plums. They ate, gained
a little strength, and entered the road through Champagne. As they proceeded, they heard the hoofbeats of running horses and said: “Let us throw ourselves on
the ground so that the approaching men do not see us.” Suddenly a great bramble bush appeared. They passed behind it and threw themselves on the ground with
drawn swords, intending to defend themselves with their spears like desperate men if they were discovered.

The riders came to that place and stopped in front of the thorny bush. While the horses urinated, one man said: “Woe to me, for these detestable men are
escaping and cannot be found! By my own salvation, if they were found, I would condemn one to the gallows and order the other cut to pieces by sword blows.” The
barbarian doing this was their master, who had come from the city of Reims in search of them. He would certainly have found them on the road if the night had
not hindered him. He then moved his horses and departed.

That same night the fugitives reached the city. Entering it, they found a man and asked where the priest Paulellus’s house was; he showed them. As they passed
through the street, the signal for matins sounded, for it was Sunday. They knocked at the priest’s door and entered, and the youth explained about his master.
The priest said: “My vision was true. This night I saw two doves fly down and settle on my hand; one was white and the other black.” The youth said: “May the
Lord reward you for His holy day. We ask you to give us something to eat, for the fourth day is dawning since we tasted bread or any dish.” The priest hid the
youths, gave them wine mixed with water and bread, and went to matins. The barbarian followed, again searching for the youths, but the priest deceived him and
he returned. The priest had an old friendship with blessed Gregory.

The youths recovered their strength with food and remained in the priest’s house for two days. They then departed and were brought safely to Saint Gregory. The
bishop rejoiced at seeing them and wept upon the neck of his nephew Attalus. He freed Leo and all his descendants from the yoke of servitude and gave him land
of his own, on which Leo lived freely with his wife and children all the days of his life.

### 16. Of Sigivald

**[017]** While Sigivald was living in the Auvergne, he did many evil things there. He seized other people’s property, and his servants did not cease from
thefts, murders, attacks, and various crimes; no one dared utter a word against them. Thus it happened that he rashly dared to seize the estate of Bulgiatensis,
which the blessed bishop Tetradius had formerly left to the basilica of Saint Julian. But as soon as he entered that house, he was driven out of his mind and
took to his bed. Then his wife, advised by a priest, had him carried on a litter to another estate, and he recovered his health. She went to him and explained
everything that he had suffered. When he heard this, he made vows to the blessed martyr and restored twofold what he had taken by force. We have also recorded
this miracle in the book of the Miracles of Saint Julian.

### 17. Of the bishops of Tours

**[018]** When Bishop Dinifius died at Tours, Ommatius governed the church for three years. He had been ordained by command of King Chlodomer, whom we mentioned
above. When Ommatius also died, Leo served for seven months. He was an energetic man and skilled in woodworking. After his death, the bishops Theodorus and
Proculus, who had come from the region of Burgundy, governed the church of Tours for three years, having been ordained by Queen Chrotchildis. When they died,
Francilio, one of the senators, was appointed in their place. In the third year of his episcopate, when the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity had shone upon the
people, the bishop, before going down to the vigil, ordered a cup to be brought to him. A servant boy came and immediately handed it to him. As soon as he had
drunk, he breathed out his spirit. It is therefore certain that he was killed by poison. Upon his death, Injuriosus, one of the citizens, obtained the episcopal
chair, the fifteenth after blessed Martin.

### 18. Of the death of the sons of Chlodomer

**[019]** While Queen Chrotchildis was staying in Paris, Childebert saw that his mother loved the sons of Chlodomer, whom we mentioned above, with undivided
affection. Moved by envy and fearing that they might be admitted to the kingdom through the queen’s favor, he sent secretly to his brother King Chlothar,
saying: “Our mother is keeping our brother’s sons with her and wishes to give them the kingdom. You must come quickly to Paris. We must take counsel together
and consider what should be done with them: whether their hair should be cut and they should live like the rest of the people, or whether they should be killed
and our brother’s kingdom divided equally between us.” Chlothar was greatly pleased by these words and came to Paris. Childebert had spread word among the
people that the kings were meeting for the purpose of raising the little boys to the kingdom. When they had joined forces, they sent to the queen, who was then
staying in that city, saying: “Send the little boys to us, so that they may be raised to the kingdom.” Rejoicing and unaware of their treachery, she gave the
boys food and drink and sent them off, saying: “I shall not feel that I have lost my son if I see you established in his kingdom.” As they went, they were
immediately seized. Their servants and attendants were separated from them, and both groups were guarded apart, the attendants in one place and the little
princes in another.

Then Childebert and Chlothar sent Archadius, whom we mentioned above, to the queen with a pair of shears and a drawn sword. He came and showed her both, saying:
“Your sons, our lords, ask your decision, most glorious queen. What do you think should be done with the boys? Do you order them to live with their hair cut, or
to have their throats cut?” Terrified by the message and deeply embittered, especially when she saw the drawn sword and the shears, she was overcome by anguish
and, not knowing in her grief what she was saying, answered without reflection: “If they are not to be raised to the kingdom, I would rather see them dead than
shorn.” He gave little thought to her grief and did not wait to learn what she might say after fuller consideration. He quickly returned and reported: “The
queen favors the work you have begun; complete your plan, for she herself wishes it carried out.”

Without delay Chlothar seized the older boy by the arm, threw him to the ground, drove a knife beneath his armpit, and cruelly killed him. As the boy cried out,
his brother threw himself at Childebert’s feet, clasped his knees, and begged with tears: “Help me, most merciful father, so that I too may not perish like my
brother.” Then Childebert, his face wet with tears, said: “I beg you, dearest brother, grant me this boy’s life as a kindness. I will give whatever you command
in return for his life; only let him not be killed.” But Chlothar answered with abuse: “Either push him away from you, or you will surely die in his place. You
are the instigator of this affair, and are you going back on your word so quickly?” When Childebert heard this, he thrust the boy away and cast him toward
Chlothar. Chlothar caught him, pierced his side with a knife, and killed him as he had killed his brother. Then they put the servants and attendants to death.

After these killings, Chlothar mounted his horse and departed, caring little about the murder of his nephews; Childebert withdrew to the suburbs. The queen had
the little bodies placed on a bier and followed them with great chanting of psalms and immense grief to the basilica of Saint Peter, where she buried them side
by side. One was ten years old and the other seven. They were unable to seize the third boy, Chlodovald, because he was rescued with the help of brave men. He
later renounced an earthly kingdom and turned to the Lord. Cutting his hair with his own hand, he became a cleric; devoted to good works, he departed from this
world as a priest. The two kings divided Chlodomer’s kingdom equally between themselves.

Queen Chrotchildis conducted herself so worthily and greatly that she was honored by everyone. She was constant in almsgiving, spent whole nights in vigils, and
always kept herself pure in chastity and every honorable practice. She provided the lands needed by churches, monasteries, and other holy places, distributing
them with generous and ready goodwill. Thus she seemed at that time not so much a queen as a handmaid of God, serving him devotedly. Neither her sons’ kingdom,
nor worldly ambition, nor wealth raised her up only to bring her to ruin; humility lifted her to grace.

### 19. Of the holy Gregory and the site of the castle of Dijon

**[020]** The blessed Gregory was then at the city of Langres, a great priest of God, renowned for signs and miracles. Since we have mentioned this bishop, I
have thought it well to include in this account a description of the site of Dijon, where he especially used to reside. The fortress stands in the middle of a
plain and is pleasantly situated, with very strong walls and extremely fertile and productive land. The fields need be cut only once by the ploughshare; then
the seed is scattered, and a great abundance of crops follows. To the south it has the river Ouche, very rich in fish; from the north another small river comes,
which enters through a gate, runs beneath a bridge, and goes out again through another gate, flowing with a calm current around the entire fortified place. In
front of the gate it drives mills with remarkable speed. Four gates face the four quarters of the world, and thirty-three towers adorn the whole structure. Its
wall is built of squared stones up to twenty feet, and above that of smaller stones; it is thirty feet high and fifteen feet thick. Why it is not called a city,
I do not know. It has excellent springs within its circuit. To the west are very rich hills covered with vineyards, which supply the inhabitants with Falernian
wine so noble that they despise the wine of Ascalon. The ancients relate that it was built by the emperor Aurelian.

### 20. How Theudebert Betrothed Visigard

**[021]** Theuderic had betrothed Wisigard, the daughter of a certain king, to his son Theudebert.

### 21. How Theudebert went into Provence

**[022]** After the death of Clovis, the Goths seized many of the places that he had acquired. Theuderic sent Theudebert, and Chlothar sent his elder son
Gunthar, to recover them. Gunthar went as far as Rodez but then turned back, for what reason I do not know. Theudebert went as far as the city of Béziers, took
the fortress of Dehas, and plundered it. He then sent messengers to another fortress named Capraria, declaring that unless its occupants surrendered, he would
burn the whole place with fire and carry off those who lived there as captives.

### 22. How he afterward took Deoteria

**[023]** There was then in that place a matron named Deoteria, a very capable and wise woman, whose husband had died in the city of Béziers. She sent
messengers to the king, saying: “No one can resist you, most merciful lord. We acknowledge you as our lord; come and do whatever is pleasing in your eyes.”
Theudebert came to the fortress and entered in peace. Seeing that the people had submitted to him, he did no harm there. Deoteria came out to meet him. Seeing
that she was beautiful, he was overcome by love for her and took her to his bed.

### 23. Of the death of Sigivald, and his flight

**[024]** In those days Theuderic killed his kinsman Sigivald with the sword. He also sent secretly to Theudebert, ordering him to put to death Sigivald’s son,
likewise named Sigivald, who was then with him. But because Theudebert had received the younger Sigivald from the sacred font as his godson, he refused to
destroy him. He gave him his father’s letter to read and said: “Flee from here, for I have received my father’s command to kill you. But if he dies and you hear
that I am reigning, then return to me in safety.” Sigivald thanked him, bade him farewell, and departed. The Goths had then seized the city of Arles, and
Theudebert was holding hostages from it; Sigivald fled there. But seeing that he was not sufficiently protected, he went to Latium and hid there.

While these things were happening, Theudebert received word that his father was gravely ill and that, unless he hurried, he would not find him alive; his uncles
would exclude him, and he would never return there. On hearing this, he set everything else aside and hastened to his father, leaving Deoteria and her daughter
in the Auvergne. Not many days after his departure, Theuderic died in the twenty-third year of his reign. Childebert and Chlothar then rose against Theudebert
and tried to take his kingdom from him. But he appeased them with gifts, was defended by his leudes, and was firmly established in the kingdom. He later sent to
the Auvergne, summoned Deoteria, and joined her to himself in marriage.

### 24. How Childebert made gifts to Theudebert

**[025]** When Childebert saw that he could not prevail against Theudebert, he sent an embassy and summoned him to come, saying: “I have no sons, and I wish to
regard you as my son.” When Theudebert came, Childebert enriched him with such gifts that everyone was astonished. He gave him three sets each of fine weapons,
clothing, and other ornaments such as a king ought to possess, and likewise of horses and dishes. When Sigivald heard that Theudebert had obtained his father’s
kingdom, he returned to him from Italy. Theudebert welcomed him joyfully, kissed him, and gave him a third of the gifts he had received from his uncle. He also
ordered that all of Sigivald’s property which his own father had placed in the treasury should be returned to him.

### 25. Of the Goodness of Theudebert

**[026]** Once firmly established in the kingdom, Theudebert showed himself great and outstanding in every kind of goodness. He ruled the kingdom justly,
honored the priests, endowed churches, relieved the poor, and conferred many benefits on many people with pious and most kindly generosity. He graciously
remitted all the tribute that the churches situated in the Auvergne used to pay to his treasury.

### 26. Of the Death of Deoteria’s Daughter

**[027]** Deoteria saw that her daughter was now fully grown. Fearing that the king would desire her and take her for himself, she placed the girl in a
carriage, harnessed untamed oxen to it, and had her thrown from a bridge. The girl died in the river. This happened at the city of Verdun.

### 27. How Theudebert took Visigard

**[028]** Seven years had now passed since Theudebert’s betrothal to Wisigard, and he still refused to marry her because of Deoteria. The Franks joined together
in strong indignation against him for abandoning his betrothed. Moved by their protest, he left Deoteria, by whom he had a young son named Theudebald, and
married Wisigard. He did not have her for long: she died, and he took another wife. But he never took Deoteria back.

### 28. How Childebert went against Chlothar

**[029]** Childebert and Theudebert called up their armies and prepared to march against Chlothar. When Chlothar heard of it, he judged that he could not
withstand their forces. He fled into a forest, made great clearings among the trees, and placed all his hope in God’s mercy. Queen Chrotchildis also heard of
it. She went to the tomb of blessed Martin, prostrated herself in prayer there, and kept vigil throughout the night, praying that no civil war might arise
between her sons.

When Childebert and Theudebert came with their armies and besieged Chlothar, intending to kill him the next day, a storm arose at daybreak in the place where
they were gathered. It scattered their tents, carried off their possessions, and overturned everything. Flashes of lightning mingled with thunder and hailstones
came down upon them. They fell face down on the hail-covered ground and were severely beaten by the falling stones, for no covering remained to them except
their shields. Above all, they feared being burned by fire from heaven. Their horses were scattered so widely that some could scarcely be found within twenty
stades, and many were never found at all. Bruised by the hailstones and prostrate on the ground, the men repented and begged God’s pardon for having intended to
do these things against their own kin.

Not a single drop of rain fell on Chlothar; no thunder was heard there, and those with him felt no blast of wind. Childebert and Theudebert sent messengers to
him and asked for peace and concord. When these were granted, they returned home. Let no one doubt that this miracle of blessed Martin was obtained through the
queen’s intercession.

### 29. How Childebert and Chlothar went into Spain

**[030]** After this King Childebert went into Spain. He and Chlothar entered the country, surrounded the city of Zaragoza with their army, and besieged it. The
inhabitants turned to God in such great humility that, clothed in haircloth and abstaining from food and drink, they went around the city walls singing psalms
and carrying the tunic of the blessed martyr Vincent. The women followed them in mourning, dressed in black garments, their hair loosened and ashes sprinkled
over them, so that one would have thought they were attending their husbands’ funerals. The whole place placed its hope in the Lord’s mercy. It was said that
the fast of the Ninevites was being celebrated there, and the people believed that nothing else could avail except to move divine mercy by their prayers.

The besiegers did not know what the besieged were doing. When they saw them going around the walls in this manner, they thought that they were practicing some
kind of sorcery. They seized a rustic from the city and asked him what was happening. He replied: “They are carrying the tunic of blessed Vincent and praying
with it that the Lord may have mercy on them.” Fearing this, the besiegers withdrew from the city. Nevertheless, after acquiring a very large part of Spain,
they returned to Gaul with great spoils.

### 30. Of the kings of the Spaniards

**[031]** After Amalaric, Theuda was made king in Spain. When he had been killed, the Goths raised Theudegisil to the throne. While Theudegisil was dining with
his friends and was in high spirits, the candles were suddenly extinguished; his enemies struck him with a sword where he reclined, and he died. Agila succeeded
him. The Goths had adopted the detestable custom of attacking with the sword any king who displeased them and then setting up as king whoever pleased them.

### 31. Of the daughter of Theuderic king of Italy

**[032]** Theoderic, king of Italy, had married King Clovis’s sister, and when he died he left a young daughter with his wife. When the girl had grown up, she
acted with foolish levity. Rejecting her mother’s plan to provide her with a king’s son, she took her own servant, named Traguila, and fled with him to a city
where she could be defended. Her mother was greatly enraged and begged her no longer to degrade her noble lineage, but to abandon the servant and accept the
royal suitor of her own rank whom her mother had chosen. She would not consent. Her enraged mother then called out an army. The soldiers came upon the couple,
killed Traguila with the sword, beat the daughter, and brought her back to her mother’s house.

They lived under the Arian sect. It was their custom for the kings, when they came to the altar, to receive from one chalice and the common people from another.
The daughter put poison in the chalice from which her mother was to receive communion. As soon as her mother drank from it, she died. There can be no doubt that
such an evil deed comes from the devil. What answer will the wretched heretics make to this, that the enemy should have a place in their holy things? We who
confess the Trinity in one equality and omnipotence believe that, even if we drink something deadly in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the
true and incorruptible God, it will not harm us.

The Italians were indignant at this woman. They invited Theodahad, king of Tuscany, and set him over themselves as king. When he learned what the harlot had
done—how she had become her mother’s murderer because of the servant she had taken—he ordered a bath to be heated intensely and had her shut inside it with a
single maid. As soon as she entered amid the overpowering vapors, she collapsed on the pavement and died, consumed by the heat.

When her cousins Kings Childebert and Chlothar, as well as Theudebert, learned that she had been killed by so shameful a punishment, they sent an embassy to
Theodahad. They reproached him for her death and said: “If you do not make compensation to us for what you have done, we will take away your kingdom and condemn
you to a similar punishment.” In fear, he sent them fifty thousand gold pieces. Childebert, always envious and crafty in his dealings with King Chlothar, joined
with his nephew Theudebert. They divided the gold between themselves and refused to give any of it to Chlothar. Chlothar then seized Chlodomer’s treasures and
took from them much more than the others had cheated him of.

### 32. How Theudebert went into Italy

**[033]** Theudebert went into Italy and acquired much territory there. But because those regions are unhealthy, as is reported, his army was afflicted by
various fevers and many of his men died there. Seeing this, Theudebert returned from Italy, with himself and his men carrying off great spoils. He is said to
have advanced at that time as far as the city of Pavia, to which he again sent Buccelin.

Buccelin captured Lesser Italy and brought it under the power of the aforesaid king, then sought Greater Italy. Fighting there many times against Belisarius, he
won the victory. When the emperor saw that Belisarius was repeatedly defeated, he removed him and put Narses in his place. He reduced Belisarius to his former
office of count of the stable, as though to humiliate him. Buccelin fought great battles against Narses. He captured all Italy, extended its boundary to the
sea, and sent great treasures from Italy to Theudebert.

When Narses reported this to the emperor, the emperor hired foreign peoples for money and sent reinforcements to Narses. Buccelin subsequently joined battle,
was defeated, and withdrew. He later occupied Sicily and sent the tribute he exacted from it to the king. He enjoyed great success in these undertakings.

### 33. Of Asteriolus and Secundinus

**[034]** Asteriolus and Secundinus were then held in high esteem by the king. Both were intelligent and trained in rhetoric. Secundinus had often been sent by
the king on embassies to the emperor; this made him boastful, and he behaved in various unreasonable ways. A bitter quarrel consequently arose between him and
Asteriolus. It went so far that they abandoned verbal accusations and beat each other with their own hands.

The king reconciled them, but Secundinus was still swollen with anger over the blows he had received, and strife broke out between them again. The king took
Secundinus’s side and handed Asteriolus over to his power. Asteriolus was severely humiliated and deprived of his office, but he was restored through Queen
Wisigard. After her death, Secundinus rose against him again and killed him.

Asteriolus left a son at his death. When the son had grown to manhood, he began to seek vengeance for the wrong done to his father. Secundinus, terrified, fled
before him from estate to estate. When he saw that the other was closing in and that he could not escape, he killed himself with poison, as is said, rather than
fall into his enemy’s hands.

### 34. Of the gift of Theudebert to the citizens of Verdun

**[035]** King Theuderic had inflicted many injuries on Desideratus, bishop of Verdun. After many disasters, losses, and sufferings, Desideratus had returned by
the Lord’s command to freedom and, as we have said, had recovered his episcopal office in the city of Verdun. Seeing that its inhabitants were extremely poor
and destitute, he grieved for them. He himself had been stripped of his property by Theuderic and had nothing of his own with which to help them. Knowing King
Theudebert’s goodness and mercy toward everyone, he sent an embassy to him, saying: “The fame of your goodness is spread throughout the whole earth, and your
generosity is so great that you give help even to those who do not ask for it. I beg you, if your charity has any money available, lend it to us so that we may
relieve our citizens. When their business activities have restored our city to the prosperity enjoyed by others, we will repay your money with lawful interest.”

Moved by compassion, Theudebert lent him seven thousand gold pieces. Desideratus received the money and distributed it among his citizens. They engaged in
trade, became rich through it, and are held in high esteem to this day. When the bishop offered to repay the money to the king, the king replied: “I have no
need to receive it back. It is enough for me that the poor who were crushed by want have been relieved through your management, at your petition and by my
generosity.” He demanded nothing and thus made the citizens wealthy.

### 35. Of the death of Syrivald

**[036]** When the bishop just mentioned died in that city, Agiricus, one of the citizens, was appointed to his see. His son Siacrius remembered the wrong done
to his father: Sirivald had accused him before King Theuderic, and he had not only been stripped of his property but also subjected to punishments. Siacrius
therefore attacked Sirivald with an armed band and killed him in the following manner.

At daybreak, when the fog was dense and the darkness was only just dispersing so that one could scarcely distinguish anything, he came to Sirivald’s estate,
named Floriacum, in the territory of Dijon. One of Sirivald’s friends came out of the house. Thinking that he was Sirivald himself, the attackers killed him. As
they were withdrawing, believing that they had overcome their enemy, a member of the household told them that they had not killed the master but a subordinate.
They returned, searched for Sirivald, and attacked the small chamber in which he usually slept. They fought for a long time at its door but could not prevail
against him. Then they broke through the wall on one side, entered, and killed him with the sword. This happened after Theuderic’s death.

### 36. Of the death of Theudebert and of the death of Parthenius

**[037]** After these events, King Theudebert fell ill. Physicians devoted great care to him, but nothing availed, because the Lord was already calling him.
After a long illness, he grew weaker and gave up his spirit.

The Franks hated Parthenius intensely because he had imposed taxes on them during the reign of the king just mentioned, and they began to pursue him. Seeing
himself in danger, he fled from the city. He humbly begged two bishops to escort him to the city of Trier and to calm the fury of the rioting people by their
preaching. While they were traveling, he was lying on his bed at night when he suddenly cried out loudly in his sleep: “Alas! Alas! Help me, you who are here;
bring aid to a man who is perishing!” Those present were awakened by the cry and asked what was wrong. He answered: “My friend Ausanius and his wife Papianilla,
whom I killed long ago, were summoning me to judgment. They said: ‘Come and answer, for you must plead your case with us before the Lord.’” Some years earlier,
moved by jealousy, he had killed his innocent wife and his friend.

When the bishops reached Trier, they could not endure the uproar of the rioting people and decided to hide Parthenius in the church. They put him in a chest and
spread over him the vestments used in the church. The people entered and searched every corner of the church. Finding nothing, they went out in a rage. Then one
man said suspiciously: “There is the chest in which our enemy has not been sought.” The guards said that it contained nothing but church ornaments, but the
crowd demanded the key, saying: “Unless you unlock it quickly, we will break it open ourselves.” At last the chest was opened, the linen cloths were removed,
and Parthenius was found and dragged out. The people clapped their hands and cried: “God has delivered our enemy into our hands!” They beat him with their fists
and spat on him. Then they bound his hands behind his back and stoned him to death against a column.

He was extremely gluttonous. He took aloes to digest his food quickly so that he might be ready to eat again sooner. He also emitted noises from his belly in
public without any regard for those who heard him. Such was the end in which he perished.

### 37. Of the severe winter

**[038]** That year there was a severe winter, harsher than usual. The streams were so bound by continuous frost that they offered people a passage like the
rest of the ground. Because of the deep snow, birds weakened by cold or hunger could be caught by hand without any human snare. From the death of Clovis to the
death of Theudebert, thirty-seven years are reckoned. Theudebert died in the fourteenth year of his reign, and his son Theudebald reigned in his place.

## Praefatio

**[001]** Vellim, si placet, parumper conferre, quae christianis beatam confitentibus Trinitatem prospera successerint et quae hereticis eandem scindentibus
fuerint in ruinam. Omittamus autem, qualiter illam Abraham veneratur ad elicem, Iacob praedicat in benedictionem, Moyses cognuscit in sentem, populus sequitur
in nubem eandemque paviscit in montem, vel qualiter eam Aaron portat in logium, aut David vaticinatur in psalmum, orans innovari se per spiritum rectum, nec
sibi auferri spiritum sanctum, atque se confirmari per spiritum principalem. Magnum et hic ego cerno mistirium, quod scilicet, quem heretici minorem adserunt,
principalem vox prophetica nuntiavit. Sed haec, ut diximus, omissa, ad nostra tempora revertamur. Arrius enim, qui huius iniquae sectae primus iniquosque
Inventur fuit, interiora in secessum deposita, infernalibus ignebus subditur, Hilarius vero beatus individuae Trinitatis defensor, propter hanc in exilium
