against us.” They refused. The Saxons then offered clothing, cattle, and all the rest of their property, saying: “Take all these things together with half our
land. Only leave our wives and little children free, and let there be no war between us.” The Franks refused even this.

King Chlothar said to them: “I beg you, abandon this plan. We have no just cause. Do not go into a battle in which you will be destroyed. If you insist on
going, I will not follow you of my own free will.” Enraged at King Chlothar, they rushed upon him, tore his tent, abused him with insults, and dragged him by
force. They were ready to kill him if he delayed going with them. Seeing this, Chlothar went with them unwillingly.

When battle was joined, the Franks were cut down by their enemies in a tremendous slaughter. So great a multitude fell on both sides that it was impossible to
estimate or count. Greatly humiliated, Chlothar sued for peace, declaring that he had not attacked the Saxons of his own free will. Peace was obtained, and he
returned home.

### 15. Of the episcopate of the holy Eufronius

**[015]** When the people of Tours heard that the king had returned from the slaughter of the Saxons, they agreed upon the priest Eufronius and went to the
king. After they presented their petition, the king replied: “I had commanded that the priest Cato be ordained there. Why has my command been disregarded?” They
answered: “We sought him, but he refused to come.”

While they were speaking, the priest Cato suddenly arrived and begged the king to expel Cautinus and appoint him to the see of Clermont. The king laughed at
him. Cato then asked to be ordained at Tours, the see he had previously despised. The king said: “I first commanded that you be consecrated bishop at Tours, but
from what I hear, you held that church in contempt. Therefore you shall be kept away from its government.” Cato departed in confusion.

When the king asked about Saint Eufronius, they told him that Eufronius was a kinsman of the blessed Gregory whom we mentioned above. The king replied: “That is
a foremost and noble lineage. Let the will of God and blessed Martin be done; let the election be completed.” A royal order was issued, and Saint Eufronius was
ordained bishop, the eighteenth after blessed Martin.

### 16. Of Chramn

**[016]** Chramn committed various evils in the Auvergne, as we have said, and always cherished hostility toward Bishop Cautinus. At that time he became so
gravely ill that his hair fell out because of the violent fever. He had with him a distinguished and entirely good citizen of Clermont named Ascovindus, who
tried earnestly to turn him away from his wickedness but could not. He also had Leo of Poitiers with him, a severe incitement to every evil deed. True to his
name, Leo was as savage as a lion in every kind of greed. He is said once to have declared that Martin and Martial, confessors of the Lord, had left nothing
useful to the resources of the treasury. Immediately struck by the power of the confessors, he became deaf and dumb and died out of his mind. The wretched man
went to the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours, kept vigils, and gave gifts, but the saint’s accustomed power did not regard him. He returned with the same
affliction he had brought.

Chramn left the Auvergne and came to the city of Poitiers. While residing there in great power, he was led astray by evil counsel and wished to defect to his
uncle Childebert, planning treachery against his father. Childebert deceitfully promised to receive him, though he ought instead to have given him spiritual
warning not to become his father’s enemy. They exchanged secret messengers, swore a conspiracy, and agreed together against Chlothar. Childebert forgot that
whenever he had acted against his brother, he had always departed in confusion.

After making this pact, Chramn returned to the Limousin and brought under his own control the region through which he had previously traveled in his father’s
kingdom. Meanwhile the people of Clermont were shut inside their walls and were dying miserably from various diseases.

King Chlothar sent his two sons Charibert and Guntram against Chramn. Passing through the Auvergne and hearing that Chramn was in the Limousin, they advanced as
far as the mountain called Black Mountain and found him. They pitched their tents opposite him and sent envoys demanding that he restore his father’s property,
which he had wrongfully seized; otherwise he should prepare a battlefield. Chramn pretended to be subject to his father and said: “I cannot give up all that I
have acquired, but I wish to retain it under my own authority with my father’s favor.” His brothers demanded that battle decide the matter. Both armies advanced
with a great array of weapons, but a sudden storm with violent lightning and thunder prevented them from fighting.

After they returned to camp, Chramn deceitfully sent an outsider to tell his brothers that their father was dead. At that time the war against the Saxons
mentioned above was still being waged. Alarmed, the brothers returned to Burgundy with all speed. Chramn sent his army after them, advanced to the city of
Chalon, besieged it, and captured it. From there he proceeded to the fortress of Dijon, where he arrived on a Sunday. I shall now relate what happened.

Saint Tetricus, whom we mentioned in an earlier book, was bishop there. The clergy placed three books on the altar—the Prophets, the Apostle, and the
Gospels—and prayed to the Lord to reveal what would happen to Chramn and whether divine power would grant him success or the ability to reign. They agreed that
each would read at Mass the first passage he found on opening a book. When the book of the Prophets was opened first, they found: “I will take away its hedge,
and it shall be laid waste; because instead of producing grapes, it produced wild grapes.” When the book of the Apostle was opened, they found: “You yourselves
know well, brothers, that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ sudden destruction will come upon them
like the pains of a woman in labor, and they will not escape.” And the Lord said through the Gospel: “Whoever does not hear my words will be like a foolish man
who built his house upon sand. The rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew and beat upon that house, and it fell; and great was its fall.”

Chramn was received by the bishop at the basilicas and ate bread there, then proceeded toward Childebert. He was not permitted to enter within the walls of
Dijon. At that time King Chlothar was fighting vigorously against the Saxons. They say that the Saxons had been incited by Childebert and had been angry with
the Franks in the previous year. They had left their own region, entered Frankish territory, plundered as far as the city of Divitia, and committed extremely
grave crimes.

### 17. How Chramn passed over to Childebert

**[017]** Chramn had by then married Willichar’s daughter. He went to Paris and bound King Childebert to himself by pledges of loyalty and affection, swearing
that he was his father’s implacable enemy. While Chlothar was fighting the Saxons, King Childebert entered the Champagne region and hastened as far as the city
of Reims, devastating everything with plunder and fire. He had heard that his brother had been killed by the Saxons. Thinking to bring everything under his own
rule, he seized all that he could reach.

### 18. Of the duke Austrapius

**[018]** Duke Austrapius also feared Chramn and took refuge in the basilica of Saint Martin. Divine assistance did not fail him in this distress. Chramn
ordered that he be confined so strictly that no one dared give him food and that he was not even permitted to draw water. He hoped that hunger would compel
Austrapius to leave the holy basilica of his own accord and go to his death. A man brought him a small vessel of water mixed with wine to drink. Austrapius
accepted it, but the judge of the place immediately rushed up, snatched it from his hand, and poured it on the ground. God’s swift vengeance and the blessed
bishop’s power followed. On the very day he committed this act, the judge was seized by fever and died at midnight. He did not live until the same hour the next
day, when he had dashed the cup from the fugitive’s hand in the saint’s basilica. After this miracle, everyone brought Austrapius abundant supplies.

When King Chlothar returned to his kingdom, Austrapius was held in high esteem by him. During Chlothar’s reign Austrapius entered the clergy and was ordained
bishop at the fortress of Selles in the diocese of Poitiers, with the intention that, when Bishop Pientius, who then governed the church of Poitiers, died,
Austrapius should succeed him. But King Charibert altered the arrangement. When Bishop Pientius departed from this life, Pascentius, then abbot of the basilica
of Saint Hilary, succeeded him at Paris by King Charibert’s command. Austrapius protested that the see was owed to him, but his words accomplished little. He
returned to his own fortress, where the Thuringians, whom he had often oppressed, rose against him. Wounded by a lance, he died a cruel death. His diocese
returned to the church of Poitiers.

### 19. Of the death of Saint Medard the bishop

**[019]** In King Chlothar’s time Saint Medard, God’s bishop, completed his course of good works and died full of days and outstanding in holiness. King
Chlothar buried him with the highest honor in the city of Soissons and began to build a basilica over him. His son Sigibert later completed and adorned it. At
his blessed tomb we have seen prisoners’ fetters and chains lying broken and shattered. They are preserved at the blessed tomb to this day as testimony to his
power. But let us return to our earlier narrative.

### 20. Of the death of Childebert and the end of Chramn

**[020]** King Childebert fell ill. After lying sick in Paris for a long time, he died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Vincent, which he himself had
built. King Chlothar took his kingdom and treasures and sent Vulthrogotha and her two daughters into exile. Chramn was brought before his father but later
proved unfaithful again. Seeing that he could not escape, he went to Brittany, where he, his wife, and his daughters hid with Chonoober, count of the Bretons.
His father-in-law Willichar took refuge in the basilica of Saint Martin.

The holy basilica was then set on fire by Willichar and his wife, because of the people’s sins and the mockeries committed there; I do not record this without a
heavy sigh. The city of Tours had also been consumed by fire a year earlier, and all the churches built there had been left desolate. By King Chlothar’s order,
the basilica of blessed Martin was immediately roofed with tin and restored to its former elegance.

Two swarms of locusts then appeared. They passed through the Auvergne and the Limousin and came, it is said, to the field of Romagnat, where they fought one
another and were destroyed in great numbers. King Chlothar, enraged with Chramn, marched with an army against him into Brittany. Chramn was not afraid to go out
against his father. When both armies were massed in one field and Chramn had drawn up his battle line with the Bretons against his father, night fell and
fighting ceased. During the night Chonoober, count of the Bretons, said to Chramn: “I consider it wrong for you to go out against your father. Let me attack him
tonight and overthrow him and his whole army.” Chramn, restrained, I believe, by God’s power, would not permit it.

At daybreak both armies advanced to battle against each other. King Chlothar went like a new David to fight against his son Absalom, lamenting and saying: “Look
down from heaven, Lord, and judge my cause, for I suffer unjust injuries from my son. Look down, Lord, and judge justly; impose the judgment that you once
imposed between Absalom and his father David.” When battle was joined, the count of the Bretons turned and fled and fell there. Chramn then fled toward ships he
had prepared at sea. But while he was trying to rescue his wife and daughters, his father’s army overwhelmed him, and he was captured and bound. When this was
reported to King Chlothar, he ordered Chramn to be burned together with his wife and daughters. They were shut inside a poor woman’s hut. Chramn was stretched
out on a bench and strangled with a cloth. The hut was then set on fire over them, and he perished with his wife and daughters.

### 21. Of the death of King Chlothar

**[021]** In the fifty-first year of his reign King Chlothar went with many gifts to the shrine of blessed Martin. Coming to the bishop’s tomb at Tours, he
reviewed all the actions that he might have performed negligently. With deep groaning he prayed that the Lord’s blessed confessor would entreat mercy for his
sins and wash away by his intercession the things Chlothar had unreasonably committed. After returning from there, still in the fifty-first year of his reign,
he was hunting in the forest of Cuise when he was seized by fever. He returned from there to the estate of Compiègne. Grievously tormented by fever, he said:
“Alas! What kind of king do you think the heavenly King is, who thus kills such mighty kings?” Worn out by illness, he breathed out his spirit. His four sons
carried him with great honor to Soissons and buried him in the basilica of blessed Medard. He died one year less a day after Chramn was killed.

### 22. The division of the kingdom among his sons

**[022]** After his father’s funeral, Chilperic took the treasures gathered at the estate of Brannacum. He sought out the more influential Franks, won them over
with gifts, and brought them under his authority. He soon entered Paris and occupied King Childebert’s seat. He was not allowed to hold it for long: his
brothers joined forces and drove him out. The four—Charibert, Guntram, Chilperic, and Sigibert—then made a lawful division among themselves. The lot assigned
Childebert’s kingdom to Charibert, with his seat at Paris; Chlodomer’s kingdom to Guntram, with his seat at Orléans; their father Chlothar’s kingdom to
Chilperic, with his seat at Soissons; and Theuderic’s kingdom to Sigibert, with his seat at Reims.

### 23. How Sigibert went against the Huns

**[023]** After King Chlothar’s death the Huns attacked Gaul. Sigibert led an army against them, fought a battle, defeated them, and put them to flight. Their
king later obtained friendly relations with Sigibert through envoys. While Sigibert was occupied with the Huns, his brother Chilperic seized Reims and took the
other cities belonging to him. Civil war, worse than the foreign conflict, arose between the brothers.

Sigibert returned victorious over the Huns and occupied the city of Soissons. Finding Theudebert, King Chilperic’s son, there, he seized him and sent him into
exile. He then advanced against Chilperic and made war on him. Chilperic was defeated and put to flight, and Sigibert restored the cities to his own control. He
ordered Chilperic’s son Theudebert to be kept under guard at the estate of Ponticon for a full year. Later, being merciful, he enriched him with gifts and
returned him safe and sound to his father, after receiving his oath never to act against Sigibert again. That oath was later broken because of sin.

### 24. Of the patriciate of Celsus

**[024]** When King Guntram had obtained his share of the kingdom like his brothers, he removed Patrician Agroecola and conferred the honor of the patriciate on
Celsus. Celsus was tall in stature, strong in the shoulders, robust in the arms, inflated in speech, ready in reply, and skilled in reading law. His desire for
possessions later became so great that he frequently seized church property and brought it under his own control. Once, when he heard a reading from the prophet
Isaiah in church—“Woe to those who join house to house and couple field to field until there is no room left”—he is said to have cried out: “That is ill-timed!
Woe to me and my sons!” He left a son who died childless and bequeathed the greater part of his property to the churches his father had despoiled.

### 25. Of the wives of Guntram

**[025]** King Guntram was a good man. He first took Veneranda, a servant woman belonging to one of his men, as his concubine and had a son by her named
Gundobad. He later married Marcatrud, daughter of Magnarius, and sent his son Gundobad to Orléans. After bearing a son herself, Marcatrud became arrogant and
plotted Gundobad’s death. They say that she sent him poison in a drink and killed him. After his death, by God’s judgment she lost her own son, incurred the
king’s hatred, and was repudiated by him. She died not long afterward. Guntram next married Austrechild, surnamed Bobilla, by whom he again had two sons. The
elder was called Chlothar and the younger Chlodomer.

### 26. Of the wives of Charibert

**[026]** King Charibert married Ingoberga and had a daughter by her who later went to Kent to take a husband. At that time Ingoberga had in her service two
girls, daughters of a poor man. The elder was called Marcovefa and wore religious clothing; the other was Merofledis. The king was deeply in love with them. As
we have said, they were the daughters of a woolworker. Ingoberga was jealous because the king loved them. She secretly had their father set to work, hoping that
when the king saw this he would despise his daughters. While the man was working, she summoned the king. Expecting to see something new, he looked from a
distance and saw the man preparing the royal wool. Angered by the sight, he left Ingoberga and married Merofledis.

He also had another girl named Theudegild, daughter of a shepherd—that is, a keeper of sheep—by whom he is said to have had a son who was carried to the tomb as
soon as he came from the womb.

During this king’s reign Leontius assembled the bishops of his province at the city of Saintes and expelled Emerius from the episcopate, asserting that he had
not received the office canonically. Emerius had obtained a decree from King Chlothar allowing him to be consecrated without the metropolitan’s consent because
the metropolitan was absent. After expelling Emerius, the bishops agreed upon Heraclius, then a priest of the city of Bordeaux. They subscribed the decision in
their own hands and sent it to King Charibert through the same priest. Heraclius came to Tours and explained the matter to blessed Eufronius, asking him to
deign to subscribe their decision. The man of God openly refused.

When the priest entered the gates of Paris and came into the king’s presence, he addressed him: “Hail, glorious king. The apostolic see sends your eminence
abundant greetings.” Charibert asked: “Have you been to the city of Rome, that you bring us its pope’s greeting?” The priest replied: “Your father Leontius and
his provincial bishops send you greeting. They report that Cymulus”—for so they used to call Emerius in his childhood—“has been expelled from the episcopate
because he sought the bishopric of Saintes in violation of the sanction of the canons. They have therefore sent their decision to you so that another may be
appointed in his place. Thus, while transgressors of the canons are properly rebuked, the power of your kingdom will be extended through long ages.”

The king was enraged by this speech. He ordered the priest to be dragged from his sight, placed on a cart heaped with thorns, and driven into exile. He said:
“Do you think there is no son of King Chlothar left to uphold his father’s acts, that these bishops have expelled without my judgment a bishop whom his will
chose?” He immediately sent religious men to restore Emerius to his see. He also sent chamberlains, who fined Bishop Leontius one thousand gold pieces and
condemned the other bishops to fines according to their means. In this way the injury to the prince was avenged.

Charibert afterward married Marcovefa, Merofledis’s sister. Bishop Saint Germanus excommunicated both the king and Marcovefa for this. When the king refused to
leave her, she was struck by God’s judgment and died. The king himself died not long after her.

After his death Theudegild, one of his queens, sent messengers to King Guntram and offered herself to him in marriage. The king replied: “Let her not hesitate
to come to me with her treasures. I will receive her and make her great among the people, so that she enjoys greater honor with me than with my recently
deceased brother.” Rejoicing, she gathered all her possessions and set out to him. Seeing this, the king said: “It is more fitting for these treasures to remain
with me than with a woman who unworthily entered my brother’s bed.” He took most of her property, left her a little, and confined her in a monastery at Arles.

She could hardly endure the fasting and vigils imposed on her. Through secret messengers she approached a certain Goth and promised that, if he would take her
to Spain and marry her, she would leave the monastery with her treasures and gladly follow him. He agreed without hesitation. She gathered her belongings and
prepared bundles in readiness to leave the monastery. But the abbess’s diligence anticipated her plan. The deception was discovered, and the abbess ordered
Theudegild to be severely beaten and placed in custody. Worn down by severe sufferings, she remained there until the end of her life.

### 27. How Sigibert took Brunhilda

**[027]** King Sigibert saw that his brothers were taking wives unworthy of themselves and, in their baseness, were even marrying servant women. He sent an
embassy to Spain and asked with many gifts for Brunhilda, daughter of King Athanagild. The girl was skilled in handiwork, beautiful in appearance, honorable and
graceful in conduct, prudent in counsel, and pleasant in speech. Her father did not refuse, but sent her with great treasures to the king. Sigibert assembled
his leading men, prepared banquets, and received her as his wife with immense joy and delight. She had been subject to Arian doctrine, but she was converted by
the bishops’ preaching and the king’s own exhortation. Confessing and believing in the blessed Trinity in unity, she was anointed with chrism. She remains
Catholic in the name of Christ.

### 28. Of the wives of Chilperic

**[028]** King Chilperic saw this and, although he already had several wives, sought Brunhilda’s sister Galswintha. He promised through envoys to put away the
others if he might obtain a wife worthy of himself and of royal lineage. Her father accepted these promises and sent his daughter to him with great wealth, as
he had sent her sister. Galswintha was older than Brunhilda. When she came to King Chilperic, she was received with great honor and joined to him in marriage.
He loved her deeply because she had brought great treasures with her. But his love for Fredegund, whom he had previously kept, caused great scandal between
them.

Galswintha had by then been converted to the Catholic faith and anointed with chrism. She repeatedly complained to the king that she suffered constant injuries
and had no honor in his household. She asked to be allowed to leave behind the treasures she had brought and return freely to her own country. He concealed his
intentions and soothed her with gentle words. Finally he ordered a servant to strangle her, and she was found dead in her bed.

After her death God displayed a great miracle. A wooden torch hanging by a cord and burning before her tomb fell to the pavement without anyone touching it when
the cord broke. The hardness of the pavement yielded before it as though it were sinking into some soft substance. It was buried halfway into the floor without
being broken at all, a great miracle to those who saw it. The king mourned her death, but a few days later he married Fredegund. His brothers judged that he had
ordered the queen’s murder and drove him from the kingdom.

Chilperic then had three sons by his former queen Audovera: Theudebert, whom we mentioned above, Merovech, and Chlodovech. But let us return to our narrative.

### 29. Of Sigibert's second war against the Huns

**[029]** The Huns attempted to invade Gaul again. Sigibert marched against them with an army and a great multitude of brave men. When battle was about to be
joined, the Huns, skilled in magical arts, produced various phantoms and utterly routed them. Sigibert’s army fled, and he himself was surrounded and held by
the Huns. But being skillful and resourceful, he later overcame by the art of gift-giving those he could not overcome by force in battle. He gave gifts and made
a treaty with their king that they would never wage war against each other for the rest of their lives. Just reason judges this more to his credit than to his
reproach. The king of the Huns also gave many gifts to King Sigibert. He was called the khagan; all the kings of that people are called by this title.

### 30. How the Arverni went to take Arles

**[030]** King Sigibert wished to capture the city of Arles and ordered the Auvergnats to mobilize. Firminus was then count of their city, and he went at their
head. Adovarius approached from another direction with an army. They entered Arles and exacted oaths on behalf of King Sigibert. When King Guntram learned of
this, he sent Patrician Celsus there with an army. Celsus went and captured Avignon, then advanced on Arles and surrounded it. He began to attack Sigibert’s
army, which was confined within the walls.

Bishop Sabaudus said to them: “Go outside and join battle. You cannot defend us or this city’s inhabitants by remaining enclosed within the walls. If you defeat
them with God’s favor, we will keep the faith we promised. If they prevail against you, you will find the gates open; come in so that you do not perish.”
Deceived by this trick, they went out and prepared for battle. Celsus’s army defeated them, and they fled. When they reached the city, they found the gates
barred. Attacked from behind by the army’s javelins and pelted with stones by the townspeople, they made for the river Rhône. Supported by their shields, they
tried to reach the farther bank. The river’s violence swept many of them away and drowned them. The Rhône then did to the Auvergnats what the Simois is said
once to have done to the Trojans: “It rolls beneath the waves the snatched shields of men, their helmets, and their strong bodies. A few swimmers appear in the
vast whirlpool.” Only with great difficulty, swimming and aided by the support of their shields, were they able to reach the level ground of the opposite shore.
Stripped of their possessions and deprived of their horses, they returned to their country in great disgrace. Firminus and Adovarius, however, were granted
leave to depart. Many noble Auvergnats died there, not only swept away by the torrent’s force but also struck down by swords. King Guntram recovered Arles and,
with his customary goodness, restored Avignon to his brother’s control.

### 31. Of the castle of Tauredunum and other signs

**[031]** A great prodigy occurred in Gaul at the fortress of Tauredunum, which stood above the river Rhône. For more than sixty days it emitted a strange
roaring sound. At last the mountain split and separated from a neighboring mountain. It plunged into the river with its men, churches, property, and houses. The
river’s channel was blocked, and the water flowed backward. That place was enclosed on both sides by mountains, and the river flowed through the narrow passage
between them. The flood covered and destroyed everything situated on the upper bank. The accumulated water then burst downward, caught people unawares, and
drowned them as it had done above. It overturned houses, destroyed cattle, and swept away and overthrew everything on those banks as far as the city of Geneva
in a violent and sudden inundation. Many relate that the mass of water was so great that it entered Geneva over its walls. This is not difficult to believe,
because, as we have said, the Rhône flows there through a narrow passage between mountains; when it was blocked, it had nowhere to turn aside. The dislodged
mountain moved and collapsed all at once, destroying everything.

After this happened, thirty monks came to the place where the fortress had fallen. Digging in the ground left behind by the mountain’s collapse, they found
bronze and iron. While doing this, they heard the mountain roaring as before. Savage greed held them there. The part that had not yet fallen came down on them,
covered them, and killed them; they were never found again.

Great prodigies likewise terrified the Auvergne before its disaster. Often three or four great lights appeared around the sun. The rustics called them suns and
said: “Look, there are three or four suns in the sky!” On one occasion, on the kalends of October, the sun appeared so darkened that not even a quarter of it
remained shining. Foul and discolored, it looked like a sack. A star that some call a comet, with a beam like a sword, appeared over that region for a whole
year. The sky seemed to burn, and many other signs appeared.

In the church at Clermont, while the morning vigils were being celebrated on a certain feast, a lark entered. It extinguished all the burning lights by putting
its wings over them with such speed that one would have thought a single hand had plunged them into water. Passing beneath the veil into the sanctuary, it tried
to extinguish the lamp there, but the doorkeepers stopped and killed it. Another bird did the same to the burning lamps in the basilica of blessed Andrew.

When the disaster itself arrived, so great a destruction of the people occurred throughout the region that the multitudes who fell there could not be counted.
When sarcophagi and planks ran out, ten or more bodies were buried in a single trench in the ground. On one Sunday three hundred corpses were counted in the
basilica of blessed Peter alone. Death was sudden. When a sore like a serpent appeared in the groin or armpit, the poison killed the person so quickly that he
breathed out his spirit on the second or third day. The force of the poison also deprived him of his senses.

The priest Cato died at that time. Many fled from the plague, but he never left the place: he buried the people and celebrated Masses for them individually.
This priest was very humane and greatly loved by the poor. I believe that this charity served as a remedy for any pride he may have had. Bishop Cautinus,
fearing the disaster, traveled through various places but returned to the city. He caught the disease and died on the day of preparation for the Lord’s Passion.
His cousin Tetradius died at the same hour. Lyon, Bourges, Chalon, and Dijon were also severely depopulated by this sickness.

### 32. Of Julian the monk

**[032]** At that time there was at the monastery of Randan in the territory of Clermont a priest of outstanding virtue named Julian. He was a man of great
abstinence, taking neither wine nor any other relish, always wearing a hair shirt beneath his tunic, prompt in vigils, and constant in prayer. By invoking the
Lord’s name and making the sign of the holy cross, he could readily heal the possessed, give sight to the blind, and drive away other infirmities. Standing
continually caused his feet to become infected with sores. When asked why he always stood beyond his body’s capacity, he used to answer with a spiritual jest:
“They do my work while life is kind, and with the Lord’s help their support does not abandon me.” We once saw him heal a possessed man with only a word in the
basilica of the blessed martyr Julian. He also often brought relief through prayer to those suffering from quartan and other fevers. During this time of plague,
full of days and virtues, he was taken from this world into rest.

### 33. Of the abbot Sunniulfus

**[033]** The abbot of that monastery also died at that time, and Sunniulf succeeded him. Sunniulf was a man of complete simplicity and charity. He often washed
the guests’ feet himself and dried them with his own hands. He governed the flock entrusted to him not by fear but by entreaty. He used to relate that he had
been led in a vision to a fiery river. Crowds rushing together from one bank were plunged into it like bees entering hives. Some stood in it up to the waist,
others up to the armpits, and some up to the chin, crying out with tears that they were being fiercely burned. A bridge over the river was so narrow that it
could scarcely accommodate the width of a single footstep. On the other bank appeared a great house, whitened on the outside. Sunniulf asked those with him what
these things meant. They replied: “Whoever is found slothful in correcting the flock entrusted to him will be thrown from this bridge. But whoever is diligent
will cross without danger and be joyfully led into the house you see beyond.” On hearing this, he awoke and thereafter appeared much sterner to the monks.

### 34. Of the monk of Bordeaux

**[034]** I will also relate what happened at a certain monastery at that time. I will not name the monk because he is still alive, lest he fall into vainglory
and relapse when this writing reaches him. A young man came to a monastery and commended himself to the abbot in order to live in God’s service. The abbot
raised many objections, telling him that the service of the place was hard and that he could not possibly fulfill all that would be required of him. Invoking
the Lord’s name, the young man promised to fulfill everything, and so the abbot received him.

A few days later, while he was conducting himself with complete humility and holiness, the monks brought grain out of the granary and spread about three heaps
in the sun to dry. They assigned him to guard it. While the others were taking refreshment and he remained watching the grain, the sky suddenly clouded over. A
heavy rainstorm, driven by a rushing wind, rapidly approached the heap of grain. The monk did not know what to do. Considering that if he called the others they
could not gather so much grain into the granaries before the rain, he set everything else aside and turned to prayer. He begged the Lord that not a drop of that
rain might fall on the wheat. He threw himself on the ground and prayed. The cloud divided, and rain poured heavily all around the grain without wetting a
single grain of wheat, if I may say so.

When the other monks and the abbot realized what was happening, they hurried to gather the grain. Seeing the miracle, they looked for the guard and found him
lying on the sand not far away, praying. At the sight the abbot prostrated himself behind him. When the rain had passed and the prayer was finished, he called
the monk to rise. He then seized him and ordered him to be beaten, saying: “You must grow humbly in the fear and service of God, my son, not glory in prodigies
and miracles.” He shut him in a cell and ordered him to fast for seven days like a guilty man, to turn vainglory away from him so that it would not become an
obstacle.

We have learned from trustworthy men that this monk now practices such abstinence that during the days of Lent he eats no bread, but only every third day drinks
a full cup of barley water. With your prayers, may the Lord deign to preserve him until the completion of his life so that he may please him.

### 35. Of the episcopate of Avitus of the Auvergne

**[035]** After Bishop Cautinus died at Clermont, as we have said, many sought the episcopate, offering much and promising still more. The priest Eufrasius, son
of the former senator Euodius, sent valuable merchandise obtained from Jews to the king through his kinsman Beregisil, hoping to obtain by rewards what he could
not obtain by merit. He was elegant in manner but unchaste in conduct. He often gave barbarians drink but seldom refreshed the needy. I believe that he failed
because he sought this honor through men rather than through God. Nor could the word spoken by the Lord through the mouth of Saint Quintianus be altered: “No
one shall arise from the stock of Hortensius to rule the church of God.”

The archdeacon Avitus assembled the clergy in the church at Clermont. He made no promises, but after receiving their consent he went to the king. Firminus, who
had obtained the countship in that city, wished to obstruct him but did not go himself. The friends sent on his behalf begged the king at least to let one
Sunday pass without Avitus being consecrated there. They promised the king one thousand gold pieces if this were made known, but the king did not consent.

The citizens of Clermont assembled together, and blessed Avitus, who was then archdeacon, was elected by clergy and people and received the episcopal see. The
king honored and loved him so greatly that, departing somewhat from canonical strictness, he ordered Avitus to be consecrated in his own presence, saying: “May
I be found worthy to receive blessed bread from his hand.” This favor caused him to be consecrated in the city of Metz.

After receiving the episcopate, Avitus showed himself great in every respect. He rendered justice to the people, aid to the poor, comfort to widows, and the
greatest assistance to orphans. A stranger who came to him was treated with such love that he felt he had found both a father and a homeland in him. Avitus
flourished in great virtues and kept with his whole heart everything pleasing to God, rooting out wrongful luxury everywhere and planting the chastity just
before God.

### 36. Of Saint Nicetius of Lyon

**[036]** When Sacerdos, bishop of Lyon, died at Paris after the synod that expelled Saffaracus, Saint Nicetius was elected by him and received the episcopate,
as we wrote in the book of his Life. He was outstanding in complete holiness and chaste conduct. The apostle commanded us to preserve charity with everyone if
possible; Nicetius practiced it toward all as far as possible, so that the Lord himself, who is true charity, could be discerned in his heart. If he was angered
by someone’s negligence, he received the person back as soon as he was corrected, as though he had never been offended. He corrected offenders and forgave
penitents. He gave alms and worked diligently. He took the greatest care in building churches, putting houses in order, sowing fields, and planting vineyards,
but these activities did not distract him from prayer.

After serving in the priesthood for twenty-two years, he departed to the Lord. He now performs great miracles at his tomb for those who pray. Through the oil of
the lamp burned daily at his tomb, he restores sight to blind eyes, drives demons from possessed bodies, restores health to contracted limbs, and is a great
protection to all the sick at this time.

Bishop Priscus, who succeeded him, and his wife Susanna began to persecute and kill many who had been close to the man of God. They had not been overcome by any
fault, convicted of any crime, or caught in any theft. Envy alone inflamed Priscus because they had been faithful to Nicetius. He and his wife uttered many
blasphemies against the saint of God. Earlier bishops had long observed the rule that a woman should not enter the house belonging to the church, but Susanna
and her maids even entered the chamber in which the blessed man had rested.

Divine majesty was at last aroused by these acts and took vengeance on Bishop Priscus’s household. His wife was seized by a demon. With her hair loose, she was
driven madly through the whole city. She proclaimed the saint of God, whose friendship with Christ she had denied while sane, and begged him to spare her. The
bishop was seized by a quartan fever and developed a tremor. Even when the fever subsided, he remained trembling and dull. His son and whole household appeared
pale and stupefied. No one can doubt that they were struck by the holy man’s power. Bishop Priscus and his household constantly barked impious words against the
saint of God and declared anyone their friend who poured out insults against him.

At the beginning of his episcopate Priscus had ordered the church house to be raised. A deacon whom Saint Nicetius, while alive, had repeatedly punished for
adultery—not only excluding him from communion but often ordering him to be beaten, without ever being able to bring him to amendment—climbed onto the roof of
that house. When he began to uncover it, he said: “I thank you, Jesus Christ, because after the death of that most wicked Nicetius I have been found worthy to
walk upon this roof.” The words were still on his lips when the surface on which he stood was pulled from beneath his feet. He fell to the ground, burst, and
died.

While the bishop and his wife were committing many unreasonable acts, the saint appeared in a dream to a certain man and said: “Go and tell Priscus to amend his
evil works and make his works good. Also tell the priest Martin: ‘Because you consent to these works, you will be chastised; if you refuse to amend your
perversity, you will die.’” On waking, the man spoke to a deacon: “Since you are a friend in the bishop’s house, please go and say these things to the bishop
and to the priest Martin.” The deacon promised to speak, but then drew back and refused. That night, when he had gone to sleep, the saint appeared to him and
said: “Why did you not repeat what the abbot told you?” He closed his fists and began beating the deacon’s throat. In the morning the deacon’s throat was
swollen and very painful. He went to the men and reported everything he had heard. They paid little attention and said it was merely a dream vision. The priest
Martin immediately fell into a fever and was ill, but recovered. Yet he continued to speak flatteringly to the bishop and consent to his evil acts and the
blasphemies they poured out against the saint. He was again seized by fever and breathed out his spirit.

### 37. Of Saint Friard the recluse

**[037]** Saint Friard also died at the same time as Saint Nicetius. He was full of days, outstanding in holiness, sublime in action, and noble in life. We
recorded some of his miracles in the book we wrote about his Life. At his passing, as Bishop Felix arrived, the whole cell shook. I do not doubt that an angelic
presence was there and made the place tremble as he departed. The bishop washed him, wrapped him in fitting garments, and committed him to burial.

### 38. Of the kings of the Spaniards

**[038]** To return to our history: when King Athanagild died in Spain, Liuva received the kingdom together with his brother Liuvigild. After Liuva died, his
brother Liuvigild took possession of the whole kingdom. Following his own wife’s death, he married Goiswintha, Queen Brunhilda’s mother. He had two sons by his
first wife; one was betrothed to Sigibert’s daughter and the other to Chilperic’s daughter. He divided the kingdom equally between them. He also killed all who
had been accustomed to murder their kings, leaving not a single one of them alive to piss against a wall.

### 39. Of the death of Palladius of the Auvergne

**[039]** Palladius, son of the former count Britianus and Caesaria, obtained the countship in the city of Javols through King Sigibert’s grant. A dispute arose
between him and Bishop Parthenius that greatly injured the people. Palladius frequently overwhelmed the bishop with insults, various reproaches, and
accusations, seizing church property and despoiling his men. As the dispute grew, they hastened into the prince’s presence and exchanged many accusations.
Palladius called the bishop soft and effeminate, saying: “Where are your husbands, with whom you live disgracefully and shamefully?” Divine vengeance soon
followed and blotted out these words spoken against the bishop.

The following year Palladius was removed from the countship and returned to the Auvergne, while Romanus sought the office. One day in the city of Clermont the
two met. While they were quarreling over the countship, Palladius heard that King Sigibert intended to have him killed. The report was found to be false and to
have originated chiefly with Romanus. Terrified, Palladius was reduced to such severe distress that he threatened to kill himself with his own hand. His mother
and his kinsman Firminus watched him closely to prevent him from carrying out his bitter intention. But after some hours he escaped his mother’s sight and
entered his chamber. Taking advantage of being alone, he drew his sword, pressed its hilt beneath his feet, and raised the point toward his breast. He threw
himself upon it: entering at one nipple, the sword came out through his back near the shoulder blade. He rose again, pierced himself similarly through the other
breast, fell, and died.

I marvel that this crime was not accomplished without the devil’s work. The first wound could have killed him if the devil had not supported him in carrying out
this impious act. His mother ran up half-dead and fell in bereavement upon her son’s body, while the whole household uttered cries of lamentation. He was
carried to the monastery of Chronon and buried, but not beside Christian corpses, nor did he receive the solemnity of Masses. It is believed that this befell
him for no other reason than the injury he had done to the bishop.

### 40. Of the empire of Justin

**[040]** After Emperor Justinian died at Constantinople, Justin obtained the empire. He was devoted to every kind of avarice, despised the poor, and despoiled
the senators. His greed was so great that he ordered iron chests to be made in which he could heap up talents of gold coin. They also say that he fell into the
Pelagian heresy. Not long afterward he lost his reason and appointed Tiberius Caesar to defend his provinces. Tiberius was a just man, an almsgiver, equitable
in judgment, victorious in war, and—what surpasses all other virtues—a most Christian man.

King Sigibert sent envoys to Emperor Justin to seek peace, namely Warnachar the Frank and Firminus the Auvergnat. Traveling by ship, they entered
Constantinople, spoke with the emperor, and obtained what they sought. They returned to Gaul in the following year.

After this the Persians captured Antioch in Egypt and Apamea in Syria, very great cities, and carried the people away captive. The basilica of Saint Julian,
martyr of Antioch, was then destroyed by a severe fire. The Armenians under Persian rule came to Emperor Justin with a great weight of woven silk. They sought
his friendship and explained that they were hostile to the Persian emperor. The Persian emperor’s envoys had come to them, saying: “The emperor’s concern
requires us to ask whether you are keeping intact the treaty made with him.” When the Armenians replied that they were keeping all their promises inviolate, the
envoys said: “It will be clear that you preserve his friendship if you worship fire as he does.” The people answered that they would never do so. The bishop who
was present said: “What divinity is there in fire, that it should be worshipped? God created it for human use. It is kindled by fuel, extinguished by water,
burns when applied, and grows cool when neglected.” As the bishop continued with these and similar words, the envoys were inflamed with fury and beat him with
fists and clubs. Seeing their bishop stained with blood, the people rushed upon the envoys, laid hands on them, and killed them. Then, as we have said, the
Armenians sought this emperor’s friendship.

### 41. How Alboin with the Lombards occupied Italy

**[041]** Alboin, king of the Lombards, who had married Chlothsinda, King Chlothar’s daughter, left his own region and went to Italy with the entire Lombard
people. Calling up their army, they departed with their wives and children, intending to settle there. They entered the region and ranged through it for about
seven years, plundering churches and killing priests, and brought it under their own power. After Alboin’s wife Chlothsinda died, he married another woman whose
father he had killed shortly before. She always hated her husband and waited for an opportunity to avenge her father’s wrong. Desiring one of the servants, she
poisoned her husband. After his death she went away with the servant, but they were captured together and killed. The Lombards then set another king over
themselves.

### 42. Of the wars of Mummolus against the Lombards

**[042]** Eunius, surnamed Mummolus, obtained the patriciate from King Guntram. I think I should go back further to explain the origin of his military career.
He was born to his father Peonius and was an inhabitant of the city of Auxerre. Peonius held the countship of that city. When he sent gifts to the king through
his son to renew his tenure, the son received his father’s property, sought his father’s countship, and supplanted the father whom he ought to have supported.
Advancing gradually from this beginning, he rose to a higher office.

When the Lombards broke into Gaul, Patrician Amatus, who had recently succeeded Celsus, went against them. Battle was joined; he fled and fell there. The
Lombards are said to have slaughtered so many Burgundians that the number of the slain could not be gathered. Laden with booty, they returned to Italy. After
their departure Eunius, also called Mummolus, was summoned by the king and received the dignity of the patriciate.

The Lombards again broke into Gaul and advanced as far as Mustiae Calmes, near the city of Embrun. Mummolus called out his army and went there with the
Burgundians. He surrounded the Lombards with his army, laid ambushes, and rushed upon them through trackless parts of the forest. He killed many, captured some,
and sent them to the king. The king ordered the captives to be dispersed and guarded in various places. Only a few escaped by flight to carry the news home. The
brothers Salonius and Sagittarius, both bishops, took part in this battle. Not guided by the heavenly cross but armed with helmet and secular breastplate, they
are said—what is worse—to have killed many men with their own hands. This was Mummolus’s first victory in battle.

Afterward the Saxons who had come with the Lombards into Italy again broke into Gaul. They pitched camp within the territory of Riez, at the estate of Stablo.
They ranged through the estates of the neighboring cities, seizing plunder, carrying off captives, and laying everything waste. When Mummolus learned of this,
he called out his army and rushed upon them. He killed many thousands and did not cease slaughtering until evening, when night put an end to it. He had caught
the men off their guard, suspecting nothing of his approach. At daybreak the Saxons drew up their army and prepared for battle, but messengers intervened and
they made peace. They gave gifts to Mummolus, left all the region’s plunder and the captives, and departed. First they swore to return to Gaul in submission to
the kings and in support of the Franks.

On returning to Italy, the Saxons took their wives, little children, and all the furnishings of their property, intending to go back to Gaul. They meant to be
gathered by King Sigibert and settled in the place from which they had originally departed. They formed two divisions, as is said. One came through the city of
Nice and the other through Embrun, following the same route as in the previous year. They joined forces in the territory of Avignon. It was harvest time, and
that place had abundant crops standing in the open; the inhabitants had stored none of them at home. The Saxons divided the crops among themselves, gathered and
threshed the grain, and ate it, leaving nothing for those who had done the work.

After consuming the produce, they reached the bank of the river Rhône, intending to cross the torrent and place themselves under King Sigibert’s rule. Mummolus
met them and said: “You shall not cross this torrent. You have devastated the region of my lord the king, gathered the crops, destroyed the cattle, burned the
houses, and cut down the olive groves and vineyards. You shall not proceed unless you first compensate those whom you have left destitute. Otherwise you will
not escape my hands: I will set the sword upon you, your wives, and your little children, and avenge the injury done to my lord King Guntram.” Greatly afraid,
they gave many thousands of gold coins as their ransom and were permitted to cross. Thus they reached the Auvergne.

It was then springtime. They produced stamped bars of bronze and passed them off as gold. Everyone who saw them believed them to be tested and proven gold, so
cleverly had they been colored by some device. Deceived by this trick, many people handed over gold, received bronze, and became poor. The Saxons then crossed
over to King Sigibert and were settled in the place from which they had originally departed.

### 43. Of the archdeacon of Marseille

**[043]** In King Sigibert’s kingdom Jovinus, governor of Provence, was removed from office, and Albinus was appointed in his place. This caused great enmity
between them. When overseas ships arrived at the harbor of Marseille, seventy men belonging to Archdeacon Vigilius stole casks, commonly called orcae,
containing oil and garum, without their master’s knowledge. When the merchant discovered that his property had been stolen, he began a careful inquiry into
where the stolen goods had been hidden. Someone told him that Archdeacon Vigilius’s men had committed the theft. The report reached the archdeacon. He
investigated and discovered the truth, but instead of making it public he began to excuse his men, saying: “No one has ever left my house who would dare commit
such a deed.”

Since the archdeacon defended them in this way, the merchant went to Albinus, laid out his case, and accused the archdeacon of complicity in the theft. On the
holy day of the Lord’s Nativity the bishop entered the church. The archdeacon, clothed in an alb, stood ready as custom required to invite the bishop to proceed
to the altar and celebrate the solemnity at the proper time. Without delay Albinus leaped from his seat, seized the archdeacon, dragged him away, beat him with
fists and kicks, and confined him in prison. Neither the bishop, nor the citizens, nor any elder, nor the cry of the whole people could persuade him to release
the archdeacon on sureties so that he might celebrate the holy day with the others and have the accusation heard later. Albinus did not even fear the sacred
solemnity enough to refrain from seizing a minister of the Lord’s altar on such a day. He condemned the archdeacon to a fine of four thousand solidi. Albinus
later came before King Sigibert and, with Jovinus pressing the case, was obliged to pay fourfold compensation.

### 44. Of the Lombards and Mummolus

**[044]** Afterward three Lombard leaders—Amo, Zaban, and Rodanus—invaded Gaul. Amo took the road through Embrun and advanced as far as the estate of Machao in
the territory of Avignon, which Mummolus had obtained by royal gift; there he pitched his tents. Zaban descended through the city of Die and came as far as
Valence, where he also established camp. Rodanus attacked the city of Grenoble and spread out his tents there. Amo overran the province of Arles and the
surrounding cities. Advancing as far as the Stony Plain near Marseille, he stripped it of cattle and people. He prepared to besiege Aix but withdrew after
receiving twenty-two pounds of silver from it. Rodanus and Zaban did likewise in the places they attacked.

When these events were reported to Mummolus, he called out his army and went to meet Rodanus, who was attacking Grenoble. The army was crossing the river Isère
with difficulty when, by God’s will, an animal entered the river, revealed a ford, and enabled the people to reach the farther bank. The Lombards saw this and
immediately attacked with drawn swords. In the ensuing battle they were cut down so severely that Rodanus, wounded by a lance, fled to the mountain heights.
Breaking through trackless forests with the five hundred men remaining to him, he reached Zaban, who was then besieging Valence, and reported everything that
had happened. After collecting all their plunder together, they returned toward Embrun. Mummolus met them there face to face with an immense army. Battle was
joined, and the Lombard ranks were cut down almost to annihilation. Their leaders returned to Italy with only a few men.

When they reached the city of Susa, the inhabitants received them harshly, especially because Sisinnius, master of the soldiers on the emperor’s side, was
residing there. A servant pretended to belong to Mummolus and produced letters for Sisinnius in Zaban’s sight. He delivered greetings in Mummolus’s name and
said: “Here he is close at hand!” Hearing this, Zaban immediately left and hurried past the city. When Amo heard this news, he collected all his plunder on the
march and set out. But the snows blocked his way; abandoning the plunder, he was barely able to escape with a few men. They were terrified of Mummolus’s power.

### 45. How Mummolus came to Tours

**[045]** Mummolus fought many wars and emerged victorious. After Charibert’s death Chilperic seized Tours and Poitiers, which had been assigned to King
Sigibert by agreement. Sigibert joined with his brother Guntram, and they chose Mummolus to recall these cities to their rightful ruler. Mummolus came to Tours
and drove out Chilperic’s son Chlodovech. After exacting oaths from the people on King Sigibert’s behalf, he advanced to Poitiers. Basilius and Sigarius,
citizens of Poitiers, assembled a multitude and tried to resist. Mummolus surrounded them from different directions, crushed, overwhelmed, and killed them. He
then entered Poitiers and exacted oaths. Let this account of Mummolus suffice for now; the rest will be related later.

### 46. Of the death of Andarcius

**[046]** Before describing Andarchius’s death, I wish first to set out his origin and homeland. They say that he was a slave of Senator Felix. Assigned to
attend his lord, he was educated alongside him and distinguished himself by his excellent training. He was thoroughly instructed in Virgil’s works, the books of
the Theodosian Code, and arithmetic. Puffed up by this knowledge, he began to despise his masters. When Duke Lupus went to Marseille by King Sigibert’s command,
Andarchius commended himself to Lupus’s protection. On returning, Lupus took Andarchius with him, carefully recommended him to King Sigibert, and placed him in
the king’s service. Sigibert sent him to various places and gave him the opportunity of military service. Regarded as a man of honor because of this, Andarchius
came to the Auvergne and formed a friendship with Ursus, a citizen of Clermont.

Being sharp-witted, he wished to betroth Ursus’s daughter. They say that he hid a breastplate in a document chest in which deeds were usually kept. He told
Ursus’s wife: “I entrust to you more than sixteen thousand of my gold pieces hidden in this chest. They can be yours if you promise your daughter to me in
betrothal.” But “accursed hunger for gold, to what do you not compel mortal hearts?” The woman believed him without suspicion and promised the girl to him in
her husband’s absence.

Andarchius returned to the king and presented an order to the local judge directing that the girl be joined to him in marriage, saying: “I have given earnest
money for her betrothal.” Ursus denied this, saying: “I do not know who you are or where you come from, and I have none of your property.” As the dispute grew
more violent, Andarchius sought to summon Ursus before the king. When Ursus came to the estate of Brinnacum, Andarchius found another man named Ursus. He
secretly brought this other man to an altar and made him swear: “By this holy place and the relics of the blessed martyrs, if I do not give you my daughter in
marriage, I will pay you sixteen thousand solidi without delay.” Witnesses stood in the sanctuary, secretly listening to the words spoken but entirely unable to
see the person who spoke.

Andarchius then soothed the real Ursus with gentle words and made him return home without appearing before the king. He had a written record of the oath
prepared and presented it to the king as he departed, saying: “Ursus made this written promise to me. I therefore request an order from your glory directing him
to give me his daughter in marriage. Otherwise, let me possess his property until I have received the sixteen thousand solidi and can withdraw from the case.”
Having obtained the order, he returned to the Auvergne and showed the king’s command to the judge.

Ursus withdrew to the territory of Villavo. While his property was being consigned to Andarchius, Andarchius came to Villavo. Entering one of Ursus’s houses, he
ordered supper to be prepared and water heated for his bath. When the servants did not appear sufficiently prompt to their rude master, he beat one with a club
and another with rods, striking several on the head until he drew blood. The terrified household prepared supper. He bathed in warm water, became drunk on wine,
and lay down on a couch. Only seven servants were with him. Buried in wine and sleep alike, they slept deeply.

The household assembled and shut the doors of the house, which was built of wooden planks. Taking the keys, they broke down the stacks of grain standing nearby
and heaped the grain around and over the house. The grain was then in sheaves, and the house appeared entirely covered with it. They set fire to it in different
places. When the burning material of the building was already falling on the unhappy men inside, they awoke and cried out, but no one came to help them. The
whole house was burned down, and the fire consumed them with it. Ursus, fearing the consequences, sought refuge in the basilica of Saint Julian. He gave gifts
to the king and recovered his property intact.

### 47. How Theudebert seized the cities

**[047]** Chilperic’s son Chlodovech was expelled from Tours and went to Bordeaux. While he was residing peacefully in Bordeaux, a certain Sigulf on Sigibert’s
side attacked him. Sigulf pursued him with trumpets and horns as though hunting a fleeing stag. Chlodovech was scarcely able to return safely to his father, but
he eventually reached him by way of Angers.

A dispute arose between Kings Guntram and Sigibert. King Guntram assembled all the bishops of his kingdom at Paris so that they might determine where the truth
lay between the two kings. But, because of sin, the kings delayed hearing them, allowing the civil war to grow more destructive. Chilperic was enraged. Through
his elder son Theudebert—who had once been captured by Sigibert and had sworn to be faithful to him—he seized Sigibert’s cities: Tours, Poitiers, and the others
situated on this side of the Loire. Theudebert came to Poitiers and fought Duke Gundovald. Gundovald’s army fled, and Theudebert inflicted great slaughter on
its men. He also burned the greater part of the region of Tours and would immediately have subdued all of it if the inhabitants had not submitted for the time
being.

Calling out his army, he overran, wasted, and overthrew the Limousin, Cahors, and the neighboring regions. He burned churches, carried off their furnishings,
killed clergy, destroyed men’s monasteries, desecrated women’s convents, and devastated everything. At that time there was greater lamentation in the churches
than during Diocletian’s persecution.

### 48. Of the monastery of Latte

**[048]** We still stand astonished and wonder why such great blows fell upon them. But let us compare what their parents did with what these men are doing.
Their ancestors were converted from pagan shrines to churches by the preaching of bishops; these men daily drag plunder out of churches. Their ancestors
venerated and obeyed the Lord’s bishops with their whole heart; these men not only refuse to obey them but persecute them. Their ancestors enriched monasteries
and churches; these men destroy and overthrow them.

What shall I say about the monastery of Latte, where relics of blessed Martin are kept? A troop of enemies approached it and prepared to cross the nearby river
to plunder the monastery. The monks cried out: “Do not cross here, barbarians! Do not! This is blessed Martin’s monastery.” Many heard them and, pierced by the
fear of God, turned back. But twenty of them, who neither feared God nor honored the blessed confessor, boarded a boat and crossed. At the enemy’s prompting
they beat the monks, destroyed the monastery, and plundered its property. They made the goods into bundles and loaded them onto the boat.

As soon as they entered the river, the boat began to toss and carried them this way and that. Having lost the use of their oars, they fixed their spear shafts
into the riverbed and tried to push themselves back. The boat split open beneath their feet. Each man’s weapon, which he was holding in front of himself, was
driven into his breast, and all were pierced and killed by their own javelins. Only one remained unharmed—the man who had rebuked them to prevent them from
committing these deeds. If anyone judges that this happened by chance, let him observe that one innocent man escaped while many guilty men perished. After they
were killed, the monks drew the bodies and their property out of the river. They buried the men and restored the goods to the monastery.

### 49. How Sigibert came to Paris

**[049]** While these things were happening, King Sigibert called out the peoples living beyond the Rhine and resolved to begin civil war against his brother
Chilperic. Hearing this, Chilperic sent envoys to his brother Guntram. They joined together and made a treaty that neither would allow his brother to be
destroyed. Sigibert arrived with those peoples, while Chilperic remained on the opposite side with his army. Sigibert wished to advance against his brother but
had no place to cross the river Seine. He sent a command to his brother Guntram: “Unless you allow me to cross this river through your share, I will march
against you with my whole army.” Fearing this, Guntram made a treaty with him and allowed him to cross.

When Chilperic perceived that Guntram had abandoned him and gone over to Sigibert, he moved camp and went as far as the village of Ablis near Chartres. Sigibert
pursued him and demanded that he prepare a battlefield. Chilperic feared that, if both armies clashed, their kingdom would also collapse. He sued for peace and
restored the cities that Theudebert had wrongfully seized. He begged that their inhabitants not be punished, since his son had acquired them unjustly by
oppression with fire and sword.

The villages around Paris were largely consumed by fire. Houses and other property were plundered by the enemy, and captives were carried away. The king adjured
them not to do these things, but he could not restrain the fury of the peoples who had come from beyond the Rhine. He endured everything patiently until they
could return to their homeland. Some of those peoples then murmured against him for withdrawing from battle. Being fearless, he mounted his horse, rode to them,
and soothed them with gentle words; afterward he ordered many of them to be stoned.

No one doubts that blessed Martin’s power enabled these men to make peace without battle. On the very day they made peace, three paralytics were brought to the
blessed man’s basilica. With the Lord’s help we shall describe this in later books.

### 50. How Chilperic made a pact with Guntram, and of the death of Theudebert his son

**[050]** It grieves the mind to relate these civil wars. A year later Chilperic again sent envoys to his brother Guntram, saying: “Let my brother come so that
we may meet, make peace, and pursue our enemy Sigibert together.” This was done: they met and honored each other with gifts. Chilperic called out his army and
advanced as far as Reims, burning and overrunning everything. Hearing this, Sigibert again summoned the peoples mentioned above and came to Paris, preparing to
march against his brother. He sent word to the men of Douai and Tours to attack Theudebert. When they evaded the order, the king sent Dukes Godegisel and
Guntram to lead them. They called out their army and advanced against Theudebert. Abandoned by his own men, Theudebert remained with only a few, but he did not
hesitate to go into battle. When battle was joined, Theudebert was defeated and laid low on the field. His enemies stripped his lifeless body, which is grievous
to relate. A certain Aunulf gathered him up, washed him, clothed him in fitting garments, and buried him in the city of Soissons. When Chilperic learned that
Guntram had again made peace with Sigibert, he fortified himself with his wife and sons within the walls of Tournai.

### 51. Of the death of King Sigibert

**[051]** That year a flash of light was seen running through the sky, as we once saw before Chlothar’s death. After obtaining the cities situated around Paris,
Sigibert advanced as far as the city of Rouen, intending to cede those cities to his enemies. His own men prevented him from doing so. He returned from there
and entered Paris, where Brunhilda came to him with her sons.

The Franks who had formerly looked to the elder Childebert sent an embassy to Sigibert, asking him to come to them, abandon Chilperic, and establish himself as
king over them. On hearing this, Sigibert sent men to besiege his brother in the city mentioned above and prepared to hasten there himself. Bishop Saint
Germanus said to him: “If you go but do not kill your brother, you will return alive and victorious. If you think otherwise, you will die. For thus the Lord
said through Solomon: ‘You will fall into the pit that you prepare for your brother.’” Because of sin, Sigibert neglected this warning.

When he came to the estate called Vitry, the whole army gathered around him. Raising him on a shield, they established him as king over them. Then two servants,
corrupted by Queen Fredegund and carrying strong knives commonly called scramasaxes smeared with poison, pretended to present another petition and struck him in
both sides. He cried out and collapsed, and not long afterward breathed out his spirit. His chamberlain Charegisel fell there too. Sigila, who had formerly come
from Gothia, was severely wounded there. King Chilperic later captured him, burned all his joints with glowing cauteries, and tore him apart limb by limb, so
that he died cruelly.

Charegisel was as frivolous in conduct as he was burdensome in greed. Rising from the lowest rank, he became great with the king through flattery. He was a
coveter of other people’s property and a breaker of wills. His end was such that, when death was imminent, he could not carry out his own will, though he had
often destroyed the wills of others.

Chilperic remained fixed in uncertainty, doubting whether he would escape or perish, until messengers came to announce his brother’s death. He then left Tournai
with his wife and sons and buried Sigibert, clothed, at the village of Lambrus. Sigibert was later translated from there to Soissons, to the basilica of Saint
Medard that he himself had built, and buried beside his father Chlothar. He died in the fourteenth year of his reign, at the age of forty. From the death of the
elder Theudebert to the death of Sigibert, twenty-nine years are reckoned. Between Sigibert’s death and that of his nephew Theudebert there were eighteen days.
After Sigibert’s death his son Childebert reigned in his place.

From the beginning to the Flood: 2,242 years. From the Flood to Abraham: 942 years. From Abraham to the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt: 462 years.
From the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt to the building of Solomon’s Temple: 480 years. From the building of the Temple to its destruction and the
exile to Babylon: 390 years. From the exile to the Lord’s Passion: 668 years. From the Lord’s Passion to the death of Saint Martin: 412 years. From the death of
Saint Martin to the death of King Clovis: 112 years. From the death of King Clovis to the death of Theudebert: 37 years. From the death of Theudebert to the
death of Sigibert: 29 years. Altogether these amount to 5,774 years.

## 1. De obito Chrodigildis regina.

**[001]** Igitur Chrodigildis regina, plena dierum bonisque operibus praedita, apud urbem Toronicam obiit tempore Iniuriosi episcopi. Quae Parisius cum magno
psallentio deportata, in sacrario basilicae sancti Petri ad latus Chlodovechi regis sepulta est a filiis suis, Childebertho atque Chlothachario regibus. Nam
basilicam illam ipsa construxerat; in qua et Genuveifa beatissima est sepulta.

## 2. Quod Chlothacharius fructuum eclesiis auferre voluit.

**[002]** Denique Chlothacharius rex indixerat, ut omnes eclesiae regni sui tertiam partem fructuum fisco dissolverent. Quod, licet inviti, cum omnes episcopi
consensissent atque subscripsissent, viriliter hoc beatus Iniuriosus respuens, subscribere dedignatus est, dicens: 'Si volueris res Dei tollere, Dominus regnum
tuum velociter aufret, quia iniquum est, ut pauperes, quos tuo debes alere horreo, ab eorum stipe tua horrea repleantur'. Et iratus contra regem nec valedicens
abscessit. Tunc commotus rex, timens etiam virtutem beati Martini, misit post eum cum muneribus, veniam praecans et hoc quod fecerat damnans, simulque et
rogans, ut pro se virtutem beati Martini antestites exoraret.

## 3. De uxoribus ac filiis eius.

**[003]** Denique ipse rex de diversis mulieribus septim filius habuit, id est de Ingunde Guntharium, Childericum, Chariberthum, Gunthchramnum, Sigyberthum et
Chlothsindam filiam; de Aregundem vero, sororem Ingundis, Chilpericum; de Chunsinam habuit Chramnum. Quae autem causa fuerit, ut uxoris suae sororem acciperet,
dicam. Cum iam Ingundem in coniugio accipisset et eam unico amore diligeret, suggestionem ab ea accepit, dicentes: 'Fecit dominus meus de ancilla sua quod
libuit et suo me stratui adscivit. Nunc ad conplendam mercide, quid famula tua suggerat, audiat dominus meus rex. Praecor, ut sorore meae, servae vestrae,
utilem atque habentem virum ordinare dignimini, unde non humilier, sed potius exaltata servire fidelius possem'. Quod ille audiens, cum esset nimium luxoriosus,
in amore Aregundis incedit et ad villam, in qua ipsa resedebat, dirigit eamque sibi in matrimonio sociavit. Quae accepta, ad Ingundem rediens, ait: 'Tractavi
mercidem illam inplere, quam me tua dulcitudo expetiit. Et requirens virum divitem atque sapientem, quem tuae sorori deberem adiungere, nihil melius quam me
ipsum inveni. Itaque noveris, quia eam coniugem aceepi, quod tibi displicere non credo'. At illa: 'Quod bonum', inquid, Videtur in oculis domini mei, faciat;
tantum ancilla tua cum gratia regis vivat'. Guntharius vero, Chramnus atque Childericus vivente patre mortui sunt. Exitum vero Chramni in posterum scripsimus.
Alboenus quoque rex Langobardorum Chlothsindam, filiam regis, accepit. Obiit autem Iniuriosus episcopus urbis Turonicae decimo et septimo episcopatus sui anno;
cui Baudinus ex domestico Chlothachari regis successit, decimus sextus post obitum beati Martini.

## 4. De Brinctanorum comitibus.

**[004]** Chanao quoque Brittanorum comes tres fratres suos interfecit. Volens autem adhuc Macliavum interfecere, conpraehensum atque catenis oneratum in
carcere retinebat. Qui per Filicem Namneticum episcopum a morte liberatus est. Post haec iuravit fratri suo, ut ei fidelis esset; sed nescio quo casu
sacramentum inrumpere voluit. Quod Chanao sentiens, iterum eum persequebatur. At ille, cum se evadere non posse videret, post alium comitem regiones illius
fugit, nomen Chonomorem. His cum sentiret persecutores eius adpropinquare, sub terra eum in loculo abscondit, conponens desuper ex more tumulum parvumque ei
spiraculum reservans, unde alitum resumere possit. Advenientibus autem persecutoribus eius, dixerunt: 'Ecce! hic Macliavus mortuos atque sepultus iacet'. Quod
illi audientes atque gaudentes et super tumulum illum bibentes, renuntiaverunt fratri, eum mortuum esse. Quod ille audiens, regnum eius integrum accepit. Nam
semper Brittani sub Francorum potestatem post obitum regis Chlodovechi fuerunt, et comites, non regis appellati sunt. Macliavus autem de sub terra consurgens,
Veneticam urbem expetiit ibique tonsoratus et episcopus ordinatus est. Mortuo autem Chanaone, hic apostatavit, et dimissis capillis, uxorem, quam post
clericatum reliquerat, cum regno fratris simul accepit, sed ab episcopis excommunicatus est. Cui qualis fuerit interitus, sequenter scribemus. Obiit autem
Baudinus episcopus anno sexto episcopatus sui. In cuius loco Guntharius abba subrogatur, XVII. post transitum sancti Martini.

## 5. De sancto Gallo episcopo.

**[005]** Denique cum beatus Quintianus, sicut supra diximus, ab hoc mundo migratus est, sanctus Gallus in eius cathedram, rege opitulante, substitutus est.
Huius tempore cum lues illa quam inguinariam vocant per diversas regiones desaeviret et maxime tunc Arelatensim provinciam depopularet, sanctus Gallus non
tantum pro se quantum pro populo suo trepidus erat. Cumque die noctuque Dominum deprecaretur, ut vivens plebem suam vastari non cernerit, per visum noctis
apparuit ei angelus Domini, qui tam caesariem quam vestem in similitudinem nivis candidam efferebat, et ait ad eum: 'Bene enim facis, o sacerdos, quod sic
Dominum pro populo tuo supplicas. Exaudita est enim oratia tua, et ecce! eris cum populo tuo ab hac infirmitate liberatus, nullusque te vivente in regione ista
ab hac strage deperiet. Nunc autem ne timeas; post octo vero annos time'. Unde manifestum fuit, transactis his annis eum a saeculo discessisse. Expergefactus
autem et Deo gratias pro hac consolatione agens, quod eum per caelestem nuntium confortare dignatus est, rogationes illas instituit, ut media quadragesima
psallendo ad basilicam beati Iuliani martyris itinere pedestri venirent. Sunt autem in hoc itinere quasi stadia 360. Tunc etiam in subita contemplatione
parietes vel domorum vel ecclesiarum signari videbantur, unde a rusticis hic scriptos Thau vocabatur. Cum autem regiones illas, ut diximus, lues illa
consumeret, ad civitatem Arvernam, sancti Galli intercedente oratione, non attigit. Unde ego non parvam censeo gratiam, qui hoc meruit, ut pastor positus oves
suas devorari defendente Domino non videret. Cum autem ab hoc mundo migrasset et ablutus in ecclesia deportatus fuisset, Cato presbiter continuo a clericis de
episcopatu laudes accepit; et omnem rem ecclesiae, tamquam si iam esset episcopus, in sua redegit potestate, ordinatores removet, ministros respuit, cuncta per
se ordinat.

## 6. De Catone presbytero.

**[006]** Episcopi tamen qui advenerant ad sanctum Gallum sepeliendum, postquam eum sepelierant, dixerunt Catoni presbitero: 'Videmus, quia te valde diligit
pars maxima populorum; veni, consenti nobis, et benedicentes consecremus te ad episcopatum. Rex vero parvulus est, et si qua tibi adscribitur culpa, nos
suscipientes te sub defensione nostra, cum proceribus et primis regni Theodovaldi regis agemus, ne tibi ulla excitetur iniuria. Nobis quoque in tantum fideliter
