et tam domus quam res reliquae ab hoste direpti sunt, ut etiam et captivi ducerentur. Obtestabat enim rex, ne haec fierent; sed furorem gentium, quae de
ulteriore Rheni amnis parte venerant, superare non poterat; sed omnia patienter ferebat, donec redire possit ad patriam. Tunc ex gentibus illis contra eum
quidam murmoraverunt, cur se a certamine subtraxisset. Sed ille, ut erat intrepedus, ascenso equo, ad eos dirigit eosque verbis lenibus demulsit, multos ex eis
postea a lapidibus obrui praecipiens. Sed nec hoc sine beati Martini fuisse vertutemambigitur, ut hi sine bello pacificarentur; nam in ipsa die, qua hi pacem
fecerunt, tres paralitici ad beati basilicam sunt directi. Quod in sequentibus libris, Domino iubente, desseruemus.

## 50. Quod Chilpericus cum Guntchramno foedus iniit.

**[050]** Dolorem enim ingerit animo ista civilia bella referre. Nam post annum iterum Chilpericus ad Guntchramnum fratrem suum legatus mittit, dicens: 'Veniat
frater meus, et videamus nos et pacificati persequamur Sigyberthum inimicum nostrum'. Quod cum fuisset factum seque vidissent ac muneribus honorassent, commoto
Chilpericus exercitu usque Remus accessit, cuncta incendens atque debellans. Quod audiens Sigyberthus, iterum convocatis gentibus illis, quarum supra memoriam
fecimus, Parisius venit et contra fratrem suum Ire disponit, mittens nuntius Dunensibus vel Toronicis, ut contra Theodoberthum ire deberent. Quod ille
dissimolantes, rex Godegiselum et Gunthchramnum duces in capite dirigit. Qui commoventes exercitum, adversus eum pergunt. Ad ille derelictus a suis, cum paucis
remansit, sed tamen ad bellum exire non dubitat. Ineuntes autem proelium, Theodoberthus evictus in campo prosternitur, et ab hostibus exanime corpus, quod dici
dolor est, spoliatur. Tunc ab Aunulfo quodam collectus ablutusque ac dignis vestibus est indutus et ad Ecolisinensim civitatem sepultus. Chilpericus vero
cognuscens, quod iterum se Gunthchramnus cum Sigybertho pacificasset, se infra Thornacinsis murus cum uxore et filiis communivit. B 1.

## 51. De obitu Sigiberthi regis.

**[051]** In eo anno fulgor per caelum discurrisse visus est, sicut quondam ante mortem Chlothari factum vidimus. Sigyberthus vero, obtentis civitatibus illis,
quae circa Parisius sunt positae, usque Rhotomaginsem urbem accessit, volens easdem urbes hostibus cedere. Quod ne faceret, a suis prohibitus est. Regressus
inde, Parisius est ingressus, ibique ad eum Brunichildis cum filiis venit. Tunc Franci, qui quondam ad Childeberthum aspexerant seniorem, ad Sigyberthum
legationem mittunt, ut ad eos veniens, derelicto Chilperico, super se ipsum regem stabilirent. Illi vero haec audiens, misitquequi fratrem suum in supra
memoratam civitatem obsederent, ipsi illuc properare deliberans. Cui sanctus Germanus episcopus dixit: 'Si abieris et fratrem tuum interficere nolueris, vivus
et victur redis; sin autem aliut1 cogitaveris, morieris. Sic enim Dominus per Salomonem dixit: Foveam quae fratri tuo parabis, in ea conrues. Quod ille,
peccatis facientibus, audire neglexit. Veniente autem illo ad villam cui nomen est Victuriaco, collectus est ad eum omnis exercitus, inpositumque super clypeum
sibi regem statuunt. Tunc duo pueri cum cultris validis, quos vulgo scramasaxos vocant, infectis vinino, malificati a Fredegundae regina, cum aliam causam
suggerire simularent, utraque ei latera feriunt. At ille vociferans atque conruens, nbn post multo spatio emisit spiritum. Ibique et Charegyselus cubicularius
eius conruit; ibi et Sigila, qui quondam ex Ghotia venerat, multum laceratus est, et postea ab Chilperico rege conpraehensus, incensis cum cauteriis candentibus
omnibus iuncturis ac membratim separatus, crudiliter vitam finivit. Fuit autem Charegyselus ille tam levis opere quam gravis cupiditate. De minimis consurgens,
magnus per adulationes cum rege effectus est; conpetitur rerum alienarum testamentorumque effractur; cui talis fuit vitae exitus, ut non meriritur voluntatem
propriam mortem inminente conplere, qui aliorum voluntates saepe distruxerat. Chilpericus autem in ancipite casu defixus, in dubium habebat, an evaderet an
periret, donec ad eum missi veniunt de fratris obitu nuntiantes. Tunc egressus a Thornaco cum uxore et filiis, eum vestitum apud Lambrus vicum sepelivit. Unde
postea Sessionas in basilica sancti Medardi, quam ipse aedificaverat, translatus, secus Chlotharium patrem suum sepultus est. Obiit autem quarto decimo regni
sui anno, aetate quadraginaria. A transito ergo Theodoberthi seniores usque ad exitum Sigyberthi supputantur anni 29. Inter exitum veroeius et nepotis sui
Theodoberthi fuere dies 18. Mortuo autem Sigybertho, regnavit Childeberthus, filius eius, pro eo. A. principio usque ad diluvium anni 2242. A diluvium autem
usque ad Abraham anni 942. Ab Abraham vero usque ad egressum filiorum Israhel ex Aegipto anni 462. Ab egressu filiorum Israhel ex Aegipto usque ad
aedificationem templi Salomonis anni 480. Ab aedificationem ergo templi usque ad dissolationem eius et transmigratione in Babilonia anni 390. A transmigratione
igitur usque ad passionem Domini anni 668. A passione Domini usque ad transitum sancti Martini anni 412. A transitum sancti Martini usque ad transitum
Chlodovechi regis anni 112. A transitum Chlodovechi regis usque ad transitum Theodoberthi anni 37. A transitum Theodoberthi usque ad exitum Sigyberthi anni 29.
Quod sunt simul anni 5774 tantum. EXPLICIT LIBER QUARTUS.

# BOOK FIVE

## LIBER QUINTUS

### Preface

**[001]** I am weary of recording the diversity of civil wars which violently crush the Frankish people and kingdom. Worse still, I now see in it the beginning
of that time of sorrows which the Lord foretold: “Father shall rise against son, son against father, brother against brother, neighbor against neighbor.” The
examples of earlier kings ought to have terrified them, for as soon as they were divided they were killed by enemies. How often has that city of cities and head
of the whole world, Rome, been destroyed by immense civil wars, and when they ceased, risen again as though from the ground! May you too, O kings, be engaged in
battles such as those in which your parents labored, so that the nations, terrified by your peace, may admire your strength! Remember what Clovis, the head of
your victories, did: he killed opposing kings, crushed harmful nations, and subjugated countries whose kingdom he left to you entire and unharmed. Yet when he
did this, he had neither gold nor silver such as is now in your treasuries. What will you do? What do you seek? In what do you not abound? Riches overflow in
your houses; wine, grain, and oil abound in your storehouses; gold and silver are heaped in your treasuries. One thing is lacking to you: because you do not
have peace, you lack God’s grace. Why does one take another’s property? Why does another covet what is not his? Beware, I beg, that saying of the apostle: “If
you bite and devour one another, take care lest you be consumed by one another.” Examine diligently the writings of the ancients, and you will see what civil
wars bring forth. Read what Orosius writes of the Carthaginians: after saying that their city and region were overthrown after seven hundred years, he added:
“What preserved it so long? Concord. What destroyed it after so long a time? Discord.” Beware discord; beware the civil wars which assail you and your people.
What else is to be expected except that, when your army has fallen, you yourselves will be left without support and immediately fall, oppressed by hostile
peoples? If civil war delights you, O king, carry on the war which the apostle records as taking place within man: let the spirit contend against the flesh, and
let vices fall before virtues. Freed from your former bondage to the root of evils, serve your head—that is, Christ.

### 1. Of the kingdom of Childebert the younger and of his mother

**[002]** After King Sigibert was killed at the estate of Vitry, Queen Brunhilda remained in Paris with her sons. When the deed was reported to her, she was
overwhelmed by grief and mourning and did not know what to do. Duke Gundovald secretly seized her little son Childebert and carried him away, rescuing him from
imminent death. He gathered the peoples over whom Childebert’s father had ruled and made the boy king when he had barely completed his fifth year. He began to
reign on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. In the first year of his reign King Chilperic came to Paris. He seized Brunhilda and sent her into exile at the city of
Rouen, and he took the treasures she had brought to Paris. He ordered her daughters to be kept in the city of Meaux. Roccolen then came to Tours with the men of
Le Mans, plundered, and committed many crimes. I shall relate later how he was struck by blessed Martin’s power for these evils and perished.

### 2. How Merovech took Brunhilda

**[003]** Chilperic sent his son Merovech with an army to Poitiers. Merovech abandoned his father’s instructions, came to Tours, and kept the holy days of
Easter there. His army greatly devastated that region. Pretending that he wished to visit his mother, he went to Rouen. There he joined Queen Brunhilda and
married her. When Chilperic heard that his son had married his uncle’s wife contrary to divine law and the canons, he was greatly embittered and hastened to the
city mentioned above. Merovech and Brunhilda learned that he intended to separate them and took refuge in the basilica of Saint Martin, built of wooden planks
above the city walls. The king arrived and tried by many devices to draw them out. They believed he was acting deceitfully and did not trust him. He swore to
them: “If it were God’s will, he himself would not try to separate them.” They accepted this oath and left the basilica. He kissed them, received them
honorably, and feasted with them. A few days later the king took Merovech with him and returned to Soissons.

### 3. The war against Chilperic, and of the malice of Rauching

**[004]** While Chilperic and Merovech were staying there, men gathered from Champagne and attacked the city of Soissons. They put Queen Fredegund and
Chilperic’s son Chlodovech to flight and wished to bring the city under their own control. When King Chilperic learned of this, he marched there with an army.
He first sent messengers asking them not to injure him and thereby bring destruction upon both armies. They ignored him and prepared for battle. When battle was
joined, Chilperic’s side prevailed and routed its opponents, striking down many brave and capable men. He put the remainder to flight and entered Soissons.

After these events the king began to suspect his son Merovech because of his marriage to Brunhilda, saying that the battle had arisen through Merovech’s
wickedness. He stripped him of his weapons, assigned guards to him, and ordered him to be kept in free custody while he considered what to do with him.

Godinus, who had gone over from Sigibert’s side to Chilperic and had been enriched by him with many gifts, had instigated this war. Defeated in the field, he
was the first to flee. The king took back the estates in the territory of Soissons that he had granted Godinus from the treasury and gave them to the basilica
of blessed Medard. Godinus himself died suddenly not long afterward.

Rauching married Godinus’s widow. He was full of every kind of vanity, swollen with pride, and insolent in arrogance. He treated his subordinates as though he
possessed no humanity. Raging against his own people beyond all measure of human malice and folly, he committed unspeakable evils. If a servant held a candle
before him while he feasted, as was customary, Rauching had the servant’s shins bared and the candle pressed against them until its light went out. When it was
relit, he did the same until the servant’s entire shins were burned. If the servant cried out or tried to move, a naked sword immediately threatened him; while
the servant wept, Rauching exulted with great delight.

They say that at that time two of his servants, a young man and a girl, loved each other, as often happens. Their love had lasted two years or more when they
went together to a church. When Rauching learned of it, he went to the local priest and demanded that his servants be returned to him immediately. The priest
said: “You know what reverence is owed to God’s churches. You cannot take them unless you guarantee the permanence of their union and promise that they will
remain free from all bodily punishment.” Rauching remained silent in doubtful thought for a long time. At last he turned to the priest, placed his hands on the
altar, and swore: “I will never separate them. Rather, I will make them remain in this union. Although I am annoyed that this was done without my knowledge and
consent, I gladly accept that he has not taken another man’s servant woman and she has not taken another master’s slave.” The priest trusted the crafty man’s
promise without suspicion and returned the servants to him.

Rauching received them, thanked the priest, and went home. He immediately ordered a tree to be felled, its trunk split with wedges, and the wood hollowed out.
He had a pit dug three or four feet deep and ordered the hollowed trunk placed in it. He laid the girl inside as though dead, had the young man thrown on top of
her, replaced the cover, filled the pit with earth, and buried them alive. He said: “I have not broken my oath: they will never be separated.” When this was
reported to the priest, he ran there quickly. Rebuking Rauching, he barely obtained permission to have them uncovered. He drew the young man out alive but found
the girl suffocated.

Rauching was exceedingly wicked in such deeds and took pleasure only in mockery, deceit, and every perverse practice. His departure from life was therefore not
undeserved; I shall describe it later. Siggo the referendary, who had held King Sigibert’s ring and had been induced by King Chilperic to retain the office he
had held under Chilperic’s brother, abandoned Chilperic and went over to Sigibert’s son King Childebert. Ansovald took possession of the property Siggo had held
in the territory of Soissons. Many others who had gone from Sigibert’s kingdom to Chilperic also withdrew. Siggo’s wife died not long afterward, and he married
another.

### 4. How Roccolenus came to Tours

**[005]** In those days Roccolen, sent by Chilperic, came to Tours with great boasting. He pitched camp beyond the Loire and sent messengers to us demanding
that we drag Duke Guntram out of the holy basilica. Guntram was then accused of Theudebert’s death. If we refused, Roccolen said he would order the city and all
its suburbs to be burned. On hearing this, we sent envoys to tell him that what he demanded had never been done in ancient times and that even now the holy
basilica could not be allowed to be violated. If it were violated, neither he nor the king who had issued the command would prosper. He ought rather to fear the
bishop’s holiness, whose power had straightened a paralytic’s limbs only the day before.

Roccolen feared none of this. While residing in a church house beyond the Loire, he cut apart the door that had been nailed shut. The men of Le Mans who had
come with him filled bellows with the nails and carried them away. They overturned the grain stores and devastated everything. While Roccolen was doing this,
God struck him. He turned yellow with jaundice, but he renewed his harsh demands: “Unless you throw Duke Guntram out of the basilica today, I will destroy all
the vegetation around the city so thoroughly that the place will be fit only for the plough.”

The holy day of Epiphany arrived, and his torment grew worse and worse. Taking counsel with his men, he crossed the river and entered the city. When the
psalm-singers came out of the church and hastened to the holy basilica, he followed the cross on horseback, with banners going before him. But as soon as he
entered the holy basilica, the fury of his threats cooled. He returned to the church house and could take no food that day. Seriously ill, he went from there to
Poitiers. It was the holy season of Lent, during which he often ate young rabbits. He made arrangements to afflict or condemn the citizens of Poitiers on the
kalends of March, but on the previous day he gave up his soul. Thus his pride and swelling ceased.

### 5. Of the bishops of Langres

**[006]** At that time Felix, bishop of Nantes, wrote me a letter full of reproaches. He even wrote that my brother had been killed because, desiring the
episcopate, he had murdered a bishop. Felix wrote this because he coveted an estate belonging to the church. When I refused to give it to him, he vomited a
thousand furious insults against me, as I have said. I once answered him: “Remember the prophet’s words: ‘Woe to those who join house to house and couple field
to field! Shall they alone inhabit the earth?’ If only Marseille had you as its bishop! Its ships would never carry oil or other merchandise, but only paper, so
that you might have more opportunity to write and defame good people. But poverty of paper puts an end to verbosity.” His greed and boasting were immense. But I
will set these matters aside so as not to resemble him, and will explain how my brother departed from this life and how swiftly the Lord avenged his murderer.

When blessed Tetricus, bishop of the church of Langres, was growing old, he deposed the deacon Lampadius, to whom he was in debt. My brother wished to help the
poor whom Tetricus had wrongfully despoiled and consented to Lampadius’s humiliation, thereby incurring Lampadius’s hatred. Meanwhile blessed Tetricus suffered
a hemorrhage. No physicians’ remedies helped him. The clergy were distressed and felt deprived of their shepherd, so they sought Munderic. With the king’s
consent he was tonsured and ordained bishop on condition that, while blessed Tetricus lived, he should govern the fortress of Tonnerre as archpriest and reside
there, succeeding Tetricus when he died.

While living in that fortress Munderic incurred the king’s anger. He was accused of having supplied provisions and gifts to King Sigibert when he came against
his brother Guntram. He was therefore taken from the fortress and confined in exile on the bank of the Rhône in a narrow, roofless tower. He remained there in
great hardship for nearly two years. Through Bishop Saint Nicetius’s intercession he returned to Lyon and lived with Nicetius for two months. Unable to obtain
the king’s permission to return to the place from which he had been expelled, he escaped by night and crossed into King Sigibert’s kingdom. He was made bishop
at the village of Arisitum, with about fifteen districts under him. The Goths had formerly held these; Bishop Dalmatius of Rodez now judges them.

After Munderic’s departure the people of Langres again asked for a bishop and chose Silvester, a kinsman either of ours or of blessed Tetricus. They did this at
my brother’s instigation. When blessed Tetricus died, Silvester was tonsured and ordained priest, receiving full authority over the church’s property. He
prepared to travel to Lyon to receive episcopal consecration. While these arrangements were being made, he was seized by epilepsy, from which he had long
suffered. He lost his senses and roared continuously for two days, breathing out his spirit on the third.

After these events Lampadius, deprived of honor and property as described above, joined Silvester’s son in hatred of the deacon Peter. He plotted with him and
assured him that his father had been killed by Peter’s sorcery. Young and foolish, Silvester’s son was aroused against Peter and publicly accused him of
parricide. When Peter heard this, an assembly was held before Saint Nicetius, bishop and my mother’s uncle, and Peter was taken to Lyon. There, in the presence
of Bishop Siagrius, many other bishops, and secular nobles, he cleared himself by oath, declaring that he had no part in Silvester’s death.

Two years later Silvester’s son, again incited by Lampadius, overtook Deacon Peter on the road, wounded him with a lance, and killed him. Peter’s body was taken
from that place to the fortress of Dijon and buried beside Saint Gregory, our great-grandfather. His killer fled to King Chilperic, leaving his property to be
confiscated by King Guntram’s treasury. He wandered from place to place because of his crime and had no secure dwelling. At last, as I believe, innocent blood
cried out against him to divine power. While traveling, he drew his sword and killed an innocent man. The man’s relatives and kinsmen grieved over his death,
rose up, drew their swords, cut the murderer to pieces, and scattered his limbs. By God’s just judgment the wretch received such an end: he who had killed an
innocent kinsman did not long survive his own guilt. This happened in the third year.

After Silvester’s death the people of Langres again asked for a bishop and received Pappolus, formerly archdeacon of Autun. They say he committed many
injustices, which I pass over so as not to appear a detractor of my brothers. But I will not omit his end. In the eighth year of his episcopate, while visiting
the districts and estates of the church, he saw blessed Tetricus in his sleep one night with a threatening expression. Tetricus said: “What are you doing here,
Pappolus? Why do you pollute my see? Why do you invade the church? Why do you scatter the sheep entrusted to me? Leave this place, abandon the see, and depart
far from this region.” As he spoke, he drove the staff he held into Pappolus’s chest with a violent blow. Pappolus awoke and wondered what it meant. A swelling
formed in that place, and he suffered extreme pain. He loathed food and drink and awaited his imminent death. On the third day he vomited blood and expired. His
body was carried away and buried at Langres.

Abbot Mummolus, surnamed Bonus, was appointed bishop in his place. Many praise him highly: he is chaste, sober, moderate, most prompt in every good work, a
lover of justice, and devoted to charity with all his heart. After becoming bishop, he learned that Lampadius had fraudulently taken much church property and
had assembled fields, vineyards, and slaves from plunder taken from the poor. He stripped Lampadius of everything and ordered him driven from his presence.
Lampadius now lives in extreme poverty and earns his bread with his own hands. Let this suffice on these matters.

### 6. Of Leunastus the archdeacon of Bourges

**[007]** In the year mentioned above—the year in which Sigibert died and his son Childebert began to reign—many miracles appeared at blessed Martin’s tomb. I
recorded them in the little books I attempted to compose about these miracles. Although my language is rustic, I have not allowed what I myself saw or learned
from trustworthy reports to remain hidden. Here I will describe only what befell those who negligently sought earthly remedies after receiving heavenly power.
His power is revealed both in gracious healings and in the chastisement of fools.

Leunast, archdeacon of Bourges, lost his eyesight as cataracts developed. He consulted many physicians but recovered no vision at all. He came to the basilica
of blessed Martin and remained there for two or three months, fasting continually and begging to recover his sight. When the feast day arrived, his eyes cleared
and he began to see. He returned home and summoned a certain Jew, who applied cupping glasses to his shoulders to increase his eyesight. After blood was drawn,
Leunast fell back into his former blindness. He returned to the holy church and remained there again for a long time, but he was not found worthy to recover his
sight.

I believe that it was withheld because of his sin, according to the Lord’s saying: “To him who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from him who has
not, even what he has will be taken away”; and again: “Behold, you are healed; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.” He would have remained healthy
if he had not placed the Jew above divine power. The apostle warns and reproves such people: “Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers. What partnership has
righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What communion has Christ with Belial? What share has a believer with an unbeliever? What
agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God. Therefore come out from among them and be separate from them, says the
Lord.” Let this case teach every Christian not to seek earthly remedies after being found worthy to receive heavenly medicine.

### 7. Of Senoch the recluse

**[008]** I also wish to commemorate the men whom the Lord called from our land this year and what kind of men they were. I consider him great and acceptable to
God who has placed such men from our land in his paradise. Blessed Senoch, a priest who lived at Tours, departed from the world in this way. He was a Thuringian
by birth. Having become a cleric at Tours, he withdrew into a cell that he had constructed between ancient walls. He gathered monks and restored an oratory that
had long lain in ruins. He performed many miracles for the sick, which we have recorded in the book of his Life.

### 8. Of the holy Germanus, bishop of Paris

**[009]** That year blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, also died. Among the many miracles he had performed while alive, this miracle at his funeral confirmed
them. When the prisoners cried out, his body became heavy in the street; when they were released, it was lifted again without effort. Those who had been
released followed his funeral freely as far as the basilica in which he was buried. Believers experience many miracles at his tomb through the Lord’s gift, so
that anyone who asks justly quickly receives what he desires. Whoever wishes to investigate diligently the miracles he performed while alive will find them all
by reading the book of his Life composed by the priest Fortunatus.

### 9. Of Caluppa the Recluse

**[010]** In the same year Caluppa the recluse also died. He had been religious from infancy. He entered monastic life at the monastery of Méallet in the
Auvergne territory and showed great humility toward the brothers, as we wrote in the book of his Life.

### 10. Of Patroclus the recluse

**[011]** In the territory of Bourges there was a recluse named Patroclus who held the honor of the priesthood. He was wonderfully holy and religious and a man
of great abstinence, often afflicted by various discomforts from fasting. He drank no wine, strong drink, or anything intoxicating except water lightly
sweetened with honey. He ate no relish. His food was bread soaked in water and sprinkled with salt. His eyes never grew dim. He was constant in prayer; if he
paused from it briefly, he read or wrote. Through prayer he often brought remedies to those suffering from chills, pustules, and other diseases. He performed
many other signs that would take too long to recount in order. He always wore a hair shirt against his pure body. Departing from the world at eighty years of
age, he went to Christ. We have also written a little book about his Life.

### 11. Of the Jews converted by Avitus the bishop

**[012]** Because our God always deigns to glorify his bishops, I will relate what happened concerning the Jews at Clermont this year. Blessed Bishop Avitus
frequently admonished them to lay aside the veil of the Mosaic law, understand the readings spiritually, and contemplate with pure hearts in the Holy Scriptures
Christ, the Son of the living God, promised by prophetic and legal authority. But there remained over their hearts not merely the veil that covered Moses’s
face, I may now say, but a wall. The bishop prayed that they would turn to the Lord and that the veil of the letter would be torn away from them.

One of them asked to be baptized at holy Easter. Born again to God through the sacrament of baptism, he proceeded in white with the others clothed in white. As
the people entered the city gate, one of the Jews, instigated by the devil, poured foul-smelling oil over the convert’s head. The whole people were horrified
and wanted to stone him, but the bishop would not permit it. On the blessed day when the Lord ascended gloriously to heaven after redeeming humanity, the bishop
was proceeding with psalmody from the church to the basilica. The whole multitude following him rushed upon the Jews’ synagogue and tore it down from its
foundations, leaving the site as level as an open field.

On another day the bishop sent envoys to the Jews, saying: “I do not compel you by force to confess the Son of God, but I preach and place the salt of knowledge
in your hearts. I am a shepherd set over the Lord’s sheep. The true Shepherd who suffered for us said of you that he has other sheep not of this fold whom he
must bring, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd. If you wish to believe as I do, become one flock under my guardianship; otherwise, depart from this
place.” After long agitation and doubt, on the third day they reached agreement, through the bishop’s intercession as I believe, and sent him this reply: “We
believe in Jesus, the Son of the living God, promised to us by the voices of the prophets. We ask to be washed in baptism so that we may no longer remain in
this error.”

The bishop rejoiced at the message. After celebrating vigils on the holy night of Pentecost, he went out to the baptistery beyond the walls. The whole multitude
prostrated itself before him and begged for baptism. Weeping for joy, he washed them all with water, anointed them with chrism, and gathered them into the bosom
of mother church. Candles blazed and lamps shone; the whole city was white with the white-clad flock. The city’s joy was no less than that which Jerusalem was
once found worthy to witness when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. More than five hundred were baptized. Those who refused baptism left the city and
went to Marseille.

### 12. Of Brachio the Abbot

**[013]** After these events Brachio, abbot of the monastery of Menat, also died. He was Thuringian by birth and formerly practiced hunting in the service of
Duke Sigivald, as we have written elsewhere.

### 13. How Mummolus wasted Limousin

**[014]** To return to our subject, King Chilperic sent his son Chlodovech to Tours. Chlodovech assembled an army, passed through the territory between Tours
and Angers, advanced as far as Saintes, and seized it. King Guntram’s patrician Mummolus crossed into the Limousin with a great army and fought Chilperic’s duke
Desiderius. In that battle five thousand of Mummolus’s army fell and twenty-four thousand of Desiderius’s. Desiderius himself barely escaped by flight.
Patrician Mummolus returned through the Auvergne, and his army devastated parts of it. He then passed into Burgundy.

### 14. How the tonsured Merovech took refuge

**[015]** After this Merovech, while held in custody by his father, was tonsured. His clothing was changed to that worn by clerics, he was ordained priest, and
he was sent to the monastery of Le Mans called Anisola to be instructed there in the priestly rule. When Guntram Boso, who was then residing in the basilica of
Saint Martin as we have said, heard this, he secretly sent Subdeacon Riculf to advise Merovech to seek the basilica of Saint Martin. Merovech set out, and his
servant Gailen arrived from another direction. Since his escort was small, Gailen rescued him from it on the journey. Covering his head and putting on secular
clothing, Merovech sought the church of blessed Martin. While we were celebrating Mass, he found the doors of the holy basilica open and entered. After Mass he
asked us to give him the blessed bread. Bishop Ragnemod of Paris, Saint Germanus’s successor, was then with us. When we refused, Merovech began to cry out that
we were wrong to suspend him from communion without the consent of his brothers. With the consent of the brother bishop present and after he had formally
invoked the canonical case, he received the blessed bread from us. I feared that, by suspending one man from communion, I might become the murderer of many. He
had threatened to kill some of our people if he did not receive communion with us. The region of Tours suffered many disasters because of this affair.

In those days Nicetius, my niece’s husband, had a case of his own and went to King Chilperic with my deacon, who was to report Merovech’s flight to the king.
When Queen Fredegund saw them, she said: “They are spies. They have come to discover what the king is doing so that they will know what to report to Merovech.”
She immediately ordered them stripped and confined in exile; they were released in the seventh month.

Chilperic then sent messengers to us: “Drive that apostate out of the basilica, or I will burn that whole region with fire.” We wrote back that what had not
been done in the time of the heretics could not now be done in a Christian age. He called out his army and sent it there. In the second year of King
Childebert’s reign, Merovech saw that his father was intent on this course. Taking Duke Guntram with him, he considered going to Brunhilda, saying: “Far be it
from me that the basilica of lord Martin should suffer violence on my account or that his region should be taken captive because of me.” He entered the basilica
to keep vigil and placed the property he had with him at blessed Martin’s tomb. He prayed that the saint would help him and grant him favor so that he could
obtain the kingdom.

Count Leudast had long set many traps for Guntram because of Fredegund’s love. Finally he treacherously surrounded and killed with the sword the servants
Guntram had sent out into the country. He wished to kill Guntram himself if he could find a favorable opportunity. Guntram, following his own counsel and
desiring revenge, seized the chief physician Marileif as he returned from the king’s presence. He had him severely beaten and took his gold, silver, and other
possessions, leaving him naked. He would have killed him if Marileif had not escaped from the hands of those beating him and fled into a church. We later
clothed him, spared his life, and sent him back to Poitiers.

Merovech spoke of many crimes committed by his father and stepmother. Although some of them were true, I believe that God was not pleased to have them made
public by his son, as I later learned. One day I attended his banquet. While we sat together, he humbly asked me to read something for the instruction of his
soul. I opened the book of Solomon and took the first verse that met my eye: “The eye that looks askance at a father, the ravens of the valleys shall pluck it
out.” Merovech did not understand, but I recognized that this verse had been provided by the Lord.

Guntram then sent a servant to a woman he had known since King Charibert’s time who had a spirit of divination, asking her to foretell what would happen. He
also asserted that she had previously predicted to him not only the year but the day and hour of King Charibert’s death. She sent back this answer through the
servants: “King Chilperic will perish this year, and Merovech will take the whole kingdom, excluding his brothers. You will hold the dukedom of his entire
kingdom for five years. In the sixth year, with the people’s favor, you will obtain the grace of the episcopate in one of the cities situated on the right bank
of the Loire. You will depart from this world old and full of days.” When the returning servants reported this to their master, he was immediately carried away
by vanity. As though he already sat in the episcopal chair of the church of Tours, he brought these words to me. Laughing at his folly, I said: “Such things
must be asked of God; the devil’s promises should not be believed. He has been a liar from the beginning and has never stood in the truth.” Guntram departed in
confusion, and I laughed heartily at a man who thought such things credible.

One night, after celebrating vigils in the holy bishop’s basilica, I lay down and fell asleep. I saw an angel flying through the air. As he passed over the holy
basilica, he said in a loud voice: “Alas! Alas! God has struck Chilperic and all his sons. None of those who came from his loins will survive to rule his
kingdom forever.” At that time Chilperic had four sons by different wives, besides his daughters. When these things were later fulfilled, I knew clearly that
the soothsayers’ promises were false.

While Merovech and Guntram were staying at the basilica of Saint Martin, Queen Fredegund, who was secretly protecting Guntram Boso concerning Theudebert’s
death, sent him a message: “If you can drive Merovech out of the basilica so that he can be killed, you will receive a great gift from me.” Thinking that
assassins were ready, Guntram said to Merovech: “Why do we sit here as though sluggish and afraid, hiding around the basilica like dullards? Let our horses be
brought. Let us take hawks and dogs, enjoy hunting, and delight in open spectacles.” He did this craftily to draw Merovech away from the holy basilica. Guntram
was otherwise a good enough man, but he was excessively ready to commit perjury. He never gave an oath to any friend without promptly abandoning it. They left
the basilica as we have described and went to the house at Jocundiacum near the city, but no one harmed Merovech.

Because Guntram was then accused of Theudebert’s death, as we have said, King Chilperic sent a written letter to Saint Martin’s tomb. It contained a request
that blessed Martin write back whether Guntram could be extracted from his basilica or not. Deacon Baudegisel, who presented the letter, placed a blank sheet
with it on the holy tomb. He waited three days and, receiving no written answer, returned to Chilperic. Chilperic sent other men to exact an oath from Guntram
that he would not leave the basilica without the king’s knowledge. Guntram swore conditionally and gave the altar cloth as surety that he would never leave
without the king’s command.

Merovech did not trust the pythoness. He placed three books on the holy tomb—the Psalter, the book of Kings, and the Gospels. Watching through the whole night,
he begged the blessed confessor to show him what would happen and whether he could obtain the kingdom, so that he might know by the Lord’s indication. He then
continued for three days in fasting, vigils, and prayers. Returning to the blessed tomb, he opened the book of Kings. The first verse on the page he opened was:
“Because you have forsaken the Lord your God and walked after foreign gods and have not done right before his sight, the Lord your God has delivered you into
the hands of your enemies.” In the Psalter he found: “Because of their deceitfulness you have brought evils upon them; you cast them down when they were lifted
up. How they are brought to desolation! They have suddenly failed and perished because of their iniquities.” In the Gospels he found: “You know that after two
days Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” Confused by these answers, Merovech wept for a long time at the blessed
bishop’s tomb. Taking Duke Guntram with him, he departed with five hundred or more men.

After leaving the holy basilica, while traveling through the territory of Auxerre, he was captured by Erpo, King Guntram’s duke. While Erpo held him, Merovech
escaped by some chance and entered the basilica of Saint Germanus. When King Guntram heard this, he was enraged. He fined Erpo seven hundred gold pieces and
removed him from office, saying: “As my brother says, you detained his enemy. If you intended to do that, you ought first to have brought him to me. Otherwise
you ought not to have touched the man you were pretending not to hold.”

King Chilperic’s army advanced as far as Tours, plundered, burned, and devastated that region. It did not spare Saint Martin’s property, but seized whatever it
touched without any regard or fear of God. Merovech remained at the basilica just mentioned for nearly two months, then fled and reached Queen Brunhilda. The
Austrasians did not receive him. His father called out an army against the people of Champagne, thinking that Merovech was hiding there, but he did no harm to
them and could not find him.

### 15. Of the war between the Saxons and the Suebi

**[016]** When Alboin entered Italy, Chlothar and Sigibert had settled the Suebi and other peoples in that region. Those who returned in Sigibert’s time—that
is, those who had been with Alboin—rose against the Suebi, wishing to drive them out of the region and destroy them. The Suebi offered them a third of the land,
saying: “We can live together without conflict.” The returning Saxons were angry because they had formerly held the land themselves and refused to make peace.
The Suebi then offered half, and afterward two-thirds, retaining only a third for themselves. When the Saxons still refused, they offered all their cattle as
well as the land if only the Saxons would refrain from war. The Saxons would not agree and sought battle.

Before the battle they discussed how they would divide the Suebi’s wives and who would take which woman after their husbands’ destruction, considering the Suebi
already as good as dead. But the Lord’s mercy, which executes justice, turned their intention in another direction. When battle was joined, there were
twenty-six thousand Saxons, of whom twenty thousand fell; there were six thousand Suebi, of whom only four hundred and eighty were struck down. The remainder
won the victory. The surviving Saxons swore that none of them would cut his beard or hair until he had avenged himself on his adversaries. When they fought
again, they fell in still greater destruction, and so the war came to an end.

### 16. Of the death of Macliavus

**[017]** These events took place in Brittany. Macliavus and Bodicus, counts of the Bretons, had once sworn to each other that whichever survived would defend
the other’s son as his own. When Bodicus died, he left a son named Theuderic. Forgetting his oath, Macliavus expelled Theuderic from his country and took his
father’s kingdom. Theuderic was a fugitive and wanderer for a long time. At last God took pity on him. He gathered men from Brittany, attacked Macliavus, and
killed him and his son Jacob with the sword. He restored to his own control the part of the kingdom his father had once held, while Macliavus’s son Waroch
claimed the other part.

### 17. Of the doubt concerning Easter

**[018]** King Guntram put two sons of the late Magnachar to the sword because they had uttered many detestable and execrable things against Queen Austregild
and her offspring. He confiscated their property for his treasury. He himself was struck by sudden illness and lost his two sons. He grieved deeply at their
deaths because he remained bereft of children.

That year there was uncertainty about Easter. In Gaul we and many cities celebrated holy Easter on the fourteenth day before the kalends of May. Others kept the
solemnity with the Spaniards on the twelfth day before the kalends of April. Yet they say that the springs in Spain that are filled by God’s will were filled at
the date of our Easter. At Chinon, a village in the territory of Tours, while Masses were being celebrated on the glorious day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the
church shook. Terrified, the people cried out with one voice that the church was falling. They all fled, even breaking down the doors. A great plague
subsequently devastated the people.

King Guntram then sent envoys to his nephew Childebert, seeking peace and asking to meet him. Childebert came to him with his nobles. They met at the bridge
called the Stone Bridge, greeted each other, and exchanged kisses. King Guntram said: “Because of my sins I have been left without children. I therefore ask
that this nephew of mine be my son.” Placing Childebert on his own chair, he handed over his whole kingdom to him, saying: “Let one shield protect us and one
spear defend us. If I have sons, I will nevertheless count you as one of them, so that the affection I promise you today with God as witness may endure among
you and them.” Childebert’s nobles made the same promise on his behalf. They ate and drank together, honored each other with fitting gifts, and departed in
peace.

They sent an embassy to King Chilperic demanding that he restore what he had taken from their kingdoms; if he delayed, he should prepare a battlefield.
Chilperic treated this demand with contempt. He ordered circuses to be built at Soissons and Paris and offered spectacles in them to the people.

### 18. Of the bishop Praetextatus and the death of Merovech

**[019]** After these events, Chilperic heard that Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, was giving gifts to the people contrary to the king’s interests, and ordered
him to be summoned. When the bishop had been examined, Chilperic discovered that Queen Brunhilda’s property had been entrusted to him. He seized it and ordered
Praetextatus to be kept in exile until an episcopal hearing. A council was then assembled and the bishop was brought before it. The bishops who had gathered
were in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle at Paris. The king said to him, “What were you thinking, bishop, when you united my enemy Merovech, who ought to
have been my son, with his aunt—that is, with his uncle’s wife? Were you unaware of what the decrees of the canons have ordained in such a case? You are proved
to have transgressed not only in this, but also to have plotted with him and given gifts so that I might be killed. You made a son his father’s enemy; you
seduced the common people with money, so that none would keep the faith they owed me; and you wished to deliver my kingdom into another’s hands.” As he spoke,
the multitude of Franks began to roar and wanted to break down the doors of the basilica, intending to drag the bishop out and stone him, but the king forbade
it.

When Bishop Praetextatus denied doing what the king had alleged, false witnesses came forward displaying various valuables and saying, “You gave us these and
those things so that we would pledge our loyalty to Merovech.” He answered, “You are telling the truth when you say that I have often given you gifts, but my
purpose was not to expel the king from his kingdom. Since you used to present me with mules, excellent horses, and other things, what else could I do but reward
you in like manner?”

When the king had returned to his quarters, we gathered and sat in the sacristy of the basilica of blessed Peter. While we were talking, Aetius, archdeacon of
the church of Paris, suddenly entered, greeted us, and said, “Listen to me, priests of the Lord assembled here. Either you will exalt your name at this time and
shine with the glory of a good reputation, or no one henceforth will regard you as priests of God, if you do not vigorously defend your own cause or permit your
brother to be destroyed.” None of the priests answered him, for they feared the fury of the queen, at whose instigation these things were being done. As they
sat silently with their fingers pressed to their lips, I said, “I beg you, most holy priests of God, to attend to my words, especially you who appear to be on
familiar terms with the king. Give him holy and priestly counsel, lest by raging against a servant of God he perish under God’s wrath and lose both kingdom and
glory.” At these words all remained silent. I continued, “Remember, my lord priests, the prophetic saying: ‘If the watchman sees a man’s iniquity and does not
speak, he will be answerable for the soul that perishes.’ Therefore do not be silent, but preach and set the king’s sins before his eyes, lest some evil befall
him and you be held accountable for his soul. Or do you not know what happened recently? How Chlodomer seized Sigismund and cast him into prison, and Avitus,
God’s priest, told him, ‘Do not lay a hand on him, and when you march into Burgundy you will gain the victory.’ But Chlodomer rejected the priest’s words, went
away and killed Sigismund with his wife and children, and then invaded Burgundy, where he was overwhelmed by the army and killed. And what of the Emperor
Maximus? When he compelled blessed Martin to share communion with a certain murderous bishop, and Martin yielded to the impious king in order more easily to
free men condemned to death, the judgment of the eternal King followed: Maximus was driven from the empire and condemned to a most wretched death.” No one
answered me; they all sat in dumb amazement. Two flatterers among them—lamentable though it is to say this of bishops—reported to the king that he had no
greater enemy to his cause than me.

Immediately one of the courtiers was sent at a run to bring me before him. When I arrived, the king was standing beside a shelter made of branches, with Bishop
Berthram on his right and Ragnemod on his left. Before them was a stool covered with bread and various dishes. When the king saw me, he said, “Bishop, you ought
to dispense justice to everyone, yet I receive no justice from you. As I see it, you consent to iniquity, and the proverb is fulfilled in you: one crow does not
peck out another crow’s eye.” I replied, “If one of us wishes to stray from the path of justice, O king, you can correct him; but if you transgress, who will
rebuke you? We speak to you, and if you are willing, you listen; but if you refuse, who will condemn you except him who declared himself to be justice?”
Incensed against me by his flatterers, he answered, “I have found justice with everyone, but with you I cannot find it. Yet I know what to do to disgrace you
before the people and make everyone perceive that you are unjust. I will summon the people of Tours and tell them, ‘Cry out against Gregory that he is unjust
and renders justice to no one.’ When they raise this cry, I will answer, ‘If I, who am king, cannot obtain justice from him, how will you, who are lesser men,
obtain it?’” I replied, “You do not know whether I am unjust. He to whom the secrets of the heart are laid bare knows my conscience. As for the people’s false
clamor at your instigation, it means nothing, because everyone knows that you prompted it. In that acclamation it is not I but you who will be disgraced. But
why say more? You have the law and the canons. You ought to examine them diligently, and if you fail to observe their commands, know that God’s judgment hangs
over you.”

Then, as though soothing me—and acting deceitfully, he thought I did not understand—he turned to the broth set before him and said, “I prepared this broth for
you. It contains nothing but poultry and a few chickpeas.” Recognizing his flattery, I said, “Our food ought to be doing God’s will, not delighting in such
delicacies, so that we never neglect his commands. You who accuse others of injustice, promise first that you will not disregard the law and the canons; then we
will believe that you are pursuing justice.” He stretched out his right hand and swore by almighty God that he would in no way neglect what the law and the
canons taught. Then I took bread, drank some wine, and departed.

That night, after the nocturnal hymns had been sung, I heard heavy blows being struck on the door of my lodging. I sent a servant and learned that messengers
from Queen Fredegund were standing there. When they were admitted, I received the queen’s greeting. The servants then begged me not to oppose her cause and
promised two hundred pounds of silver if Praetextatus were crushed despite my resistance. “We already have the promise of all the bishops,” they said. “Only do
not proceed against us.” I answered, “Even if you gave me a thousand pounds of gold and silver, what else could I do except what the Lord commands? I promise
only this: I will follow whatever the others agree upon in accordance with the decrees of the canons.” Not understanding what I meant, they thanked me and left.
In the morning some bishops came to me with a similar message, and I gave them a similar answer.

When we assembled in the basilica of Saint Peter, the king arrived in the morning and said, “The authority of the canons has ordained that a bishop caught in
theft be removed from the episcopal office.” We asked who the bishop was against whom the charge of theft was brought. The king replied, “You have seen the
valuables that he stole from us.” Three days earlier he had shown us two bundles filled with valuables and various ornaments, valued at more than three thousand
solidi, as well as a small purse containing about two thousand gold pieces. He claimed that the bishop had stolen these things from him.

Praetextatus answered, “I believe you remember that when Queen Brunhilda left the city of Rouen, I came to you and told you that I held five packages of her
property in trust. Her servants kept coming to me to recover them, but I was unwilling to return them without your advice. You, O king, said to me, ‘Get these
things out of your hands and let the woman’s property return to her, lest enmity arise between me and my nephew Childebert because of them.’ When I returned to
the city, I handed one bundle to the servants, for they could not carry more. They came back and demanded the others. Again I sought your magnificence’s advice,
and you ordered me, saying, ‘Get rid of them, bishop, get rid of them, lest this matter cause scandal.’ I handed two more over to them, but the remaining two
stayed with me. Why do you now slander me and accuse me of theft, when this matter should be regarded as custody, not theft?”

The king replied, “If this deposit was in your hands for safekeeping, why did you open one of the bundles, cut into pieces an embroidered border woven with gold
thread, and give them to men who were to drive me from the kingdom?” Bishop Praetextatus answered, “I have already told you that I had accepted gifts from them.
Since I had nothing at hand to give in return, I took these things and gave them reciprocal gifts. What belonged to Merovech, my son, whom I received from the
font of regeneration, I regarded as my own.”

Seeing that he could not overcome Praetextatus with these calumnies, King Chilperic, greatly astonished and troubled in conscience, left us, summoned some of
his flatterers, and said, “I confess that I have been defeated by the bishop’s words, and I know that what he says is true. What am I to do now so that the
queen’s will concerning him may be fulfilled?” He then told them, “Go to him and speak as though offering advice on your own initiative: ‘You know that King
Chilperic is pious and tenderhearted and quickly moved to mercy. Humble yourself before him and say that you committed the acts of which he accuses you. Then we
will all prostrate ourselves at his feet and obtain pardon for you.’” Deceived by these words, Bishop Praetextatus promised to do so.

In the morning we assembled at the customary place. The king arrived and said to the bishop, “If you gave these men gifts in return for gifts, why did you
demand oaths that they would keep faith with Merovech?” The bishop answered, “I confess that I sought their friendship for him. I would have summoned not only a
man but, if it had been lawful, an angel from heaven to be his helper, for, as I have often said, he was my spiritual son through baptism.” As the altercation
grew more intense, Bishop Praetextatus prostrated himself on the ground and said, “I have sinned against heaven and before you, most merciful king. I am a vile
murderer; I wished to kill you and set your son upon your throne.” At these words the king prostrated himself at the feet of the bishops, saying, “Hear, most
pious priests, this guilty man confessing an abominable crime.” Weeping, we raised the king from the ground. He ordered Praetextatus to leave the basilica and
withdrew to his own quarters.

He then sent a book of canons containing a newly attached quaternion with what purported to be apostolic canons, including this: “A bishop convicted of murder,
adultery, or perjury shall be deposed from the priesthood.” When these had been read and Praetextatus stood dumbfounded, Bishop Berthram said, “Hear, brother
and fellow bishop: since you do not possess the king’s favor, you cannot enjoy our affection either until you merit the king’s indulgence.” After this the king
demanded that either Praetextatus’s tunic be torn, or the hundred and eighth psalm, which contains the curses against Judas Iscariot, be recited over his head,
or at least that judgment be written against him so that he might never again receive communion. I resisted these demands in accordance with the king’s promise
that nothing would be done outside the canons.

Praetextatus was then taken from our sight and placed under guard. When he tried to escape from custody at night, he was severely beaten and driven into exile
on an island in the sea near the city of Coutances.

After this a report spread that Merovech was again attempting to seek sanctuary in Saint Martin’s basilica. Chilperic ordered the basilica to be guarded and all
its entrances closed. The guards left one door open, through which a few clergy could enter for the services, and kept the other doors shut, which caused much
distress to the people.

While we were staying at Paris, signs appeared in the sky: twenty rays in the north, rising in the east and hastening toward the west. One was longer and
another stood out above the rest; when it had risen high, it soon faded, and then the others that had followed disappeared. I believe they foretold Merovech’s
death.

While Merovech was hiding in the Champagne region of Rheims and did not trust himself openly to the Austrasians, he was surrounded by the men of Tarabanna. They
said that if he came to them, they would abandon his father Chilperic and submit to him. He quickly took his strongest men and went to them. Revealing the
snares they had prepared, they confined him in a certain villa, surrounded him with armed men, and sent messengers to his father. On hearing this, Chilperic
resolved to hasten there. Merovech, held in a small lodging and fearing that he would suffer many torments in vengeance for his enemies, summoned his retainer
Gailen and said, “Until now we have shared one soul and one purpose. I beg you not to allow me to be delivered into my enemies’ hands. Take a sword and strike
me down.” Gailen did not hesitate, but stabbed him with a knife. When the king arrived, Merovech was found dead. Some then asserted that the words of Merovech
reported above had been invented by the queen, and that Merovech had in fact been secretly killed by her order.

Gailen was seized, and after his hands and feet had been cut off, his ears and the tips of his nostrils severed, and many other tortures inflicted, they put him
to a miserable death. They also raised Grindio high, bound to a wheel; and they beheaded and killed Ciucilo, who had once been count of King Sigibert’s palace.
Many others who had come with Merovech were cruelly put to death by various torments. People were also saying at the time that Bishop Egidius and Guntram Boso
had played the leading part in this entrapment: Guntram because Queen Fredegund had secretly befriended him for the murder of Theudebert, and Egidius because he
had long enjoyed her favor.

### 19. Of the almsgivings of Tiberius

**[020]** When the Emperor Justin lost his reason and became insane, and the empire was governed solely through the Augusta Sophia, the people, as I have
already said in the preceding book, chose Tiberius as Caesar. He was energetic, vigorous, and wise, generous in almsgiving and an excellent defender of the
poor. He distributed to the poor much of the treasure that Justin had accumulated. The Augusta frequently rebuked him for reducing the state to poverty, saying,
“What I gathered over many years you are scattering and squandering in a short time.” But he answered, “Our treasury will not be exhausted, provided that the
poor receive alms and captives are ransomed. For this is the great treasure, since the Lord says, ‘Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust
nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal.’ Therefore let us gather in heaven, through the poor, from what God has given us, so that the
Lord may deign to increase our wealth in this world.” Because he was, as I have said, a great and true Christian, the more cheerfully he assisted the poor by
his distributions, the more abundantly the Lord provided for him.

While walking through the palace, he saw in the pavement of a room a marble slab on which the Lord’s cross was carved. He said, “Lord, we protect our foreheads
and breasts with your cross, and behold, we trample a cross beneath our feet!” He immediately ordered it to be removed. When the slab had been dug out and
raised, they found another beneath it bearing the same sign. This was reported to him, and he ordered that slab removed as well. When it was taken away, they
found a third, which was likewise removed at his command. Beneath it they discovered a great treasure containing more than a thousand hundredweight of gold. The
gold was carried away, and he distributed it to the poor still more generously, as had been his custom; and because of his good will the Lord never allowed him
to lack anything.

I will not omit what the Lord sent him afterward. Narses, the commander in Italy, had a large house in a certain city. When he left Italy with many treasures,
he came to that city and secretly dug a large cistern in his house, in which he deposited many thousands of hundredweight of gold and silver. He killed those
who knew of it and entrusted the hidden treasure to only one old man, binding him by an oath. After Narses died, these riches lay hidden underground. When the
old man observed Tiberius’s continual almsgiving, he went to him and said, “Caesar, if it would benefit me in some way, I will disclose something of great
importance to you.” Tiberius replied, “Tell me whatever you wish. It will benefit you if you report something that will be of use to me.” The old man said, “I
know where Narses’s treasure is hidden, and now that I am at the end of my life I cannot keep it secret.” Caesar Tiberius rejoiced and sent his servants to the
place. The old man led the way, and they followed in astonishment. They came to the cistern, uncovered it, and entered. There they found so much gold and silver
that those carrying it away could scarcely empty it over many days. From this treasure Tiberius distributed still more to the needy with cheerful generosity.

### 20. Of Salonius and Sagittarius the bishops

**[021]** A disturbance now arose concerning the bishops Salonius and Sagittarius. They had been brought up by Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, and had received
the office of deacon. In his time Salonius was appointed bishop of the church of Embrun and Sagittarius of that of Gap. But once they had obtained their
episcopates and were left to their own discretion, they began to revel with insane fury in violent seizures, assaults, murders, adulteries, and various crimes.
On one occasion, while Victor, bishop of Troyes, was celebrating the anniversary of his birth, they sent out a band of men and rushed upon him with swords and
arrows. The attackers tore his garments, beat his servants, and carried off the vessels and all the provisions for the banquet, leaving the bishop in deep
humiliation.

When King Guntram learned of this, he ordered a synod to assemble in the city of Lyons. The bishops met with the blessed patriarch Nicetius, examined the case,
and found Salonius and Sagittarius clearly guilty of the crimes of which they were accused. They decreed that men who had committed such acts should be deprived
of the honor of the episcopate. But the two, knowing that the king was still favorably disposed toward them, approached him, protesting that they had been
unjustly removed and asking permission to go to the pope of the city of Rome. The king granted their petition, gave them letters, and allowed them to depart.
Appearing before Pope John, they declared that they had been removed without any legitimate grounds. The pope sent letters to the king directing that they be
restored to their sees. The king obeyed without delay, though not before rebuking them at length. But, worse still, no amendment followed.

They nevertheless sought peace with Bishop Victor and surrendered the men whom they had sent to make the attack. Victor remembered the Lord’s command not to
return evil for evil to one’s enemies, did them no harm, and allowed them to go free. For this he was afterward suspended from communion, because, after
accusing them publicly, he had privately spared his enemies without consulting the brethren before whom he had made the accusation. Through the king’s favor,
however, he was later restored to communion.

Salonius and Sagittarius became involved daily in greater crimes. In the battles which, as I mentioned above, Mummolus fought against the Lombards, they armed
themselves like laymen and killed many with their own hands. Among their own citizens, they would rage until blood flowed, beating some with clubs when moved to
anger. The people’s outcry therefore reached the king once more, and he ordered the two bishops to be summoned. When they arrived, he refused to admit them to
his presence, intending that a hearing should first be held and that only if they were found worthy should they be allowed to appear before the king.

Sagittarius, moved to wrath and taking this procedure badly, being fickle, vain, and prone to streams of irrational talk, began to declaim at length against the
king. He declared that the king’s sons could not inherit the kingdom because their mother had been taken from the household of Magnachar and brought to the
king’s bed. He did not understand that, whatever the rank of the women, the children born of kings are called kings’ sons. When the king heard this, he was
greatly angered. He took away their horses, servants, and everything else they possessed and ordered them to be confined in monasteries far from him, where they
were to do penance, leaving each only a single cleric. He sternly warned the local judges to guard them with armed men and to allow no one access to visit them.

At that time the king’s sons were still alive, and the elder fell ill. The king’s intimates approached him and said, “If the king would graciously deign to hear
his servants’ words, we would speak in your ears.” He answered, “Say whatever you wish.” They said, “Perhaps these bishops were innocent and have been condemned
to exile, and the king’s sin is thereby increased in some respect; perhaps that is why our lord’s son is dying.” He replied, “Go at once and release them,
asking them to pray for our little children.” They went, and the bishops were released.

On leaving the monasteries, Salonius and Sagittarius met, embraced and kissed one another because they had not seen each other for so long, and returned to
their cities. They appeared so contrite that they seemed never to cease chanting psalms, observed fasts, gave alms, and spent their days and nights completing
the book of David’s songs, meditating on hymns and readings. But this holiness did not long remain unimpaired, and they turned backward once again. They often
spent the nights feasting and drinking so that, while their clergy were celebrating matins in church, they would call for cups and pour out wine. There was no
mention of God at all, and no course of recollection was observed. When dawn broke, they would rise from dinner, wrap themselves in soft coverings, and, buried
in sleep and wine, sleep until the third hour of the day. Nor were women lacking with whom they could defile themselves. On rising, they bathed and reclined at
table; when they rose from that meal in the evening, they longed for dinner until the hour of daylight mentioned above. They behaved in this way every day until
God’s wrath crashed down upon them, as I shall relate later.

### 21. Of Winnoc the Briton

**[022]** At that time Winnoch the Briton came from Brittany to Tours, practicing extreme abstinence and wishing to go to Jerusalem. He wore no garment except
one made from sheepskins stripped of their wool. Because he seemed to me a very religious man, and in order to retain him more easily, I honored him with the
grace of the presbyterate.

The religious woman Ingitrude was accustomed to collect water from Saint Martin’s tomb. When this water ran short, she asked that a vessel of wine be brought to
the blessed tomb. After a night had passed, she ordered some of it to be taken from there in the presence of this priest. When it was brought to her, she said
to him, “Remove the wine, and pour in only one drop of the little holy water that remains.” When he had done so, wonderful to relate, at the descent of that
single drop the vessel, which had been half empty, was filled. It was emptied two or three times and each time refilled by only one drop. There is no doubt that
blessed Martin’s power was at work in this as well.

### 22. Of the death of Samson, Chilperic's son

**[023]** After these events, Samson, King Chilperic’s younger son, was seized by dysentery and fever and departed this life. He had been born while King
Chilperic was being besieged at Tournai by his brother. His mother, fearing death, cast him away and wanted to destroy him. Unable to do so, and rebuked by the
king, she ordered him to be baptized. He was baptized and received from the font by the bishop himself, but died before completing a single five-year period.
His mother Fredegund also became gravely ill during those days, but recovered.

### 23. Of the prodigies shown

**[024]** Afterward, on the night of the third day before the Ides of November, while I was celebrating the vigils of blessed Martin, a great portent appeared
to me. A shining star seemed to gleam in the middle of the moon, and other stars appeared close above and below it. The halo that usually signifies rain also
appeared around it. What these things signified I do not know. This year I also saw the moon frequently turn black, and there were severe thunderstorms before
the Lord’s Nativity. Those bright lights around the sun, which country people call “suns,” also appeared, as I mentioned they had before the disaster in
Auvergne. It is said that the sea advanced beyond its usual limits, and many other signs appeared.

### 24. How Chilperic seized Poitiers

**[025]** Guntram Boso came to Tours with a few armed men, forcibly carried off his daughters, whom he had left in the holy basilica, and took them to the city
of Poitiers, which belonged to King Childebert. King Chilperic also invaded Poitiers, and his nephew’s men were driven out by Chilperic’s men. They brought
Ennodius from his office as count into the king’s presence. He was condemned to exile, and his property was surrendered to the treasury. A year later, however,
he was restored to both his native land and his possessions. Guntram Boso left his daughters in the basilica of blessed Hilary and went over to King Childebert.

### 25. Of the death of Dacco and Dracolenus

**[026]** In the third year of King Childebert’s reign, which was the seventeenth year of Chilperic and Guntram, Dacco, the son of the late Dagaric, abandoned
King Chilperic and wandered from place to place. He was treacherously seized by Duke Dracolenus, who was also called Industrius. Dracolenus took him in chains
to King Chilperic at Brannacum, having given Dacco an oath that he would obtain his life from the king. But he forgot his oath, made wicked allegations against
Dacco before the king, and arranged for his death. While Dacco was being held in chains and saw that there was no possibility of escape, he sought penance from
a priest without the king’s knowledge. After receiving it, he was killed.

When Dracolenus was swiftly returning to his own country, Guntram Boso was at that time attempting to take his daughters away from Poitiers. Hearing of this,
Dracolenus threw himself in Guntram’s path, but Guntram and his companions, being prepared, resisted and tried to defend themselves. Guntram sent one of his
friends to Dracolenus with this message: “Go and tell him, ‘You know that we have entered into an alliance with one another. I beg you to abandon your ambush
against me. I do not forbid you to take whatever property you wish; only let me, even stripped bare, go wherever I wish with my daughters.’”

But Dracolenus, vain and fickle as he was, replied, “Here is the rope with which other guilty men have been led bound to the king at my direction. Today this
man too will be tied with it and taken there in chains.” Having said this, he spurred his horse with his heels and charged at Guntram at full speed. He struck a
useless blow, his spear shaft broke, and his sword fell to the ground. Seeing death hanging over him, Guntram called upon the Lord’s name and the great power of
blessed Martin, raised his spear, and gripped Dracolenus by the throat. While he held him suspended above the horse, one of Guntram’s friends struck Dracolenus
in the side with a lance and finished him. His companions fled, and after stripping the body Guntram departed freely with his daughters.

Afterward Severus, Guntram’s father-in-law, was gravely accused before the king by his sons. On hearing this, Severus went to the king with rich gifts. He was
seized on the road, stripped of his property, taken into exile, and ended his life by a most wretched death. His two sons, Burgolenus and Dodo, were condemned
to death on a charge of treason. One was forcibly killed by the army; the other was captured in flight and died after his hands and feet had been cut off. All
their property and their father’s was surrendered to the treasury, for they possessed great treasures.

### 26. How the army went into Brittany

**[027]** Then, by King Chilperic’s command, the men of Tours, Poitiers, Bayeux, Le Mans, and Angers, together with many others, went into Brittany and took up
positions against Waroch, son of the late Macliav, on the river Vicinonia. Waroch made a treacherous night attack on the Saxons of Bayeux and killed a great
many of them. Three days later he made peace with King Chilperic’s commanders, gave his son as a hostage, and bound himself by an oath to remain faithful to
King Chilperic. He also surrendered the city of Vannes on condition that he be allowed to govern it by the king’s command and pay the tribute and all other dues
arising from it every year without being reminded. When this had been done, the army withdrew from the region.

Afterward King Chilperic ordered fines to be exacted from the poor and the junior members of churches and basilicas because they had not marched with the army,
although it had not been customary for them to perform any public service. Waroch later forgot his promise. Wishing to break what he had done, he sent Eunius,
bishop of the city of Vannes, to King Chilperic. The king, moved to anger, rebuked Eunius and ordered him to be condemned to exile.

### 27. Of the deposition of Salonius and Sagittarius

**[028]** In the fourth year of Childebert’s reign, the eighteenth year of Kings Guntram and Chilperic, a synod was held in the city of Chalon by command of
King Guntram. Various cases were considered, and the old calamity concerning the bishops Salonius and Sagittarius was renewed. Charges were brought against
them: they were accused not only of adultery but also of murder. The bishops judged that these offenses could be expiated by penance, but the further charge was
added that they were guilty of treason and betrayal of their country. For this reason they were deprived of the episcopate and thrust under guard into the
basilica of blessed Marcellus. They escaped from it by flight and departed, wandering in different directions, until other bishops were appointed in their
cities.

### 28. Of the tax-registers of Chilperic

**[029]** King Chilperic ordered new and oppressive tax assessments to be made throughout his kingdom. Many people therefore abandoned their cities or their own
property and sought other kingdoms, considering it better to live as strangers elsewhere than to be subjected to such danger. It had been decreed that a
landowner should render one amphora of wine for every arpent of his own land. Many other levies were also imposed on the remaining lands and on slaves, and the
people could not meet them.

When the people of Limoges saw themselves burdened by such an exaction, they assembled on the Kalends of March and wanted to kill Mark the referendary, who had
been ordered to carry out these measures. They would certainly have done so had Bishop Ferreolus not rescued him from imminent danger. The assembled multitude
also seized the tax registers and burned them. The king was greatly incensed and sent agents from his own entourage, who afflicted the people with enormous
losses, terrified them with punishments, and punished them with death. It is also reported that abbots and priests were stretched upon stakes and subjected to
various torments, because the royal envoys falsely alleged that they had assisted the insurgents in burning the registers. Still harsher tributes were imposed
afterward.

### 29. Of the devastation of the Bretons

**[030]** The Bretons also devastated the region of Rennes severely with fire, plunder, and captivity. They advanced as far as the village of Cornutium,
fighting as they went. Bishop Eunius was brought back from exile but was assigned to Angers for his maintenance and was not permitted to return to his own city
of Vannes. Duke Bippolenus was sent against the Bretons and ravaged several parts of Brittany with sword and fire, which provoked still greater fury.

### 30. Of the empire of Tiberius

**[031]** While these things were happening in Gaul, Justin completed the eighteenth year of his reign and ended both his madness and his life. After his
burial, Caesar Tiberius assumed the empire to which he had long since been admitted. When the people, according to local custom, expected him to proceed to the
spectacle in the circus, and were planning an ambush against him on behalf of Justinian, who was then regarded as Justin’s nephew, Tiberius instead went in
procession through the holy places. When the prayer was completed, he summoned the pope of the city and entered the palace with the consuls and prefects. He was
then clothed in purple, crowned with the diadem, and seated upon the imperial throne, and his rule was confirmed amid immense acclamations. When the circus
factions learned what had happened, they covered their heads in confusion and withdrew without achieving anything, unable to harm a man who had placed his hope
in God.

A few days later Justinian came and threw himself at the emperor’s feet, bringing him fifteen hundredweight of gold as a token of gratitude. With his customary
patience, Tiberius raised him up and ordered him to remain in the palace. But the Augusta Sophia, forgetting the promise she had once made to Tiberius, tried to
