lay snares for him. When Tiberius went to his estate to enjoy the vintage for thirty days according to imperial custom, Sophia secretly summoned Justinian and
wished to elevate him to the empire. On discovering this, Tiberius returned swiftly to Constantinople, seized the Augusta, and stripped her of all her
treasures, leaving her only her daily sustenance. He removed her servants and replaced them with others chosen from his own faithful men, expressly commanding
that none of her former attendants should have access to her. Justinian he merely rebuked, and afterward loved him so greatly that he promised his own daughter
to Justinian’s son and in turn sought Justinian’s daughter for his own son; but this arrangement was never carried out. Tiberius’s army defeated the Persians
and returned victorious with such a mass of booty that it seemed sufficient to satisfy human greed. Twenty captured elephants were brought to the emperor.

### 31. Of the Attacks of the Bretons

**[032]** That year the Bretons were extremely aggressive around the cities of Nantes and Rennes. They carried off immense plunder, overran the fields, stripped
the vineyards of their fruit, and led away captives. Bishop Felix sent an embassy to them, and although the Bretons promised to make amends, they refused to
fulfill any of their promises.

### 32. Of the basilica of Saint Denis outraged by a woman

**[033]** At Paris a certain woman fell under accusation, many people alleging that she had left her husband and was having intercourse with another man. Her
husband’s relatives approached her father and said, “Either prove your daughter’s innocence, or let her die, so that this shameful conduct does not bring
disgrace upon our family.” The father answered, “I know my daughter to be entirely innocent; what these wicked people are saying is not true. Nevertheless, so
that the accusation may go no further, I will establish her innocence by an oath.” They said, “If she is innocent, affirm it by an oath over the tomb of the
blessed martyr Denis.” The father agreed. When the appointed day came, they assembled at the holy martyr’s basilica. The father raised his hands over the altar
and swore that his daughter was not guilty. The husband’s party, on the other hand, declared that he had perjured himself.

As they argued, they drew their swords, rushed at one another, and slaughtered each other before the altar itself. They were men of high rank and among the
foremost at King Chilperic’s court. Many were wounded by swords; the holy basilica was spattered with human blood; its doors were pierced by javelins and
swords; and the impious missiles raged as far as the tomb itself. When the violence was with difficulty calmed, services ceased at the place until all these
events were brought to the king’s attention. The men hastened into the king’s presence but were not received into favor. They were sent back to the local bishop
with instructions that, if they were not found guilty of this crime, they should be admitted to communion. They then made amends for their misconduct before
Bishop Ragnemod, who presided over the church of Paris, and were received back into ecclesiastical communion. Not many days later, when the woman was summoned
to judgment, she ended her life with a noose.

### 33. Of the prodigies

**[034]** In the fifth year of King Childebert’s reign, great floods afflicted the region of Auvergne. Rain did not cease for twelve days, and the Limagne was
so inundated that many people were prevented from sowing their seed. The rivers Loire and Allier, the latter also called the Elacer, as well as the other
torrents flowing into it, swelled so greatly that they passed boundaries they had never crossed before. They caused great destruction of livestock, loss of
crops, and the wreck of buildings. Similarly, the Rhône and Saône joined together, burst their banks, brought severe losses upon the people, and overthrew part
of the wall of the city of Lyons. When the rains ceased, the trees blossomed a second time, for it was the month of September.

In the Touraine that year, in the morning before daylight, a flash was seen to run across the sky and fall toward the east. A sound like trees crashing down was
heard throughout that land. It cannot be supposed to have come from trees, because it was heard for fifty miles or more. That same year the city of Bordeaux was
violently shaken by an earthquake, and the city walls were in danger of being overthrown. The whole population was so terrified of death that they thought they
would be swallowed up with the city if they did not flee. Many therefore moved to other cities. The tremor extended to neighboring cities and reached as far as
Spain, though less violently. Immense rocks were dislodged from the Pyrenees and struck down cattle and men.

A fire of divine origin also burned a suburb of Bordeaux. Houses and threshing floors with their grain were suddenly caught by the flames and consumed, with no
external source of ignition, perhaps by divine command. The city of Orléans likewise suffered a severe conflagration, so that nothing at all remained to the
wealthier inhabitants; and if anyone rescued anything from the fire, it was snatched away by thieves who pressed in. In the territory of Chartres, blood flowed
from a loaf that had been broken. The city of Bourges was also severely battered by hail at that time.

### 34. Of the disease of the dysentery and the death of Chilperic's sons

**[035]** These portents were followed by a most severe pestilence. While the kings were quarreling and again preparing civil war, dysentery spread through
nearly all Gaul. Those who suffered had a violent fever with vomiting, severe pain in the loins, and heaviness of the head or neck. What they brought up from
their mouths was saffron-colored or green. Many asserted that it was a hidden poison, while the country people called the pustules “coral pustules.” This is not
incredible, because cupping vessels applied to the shoulders or legs brought relief to many: blisters swelled and burst, the corrupt matter drained away, and
they were freed. Herbs that counteract poisons, when taken as drinks, also brought relief to many.

This illness began in the month of August and first seized small children and youths, laying them on their sickbeds. I lost sweet and beloved little children
whom I had cherished in my lap, carried in my arms, or fed with my own hand, nourishing them with the most attentive care by serving them food. But, wiping away
my tears, I say with blessed Job, “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so has it been done. Blessed be his name forever.”

At this time King Chilperic became gravely ill. When he recovered, his younger son, who had not yet been reborn by water and the Holy Spirit, fell sick. Seeing
that he was at the point of death, they washed him in baptism. When he improved slightly, his elder brother Chlodobert was seized by the same disease. His
mother Fredegund, seeing him in danger of death, repented too late and said to the king, “Divine goodness has long borne with us in our evil conduct. It has
often afflicted us with fevers and other troubles, but no amendment followed. Behold, we are now losing our sons. The tears of the poor, the laments of widows,
and the sighs of orphans are destroying them, and no hope remains for us to accumulate wealth for anyone. We store up treasure without knowing for whom we are
gathering it. Behold, our treasures remain without an owner, filled with plunder and curses. Were our storehouses not overflowing with wine? Were our granaries
not filled with grain? Were our treasuries not crammed with gold, silver, precious stones, necklaces, and the other ornaments of empire? Behold, we are losing
the fairest thing we possessed. Come now, if it pleases you: let us burn all the unjust tax registers, and let our treasury be content with what sufficed for
your father, King Chlothar.”

Having spoken, the queen beat her breast with her fists and ordered the registers that had come from her cities through Mark to be brought and thrown into the
fire. Turning again to the king, she said, “Why do you delay? Do as you have seen me do, so that even if we lose our sweet children, we may at least escape
perpetual punishment.” Then the king, stricken at heart, consigned all the tax registers to the flames. Once they had been burned, he sent men to prohibit
future assessments.

Afterward the younger child wasted away under the violence of the disease and died. With the deepest grief they carried him from the villa of Brinnacum to Paris
and ordered him to be buried in the basilica of Saint Denis. Chlodobert was placed on a bier and taken to Soissons, to the basilica of Saint Medard. They laid
him beside the holy tomb and made vows for him, but in the middle of the night, exhausted and faint, he breathed his last. They buried him in the basilica of
the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian. There was great lamentation among all the people: mourning men and women dressed in dark garments followed this funeral
as is customary at the funerals of husbands and wives. King Chilperic afterward distributed many gifts to churches, basilicas, and the poor.

### 35. Of Queen Austregild

**[036]** In these days Austrigildis, the queen of King Guntram, was carried off by this disease. Before she breathed out her wretched spirit, seeing that she
could not escape, she drew deep sighs and wished to have companions in her death, arranging that others’ funerals should be mourned at her own obsequies. It is
said that, in the manner of Herod, she made this request of the king: “I would still have had hope of living had I not perished at the hands of wicked
physicians, for the potions I received from them have violently taken away my life and caused me to lose this light swiftly. Therefore, so that my death may not
pass unavenged, I beg and adjure you with an oath that, as soon as I depart this light, those men be slaughtered by the sword. Just as I can live no longer, let
them not glory after my death; let there be one grief for our friends and theirs alike.” Having spoken, she yielded up her unhappy soul. When the customary
funeral rites had been completed, the king, constrained by his wicked wife’s oath, fulfilled her iniquitous command. He ordered the two physicians who had
attended her to be struck down by the sword. The judgment of many wise people was that this deed was not free from sin.

### 36. Of the bishop Heraclius and the count Nanthinus

**[037]** Count Nanthinus of Angoulême was also wasted by this disease and died. But his actions against priests and the churches of God require a fuller
account. His uncle Maracharius had long held the office of count in that city. When his term was completed, he joined the Church, became a cleric, and was
ordained bishop. He built and repaired churches and ecclesiastical houses with great vigilance. In the seventh year of his episcopate, enemies put poison in his
fish; he accepted it unsuspectingly and was cruelly killed. Divine mercy did not long leave his death unavenged. Frontonius, on whose advice the crime had been
committed, immediately took the episcopate, but God’s judgment overtook him and he died after occupying it for one year.

After Frontonius’s death, Heraclius, a priest of Bordeaux who had once served as an envoy of Childebert the Elder, was ordained bishop. Nanthinus sought the
office of count in that city in order to avenge his uncle’s death. Once he had obtained it, he inflicted many injuries on the bishop. He said, “You keep with
you the murderers who killed my uncle, and you admit to your table priests involved in this crime.” As the enmity grew, he gradually began to seize by force the
church estates that Maracharius had left by written testament, asserting that the Church ought not to acquire the property of a testator who had been killed by
its own clergy. Later, having killed some laymen, he went further: he seized a priest, bound him, and pierced him with a spear. While the priest still lived,
Nanthinus had his hands twisted behind his back and fastened him to a stake, seeking to force from him an admission that he had been involved in the affair. The
priest denied it and, as blood poured from the wound, gave up his spirit. The bishop, aroused by this, ordered Nanthinus to be barred from the doors of the
church.

When the bishops assembled at the city of Saintes, Nanthinus begged to obtain the bishop’s peace, promising to restore all the church property that he had
wrongfully taken and to show himself humble before the bishop. Heraclius, desiring to obey his brethren’s instructions, granted everything requested;
nevertheless, he commended the priest’s cause to almighty God and received the count back in charity. Nanthinus returned to the city and stripped, shattered,
and demolished the houses that he had wrongfully seized, saying, “Even if the Church recovers them, let it find them desolate.” The bishop was moved once more
and suspended him from communion. While these things were happening, the blessed bishop completed the course of his life and departed to the Lord.

A few months later Nanthinus was seized by the disease mentioned above, after some bishops had admitted him to communion in return for gifts and flattery.
Consumed by an intense fever, he cried out, “Alas, alas! I am being burned by Bishop Heraclius; I am tormented by him; I am summoned by him to judgment. I
acknowledge my crime; I remember that I unjustly inflicted injuries on the bishop. I beg for death, so that I may no longer be tormented by this torture.” As he
cried these words in the height of his fever, his bodily strength failed and he poured out his unhappy soul, leaving unmistakable evidence that this had
happened to him in vengeance for the blessed bishop. His lifeless body turned so black that one would have thought it had been burned over hot coals. Let
everyone be astonished at these things, marvel at them, and fear to inflict injuries on priests, for the Lord is the avenger of his servants who hope in him.

### 37. Of Martin of Galicia the bishop

**[038]** At this time the blessed Martin, bishop of Galicia, also died, causing great mourning among his people. He was born in Pannonia and, setting out from
there to visit the holy places of the East, became so learned that no one of his time was considered his superior. He then came to Galicia, where he was
ordained bishop while the relics of blessed Martin were being carried there. Having spent about thirty years in that episcopate, he departed to the Lord full of
virtues. He himself composed the verses over the southern door of the basilica of Saint Martin.

### 38. Of the persecution of the Christians in Spain

**[039]** There was a great persecution of Christians in Spain that year. Many were sent into exile, deprived of their property, wasted by hunger, imprisoned,
scourged, and slaughtered by various torments. The chief instigator of this crime was Goisuintha, whom King Leovigild had married after her union with King
Athanagild. Divine vengeance followed, and she who had branded God’s servants with the mark of humiliation was herself made notorious before all peoples: a
white cloud covered one of her eyes and drove from her eyelids the light that her mind did not possess.

King Leovigild had two sons by another wife. The elder had been betrothed to the daughter of Sigibert, King Chilperic’s younger brother. Ingund, King Sigibert’s
daughter, was sent to Spain with a great retinue and was received with much rejoicing by her grandmother Goisuintha. Goisuintha would not allow her to remain
long in the Catholic religion, but began to entice her with flattering words to be rebaptized into the Arian heresy. Ingund resisted courageously and said, “It
is enough that I was once washed from original sin in saving baptism and confessed the Holy Trinity in one equality. I declare that I believe this with my whole
heart, and I will never turn back from this faith.” On hearing this, Goisuintha burned with furious anger, seized the girl by the hair, and dashed her to the
ground. After kicking her for a long time until she was covered with blood, she ordered her to be stripped and plunged into a baptismal pool. But, as many
assert, Ingund never turned her mind away from our faith.

Leovigild gave the couple a city in which to reside and rule. When they had gone there, Ingund began to urge her husband to abandon the deceit of heresy and
acknowledge the truth of the Catholic law. He resisted for a long time, but at length, moved by her preaching, he was converted to the Catholic faith and
received the name John when he was anointed with chrism. When Leovigild heard this, he began seeking an opportunity to destroy him. Hermenegild understood this
and joined the emperor’s side, forming an alliance with the imperial general who was then attacking Spain. Leovigild sent messengers to him, saying, “Come to
me, for there are matters that we should discuss together.” Hermenegild replied, “I will not go, because you are hostile to me now that I am a Catholic.”
Leovigild then gave the emperor’s general thirty thousand solidi to withdraw his support and marched against his son with an army.

Hermenegild summoned the Greeks and went out against his father, leaving his wife in the city. When Leovigild approached from the opposite direction and
Hermenegild found himself abandoned by his allies and saw that he could accomplish nothing, he sought refuge in a nearby church, saying, “Let my father not come
upon me. It is unlawful for either a father to be killed by a son or a son by a father.” On hearing this, Leovigild sent Hermenegild’s brother to him. The
brother gave an oath that Hermenegild would not be humiliated and said, “Come yourself and prostrate yourself at our father’s feet, and he will forgive you
everything.” Hermenegild asked that his father be summoned. When Leovigild entered, Hermenegild prostrated himself at his feet. His father seized and kissed
him, soothed him with flattering words, and led him to the camp. Then, forgetting his oath, he signaled to his men, who seized Hermenegild, stripped him of his
garments, and dressed him in vile clothing. Leovigild returned to the city of Toledo, removed Hermenegild’s attendants, and sent him into exile with only one
young servant.

### 39. Of the death of Chlodovech

**[040]** After the death of his sons, King Chilperic, full of grief, withdrew with his wife to the forest of Cothia in the month of October. At the queen’s
instigation he sent his son Clovis to Brinnacum, evidently so that Clovis too might perish in the same destruction. The disease that had killed his brothers was
raging severely there at the time, but Clovis suffered no harm. The king himself then came to the villa of Cala in the city of Paris. A few days later he
ordered Clovis to come to him. I will not be reluctant to describe the manner of Clovis’s death.

While he was living with his father at the villa mentioned above, Clovis began to boast and speak immaturely: “Behold, my brothers are dead, and the whole
kingdom remains to me. All Gaul will be subject to me, and fate has granted me the entire empire. Behold, my enemies are in my hands, and I will inflict on them
whatever I please.” He also made unseemly disparaging remarks about his stepmother, Queen Fredegund. When she heard this, she was seized with overwhelming fear.
Some days later a certain man came and told the queen, “It is Clovis’s treachery that has caused you to sit bereaved of your sons. Desiring the daughter of one
of your servant women, he killed your sons through sorcery practiced by her mother. I warn you therefore not to expect anything better for yourself, now that
the hope through which you were to reign has been taken away.”

Terrified, inflamed with fury, and stricken by this fresh bereavement, the queen seized the girl whom Clovis had desired, had her severely beaten, ordered her
hair to be cut off, and commanded that she be fixed upon a split log in front of Clovis’s lodging. She also had the girl’s mother driven away and tortured for a
long time until she extorted from her a confession affirming that these allegations were true. Fredegund then reported these and similar things to the king and
demanded vengeance upon Clovis.

The king went hunting and ordered Clovis to be summoned secretly. When he arrived, Dukes Desiderius and Bobo seized him by the king’s command and placed him in
handcuffs. He was stripped of his weapons and clothing, covered with a vile garment, and brought in chains to the queen. She ordered him to be kept in custody,
wishing to force from him whether matters were as she had heard, whose advice he had followed, at whose instigation he had acted, and with whom he had formed
close friendships. He denied the other charges but disclosed friendships with many people.

After three days the queen ordered him to be taken in chains across the river Marne and guarded at a villa called Nocitum. While in custody there he was struck
with a knife and died, and he was buried in that very place. Meanwhile messengers came to the king saying that Clovis had pierced himself with his own blow, and
they affirmed that the knife with which he had struck himself was still fixed in the wound. King Chilperic was deceived by these words and did not weep for the
son whom he himself, so to speak, had delivered to death at the queen’s instigation.

Clovis’s servants were scattered in different directions. His mother was cruelly killed; his sister was sent to a monastery after being deceived by the queen’s
servants, and she remains there now, having taken the habit. All their wealth was transferred to the queen. The woman who had made the accusation against Clovis
was condemned to be burned alive. As she was being led away, the wretched woman began to cry out that she had spoken lies, but her words accomplished nothing.
She was tied to a stake and burned alive in the flames.

Clovis’s treasurer was brought back from Bourges by Chuppa, count of the stable, and sent in chains to the queen to be subjected to various tortures. But the
queen ordered him to be released from both punishment and chains, and at my intercession with the king she allowed him to go free.

### 40. Of the bishops Elafius and Eunius

**[041]** Afterward Elafius, bishop of Châlons, was sent as an envoy to Spain on business for Queen Brunhilda. Seized by a severe fever, he breathed his last;
his body was carried back and buried in his own city. Bishop Eunius, whose binding by the Bretons I mentioned above, was not permitted to return to his own
city, and the king ordered that he be maintained at public expense in Angers. When he came to Paris and was celebrating the sacred mysteries on the Lord’s day,
he uttered a cry like a whinny and fell to the ground. Blood poured from his mouth and nostrils, and he was carried away in men’s hands, but he recovered. He
was excessively devoted to wine and was often so disgracefully drunk that he could not walk.

### 41. Of the legates of Galicia and the prodigies

**[042]** Mir, king of Galicia, sent envoys to King Guntram. As they were passing through the territory of Poitiers, which King Chilperic then held, their
presence was reported to him. He ordered them to be brought before him under guard and kept in custody at Paris. At that time a wolf came from the woods into
the city of Poitiers and entered through a gate. The gates were closed, and it was trapped within the city walls and killed. Some people also asserted that they
had seen the sky on fire. The river Loire rose higher than in the previous year after the torrent of the Cher joined it. An exceedingly violent south wind blew,
flattening forests, tearing up houses, carrying away fences, and rolling people along until they were destroyed. Its path was about seven acres wide, but its
length could not be estimated. Cocks also often crowed loudly at the beginning of the night. The moon was eclipsed, and a comet appeared. A severe pestilence
among the people followed. After a year the Suebi envoys were released and returned home.

### 42. Of Maurilius bishop of Cahors

**[043]** Maurilius, bishop of the city of Cahors, was gravely ill with gout, but in addition to the pains caused by the disease itself he inflicted great
torments upon himself: he often pressed red-hot iron against his shins and feet in order to increase his suffering. Since many were seeking his episcopate, he
chose Ursicinus, who had once been referendary to Queen Ultrogotha. Maurilius asked that Ursicinus be consecrated while he himself still lived, and then
departed from this world.

Maurilius was very generous in almsgiving and deeply instructed in the ecclesiastical Scriptures. He could usually recite from memory the succession of the
various generations described in the books of the Old Testament, which many find difficult to retain. He was also just in judgment and defended the poor of his
church against the hands of wicked judges, according to the words of Job: “I delivered the poor from the hand of the powerful, and helped the needy who had no
helper. The mouth of the widow blessed me, for I was an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame, and a father to the helpless.”

### 43. Of the altercation with the heretic

**[044]** King Leovigild sent Agila as an envoy to Chilperic, a man endowed with no intelligence or capacity for ordered reasoning, but perverse in his will
concerning the Catholic faith. When his journey brought him to Tours, he began to provoke me about the faith and attack the doctrines of the Church. “The
sentence pronounced by the ancient bishops was unjust,” he said, “when it asserted that the Son is equal to the Father. How can he be equal to the Father in
power when he says, ‘The Father is greater than I’? It is not right that he should be considered like one to whom he declares himself inferior, for whom he
groans with the anguish of death, and to whom finally, as he dies, he commends his spirit as though possessing no power. It is therefore evident that he is
inferior to the Father in both age and power.”

I asked whether he believed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and whether he acknowledged him to be God’s wisdom, light, truth, life, and righteousness. He
replied, “I believe that the Son of God is all these things.” I said, “Then tell me when the Father was without wisdom, without light, without life, without
truth, or without righteousness. Just as the Father could not exist without these, neither could he exist without the Son. These attributes belong supremely to
the mystery of the Lord’s name. Nor would the Father be Father if he had no Son. As for your saying that he declared, ‘The Father is greater than I,’ know that
he said this from the humility of the flesh he assumed, so that you may understand that redemption was accomplished through humility, not through power. You who
say, ‘The Father is greater than I,’ ought to remember that elsewhere he says, ‘I and the Father are one.’ Both the fear of death and the commendation of the
spirit must be referred to the weakness of the body, so that he may be believed to be true man just as he is true God.”

He answered, “Whoever fulfills another’s will is also inferior to him. A son is always inferior to his father, because he does his father’s will, while the
father is not shown to do the son’s will.” I replied, “Understand that the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father always subsist in one Godhead. So that
you may know that the Father does the Son’s will, if evangelical faith remains in you, hear what our God Jesus himself said when he came to raise Lazarus:
‘Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may
believe that you sent me.’ And when he came to his Passion, he said, ‘Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.’ The
Father answered from heaven, ‘I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.’ The Son is therefore equal in the Godhead, not inferior and possessing
nothing less. For if you confess God, you must acknowledge him complete and lacking nothing; if you deny that he is truly complete, you do not believe him to be
God.”

He said, “Did God’s Son begin to be called such from the man he assumed? For there was a time when he did not exist.” I answered, “Hear David speaking in the
person of the Father: ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.’ And John the Evangelist says, ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with
God, and the Word was God.’ This Word was therefore made flesh and dwelt among us, and through him all things were made. Blinded by the poison of persuasion,
you people think nothing worthy of God.”

He asked, “Do you also call the Holy Spirit God and declare him equal to the Father and the Son?” I replied, “In the three there is one will, one power, and one
operation: one God in Trinity and threefold in unity; three persons, but one kingdom, one majesty, one power and omnipotence.” He said, “The Holy Spirit, whom
you proclaim equal to the Father and the Son, is understood to be inferior to both, because he is promised by the Son and described as sent by the Father. No
one promises anything unless it is subject to his own dominion, and no one sends anyone except an inferior, as the Son himself says in the Gospel: ‘Unless I go
away, the Paraclete will not come; but if I go, I will send him to you.’”

I answered, “The Son spoke rightly before his Passion, because unless he returned victorious to the Father and prepared in man, by redeeming the world with his
own blood, a dwelling worthy of God, the Holy Spirit, himself God, could not descend into a heart defiled by fanaticism and infected with the stain of original
sin. For Solomon says, ‘The Holy Spirit will flee deceit.’ If you have any hope of resurrection, do not speak against the Holy Spirit, because according to the
Lord’s sentence, ‘Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this world or in the world to come.’” He replied, “He who sends is
God; he who is sent is not God.”

I asked whether he believed the teaching of the apostles Peter and Paul. When he answered, “I believe it,” I added, “When the apostle Peter rebuked Ananias for
fraud concerning a field, consider what he said: ‘Why did you think to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men, but to God.’ And Paul, distinguishing
the degrees of spiritual gifts, says, ‘One and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills.’ One who does what he wills is
reduced to no one’s power. As I said above, you people think nothing rightly about the Holy Trinity, and the death of your own founder, Arius, demonstrated how
iniquitous is the perversity of this sect.”

He answered, “Do not blaspheme a law you do not observe. We do not believe what you believe, yet we do not blaspheme it, because it is not considered a crime if
both are worshipped. In common speech we say that it is not harmful if someone passing between pagan altars and God’s church venerates both.” Seeing his folly,
I said, “As I see, you show yourself both a defender of pagans and a champion of heretics, since you defile ecclesiastical doctrine and preach that the filth of
the pagans should be adored. You would do better if that faith armed you which Abraham saw at the oak, Isaac in the ram, Jacob in the stone, and Moses in the
bush; which Aaron bore on his breastplate, David exulted in with the timbrel, and Solomon preached in understanding; which all the patriarchs, the prophets, and
the law itself either sang in oracles or prefigured in sacrifices; and which our Martin, still present with us, now supports by his intercession, possesses in
his heart, and displays in his works. Then you too would be converted and believe in the inseparable Trinity; you would receive a blessing from me, your heart
would be purged of the poison of false belief, and your iniquities would be blotted out.”

Moved to fury and gnashing his teeth like a madman, he said, “May my soul escape from the bonds of this body before I receive a blessing from any priest of your
religion.” I answered, “May the Lord never allow my religion or faith to grow so lukewarm that I would distribute his holy things to dogs and offer the sacred
pearls of great price to filthy swine.” At this he abandoned the argument, rose, and departed. Afterward, when he had returned to Spain, he was weakened by
illness and, compelled by necessity, was converted to our religion.

### 44. Of what Chilperic wrote

**[045]** At the same time King Chilperic wrote a short treatise maintaining that the Holy Trinity should not be named with any distinction of persons, but only
as God. He asserted that it was unworthy to speak of God as a person in the way one speaks of a man of flesh, and affirmed that he who is the Father is also the
Son, and that he who is Father and Son is likewise the Holy Spirit. “Thus,” he said, “he appeared to the prophets and patriarchs, and thus the law itself
proclaimed him.” When he had ordered these things to be read to me, he said, “This is what I wish you and the other teachers of the churches to believe.”

I replied, “Abandon this belief, pious king. You ought to follow what the other teachers of the Church after the apostles have left me, what Hilary and Eusebius
taught, and what you yourself confessed at baptism.” The king angrily replied, “It is plain to me that in this matter I have Hilary and Eusebius as powerful
enemies.” I answered, “You ought to take care not to offend either God or his saints. Know that the Father is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit
another. Neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, but the Son, so that he who was the Son of God might also be called the son of a virgin for the
redemption of man. Neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit suffered, but the Son, so that he who had assumed flesh in the world might himself be offered for the
world. What you say about persons must be understood not corporeally but spiritually. In these three persons there is one glory, one eternity, and one power.”

Moved to anger, he said, “I will expound these things to men wiser than you, and they will agree with me.” I answered, “Anyone willing to follow what you
propose will never be wise, but foolish.” Gnashing his teeth, he fell silent. Not many days later, when Salvius, bishop of Albi, arrived, Chilperic ordered
these things to be recited to him and begged him to agree. Salvius rejected them so completely that, if he could have laid hands on the sheet in which they were
written, he would have torn it to pieces. The king accordingly abandoned this undertaking.

The same king wrote other books in verse, as though following Sedulius, but his verses did not conform in any respect to the rules of meter. He also added
letters to my alphabet—namely ō, as the Greeks have, æ, th, and uui—whose characters are these: Δ ϸ. He sent letters to all the cities of his kingdom directing
that boys be taught in this way and that books written in former times be smoothed with pumice and rewritten.

### 45. Of the death of Agroecula the bishop

**[046]** At this time Agroecula, bishop of Chalon, died. He was a very distinguished and prudent man of senatorial family. He erected many buildings in that
city, restored houses, and built a church, which he supported with columns, adorned with various marbles, and decorated with mosaic. He practiced great
abstinence: he never took luncheon, only dinner, and he sat at it at such a time that he rose while the sun was still above the horizon. He was not particularly
gracious, but very eloquent. He died in the forty-eighth year of his episcopate and the eighty-third year of his life. Flavus, King Guntram’s referendary,
succeeded him.

### 46. Of the death of Dalmatius the bishop

**[047]** At the same time Dalmatius, bishop of the city of Rodez, departed from this world. He was a man eminent in every holiness, abstinent in food and from
the desires of the flesh, very generous in almsgiving and kind to all, and steadfast in prayer and vigils. He built a church, but because he repeatedly
demolished it in order to improve it, he left it unfinished. After his death many sought the episcopate, as usually happens. The priest Transobadus, who had
formerly been his archdeacon, pursued it most actively, confident because he had entrusted his son to Gogo, who was then the king’s foster-father.

The bishop had drawn up a testament in which he specified what gift the king should receive after his death, and adjured them under terrible oaths that no
outsider, no greedy man, and no man bound by the marriage tie should be ordained in that church. Instead, a man free from all these things, occupied solely in
the praises of the Lord, was to be appointed. The priest Transobadus prepared a banquet for the clergy in that city. While they were reclining at table, one of
the priests began to revile the deceased bishop with shameful language and went so far as to call him deranged and foolish. As he was speaking, a cupbearer
arrived to offer him a drink. He took the cup, but as he brought it toward his mouth he began to tremble. The cup slipped from his hand, and leaning his head on
another priest beside him, he gave up his spirit. He was carried from the banquet to the grave and covered with earth. Afterward the bishop’s testament was set
aside, and Theodosius, who then held the archdeaconate of that city, was ordained bishop in the presence of King Childebert and his nobles.

### 47. Of the countship of Eunomius

**[048]** When Chilperic heard of all the evils that Leudast was inflicting on the churches of Tours and the entire population, he sent Ansovald there. Ansovald
arrived for Saint Martin’s festival and gave me and the people a choice, and Eunomius was raised to the office of count. Leudast, seeing himself removed, went
to Chilperic and said, “Until now, most pious king, I have guarded the city of Tours. Now that I have been removed from office, see how it will be guarded. Know
that Bishop Gregory intends to deliver it to Sigibert’s son.” On hearing this, the king replied, “By no means. You are adding these accusations because you have
been removed.” Leudast answered, “The bishop says still worse things about you. He says that your queen is committing adultery with Bishop Berthram.” The king
was enraged and ordered Leudast to be beaten with fists and heels, loaded with irons, and shut up in prison.

### 48. Of the malice of Leudast

**[049]** Since this book demands an ending, I wish to relate something of Leudast’s actions, but first it seems appropriate to describe his family, native
country, and character. There is an island near Poitiers called Gracina, where he was born to a slave named Leuchadius who belonged to a royal vine-grower.
Summoned from there to service, he was assigned to the royal kitchen. Because his eyes were sore in his youth and could not endure the harshness of the smoke,
he was removed from the pestle and promoted to the bread-basket. But while pretending to delight in working the kneaded masses of dough, he ran away and
abandoned his service. Brought back from flight two or three times and unable to be restrained from running away again, he was punished by having one ear slit.
Later, unable by any means to conceal the mark inflicted on his body, he fled to Queen Marcoveifa, whom King Charibert loved excessively and had taken to his
bed in place of her sister. She received him gladly, promoted him, and appointed him keeper of her finest horses.

Now possessed by vanity and given over to pride, he sought the office of count of the stables. Once he had obtained it, he despised and neglected everyone, was
inflated with vanity, dissolute in luxury, inflamed with greed, and was carried here and there as his patroness’s own fosterling in her affairs. After her
death, enriched with estates, he offered gifts to King Charibert and retained the same position. Afterward, when the sins of the people brought their
consequences, he was appointed count of Tours. There he boasted still more with the arrogant pride of glorious honor, showing himself rapacious in plunder,
swollen with quarrels, and filthy with adulteries. By sowing discord and bringing false accusations, he amassed considerable treasures.

After Charibert’s death, when that city had fallen to Sigibert’s share, Leudast went over to Chilperic, and all that he had unjustly accumulated was plundered
by the adherents of the king I have named. When King Chilperic invaded the city of Tours through his son Theudebert, I had already come to Tours, and Theudebert
strongly commended Leudast to me so that he might obtain the office of count he had previously held. Leudast made himself exceedingly humble and submissive
toward me, repeatedly swearing over the holy bishop’s tomb that he would never act contrary to the order of reason and that he would be faithful to me in all
things, both in my own affairs and in the needs of the Church. For he feared what later happened, namely that King Sigibert might again bring that city under
his own dominion. After Sigibert died and Chilperic again succeeded to the kingdom, Leudast entered upon the office of count. When Merovech came to Tours,
however, he plundered all Leudast’s property wherever it could be found. Leudast himself had hidden in Brittany during the two years when Sigibert held Tours.

Once he had obtained the countship, as I have said, he was carried away by such fickleness that he would enter the church house wearing a breastplate and coat
of mail, girt with a quiver, carrying a spear in his hand, and with a helmet on his head. He felt safe from no one because he was hostile to everyone. If he sat
in judgment with elders, whether laymen or clergy, and saw anyone pursuing justice, he would immediately fly into a rage and belch out insults against the
citizens. He ordered priests to be dragged out in handcuffs and soldiers to be beaten with clubs, exercising a cruelty that can scarcely be described. When
Merovech, who had plundered his property, departed, Leudast became my accuser, falsely asserting that Merovech had followed my advice in taking his possessions.
But after inflicting these losses he again swore oaths and gave the pall from blessed Martin’s tomb as surety that he would never oppose me.

### 49. Of the snares which he made for us

**[050]** It would take too long to recount in order all Leudast’s perjuries and other evil deeds. Let me come instead to the way he tried to supplant me with
unjust and abominable calumnies, and the way divine vengeance descended upon him, fulfilling the words, “Everyone who supplants will be supplanted,” and again,
“He who digs a pit will fall into it.”

After the many evils he inflicted on me and mine, and after many plunderings of ecclesiastical property, he joined to himself the priest Riculf, a man perverted
by similar malice, and went so far as to say that I had alleged a crime against Queen Fredegund. He asserted that if my archdeacon Plato or my friend Galienus
were subjected to punishment, they would certainly prove that I had spoken these words. The king was enraged and, as I said above, ordered Leudast to be beaten
with fists and heels, loaded with chains, and shut up in prison. Leudast claimed that he had the cleric Riculf through whom I was supposed to have spoken.

This Riculf, a subdeacon equally prone to fickleness, had taken counsel with Leudast about the affair a year earlier and sought grounds for taking offense, so
that he might take offense at me and go over to Leudast. Having finally found them, he went to Leudast, prepared every deceit and snare for four months, and
then returned to me with Leudast himself, begging me to receive him back with his pardon. I confess that I did so, and publicly received a secret enemy into my
house. When Leudast departed, Riculf prostrated himself at my feet and said, “Unless you help me quickly, I am going to perish. Behold, at Leudast’s instigation
I have said what I ought not to have said. Send me away to another kingdom; if you do not, I will be seized by the royal officers and suffer mortal punishment.”
I answered, “If you have uttered anything contrary to reason, your word will fall upon your own head. I will not send you to another kingdom, lest I become
suspect in the king’s eyes.”

Leudast then became Riculf’s accuser, saying that he had heard the aforementioned statements from the subdeacon Riculf. Riculf was again placed in chains and
committed to custody, while Leudast was released. Riculf said that Galienus and the archdeacon Plato had been present on the day when the bishop uttered these
words. Meanwhile the priest Riculf, who had already received Leudast’s promise of the episcopate, was so elated that he equaled the pride of Simon Magus.
Although he had sworn an oath to me three times or more over Saint Martin’s tomb, on the Friday of Easter week he assailed me with such insults and spitting
that he could scarcely keep his hands off me, confident in the snare he had prepared.

The next day, Holy Saturday itself, Leudast came to the city of Tours. Pretending to be engaged in other business, he seized the archdeacon Plato and Galienus,
bound them in chains, and ordered them to be led to the queen chained and stripped of their clothing. When I heard this while sitting in the church house, sad
and troubled, I entered the oratory and took up the book of David’s songs, hoping that when opened it would offer some verse of consolation. There I found: “He
led them forth in hope, and they were not afraid; and the sea covered their enemies.” Meanwhile the prisoners entered the river on the bridge, which was
supported by two boats. The boat carrying Leudast sank, and had he not saved himself by swimming, he might have perished with his companions. The other boat,
which was lashed to it and carried the prisoners, was held up above the water by God’s help.

The prisoners were brought before the king and vehemently accused, so that they might be sentenced to death. But the king reconsidered, released them from their
chains, and kept them unharmed under free custody. Duke Berulf and Count Eunomius came to Tours and invented a story that King Guntram wished to capture the
city. They said that the city must therefore be secured by guards to prevent any negligence. They deceitfully posted guards at the gates who, while pretending
to protect the city, were actually guarding me. They also sent men to advise me to take the church’s finest possessions and flee secretly to Auvergne, but I did
not consent.

The king summoned the bishops of his kingdom and ordered the case to be diligently examined. While the cleric Riculf was repeatedly questioned in secret and
spread many falsehoods against me and mine, a certain carpenter named Modestus said to him, “You wretched man, why do you stubbornly devise these things against
your bishop? It would be better for you to be silent, seek the bishop’s pardon, and obtain his favor.” Riculf began to shout aloud, “Here is the man who orders
me to be silent so that I may not pursue the truth! Here is the queen’s enemy, who will not allow the charge against her to be investigated!” This was
immediately reported to the queen. Modestus was seized, tortured, scourged, bound in chains, and placed in custody. Held in chains and stocks between two
guards, at midnight, while the guards slept, he poured out a prayer to the Lord, begging him to deign in his power to visit the wretched man, and asking that he
who had been bound though innocent might be released through the visitation of bishops Martin and Medard. Soon his bonds burst apart, the stocks broke, the door
opened, and while I was keeping vigil at night he entered the basilica of Saint Medard.

The bishops assembled at the villa of Brinnacum and were ordered to sit together in one house. The king then arrived, greeted everyone, received a blessing, and
sat down. Berthram, bishop of the city of Bordeaux, who had been implicated in this charge with the queen, presented the case and challenged me, saying that I
had alleged the crime against him and the queen. I truthfully denied having said it, though I acknowledged that I had heard others say it, not that I had
invented it. Outside the house there was a great outcry among the people: “Why are these charges brought against God’s priest? Why does the king pursue such
things? Could the bishop have said such things even about a slave? Alas, alas, Lord God, give help to your servant!”

The king said, “A charge against my wife is regarded as a reproach to me. If you judge that witnesses should be produced against the bishop, behold, they are
here. But if you decide that this should not be done and that the matter should be committed to the bishop’s word, say so; I will willingly hear your
instructions.” Everyone marveled at the king’s prudence and patience. When all declared, “An inferior person cannot be believed against a priest,” the
resolution was that Masses should be celebrated at three altars and that I should clear myself of these words by an oath. Although this was contrary to the
canons, it was nevertheless carried out for the king’s sake. I will not conceal that Queen Rigunthis, sharing my distress, fasted with her entire household
until a servant brought word that I had fulfilled everything exactly as prescribed.

The bishops then returned to the king and said, “The bishop has fulfilled everything that was commanded. What now remains for you, O king, except to deprive
Berthram, his brother’s accuser, of communion?” Berthram answered, “I have only reported what I heard.” When they asked who had told him, he replied that he had
heard it from Leudast. Leudast, true to the weakness of his counsel and purpose, had already fled. All the bishops then resolved that the sower of scandal,
defamer of the queen, and accuser of the bishop should be barred from every church because he had withdrawn himself from the hearing. They sent a subscribed
letter to the other bishops who had not been present, and each returned to his own place.

When Leudast heard this, he sought refuge in the basilica of Saint Peter at Paris. But when he heard the king’s edict that no one in his kingdom should shelter
him, and especially when he learned that his son whom he had left at home had died, he came secretly to Tours and transferred his best possessions to Berry. The
king’s servants pursued him, but he escaped by flight. His wife was captured and confined in exile in the district of Tournai. The cleric Riculf was condemned
to death. I with difficulty obtained his life, but could not secure exemption from torture. No object and no metal could have endured such blows as this most
wretched man. From the third hour of the day he hung suspended from a tree with his hands tied behind his back. At the ninth hour he was taken down, stretched
on the rack, and beaten with clubs, rods, and doubled leather straps, not by one or two men, but by as many torturers as could crowd around his wretched limbs.
When he was at the point of death, he revealed the truth and publicly laid bare the secrets of the plot. He said that the charge had been brought against the
queen so that she might be expelled from the kingdom; then, after her brothers and father had been killed, Clovis would obtain the kingdom, Leudast the duchy,
and the priest Riculf—who had been Clovis’s friend since the time of blessed Bishop Eufronius—would seek the episcopate of Tours, having promised the
archdeaconate to the cleric Riculf.

When I returned to Tours by God’s grace, I found the church thrown into confusion by the priest Riculf. Under Bishop Eufronius he had been advanced from among
the poor and ordained archdeacon; subsequently promoted to the presbyterate, he had withdrawn to his own property. He was always elated, inflated, and
presumptuous. While I was still staying with the king, he impudently entered the church house as though he were already bishop, inventoried the church’s silver,
and brought its remaining property under his own authority. He enriched the senior clergy with gifts, bestowed vineyards, and distributed meadows, but afflicted
the junior clergy with many blows from clubs and even with his own hand, saying, “Acknowledge your lord, who has obtained victory over his enemies and whose
genius has cleansed the city of Tours of the people of Auvergne.” The wretch did not know that, apart from five bishops, all the others who have held the
episcopate of Tours were related to the stock of my ancestors. He often used to tell his intimates that a prudent man could be deceived only by perjuries.

Even after my return he continued to despise me. He did not come to greet me as the other citizens had done, but rather threatened to kill me. On the advice of
the provincials I ordered him to be removed to a monastery. When he was being strictly confined there, messengers from Bishop Felix, who had supported the
affair mentioned above, intervened. The abbot was circumvented by perjuries, and Riculf escaped and went to Bishop Felix, who eagerly received a man whom he
ought to have abhorred.

Leudast meanwhile went to Berry, taking with him all the treasures he had stripped from the poor. Not long afterward the men of Berry, together with the local
judge, rushed upon him and took all the gold, silver, and other things he had brought, leaving him nothing but what he wore. They would have taken his life as
well had he not escaped by flight. Recovering his strength, he returned with some men of Tours and attacked his robbers, killed one, recovered part of the
property, and came back to the Touraine. When Duke Berulf heard this, he sent his servants with arms to seize him. Seeing that capture was imminent, Leudast
abandoned his possessions and sought refuge in the basilica of Saint Hilary at Poitiers. Duke Berulf sent the captured property to the king. Leudast would leave
the basilica, burst into various people’s houses, and openly carry off plunder. He was also often caught in adultery in the holy portico itself. The queen,
indignant that a place consecrated to God should be polluted in this way, ordered him to be expelled from the holy basilica. Once expelled, he went back to his
hosts in Berry and begged them to hide him.

### 50. What the blessed Salvius foretold of Chilperic

**[051]** Although I ought to have mentioned above my conversation with the blessed bishop Salvius, it escaped my mind, and I do not consider it sacrilegious to
write it down afterward. After the synod mentioned above, when I had already taken leave of the king and wished to return home, I resolved not to depart until I
had kissed this man and taken leave of him. I looked for him and found him in the atrium of the house at Brinnacum. I told him that I was now about to return
home. We withdrew a short distance, and while we were conversing he said to me, “Do you see above this roof what I behold?” I answered, “I see the new roofing
that the king recently ordered to be put on.” He asked, “Do you see nothing else?” I replied, “I see nothing else.” I suspected that he was speaking jokingly,
and added, “If you see something more, describe it.” Drawing a deep sigh, he said, “I see the drawn sword of divine wrath hanging over this house.” The priest’s
words did not prove false, for twenty days later the king’s two sons, whose deaths I described above, died.

HERE ENDS THE FIFTH BOOK, COMPLETED IN THE FIFTH YEAR OF KING CHILDEBERT’S REIGN.


## Praefatio

**[001]** Taedit me bellorum civilium diversitatis, que Francorum gentem et regnum valde proterunt, memorare; in quo, quod peius est, tempore illud quod Dominus
de dolorum praedixit initium iam videmus: Consurgit pater in filium, filius in patrem, frater in fratrem, proximus in propinquum. Debebant enim eos exempla
anteriorum regum terrere, qui, ut divisi, statim ab inimicis sunt interempti. Quotiens et ipsa urbs urbium et totius mundi capud ingens bella civilia diruit;
quae cessante, rursum quasi ab humo surrexit. Utinam et vos, o regis, in his proelia, in quibus parentes vestri desudaverunt, exercimini, ut gentes, vestra pace
conterritae, vestris viribus praemirentur! Recordamini, quid capud victuriarum vestrarum Chlodovechus fecerit, qui adversos reges interficet, noxias gentes
elisit, patrias subiugavit, quarum regnum vobis integrum inlesumque reliquit! Et cum hoc facerit, neque aurum neque argentum, sicut nunc est in thesauris
vestris, habebat. Quid agetis? Quid quaeritis? Quid non habundatis? In domibus dilitiae supercrescunt, in prumtuariis vinum, triticum oleumque redundat, in
thesauris aurum atque argentum coacervatur. Unum vobis deest, quod, pacem non habentes, Dei gratiam indegetis. Cur unus tollit alteri suum? Cur alter
concupiscit alienum? Cavete illo, quaeso, apostoli: Si ab invicem mordetis et comeditis, vidite, ne ab invicem consummamini. Scrutamini diligenter veterum
scripta, et videbitis, quid civilia bella parturiant. Requirite, quod de Carthaginensibus scribat Orhosius, qui, cum post septingentos annos subversam dicat
civitatem et regionem eorum, addidit: Quae res eam tamdiu servavit? Concordia. Quae res eam post tanta distruxit tempora? Discordia. Cavete discordiam, cavete
bella civilia, quae vos populumque vestrum expugnant. Quid aliud sperandum erit, nisi cum exercitus vester caeciderit, vos sine solatio relicti atque a gentibus
adversis oppressi protinus conruatis? Si tibi, o rex, bellum civili delectat, illut quod apostolus in hominem agi meminit exerce, ut spiritus concupiscat
adversus carnem et vitia virtutibus caedant; et tu liber capite tuo, id est Christo, servias, qui quondam radicem malorum servieras conpeditus.

## 1. De Childeberthi iunioris regno et matre eius.

**[002]** Igitur interempto Sigybertho rege apud Victuriacum villam, Brunichildis regina cum filiis Parisius resedebat. Quod factum cum ad eam perlatum fuisset
et, conturbata dolore aclucto, quid ageret ignoraret, Gundovaldusduxadpraehensum Childeberthum, filium eius parvolum, furtim abstulit ereptumque ab immenente
morte, collectisque gentibus super quas pater eius regnum tenuerat, regem instituit, vix lustro aetatis uno iam peracto. Qui die dominici natalis regnare
coepit. Anno igitur primo regni eius Chilpericus rex Parisius venit adpraehensamque Brunichildem apud Rodomaginsem civitatem in exilio trusit thesaurisque eius,
quos Parisius detulerat, abstulit; filias vero eius Meledus urbe tenire praecipit. Tunc Roccolenus cum Cinomannicis Toronus venit et praedas egit et multa
scelera fecit, quod in sequenti, qualiter a virtute beati Martini pro tantis malis quae gessit percussus interiit, memoramus.

## 2. Quod Merovechus Brunechilde accepit.

**[003]** Chilpericus vero filium suum Merovechum cum exercitu Pectavus dirigit. At ille, relictam ordinationem patris, Toronus venit ibique et dies sanctos
paschae tenuit. Multum enim regionem illam exercitus eius vastavit. Ipsi vero simolans ad matrem suam ire velle, Rodomago petiit; et ibi Brunichilde reginae
coniungitur, ea quoque sibi in matrimonio sociavit. Haec audiens Chilpericus, quod scilicet contra fas legemque canonicam uxorem patrui accepisset, valde amarus
dicto citius ad supra memoratum oppidum dirigit. At ille, cum haec cognovissent, quod eosdem separare decernerit, ad basilicam sancti Martini, quae super murus
civitatis ligneis tabulis fabrecata est, confugium faciunt. Rex vero adveniens, cum in multis ingeniis eos exinde auferre niteretur et illi, dolosae eum
potantes facere, non crederent, iuravit eis, dicens: 'Si', inquid, 'voluntas Dei foret, ipse hos separare non conaretur'. Haec illi sacramenta accipientes, de
basilica egressi sunt; exosculatisque et dignanter acceptis, epulavit cum eis. Post dies vero paucus adsumpto secum rex Merovecho Sessionas rediit.

## 3. Bellum contra Chilpericum, et de malitia Rauchingi.

**[004]** Cum autem ibidem commorarentur, collecti aliqui de Campania Sessionas urbe adgrediuntur, fugatamque ex ea Fredegundem regina atque Chlodovechum,
filium Chilperici, volebant sibi subdere civitatem. Quod ut Chilpericus rex conperit, cum exercitu illuc dirigit, mittens nuntius, ne sibi iniuriam facerent et
excidium de utroque eveniret exercitu. Illi autem haec neglegentes, praeparantur ad bellum; commissoque proelio, invaluit pars Chilperici atque fugavit partem
sibi adversam, multus ex ea strenuos atque utilis viros prosternens; fugatusque reliquos, Sessionas ingreditur. Quae postquam acta sunt, rex propter
coniugatione Brunichildis suspectum habere coepit Merovechum, filium suum, dicens, hoc proelium eius nequitia surrexisse; spoliatumque ab armis, datis
custodibus, libere custodire praecipit, tractans, quid de eo in posterum ordinaret. Godinus autem, qui a sorte Sigyberthi se ad Chilpericum transtulerat et
multis ab eo muneribus locopletatus est, caput belli istius fuit; sed in campo victus, primus fuga dilabitur. Villas vero, quas ei rex a fisco in territurio
Sessionico indulserat, abstulit et basilicae contulit beati Medardi. Ipse quoque Godinus non post multum tempus repentina morte praeventus, interiit. Cuius
coniugem Rauchingus accepit, vir omni vanitate repletus, superbia tumidus, elatione protervus, qui se ita cum subiectis agebat, ut non cognusceret in se aliquid
humanitatis habere, sed ultra modum humanae malitiae atque stultitiae in suos deseviens, nefanda mala gerebat. Nam si ante eum, ut adsolet, convivio utenti puer
cereum tenuisset, nudari eius tibias faciebat atque tamdiu in his cereum comprimi, donec lumine privaretur; iterum cum inluminatus fuisset, similiter faciebat,
usque dum totae tibiae famuli tenentes exurirentur. Quod si vocem emittere aut se de loco illo alia in parte movere conatus fuisset, nudus ilico gladius
imminibat, fiebatque, ut, hoc flente, iste magna laetitia exultaret. Aiebant enim quidam, quod eo tempore duo de famulis eius, ut sepe contingit, mutuo se amore
dilixisse, virum scilicet et puella. Cumque haec dilectio per duorum annorum aut eo amplius spatio traheretur, coniuncti pariter aeclesiam petierunt. Quod cum
Rauchingus conperisset, accedit ad sacerdotem loci; rogat, sibi protinus reddi suos famulos excusatus. Tunc sacerdos ait ad eum: 'Nosti enim, quae veneratio
debeat inpendi aeclesiis Dei; non enim poteris eos accepere, nisi ut fidem facias de permanente eorum coniunctione; similiter et ut de omni poena corporali
liberi maneant repromittas'. At ille, cum diu ambiguus cogitatione siluisset, tandem conversus ad sacerdotem, posuit manus suas super altarium cum iuramento,
dicens, quia: 'Numquam erunt a me separandi, sed potius ego faciam, ut in hacconiunctionepermaneant, quia, quamquam mihi molestum fuerit, quod absque mei
consilii coniventia ista sint gesta, illud tamen libens amplectur, quod nec hic ancillam alterius neque haec extranei servum acceperit'. Crededit sacerdus illi
simpliciter promissionem hominis callidi reddeditque hominis excusatos. Quibus ille acceptis et gratias agens, abscessit ad domum suam. Et statim iussit elidere
arborem truncatamque colomnam eius per capita cuneo scissam praecipit excavare; effossamque in altitudine trium aut quattuor pedum humum, deponi vas iubet in
foveam. Ibique puellam ut mortuam conponens, puerum desuper iactare praecipit, positoque operturium, fossam humo replevit sepelivitque eos viventes, dicens,
quia: 'Non frustravi iuramentum meum, ut non separarentur hi in sempiternum'. Qui cum sacerdote nuntiata fuissents, cucurrit velociter; et increpans hominem,
vix obtenuit, ut detegerentur. Verumtamen puerum vivum extraxit, puellam vero repperit suffocatam. In talibus enim operibus valde nequissimus erat, nullam
habens aliam potius utilitatem, nisi in caccinnis ac dolis omnibusque perversis rebus. Unde non inmerito taliter excessit a vita, qui talia gessit, cum
frueretur hanc vitam; quod in posterum degesturi sumus. Siggo quoque referendarius, qui anolum regis Sigyberthi tenuerat et ab Chilperico rege ita provocatus
erat, ut servitium, quod tempore fratris sui habuerat, obteneret, ad Childeberthum regem, Sigyberthi filium, relicto Chilperico, transivit resque eius, quas in
Sessionico habuerat, Ansovaldus obtinuit. Multi autem et alii de his, qui se de regno Sigyberthi ad Chilpericum tradiderant, recesserunt. Uxor quoque Siggonis
non post multum temporis spatio obiit; sed ille aliam rursus accepit.

## 4. Quod Roccolenus Toronus venit.

**[005]** His diebus Roccolenus, ab Chilperico missus, Toronus advenit cum magna iactantia, et ultra Legerem castra ponens, nuntios ad nos dirixit, ut scilicit
Gunthchramnum, qui tunc de morte Theudoberthi inpetebatur, a basilica sancta deberemus extrahere. Quod si non facerimus, et civitatem et omnia suburbana eius
iuberet incendio concremare. Quo auditu, mittimus ad eum legationem, dicentes, haec ab antiquo facta non fuisse, quae hic fieri deposcebat, sed nec modo
permitti posse, ut basilica sancta violaretur; quod si fierit, nec sibi fore prosperum nec rege, qui haec iussa mandasset; metueretque magis sanctitatem
antestetis, cuius virtus hesterna die paralitica membra dirixisset. Nihil his ille furmidans, cum in domo aeclesiae ultra Legerem resederet, domum ipsam, quae
clavis adfixerat, dissecet. Ipsos quoque clavos Caenomannici, qui tunc cum eodem advenerant, inpletis follibus portant, annonas evertunt et cuncta devastant.
Sed dum haec Roccolenus agit, a Deo percutitur, morboque regio croceus effectus, mandata aspera remittit, dicens: 'Nisi hodie proieceritis Gunthchramnum ducem
de basilica, ita cuncta virentia quae sunt circa urbem atteram, ut dignus fiat aratro locus ille'. Interim advenit dies sanctus epifaniae; et hic magis ac magis
torquere coepit. Tunc accepto a suis consilio, amne transacto, ad civitatem accedit. Denique cum psallentes de ęclesiam egressi, ad sanctam basilicam
properarent, hic post crucem, praecidentibus signis, aequo superpositus ferebatur. Verum ubi basilicam sanctam introit, mox furor minantis intepuit;
regressusque ad eclesiam, nihil cibi ea die accipere potuit. Exinde cum valde anillus esset, Pectavo abiit. Erant enim dies sanctae quadraginsimae, in qua fetus
cunicolorum saepe comedit. Dispositis vero actionibus, quibus in Kalendas Martias cives Pectavus vel adfligeret vel damnaret, pridie animam reddedit; et sic
superbia tumorque quievit.

## 5. De episcopis Lingonicis.

**[006]** Eo tempore Felix Namneticae urbis episcopus litteras mihi scripsit plenas opprobriis, scribens etiam fratrem meum ob hoc interfectum, eo quod ipse
cupidus episcopati episcopum interfecisset. Sed ut haec scriberet, villam ecclesiae concupivit. Quam cum dare nollem, evomit in me, ut dixi, plenus furore
opprobria mille. Cui aliquando ego respondi: 'Memento dicti prophetici: Vae his qui iungunt domum ad domum et agrum ad agrum copulant! Numquid soli inhabitabunt
terram? O si te habuisset Massilia sacerdotem! Numquam naves oleum aut reliquas species detulissent, nisi caitam tantum, quo maiorem oportunitatem scribendi ad
bonos infamandos haberes. Sed paupertas cartae finem inponit verbositati'. Inmensae enim erat cupiditatis atque iactantiae. Sed ego ista postponens, ne illi
similis appaream, illud explicabo, qualiter germanus meus ab hac luce migraverit, et quam velocem in percussorem eius Dominus praestiterit ultionem.
Consenescente beato Tetrico ecclesiae Lingonicae sacerdote, cum Lampadio diacono, quem creditorem habuit, deicisset et frater meus, dum pauperibus, quos ille
male spoliaverat, opitulare cupiens, consensisset in eius humiliatione, odium ex hoc incurrit. Interea beatus Tetricus a sanguine sauciatur. Cui cum nulla
medicorum fomenta valerent, conturbati clerici et a pastore utpote destituti, Mundericum expetunt. Qui a rege indultus ac tonsoratus, episcopus ordinatur, sub
ea specie, ut, dum beatus Tetricus viveret, hic Ternoderinsim castrum ut archipresbiter regerit atque in eo commoraretur, migrante vero decessore, iste
succederet. In quo castro dum habitaret, iram regis incurrit. Adserebatur enim contra eum, quod ipse Sigibertho regi adversus fratrem suum Guntchramnum venienti
alimenta et munera praebuisset. Igitur extractus a castro, in exilio super ripam Rhodani in turre quadam arta atque detecta retruditur; in qua per duos fere
annos cum grandi exitu commoratus, obtinente beato Nicetio episcopo, Lugduno regreditur habitavitque cum eo per duos menses. Sed cum obtinere non posset a rege,
ut in loco, unde eiectus fuerat, restitueretur, nocte per fugam lapsus, ad Sigiberti regnum pertransiit et apud Arisitensim vicum episcopus instituetur, habens
sub se plus minus dioceses XV, quas primum quidem Gothi tenuerant, nunc vero Dalmatius Rutenensis episcopus iudicat. Quo abeunte, iterum Lingonici Silvestrum,
propinquum vel nostrum vel beati Tetrici, episcopum expetunt. Sed ut eum peterent, fratris mei hoc instinctu fecerunt. Interea transeunte beato Tetrico, hic,
tonso capite, presbiter ordinatur, accepta omni potestate de rebus ecclesiae. Qui vero, ut benedictionem episcopalem Lugduno accipiat,' iter parat. Quae dum
aguntur, ipse, quia iam diu epilenticus erat, ab hoc morbo correptus, asperius ex sensu factus et per dies duos assiduae dans mugitum, tertia die spiritum
exalavit. Quae peracta, Lampadius, ut superius dictum est, ab honore et facultate privatus, in odio Petri diaconi cum filio Silvestri coniungitur, machinans
atque confirmans, patrem suum ab ipso fuisse maleficiis interfectum. At ille aetate iuvenis, sensu levis contra eum commovetur, ipsum inpetens publice
parricidam. Porro ille haec audiens, facto placito in praesentia sancti Niceti episcopi, avunculi matris meae, Lugduno dirigitur; et ibi, Siagrio episcopo coram
adstante vel aliis sacerdotibus multis cum saecularium principibus, se sacramento exuit, numquam se in morte Silvestri mixtum fuisse. Post duos vero annos
instigatus iterum a Lampadio filius Silvestri, adsecutus in via Petrum diaconum, lancea sauciatum interfecit. Quod cum factum fuisset, de eo loco elevatus et ad
Divionensim delatus castrum, secus sanctum Gregorium, proavum nostrum, sepelitur. Iste vero fugam iniens, ad Chilpericum regem transiit, facultatibus suis fisco
regis Guntchramni dimissis. Cumque per diversa vagaretur pro commisso scelere nec ei essit locus firmus ad commorandum, tandem, ut credo, contra eum sanguine
insonte ad divinam potentiam proclamante, in quodam loco, dum iter ageret, innocentem hominem evaginato gladio interemit. Cuius parentes condolentes propinqui
exitum, commota seditione, extractis gladiis, eum in frustra concidunt membratimque dispergunt. Tale iusto iudicio Dei exitum miser accepit, ut, qui propinquum
innocentem interimerat, ipse nocens diutius non maneret. Nam tertio ei haec evenerunt anno. Denique Silvestri post transitum Lingonici iterum episcopum
flagitantes, Pappolum, qui quondam archidiaconus Agustidunensis fuerat, accipiunt. Qui multa, ut asserunt, egit iniqua, quae a nobis praetermittuntur, ne
detractores fratrum esse videamur. Tamen, quale habuerit exitum, non omittam. Anno octavo episcopatus sui, dum dioceses ac villas ecclesiae circuiret, quadam
nocte dormienti apparuit beatus Tetricus vultu minaci. Cui ita: 'Quid tu', inquit, 'hic Pappole? Ut quid sedem meam polluis? Ut quid ecclesiam pervadis? Ut quid
oves mihi creditas sic dispergis? Cede loco, relinque sedem, abscede longius a regione'. Et haec dicens, virgam quam habebat in manu pectori eius cum ictu
valido inpulit. In quo ille evigilans, dum cogitat, quid hoc esset, ficta in loco illo defigitur ac dolore maximo cruciatur. Abhorret cibum potumque et mortem
iam sibi proximam praestolatur. Quid plura? Tertia die, cum sanguinem ore proicerit, exspiravit; exinde elatus, Lingonas est sepultus. In cuius loco Mummolus
abba, quem Bonum cognomento vocant, episcopus substituitur. Quem multi magnis laudibus prosecuntur: esse eum castum, sobrium, moderatum ac in omni bonitate
promptissimum, amantem iustitiam, caritatem omni intentione diligentem. Qui, accepto episcopatu, cognoscens, quod Lampadius multum de rebus fraudasset ecclesiae
ac de spoliis pauperum agros vineasque vel mancipia congregasset, eum ab omni re nudatum a praesentia sua iussit abigi. Qui nunc in maxima paupertate degens,
manibus propriis victum quaerit. Haec de his sufficiant.

## 6. De Leunaste archidiacono Bitorigo.

**[007]** Anno vero quo supra, id est quo, mortuo Sigybertho, Childeberthus, filius eius, regnare coepit, multae virtutes ad sepulchrum beati Martini
apparuerunt, quas in illis libellis scripsi, quos de ipsis miraculis conponere temptavi. Et licet sermone rustico, tamen celare passus non sum, quae aut ipse
vidi aut a fidelibus relata cognovi. Hic tantum, quid neglegentibus evenerit, qui post virtutem caelestem terrena medicamenta quaesierunt, exsolvam, quia, sicut
per gratiam sanitatum, ita et in castigationem stultorum virtus eius ostenditur. Leonastis Biturigus archidiaconus, decedentibus cataractis, lumen caruit
oculorum. Qui cum, per multos medicos ambulans, nihil omnino visionis recipere possit, accessit ad basilicam beati Martini; ubi per duos aut tres menses
consistens et ieiunans assiduae, lumen ut reciperet flagitabat. Adveniente autem festivitate, clarificatis oculis cernere coepit; regressus quoque domum, vocato
quodam Iudaeo, ventosas, quorum beneficio oculis lumen augeret, humeris superponit. Decedente quoque sanguine, rursus in redeviva caecitate redigitur. Quod cum
factum fuisset, rursum ad sanctum templum regressus est. Ibique iterum longo spatio commoratus, lumen recipere non meruit. Quod ei ob peccatum non praestitum
reor iuxta illud dominicum oraculum: Qui habet, dabitur ei et habundavit; et qui non habet, ipsum quod habet aufertur ab eo; et illud: Ecce sanus factus es, iam
noli peccare, ne quid tibi deterius eveniat. Nam perstiterat hic in sanitate, si Iudaeum non induxisset super divinam virtutem. Tales enim et monet et arguit
apostulus, dicens: Nolite enim iugum ducere cum infidelibus. Quae enim participatio iustitiae cum iniquitate? Aut quae societas luci cumtenebris? Quae autem
communicatio Christi cum Belial? Aut quae pars fideli cum infidele? Qui autem consensus templo Dei cum idolis? Vos estis enim templum Dei vivi. Propterea exite
de medio eorum et separamini ab his, ait Dominus. Ideo doceat unumquemque christianum haec causa, ut, quando caelestem accipere meruerit medicinam, terrena non
requirat studia.

## 7. De Senoch reclauso.

**[008]** Sed et illud commemorare libet, qui vel quales viri hoc anno a Domino sunt vocati. Unde magnum eum et Deo acceptabilem ego censeo, qui tales de nostra
terra suo paradiso collocavit. Nam benedictus Senoch presbiter, qui apud Turonus morabatur, sic migravit a saeculo. Fuit enim genere Theifalus, et in Turonico
clericus factus, in cellulam, quam ipse inter parietes antiquos conposuerat, se removit, collectisque monachis, oratorium, quod multo tempore dirutum fuerat,
reparavit. Idem super infirmos multas virtutes fecit, quas in libro vitae eius scripsimus.

## 8. De sancto Germano Parisiorum episcopo.

**[009]** Eo anno et beatus Germanus Parisiorum episcopus transiit. In cuius exsequiis multis virtutibus, quas in corpore gesserat, hoc miraculum confirmationem
fecit. Nam carcerarius adclamantibus, corpus in platea adgravatum est, solutisque eisdem, rursum sine labore levatur. Ipsi quoque, qui soluti fuerant, in
obsequium funeris usque basilicam, in qua sepultus est, liberi pervenerunt. Ad sepulchrum autem eius multas virtutes, Domino tribuente, credentes experiuntur,
ita ut quisque iusta petierit velociter exoptata reportet. Quis tamen strenuus virtutes illius, quas in corpore fecit, sollicite vult inquirere, librum vitae
illius, qui a Fortunato presbitero conpositus est, legens, cuncta repperiet.

## 9. De Caluppane reclauso.

**[010]** Eodem quoque anno et Caluppa reclausus obiit. Hic autem ab infantia sua semper religiosus fuit, et apud monasterium Melitensim termini Arverni
conversus, in magna se humilitate fratribus praebuit, sicut in libro vitae eius scripsimus.

## 10. De Patroclo reclauso.

**[011]** Fuit autem in Biturigo termino reclausus nomine Patroclus, presbiterii honore praeditus, mirae sanctitatis ac religionis, vir magnae abstinentiae, qui
plerumque ab inaedia diversis incommodis vexabatur. Vinum, sicera vel omne quod inebriare potest non bibebat praeter aquam parumper melle linitam; sed nec
pulmentum aliquod utebatur. Cuius victus erat panis in aqua infusus atque sale respersus. Huius oculi numquam caligaverunt. Erat enim in oratione assiduus, quam
si parumper praetermisisset, aut legebat aut scribebat. Frigoriticis, pustulis laborantibus vel reliquis morbis saepe per orationem remedia conferebat. Sed et
alia signa multa fecit, quae per ordinem longum est enarrare. Cilicium semper puro adhibens corpori. Qui octogenaria aetate abscedens a saeculo, migravit ad
Christum. Scripsimus et de huius vita libellum.

## 11. De Iudaeis conversis per Avitum episcopum.

**[012]** Et quia semper Deus noster sacerdotes suos glorificare dignatur, quid Arverno de Iudaeis hoc anno contigerit pandam. Cum eosdem plerumque beatus
Avitus episcopus commoneret, ut, relicto velamine legis Moysaicae, spiritaliter lecta intellegerent et Christum, filium viventis Dei, prophetica et legali
auctoritate promissum, corde purissimo in sacris litteris contemplarent, manebat in pectoribus eorum, iam non dicam, velamen illud, quod facies Moysi
obumbrabatur, sed paries. Sacerdos quoque orans, ut, conversi ad Dominum, velamen ab eis litterae rumperetur, quidam ex his ad sancta pascha ut baptizaretur
expetiit, renatusque Deo per baptismi sacramentum, cum albatis reliquis in albis et ipse procedit. Ingredientibus autempopulis portam civitatis, unus Iudaeorum
super capud conversi Iudaei oleum foetidum, diabulo instigante, diffudit. Quod cum cunctus aborrens populus voluissent eum urguere lapidibus, pontifex ut fieret
non permisit. Die autem beato, quo Dominus ad caelos post redemptum hominem gloriosus ascendit, cum sacerdos de aeclesiam ad basilicam psallendo procederet,
inruit super sinagogae Iudaeorum multitudo tota sequentium, distructamque a fundamentis, campi planitiae locus adsimilatur. Alia autem die sacerdos eis legatos
mittit, dicens: 'Vi ego vos confiteri Dei Filium non inpello, sed tamen praedico et salem scientiae vestris pectoribus trado. Pastor sum enim dominicis ovibus
superpositus; et de vobis ille verus Pastor, qui pro nobis passus est, dixit, habere se alias oves quae non sunt ex ovili suo, quas eum oporteat adducere, ut
fiat unus grex et unus pastor. Ideoque si vultis credere ut ego, estote unus grex, costodi me posito; sin vero aliud, abscedite a loco. Illi autem diu
aestuantes atque dubitantes, tertia die, ut credo, obtentum pontificis coniuncti in unum, ad eum mandata remittunt, dicentes: 'Credimus Iesum, filium Dei vivi,
nobis prophetarum vocibus repromissum; et ideo petimus, ut abluamur baptismum, ne in hoc delicto permaneamus. Gavisus autem nuntio pontifex, noctem sanctam
