inconpositam dereliquit. Post cuius obitum multi, ut fit, episcopatum petibant. Transobadus vero presbiter, qui quondam archidiaconus eius fuerat, maxime in hoc
intendibat, fidus, quod filium suum cum Gogone, qui tunc regis erat nutricius, commendaverat. Condidirat autem episcopus testamentum, in quo regis exenium quid
post eius obitum accepiret indecabat, adiurans terribilibus sacramentis, ut in ecclesia illa non ordinaritur extraneus, non cupidus, non coniugali vinculo
nexus, sed ab his omnibus expeditus, qui in solis tantum dominicis laudibus degebat, substitueritur. Transobadus autem presbiter epulum in ipsa urbe clericis
praeparat. Resedentibus autem illis, unus praesbiterorum coepit antestitem memoratum inpudicis blasphemare sermonibus et usque ad hoc erupit, ut eum delerum et
fatuum nominaret. Haec eo dicente, pincerna poculum oblaturus advenit. At ille acceptum dum ori proximat, tremire coepit, laxatumque de manu calicem, super
alium, qui sibi erat proximus, caput reclinans, reddidit spiritum, ablatusque ab epulo ad sepulchrum, humo contectus est. Post haec relicto testamento
antestitis in praesentia Childeberthi regis ac procerum eius, Theodosius, qui tunc archediaconatum urbis illius potiebatur, episcopus ordinatus est.

## 47. De comitatu Eunomii.

**[048]** Audiens autem Chilpericus omnia mala, quae faciebat Leudastis ecclesiis Toronicis vel omni populo, Ansovaldum illuc dirigit. Qui veniens ad
festivitatem sancti Martini, data nobis populo optionem, Eunomius in comitatum erigitur. Denique Leudastis cernens se remotum, ad Chilpericum dirigit, dicens:
'Usque nunc, o piissime rex, custodivi civitatem Turonicam; nunc autem, me ab actione remoto, vide, qualiter custodiatur. Nam noveris, quia Gregorius episcopus
eam ad filium Sygiberthi tradere distinat'. Quod audiens rex, ait: 'Nequaquam, sed quia remotus es, ideo haec adponis'. Et ille: 'Maiora', inquit, 'de te ait
episcopus; dicit enim, reginam tuam in adulterio cum episcopo Berthramno misceri'. Tunc iratus rex, caesum pugnis et calcibus, oneratum ferro recludi praecepit
in carcere.

## 48. De malitia Leudastis.

**[049]** Sed quia liber finem postulat, narrare aliquid de eius actionibus libet; sed prius videtur genus ac patriam moresque ordiri. Gracina Pictavensis
insula vocitatur, in qua a fiscalis vinitoris servo Leuchadio nomine nascitur. Exinde ad servitium arcessitus, culinae regiae deputatur. Sed quia lippis erat in
adolescentia oculis, quibus fumi acerbitas non congruebat, amotus a pistillo, promovitur ad cophinum. Sed dum inter firmentatas massas se delectari consimulat,
servitium fugam iniens dereliquit. Cumque bis aut tertio reductus a fugat lapsu teneri non possit, auris unius incisione multatur. Dehinc cum notam inflictam
corpori occulere nulla auctoritate valeret, ad Marcoveifam reginam, quam Chariberthus rex nimium diligens in loco sororis toro adsciverat, fugit. Quae libenter
eum colligens, provocat equorumque meliorum deputat esse custodem. Hinc iam obsessus vanitate ac superbiae deditus, comitatum ambit stabulorum; quo accepto,
cunctos despicit ac postponit, inflatur vanitate, luxuria dissolvitur, cupiditate succenditur et in causis patronae alumnus proprius huc illucque defertur.
Cuius post obitum refertus praedis, locum ipsum cum rege Charibertho, oblatis muneribus, tenere coepit. Post haec, peccatis populi ingruentibus, comes Turonus
destinatur ibique se amplius honoris gloriosi supercilio iactitat, ibique se exhibete rapacem praedis, turgidum rixis, adulteriis lutulentum. Ubi seminando
discordias et inferendo calumnias non modicos thesauros adgregavit. Post obitum vero Chariberthi, cum in Sigiberthi sorte civitas illa venisset, transeunte eo
ad Chilpericum, omnia quae inique adgregaverat a fidelibus nominati regis direpta sunt. Pervadente igitur Chilperico rege per Theodobertum, filium suum, urbem
Turonicam, cum iam ego Turonus advenissem, mihi a Theodobertho strenue commendatur, ut scilicet comitatum, quem prius habuerat, potiretur. Multum se nobis
humilem subditumque reddebat, iurans saepius super sepulchrum sancti antistitis, numquam se contra rationis ordinem esse venturum seque mihi tam in causis
propriis quam in ecclesiae necessitatibus in omnibus esse fidelem. Timebat enim, quod postea evenit, ne urbem illam iterum rex Sigiberthus in suo dominio
revocaret. Quo defuncto, succedente iterum Chilperico in regno, iste in comitatum accedit. Adveniente autem Turonus Merovecho, omnes res eius usquequaque
diripuit. Sed hic, dum Sigiberthus duos annos Turonus tenuit, hic in Brittaniis latuit. Qui, adsumpto, ut diximus, comitatu, in tali levitate elatus est, ut in
domo ecclesiae cum toracibus atque loricis, praecinctus pharetra et contum manu gerens, capite galeato ingrederetur, de nullo securus, quia omnibus erat
adversus. Iam si in iudicio cum senioribus vel laicis vel clericis resedisset et vidisset hominem iustitiam prosequentem, protinus agebatur in furias, ructabat
convicia in civibus; presbiteros manicis iubebat extrahi, milites fustibus verberari, tantamque utebatur crudelitatem, ut vix referri possit. Discedente autem
Merovecho, qui res eius diripuerat, nobis calumniator existit, adserens fallaciter Merovechum nostro usum consilio, ut res eius auferret. Sed post inlata damna
iterat iterum sacramenta pallamque sepulchri beati Martini fideiussorem donat, se nobis numquam adversaturum.

## 49. De insidiis, quas nobis fecit.

**[050]** Sed quia longum est per ordinem prosequi periurias vel reliqua mala eius, veniamus ad illud, qualiter me voluit iniquis ac nefariis calamniis
supplantare, vel qualiter in eum ultio divina descendit, ut illud adimpleretur: Omnis subplantans subplantabitur; et iterum: Qui fodit foveam, incidit in ea.
Igitur post multa mala quae in me meisque intulit, post multas direptiones rerum ecclesiasticarum, adiuncto sibi Riculfo presbitero simili malitia perverso, ad
hoc erupit, ut diceret, me crimen in Fredegundem reginam dixisse; adserens, si archidiaconus meus Plato aut Galienus amicus noster subdirentur poenae,
convincerent me utique haec locutum. Tunc rex iratus, ut supra diximus, iussit eum pugnis calcibusque caesum oneratumque catenis recludi in carcerem. Nam
Riculfum clericum se habere dicebat, per quem haec locutus fuisset. Hic vero Riculfus subdiaconus, simili levitate perfacilis, ante hoc anno consilio cum
Leudaste de hac causa habito, causas offensionis requirit, quibus scilicet me offenso ad Leudastem transiret; nanctisque tandem, ipsum adivit, ac per menses
quattuor dolos omnes ac muscipulas praeparatas, ad me cum ipso Leudaste revertitur, deprecans, ut eum debeam recipere excusatum. Feci, fateor, et occultum
hostem publice in domo suscepi. Discedente vero Leudaste, ipse se pedibus meis sternit, dicens: 'Nisi succurras velociter, periturus sum. Ecce, instigante
Leudaste, locutus sum quod loqui non debui! Nunc vero aliis me regnis emitte; quod nisi feceris, a regalibus conprehensus, mortales poenas sum lueturus'. Cui
ego aio: 'Si quid incongruum rationi effatus es, sermo tuus in caput tuum erit; nam ego altero te regno non mittam, ne suspectus habear coram rege'. Post ista
Leudastis extitit accusator eius, dicens, se sermones iam dictos a Riculfo audisse subdiacono. At ille iterum vinctus, relaxato Leudaste, custodiae deputatur,
dicens, Galienum eadem die et Platonem archidiaconem fuisse praesentes, cum haec est episcopus elocutus. Sed Riculfus presbiter, qui iam promissionem de
episcopatu a Leudaste habebat, in tantum elatus fuerat, ut magi Simonis superbia aequaretur. Qui tertio aut eo amplius mihi sacramentum super sepulchrum sancti
Martini dederat, in die sexta paschae in tantum me conviciis et sputis egit, ut vix manibus temperaret, fidus scilicet doli quem praeparaverat. In crastina
autem die, id est sabbati in ipsa pascha, venit Leudastis in urbe Turonica, adsimilansque aliud negotii agere, adprehensis Platonem archidiaconem et Galienum in
vincla conectit, catenatosque ac exutos veste iubet eos ad reginam deduci. Haec ego audiens, dum in domo ecclesiae residerem, mestus turbatusque ingressus
oratorium, Davitici carminis sumo librum, ut scilicet apertus aliquem consolationis versiculum daret. In quo ita repertum est: Eduxit eos in spe, et non
timuerunt; et inimicos eorum operuit mare. Interea ingressi in fluvium super pontem, qui duabus lintribus tenebatur, navis illa, quae Leudastem vehebat,
dimergitur, et nisi natandi fuisset adminiculo liberatus, cum sociis forsitan interisset. Navis vero alia quae huic innexa erat, quae et vinctos vehebat, super
aquas Dei auxilio elevatur. Igitur deducti ad regem qui vincti fuerant, incusantur instanter, ut capitali sententia finirentur. Sed rex recogitans, absolutos a
vinculo libera custodia reservat inlaesos. Ad civitatem vero Turonuse Berulfus dux cum Eunomio comite fabulam fingit, quod Gunthramnus rex capere vellet
Turonicam civitatem, et idcirco, ne aliqua neglegentia accederet, oportere, ait, urbem custodia consignari. Ponunt portis dolose custodes, qui civitatem tueri
adsimilantes, me utique custodirent. Mittunt etiam qui mihi consilium ministrarent, ut ad occultum, adsumptis melioribus rebus ecclesiae, Arverno fuga
secederem; sed non acquievi. Igitur rex, arcessitis regni sui episcopis, causam diligenter iussit exquiri. Cumque Biculfus clericus saepius discuteretur occulte
et contra me vel meos multas fallacias promulgaret, Modestus quidam faber lignarius ait ad eum: 'O infelix, qui contra episcopum tuum tam contumaciter ista
meditaris! Satius tibi erat silere, et, petita venia episcopi, gratiam inpetraris'. Ad haec ille clamare coepit voce magna ac dicere: 'En ipse, qui mihi
silentium indicit, ne prosequar veritatem! En reginae inimicum, qui causam criminis eius non sinet inquiri!' Nuntiantur protinus haec reginae. Adprehenditur
Modestus, torquetur, flagellatur, et in vincla compactus, custodiae deputatur. Cumque inter duos custodes catenis et cippo teneretur vinctus, media nocte,
dormientibus custodibus, orationem fudit ad Dominum, ut dignaretur eius potentia miserum visitare, et qui innocens conligatus fuerat, visitatione Martini
praesulis ac Medardi absolveretur. Mox, disruptis vinculis, confracto cippo, reserato ostio, sancti Medardi basilicam, nocte nobis vigilantibus, introiit.
Congregati igitur apud Brinnacum villam episcopi, in unam domum resedere iussi sunt. Dehinc adveniente rege, data omnibus salutatione ac benedictione accepta,
resedit. Tunc Berthramnus Burdegalensis civitatis episcopus, cui hoc cum regina crimen inpactum fuerat, causam proponit meque interpellat, dicens, a me sibi ac
reginae crimen obiectum. Negavi ego in veritate haec locutum, et audisse quidem haec alios, nam non excogitasse. Nam foris domum rumor in populo magnus erat,
dicentium: 'Cur haec super sacerdotem Dei obiciuntur? Cur talia rex prosequitur? Numquid potuit episcopus talia dicere vel de servo? Heu, heu, domine Deus,
largire auxilium servo tuo!' Rex autem dicebat: 'Crimen uxoris meae meum habetur obprobrium. Si ergo censitis, ut super episcopum testes adhibeantur, ecce
adsunt! Certe, si videtur, ut haec non fiant et in fidem episcopi committantur, dicite; libenter audiam quae iubetis'. Mirati sunt omnes regis vel prudentiam
vel patientiam simul. Tunc cunctis dicentibus: 'Non potest persona inferior super sacerdotem credi', restitit ad hoc causa, ut, dictis missis in tribus
altaribus, me de his verbis exuerem sacramento. Et licet canonibus essent contraria, pro causa tamen regis impleta sunt. Sed nec hoc sileo, quod Rigunthis
regina, condolens doloribus meis, ieiunium cum omni domo sua celebravit, quousque puer nuntiaret, me omnia sic implesse, ut fuerant instituta. Igitur regressi
sacerdotes ad regem aiunt: 'Impleta sunt omnia ab episcopo quae imperata sunt. O rex, quid nunc ad te, nisi ut cum Berthramno accusatore fratris communione
priveris?' Et ille: 'Non', inquid, 'ego nisi audita narravi'. Quaerentibus illis, quis hoc dixerit, respondit, se haec a Leudaste audisse. Ille autem secundum
infirmitatem vel consilii vel propositionis suae iam fugam inierat. Tunc placuit omnibus sacerdotibus, ut sator scandali, infitiator reginae, accusator
episcopi, ab omnibus arceretur ecclesiis, eo quod se ab audientia subtraxisset. Unde et epistolam subscriptam aliis episcopis qui non adfuerant transmiserunt.
Et sic unusquisque in loco suo regressus est. Leudastis vero haec audiens, basilicam sancti Petri Parisius expetiit. Sed cum audisset edictum regis, ut in suo
regno a nullo colligeretur, et praesertim quod filius eius, quem domi reliquerat, obisset, Turonus occulte veniens, quae melius habuit in Biturigo transposuit.
Prosequentibus vero regalibus pueris, ipse per fugam labitur. Capta quoque uxore eius, in pago Tornacensi exilio recluditur. At Riculfus clericus ad
interficiendum deputatur. Pro cuius vita vix obtinui, tamen de tormentis excusare non potui. Nam nulla res, nullum metallum tanta verbera potuit sustinere,
sicut hic miserrimus. Nam ab hora tertia diei, revinctis postergum manibus, suspensus ad arborem dependebat; ad horam vero nonam depositus, extensus ad
trocleas, caedebatur fustibus, virgis ac loris duplicibus, et non ab uno vel duobus, sed quanti accedere circa miseros potuerunt artus, toti caesores erant. Cum
autem iam in discrimine esset, tunc aperuit veritatem et archana doli publice patefecit. Dicebat enim ob hoc reginae crimen obiectum, ut, eiecta de regno,
interfectis fratribus et patre, Chlodovechus regnum acciperet, Leudastis ducatum, Riculfus vero presbiter, qui iam a tempore beati Eufronii episcopi amicus erat
Chlodovechi, episcopatum Turonicum ambiret, huic Riculfo clerico archidiaconatu promisso. Nos vero cum Dei gratia Turonus reversi, invenimus ecclesiam
conturbatam pei Riculfum presbiterum. Nam hic sub Eufronio episcopo de pauperibus provocatus, archidiaconus ordinatus est. Exinde ad presbiterium admotus,
recessit ad propria. Semper elatus, inflatus, praesumptiosus; nam, me adhuc commorante cum rege, hic, quasi iam esset episcopus, in domo ecclesiae ingreditur
impudenter, argentum describit ecclesiae reliquasque res sub sua redegit potestate. Maiores clericos muneribus ditat, largitur vineas, prata distribuit;
minoribus vero fustibus plagisque multis etiam manu propria adfecit, dicens: 'Recognoscite dominum vestrum, qui victoriam de inimicis obtinuit, cuius ingenium
Turonicam urbem ab Arvernis populis emundavit'; ignorans miser, quod praeter quinque episcopos reliqui omnes, qui sacerdotium Turonicum susceperunt, parentum
nostrorum prosapiae sunt coniuncti. Illud saepe suis familiaribus dicere erat solitus, hominem prudentem non aliter nisi in periuriis quis decipere possit. Sed
cum me reverso adhuc despiceret nec ad salutationem meam, sicut reliqui cives fecerant, adveniret, sed magis me interficere minitaret, cum consilio
provincialium eum in monasterio removeri praecipio. Cumque ibidem artius distringeretur, intercedentibus Felicis episcopi missis, qui memoratae causae fautor
extiterat, circumventum periuriis abbatem, fuga labitur et usque ad Felicem accedit episcopum, eumque ille ambienter collegit, quem execrare debuerat. Leudastis
vero in Biturigo pergens, omnes thesauros quos de spoliis pauperum detraxerat secum tulit. Nec multo post, inruentibus Biturigis cum iudice loci super eum, omne
aurum argentumque vel quod secum detulerat abstulerunt, nihilque ei nisi quod super se habuit relinquentes; ipsamque abstulissent vitam, nisi fuga fuisset
elapsus. Resumptis dehinc viribus, cum aliquibus Turonicis iterum inruit super praedones suos, interfectoque uno, aliqua de rebus ipsis recepit et in Turonico
revertitur. Audiens haec Berulfus dux, misit pueros suos cum armorum apparatu, ut apprehenderent eum. Ille vero cernens, se iam iamque capi, relictis rebus,
basilicam sancti Hilarii Pictavensis expetiit. Berulfus vero dux res captas regi transmisit. Leudastis enim egrediebatur de basilica, et inruens in domibus
diversorum, praedas publice exercebat. Sed et in adulteriis saepe in ipsam sanctam porticum deprehensus est. Commota autem regina, quod scilicet locus Deo
sacratus taliter pollueretur, iussit eum a basilica sancta eici. Qui eiectus, ad hospites suos iterum in Biturigo expetiit, deprecans, se occuli ab eis.

## 50. Quae beatus Salvius de Chilperico praedixit.

**[051]** Et licet de beati Salvii episcopi conlocutione superius memorare debueram, sed quia mentem excessit, esse sacrilegum non arbitror, si in posterum
scribatur. Igitur cum, vale post sinodum memoratam regi iam dicta, ad propria redire vellimus, non ante discidere placuit, nisi hunc virum, libatis osculis,
linquerimus. Quem quesitum in atrio Brinnacinsis domus repperi. Cui dixi, quia iam eram ad propriam rediturus. Tunc remoti paululum, dum hinc inde
sermocinaremur, ait mihi: 'Videsne super hoc tectum quae ego suspicio?' Cui ego: 'Video enim supertegulum, quod nuper rex poni praecepit'. Et illi: 'Aliud,
inquid, 'non aspicis?' Cui ego: 'Nihil aliud video'. Suspicabar enim, quod aliquid ioculariter loqueretur. Et adiaci: 'Si tu aliquid magis cernis, enarra'. At
ille, alta trahens suspiria, ait: 'Video ego evaginatum irae divinae gladio super domum hanc dependentem'. Verumtamen non fefellit dictio sacerdotem; nam post
dies viginti duo filii regis, quos superius mortuos scripsimus, obierunt. EXPLICIT LIBER QUINTUS, FINITUS IN ANNO QUINTO CHILDEBERTI REGIS.

---

# BOOK SIX

## LIBER SEXTUS

### 1. How Childebert passed over to Chilperic, and of the flight of Mummolus

**[001]** In the sixth year of his reign, King Childebert rejected his peace with King Guntram and allied himself with Chilperic. Not long afterward Gogo died,
and Wandelenus was appointed in his place. Mummolus escaped by flight from King Guntram’s kingdom and shut himself within the protecting walls of Avignon. A
synod of bishops assembled at Lyons, considered various disputed cases, and condemned the negligent by its judgment. The synod returned to the king, discussing
at length the flight of Duke Mummolus and, to some extent, the discords between the kings.

### 2. Of the legates of Chilperic returned from the East

**[002]** Meanwhile King Chilperic’s envoys, who had gone to the Emperor Tiberius three years earlier, returned, though not without severe loss and hardship.
Because the kings were at odds, they had not dared to enter the port of Marseille and instead came to the city of Agde, situated in the kingdom of the Goths.
Before they reached shore, their ship was driven by the wind, struck the land, and broke to pieces. Seeing themselves and their servants in danger, the envoys
seized planks and with difficulty reached the bank. Many servants were lost, but most escaped. The inhabitants seized the goods that the waves washed ashore,
though the envoys recovered the better items and carried them back to King Chilperic. The people of Agde kept many of them for themselves.

I had then gone to the villa of Novigentum to meet the king. There he showed me a great ceremonial dish that he had caused to be made of gold and gems, weighing
fifty pounds, and said, “I made this to adorn and ennoble the Frankish people. If life accompanies me, I will make many more.” He also displayed gold pieces,
each weighing a pound, sent by the emperor. On one side they bore a likeness of the emperor and the circular inscription TIBERIUS CONSTANTINE, PERPETUAL
AUGUSTUS; on the other, a four-horse chariot with its driver and the inscription GLORY OF THE ROMANS. He showed me many other ornaments presented by the envoys
as well.

### 3. Of the legates of Childebert to Chilperic

**[003]** While Chilperic was staying at the same villa, Egidius, bishop of Rheims, came with King Childebert’s leading nobles as envoys to King Chilperic.
After they had discussed joining together in peace and taking away King Guntram’s kingdom, King Chilperic said, “Because my sins increased, no sons remain to
me, and I now have no other heir except my brother Sigibert’s son, King Childebert. Therefore let him be heir to everything over which I have been able to
labor; only let me hold everything without question or dispute for as long as I live.” They thanked him, confirmed their statements in written agreements, and
returned to Childebert with rich gifts. When they departed, King Chilperic sent Bishop Leudovald with the leading men of his kingdom. Having given and received
oaths of peace and confirmed the agreements, they returned laden with gifts.

### 4. How Lupus was driven from Childebert's kingdom

**[004]** Duke Lupus of Champagne had long been harassed and continually plundered by various men, especially Ursio and Berthefred. At last they made an
agreement to kill him and raised an army against him. Queen Brunhilda, seeing this and grieving over the unjust persecution of her faithful servant, girded
herself like a man and burst into the middle of the hostile squadrons, saying, “Do not, men, do not do this evil. Do not persecute an innocent man. Do not join
battle over one man and thereby destroy the strength of the region.” Ursio answered her, “Withdraw from me, woman. It was enough for you to hold the kingdom
while subject to your husband. Now your son reigns, and his kingdom is preserved not by your protection but by mine. Withdraw from me, or my horses’ hooves will
trample you into the earth.” After they had exchanged these and other words at great length, the queen’s intervention prevented them from fighting.
Nevertheless, on leaving that place they attacked Lupus’s houses, seized all his resources, and carried them to their own homes while pretending to deposit them
in the king’s treasury. They threatened Lupus, saying, “You will not escape my power alive.” Seeing himself in danger, Lupus placed his wife safely within the
walls of Lyon-la-Clavate and fled to King Guntram. Guntram received him kindly, and Lupus remained hidden with him, waiting for Childebert to reach lawful age.

### 5. The altercation with the Jew

**[005]** While King Chilperic was still staying at the villa mentioned above, he ordered the baggage to be moved and prepared to come to Paris. When I
approached him to take my leave, a certain Jew named Priscus, who was on familiar terms with him as a purchaser of goods, arrived. The king gently took hold of
Priscus’s hair and said to me, “Come, priest of God, and lay your hand on him.” When Priscus resisted, the king said, “O hard mind and ever unbelieving
generation! You do not understand that God’s Son was promised to you by the voices of the prophets, nor do you understand that the mysteries of the Church were
prefigured in your sacrifices.”

The Jew answered, “God has not entered into marriage, is not endowed with offspring, and permits no one to share his kingdom. Through Moses he says, ‘See, see
that I am the Lord, and there is no God besides me. I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike and I will heal.’” The king replied, “God begot his eternal
Son from a spiritual womb, not younger in age or lesser in power. Of him God himself says, ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.’ In the last
ages he sent into the world as healer this Son born before the ages, as your prophet says, ‘He sent his Word and healed them.’ As for your assertion that God
does not beget, hear your prophet speaking in the Lord’s voice: ‘Shall I who make others give birth not give birth myself?’ He says this concerning the people
who are reborn in him through faith.”

The Jew answered, “Could God become man, be born of a woman, be subjected to blows, and be condemned to death?” When the king fell silent, I joined the
discussion and said, “That God’s Son, as God, became man was required not by his necessity but by mine. He could not redeem man, who was captive to sin and
subjected to the devil’s servitude, without assuming human nature. I will offer testimony not from the Gospels and the apostle, which you do not believe, but
from your own books, and pierce you with your own sword, just as David is recorded once to have slaughtered Goliath.

“Hear your prophet saying that God was to become man: ‘He is God and Man, and who has known him?’ And elsewhere: ‘This is our God, and no other can be compared
with him. He found the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen on earth and conversed with men.’
Hear your prophet likewise saying that he is born of a virgin: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called
Emmanuel, which interpreted means God with us.’ Another prophet says that he was to be subjected to blows, fastened with nails, and exposed to other injuries:
‘They pierced my hands and my feet; they divided my garments among them,’ and so forth. And again: ‘They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me
vinegar to drink.’ David also says that through the gibbet of the cross he restored to his kingdom the fallen world subject to the devil’s dominion: ‘The Lord
reigned from the tree.’ This does not mean that he had not previously reigned with the Father, but that he began a new reign over the people whom he had freed
from servitude to the devil.”

The Jew answered, “What necessity compelled God to suffer these things?” I replied, “I have already told you: God created man innocent, but man was ensnared by
the serpent’s cunning and became a transgressor of the commandment. Cast out of paradise, he was therefore consigned to worldly labors. Through the death of
Christ, God’s only-begotten Son, he was reconciled to God the Father.”

The Jew said, “Could God not have sent prophets or apostles to call man back to the way of salvation without humbling himself in the flesh?” I answered, “From
the beginning God always loved the human race, but neither the submersion of the flood, nor the burning of Sodom, nor the plagues of Egypt, nor the miracle of
the divided sea and Jordan ever terrified it. It always resisted God’s law and did not believe the prophets; indeed, it not only disbelieved but killed those
very preachers of repentance. Therefore no other could have accomplished this if he himself had not descended to redeem it. Reborn through his birth, washed by
baptism, healed by his wound, raised by his resurrection, we are glorified by his ascension. Your prophet said that he would come to heal my diseases: ‘By his
bruise we have been healed.’ Elsewhere: ‘He himself will bear my sins and pray for transgressors.’ And again: ‘He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and
like a lamb dumb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who shall declare his generation? His name is
the Lord of hosts.’

“Jacob too, from whose race you boast to have come, spoke as though addressing Christ himself, God’s Son, in his blessing upon his son Judah: ‘The sons of your
father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s whelp. From the shoot, my son, you have ascended. Stooping down, you slept like a lion, like a lion’s whelp. Who
will rouse him? His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.’ Who, Jacob asks, will rouse him? Although Christ himself said, ‘I have
power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again,’ the apostle Paul nevertheless says, ‘Whoever does not believe that God raised him from the
dead cannot be saved.’”

Despite these and other words, the wretched man was never moved to believe. When the king saw that he was silent but not moved by my discourse, he turned to me
and asked that I give him a blessing and depart. He said, “I will say to you, priest, what Jacob said to the angel who spoke with him: ‘I will not let you go
unless you bless me.’” He ordered water to be brought for my hands. When I had washed and prayed, I took bread, gave thanks to God, ate some myself, and offered
it to the king. After drinking unmixed wine and taking my leave, I departed. The king mounted his horse and returned to Paris with his wife, daughter, and
entire household.

### 6. Of Saint Hospitius the recluse, his abstinence and miracles

**[006]** At that time there lived in the city of Nice a recluse named Hospitius, a man of great abstinence. His pure body was bound with iron chains, over
which he wore a hair shirt, and he ate nothing but plain bread with a few dates. During the days of Lent he sustained himself on the roots of Egyptian herbs
used by hermits, which merchants brought him. At first he drank the broth in which they had been cooked, and afterward ate the roots themselves. The Lord
deigned to work great miracles through him.

On one occasion, with the Holy Spirit revealing it to him, he foretold the coming of the Lombards into Gaul: “The Lombards will come into Gaul and devastate
seven cities, because their malice has increased in the Lord’s sight. There is no one who understands and no one who does good to appease God’s wrath. The whole
people is faithless, given to perjury, liable to theft, and prone to murder, and no fruit of justice springs from these things. Tithes are not paid, the poor
are not fed, the naked are not clothed, and strangers are not received in hospitality or satisfied with sufficient food. Therefore this blow is coming. Now I
tell you: gather all your substance within the circuit of your walls so that it may not be plundered by the Lombards, and fortify yourselves in the strongest
places.” All were astonished at his words, took their leave, and returned home in great wonder.

He also told the monks, “Depart from this place too, taking your possessions with you. Behold, the people I foretold is approaching.” When they answered, “We
will not leave you, most holy father,” he said, “Do not fear for me. They will inflict injuries on me, but they will not kill me.” After the monks departed,
that people came. While devastating everything they found, they reached the place where God’s holy recluse lived. He showed himself to them through the tower
window. They circled the tower but could find no entrance by which to reach him. Two of them climbed up, removed the roof, and saw him bound in chains and
wearing a hair shirt. They said, “This man is a criminal and has committed murder; that is why he is kept bound in these fetters.” Summoning an interpreter,
they asked him what evil he had done to be confined in such punishment. He confessed that he was a murderer and guilty of every crime.

One Lombard drew his sword to strike off his head, but his right hand stiffened in the very act of striking, and he could not draw it back. He dropped the sword
and it fell to the ground. Seeing this, his companions raised a cry to heaven, begging the saint to tell them mercifully what they should do. He made the sign
of salvation and restored the arm to health. The man was converted in that very place, received the tonsure, and is now regarded as a most faithful monk. Two
commanders who listened to Hospitius returned safely to their own country, but those who despised his command died miserably in that province. Many of them were
seized by demons and cried, “Why, most holy and blessed man, do you torture and burn us like this?” He laid his hand on them and cleansed them.

After this there was a man living in Angers who had lost both speech and hearing through a severe fever. When the fever subsided, he remained deaf and mute. A
deacon from that province was sent to Rome to obtain tokens of the blessed apostles and other saints who protect that city. When the sick man’s relatives
learned of this, they asked the deacon to take him as a traveling companion, confident that if he visited the tombs of the most blessed apostles he would
immediately obtain healing. On their journey they came to the place where blessed Hospitius lived. After greeting and kissing him, the deacon explained the
reason for his journey, said that he was going to Rome, and asked Hospitius to commend him to his friends among the shipmasters. While the deacon was still
there, the holy man perceived through the Lord’s spirit that divine power was present. He said to the deacon, “I beg you to bring before me the sick man who is
now your traveling companion.” The deacon went quickly to his lodging without delay and found the sick man full of fever, indicating by signs that his ears were
ringing. He took him and led him to the man of God. Hospitius grasped his hair and drew his head to the window. Taking oil sanctified by a blessing, he held the
man’s tongue with his left hand and poured the oil into his mouth and over the top of his head, saying, “In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, may your ears be
opened, and may that power which once drove the harmful demon from a deaf and mute man unlock your mouth.” Then he asked his name, and the man answered clearly
and told him.

Seeing this, the deacon said, “I give immeasurable thanks to you, Christ, for deigning to reveal such things through your servant. I was seeking Peter, Paul,
Laurence, and the others who glorify Rome with their own blood; here I have found them all, here I have discovered every one.” As he spoke with tears and great
wonder, the man of God, avoiding vainglory with all his resolution, said, “Be silent, be silent, dearest brother. It is not I who do these things, but he who
created the world from nothing, who for our sake assumed humanity, gives sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the mute, restores their former
skin to lepers, life to the dead, and abundant healing to all the sick.” The deacon departed rejoicing, taking leave and going with his companions.

After they had gone, a man named Dominic, blind from birth, came to test the power of this miracle-worker. He stayed in the monastery for two or three months,
devoting himself to prayer and fasting. At length the man of God summoned him and asked, “Do you wish to receive your sight?” Dominic answered, “My desire was
to learn what was unknown to me. I do not know what light is. I know only that everyone praises it, but from the beginning of my life until now I have not been
privileged to see.” Hospitius made the holy cross over his eyes with blessed oil and said, “In the name of Jesus Christ my Redeemer, let your eyes be opened.”
His eyes were immediately opened, and he stood in amazement, beholding the mighty works of God visible in this world.

Next a woman who, by her own account, had three demons was brought to him. After he had blessed her with his sacred touch and made the sign of the cross on her
forehead with holy oil, the demons were cast out and she departed cleansed. He also healed a girl tormented by an unclean spirit through his blessing.

When the day of his death was approaching, he summoned the monastery’s superior and said, “Bring tools, break through the wall, and send messengers to the
bishop of the city to come and bury me. On the third day I will depart from this world and enter the appointed rest that the Lord has promised me.” The superior
sent messengers to the bishop of Nice with this news. Afterward a man named Crescens came to the window and, seeing him bound in chains and full of worms, said,
“My lord, how can you endure such severe torments so courageously?” Hospitius answered, “He for whose name I suffer these things strengthens me. I tell you that
I am now being released from these bonds and entering my rest.”

On the third day he removed the chains with which he had been bound and prostrated himself in prayer. After praying with tears for a very long time, he sat on a
stool, stretched out his feet, raised his hands to heaven, gave thanks to God, and yielded up his spirit. Immediately all the worms that had been boring into
his holy limbs vanished. Bishop Austadius came and committed his blessed body to burial with the greatest care. I learned all these things from the lips of the
man whom I described above as healed by him from muteness and deafness. He told me many other things about Hospitius’s powers, but the fact that I have heard
his life has been written by many prevents me from relating them.

### 7. Of the death of Ferreolus, bishop of Uzès

**[007]** At that time Ferreolus, bishop of Uzès, a man of great holiness, died full of wisdom and understanding. Following Sidonius, he had composed several
books of letters. After his death Albinus, formerly a prefect, obtained the episcopate through Dynamius, governor of Provence, without the king’s consent. He
held it for no more than three months and died when proceedings had been initiated to remove him. Jovinus, also a former governor of Provence, then received a
royal command granting him the episcopate. But the deacon Marcellus, son of the senator Felix, forestalled him: he summoned his fellow provincials and was
ordained bishop on Dynamius’s advice. When Jovinus subsequently pressed for his removal, Marcellus shut himself in the city and tried to defend himself by
force; unable to succeed, he prevailed by gifts.

### 8. Of Eparchius the recluse of the city of Angoulême

**[008]** Eparchius, the recluse of Angoulême, also died. He was a man of magnificent holiness, through whom God displayed many miracles; omitting most of them,
I will touch upon only a few. He was an inhabitant of Périgueux. After his conversion he became a cleric, came to Angoulême, and built himself a cell. Gathering
a few monks there, he remained constantly at prayer. Any gold or silver offered to him he distributed for the needs of the poor or the redemption of captives.
No bread was ever baked in that cell during his lifetime; devoted people brought it in when necessity required. He redeemed a great host of people with the
offerings of the devout, often suppressed the poison of malignant pustules with the sign of the cross, and drove demons from possessed bodies by prayer. He
frequently commanded judges with overflowing gentleness, rather than merely asking them, to pardon the guilty. His speech was so gentle that they could not
refuse when he begged for indulgence.

On one occasion a man was being led away to be hanged for theft. The inhabitants also accused him of many other crimes, including theft and murder. When
Eparchius was told, he sent one of his monks to beg the judge to spare the culprit’s life. But the crowd jeered and shouted that neither the region nor the
judge would be safe if the man were released, and the petition was refused. The prisoner was stretched on the rack, beaten with rods and clubs, and condemned to
the gallows. When the monk sorrowfully reported this to the abbot, Eparchius said, “Go some distance away. Know that the Lord will restore by his gift the man
whom a human being refused to hand back. When you see him fall, seize him at once and bring him to the monastery.” While the monk carried out these
instructions, Eparchius prostrated himself in prayer and poured out petitions to God with tears until the hanged man’s bolt and chains broke and he was restored
to the ground. The monk seized him and presented him unharmed before the abbot.

Eparchius gave thanks to God and ordered the count to be summoned. He said, “Dearest son, you were always accustomed to hear me with a kindly spirit. Why have
you hardened yourself today and refused to release the man for whose life I asked?” The count replied, “I willingly listen to you, holy bishop, but when the
crowd rose up I could do nothing else, fearing that a rebellion would be stirred against me.” Eparchius said, “You did not listen to me, but God deigned to hear
me, and the man you handed over to death he has restored to life. Behold, he stands before you unharmed.” As he spoke, the man prostrated himself at the feet of
the astonished count, who saw alive the man he had left in the destruction of death. I learned this from the count’s own lips. Eparchius performed many other
deeds that I have considered too lengthy to recount. After forty-four years of enclosure he was afflicted by a slight fever and yielded up his spirit. He was
carried from his cell and committed to burial, and, as I have said, a great company of those he had redeemed joined his funeral procession.

### 9. Of Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans

**[009]** Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans, fell ill. In King Chlothar’s time he had presided over the monastic community at the basilica of Saint Laurence in Paris.
Because he had always remained faithful to King Chlothar while Childebert the Elder was alive, and had often concealed messengers sent to spy on the king, the
king was waiting for an opportunity to give him episcopal honor. When the bishop of Avignon died, Chlothar intended to appoint him there. But blessed Domnolus
heard of this and went to the basilica of Saint Martin, where King Chlothar had then come to pray. Keeping vigil all night, he made a petition to the king
through the leading men present, asking not to be removed like a captive from the king’s sight and not to have his simplicity wearied among sophisticated
senators and philosophical judges. He asserted that such a position would mean humiliation rather than honor for him. The king consented and, when Innocentius,
bishop of Le Mans, died, appointed Domnolus bishop of that church.

Once he had obtained the episcopate, he showed himself so great and so holy that, raised to the summit of supreme holiness, he restored the use of their steps
to the lame and sight to the blind. After twenty-two years as bishop, seeing himself gravely afflicted by jaundice and gallstones, he chose Abbot Theodulf to
take his place. The king assented to his wish, but not long afterward changed his mind, and the choice was transferred to Badegisil, mayor of the royal palace.
Badegisil received the tonsure and ascended through the grades allotted to clerics; forty days later, when the bishop died, he succeeded him.

### 10. Of the breaking into the basilica of Saint Martin

**[010]** In these days Saint Martin’s basilica was broken into by thieves. They placed against a window of the apse a grating that stood over a dead man’s
tomb, climbed up it, broke the glass, and entered. They carried off a large quantity of gold, silver, and all-silk palls, not fearing to set foot on the holy
tomb where I scarcely presume even to touch my lips. But the saint’s power chose to reveal their rashness with terrible judgment. After committing the crime
they came to the city of Bordeaux, where a quarrel arose and one killed the other. Their deed was thus exposed and the theft discovered; broken silver and palls
were taken from their lodging. When this was reported to King Chilperic, he ordered them to be bound in chains and brought before him. Fearing that men would
die on account of one who, while living in the body, had often prayed for the lives of the lost, I sent the king a letter of petition, asking that they not be
killed since I, to whom the prosecution belonged, was not accusing them. He received this kindly and spared their lives. He carefully reassembled the valuables
that had been scattered and ordered them to be restored to the holy place.

### 11. Of Bishop Theodore and Dynamius

**[011]** In the city of Marseille, Dynamius, governor of Provence, began to lay grave snares for Bishop Theodore. When Theodore prepared to hasten to the king,
Dynamius seized him, detained him in the middle of the city, and treated him outrageously before finally releasing him. The clergy of Marseille were plotting
with Dynamius to expel him from the episcopate. But while Dynamius was traveling to King Childebert, King Guntram ordered him and the former prefect Jovinus to
be detained. When the clergy of Marseille heard this, they were filled with great joy that he was now detained and assigned to exile, and that matters had
reached the point that he would never return to Marseille. They seized the church houses, inventoried the furnishings, opened the store-chests, stripped the
storerooms, and took possession of all the church property as though the bishop were already dead, uttering various charges against him which, with Christ’s
guidance, were later proved false.

After Childebert made peace with Chilperic, he sent envoys to King Guntram demanding the return of the half of Marseille that Guntram had given him after his
father’s death. If Guntram refused, he was to know that he would lose much by retaining this portion. When Guntram refused to return it, he ordered the roads
closed so that no one would have passage through his kingdom. Seeing this, Childebert promoted Gundulf from household officer to duke, a man of senatorial
family, and sent him to Marseille. Not daring to travel through Guntram’s kingdom, Gundulf came to Tours. I received him kindly, recognized him as my mother’s
great-uncle, kept him with me for five days, supplied his needs, and allowed him to depart.

When he proceeded farther, he was unable to enter Marseille because Dynamius resisted him. Nor was the bishop, who had by then joined Gundulf, received back
into his church. Dynamius and the clergy barred the city gates, jeering at and despising both bishop and duke. At last Dynamius was invited to a conference with
the duke and came to the basilica of blessed Stephen near the city. Doorkeepers guarded the entrance so that the doors would be shut immediately after Dynamius
entered. This was done, and the crowds of armed men following Dynamius were excluded and could not enter. Unaware of this, he discussed various matters with
Gundulf at the altar. They then left the altar and entered the reception room. When Dynamius entered with them, now stripped of his companions’ support, they
sternly rebuked him. The armed attendants who were clamoring around after he had been led away were put to flight. The duke and bishop then assembled the senior
citizens so that they might enter the city. Seeing all this, Dynamius begged pardon, gave the duke many gifts, and swore oaths that he would henceforth be
faithful to the bishop and king, whereupon his clothing was restored to him. The gates of the city and the doors of the sacred buildings were opened, and both
duke and bishop entered with standards, acclamations, and various honorary banners. The clergy involved in this crime, whose leaders were Abbot Anastasius and
the priest Proculus, fled beneath Dynamius’s roof, seeking refuge from the very man who had incited them. Many of them were released on suitable sureties and
ordered to go to the king.

Meanwhile Gundulf returned to King Childebert after subjecting the city to Childebert’s rule and restoring the bishop to his place. But Dynamius forgot the
faith he had promised King Childebert and sent messengers to King Guntram, saying that through the bishop he would lose the portion of the city due to him and
would never possess Marseille under his own dominion unless Theodore were expelled. Moved to anger, Guntram ordered, contrary to religious law, that the bishop
of the supreme God be brought before him confined in chains, saying, “Let the enemy of my kingdom be thrust into exile so that he can no longer harm me.”

Because the bishop suspected these designs and could not easily be dragged from the city, his enemies waited for the dedication festival of an oratory in the
suburban countryside. As he left the city and hastened to the feast, armed men suddenly poured from a hidden ambush with a great uproar and surrounded the holy
bishop. They threw him from his horse, scattered all his companions, bound his servants, beat his clergy, placed him on a miserable hack, and led him to the
king’s presence without allowing any of his own people to follow. As they passed through the city of Aix, Bishop Pientius, grieving for his brother bishop,
supplied clergy to assist him and provided necessities before allowing him to proceed.

While this was happening, the clergy of Marseille again opened the church houses, ransacked private places, inventoried some property, and carried other
property to their own homes. The bishop was brought before the king, found innocent, and permitted to return to his city, where the citizens received him with
great acclamation. Grave enmity consequently arose between King Guntram and his nephew Childebert; their treaty was broken, and they began laying snares for one
another.

### 12. Of the army moved against Bourges

**[012]** King Chilperic, seeing these discords springing up between his brother and nephew, summoned Duke Desiderius and ordered him to inflict some injury on
his brother. Desiderius raised an army, put Duke Ragnovald to flight, and invaded Périgueux. After exacting oaths he proceeded to Agen. When Ragnovald’s wife
heard that her husband had been put to flight and these cities were being brought under King Chilperic’s power, she sought refuge in the basilica of the holy
martyr Caprasius. She was dragged out, stripped of her property and her servants’ support, and sent to Toulouse after giving sureties. There she again entered
the basilica of Saint Saturninus and remained. Desiderius took all the cities in that region belonging to King Guntram and subjected them to King Chilperic’s
rule. Duke Berulf, hearing that the men of Bourges were murmuring that they would enter the territory of Tours, raised an army and stationed himself on their
borders. The districts of Isiodore and Berrave in the city of Tours were then severely devastated. Those who could not be present at this siege were afterward
cruelly condemned. Duke Bladast went into Gascony and lost the greater part of his army.

### 13. Of Lupus and Ambrose, citizens of Tours, slain

**[013]** Lupus, a citizen of Tours, wished to enter the clergy after losing his wife and children, but his brother Ambrosius prevented him, fearing that if
Lupus joined the Church he would make God’s Church his heir. His misguiding brother provided him with another wife and appointed a day on which they would be
joined and the betrothal gifts presented. The brothers then came together to the fortress of Chinon, where they had lodging. Ambrosius’s wife, an adulteress who
loved another man with harlot’s passion and hated her husband, laid a snare for him. After the brothers had feasted together and soaked themselves in wine until
drunk late into the night, they lay down together on one bed. During the night, while everyone was sleeping heavily with wine, Ambrosius’s wife’s lover arrived.
He lit a fire of straw to see what he was doing, drew his sword, and struck Ambrosius on the head so violently that the sword descended through his eyes and
split his head.

Awakened by the blow and finding himself wallowing in blood, Lupus cried loudly, “Alas, alas! Help! My brother has been killed!” The adulterer, who was already
leaving after committing the crime, heard this, returned to the bed, and attacked Lupus. Lupus resisted, but the adulterer overwhelmed him, mangled him with
many wounds, and left him half alive with a mortal injury. No one in the household noticed. In the morning everyone was appalled by so great a crime. Lupus was
found still alive and, after relating what had happened, breathed his last. The harlot did not allow herself even a short period of mourning; after a few days
she joined her lover and departed.

### 14. Of the prodigies that appeared

**[014]** In the seventh year of King Childebert’s reign, the twenty-first year of Chilperic and Guntram, there were heavy rains, lightning, and severe
thunderstorms in January, and flowers appeared on the trees. The star I earlier called a comet appeared with a great darkness around it; it shone through the
darkness as though set in an opening, sparkling and spreading its hair. A ray of marvelous size issued from it, looking from a distance like the great smoke of
a conflagration. It was seen in the west at the beginning of the first watch of the night.

On the holy day of Easter the sky appeared to be on fire at the city of Soissons, so that two conflagrations seemed visible, one larger and the other smaller.
After two hours they joined together, formed a great pyramid, and vanished. In the territory of Paris real blood flowed from a cloud and fell upon many people’s
garments, staining them so corruptly that they themselves rejected their own clothing in horror. This portent appeared in three places within the territory of
that city. In the territory of Senlis a man’s house was found spattered with blood inside when he rose in the morning.

There was a great pestilence among the people that year: various illnesses and eruptive fevers with pustules and blisters afflicted many people to death, though
many who took care escaped. I heard that the inguinal plague was raging severely in the city of Narbonne that year, so that once a man had been seized by it
there was no interval before death.

### 15. Of the death of Felix the bishop

**[015]** Felix, bishop of the city of Nantes, succumbed to this illness and became gravely sick. He summoned the neighboring bishops and begged them to confirm
with their subscriptions the consent he had given to his nephew Burgundio. When this had been done, they sent Burgundio to me. He was then about twenty-five
years old. He came and asked me to go to Nantes, tonsure him, and consecrate him bishop in place of his uncle, who was still alive. I refused because I knew
this was contrary to the canons. But I offered advice: “It is written in the canons, my son, that no one may enter the episcopate without first receiving the
ecclesiastical grades in due order. Return there, dearest son, and ask the man who chose you to tonsure you himself. When you have received the honor of the
presbyterate, attend church assiduously; and when God wills Felix to depart, you will easily ascend to the episcopal grade.”

He returned but neglected to follow the advice he had received, because Bishop Felix appeared to be improving. After the fever departed, however, pustules
caused by the humor broke out on his shins. He applied an excessively strong plaster of Spanish flies; his shins putrefied, and he ended his life in the
thirty-third year of his episcopate, at the age of seventy. His cousin Nonnichius succeeded him by royal appointment.

### 16. How Pappolenus received back his wife

**[016]** When Pappolenus heard of Felix’s death, he took back Felix’s niece, from whom he had been separated. Before this he had been betrothed to her, but
while Bishop Felix was delaying the marriage, Pappolenus came with a large band, dragged the girl from an oratory, and took refuge in the basilica of blessed
Albinus. Bishop Felix, moved to anger, deceived the girl and separated her from her husband. He changed her clothing and placed her in a monastery in the city
of Bazas. But Pappolenus secretly sent servants to rescue her from the place where she had been put and bring her to him. He did not refuse; he took her from
the monastery and joined her to himself in marriage. Protected by royal decrees, he had no reason to fear her relatives’ threats.

### 17. Of the Jews converted by King Chilperic

**[017]** King Chilperic ordered many Jews to be baptized that year and received several of them himself from the holy font. Some, however, were washed only in
body, not in heart. They lied to God and returned to their former perfidy, appearing to observe the Sabbath and honor the Lord’s day at the same time. Priscus
could by no means be deflected into acknowledging the truth. The angry king ordered him to be committed to custody, intending to compel the man who would not
believe voluntarily to hear and believe even against his will. Priscus offered certain gifts and asked for time until his son could marry a Hebrew woman at
Marseille, falsely promising that he would then fulfill the king’s command.

Meanwhile a quarrel arose between Priscus and Phatir, a convert from Judaism who was now the king’s godson through baptism. On the Sabbath Priscus girded
himself with a prayer shawl and, carrying no iron weapon in his hand as though observing the Mosaic law, entered a secluded place. Phatir suddenly arrived and
killed Priscus and the companions who were with him with a sword. After killing them, Phatir fled with his servants, who were in a nearby street, to the
basilica of Saint Julian. While they were there, they heard that the king, hoping to save Phatir’s life, would order the servants to be dragged from the
basilica and killed as criminals. One of them drew his sword after his master had escaped and killed his companions. He then left the basilica with his sword,
but the crowd rushed upon him and cruelly killed him. Phatir obtained permission and returned to King Guntram’s kingdom, from which he had come, but not many
days later he was killed by Priscus’s relatives.

### 18. Of the legates of King Chilperic returned from Spain

**[018]** King Chilperic’s envoys Ansovald and Domegisel, who had been sent to Spain to inspect the dowry, returned. In those days King Leovigild was encamped
with his army against his son Hermenegild and had taken the city of Mérida from him. I have already explained above how Hermenegild allied himself with the
Emperor Tiberius’s commanders. This affair also delayed the envoys and caused them to return later. On seeing them, I was anxious to know how faith in Christ
was flourishing among the few Christians remaining in that region. Ansovald replied, “The Christians now living in Spain preserve the Catholic faith intact, but
the king is now using a new device to drive it out. He deceitfully pretends to pray both at the martyrs’ tombs and in the churches of our religion. He says, ‘I
have clearly recognized that Christ the Son of God is equal to the Father, but I do not believe at all that the Holy Spirit is God, because in no book is he
described as God.’” Alas, what an iniquitous sentence, what a venomous understanding, what a perverse mind! Where is the Lord’s saying, “God is spirit”? Where
is Peter’s saying to Ananias, “Why did you think to tempt the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men, but to God”? And where is Paul’s statement, when recounting
the mystical gifts, “One and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills”? One who works what he wills is known to be subject to no
one. When Ansovald reached King Chilperic, a Spanish embassy followed; it proceeded from Chilperic to Childebert and then returned to Spain.

### 19. Of the men of King Chilperic at the bridge of the Oureq

**[019]** King Chilperic had posted guards at the bridge of Urbia in the city of Paris to keep plotters from his brother’s kingdom from causing harm. The former
duke Asclipius learned of this in advance, attacked at night, killed them all, and severely devastated the district nearest the bridge. When this was reported
to King Chilperic, he sent messengers to his counts, dukes, and other officers, directing them to assemble an army and invade his brother’s kingdom. But good
counselors restrained him, saying, “They acted wickedly; you act wisely. Send messengers to your brother. If he is willing to make amends for your injury, do no
evil; if he refuses, you can then consider what course to follow.” Accepting this reasoning, he stopped the army and sent an embassy to his brother. Guntram
made amends for everything and sought his brother’s undiminished affection.

### 20. Of the death of Duke Chrodinus

**[020]** Chrodinus died that year. He was a man of magnificent goodness and piety, very generous in almsgiving and a refresher of the poor, a lavish benefactor
of churches and a nourisher of clergy. He often founded new estates, planted vineyards, built houses, and established farms. He would then invite bishops whose
resources were small, give them a banquet, and generously distribute those houses with their farms and cultivated fields, together with silver, bedding,
utensils, servants, and attendants. He would say, “Let these things be given to the Church so that, when the poor are refreshed from them, they may obtain
pardon for me before God.” I heard many other good things about this man, which would take too long to recount. He died at the age of seventy.

### 21. Of the signs shown

**[021]** Repeated signs appeared that year. The moon suffered an eclipse; real blood flowed from a broken loaf within the territory of Tours; the walls of the
city of Soissons collapsed; the earth shook in the city of Angers; wolves entered within the walls of the town of Bordeaux and devoured dogs without any fear of
man; and fire was seen running across the sky. The city of Bazas was also consumed by fire, so that churches and ecclesiastical houses were destroyed, though I
learned that all the furnishings were rescued.

### 22. Of the bishop Cartherius

**[022]** After King Chilperic had seized his brother’s cities, he appointed new counts and ordered all the tributes of the cities to be brought to him. I
learned that this was carried out. In those days two men were arrested by Nunnichius, count of the city of Limoges, carrying letters in the name of Cartherius,
bishop of Périgueux, which contained many insults against the king. Among other things the bishop was made to complain that he had descended from paradise into
hell, meaning that he had been transferred from King Guntram’s kingdom to Chilperic’s rule. The count sent these letters with the men to the king under close
guard. The king patiently, for the bishop’s sake, sent men to bring Cartherius before him, intending to examine whether the charges were true. When the bishop
arrived, the king presented the men with the letters and asked whether the bishop had sent them. He denied sending them. The men were asked from whom they had
received them and named the deacon Frontonius. The bishop was questioned about the deacon and answered that Frontonius was his particular enemy and that there
could be no doubt the wickedness was his, since he had often stirred up unjust proceedings against him. The deacon was brought without delay and questioned by
the king. He confessed against the bishop, saying, “I dictated this letter at the bishop’s command.” The bishop protested that Frontonius had often sought
devices to cast him from the episcopate. The king, moved to mercy and commending his own cause to God, yielded to both: he gently begged the bishop on the
deacon’s behalf and asked the bishop to pray for him. Cartherius was then sent back to his city with honor. Two months later Count Nunnichius, who had sown this
scandal, was stricken with hemorrhage and died; because he had no children, the king granted his property to various persons.

### 23. That a Son Was Born to King Chilperic

**[023]** After the many deaths of his sons, a son was born to King Chilperic. The king therefore ordered all prisons opened, the bound released, and the
composition payments owed to the treasury by negligent persons not to be exacted at all. This infant later committed a great outrage.

### 24. Again of the snares of Bishop Theodore, and of Gundovald

**[024]** Fresh hostilities again arose against Bishop Theodore. Gundovald, who claimed to be King Chlothar’s son, came from Constantinople and landed at
Marseille. I wish briefly to record something of his origin. He was born in Gaul and reared with the diligent care customary among those kings, with locks of
hair hanging down his back, and was instructed in letters. His mother presented him to King Childebert, saying, “Behold your nephew, King Chlothar’s son.
Because his father dislikes him, receive him, for he is your own flesh.” Childebert, having no sons, accepted him and kept him with him. When this was reported
to King Chlothar, he sent messengers to his brother, saying, “Send the boy to me.” Childebert sent the youth without delay. On seeing him, Chlothar ordered the
hair of his head to be cut, saying, “I did not beget him.”

After King Chlothar’s death, Gundovald was received by King Charibert. King Sigibert summoned him, again cut off his hair, and sent him to the city of
Agrippina, now called Cologne. He escaped from there, again let his hair grow, and went to Narses, who then governed Italy. There he married, begot sons, and
went to Constantinople. It is said that after a long time someone invited him to return to Gaul. He landed at Marseille and was received by Bishop Theodore.
Theodore also supplied him with horses, and he joined Duke Mummolus, who was then in the city of Avignon, as I mentioned above.

Duke Guntram Boso seized Bishop Theodore and thrust him into custody for this affair, demanding to know why he had brought a foreigner into Gaul and sought
through these actions to subject the kingdom of the Franks to imperial rule. Theodore produced a letter said to be subscribed by the hand of King Childebert’s
leading men and said, “I did nothing on my own initiative except what my lords and seniors commanded me.” The bishop was guarded in a cell and not permitted to
approach the church. One night, while he was praying earnestly to the Lord, the cell shone with overwhelming splendor, so that the count guarding him was seized
with immense terror. A globe of immense light was seen above him for two hours. In the morning the count recounted this to the others with him.

Theodore was afterward brought before King Guntram with Bishop Epiphanius, who had fled from the Lombards and was then staying at Marseille because he too was
alleged to have known of this affair. The king examined them and found no crime in either, but nevertheless ordered them to remain in custody. After many
torments in custody, Bishop Epiphanius died. Gundovald withdrew to an island in the sea to await the outcome. Duke Guntram Boso, together with King Guntram’s
duke, divided Gundovald’s property and carried to Auvergne an immense weight of silver, gold, and other things, as it is said.

### 25. Of the signs

**[025]** In the eighth year of King Childebert’s reign, on the day before the Kalends of February, the signal for matins sounded on a Sunday in the city of
Tours and the people rose and gathered at church. Though the sky was cloudy and rainy, a great globe of fire fell from heaven and ran through the air over a
great distance. It gave so much light that everything could be seen as though it were midday. When the cloud received it again, night returned. The waters also
rose beyond their usual strength: the Seine and Marne caused such inundations around Paris that shipwrecks often occurred between the city and the basilica of
Saint Laurence.

### 26. Of Gunthchramn and Mummolus

**[026]** Duke Guntram Boso returned to Auvergne with the treasures mentioned above and went to King Childebert. When he came back from there with his wife and
daughters, King Guntram seized and detained him, saying, “Your invitation brought Gundovald into Gaul, and that is why you went to Constantinople years ago.”
Guntram Boso answered, “Your own Duke Mummolus received him and kept him with him in Avignon. Now permit me to bring Mummolus himself to you, and then I will be
free from the charges made against me.” The king replied, “I will not permit you to go unless you pay fitting penalties for what you have done.” Seeing death
near, Guntram Boso said, “Behold my son. Take him as a hostage for what I promise my lord the king. If I do not bring Mummolus to you, let me lose my little
child.” The king allowed him to depart but retained his infant son.

Taking with him men from Auvergne and the Vellavi, Guntram Boso went to Avignon. Mummolus treacherously had unsound boats prepared on the Rhône. Guntram’s men
boarded unsuspectingly, and when they reached the middle of the river the boats filled with water and sank. In this danger some escaped by swimming, others
seized planks from the boats and reached shore, but many less resourceful men drowned in the river.

Duke Guntram reached Avignon. After entering that city’s walls, Mummolus had observed that a small part was not protected by the Rhône. He had diverted a branch
of the river so that the whole place was protected by its floodwater. There he dug very deep ditches, and running water concealed the snares he had prepared.
When Guntram arrived, Mummolus called from the wall, “If good faith is intact, let him come from one side of the bank and I from the other, and let him say what
he wishes.” When this was agreed, Guntram said from the opposite side—for a branch of the river lay between them—“If I may, I will cross, for there are things
we should discuss more privately.” Mummolus replied, “Come; do not be afraid.” Guntram entered with one friend, weighed down by the weight of his coat of mail.
As soon as his friend reached the river ditch, he sank beneath the water and was never seen again. Guntram too was sinking and being carried away by the swift
current when one of the bystanders held out his spear-shaft and brought him back to the bank. After exchanging insults, Guntram and Mummolus departed.

While Guntram was besieging the city with King Guntram’s army, these events were reported to Childebert. Angry that this had been done without his command, he
sent the aforementioned Gundulf there. Gundulf lifted the siege and brought Mummolus to Auvergne, but Mummolus returned to Avignon a few days later.

### 27. How King Chilperic entered Paris

**[027]** King Chilperic went to Paris on the day before Easter. So that he might escape the curse written into his pact with his brothers, forbidding any of
them to enter Paris without another’s consent, he entered the city with the relics of many saints borne before him. He celebrated Easter with great rejoicing
and presented his son for baptism. Ragnemod, bishop of that city, received him from the holy font and ordered him to be named Theuderic.

### 28. Of Marcus the Referendary

**[028]** The referendary Mark, whom I mentioned above, was suddenly seized by a pain in his side after amassing treasures from the unjust tax assessments. He
beat his head, received penance, and breathed his last, and his property was surrendered to the treasury. Great treasures of gold, silver, and many kinds of
valuables were found there. He carried nothing away with him except the injury to his soul.

### 29. Of the girls of the monastery of Poitiers

**[029]** The envoys returning from Spain reported nothing certain because Leovigild was encamped with his army against his elder son. In the monastery of
blessed Radegund a girl named Disciola, niece of the blessed Salvius, bishop of Albi, died in the following manner. When she fell ill, the other sisters
attended her assiduously. The day came for her departure from the body, and about the ninth hour she said to the sisters, “Behold, I already feel easier;
behold, I feel no pain. There is now no need for your solicitude to expend further care on me. Rather, withdraw from me so that I may relax more easily in
sleep.” On hearing this, her sisters withdrew from the cell for a short time and then returned. Standing before her, they waited to hear what she would say. She
stretched out her hands, begging a blessing from someone unseen, and said, “Bless me, holy handmaidens of God on high. Behold, you are already being troubled
for the third time today on my account. Why, holy ones, do you endure repeated trouble for a weak little woman?” When the sisters asked to whom she was
speaking, she gave no answer. After a short interval she gave a loud cry with a laugh and yielded up her spirit.

Behold, a certain demoniac who had come to be cleansed for the feast of the blessed Cross seized his own hair and dashed himself to the ground, saying, “Alas,
alas for me, who have suffered such a loss! If only I might have investigated the matter beforehand; then this soul would not have been taken from my power.”
When those present asked what he meant, he replied, “Behold, the angel Michael has received the girl’s soul and raised her to the heavens. My prince, whom you
call the devil, has no share in her.”

Afterward her body was washed with water and shone with such snowy whiteness that the abbess could find no linen in the store that appeared whiter than the
body. She was clothed in clean linens and committed to burial.

Another girl of this monastery also had a vision, which she related to the sisters. She thought she was making a journey and desired to reach a living fountain.
Not knowing the way, she met a man who said, “If you wish to reach the living fountain, I will guide your journey.” Thanking him, she followed as he led.
Walking together, they came to a great fountain whose waters shone like gold, while the herbs around it gleamed with verdant light like various gems. The man
said to her, “Behold the living fountain you sought with such labor. Drink your fill of its streams, so that it may become in you a fountain of living water
springing up into eternal life.” As she eagerly drank, the abbess approached from the other side and clothed the naked girl in a royal robe shining with such
light, gold, and necklaces that one could scarcely look at it. The abbess said, “Your bridegroom sends you these gifts.”

When the girl saw this vision, she was stricken at heart. A few days later she asked the abbess to prepare a cell in which she could be enclosed. The abbess
quickly completed it and said, “Behold the cell. What do you now desire?” The girl asked to be enclosed. When this was granted, the virgins gathered with loud
psalmody and burning lamps. Blessed Radegund herself took the girl by the hand and led her to the place. She bade everyone farewell, kissed each one, and was
enclosed. The entrance by which she had gone in was walled up, and there she now devotes herself to prayer and reading.

### 30. Of the death of the emperor Tiberius

**[030]** The Emperor Tiberius departed from this world that year, leaving the people in deep mourning at his death. He was supremely good, ready in almsgiving,
just in judgments, and most cautious in judging. He despised no one but embraced everyone with good will. Loving all, he was loved by all. When he fell ill and
despaired of living, he summoned the Augusta Sophia and said, “Behold, I feel that the time of my life is fulfilled. Now, on your advice, I will choose who
should preside over the state. I must choose an energetic man to exercise this power.” Sophia chose a certain Maurice, saying, “This man is very energetic and
sagacious. He has often fought the enemies of the state and gained victories.” She said this because, once Tiberius had departed, she hoped to be joined in
marriage to Maurice. But when Tiberius learned of the Augusta’s consent to this choice, he ordered his daughter to be adorned with imperial ornaments, summoned
Maurice, and said, “Behold, with the Augusta Sophia’s consent you have been chosen for the empire. To make you more secure in it, I will give you my daughter.”
The girl approached, and her father gave her to Maurice, saying, “Let my empire be granted to you together with this girl. Enjoy it prosperously, always
remembering to delight in equity and justice.” Maurice took the girl and led her to his house. When the wedding ceremony had been completed, Tiberius died.
After the funeral rites, Maurice was clothed in the diadem and purple, proceeded to the circus, received acclamations and praises, distributed gifts to the
people, and was confirmed in the empire.

### 31. Of the many evils which King Chilperic commanded to be done in his brother's cities, or did himself

**[031]** King Chilperic received envoys from his nephew Childebert, the foremost of whom was Egidius, bishop of Rheims. When admitted to the king, they
presented their proposal: “My lord, your nephew, asks you to preserve in every way the peace you made with him. He cannot have peace with your brother, because
after his father’s death Guntram took from him his part of Marseille, retains his fugitives, and refuses to return them. Your nephew Childebert therefore wishes
to preserve intact the affection he now maintains with you.” Chilperic answered, “My brother has been culpable in many respects. If my son Childebert examines
the order of events, he will immediately discover that his father was killed through Guntram’s collusion.” Bishop Egidius then said, “If you join with your
nephew and he joins with you, I can raise an army and swiftly inflict upon Guntram the vengeance that is owed.” When they had confirmed this by oath and
exchanged hostages, they departed.

Trusting their promises, Chilperic raised the army of his kingdom and came to Paris, where his stay caused the inhabitants great losses. Duke Berulf came with
the men of Tours, Poitiers, Angers, and Nantes to the border of Berry. Desiderius and Bladast, with the entire army of the province entrusted to them,
surrounded Bourges from the other side, devastating the regions through which they passed. Chilperic ordered the army that had joined him to pass through Paris.
After it crossed, he crossed himself and went to the fortress of Meudon, burning and devastating everything. Although his nephew’s army had not joined him,
Childebert’s commanders and envoys were with him. He sent messengers to the dukes mentioned above, saying, “Enter Berry, advance to the city, and exact oaths of
fidelity in my name.”

The men of Bourges assembled fifteen thousand strong at the fortress of Mediolanum and fought against Duke Desiderius. The slaughter was so great that more than
seven thousand men fell from each army. The dukes and the rest of the people reached the city, plundering and devastating everything. The depredation there was
such as had never been heard of in former times: no house, vineyard, or tree remained; they cut down, burned, and destroyed everything. They also took the
sacred vessels from the churches and burned the churches themselves.

King Guntram advanced against his brother with an army, placing all his hope in God’s judgment. One evening he sent out his army and killed the greater part of
his brother’s forces. In the morning envoys met, and the kings made peace, each promising the other that whichever party had transgressed the law would make
amends as the bishops and leading men of the people judged. They then departed in peace. King Chilperic could not restrain his army from plundering and struck
down the count of Rouen with a sword. He returned to Paris, abandoning all the booty and releasing the captives. The forces besieging Bourges received orders to
return home and carried off such quantities of booty that the whole region from which they had come seemed utterly emptied of both men and cattle.

The army of Desiderius and Bladast also passed through the Touraine, causing fires, plunder, and murders on the scale usually inflicted on enemies. They led
away captives, many of whom they later released after stripping them. A cattle plague followed this destruction, so that scarcely any stock remained, and it was
a novelty to see a bullock or heifer.

While these things were happening, King Childebert remained encamped with his army in one place. One night the common soldiers in the army were stirred up,
raised a great murmur against Bishop Egidius and the king’s dukes, and began to cry out publicly: “Remove from the king’s presence those who sell his kingdom,
subject his cities to another’s dominion, and deliver his people into the rule of another prince!” As they shouted these and similar words, morning came. They
