where he still resides with his surviving mother.

### 18. Of that which was said to the king

**[018]** While the king was staying in Paris, a poor man came and said, “Hear the words of my mouth, O king. Know that Faraulf, formerly your brother’s
chamberlain, is seeking to kill you. I have heard his plan to attack you with a knife or pierce you with a spear as you go to church for morning prayer.” The
astonished king sent for Faraulf. Faraulf denied it, but the king, fearing for his life, protected himself strongly with arms and never proceeded to holy places
or anywhere else except surrounded by armed guards. Faraulf died not long afterward.

### 19. How the queen was bidden to go to a villa

**[019]** When a great outcry arose against those who had been powerful under King Chilperic because they had taken estates and other property belonging to
others, the king ordered everything unjustly taken to be restored, as I have already mentioned. He also ordered Queen Fredegund to go to the villa of Rodoiale,
situated in the territory of Rouen. All the highest-born men of Chilperic’s kingdom followed her. There they left her with Bishop Melanius, who had been removed
from Rouen, and transferred themselves to her son, promising that he would be reared by them with the greatest care.

### 20. How he sent one who should wound Brunhilda

**[020]** After Queen Fredegund went to the villa mentioned above, she was deeply grieved that part of her power had been taken away. Considering Brunhilda
superior to herself, she secretly sent a cleric in her confidence to circumvent Brunhilda with deceit and kill her. He was to insinuate himself subtly into
Brunhilda’s service, gain her trust, and then strike secretly. When the cleric arrived, he commended himself to her with various devices, saying, “I am fleeing
from Queen Fredegund’s presence and seeking your help.” He began to make himself humble, dear, obedient, and personally devoted to the queen in everything. Not
long afterward they discovered that he had been sent treacherously. He was bound and beaten, and when he had revealed the secret plot he was allowed to return
to his patroness. He disclosed what had happened and said that he had been unable to carry out her orders; she punished him by cutting off his hands and feet.

### 21. Of the flight and custody of Eberulfus

**[021]** After these events King Guntram returned to Chalon and tried to investigate his brother’s death. The queen imputed the crime to the chamberlain
Eberulf. She had asked him to remain with her after the king’s death, but he had been unable to do so. As this enmity grew, the queen asserted that Eberulf had
killed the king, taken much of his treasure, and then withdrawn to the Touraine. If the king desired to avenge his brother’s death, she said, he should know
that Eberulf was the standard-bearer of this crime. The king then swore before all his nobles that he would destroy not only Eberulf but his progeny to the
ninth generation, so that by their slaughter the wicked custom of killing kings might be abolished.

When Eberulf learned this, he sought refuge in Saint Martin’s basilica, whose property he had often seized. An arrangement was made to guard him, and the men of
Orléans and Blois came alternately to keep watch. After fifteen days they returned with much plunder, driving off pack animals, cattle, and whatever else they
could seize. Men who had driven off blessed Martin’s beasts quarreled and pierced one another with lances. Two others who were stealing mules approached a
neighbor’s house and began demanding drink. When he said he had none, they raised their lances to pierce him, but he drew his sword and ran both through; both
fell dead. Saint Martin’s animals were nevertheless returned. The men of Orléans committed so many evils there that they cannot be described.

### 22. Of his malice

**[022]** While this was happening, Eberulf’s property was granted to various persons. He displayed in public the gold, silver, and other valuable goods that he
retained with him, while what he had entrusted to others was confiscated. His herds of horses, pigs, and pack animals were plundered. His house within the
walls, which he had taken from the Church’s dominion and filled with grain, wine, hides, and many other things, was completely stripped, and nothing remained
there except empty walls. He regarded me with particular suspicion because I faithfully supported his interests and often promised that, if he ever regained the
king’s favor, he would avenge on me what he was now suffering. God, to whom the secrets of the heart are revealed, knows that I offered him assistance with a
pure heart as far as I could. Although he had previously laid many snares for me concerning Saint Martin’s property, there was reason for me to forget them
because I had received his son from the holy font. But I believe it was a great obstacle to the unfortunate man that he showed no reverence to the holy bishop.

He often held banquets in the very atrium at the blessed saint’s feet, continually practicing drunkenness and vanity. When a priest delayed to give him wine,
though he already appeared drunk, Eberulf crushed him against a stool and beat him with his fists and various blows until the priest seemed about to give up his
soul. He might indeed have done so had the physicians’ cupping vessels not come to his aid. Out of fear of the king, Eberulf had his lodging in the reception
room of the blessed basilica. When the priest who kept the door key had closed the other doors and departed, girls and Eberulf’s other servants entered through
the reception-room door, looked at the wall paintings, and examined the ornaments of the blessed tomb, which religious people considered highly criminal. When
the priest learned this, he fixed bolts on the door and fitted bars inside. After dinner Eberulf, soaked in wine, noticed this while I was chanting psalms in
the basilica at the beginning of the night for prayer. He entered in a fury and began to assail me with insults and curses, reproaching me among other things
with wishing to separate him from the holy bishop’s fringes. Astonished at the madness that had seized the man, I tried to soothe him with gentle words. Unable
to overcome his fury with soft speech, I resolved to be silent. Seeing me silent, he turned to the priest and vomited out many insults against him, attacking
him with shameless words and me with various reproaches. Seeing that he was, so to speak, driven by a demon, I left the holy basilica and ended the scandalous
vigil. What I found hardest to bear was that he had stirred up this quarrel without reverence for the saint, before the bishop’s very tomb.

In those days I saw a dream that I related to him in the holy basilica: “I dreamed that I was celebrating the solemn Mass in this basilica. When the altar with
its offerings had been covered with a silk pall, I suddenly saw King Guntram enter and shout loudly, ‘Drag out the enemy of my family; tear the murderer away
from God’s holy altar.’ Hearing this, I turned to you and said, ‘Wretched man, seize the altar pall that covers the sacred gifts so that you may not be cast
out.’ You seized it but held it with a slack hand, not manfully. With outstretched arms I pressed my breast against the king’s, saying, ‘Do not drive this man
from the holy basilica, or you will suffer mortal danger and the holy bishop will strike you with his power. Do not kill yourself with your own javelin; if you
do, you will lose both present and eternal life.’ While the king resisted me, you released the pall and came behind me. I was deeply troubled by you. When you
returned to the altar, you seized the pall but again let it go. While you held it feebly and I resisted the king vigorously, I awoke terrified, not knowing what
the dream meant.”

When I had told him this, he said, “The dream you saw is true and agrees exactly with my own thoughts.” I asked, “What have your thoughts contemplated?” He
answered, “I had resolved that if the king ordered me dragged from this place, I would hold the altar palls with one hand and, drawing my sword with the other,
first kill you and then strike down as many clergy as I could find. After that it would be no injury for me to perish in death if I had taken vengeance on this
saint’s clergy.” Hearing this in astonishment, I marveled that the devil was speaking through his mouth. He never had any fear of God. While he was free, his
horses and cattle were let loose in the poor people’s crops and vineyards. If the owners whose labor they destroyed drove them off, Eberulf’s men immediately
beat them. In the straits in which he found himself he often recalled that he had unjustly taken the blessed bishop’s property. The previous year he had induced
a certain fickle citizen to bring an action against the church’s agents. Setting justice aside, he took away under the appearance of purchase property the
Church had long possessed and gave that man a gold section of his own belt. He did many other perverse things until the end of his life, which I shall describe
later.

### 23. Of the Jew slain with his companions

**[023]** This year Armentarius the Jew came to Tours with one adherent of his own sect and two Christians to collect the bonds that Injuriosus, formerly
vicarius, and Eunomius, formerly count, had deposited with him on account of public taxes. When he had called upon these men, he received a promise of repayment
of the money lent with interest. They further told him, “If you come to my house, I will pay what is owed and honor you with other gifts as you deserve.” He
went, was received by Injuriosus, and was seated at a banquet. When the feast was over and night approached, they moved from that place to another. It is said
that Injuriosus’s men then killed the Jews and the two Christians and threw them into a well near his house. Their relatives heard what had happened and came to
Tours. Receiving information from certain men, they found the well and drew out the bodies, although Injuriosus strongly denied being implicated in the affair.
He afterward appeared in judgment. Since he vigorously denied the charge and they had no means of proving it, judgment was given that he should clear himself by
oath. When they refused to accept this, a hearing was appointed in King Childebert’s presence. Neither the dead Jew’s money nor his bonds were found. Many
people then said that the tribune Medard had been involved in the crime because he too had borrowed money from the Jew. Injuriosus came to the hearing before
King Childebert and waited for three days until sunset. When the accusers did not come and no one charged him in the case, he returned home.

### 24. Of the plunder of the city of Poitiers

**[024]** In the tenth year of King Childebert’s reign, King Guntram summoned the peoples of his kingdom and assembled a great army. The larger part, with the
men of Orléans and Bourges, went to Poitiers because the Poitevins had broken the faith they had promised the king. They first sent an embassy to learn whether
they would be received. Maroveus, the local bishop, received the messengers harshly. The army entered the territory and committed plunder, arson, and murder.
Those returning with booty passed through the Touraine and treated in the same way people who had already given oaths, even burning churches and plundering
whatever they could find. This happened repeatedly while the others were being returned unwillingly to the king. When the army drew nearer the city and the
greater part of the region was seen to be devastated, the Poitevins sent messengers acknowledging themselves faithful to King Guntram. The soldiers were
received within the city walls and then attacked the bishop, calling him faithless. Seeing himself hard pressed, he broke up a golden chalice from the sacred
vessels, converted it into coin, and ransomed himself and the people.

### 25. Of the spoiling of Marileif

**[025]** They also surrounded Marileif, who had been regarded as the chief physician in King Chilperic’s household, with great violence. Duke Gararic had
already plundered him severely, and these men now stripped him again until no substance remained. They carried off his horses, gold, silver, and best valuables
and subjected him to ecclesiastical servitude. His father’s service had been to attend the church mills, and his brothers, cousins, and other relatives were
subject to the royal estates and bakery.

### 26. How Gundovald went about the cities

**[026]** Gundovald wished to approach Poitiers but feared to do so because he had heard that an army was already being raised against him. In the cities that
had belonged to King Sigibert he received oaths in King Childebert’s name; in the others that had belonged to Guntram or Chilperic they swore in his own name to
keep faith with him. He then came to Angoulême, received oaths, rewarded the leading men, and proceeded to Périgueux. He left its bishop gravely injured because
he had not received him honorably.

### 27. Of the injury to Bishop Magnulf

**[027]** From there Gundovald went to Toulouse and sent messengers to Magnulf, bishop of the city, asking to be received by him. Remembering the earlier injury
he had suffered through Sigulf, who had once wished to raise himself to the kingdom, Magnulf told his citizens, “I know that Guntram and his nephew are kings,
but I do not know where this man comes from. Be prepared, therefore, and if Duke Desiderius wishes to bring this calamity upon me, let him perish in the same
way as Sigulf. Let this be an example to everyone that no foreigner may dare violate the kingdom of the Franks.” While they resisted and prepared for war,
Gundovald arrived with a great army. Seeing that they could not withstand him, they received him.

Afterward the bishop sat at dinner with Gundovald in the church house and said, “You assert that you are King Chlothar’s son, but I do not know whether that is
true. Even if you can justify your undertaking, my mind finds it incredible.” Gundovald replied, “I am King Chlothar’s son, and I shall now receive my part of
the kingdom. I will swiftly go to Paris and establish the seat of my kingdom there.” The bishop asked, “Is it true, then, that no one of the stock of the
Frankish kings remains, if you accomplish what you say?” When Mummolus overheard these exchanges, he raised his hand and struck the bishop with blows, saying,
“Are you not ashamed to answer so great a king like a degenerate fool?” When Desiderius learned what had been said on the bishop’s advice, he too was moved to
anger and laid hands on him. Together they beat him with spear-shafts, fists, and heels, bound him with a rope, and condemned him to exile, taking away both his
own property and the Church’s in full. Waddo, who was Queen Rigunthis’s mayor of the palace, joined them. The others who had accompanied him escaped by flight.

### 28. That the Army Advanced Farther

**[028]** Afterward the army withdrew from Poitiers and proceeded farther after Gundovald. Many men of Tours followed him for the sake of gain, but when the
Poitevins attacked them some were killed and most returned stripped. Those who had joined the army earlier went on together. The army reached the river Dordogne
and began waiting to learn what would become of Gundovald. Duke Desiderius and Bladast, together with Waddo, Queen Rigunthis’s mayor of the palace, had already
joined him, as I said above. Bishop Sagittarius and Mummolus were among his foremost adherents, Sagittarius having already received a promise of the episcopate
of Toulouse.

### 29. Of the death of Eberulfus

**[029]** While this was happening, King Guntram sent a man named Claudius, saying, “If you go and either kill Eberulf with the sword after driving him from the
basilica or bind him in chains, I will enrich you with great gifts; but I strictly warn you not to injure the holy basilica.” Claudius, devoted to vanity and
avarice, flew swiftly to Paris, for his wife came from the territory of Meaux. He began considering whether to see Queen Fredegund, thinking, “If I see her, I
can obtain some gift from her. I know that she is an enemy of the man to whom I am being sent.” He approached her, immediately received great gifts, and
elicited many promises that he would either kill Eberulf after dragging him from the basilica, deceive and bind him in chains, or slaughter him in the atrium
itself.

Claudius returned to the fortress of Dun and induced the count to assign him three hundred men, ostensibly to guard the gates of Tours, so that with their help
he could overwhelm Eberulf when he arrived. While the local count was assembling these men, Claudius proceeded to Tours. On the journey he began, as is the
barbarian custom, to observe omens and say that they were unfavorable to him. He also asked many people whether blessed Martin’s power was still manifested
against the perfidious, and whether vengeance followed immediately when anyone injured those who hoped in him. Leaving behind the men who were to come to his
aid, as I have said, he approached the holy basilica. He immediately joined the unfortunate Eberulf and began giving oaths, swearing by everything sacred and by
the power of the bishop present there that no one would be more faithful in Eberulf’s cause or better able to plead it with the king. The wretched man had
privately resolved, “Unless I deceive him by perjury, I will not overcome him.” When Eberulf saw Claudius making such promises with oaths in the basilica itself
and throughout the porticoes and each venerable part of the atrium, the wretch believed the perjurer.

The next day, while I was staying at a villa about thirty miles from the city, Eberulf was invited with Claudius and other citizens to a banquet at the holy
basilica. Claudius wished to strike him there with a sword, provided Eberulf’s servants stood far enough away, but Eberulf, vain as he was, never noticed. When
the banquet ended, Eberulf and Claudius began walking together through the atrium of the basilica house, repeatedly promising each other fidelity and affection
with oaths. As they spoke, Claudius said to Eberulf, “I would enjoy taking a drink at your lodging, if you have wines mixed with spices, or if your energy would
provide a libation of stronger wine.” Eberulf gladly answered that he had some: “You will find everything you wish at my lodging, provided only that my lord
deigns to enter the hut where I dwell.” He sent one servant after another to obtain the stronger wines, namely Laticinian and Gazitinian. When Claudius saw
Eberulf left alone by the servants, he raised his hand toward the basilica and said, “Most blessed Martin, let me soon see my wife and parents.” The unfortunate
man was in a dilemma: he intended to kill Eberulf in the atrium, yet feared the holy bishop’s power.

Then one of Claudius’s stronger servants seized Eberulf from behind and held him in powerful arms, preparing to expose his chest for slaughter. Claudius drew a
sword from his belt and approached him. But Eberulf too, though held, prepared a weapon drawn from his belt to strike. Claudius raised his right hand and drove
his knife into Eberulf’s chest, while Eberulf for his part fixed a dagger beneath Claudius’s armpit. Eberulf then drew it back and, aiming another blow, cut off
Claudius’s thumb. Claudius’s servants gathered at this and wounded Eberulf with various sword blows. He slipped from their hands and tried to flee, already
exhausted. Drawing their swords, they struck his head most violently; his brain poured out, and he fell dead. He did not deserve to be saved by the saint whom
he had never understood faithfully to invoke.

Terrified, Claudius sought the abbot’s little cell, wishing to be protected by the abbot although he had not known how to show reverence to the abbot’s patron.
As he sat there he said, “An immense crime has been committed, and unless you help me, I will perish.” While he spoke, Eberulf’s servants rushed in with swords
and lances. Finding the door barred, they broke the cell’s windows and hurled spears through the openings in the wall, piercing Claudius and leaving him half
alive. His attendants hid behind doors and under beds. The abbot was seized by two clerics and with difficulty rescued alive from among the sword-blades. The
doors were opened, and the crowd of swordsmen entered. Some of the registered poor and other paupers also tried to overthrow the cell’s roof because of the
crime committed. Demoniacs and various needy people came with stones and clubs to avenge the violence done to the basilica, indignant that such things, which
had never happened before, had been perpetrated there. In short, the fugitives were dragged from their hiding places and cruelly slaughtered, and the cell’s
pavement was stained with gore. After they were killed, they were dragged outside and left naked on the cold ground. The killers seized plunder and escaped by
flight the following night. God’s vengeance immediately fell upon those who had polluted the blessed atrium with human blood. Nor was Eberulf’s crime considered
small, since the blessed bishop had allowed him to suffer such things. The king was greatly angered but became calm when the circumstances were known. He
granted the unfortunate man’s remaining movable and immovable property to his own faithful servants. They left Eberulf’s wife, severely stripped, in the holy
basilica. The nearest relatives carried away the bodies of Claudius and the others and buried them in their own region.

### 30. Of Gundovald’s Envoys

**[030]** Gundovald sent two clerics as envoys to his friends. One, an abbot of the city of Cahors, hid the letters he had received beneath the wax in a
hollowed wooden tablet. He was seized by King Guntram’s men, the letters were found, and he was brought before the king. After being most severely beaten, he
was thrust into custody.

### 31. Of the relics of Saint Sergius the martyr

**[031]** At that time Gundovald was in Bordeaux and greatly loved by Bishop Berthram. While inquiring what assistance might support his cause, he was told that
a certain king in the East had taken a thumb of the holy martyr Sergius and fastened it to the right arm of his own body. When necessity required him to repel
enemies, he trusted in this help: wherever he raised the forearm of his right arm, a multitude of enemies immediately fled as though overwhelmed by the martyr’s
power. Hearing this, Gundovald began to inquire carefully whether anyone in that region had been privileged to obtain relics of Saint Sergius.

Meanwhile Bishop Berthram, out of enmity and greed for his property, betrayed the merchant Eufron, whom he had once tonsured against his will. Eufron had
escaped by moving to another city and returned when his hair had grown. The bishop said, “There is a certain Syrian here named Eufron who made a church of his
house and placed this saint’s relics in it. With the martyr’s assistance he has seen very many signs from them. When the city of Bordeaux was once burning in a
great conflagration, this house, though surrounded by flames, was not burned at all.”

Immediately Mummolus went at a run with Bishop Berthram to the Syrian’s house. They surrounded the man and ordered the holy pledges to be shown to them. He
refused. Thinking that this snare had been prepared out of malice, he said, “Do not weary an old man or injure the saint. Take a hundred gold pieces from me and
depart.” When Mummolus insisted on seeing the holy relics, Eufron offered two hundred gold pieces, but could not even then induce him to leave unless the
pledges themselves were displayed. Mummolus ordered a ladder raised against the wall—the relics were enclosed in a little casket high on the wall opposite the
altar—and directed his deacon to climb. As the deacon ascended the rungs and seized the casket, he was so shaken by trembling that it seemed he would never
return to the ground alive. Nevertheless, he took the casket hanging on the wall and brought it down. Mummolus examined it and found a bone from the saint’s
finger, which he did not fear to strike with a knife. He laid the knife on it and struck the knife with another object. After many blows the bone could scarcely
be broken; when the little bone was divided into three parts, the pieces flew in different directions. I believe this deed was not acceptable to the martyr.

While Eufron wept bitterly, they all prostrated themselves in prayer, begging God to deign to reveal what had been taken from human eyes. After the prayer the
particles were found. Mummolus took one and departed, but not, I believe, with the martyr’s favor, as the sequel showed.

While they were staying in Bordeaux, they ordered the priest Faustianus to be ordained bishop of Agen. The bishop of Agen had recently died, and Nicetius, count
of that place and brother of Rusticus, bishop of Vic, had obtained a command from Chilperic that, after receiving the tonsure, he should be given to that city
as bishop. Gundovald, seeking to annul Chilperic’s decrees, summoned the bishops and ordered Faustianus to be consecrated. Bishop Berthram, the metropolitan,
guarding against future consequences, assigned the consecration to Palladius of Saintes. Berthram’s eyes were also afflicted by soreness at the time. Orestes,
bishop of Bazas, was present at this ordination but later denied it before the king.

### 32. Of other legates of Gundovald

**[032]** Afterward Gundovald again sent two envoys to the king with consecrated staffs according to Frankish custom, so that no one would harm them and they
might present their message and return with an answer. But they incautiously disclosed their demands to many people before seeing the king. Word immediately
reached the king, and they were brought before him bound in chains. Not daring to deny what they sought, to whom they had been sent, or by whom, they said,
“Gundovald, who recently came from the East and claims to be the son of your father, King Chlothar, sent me so that he may receive the portion of the kingdom
due to him. If you do not return it, know that he will come into these parts with an army. All the strongest men of the region beyond the Dordogne belonging to
Gaul have joined him. He says, ‘God will judge when we meet on the level ground of a single field whether I am Chlothar’s son or not.’”

Inflamed with fury, the king ordered them stretched on the rack and severely beaten so that they might more clearly prove whether their statements were true and
the force of torture might extort any deceit still hidden in their breasts. As their torments increased, they said that Gundovald’s niece, King Chilperic’s
daughter, had been condemned to exile with Magnulf, bishop of Toulouse; that Gundovald had taken all the treasures; and that he had been invited by all King
Childebert’s leading men, especially when Guntram Boso went to Constantinople years earlier.

### 33. How Childebert came to his uncle Guntram

**[033]** After the men had been beaten and thrust into prison, the king ordered his nephew Childebert to be summoned, so that together they might hear what
these men had to say. When the two kings were assembled and questioned the men, they repeated in the presence of both rulers what King Guntram alone had
previously heard. They also steadfastly maintained that, as we have already said, this whole affair was known to all the leading men in King Childebert’s
kingdom. For this reason some of Childebert’s chief men who were thought to have participated in the plot were then afraid to leave the assembly. Afterwards
King Guntram placed a spear in King Childebert’s hand and said: ‘This is the sign that I have handed over my entire kingdom to you. Go now, and bring all my
cities under the dominion of your authority as though they were your own. For, because of my sins, no one of my stock remains except you alone, my brother’s
son. You shall therefore succeed as heir to my whole kingdom, and all others shall be excluded from the inheritance.’ Then, leaving everyone else, he took the
boy aside and spoke with him privately, first adjuring him most earnestly not to reveal their secret conversation to anyone. He told him whom he should retain
as counsellors and whom he should exclude from his confidence, whom he should trust and whom avoid, whom he should honour with gifts and whom deprive of office.
Among other things, he charged him on no account to trust or retain Bishop Egidius, who had always been his enemy, because he had repeatedly perjured himself
against both Childebert and his father. Then, when they had assembled for a banquet, King Guntram addressed the whole army, saying: ‘See, my men, my son
Childebert has now become a grown man. See to it that you no longer treat him as a little child. Abandon now the perversity and presumption which you have
practised, for he is the king whom you must henceforth serve.’ After speaking these and similar words, they feasted and made merry for three days, enriched one
another with many gifts, and departed in peace. King Guntram then restored to Childebert everything that his father Sigibert had possessed, adjuring him not to
go to his mother, lest she be given an opportunity to write to Gundovald or receive letters from him.

### 34. How Gundovald went to Comminges

**[034]** When Gundovald heard that the army was approaching him, deserted by Duke Desiderius, he crossed the Garonne with Bishop Sagittarius, Dukes Mummolus
and Bladast, and Waddo, making for Comminges. This city stands on the summit of a mountain and is not joined to any other height. A great spring bursts forth at
the foot of the mountain and is enclosed by a very strong tower; the townspeople descend to it from the city through a tunnel and draw water in secret.
Gundovald entered this city at the beginning of Lent and addressed the citizens, saying: ‘Know that I have been chosen king by all who are in Childebert’s
kingdom, and that I have no small support with me. But since my brother King Guntram has raised an immense army against me, you must store food and all your
household goods within the protection of the walls, so that, while divine goodness increases my support, you may not perish from want.’ They believed him,
placed whatever they possessed in the city, and prepared to resist. At that time King Guntram sent a letter to Gundovald in Queen Brunhild’s name, instructing
him to dismiss his army and order it to return home, while he himself withdrew farther away to spend the winter at Bordeaux. Guntram had written this
deceitfully in order to learn more fully what Gundovald was doing. While Gundovald remained at Comminges, he said to the inhabitants: ‘The army is now
approaching; go out to resist it.’ When they went out, Gundovald’s men seized and closed the gates, shutting out the people together with the bishop of the
place, and brought everything they could find in the city under their own control. Such an abundance of grain and wine was found there that, if they had held
out courageously, they would not have lacked provisions for many years.

### 35. Of the basilica of Saint Vincent the martyr of Agen laid waste

**[035]** King Guntram’s commanders had heard at that time that Gundovald had halted beyond the Garonne with a vast multitude of armed men, and that he still
retained the treasures which Rigunthis had brought. Making an attack, they swam across the Garonne with their horses, though some of the army were drowned in
the river. The rest came ashore and, searching for Gundovald, found camels laden with an enormous weight of gold and silver, as well as horses which he had
abandoned exhausted along the roads. Hearing next that Gundovald was staying within the walls of Comminges, they left their wagons and various baggage with the
less able men, while the stronger men resolved to pursue him across the Garonne as they had already done. As they hastened on, they came to the basilica of
Saint Vincent within the territory of Agen, where the martyr himself is said to have completed his contest for Christ’s name, and found it filled with the
inhabitants’ various treasures. The people had hoped that Christians would not violate the basilica of so great a martyr, and its doors had been barred with the
greatest care. Without delay the army approached and, when it could not open the doors of the church, set them on fire. Once the doors had been consumed, the
soldiers carried off all the property and furnishings they could find, together with the sacred vessels. But divine vengeance struck many of them there. The
hands of several were supernaturally burned and emitted a great smoke, as usually rises from a fire. Some were seized by a demon and raved in madness, crying
out upon the martyr. Many who had kept apart from the tumult wounded themselves with their own javelins. The rest of the crowd went forward in great fear. What
more need be said? They assembled at Comminges—for so I have called the city—and the whole army pitched camp on the plain outside the city, remaining there with
their tents spread out. The entire surrounding region was devastated; but some soldiers who strayed farther afield, driven by the sharper goad of avarice, were
killed by the inhabitants.

### 36. Of the conference of Gundovald with the army

**[036]** Many of the soldiers climbed the hill and repeatedly spoke with Gundovald, heaping abuse upon him and saying: ‘Are you that painter who, in King
Chlothar’s time, used to paint the walls and ceilings of oratories? Are you the man whom the inhabitants of Gaul so often called Ballomer? Are you the man who
was repeatedly tonsured and exiled by the Frankish kings because of these same pretensions which you now put forward? Tell us, most wretched of men, who brought
you to this region. Who gave you such audacity that you dared to enter the territory of our lords and kings? If anyone summoned you, declare it loudly. See,
death lies exposed before your eyes; see the very pit of destruction for which you have so long searched and into which you will be cast headlong. Tell the
truth about your accomplices, and reveal who invited you.’ Hearing this, Gundovald stood nearer above the gate and said: ‘No one is unaware that my father
Chlothar hated me, and everyone knows that I was tonsured by him and afterwards by my brothers. This affair brought me into association with Narses, the
commander in Italy. There I took a wife and begot two sons. When she died, I took my children with me and went to Constantinople. The emperors received me most
kindly, and I lived there until this time. Some years ago, when Guntram Boso went to Constantinople, I anxiously inquired carefully into my brothers’ affairs
and learned that our line had been greatly reduced. Only Kings Childebert and Guntram remained of our stock—that is, my brother and my brother’s son. King
Chilperic’s sons had died with him, leaving only one small child. My brother Guntram had no sons, and our nephew Childebert was not yet strong. Then Guntram
Boso, having carefully explained all this to me, invited me, saying: “Come, for all the leading men of King Childebert’s kingdom invite you, and no one dares
utter a word against you. I all know that you are Chlothar’s son, and no one remains in Gaul who can rule that kingdom unless you come.” I gave him many gifts
and received oaths from him at twelve holy places, so that I might enter this kingdom in safety. I came to Marseilles, where the bishop received me with the
greatest kindness, for he had letters from the leading men of my nephew’s kingdom. From there I went to Avignon in accordance with the wishes of the patrician
Mummolus. Guntram, however, forgot his oath and promise, stole my treasures, and brought them under his own control. Now recognize that I am king, just as my
brother Guntram is. But if your minds are so inflamed with hatred of me, let me be conducted to your king; if he acknowledges me as his brother, let him do what
he wishes. If you will not agree even to this, at least permit me to return whence I came. I will depart and do no injury to anyone. But so that you may know
that what I say is true, question Radegund of Poitiers and Ingitrude of Tours. They will affirm to you that my words are certain.’ As he said this, many pursued
his words with abuse and reproaches.

### 37. Of the war against the city

**[037]** The fifteenth day of the siege had dawned, and Leudegisel was preparing new engines for destroying the city: wagons fitted with battering rams and
covered with wicker frames and planks, beneath which the army could advance to demolish the walls. But when they approached, they were so overwhelmed with
stones that all who came near the wall fell. The defenders hurled down barrels filled with burning pitch and fat, and threw others filled with stones upon them.
When night put an end to the fighting, the army returned to camp. Chariulf, a very rich and powerful man, was also with Gundovald, and the city was well stocked
from his storehouses and granaries; the besieged lived chiefly upon his supplies. Bladast, seeing what was happening and fearing that Leudegisel would gain the
victory and put them to death, set fire to a building belonging to the church. While those shut inside rushed to extinguish the blaze, he slipped away and
escaped. At daybreak the army again rose for battle and made bundles of brushwood, intending to fill a deep ravine on the eastern side; but this device
accomplished nothing. Bishop Sagittarius frequently went around the walls under arms and often threw stones at the enemy with his own hand.

### 38. Of the death of Gundovald

**[038]** When the besiegers saw that they were accomplishing nothing, they sent secret messengers to Mummolus, saying: ‘Acknowledge your lord and at last
abandon this perversity. What madness possesses you, that you submit to an unknown man? Your wife and sons have already been taken captive, and your sons have,
I believe, already been killed. Where are you rushing, and what do you await, except your own destruction?’ Receiving this message, Mummolus said: ‘As I see, my
kingdom has reached its end and its power is falling. One thing remains: if I learn that my life will be spared, I can relieve you of much labour.’ When the
messengers departed, Bishop Sagittarius went with Mummolus, Chariulf, and Waddo to a church, where they swore that, if they were assured their lives would be
spared, they would abandon their friendship with Gundovald and hand him over to the enemy. The messengers returned and again promised them safety of life.
Mummolus said: ‘Let only this be done: I will deliver him into your hands, and, acknowledging the king as my lord, I will hasten into his presence.’ They
promised that, if he fulfilled this, they would receive him in friendship and, if they could not obtain his pardon from the king, would place him in a church so
that he would not be punished with death. Having made these promises with oaths, they departed. Mummolus then went with Bishop Sagittarius and Waddo to
Gundovald and said: ‘You yourself know the oaths of fidelity which I swore to you while you were present. Now accept salutary counsel: leave this city and
present yourself to your brother, as you have often requested. I have spoken with these men, and they say that the king does not wish to destroy your support,
since so little of your family remains.’ Perceiving their deception, Gundovald burst into tears and said: ‘It was at your invitation that I was brought to this
land of Gaul. Of my treasures, which contain an immense weight of silver, gold, and various precious objects, part is retained at Avignon and part was seized by
Guntram Boso. Relying entirely upon God’s help, I placed all my hope in you, entrusted my counsel to you, and always desired to reign through you. Now God will
judge between us if you have spoken any falsehood to me; let Him judge my cause.’ When he had spoken, Mummolus replied: ‘I am saying nothing deceitful to you.
See, very brave men are standing at the gate awaiting your arrival. Now take off my golden belt which you are wearing, lest you appear to go forth in
ostentation; gird on your own sword and restore mine to me.’ Gundovald said: ‘I do not accept these words as innocent, since you seek to take from me what I
have until now used as tokens of your friendship.’ But Mummolus declared with an oath that no harm would be done to him. They therefore went out of the gate,
and Gundovald was received by Ollo, count of Bourges, and Boso. Mummolus returned into the city with his followers and barred the gate most securely. When
Gundovald saw that he had been delivered into his enemies’ hands, he raised his hands and eyes to heaven and said: ‘Eternal Judge and true Avenger of the
innocent, O God, from whom all justice proceeds, who takes no pleasure in falsehood, and in whom there is no deceit or crafty malice, I commit my cause to You,
praying that You may swiftly take vengeance upon those who have delivered me, an innocent man, into the hands of my enemies.’ Having said this and signed
himself with the Lord’s cross, he began to go with the men named above. When they had gone some distance from the gate, where the whole valley around the city
falls away precipitously, he was pushed by Ollo and fell. Ollo cried: ‘Behold your Ballomer, who calls himself the king’s brother and son!’ He thrust a lance at
him and tried to transfix him, but it was turned aside by the rings of his mail and did him no harm. Then, as Gundovald struggled to rise and climb back up the
hill, Boso hurled a stone and struck his head. He fell and died. The whole crowd came, fixed their lances in him, bound his feet with a rope, and dragged him
through all the army camps. They tore out his hair and beard and left him unburied in the place where he had been killed. During the following night the leading
men secretly carried off all the treasures they could find in the city, together with the church vessels. In the morning the gates were opened and the army sent
in. They put all the people shut inside to the sword, slaughtering the Lord’s priests and their ministers at the very altars of the churches. After they had
killed everyone, so that not a male was left, they burned the whole city with its churches and other buildings, leaving nothing there but bare ground.

### 39. Of the death of Bishop Sagittarius and of Mummolus

**[039]** Leudegisel then returned to camp with Mummolus, Sagittarius, Chariulf, and Waddo, and secretly sent messengers to the king to ask what he wished to be
done with them. The king ordered them to be executed. Waddo and Chariulf then left them, leaving their sons as hostages. When word of their intended execution
arrived and Mummolus learned of it, he girded on his arms and went to Leudegisel’s hut. Seeing him, Leudegisel said: ‘Why do you come thus, as though fleeing?’
Mummolus answered: ‘As I see, none of the promised faith is being kept, for I perceive that I am faced with death.’ Leudegisel said: ‘I will go outside and calm
everything.’ When he went out, the house was immediately surrounded at his command so that Mummolus might be killed. Mummolus resisted the attackers for a very
long time and reached the doorway; as he was coming out, two men struck him in both sides with lances. He fell and died. Seeing this, the bishop was stricken
with terror, and one of those standing nearby said: ‘See with your own eyes, bishop, what is happening. Cover your head so that you will not be recognized, make
for the forest, and hide for a little while; when their anger has passed, you may escape.’ He accepted the advice and tried to flee with his head covered, but a
man drew his sword and cut off his head together with the hood. Then everyone returned home, committing great plunder and murder along the way. In those days
Fredegund sent Chuppa to Toulouse to rescue her daughter from there by whatever means he could. Many said that he had been sent for the additional purpose that,
if he found Gundovald alive, he might entice him with many promises and bring him to her. Unable to do this, Chuppa took Rigunthis and brought her back from
that place, not without great humiliation and disgrace.

### 40. Of the treasures of Mummolus

**[040]** Duke Leudegisel then came to the king with all the treasures mentioned above, which the king afterwards distributed to the poor and the churches. The
king seized Mummolus’s wife and began to question her about what had become of the treasures which these men had collected. Knowing that her husband had been
killed and that all their pride had utterly collapsed into the dust, she revealed everything. She said that much gold and silver still remained at Avignon which
had not come to the king’s attention. The king immediately sent men to bring it back, accompanied by a servant whom Mummolus had greatly trusted and to whom he
had entrusted these things. They went and took everything that had been left in the city. It is said that there were two hundred and fifty talents of silver and
more than thirty of gold, and that Mummolus had taken this from an ancient treasure which he had discovered. The king divided it with his nephew King Childebert
and gave most of his own share to the poor, leaving the woman nothing beyond what she had inherited from her parents.

### 41. Of the Giant

**[041]** At that time a member of Mummolus’s household, a man of immense stature, was also brought before the king. He was of such great height that he was
thought to stand two or three feet above the tallest men. He was a carpenter and died not long afterwards.

### 42. Of the power of Saint Martin

**[042]** Afterwards the judges issued an edict that those who had been slow to join this expedition should be punished. The count of Bourges also sent his
servants to despoil men of this kind in a house of blessed Martin situated within that territory. But the steward of the house began to resist vigorously,
saying: ‘These are Saint Martin’s men. Do them no injury, for they have not been accustomed to go on such expeditions.’ They replied: ‘Your Martin, whom you
always invoke vainly in these affairs, is nothing to us. Both you and they shall pay the penalty for having neglected the king’s command.’ Saying this, he
entered the courtyard of the house. He was immediately struck by pain, fell, and became gravely ill. Turning to the steward, he said in a tearful voice: ‘I beg
you to make the sign of the Lord’s cross over me and invoke blessed Martin’s name. I now know that his power is great. For as I entered the courtyard, I saw an
old man holding a tree in his hand, which soon spread its branches and covered the whole courtyard. One of its branches touched me, and I fell, overwhelmed by
its blow.’ Beckoning to his men, he asked to be carried out of the courtyard. Once outside, he began to invoke blessed Martin’s name more earnestly, and
thereafter he recovered and was healed.

### 43. Of Desiderius and Waddo

**[043]** Desiderius protected himself and his property within the fortifications of the camp. Waddo, Rigunthis’s major-domo, went over to Queen Brunhild; she
received him and dismissed him with gifts and favour. Chariulf sought refuge in Saint Martin’s basilica.

### 44. Of the woman with the pythonic spirit

**[044]** At that time there was a woman who possessed a spirit of divination and brought her masters great profit by her prophecies. She advanced so far in
their favour that she was freed by them and allowed to follow her own wishes. Whenever anyone suffered a theft or some other loss, she would at once declare
where the thief had gone, to whom he had handed over the property, or what he had done with it. She accumulated gold and silver daily and went about in finery,
so that the people thought there was something divine in her. When these things were reported to Ageric, bishop of Verdun, he sent men to arrest her. She was
seized and brought before him, and, in accordance with what I read in the Acts of the Apostles, he recognized that an unclean spirit of divination was in her.
While he pronounced an exorcism over her and anointed her forehead with holy oil, the demon cried out and revealed to the bishop what it was. But since it was
not expelled from the woman by him, she was permitted to depart. Seeing that she could not remain in that place, she went to Queen Fredegund and hid there.

### 45. Of the famine of the present year

**[045]** A great famine afflicted almost the whole of Gaul this year. Many people made bread from grape seeds, hazel flowers, or, in some cases, dried fern
roots ground into powder and mixed with a little flour. Many cut down the green growth among the standing grain and did the same. There were also many who had
no flour at all; they gathered and ate various herbs, became swollen, and died. Very many wasted away from starvation and perished. Merchants then cruelly
despoiled the people, scarcely selling a measure of grain or half a measure of wine for a triens. The poor submitted themselves to servitude in order to obtain
even the smallest amount of food.

### 46. Of the death of Christoforus

**[046]** In those days the merchant Christopher went to Orléans, having heard that a great quantity of wine had been brought there. He bought wine, loaded it
into boats, received a large sum of money from his father-in-law, and travelled on horseback with two Saxon servants. The servants had long hated their master
and had often run away because they were frequently and severely beaten. When they came into a forest, their master rode ahead, and one servant hurled a lance
with great force and transfixed him. As he fell, the other hacked at his head with a framea. Cut to pieces by both of them, he was left lifeless. They took the
money and escaped. After Christopher’s brother had buried his body, he sent his men after the servants. They captured the younger, while the elder escaped with
the money. As the captors were returning, they left the prisoner rather loosely bound; he seized a lance and killed one of the men leading him. The others
brought him to Tours, where he was subjected to various tortures, mutilated, and hung lifeless on a gibbet.

### 47. Of the civil war among the citizens of Tours

**[047]** A serious civil feud then arose among the citizens of Tours. Sichar, the son of the late John, was celebrating the feast of the Lord’s Nativity with
Austrigisel and other local people in the village of Manthelan, when the priest of the place sent a servant to invite some men to come to his house for a drink.
When the servant arrived, one of those invited did not hesitate to draw his sword and strike him. He immediately fell dead. Sichar, who was on friendly terms
with the priest, heard that his servant had been killed; he took up arms and went to the church to await Austrigisel. Hearing this, Austrigisel gathered his
weapons and set out against him. Both sides joined battle, and Sichar was rescued by the clergy and fled to his estate, leaving four wounded servants, together
with silver and clothing, in the priest’s house. After his flight, Austrigisel attacked again, killed the servants, and carried off the gold, silver, and other
property. The parties then came before the citizens’ tribunal, and it was decided that Austrigisel, who had committed murder and, after killing the servants,
had seized property without a hearing, should be condemned according to law. An agreement was made, but within a few days Sichar heard that the property which
Austrigisel had seized was being kept by Auno, his son, and his brother Eberulf. Disregarding the settlement and joining Audinus, he raised a disturbance and
attacked them at night with armed men. Breaking into the lodging where they slept, he killed the father, brother, and son, killed the servants, and carried off
their property and cattle. Hearing of this, I was greatly disturbed and, with the judge, sent envoys to them, asking them to come before me so that, after a
hearing, they might depart in peace and the quarrel spread no farther. When they came and the citizens had assembled, I said: ‘Do not continue in these crimes,
my men, lest the evil spread farther. I have lost sons of the Church; let us now fear that we may lose others in this strife. Be peaceful, I beg you; let him
who has done evil make compensation without destroying friendship, so that you may be peaceful sons worthy to receive the kingdom of God by the Lord’s gift. For
He Himself says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God.” If the guilty man has insufficient means, he shall be redeemed with
the Church’s silver; meanwhile, let no man’s soul perish.’ Saying this, I offered the Church’s money; but Chramnesind’s party, which sought vengeance for the
death of his father, brother, and uncle, would not accept it. When they departed, Sichar prepared to go to the king and set out for Poitiers to see his wife.
While urging a servant to do his work and beating him with a raised stick, the servant drew the sword at his belt and did not hesitate to wound his master.
Sichar fell to the ground; his friends ran up, seized the servant, cruelly beat him, cut off his hands and feet, and condemned him to the gibbet. Meanwhile a
report reached Tours that Sichar had died. When Chramnesind heard this, he summoned his relatives and friends and hastened to Sichar’s house. He plundered it,
killed several servants, burned all the houses belonging both to Sichar and to the others who shared that estate, and carried off the cattle and everything
movable. The judge then brought the parties to the city, where they pleaded their causes. The judges decided that the party which had refused the earlier
compensation and burned the houses should forfeit half the sum awarded to it—contrary to the law, but in order to restore peace—and that Sichar should pay the
other half of the compensation. The Church supplied the money which they had awarded; Sichar paid the compensation, security was given, and the parties swore
mutual oaths that neither would ever again trouble the other. Thus the dispute came to an end.

# LATIN TEXT

*INCIPIT LIBER VII.*

## 1. De obitu sancti Salvii episcopi.

**[001]** Licet sit studium historiam prosequi, quam priorum librorum ordo reliquid, tamen prius aliqua de beati Salvii obitu exposcit loqui devotio, qui hoc
anno obisse probatur. Hic enim, ut ipse referre erat solitus, diu in habitu saeculari commoratus, cum iudicibus saeculi mundialis causas est exsecutus; numquam
tamen se in his concupiscentiis oblegans, quibus adoliscentum animus solitus est inplicari0. Iam cum divini spiramenti odor interna viscerum attigisset, relicta
saeculari militia, monastyrio expetivit; intellexitque vir iam tunc divinitati deditus, melius esse uti paupertatem cum Dei timore quam saeculi pereuntis lucra
sectari. In quo monastyrio diu sub regula a patribus instituta versatus est. Iam vero cum in robore maiori tam intellectus quam aetatis evectus esset, defuncto
abbate, qui huic monasterio praeerat, alendi gregis suscepit officium; et qui se magis fratribus publicum pro correctione reddere debuerat, fit, adsumpto
honore, remutior. Ilico sibi secretiorem cellolam quaerit; nam in priore, ut ipse adserebat, amplius quam novem vicibus, nimia excesus abstinentia, pellem
corporis demutavit. Denique accepto honore, cum in hac contentus parsimonia orationi et lectioni vacaret, illud plerumque revolvebat, melius sibi fieri, si
esset inter monachos occultus, quam nomen acciperit abbatis in populos. Quid plura? Includitur vale dicens fratribus sibique ipsis vale dicentibus. In qua
inclusione in omni abstinentia magis, quam prius egerat, commoratur, studens pro caritatis obsequio, ut, cum quisque venisset extraneus, et orationem tribuerit
et eoglogias gratiam plenissimam ministraret; quae multis infirmis plerumque salutem integram detulerunt. Quodam autem tempore, febre nimia exaustus, hanillus
iacebat in lectulo, et ecce! subito magno lumine cellola clarificata contremuit. Ad ille, extensis ad caelum manibus, cum gratiarum actione spiritum exalavit.
Mixto quoque ululatu monachi cum ipsius genetrice corpus defuncti extrahunt, aqua diluunt, vestimentis induunt et feretro superponunt, adque in psallentio
fletuque labentem exegunt noctem. Mane autem facto, funeris officio praeparato, corpus movere coepit in feretro. Et ecce! malis robiscentibus, vir, quasi de
gram somno suscitatus, excutitur, apertisque oculis, manibus elevatis, ait: 'O Domine misericors, quid fecisti mihi, ut me in hunc tenebrosum mundanae
habitationis locum redire permitteris, cum mihi melior esset in caelo tua misericordia quam istius mundi vita nequissima?' Stupentibus autem suis et
interrogantibus, quid fuerit tale prodigium, nihil interrogantibus ille respondit. Surgens autem de feretro, nihil mali sentiens de incommodo quod laboraverat,
triduo absque cibi ac poculi perstetit alimento. Die autem tertio convocatis monachis et matrem, ait: 'Audite, o dilectissimi, et intellegite, quia nihil est,
quod cernitis in hoc mundo; sed sunt iuxta id quae Salomon propheta cecinit: Omnia vanitas. Felix est enim qui ea agere potest in saeculo, ut gloriam Dei
cernere mereatur in caelo'. Et cum haec dicerit, dubitare coepit, utrum loqueretur amplius an sileret. Quo tacente, inplicitus fratrum praecibus, ut quid
vidisset exponerit, ait: 'Cum me ante hos quattuor dies, contremiscente cellola, exanimem vidistis, adpraehensus a duobus angelis in caelorum excelsa sublatus
sum, ita ut non solum hunc squalidum saeculum, verum etiam solem ac lunam, nubes et sidera sub pedibus habere potarem. Deinde per portam luce ista clariorem
introductus sum in illud habitaculum, in quo omne pavimentum erat quasi aurum argentumque renitens, lux ineffabilis, amplitudo inenarrabilis; quam ita multitudo
promiscui sexus obtexerat, ut longitudo ac latitudo catervae prorsus pervidere non possit. Cumque nobis via inter conpraementes ab his qui praecedebant angelis
pararetur, pervenimus ad locum, quem iam de longinquo contemplabamus; in quo superpendebat nubs omne luce lucidior, in quo non sol, non luna, non astrum cerni
poterat, sed super his omnibus naturali luce splendidius effulgebat, et vox procedebat e nubi, tamquam vox aquarum multarum. Ibi etiam me peccatori humiliter
salutabant viri in veste sacerdotali ac saeculari; quos mihi qui praecedebant enarraverunt esse martyres ac confessores, quos hic summo excolemus famulatu.
Stans igitur in loco in quo iussus sum, operuit me odor nimiae suavitatis, ita ut, ab hac suavitate refectus, nullum adhuc cybum potumque desiderarem. Et audivi
vocem dicentem: „Revertatur hic in saeculo, quoniam necessarius est aeclesiis nostris". Vox enim audiebatur; nam qui loqueretur, paenitus cerni non poterat. Et
ego prostratus super pavimentum cum fletu dicebam: „Heu, heu, Domine, quur mihi haec ostendisti, si ab his frustrandus eram! Ecce hodie eiecis me a facie tua,
ut revertar ad saeculum fragilem et hic ultra redire non valeam. Ne, queso, Domine, auferas misericordiam tuam a me, sed depraecor, ut permittas me hic
habitare, ne illic decidens peream". Et ait vox, quae loquebatur mihi: „Vade in pace. Ego enim sum custus tuus, donec reducam te in hoc loco". Tunc relictus a
comitibus meis, discedens cum fletu, per portam quam ingressus fueram hic sum regressus'. Haec eo loquente, stupentibus cunctis qui aderant, coepit iterum
sanctus Dei cum lacrimis dicere: 'Vae mihi, quia talem misterium ausus sum revelare. Ecce enim odor suavitatis, quam de loco sancto hauseram, et in quo per hoc
triduum sine ullo cybo potuque sustentatus sum, recessit a me. Sed et lingua mea gravibus est operta vulneribus et ita tumefacta, ut omne os meum videatur
implere. Et scio, quia non fuit bene placitum domino Deo meo, ut haec arcana vulgarentur. Sed tu nosti, Domine, quia in simplicitate cordis haec feci, non in
iactantia mentis. Sed, quaeso, indulgeas et non me derelinquas iuxta pollicitationem tuam'. Et haec dicens siluit et accepit cybum potumque. Ego vero haec
scribens vereor, ne alicui legenti sit incredibile, iuxta id quod Salustius historiam scribens ait: Ubi de virtute adque gloriam bonorum memores, quae sibi
quisque facilia factu putat, aequo animo accepit; supra ea veluti ficta pro falsis ducit. Nam testor Deum omnipotentem, quia ab ipsius ore omnia quae rettuli
audita cognovi. Post multum vero tempus ipse vir beatus a cellola sua extractus, ad episcopatum electus, invitus est ordinatus. In quo, ut opinor, decimo anno
cum agerit, invalescente apud Albigensem urbem inguinario morbo et maxima iam parte de populo illo defuncta, cum iam pauci de civibus remanerent, vir beatus
tamquam bonus pastor numquam ab illo loco recedere voluit; sed semper ortabatur eos, qui relicti fuerant, oratione incumbere ac vigiliis instanter insistere et
bona semper tam in operibus quam in cogitatione versare, dicens: 'Haec agite, ut, si vos Deus de hoc mundo migrare voluerit, non in iudicium, sed in requiem
introire possitis'. Cum autem, ut credo, iam revelante Domino, tempus suae vocationis agnusceret, ipse sibi sarcofagum conposuit, corpus abluit, vestem induit;
et sic intentum semper caelo beatum spiritum exalavit. Fuit autem magnae sanctitatis minimaeque cupiditatis, aurum numquam habere volens. Nam, si coactus
accepisset, protinus pauperibus erogabat. Cuius tempore cum Mummolus patricius multos captivos ab ea urbe duxisset, prosecutus ille omnes redemit. Tantamque ei
Dominus gratiam cum populo illo tribuit, ut ipsi etiam qui captivos duxerant et de praetio ei concederent et in reliquo munerarent; et sic patriae suae captivos
libertati pristinae restauravit. Multaque de hoc viro bona audivi; sed dum ad historiae ceptum reverti cupio, plurima praetermitto.

## 2. De conlisione Carnotenorum et Aurilianensium.

**[002]** Defuncto igitur Chilperico inventamque, quam diu quaesierat, mortem, Aurilianensis cum Blesensibus iuncti super Dunenses inruunt eosque inopinantes
proterunt; domos annonasque vel quae moveri habele non poterant incendio tradunt, pecora diripiunt adque res quas levare poterant sustulerunt. Quibus
discedentibus, coniuncti Dunenses cum reliquis Carnotenis, de vestigio subsecuntur, simile sorte eos adficientes, qua ipsi adfecti fuerant, nihil in domibus vel
extra domus vel de domibus relinquentes. Cumque adhuc inter se iurgia commoventes desevirent et Aurilianensis contra hos arma concuterent, intercedentibus
comitibus, pax usque in audientia data est, scilicet ut in die, quo iudicium erat futurum, pars, quae contra partem iniuste exarserat, iusticia mediante,
conponerit. Et sic a bello cessatum est.

## 3. De interitu Vidastis cognomento Avi.

**[003]** Vidastis cognomento Avus, qui ante hos annos Lupum Ambrosiumque pro amore uxoris Ambrosii interfecerat et ipsam sibi, quae consubrina sua esse
dicebatur, in matrimunio acceperat, dum multa scelera infra Pectavum terminum perpetraret, quodam loco cum Chulderico Saxone coniunctus, dum se invicem
convitiis lacesserent, unus ex pueris Chulderici Avonem hasta transfixit. Qui ad terram ruens, plerisque adhuc ictibus sauciatus, iniquam animam, sanguine
defluente, refudit; fuitque ultrix divina maiestas sanguinis innocentis, quem propria effuderat manu. Multa enim furta, adulteria homicidiaque miserrimus saepe
conmiserat, quae silere melius poto. Conposuit tamen filiis Saxo ille mortem eius.

## 4. Quod Fredegundis in aeclesia confugit.

**[004]** Interea Fredegundis regina iam viduata Parisius advenit et cum thesauris, quos infra murorum septa concluserat, ad aeclesiam confugit adque a
Ragnemodo fovetur episcopo. Reliquos vero thesauros, qui apud villam Calam remanserant, in quibus erat missurium illud aureum quod nuper fecerat, thesaurarii
levaverunt et ad Childeberthum regem, qui tunc apud Meldensem conmorabatur urbem, velociter transierunt.

## 5. Quod Gunthramnus rex Parius venit.

**[005]** Fredegundis igitur regina, accepto consilio, legatos ad Gunthchramnum regem mittit, dicens: 'Veniat dominus meus et suscipiat regnum fratris sui.
Est', inquid, 'mihi infans parvolus, quem in eius ulnis ponere desiderans, me ipsam eius humilio dicioni'. Conperto autem Gunthchramnus rex de fratris excessu
amarissime flevit. Moderato quoque planctu, conmoto exercitu, Parisius dirigit. Cumque ille infra muros susceptus fuisset, Childeberthus rex, nepus eius, ab
alia advenit parte.

## 6. Quod idem rex ea que de Charibertho erant sibi subegit.

**[006]** Sed cum eum Parisiaci recipere nollent, legatos ad Gunthchramnum regem diregit, dicens: 'Scio, piissime pater, non latere pietati tuae, qualiter
utrumque usque praesens tempus pars obpraesserit inimica, ut nullus de rebus sibi debitis possit invenire iustitiam. Idcirco supplex nunc depraecor, ut placita,
quae inter nos post patris mei obitum sunt innexa, custodiantur'. Tunc Gunthchramnus rex legatis illius ait: 'O miseri et semper perfidi, nihil in vobis verum
habentes neque in promissis permanentes, ecce omnia quae mihi polliciti estis relictis, cum Chilperico rege novam pactionem scripsistis, ut, me a regno depulso,
civitates meas inter se dividerent. Ecce pactiones ipsas, ecce manus vestrae subscriptiones, quibus hanc conibentiam confirmastis! Et qua nunc fronte quaeritis,
ut nepotem meum Childeberthum suscipere debeam, quem mihi vestra perversitate voluistis facere inimicum?' Cui legati dixerunt: 'Si tantum mentem iracundia
coepit, ut nihil nepote tuo de his quae pollicitus es indulgeas, vel illa quae de regno Chariberthi debentur auferre desiste'. Quibus ille ait: 'Ecce pactiones,
quae inter nos factae sunt, ut, quisque sine fratris voluntatem Parisius urbem ingrederetur, amitteret partem suam, essetque Polioctus martyr cum Hylario adque
Martino confessoribus iudex ac retributor eius. Post haec ingressus est in ea germanus meus Sigyberthus, qui iudicio Dei interiens amisit partem suam, Similiter
et Chilpericus gessit. Per has ergo transgressiones amiserunt partes suas. Ideoque, quia illi iuxta Dei iudicium et maledictionibus pactionum defecerunt, omnem
regnum Chariberthi cum thesauris eius meis ditionibus, lege opitulante, subiciam nec exinde alicui quicquam nisi spontanea voluntate indulgeam. Absistete
igitur, vos semper mendaces ac perfidi, et haec regi vestro referte'.

## 7. Quod legati Childeberthi Fredegundem requirunt.

**[007]** Quibus discedentibus, legati iterum Childeberthi ad antedictum regem veniunt, Fredegundem reginam requirentes atque dicentes: 'Redde homicidam, quae
amitam meam suggillavit, quae patrem interfecit et patruum, quae ipsus quoque consobrinus meus gladio interemit'. At ille: 'In placito', inquid, 'quem habemus,
cuncta decernimus, tractantes, quid oporteat fieri'. Nam Fredegunde patrocinio suo fovebat, ipsamque sepius ad convivium evocans, promittens, se ei fieri
maximum defensorem. Quadam vero die, dum pariter ad mensam epolarentum, regina consurgens et vale dicens, a rege detenebatur, dicente sibi: 'Adhuc aliquid cybi
sume'. Cui illa: 'Indulge', inquid, 'depraecor, domini mi, quia iuxta consuetudinem mulierum contigit mihi, ut pro conceptu consurgam'. Haec ille audiens,
obstipuit, sciens, quartum esse mensem, ex quo alium ediderat filium; tamen permisit eam consurgere. Prioribus quoque de regno Chilperici, ut erat Ansovaldus,
et reliqui ad filium eius, qui erat, ut superius diximus, quattuor mensuum, se colligerunt, quem Chlotharium vocitaverunt, exegentes sacramenta per civitates,
quae ad Chilpericum prius aspexerant, ut scilicit fidelis esse debeant Gunthchramno rege ac nepote suo Chlothario. Gunthchramnus vero rex omnia, quae fidelis
regis Chilperici non recte diversis abstulerant, iusticia intercedente, restituit, multa et ipsi eclesiis conferens; testamenta quoque defunctorum, qui eclesias
heredis instituerant et ad Chilperico conpressa fuerant, restauravit, multisque se benignum exhibens ac multa pauperibus tribuens.

## 8. Quod rex populum petiit, ne ut fratres eius interematur.

**[008]** Sed quia non erat fidus ab hominibus inter quos venerat, armis se munivit, nec umquam ad eclesiam aut reliqua loca, qua ire delectabat, sine grande
pergebat custodia. Unde factum est, ut quadam die dominica, postquam diaconus silentium populis, ut missae abscultarentur, indixit, rex conversus ad populum
dicerit: 'Adiuro vos, o viri cum mulieribus qui adestis, ut mihi fidem inviolatam servare dignimini nec me, ut fratres meus nuper fecistis, interematis,
liceatque mihi vel tribus annis nepotis meus, qui mihi adoptivi facti sunt filii, enutrire, ne forte contingat, quod Divinitas aeterna non patiatur, ut illis
parvolis, me defuncto, simul pereatis, cum de genere nostro robustus non fuerit qui defensit'. Haec eo dicente, omnes populus orationem pro rege fudit ad
Dominum.

## 9. Quod Rigunthis a Desiderio, thesauris ablatis, retenta est.

**[009]** Dum haec agerentur, Rigunthis, Chilperici regis filia, cum thesauris supra scriptis usque Tholosam accessit. Et cernens se iam ad terminum Gothorum
esse propinquam, moras innectire coepit, dicentibus sibi tum praeterea suis, oportere eam ibidem commorari, cum ipsi fatigati de itenere vestimenta haberent
inculta, calciamenta scissa, ipsosque equorum adque carrucarum apparatos adhuc, sicut plaustris evecti erant, seorsum esse disiunctos. Oportere potius omnia
haec prius diligenter stabilire et sic in itenere proficisci ac suscepi cum omni elegantia ab sponso, ne forte, si inculti inter Gothos apparerent, inriderentur
ab ipsis. Dum ergo his retardarentur ex causis, mors Chilperici regis in aures Desiderii ducis inlabitur. Ipse quoque, collectis secum viris fortissimis,
Tholosam urbem ingreditur repertusque thesauros abstulit de potestate reginae et in domo quadam sub sigillorum munitione ac virorum fortium custodia mancipat,
deputans reginae victum artum, donec ad urbem regrederetur.

## 10. Quod Gundovaldus in regno elevatus est.

**[010]** Ipse vero ad Mummolum, cum quo foedus ante duos annos inierat, pro peravit. Morabatur tunc Mummolus infra murus Avennicae urbis cum Gundovaldo, cui in
libro superiore memimmus. Qui coniunetus cum supradictis ducibus Limovicinum accedens, Briva-Curretia vicum, in quo sanctus Martinus, nostri, ut aiunt, Martini
discipulus, requiescit, advenit, ibique parmae superpositus, rex est levatus. Sed cum tertio cum eodem girarent, cecidisse fertur, ita ut vix manibus
circumstantium sustentare potuisset. Deinde ibat per civitates in circuitu positas. Rigunthis vero in basilica sanctae Mariae Tholosa, in qua Ragnovaldi uxor,
cui supra meminimus, Chilpericum metuens confugerat, resedebat. Ragnovaldus vero de Hispaniis rediens, uxori facultatique restituetur. Legationis enim causa
Hispaniam petierat, a rege Gunthchramno directus. Magno ea tempestate incendio basilica antedicti Martini beati apud Brivam vicum ab inminente hoste cremata
est, ita ut tam altarium quam columnae, quae de diversis marmorum generibus aptatae erant, ab igne dissolverentur. Sed ita haec aedes in posterum a Ferreolo
episcopo reparata est, tamquam si nihil mali pertulerit. Vehementer enim admirantur veneranturque hunc sanctum incole, eo quod plerumque virtutes eius
experiantur.

## 11. De signis quae apparuerunt.

**[011]** Erat enim, cum haec agebatur, mensis decimus. Tunc apparuerunt in codicibus vinearum palmites novi cum uvis deformatis, in arboribus flores; pharus
magna per caelum discurrens, quae, priusquam lux fierit in die, late mundum inluminavit. Apparuerunts etiam in caelo et radii. A parte septentrionali columna
ignea, quasi de caelo pendens, per duarum horarum spatium visa est, cui stella magna superposita erat. In Andecavo enim terra tremuit, et multa alia signa
apparuerunt, quae, ut opinor, ipsius Gundovaldi interitum nuntiarunt.

## 12. De incendio regionis Toronicae et virtute sancti Martini.

**[012]** Igitur Gunthchramnus rex comites suos ad conpraehendendas civitates, quas condam Sigyberthus de regno Chariberthi fratris sui acciperat, direxit, ut
exegentes sacramenta suis eas ditionibus subiugarent. Toronici vero adque Pectavi ad Childeberthum, Sigyberthi filium, transire voluerunt, sed commoti Biturigi
contra eos venire disponunt adque infra terminum Toronicum incendia facere coeperunt. Tunc Maroialensim aeclesiam termini Toronici, in qua sancti Martini
reliquiae habibantur, incendio concremarunt; sed virtus beati adfuit, ut in tam valido incendio pallolae, quae super altarium fuerant positae, non consumerentur
ab igne. Et non solum ipse, sed etiam herbolae olim collectae altarioque locatae nequaquam exustae sunt. Qua incendia videntes Toronici legationem mittunt,
dicentes, melius sibi esse ad tempus Gunthchramno rege subdi quam cuncta incendio ac ferro vastari.

## 13. De incendio et praedes Pectavi urbis.

**[013]** Confestim autem post mortem Chilperici Gararicus dux Limovicas accesserat et sacramenta de nomine Childeberthi susceperat. Exinde Pectavis veniens, ab
ipsis receptus est et ibi morabatur. Audiens vero quae Toronici patiebantur, mittit legationem, obtestans, ne nos ad partem Gunthchramni regis tradere
deberimus, si nobis vellimus esse consultum; sed meminirimus potius Sigyberthi, qui quondam genitur Childeberthi fuit. Nos vero haec rursum episcopo et civibus
mandata remisimus, quod, nisi se ad tempus Gunthchramno rege subderent, similia paterentur, adserentes, hunc esse nunc patrem super duos filios, Sigyberthi
scilicet et Chilperici, qui ei fuerant adoptati; et sic tenere regni principatum, ut quondam Chlotharius rex fecerat, pater eius. His quoque non
adquiescentibus, Gararicus de civitate egreditur, quasi exercitum adducturus, in urbe vero Eberonem cubicularium Childeberthi regis relinquens. Sicharius vero
cum Willachario Aurilianense comite, qui tunc Toronus acceperat, exercitum contra Pectavos commovit, ut scilicet ab una parte Toronici, ab alia Biturigi commoti
cuncta vastarent. Qui cum ad terminum propinquassent ac domus cremare coepissent, miserunt ad eos Pectavi legatos, dicentes: 'Petemus, ut usque in placito, quod
inter se Gunthchramnus et Childeberthus regis habent, susteneatis. Quod si convenit, ut pagos hos rex Gunthchramnus accipiat, non resistemus; sin aliud, dominum
nostrum recognuscimus, cui servire plenius debeamus'. Ad haec illi responderunt: 'Nihil nobis de hac causa pertinet, nisi tantum iussa principis adimplere. Nam
si nolueritis, cuncta ut coepimus devastamus'. Cumque in hoc res ageretur, ut universa incendio, praedae adque captivitati traderentur, eiectis de civitate
hominibus Childeberthi, sacramenta Gunthchramno rege dederunt, non longo tempore ea custodientes.

## 14. De legatis Childeberthi regis ad Gunthramno missis.

**[014]** Igitur, adveniente placito, directi sunt ad Childebertho rege Egidius episcopus, Gunthchramnus Boso, Sigyvaldus et alii multi ad Gunthchramno regem;
ingressique ad eum, ait episcopus: 'Gratias agimus Deo omnipotenti, o piissime rex, quod te post multos labores regionibus tuis regnoque restituit'. Cui rex
ait: 'Illi enim dignae sunt gratiae referendae, qui est rex regum et dominus dominorum, qui haec sua miseratione operare dignatus est. Nam non tibi, cuius
consilio doloso ac periuriis regionis meae anno superiore incensae sunt, qui numquam fidem integram cum ullo homine habuisti, cuius dolositas ubique
dispergitur, qui non sacerdotem, sed inimicum regni nostri te esse declaras'. Ad haec verba episcopus iracundia commotus siluit. Unus autem ex legatis dixit:
'Supplecat nepus tuus Childeberthus, ut civitates, quas pater eius tenuit, reddi iubeas '. Ad haec ille respondit: 'Iam dixi vobis prius, quia pactiones nostrae
mihi haec conferunt, ideoque eas reddere nolo'. Alius quoque legatorum ait: 'Rogat nepus tuus, ut Fredegundem maleficam, per quam multi reges interfecti sunt,
reddi iubeas ad ulciscendam mortem patris, patrui vel consubrinorum suorum'. At ille: 'Tradi ei', inquid, 'in potestate non poterit, quia filium regem habet.
Sed et ea quae contra illam adseretes, vera esse non credo'. Post hos Gunthchramnus Boso, quasi aliquid suggesturus, ad regem accedit. Et quia sonuerat,
Gundovaldum manifeste regem levatum, antecipans rex verba eius, ait: 'O inimici regionis regnique nostri, qui propterea ante hos annos Orientem adgressus es, ut
Ballomerem quendam – sic enim vocabat rex Gundovaldum – super regnum nostrum adduceris, semper perfide et numquam custodiens quae promittis!' Cui ille: 'Tu',
inquid, 'dominus et rex regali in solio resedis, et nullus tibi ad ea quae loqueris ausus est respondere. Insontem enim me de hac causa profiteor. At si aliquis
est similis mihi, qui hoc crimen inpingat occulte, veniat nunc palam et loquatur. Tunc, o rex piissime, ponens hoc in Dei iudicium, ut ille discernat, cum nos
in unius campi planitiae viderit demicare'. Ad haec, cunctis silentibus, addedit rex: 'Omnibus autem haec causa animus accendere debet, ut repellatur a finibus
nostris advena, cuius pater molinas gobernavit, et ut vere dicam, pater eius pectinibus insedit lanasque conposuit'. Et quamquam possit fieri, ut unus homo
utriusque artificii magisterio subderetui, ad increpationem tamen regis quidam ex ipsis respondit: 'Ergo duos, ut adseris, patres hic homo habuit, lanarium
simul molinariumque. Absit a te, o rex, ut tam inculte loquaris. Non enim auditum est, unum hominem praeter spiritalem causam duos habere posse pariter
genitores'. Dehinc, cum multi solverentur in risu, respondit alius legatorum, dicens: 'Vale dicimus tibi, o rex. Nam quia reddere noluisti civitatis nepotis
tui, scimus, salvam esse securem, quae fratrum tuorum capitibus est defixa. Celerius tuum libravit defixa cerebrum'. Et sic cum scandalum discesserunt. Tunc rex
his verbis succensus, iussit super capita euntium proici aequorum stercora, putrefactas astulas, paleas ac faenum putridine dissolutum ipsumque foetidum urbis
lutum. Quibus de rebus maculati graviter, non sine inmensa iniuria adque contumilia abierunt.

## 15. De malitia Fredegunde.

**[015]** Resedente vero Fredegunde regina in aeclesia Parisiaca, Leonardus ex domestico, qui tunc ab urbe Tholosa ad venerat, ingressus ad eam, causas
contumiliae iniuriasque filiae eius narrare coepit, dicens, quia: 'Iuxta imperium tuum accessi cum regina Rigunthe ac vidi humilitatem eius, vel qualiter
expoliata est a thesauris et omnibus rebus; ego vero per fugam dilapsus, veni nuntiare dominae meae quae gesta sunt'. Haec illa audiens furore commota, iussit
eum in ipsa aeclesia spoliare, midatumque vestimentis ac balteo, quod ex munere Chilperici regis habebat, discedere a sua iubet praesentia. Cocos quoque sive
pistores, vel quoscumque de hoc itenere regressus esse cognovit, caesos spoliatosque ac demanicatos reliquid. Nectarium autem, Baudegysili episcopi fratrem,
nefandis accusationibus cum rege temptavit obruere, adserens, eum de thesauro regis mortui multa portasse. Sed et de prumptuariis tam tergora quam vina multa
eum abstulisse dicebat, petens, ut vinctus carceralibus tenebris truderetur. Sed patientia regis fratrisque auxilium fieri non permisit. Multa quidem ibi vana
exercens, non metuebat Deum, in cuius aeclesiam petebat auxilium. Habebat tunc temporis secum Audonem iudicem, qui ei tempore regis in multis consenserat malis.
