content to live with the brothers.’

### 16. And what he related of the virtues of Saint Martin

**[016]** When I asked him to describe some of blessed Martin’s miracles performed in that place, he related the following: ‘The son of a certain Frank, a most
noble man among his people, was mute and deaf. His parents brought him to this basilica, and I ordered him to rest on a small bed in the holy church itself with
my deacon and another minister. During the day he devoted himself to prayer, and at night he slept in the church as I have said. At last God took pity, and
blessed Martin appeared to me in a vision, saying: “Put the lamb out of the basilica, for he has now been healed.” In the morning, while I was wondering what
this dream meant, the boy came to me, uttered sounds, and began to thank God. Turning to me, he said: “I thank almighty God, who has restored both speech and
hearing to me.” Healed, he returned home. Another man, often involved in thefts and various crimes and accustomed to perjure himself, was once accused of theft
and said: “I will go to blessed Martin’s basilica, clear myself by oaths, and be declared innocent.” As he entered, the axe slipped from his hand and he fell at
the doorway, struck by a grievous pain in his heart. The wretched man confessed in his own words what he had come to deny by perjury. Another man, similarly
accused of burning his neighbour’s house, said: “I will go to Saint Martin’s church and give my oath, and I shall be cleared of this charge.” It was well known
that he had burned the house. When he went to swear, I turned to him and said: “According to your neighbours’ statements, you are not innocent of this crime.
God is everywhere, however, and His power outside is the same as within. But if vain confidence has possessed you, so that you think God and His saints do not
avenge perjury, behold the holy church opposite; swear as you wish. You will not be permitted to tread upon its sacred threshold.” He raised his hands and said:
“By almighty God and the power of His bishop blessed Martin, I did not commit this arson.” Having sworn, as he withdrew he seemed to himself to be surrounded by
fire. He immediately fell to the ground and began to cry out that the blessed bishop was fiercely burning him. The wretched man said: “I call God to witness
that I saw fire fall from heaven; it surrounds me and scorches me with mighty heat.” As he spoke, he breathed his last. This event taught many never again to
dare perjure themselves in this place.’ The deacon related many more miracles, but I have thought it too long to recount them all.

### 17. Of the signs which appeared

**[017]** While I was staying in that place, for two nights I saw signs in the sky: rays in the north shining so brightly that none had ever before appeared
like them, and blood-red clouds on both sides, east and west. On the third night these rays appeared about the second hour. While I was gazing at them in
amazement, other similar rays arose from the four quarters of the world, and I saw the whole sky covered by them. In the centre of the sky was a shining cloud,
towards which these rays gathered like a tent which, beginning with broader bands below and narrowing above, is often drawn together into a single peaked hood.
Between the rays were other clouds flashing like bright lightning. This great sign filled me with fear, for I expected some calamity to be sent upon me from
heaven.

### 18. How Childebert sent an army into Italy

**[018]** Urged on by imperial envoys who demanded the gold given the previous year, King Childebert sent an army into Italy. There was a report that his sister
Ingund had already been taken to Constantinople. But the commanders quarrelled among themselves and returned without gaining any profit. Duke Wintrjo was
expelled by his own people and deprived of his dukedom; he would have lost his life had flight not saved him. Afterwards, when the people had been pacified, he
recovered the dukedom. Nicetius, removed from the countship of Clermont through Eulalius’s scheming, sought a dukedom from the king and gave immense gifts for
it. He was appointed duke over Clermont, Rodez, and Uzès. Though very young, he was shrewd and established peace in Auvergne and the other places under his
authority. Chulderic the Saxon, having offended King Guntram for the reason mentioned above, sought refuge in blessed Martin’s basilica, leaving his wife in
that king’s kingdom. Guntram had adjured her not to presume to see her husband until he had been reconciled to royal favour. I repeatedly sent envoys on his
behalf and finally obtained permission for him to receive his wife and live on this side of the Loire, though he was not to presume to cross over to King
Childebert. But once he received liberty to recover his wife, he secretly crossed to Childebert, obtained a ducal appointment over cities beyond the Garonne
under that king’s power, and went there. King Guntram, wishing to govern the kingdom of his nephew Chlothar, Chilperic’s son, appointed Theodulf count of
Angers. When he entered the city, the citizens, especially Domigisel, humiliatingly rejected him. He returned to the king, received another command, was
admitted by Duke Sigulf, and governed the countship of that city. Gundovald contended with Werpinus for the countship of Meaux, entered the city, and began to
conduct judicial business. While touring the city’s district in this office, he was killed by Werpinus at an estate. Gundovald’s relatives assembled, attacked
Werpinus, trapped him in an upper room, and killed him. Thus both departed from the countship through imminent death.

### 19. Of the death of the abbot Dagulfus

**[019]** Abbot Dagulf was frequently accused of crimes, for he often committed theft and murder and was exceedingly dissolute in adultery. At one time he
coveted his neighbour’s wife and had intercourse with her. Seeking various opportunities to destroy the adulteress’s husband, who lived on the monastery’s land,
he finally threatened him, saying that he would be punished if he went to his wife. When the husband left his lodging, Dagulf came at night with a cleric and
entered the harlot’s house. After drinking until they were very drunk, they lay down in one bed. While they slept, the husband arrived, lit some straw, raised a
double axe, and killed them both. Let this event therefore teach clerics not to enjoy the company of unrelated women contrary to the canons, since both
canonical law and all the Holy Scriptures forbid it, except with those women about whom no suspicion can arise.

### 20. What was done in the synod of Mâcon

**[020]** Meanwhile the appointed day arrived, and the bishops assembled at Mâcon by King Guntram’s command. Faustianus, who had been ordained bishop of Agen at
Gundovald’s command, was removed on condition that Bertram, Orestes, and Palladius, who had consecrated him, support him in turn and provide him with one
hundred gold pieces each year. Nicetius, however, though a layman, obtained the bishopric in that city, having previously secured a command from King Chilperic.
Ursicinus, bishop of Cahors, was excommunicated because he publicly confessed that he had received Gundovald. A settlement was made that he should do penance
for three years, neither cut his hair nor beard, abstain from wine and meat, and not presume to celebrate Mass, ordain clerics, consecrate churches or chrism,
or distribute blessed bread; nevertheless, the administration of the Church was to be carried out entirely under his direction as before. At this synod one
bishop asserted that a woman could not be called a human being. He was pacified when the bishops explained that the sacred book of the Old Testament teaches
that at the beginning, when God created humanity, it says: ‘Male and female He created them, and He called their name Adam,’ which means earthly human being,
thus calling woman as well as man human; He called both human. The Lord Jesus Christ is likewise called the Son of Man because He is the Son of the Virgin, that
is, of a woman. When He was about to turn water into wine, He said to her: ‘Woman, what have I to do with you?’ and so on. This contention was refuted by these
and many other testimonies and came to rest. Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, recited before the bishops the prayers he had composed in exile. Some approved of
them, while others criticized them because he had not followed the rules of composition; nevertheless, their style was in places ecclesiastical and reasonable.
There was also a great slaughter between the servants of Bishop Priscus and Duke Leudegisel, though Bishop Priscus offered a large sum to purchase peace. In
those days King Guntram became so gravely ill that some thought he could not possibly survive. I believe divine providence caused this, for he had been planning
to drive many bishops into exile. Bishop Theodore returned to his own city and was received with praise by the whole favourable population.

### 21. Of the pact at Belsonacum and of the violated tomb

**[021]** While this synod was being held, King Childebert met his men at the estate of Belsenan, situated in the middle of the Ardennes forest. Queen Brunhild
complained to all the leading men about her daughter Ingund, still held in Africa, but obtained little consolation. Then a charge arose against Guntram Boso. A
few days earlier a childless relative of his wife had died and been buried in a basilica at Metz with costly ornaments and much gold. A few days later came the
feast of blessed Remedius, celebrated at the beginning of the eighth month. Many people left the city with the bishop, especially the city’s leading men with
the duke. Guntram Boso’s servants came to the basilica where the woman was buried, entered, locked the doors behind them, opened the tomb, and took all the
ornaments they could find from the corpse. The basilica’s monks perceived what was happening and came to the door but were not admitted. Seeing this, they
reported it to their bishop and the duke. Meanwhile the servants took the goods, mounted their horses, and began to flee. Fearing that they would be caught on
the road and subjected to various punishments, they returned to the basilica. They placed the goods upon the altar but did not dare go outside, crying out: ‘We
were sent by Guntram Boso!’ When Childebert and his nobles assembled at the estate mentioned above, Guntram Boso was questioned about this but gave no answer
and fled. All the property he had acquired in Auvergne as a gift from the fisc was subsequently taken from him, and he also left behind in disgrace various
possessions which he had wrongfully seized.

### 22. Of the death of the bishops and of Wandelenus

**[022]** Laban, bishop of Elusa, died this year, and the layman Desiderius succeeded him, although the king had promised on oath that he would never appoint a
bishop from among laymen. But what does the accursed hunger for gold not compel human hearts to do? Returning from the synod, Bertram was seized by fever. He
summoned the deacon Waldo, who had also been named Bertram at baptism, and entrusted to him the government of the bishopric together with all the provisions of
his will and the disposal of his goods. After the deacon departed, Bertram died. The deacon returned and hastened to the king with gifts and the citizens’
consent, but obtained nothing. The king issued a command for Gundegisil, count of Saintes, surnamed Dodo, to be ordained bishop, and this was done. Before the
synod many clerics of Saintes, with Bishop Bertram’s consent, had written accusations against their bishop Palladius to bring humiliation upon him. After
Bertram’s death, Palladius arrested them and had them severely beaten and stripped. At this time Wandelenus, King Childebert’s foster-father, also died. No one
was appointed in his place because the queen mother wished to take personal charge of her son. Whatever he had acquired from the fisc was restored to the fisc.
Duke Bodygisel also died in those days, full of years, but his sons’ inheritance was not diminished. The priest Saius was appointed in place of Faustus, bishop
of Auch. After holy Salvius’s death, Desideratus was given this year as bishop to the people of Albi.

### 23. Of the Floods

**[023]** There were great rains this year, and the rivers rose so high that shipwrecks frequently occurred. Overflowing their banks and covering nearby crops
and meadows, they caused severe destruction. The spring and summer months were so wet that the season seemed winter rather than summer.

### 24. Of the islands of the sea

**[024]** Two islands in the sea were burned this year by a divinely sent fire. For seven days they were consumed and overwhelmed together with their people and
cattle. Those who fled into the sea and plunged into deep water were consumed in the very water into which they sank; those who did not immediately die were
burned with still greater torment. When everything had been reduced to ashes, the whole sea was covered with them. Many also said that the signs which I
described seeing in the eighth month, as though the sky were burning, came from the glare of this fire.

### 25. Of the Island on Which Blood Appeared

**[025]** On another island near the city of Vannes there was a deep lake full of fish, which turned to blood to a depth of one cubit. An incalculable multitude
of dogs and birds gathered for many days, lapped up the blood, and departed satiated in the evening.

### 26. Of Berulfus who had been duke

**[026]** Ennodius was appointed duke over Tours and Poitiers. Berulf, who had previously governed these cities, was suspected together with his associate
Arnegisel of secretly stealing King Sigibert’s treasures. When he sought the dukedom over these cities, Duke Rauching captured him and his followers by a trick.
Servants were immediately sent to their houses and plundered everything. Much of their own property and some of the treasures mentioned above were found there,
all of which were brought to King Childebert. When matters had reached the point where the sword was about to fall upon their necks, the bishops intervened and
their lives were spared, but they recovered none of the property taken from them.

### 27. How Desiderius went to the king

**[027]** Duke Desiderius hastened to King Guntram with several bishops, Abbot Aridius, and Antestius. Although the king was reluctant to receive him, he was
overcome by the bishops’ prayers and restored Desiderius to favour. Eulalius was also there, intending to make a complaint concerning his wife, who had rejected
him and gone over to Desiderius; but he was reduced to ridicule and humiliation and fell silent. Desiderius was rewarded by the king and returned in his favour.

### 28. Of Hermenegild and Ingund

**[028]** As I have often said, Ingund was abandoned by her husband with the imperial army and died and was buried in Africa while being conducted to the
emperor with her small son. Leovigild put to death his son Hermenegild, whom the woman just named had borne. Angered by these events, King Guntram resolved to
send an army into Spain, intending first to bring Septimania, still within the borders of Gaul, under his control and then advance farther. While this army was
on the move, a letter was found with some rustic men. They sent it to King Guntram to be read. It was written as though Leovigild were addressing Fredegund,
asking her to prevent the army’s advance by any means and saying: ‘Quickly kill our enemies Childebert and his mother, and make peace with King Guntram,
purchasing it with many gifts. If you lack money, I will secretly send it, provided only that you carry out my request. When I have avenged myself upon my
enemies, reward Bishop Amelius and the matron Leuba, through whom my envoys gain access to you.’ Leuba was Duke Bladast’s mother-in-law.

### 29. How Fredegund sent men to kill Childebert

**[029]** Although this letter was brought to King Guntram and communicated to his nephew Childebert, Fredegund nevertheless ordered two iron knives to be made,
deeply engraved and smeared with poison, so that if a mortal thrust did not destroy the vital organs, the poison itself might more quickly extinguish life. She
handed these knives to two clerics with these instructions: ‘Take these swords and go as quickly as possible to King Childebert, pretending to be beggars. When
you have prostrated yourselves at his feet as though asking alms, pierce both his sides, so that Brunhild, who derives her arrogance from him, may fall with him
and become subject to me. If the boy is so closely guarded that you cannot approach him, kill my enemy Brunhild herself. Your reward will be that, if you die in
this work, I will bestow goods upon your relatives, enrich them with gifts, and make them the foremost men in my kingdom. Meanwhile cast off all fear and let
there be no dread of death in your hearts. Remember that death awaits all men. Strengthen your minds with courage and consider how often brave men fall in
battle, while their relatives are afterwards ennobled and raised above all others by immense wealth.’ As the woman spoke, the clerics began to tremble, thinking
her orders difficult to carry out. Seeing their uncertainty, she gave them a drugged potion and directed them where to go. Their courage immediately increased,
and they promised to fulfil all her commands. She also ordered them to take a flask filled with this potion, saying: ‘On the day when you do what I command,
take this drink in the morning before beginning the work. It will give you great resolution.’ Thus equipped, she sent them off. As they travelled and approached
Soissons, Duke Rauching captured and questioned them; they revealed everything and were imprisoned. A few days later Fredegund, now convinced that her orders
had been carried out, sent a servant to learn what the people were reporting or to find anyone who would say that Childebert had been killed. The servant left
her and came to Soissons. Hearing that the men were held in prison, he approached the door, but when he began speaking to the guards he too was captured and
detained. All were then sent together to King Childebert. Questioned, they revealed the truth, stating that Fredegund had sent them to kill him, and saying: ‘At
the queen’s command we were to disguise ourselves as paupers. When we prostrated ourselves at your feet seeking alms, we intended to stab you with these swords.
If the sword did not penetrate with sufficient force, the poison smeared upon the iron would quickly destroy your life.’ As they spoke, they were subjected to
various tortures; their hands, ears, and noses were cut off, and they were put to death in various ways.

### 30. How the army went into Septimania

**[030]** King Guntram ordered the army to march into Spain, saying: ‘First subject the province of Septimania, which is adjacent to Gaul, to my authority, for
it is disgraceful that the territory of the dreadful Goths should extend into Gaul.’ He assembled the whole army of his kingdom and sent it there. But the
peoples living beyond the Saône, Rhône, and Seine joined the Burgundians and severely devastated the banks of the Saône and Rhône, taking both crops and cattle.
They committed many murders, burnings, and robberies in their own region, stripped churches, and killed clerics, bishops, and the rest of the people at the very
altars consecrated to God, advancing as far as Nîmes. Likewise the men of Bourges, Saintes, Périgueux, and the other cities then subject to the king advanced as
far as Carcassonne and committed similar evils. When they reached that city, the inhabitants voluntarily opened the gates and they entered unopposed, but after
some quarrel with the people of Carcassonne they left the city. Terentiolus, formerly count of Limoges, was struck by a stone thrown from the wall and killed.
His head was cut off and carried into the city as vengeance against his enemies. The whole army was terrified and resolved to return home, abandoning everything
it had acquired along the way or brought with it. The Goths ambushed and killed many after robbing them. Then they fell into the hands of the people of
Toulouse, whom they had greatly injured on their march; robbed and beaten, they scarcely reached their homes. Those who had attacked Nîmes devastated the whole
region, burned houses and crops, cut down olive trees and vines, and, unable to harm those shut inside, moved on to other cities. These were strongly fortified
and fully stocked with food and other necessities, so the army devastated their outskirts but could not break into them. Duke Nicetius, marching with the men of
Clermont on this expedition, also took part in the siege. When he could accomplish nothing, he came to a fortress. Its inhabitants opened the gates voluntarily
after receiving an oath and trustingly admitted the men as peaceful visitors. But once inside, the soldiers disregarded their oath, plundered all the stores,
and took the people captive. Then by common counsel everyone returned home. Along the way they committed such crimes, murders, robberies, and plunder in their
own region that it would take too long to recount them all. Because they had burned the crops of Provence, they themselves died of hunger and starvation along
the road; some drowned in rivers and many were killed in disturbances. It was said that more than five thousand perished in these disasters, yet the deaths of
others did not restrain the survivors. Churches in Auvergne near the public roads were stripped of their furnishings, and there was no end to their wrongdoing
until each man reached home. Their return filled King Guntram with bitter grief. The army’s commanders sought refuge in the basilica of the martyr Saint
Symphorian. When the king came for the saint’s feast, they were brought before him on condition of a future hearing. Four days later the king assembled the
bishops and the senior laymen and began to question the commanders, saying: ‘How can I obtain victory now, when I do not keep the ways my fathers followed? They
built churches, placed all their hope in God, honoured the martyrs, and revered the bishops; thus they gained victories and often subjected hostile peoples with
sword and shield through divine aid. I not only fail to fear God but devastate His sanctuaries, kill His ministers, and tear apart and destroy the saints’ very
relics in mockery. Victory cannot be gained where such things are done. Therefore my hands are weak, the sword grows dull, and the shield no longer defends and
protects me as it used to. If this is attributed to my fault, let God exact it from my own head. But if you despise royal commands and delay fulfilling my
orders, the axe ought to fall upon your necks. The execution of one commander will teach the whole army. I must now determine what ought to be done. Let anyone
who intends to follow justice do so; if anyone refuses, let public vengeance hang over his neck. It is better that a few obstinate men perish than that God’s
anger descend upon an entire innocent region.’ The commanders replied: ‘Your great goodness cannot easily be described, best of kings: your fear of God, love
for the churches, reverence for bishops, compassion for the poor, and provision for the needy. But since everything your majesty says is judged right and true,
what shall we do when the whole people has sunk into vice and everyone delights in wrongdoing? No one fears the king, no one fears the duke, no one respects the
count. If anyone disapproves and tries to correct these things for the preservation of your life, sedition and tumult immediately arise among the people.
Everyone is so fiercely enraged against his superior that he scarcely believes he can escape if he does not withdraw quickly enough.’ The king answered: ‘If
anyone follows justice, let him live; if anyone rejects the law and my command, let him perish, so that I may no longer continue this blasphemy.’ As he spoke, a
messenger arrived and said: ‘Reccared, Leovigild’s son, has come out of Spain, captured the fortress of Cabaret, devastated most of the district of Toulouse,
and carried off captives. He has broken into the Arles fortress of Ugernum, taken all its property and people, and shut himself within the walls of Nîmes.’
Hearing this, the king appointed Leudegisel duke in place of Calumniosus, surnamed Aegyla, entrusted to him the whole province of Arles, and stationed more than
four thousand men as guards along the frontier. Nicetius, duke of Clermont, likewise went with guards and patrolled the region’s borders.

### 31. Of the slaying of Bishop Praetextatus

**[031]** While these events were taking place and Fredegund was staying at Rouen, she exchanged bitter words with Bishop Praetextatus, saying that a time would
come when he would return to the exile in which he had been detained. He replied: ‘I have always been, am, and shall be a bishop, whether in exile or out of it;
but you will not always enjoy royal power. By God’s gift I am promoted from exile to a kingdom, while you shall be plunged from this kingdom into the abyss. You
would do better to abandon folly and malice, turn to better things, and withdraw from the pride which continually inflames you, so that you may obtain eternal
life and bring the little son you bore to lawful maturity.’ When he had spoken, the woman took his words badly and withdrew from his presence boiling with gall.
On the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the bishop hurried early to church to perform the ecclesiastical offices and began the antiphons in order according to
custom. While he reclined on a bench during the psalmody, a cruel murderer approached, drew a knife from his belt, and struck the bishop beneath the armpit as
he rested on the bench. Praetextatus cried out for the clergy present to help him, but none of the many bystanders assisted him. Stretching his blood-filled
hands over the altar, pouring out prayer, and thanking God, he was carried in the hands of the faithful to his chamber and laid upon his bed. Fredegund
immediately arrived with Duke Beppolen and Ansovald, saying: ‘It was not right, holy bishop, that this should happen to you while we and the rest of your people
were present. If only the man who dared to do this were identified, so that he might suffer fitting punishment for the crime!’ Knowing that she spoke
deceitfully, the bishop said: ‘Who did this except the one who has destroyed the laws, often shed innocent blood, and committed various evils in this kingdom?’
The woman answered: ‘We have most skilful physicians who can treat this wound. Allow them to come to you.’ He said: ‘God has already commanded me to be called
from this world. You, who are found to be the author of these crimes, shall be cursed in this world, and God shall avenge my blood upon your head.’ After she
departed, the bishop set his household in order and died. Romacharius, bishop of Coutances, came to bury him. Great grief then seized all the citizens of Rouen,
especially the senior Franks of that place. One of these leading men came to Fredegund and said: ‘You have committed many evils in this world, but you had never
yet done worse than ordering a priest of God to be killed. May God swiftly avenge innocent blood! We shall all seek out the author of this crime, so that you
may no longer be permitted to practise such cruelty.’ When he said this and left the queen’s presence, she sent someone to invite him to a banquet. He refused,
and she asked that, if he would not dine with her, he at least drink a cup and not leave the royal house fasting. He waited, accepted the cup, and drank
absinthe mixed with wine and honey, as is the barbarian custom; but the drink was poisoned. As soon as he drank, he felt violent pain assail his chest and cried
out to his companions as though he were being cut open inside: ‘Flee, wretched men, flee this evil, lest you perish with me!’ They did not drink but hurried
away. He was immediately blinded, mounted a horse, and fell dead three furlongs from that place. Afterwards Bishop Leudovald sent letters to all the bishops
and, by common counsel, closed the churches of Rouen so that the people could not celebrate the divine offices there until the author of the crime was
discovered by a common investigation. He also arrested some men and extorted by torture the truth that these things had been done on Fredegund’s advice, but he
could not avenge them because she protected the guilty. It was also said that assassins came against Leudovald himself because he was determined to investigate
vigorously, but his men surrounded and protected him so that they could do him no harm. When these events were reported to King Guntram and the crime was
imputed to the woman, he sent three bishops to the child said to be Chilperic’s son, whom I mentioned above as Chlothar: Artemius of Sens, Veranus of Cavaillon,
and Agricius of Troyes. They were to investigate with the child’s guardians who was responsible for the crime and bring the person before him. After the bishops
had spoken, the leading men replied: ‘I entirely disapprove of this deed and increasingly desire to avenge it. But if anyone among us is found guilty, he cannot
be brought before your king, since I can pay for our offences according to royal decree.’ The bishops said: ‘Know that if the person who committed this is not
produced, our king will come here with an army and devastate this whole region with sword and fire, because it is evident that the woman who ordered a Frank to
be killed by witchcraft has also had the bishop killed by the sword.’ With these words they departed without receiving a reasonable answer, adjuring them
solemnly that Melantius, who had previously been appointed in Praetextatus’s place, should never perform the episcopal office in that church.

### 32. Of the death of Domnola, wife of Nectarius

**[032]** Many evils were committed at this time. Domnola, widow of the late Burgulinus and daughter of Victorius, bishop of Rennes, whom Nectarius had married,
had a dispute over vineyards with Bobolenus, Fredegund’s referendary. Hearing that she had entered these vineyards, he sent messengers adjuring her not to
presume to set foot in the property. She disregarded this, declared that it had been her father’s property, and entered. He then raised a disturbance and
attacked her with armed men. He killed her, recovered the vineyards, plundered the property, and put to the sword both the men and women with her; only those
able to escape survived.

### 33. Of the burning of the city of Paris

**[033]** In those days a woman at Paris said to the inhabitants: ‘Flee from the city, and know that it shall be burned with fire.’ Many ridiculed her, thinking
she spoke from some omen of lots, had dreamed something vain, or was certainly speaking at the instigation of the noonday demon. She replied: ‘It is not as you
say. I speak the truth, for in a dream I saw a shining man come from Saint Vincent’s basilica holding a candle and setting the merchants’ houses on fire one
after another.’ On the third night after the woman spoke, at twilight, a citizen lit a lamp and entered his storeroom. He took oil and other necessities and
departed, leaving the lamp beside a small cask of oil. His house was the first beside the gate opening to the south. The house caught fire from the lamp and
burned, and others began to catch fire from it. As the flames fell upon the prisoners’ chains, blessed Germanus appeared to them, broke the beam and the chains
binding them, opened the prison door, and allowed them to depart unharmed. They went out and took refuge in Saint Vincent’s basilica, where the blessed bishop’s
tomb is. While the wind drove flames throughout the city and the fire raged with full force, it began to approach another gate containing an oratory of blessed
Martin. This had been built because Martin had once driven away a leprous man’s disease there with a kiss. The man who had built the oratory high with
interwoven branches trusted in the Lord and did not doubt blessed Martin’s power. He enclosed himself and his possessions within its walls, saying: ‘I believe
and am confident that he who often commanded fires and cleansed a leper’s skin here with a healing kiss will drive the fire away from this place.’ As the fire
approached, great balls of flame were carried against the oratory wall but immediately died down upon striking it. Men and women among the people cried out:
‘Flee, wretched people, so that you may escape! A mass of fire is already falling upon you; ashes and burning coals are spreading towards you like heavy rain!
Leave the oratory, lest you be burned with it!’ But they prayed and were never moved by these cries. Nor did the woman ever leave the window through which
flames occasionally entered, for she was fortified with firmest hope in the blessed bishop’s power. So great was the blessed bishop’s power that he not only
saved this oratory with his own foster-child’s house, but did not permit the raging flames to harm the surrounding houses either. The fire which had begun
raging from one bridge subsided there. On the other side everything burned so fiercely that only the river stopped it. Yet the churches and their houses were
not burned. People said that this city had been consecrated in ancient times so that fire could not prevail there and no snake or dormouse would appear.
Recently, however, when a conduit of the bridge was cleaned and the mud filling it removed, they found a bronze serpent and dormouse. After these were removed,
countless dormice and snakes subsequently appeared there, and the city began to suffer fires.

### 34. Of the recluses tempted

**[034]** Because the prince of darkness has a thousand ways of doing harm, I will relate what recently happened to recluses devoted to God. Vennocus the
Breton, honoured with the priesthood and mentioned in another book, devoted himself to such abstinence that he wore only skins, ate uncooked wild herbs, and
merely raised the wine vessel to his mouth, seeming rather to touch it with a kiss than drink. But when devout people often generously offered him vessels full
of this liquor, he learned—what is worse—to drink immoderately and became so overcome that he was frequently seen drunk. As time passed and his drunkenness
increased, he was seized by a demon and tormented with madness, so that he would seize a knife or any weapon, stone, or club he could grasp and chase people in
insane fury. It became necessary to bind him with chains and guard him in a cell. Raving under this affliction for two years, he died. Another man, Anatolius of
Bordeaux, was, it is said, a twelve-year-old boy serving a merchant when he asked permission to become a recluse. His master long resisted, thinking that he was
too weak at that age to accomplish what he sought, but finally overcome by the servant’s prayers he permitted him to fulfil his desire. There was an ancient
crypt there, beautifully vaulted and elegantly constructed, in one corner of which a small cell had been enclosed with squared stones, scarcely large enough to
hold one standing man. The boy entered this cell and lived there for eight years or more, content with scant food and drink and devoting himself to vigils and
prayers. Afterwards he suffered a violent terror and began to cry out that he was being tormented within. Then, with the aid, I believe, of the devil’s
soldiers, he removed the squared stones enclosing him, broke the wall to the ground, clapped his hands, and cried that God’s saints were burning him. He
remained in this madness for a very long time, often invoking Saint Martin’s name and saying that Martin was tormenting him more than the other saints. He was
brought to Tours, but the evil spirit, suppressed, I believe, by the saint’s power and greatness, did not harm the man there. After spending a year in that
place without suffering anything, he returned, but again incurred the afflictions from which he had been free.

### 35. Of the legates of the Spaniards

**[035]** Envoys from Spain came to King Guntram with many gifts seeking peace, but received no definite answer. In the previous year, when the army attacked
Septimania, ships which had gone from Gaul to Galicia were ravaged at King Leovigild’s command; their goods were taken, men were beaten and killed, and some
were carried off captive. A few escaped in skiffs and reported to their homeland what had happened.

### 36. Of the death of Magnovaldus

**[036]** Magnovald was then killed at King Childebert’s command for secret reasons in the following manner. While the king stood in the palace at Metz watching
a spectacle in which an animal surrounded by a pack of dogs was being exhausted, Magnovald was summoned. He came unaware of what was intended and, laughing
freely with the others, began to watch the beast. When the man assigned the task saw him intent upon the spectacle, he swung an axe and struck his head.
Magnovald fell dead, was thrown through a window of the house, and was buried by his own people. His property was immediately plundered and, as far as it could
be found, brought into the public treasury. Some asserted that the reason for his death was that after his brother’s death he had beaten his wife to death with
various blows and taken his brother’s wife to his own bed.

### 37. That a son was born to Childebert

**[037]** Afterwards a son was born to King Childebert. Magneric, bishop of Trier, received him from the sacred font, and he was named Theudebert. King Guntram
was so delighted that he immediately sent envoys with many gifts, saying: ‘Through him God in the mercy of His own majesty will deign to raise up the kingdom of
the Franks, if his father or he himself lives.’

### 38. How the Spaniards Burst into Gaul

**[038]** In the eleventh year of King Childebert’s reign, envoys again came from Spain seeking peace, but returned without obtaining any definite answer.
Reccared, Leovigild’s son, came as far as Narbonne, took plunder within the territory of Gaul, and secretly withdrew.

### 39. Of the death of the bishops

**[039]** Many bishops died that year, including Badegisel, bishop of Le Mans, a very savage man towards the people, who wrongfully took and plundered others’
property. His still more savage wife had accommodated herself to his harsh and pitiless mind and goaded him with counsels to commit the most wicked crimes. No
day or moment passed without his raging in plundering citizens or in various quarrels. He daily conducted cases with judges, exercised secular offices, raged
against some, pursued others with slaughter, beat many with his own hands, trampled them, and said: ‘Because I have become a cleric, shall I therefore not be
the avenger of my own injuries?’ What shall I say of others when he did not spare even his own brothers but rather plundered them most of all? They could never
obtain justice from him concerning their paternal or maternal property. Having completed the fifth year of his episcopate and entered the sixth, he prepared a
banquet for the citizens with immense rejoicing, but was seized by fever and immediately ended by death the year he had begun. Bertram, archdeacon of Paris, was
appointed in his place. He is known to have had many disputes with the dead bishop’s widow because she retained as her own property given to the Church in
Bishop Badegisel’s time, saying: ‘This was my husband’s service.’ Although unwilling, she restored everything. Badegisel had been of unspeakable malice: he
often cut men’s genitals together with the skin of their bellies and burned women’s private parts with heated metal plates, and committed many other iniquities
which I have thought better to leave unmentioned. Sabaudus, bishop of Arles, also died, and Licerius, King Guntram’s referendary, was chosen in his place. A
severe plague then ravaged Provence itself. Evantius, bishop of Vienne, died too, and Virus, a priest of senatorial family, was appointed to his see at the
king’s choice. Many bishops departed from this world that year; I have wished to pass over most of them because each has left his own memorial in his own city.

### 40. Of Pelagius of Tours

**[040]** There was also in Tours a certain Pelagius, practised in every wickedness, who feared no judge because the keepers of the fiscal horses were under his
authority. He therefore continually committed theft, assault, violent seizure, murder, and various crimes on rivers as well as on land. I often summoned him and
tried with threatening and gentle words to deter him from this wickedness, but received from him hatred rather than any fruit of justice, according to Solomon’s
proverb in Wisdom: ‘Rebuke a fool, and he will hate you more.’ The wretched man hated me so much that he often robbed and beat the holy Church’s men and left
them half dead, seeking opportunities to injure the Church and Saint Martin’s basilica. On one occasion, when our men came bringing church vessels, he beat and
trampled them and stole the vessels. When I learned of this, I suspended him from communion, not to avenge my own injury but to correct him more easily and free
him from this madness. He came with twelve chosen men to clear himself of the crime by oath. I wished to accept no oath, but, pressed by him and my citizens, I
set aside the others and accepted his oath alone, ordering him restored to communion. It was then the first month. When the fifth month came, in which meadows
are usually mown, he seized a meadow belonging to nuns which adjoined his own. As soon as he put his sickle into it, he was seized by fever and died on the
third day. He had prepared a tomb for himself in Saint Martin’s basilica at the village of Candé, but his men found it broken open and shattered. He was
therefore buried afterwards in the basilica’s portico. The church vessels over which he had perjured himself were brought from his storeroom after his death.
Thus was manifested the power of blessed Mary, in whose basilica the wretched man uttered his false oath.

### 41. Of those who slew Bishop Praetextatus

**[041]** When the report spread throughout the land that Bishop Praetextatus had been killed by Fredegund, she ordered a servant arrested and severely beaten
to clear herself more easily of the crime, saying: ‘You brought this accusation against me by attacking Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, with a sword.’ She handed
him over to the bishop’s nephew. When the nephew put him to torture, he revealed the whole affair clearly and said: ‘I received one hundred solidi from Queen
Fredegund to do this, fifty from Bishop Melantius, and another fifty from the city’s archdeacon. I was also promised freedom for myself and my wife.’ At these
words the man drew his sword and cut the accused to pieces. Fredegund then established Melantius, whom she had previously appointed bishop, over the church.

### 42. How Bippolinus was given as duke

**[042]** Because Duke Beppolen was greatly harassed by Fredegund and not shown the honour due to his rank, seeing himself despised, he went to King Guntram.
Receiving from him ducal authority over the cities belonging to Chlothar, King Chilperic’s son, he proceeded with great power, but the people of Rennes did not
receive him. Coming to Angers, he committed many evils, devastating the grain, hay, wine, and whatever else he could find in citizens’ houses without waiting
for keys but breaking down the doors. He beat and trampled many inhabitants. He also frightened Domigisel but was afterwards reconciled with him. While feasting
with various people in a tavern near the city, the raised floor of the house suddenly collapsed; he escaped barely alive and many were crippled, yet he
persisted in the same evils as before. Fredegund then confiscated much of his property in her son’s kingdom. Returning to Rennes and wishing to subject its
people to King Guntram, he left his son there. Not long afterwards the people of Rennes attacked and killed the son together with many distinguished men. Many
signs appeared this year: in the seventh month trees were seen to flower, and many which had already borne fruit produced new fruit which remained on the trees
until the Lord’s Nativity. Lightning seemed to run across the sky like a serpent.

### 43. How Nicetius was ordained rector of Provence

**[043]** In King Childebert’s twelfth year, Nicetius of Clermont was appointed governor of the province of Marseilles and the other cities in those parts
belonging to Childebert’s kingdom. Antestius was sent to Angers by King Guntram and inflicted many penalties upon those involved in the death of Domnola,
Nectarius’s wife. Bobolenus’s property was confiscated by the fisc because he had been the author of the crime. Antestius then came to Nantes and began to
attack Bishop Nonnichius, saying: ‘Justice demands that your son, who was involved in this crime, suffer the punishment his offence deserves.’ Terrified by his
accusing conscience, the young man fled to Chlothar, Chilperic’s son. Antestius accepted sureties from the bishop that he would appear before the king and went
to Saintes. A report had circulated in those days that Fredegund had secretly sent envoys to Spain and that Palladius, bishop of Saintes, had secretly received
them and sent them onward. It was holy Lent, and the bishop had withdrawn to an island in the sea to pray. According to custom he was returning to his church
for the feast of the Lord’s Supper while the people awaited him, but Antestius intercepted him on the road. Without examining the truth of the matter, Antestius
said: ‘You shall not enter the city but shall be condemned to exile, because you received envoys of our lord king’s enemy.’ Palladius replied: ‘I do not know
what you mean. But since the holy days are approaching, let us go to the city; after the holy feasts have been celebrated, bring whatever charges you wish and I
will answer, for your suspicion is baseless.’ Antestius said: ‘No. You shall not approach the threshold of your church, because you have proved disloyal to our
lord king.’ In short, the bishop was detained on the road, the church house was seized, and its property plundered. The citizens could not obtain from Antestius
even permission for the bishop’s case to be heard after Easter. While they pleaded and he refused, he finally revealed the desire hidden in his breast: ‘If he
conveys to me by sale the house he is known to possess in the territory of Bourges, I will do what you ask; otherwise he shall not escape my hands but shall be
driven into exile.’ The bishop did not dare refuse; he wrote and signed a deed and transferred the land. Then, after giving sureties to appear before the king,
he was permitted to enter the city. When the holy days were over he went to the king. Antestius was present but could prove none of his charges against the
bishop. The bishop was ordered to return to his city, with the case deferred until a future synod in case any of the charges could be more clearly established.
Bishop Nonnichius was also present and departed after giving many gifts.

### 44. Of him who wished to kill King Guntram

**[044]** Fredegund sent envoys to King Guntram ostensibly in her son’s name. Having presented their petition and received an answer, they said farewell and
departed, but for some reason lingered a little at their lodging. In the morning the king went to matins preceded by a candle. A man was seen sleeping like a
drunkard in a corner of the oratory, girt with a sword whose hilt rested against the wall. Seeing him, the king exclaimed that it was not innocent for a man to
rest in such a place in the dread of night. The man was seized, bound with straps, and questioned about his purpose and actions. Subjected to torture without
delay, he said that the newly arrived envoys had sent him to kill the king. Fredegund’s envoys were then arrested but confessed nothing when questioned, saying:
‘We were sent for no purpose except to deliver the message we presented.’ The king ordered the man to be beaten in various ways and imprisoned, and condemned
the envoys to exile in different places. It was quite evident that they had been sent by Fredegund in this plot to kill the king, which the Lord’s mercy did not
permit. Baddo was the eldest among them.

### 45. Of the death of Duke Desiderius

**[045]** Although envoys from Spain repeatedly came to King Guntram, they could obtain no favour of peace and hostility only increased. King Guntram therefore
restored the city of Albi to his nephew Childebert. Duke Desiderius, who had established the greater part of his property in that city’s territory, saw this and
feared that vengeance would be exacted from him because of an old enmity: he had once severely defeated an army of King Sigibert of glorious memory in that
city. With his wife Tetradi, whom he had taken from Eulalius, now count of Clermont, he crossed into the territory of Toulouse with all his possessions. He
assembled an army and prepared to march against the Goths, having first, it is said, divided his property among his sons and wife. Taking Count Austrovald with
him, he made for Carcassonne. The citizens had heard of his approach and prepared to resist. When battle was joined, the Goths began to flee, and Desiderius and
Austrovald pursued the enemy from behind. After their flight Desiderius approached the city with only a few men, for his companions’ horses were exhausted.
Coming to the gate, he was surrounded by the citizens within the walls and killed with all who had followed him; scarcely a few escaped to report what had
happened. Hearing that Desiderius was dead, Austrovald turned back and went to the king, who soon appointed him duke in Desiderius’s place.

### 46. Of the death of King Leuvigild

**[046]** Afterwards Leovigild, king of the Spains, fell ill. As some assert, he did penance for his heretical error, adjured everyone not to agree with that
heresy, and passed over to the Catholic faith. Continuing in tears for seven days over the iniquities he had devised against God, he died. His son Reccared
reigned in his place.

# LATIN TEXT

---

*IN CHRISTI NOMEN INCIPIT LIBER VIII.*

## 1. De eo quod rex Aurilianis venit.

**[001]** Igitur Gunthchramnus rex anno XXIIII. regni sui de Cavillonno progressus, Nevernensem urbem adgreditur. Invitatus enim Parisius veniebat, ut
Chilperici filium, quem iam Chlotliacharium vocitabant, a sacro regenerationes fonte deberet excipere. Digressus vero a Neverno ad Aurilianensem urbem venit,
magnum se tunc civibus suis praebens. Nam per domibus eorum invitatus abibat et prandia data libabat; multum ab his muneratus muneraque ipsis proflua
benignitate largitus est. Sed cum ad urbem Aurilianensem venisset, erat ea die solemnitas beati Martini, id est quarto Nonas mensis quinti. Prccessitque in
obviam eius inmensa populi turba cum signis adque vixillis, canentes laudes. Et hinc lingua Syrorum, hinc Latinorum, hinc etiam ipsorum Iudaeorum in diversis
laudibus variae concrepabat, dicens: 'Vivat rex, regnumque eius in populis annis innumeris dilatetur'. Iudaei vero, qui in his laudibus videbantur esse
participes, dicebant: 'Omnes gentes te adorent tibique genu flectant adque tibi sint subditi'. Unde factum est, ut, celebratis missis, cum rex ad convivium
resederet, diceret: 'Vae genti Iudaicae malae et perfidae ac subdolo semper sensu viventi. Ob hoc enim mihi', inquid, 'hodie laudes adulaturias adclamabant, ut
me cunctae gentes quasi dominum adorarent, ut synagoga eorum, quae dudum a christianis deruta est, iuberem ope publica sublevare; quod, iubente Domino, numquam
ero facturus'. O regem admirabili prudentia clarum! Sic intellexit dolositatem hereticorum, ut ei paenitus non valerent subripere, quae erant postmodum
suggesturi. Iam enim mediante epulo rex loeutus est sacerdotibus qui aderant, dicens: Rogo, ut in domo mea crastina die vestram promerear benedictionem, fiatque
mihi salus in ingressu vestro, ut ex hoc salvus fiam, cum super me humilem vestrarum benedictionum verba defluxerint'. Haec eo dicente, omnes gratias agentes,
epulo expleto, surreximus.

## 2. Qualiter ei episcopi praesentati sunt, et qualiter ipse convivium praeparavit.

**[002]** Mane autem facto, dum rex loca sanctorum orationis gratia visitaret, ad metatum nostrum advenit. Erat enim ibi basilica sancti Aviti abbatis, cui in
libro Miraculorum meminimus. Surrexi gavisus, fateor, ad occursum eius et, data oratione, depraecor, ut in mansione mea euglogias beati Martini dignaretur
accipere. Quod ille non respuens, benigno animo ingressus, hausto poculo, admonitis nobis ad convivium, laetus abscessit. Tunc Berthchramnus Burdegalensis
episcopus cum Palladio Santonico valde regi infensus erat pro susceptione Gundovaldi, cui supra meminimus. Sed et Palladius episcopus ob hoc maxime regem
incurrerat, quod ei saepius fallacias intulisset. Discussi enim ante paulolum fuerant a reliquis episcopis et optimatibus regis, cur Gundovaldum suscepissent,
cur Faustianum Aquis episcopum ad praeceptionem eius levissimam ordinassent. Sed hanc causam ordinationis Palladius episcopus a Bertechramno metropole suo
auferens, super se divolvit, dicens: 'Oculi metropolis mei valde doloribus artabantur, et ego spoliatus et contemptus, invitus in eo loco adductus sum. Non
potui aliud facere, nisi quae ille, qui omnem principatum Galliarum se testabatur accipere, imperabat'. Cum haec rege nuntiata fuissent, valde commotus est, ita
ut vix obtineri possit, ut eos ad convivium provocaret, quos antea non viderat. Introeunte itaque Bertliramno, interrogat rex: 'Quis', ait, 'est iste?' Diu enim
erat, quod ab eo visus non fuerat. Dixeruntque: 'Hic est Berthchramnus Burdegalinsis urbis episcopus'. Cui ille: 'Gratias', inquid, agimus, quod sic custodisti
fidem generationi tuae. Scire enim te oportuerat, dilectissime pater, quod parens eras nobis ex matre nostra, et super gentem tuam non debueras inducere pestem
extraneam'. Cumque talia et his similia Berthchramnus audisset, conversus ad Palladium rex ait: 'Nec tibi, o Palladi episcope, nimium sunt gratiae referendae.
Tertio enim mihi, quod de episcopo dici iniquum est, periurasti, mittens indicolos dolositate plenus. A me excusabaris per epistolas, et germanum meum cum
scriptis aliis invitabas. Iudicavit enim Deus causam meam, cum ego provocare vcs semper tamquam aeclesiae patres studui et vos circa me semper egistis dolose'.
Nicasio autem et Antidio episcopis dixit: 'Quid vos, o sanctissimi patres, pro regiones utilitate vel regni nostri sospitate tractastis, edicite'. Illis quoque
tacentibus, ablutis rex manibus, accepta a sacerdotibus benedictione, ad mensam resedit laeto vulto et hilare faciae, quasi nihil de contempto suo fuisset
effatus.

## 3. De cantoribus et argento Mummoli.

**[003]** Interea iam medium prandii peractum, iubet rex, ut diaconem nostrum, qui ante die ad missas psalmum responsurium dixerat, canere iuberem. Quo canente,
iubet iterum mihi, ut omnes sacerdotes qui aderant per meam commonitionem, datis ex officio suo singulis clerecis, coram rege iuberentur cantare. Per me enim
secundum regis imperium admoniti, quisque, ut potuit, in regis praesentia psalmum responsurium decantavit. Cum autem fercula profererentur, dixit rex: 'Argentum
omne, quod cernitis, Mummoli illius periuris fuit; sed nunc, gratia Domini tribuente, in nostra dominatione translatum est. Nam quindecim ex eo catinos, ut
istum maiorem cernitis, iam concidi, et non exinde amplius quam hunc et alium de cento septuaginta libris reservavi. Et quid amplius quam opus cotidianum? Non
ego, quod peius est, alium filium praeter Childeberthum habeo, cui satis sit de thesauris, quos ei pater reliquid', et quae iam de huius miserrimi rebus, quae
Avennione inventae sunt, transmittere curavi. Reliqua vero pauperum et aeclesiarum erunt necessitatibus tribuenda.

## 4. Laus Childeberthi regis.

**[004]** Unum vos tantummodo, sacerdotes Domini, depraecor, ut pro filio meo Childebertho Domini misericordiam exoretis. Est enim vir sapiens adque utilis, ut
de multorum annorum aevo vix ita tam cautus homo repperire possit ac strinuus. Quia, si hunc Deus his Galliis concedere dignabatur, fortassis spes erat, de
eodem gentem nostram, quae valde exinanita est, posse consurgere. Quod fieri iuxta eius misericordiam non diffido, eo quod tale fuerit pueri nativitates
praesagium. Nam in diem sanctum paschae, stante fratre meo Sigybertho in aeclesia, procedente diacono cum sancto euangeliorum libro, nuntius regi advenit,
unaque vox fuit pronuntiantes lectionem euangelicam ac nuntii dicentis: „Filius natus est tibi". Unde factum est, ut omnis populus in utraque adnuntiatione
pariter proclamaret: „Gloria Deo omnipotenti". Sed et baptismum in die sanctum pentecosten accepit, et rex nihilominus in diem sanctum dominicae nativitatis est
elevatus. Unde, si oratio vestra prosequitur, poterit hic, Domino annuente, regnare'. Haec rege dicente, omnes orationem fuderunt ad Dominum, ut utrumque regem
eius misericordia conservaret. Adiecitque rex: 'Verum quia mater eius Brunichildis me minatur interimere, sed nihil mihi ex hoc formidinis est. Dominus enim,
qui me eripuit de manibus inimicorum meorum, et de huius insidiis liberavit me'.

## 5. De visiones, quas rex vel nos de Chilperico vidimus.

**[005]** Multa tunc et in Theodorum adversa locutus est, protestans, quod, si ad synodum veniret, iterum exilio truderetur, dicens: 'Scio enim, quod horum
causa germanum meum Chilpericum interfeci fecit. Denique nec nos pro viris habere debemur, si eius necem ulciscere non valemus hoc anno. Cui ego respondi: 'Et
quis Chilpericum interemit, nisi malitia sua tuaque oratio? Multas enim tibi contra iustitiam tetendit insidias, quae ei mortis exitium intulerunt. Quod ut
dicam, valde hoc per visionem somnii inspexi, cum viderem eum, ante tonsorato capite, quasi episcopum ordinari; deinde super cathedram puram, sola fuligine
tectam, inpositum ferri, praelucentibus coram eo lyghnis ac cereis'. Me haec narrante, rex ait: 'Vidi et ego aliam visionem, quae huius interitum nuntiavit.
Adducebatur enim in conspectu meo a tribus episcopis vinctus catenis, quorum unus Tetricus, alius Agroecula, tertius vero Nicetius Lugduninsis erat. E quibus
dicebant duo: „Solvite, quaesumus, eum et castigatum abire permittite". Quibus e contrario cum amaritudine Tetricus episcopus respondebat: „Non fiet ita, sed
igni concremabitur pro sceleribus suis". Et cum diu multumque quasi altercantes haec inter se verba proferrent, conspicio eminus aeneum super ignem positum
fervere vehementer. Tunc me flente, adpraehensum infilicem Chilpericum, confractis membris, proiciunt in aeneum. Nec mora, inter undarum vapores ita dissolutus
ac liquefactus est, ut nullum ex eo paenitus indicium remaneret'. Haec rege dicente, admirantibus nobis, epulo expleto, surreximus.

## 6. De his quos praesentavimus.

**[006]** Rex igitur in crastinum in venatione progressus est. Quo redeunte, Garacharius comis Burdigalensis adque Bladastis a nobis repraesentat sunt, quia, ut
superius diximus, in basilica sancti Martini confugium fecerant, pro eo quod Gundovaldo coniuncti fuissent. Nam cum prius, pro his depraecatus, nihil obtinere
potuissem, haec in sequenti locutus sum: 'Audiat, o rex, potestas tua. Ecce! a domino meo in legatione ad te directus sum. Vel quid renuntiabo ei qui me misit,
cum nihil mihi responsi reddere vellis?' At ille obstupefactus ait: 'Et quis est dominus tuus, qui te misit?' Cui ego subridens: 'Beatus Martinus', inquio,
'misit me'. Tunc ille iussit sibi repraesentari viros. Sed cum in eius conspectu venissent, multas eis perfidias ac periurias exprobravit, vocans eos saepius
vulpis ingeniosas, sed restituit eos gratiae suae, reddens quae illis ablata fuerant.

## 7. De Palladio episcopo, qualiter missas dixit.

**[007]** Adveniente quoque die dominico, rex ad aeclesiam ad spectanda missarum solemnia petit. Fratres vero consacerdotesque, qui aderant, locum Palladio
episcopo ad agenda festa praebuerunt. Quo incipiente prophetiam, rex interrogat, quis esset. Cumque Palladium episcopum initiasse pronuntiassent, statim
commotus rex ait: 'Qui mihi semper infidelis et perfidus fuit, ille nunc sacrata verba praedicavit? Egrediar prursus ab haec aeclesia, ne inimicum meum audiam
praedicantem'. Et haec dicens, egredi coepit aeclesiam. Tunc conturbati sacerdotes de fratres humilitate, dixerunt regi: Tidimus enim eum convivio tuo adesse ac
de eius manu te benedictionem accipere; et cur eum nunc rex aspernatur? Si enim scissemus tibi exosum, declinassemus utique ad alium, qui haec agere debuisset.
Nunc, si permittis, caelebret, quae coepit; in posterum autem, si aliquid opposueris, canonicae sanctionis censura finiatur'. lam enim Palladius episcopus in
sacrario cum grande humilitate discesserat. Tunc rex iussit eum revocare, et sic quae agere coeperat expedivit. Nam cum iterato ad convivium regis Palladius
atque Berthchramnus acciti fuissent, commoti in invicem multa sibi de adulteriis ac fornicatione exprobraverunt, nonnulla etiam de periuriis. Quibus de rebus
multi ridebant, nonnulli vero, qui alacriores erant scientiae, lamentabant, cur inter sacerdotes Domini taliter zezania diabuli pollularet. Discedentes itaque a
regis praesentia, cautiones et fideiussores dederunt, ut decimo Kalendas mensis noni ad sinodum convenirent.

## 8. De signis ostensis.

**[008]** Tunc apparuerunt signa, id est radii a parte aquilonis, sicut saepius apparere solent. Fulgor per caelum cucurrisse visus est, floresque in arboribus
ostensi sunt. Erat enim mensis quintus.

## 9. De sacramento pro filio Chilperici dato.

**[009]** Post haec rex Parisius venit et coram omnibus loqui coepit, dicens: ' Germanus meus Chilpericus moriens dicitur filium reliquisse, cuius nutritores,
matre depraecante, petierunt, ut eum de sancto lavacro in dominici natalis solemnitate deberem excipere, et non venerunt. Rogaverunt deinceps, ut ad sanctum
pascha baptizaretur, sed nec tunc adlatus est infans. Depraecati sunt autem tertio, ut ad festivitatem sancti Iohannis exhiberetur, sed nec tunc venit. Moverunt
itaque me per tempus sterile de loco ubi abitabam. Veni igitur, et ecce! absconditur nec ostenditur mihi puer. Unde, quantum intellego, nihil est quod
promittitur, sed, ut credo, alicuius ex leudibus nostris sit filius. Nam si de stirpe nostra fuisset, ad me utique fuerat deportatus. Ideoque noveritis, quia a
me non suscipitur, nisi certa de eo cognuscam indicia'. Haec audiens Fredegundis regina, coniunctis prioribus regni sui, id est cum tribus episcopis et
tricentis viris optimis, sacramenta dederunt, hunc ab Chilperico rege generatum fuisse; et sic suspicio ab animis regis ablata est.

## 10. De corporibus Merovechi et Chlodovechi.

**[010]** Denique cum interitum Merovechi adque Chlodovechi saepius lamentaret nesciretque, ubi eos postquam inteificerant proiecissent, venit ad regem homo,
qui diceret: 'Si mihi contrarium in posterum non habetur, indicabo, in quo loco Chlodovechi cadaver sit positum'. Iuravit rex, nihil ei molestum fieri, sed
potius muneribus ampliari. Tunc ille: 'Veritatem', inquid, 'me loqui, o rex, ipsa ratio quae acta est conprobabit. Nam quando Chlodovechus interfectus est ac
sub stillicidio oraturii cuiusdam sepultus, metuens regina, ne aliquando inventus cum honore sepeliretur, iussit eum in alveum Matronae fluminis proici. Tunc
intra lapsum, quod opere meo ad capiendorum piscium necessitatem praeparaveram, repperi. Sed cum ignorarem, quisnam esset, a caesariae prolixa cognovi
Chlodovechum esse, adpraehensumque in humeris ad litus detuli ibique eum cespite superposito tumulavi. Ecce, salvatis artubus, quod volueris effice!' Quod cum
rex conperisset, confingens se ad venationem procedere, detectoque tumulo, repperit corpusculum integrum et inlaesum. Una tantum pars capillorum, quae subter
fuerat, iam defluxerat, alia vero cum ipsis crinium flagellis intacta durabat. Cognitumque est, hunc esse, quem rex intento animo requirebat. Convocato igitur
episcopo civitatis, cum clero et populo ac cereorum innumerabilium ornato ad basilicam sancti Vincenti detulit tumulandum, non minus plangens nepotes mortuos,
quam cum vidit filios proprios iam sepultus. Post haec misit Pappolum Carnotenae urbis episcopum, qui Merovechi cadaver requirens, iuxta Chlodovechi tumulum
sepelivit.

## 11. De ostiariis et interito Boanti.

**[011]** Ostiarius vero quidam de alio ostiario dixit: 'Domine rex, hic, accepto praemio, consinsit, ut tu interficiaris'. Adpraehensusque ostiarius, de quo
dixerat, caesus suppliciisque multis adfectus, nihil de causa, qua interrogabatur, aperuit. Loquebantur enim tunc multi hoc in insidiis et invidia factum, quod
ostiarius ille, cui hoc crimen inpactum fuerat, plurimum a reges diligeretur. Ansovaldus autem, nescio qua suspicione tactus, nec vale dicens, a rege discessit.
Rex vero Cavillonum regressus, iussit Boantum, qui sibi semper fuerat infidelis, gladio percuti. Qui vallatus in domo sua, ab hominibus regis peremptus
interiit, resque suae fisci dicionibus subiugatae sunt.

## 12. De Theudoro episcopo et plaga super Ratharium.

**[012]** Denique cum rex maxima intentione Theodorum episcopum iterum persequi conaretur et Massilia iam in Childeberthi regis dominatione revocata fuisset, ad
discutiendas causas Ratharius illuc quasi dux a parte regis Childeberthi diregitur. Sed postposita actione, quae ei a rege iniuncta fuerant, episcopum vallat,
fideiussores requirit et ad praesentiam regis Gunthchramni direxit, ut scilicet ad synodum, quod Matiscone futurum erat, quasi ab episcopis damnandus adesset.
Nec defuit ultio divina, quae servos suos ab ore canum rabidorum defensare consuevit. Nam egrediente episcopo a civitate, statim res aeclesiae direpit et alia
quidem sibi vindicat, alia sub sigillorum munitione concludit. Cumque hoc fecisset, protenus famulus eius saevissimus invadit morbus exhaustusque febre peremit;
filius eius ab hcc incommodo defecit, quem suburbano Massiliae ipsius cum gravi gemitu sepelivit. Fuitque talis domui eius plaga, ut, cum ab urbe illa est
digressus, vix ad patriam suam regredi putaretur. Theodorus vero episcopus a Gunthchramno rege detentus est, sed nihil ei rex nocuit. Est enim vir egregiae
sanctitatis et in oratione assiduus, de quo mihi Magnericus Treverensis episcopus haec retulit: Ante hos annos cum ad praesentia Childeberthi regis ita sub
ardua custodia duceretur, ut, quandoque ad urbem aliquam venisset, neque episcopum neque quemquam de civibus videre permitteretur, adveniens Treverus, nuntiatum
est episcopo, hunc iam in navi positum clam abduci. Surrexitque sacerdus tristis, ac velociter prosecutus, repperit eum ad litus; causatusque cum custodibus,
cur tanta esset impietas, ut non liceret fratri fratrem aspicere, visoque tandem, osculatus eum, indulgens aliquid vestimenti, discessit. Veniens itaque ad
basilicam sancti Maximini, prosternitur sepulchro, illud apostoli Iacobi retinens: Orate pro invicem, ut salvimini. Fusaque diu oratione cum lacrimis, ut fratre
dignaretur Dominus adiuvare, egressus est foris. Et ecce! mulier, quam spiritus erroris agitabat, clamare sacerdoti coepit ac dicere: 'O sceleste et inveterate
dierum, qui pro inimico nostro Theodore orationem fundis ad Dominum, ecce! nos cotidie querimus, qualiter ab his Galliis extrudatur, qui nos cotidianis
incendiis conflat, et tu pro eo rogare non desinis! Satius enim tibi erat, res aeclesiae tuae diligenter inquirere, ne pauperibus aliquid deperiret, quam pro
hoc tam intente deposcere'. Et agebat: 'Vae nobis, qui eum non possumus expugnare'. Et licet daemoniis credi non debeat, tamen qualis esset sacerdus, de quo
haec daemon condolens declamabat, apparuit. Sed ad coepta redeamus.

## 13. De legationem Gunthchramni ad Childeberthum directa.

**[013]** Igitur legatus ad nepotem suum Childeberthum rex diregit, qui morabatur tunc ad castrum Confluentis, qui ob hoc nomen accepit, pro eo quod Musella
Rhenusque amnes pariter confluentes in eodem loco iungantur. Et quia placitum fuerat, ut Trecas Campaniae urbem de utrumque regnum coniungerent, sacerdotibusque
de regno Childeberthi congruum non fuit, Felix legatus, salutatione praemissa, ostensis litteris, ait: 'Patruus tuus, o rex, diligenter interrogat, quis te ab
hac promissione retraxit, ut sacerdotes regni vestri ad concilium, quod simul decreveratis, venire differrent. An forsitan mali homines aliquam inter vos
discordiae radicem faciunt pullulare?' Tunc ego, rege tacente, respondi: 'Nimirum, si zizania seratur in populus; nam inter hos quo radicem obligit protenus non
potest repperiri. Nulli enim latet, quod Childeberthus rex alium patrem nisi patruum non habet, neque ille alium filium nisi hunc habere disponit, iuxta id quod
eum anno praesenti audivimus loqui. Absit ergo, ut inter eos radix discordiae germinet, cum se pariter et tuere debeant et amare'. Tunc vocato secretius Felice
legato, Childeberthus rex rogavit, dicens: 'Depraecor dominum et patrem meum, ut Theodoro episcopo nihil iniuriae inferat; quod si fecerit, confestim inter nos
scandalum germinavit, erimusque, discordia inpediente, disiuncti, qui debemus amorem tuendo esse pacifici'. Acceptoque et de aliis causis responso, legatus
discessit.

## 14. De periculo in flumine.

**[014]** Nobis itaque in antedicto castro cum regem commorantibus, dum ad convivium principis usque obscura nocte reteneremur, epulo expleto, surreximus,
venientesque ad fluvium, offendimus navem in litus, quae nobis fuerat praeparata. Ascendentibusque nobis, inruit turba hominum diversorum, impletaque est navis
tam hominibus quam aquis. Sed virtus Domini adfuit non sine grande miraculo, ut, cum usque labium impleta fuisset, mergi non possit. Habebamus enim nobiscum
beati Martini reliquias cum aliorum sanctorum, quorum virtutem nos credimus fuisse salvatos. Ad vero nave ad litus unde egressi fuimus redeunte, evacuata vel ab
hominibus vel a lymphis, repulsis extraneis, sine inpedimento transivimus. In crastino autem vale regi dicentes, abscessimus.

## 15. De conversione Vulfelaici diaconi.

**[015]** Profecti igitur in itenere, ad Eposium castrum accessimus, ibique a Vulfilaico diacono nancti, ad monasterium eius deducti, benignissime suscepti
sumus. Est enim hoc monasterium quasi milibus octo ab antedicto castro in montis cacumine collocatum. In quo monte magnam basilicam aedificavit, quam beati
Martini vel reliquorum sanctorum reliquiis inlustravit. Commorantes autem ibi, petere ab eo ccepimus, ut nobis aliqua de conversionis suae bono narraret, vel
qualiter ad clericatus officium advenissit, quia erat genere Langobardus. Sed nequibat exponere, vanam tcta intentione cupiens gloriam evitare. Quem ego
terribilibus sacramentis coniurans, pollicitus primo, ut nulli quae referebat expanderem, rogare coepi, ut nihil mihi de his quae interrogabam cccoleret. Cumque
diutissime reluctasset, victus tandem tam praecibus quam obsecrationibus meis, haec effatus est: 'Dum essem', inquid, 'puer parvolus, audito beati Martini
nomine, nesciens adhuc, utrum martyr an confessor esset, vel quid boni in mundo gessisset, vel quae regio beatus artus tumulo meruisset accipere, iam in eius
honore vigilias celebrabam ac, si aliquid inter manus numismatis advenisset, aelimosinas faciebam. Iamque in maiore aetate proficiens, litteras discere studui;
ex quibus prius scribere potui, quam ordinem scriptarum litterarum scirem. Deinde Aridio abbati coniunctus ab eoque edoctus, beati Martini basilicam adii.
Revertensque cum eo, ille parumper pulveris beati sepulchri pro benedictione sustulit, quod in capsulam positum ad collum meum dependit. Devectique ad
monasterium eius Limovicino in termino, accepta capsula, ut eam in oraturio suo locaret, in tantum pulvis adcrevit, ut non solum totam capsam repleret, verum
etiam foris inter iuncturas, ubi aditum repperire potuit, scatiret. Ex hoc mihi miraculi lumine animus magis accendit totam spem meam in eius virtute defigere.
Deinde territurium Trevericae urbis expetii, et in quo nunc estis monte habitaculum quod cernitis proprio labore construxi. Repperi tamen hic Dianae simulacrum,
quod populus hic incredulus quasi deum adorabat. Colomnam etiam statui, in qua cum grandi cruciatu sine ullo pedum perstabam tegmine. Itaque cum hiemis tempus
solite advenisset, ita rigore glaciali urebar, ut ungues pedum meorum saepius vis rigoris excuteret et in barbis meis aqua gelu conexa candelarum more
dependeret. Magnam enim hiemem regio illa persaepe dicitur sustenere '. Sed cum nos sollicite interrogaremus, qui ei cybus aut potus esset, vel qualiter
simulacra montis illius subvertisset, ait: 'Potus cybusque meus erat parumper panis et oleris ac modicum aquae. Verum ubi ad me multitudo vicinarum villarum
confluere coepit, praedicabam iugiter, nihil esse Dianam, nihil simulacra nihilque quae eis videbatur exercere cultura; indigna etiam esse ipsa, quae inter
pocula luxuriasque profluas cantica proferebant; sed potius Deo omnipotenti, qui caelum fecit ac terram, dignum sit sacrificium laudis inpendere. Orabam etiam
saepius, ut simulacrum Dominus dirutum dignaretur populum illum ab hoc errore discutere. Flexit Domini misericordia mentem rusticam, ut inclinaret aurem suam in
verba oris mei, ut scilicet, relictis idolis, Dominum sequeretur. Tunc convocatis quibusdam ex eis, simulacrum hoc inmensum, quod elidere propria virtute non
poteram, cum eorum adiutorio possim eruere; iam enim reliqua sigillorum, quae faciliora fuerant, ipse confringeram. Convenientibus autem multis ad hanc Dianae
statuam, missis funibus, trahere coeperunt; sed nihil labor eorum proficere poterat. Tunc ego ad basilicam propero, prostratusque solo, divinam misericordiam
cum lacrimis flagitabam, ut, quia id humana industria evertere non valebat, virtus illud divina destrueret. Egressusque post orationem, ad operarius veni,
adprehensumque funem, ut primo ictu trahere coepimus, protenus simulacrum ruit in terra, confractumque cum malleis ferreis in pulverem redegi. Ipsa quoque hora,
cum ad cibum capiendum venissem, ita omne corpus meum a vertice usque ad plantam pusulis malis repletum est, ut locus, quem unus digitus tegerit, vacuus
invenire non possit. Ingressusque basilicam solus, denudavi me coram sancto altario. Habebam enim ibi ampullam cum oleo plenam, quam de sancti Martini basilicam
detuleram; ex qua propriis manibus omnes artus perunxi, moxque sopori locatus sum. Expergefactus vero circa medium noctis, cum ad cursum reddendum surgerem, ita
corpus totum incolomem repperi, acsi nullum super me ulcus apparuisset. Quae vulnera non aliter nisi per invidiam inimici emissa cognovi. Et quia semper ipse
invidus Deum quaerentibus nccere conatur, advenientibus episcopis, qui me magis ad hoc cohortare debuerant, ut coeptum opus sagaciter explicare deberem,
dixerunt mihi: „Non est aequa haec via, quam sequeris, nec tu ignobilis Symeoni Anthiochino, qui colomnae insedit, poteris conparare. Sed nec cruciatum hoc te
sustenere patitur loci positio. Discende potius et cum fratribus, quos adgregasti tecum, inhabita". Ad quorum verba, quia sacerdotes non obaudire adscribitur
crimini, discendebam, fateor, et ambulabam cum eisdem ac cybum pariter capiebam. Quadam vero die, provocans me episcopus longius ad villam, emisit operarius cum
scutis et malleis ac securibus, et eliserunt colomnam, in qua stare solitus eram. In crastinum autem veniens, inveni omnia dissipata. Flevi vehementer, sed
erigere nequivi quae distruxerant, ne dicerer contrarius iussionibus sacerdotum; et ex hoc, sicut nunc habito, cum fratribus habitare contentus sum'.

## 16. Et quae de virtutibus sancti Martini retulit.

**[016]** Cui cum de virtutibus beati Martini, quas in eo loco operatus est, aliquam ut declararet exposcirem, haec retulit: 'Franci cuiusdam et nobilissimi in
gente sua viri filius mutus surdusque erat; adductusque a parentibus ad hanc basilicam, iussi eum cum diacono meo et alio ministro in ipsum templum sanctum in
lectulo requiescere. Et per diem quidem orationi vacabat, nocte autem in ipsa, ut diximus, aede dormiebat. Quandoque misertus Deus, apparuit mihi in visione
beatus Martinus, dicens: „Eiece agnum de basilica, quia iam sanus factus est". Mane autem facto, cogitanti mihi, quod esset hoc somnium, venit ad me puer, et
emittens vocem, gratias agere Deo coepit, conversusque ad me, ait: „Gratias ago Deo omnipotenti, qui mihi et eloquium reddedit et auditum". Ex hoc sanus
redditus, ad domum rediit. Alius vero, qui plerumque in furtis diversisque sceleribus conmixtus, periurare consueverat, cum aliquando a quibusdam pro furtu
argueritur, ait: „Ibo ad basilicam beati Martini, et sacramentis me exuens, innocens reddar". Quo ingrediente, elapsa secure de manu eius, ad usteum ruit, gravi
cordis dolore perculsus. Confessusque est miser verbis propriis quae venerat excusare periuriis. Alius simili modo cum de incendiis domus vicini sui argueritur,
ait: „Vadam ad templum sancti Martini et, fide data, insons redditurus ero ab hoc crimine". Manifestum erat enim, hunc domum illam incendio concremasse. Abiens
autem ad sacramenta danda, conversus ad eum, dixi ei: „Quantum vicinorum tuorum dictat assertio, non eris innocens ab hoc scelere; sed tamen Deus ubique est, et
virtus eius ipsa est forinsecus, quae habetur intrinsecus. Tamen si ita te vana fiducia coepit, quod Deus vel sancti eius in periuribus non ulciscantur, ecce!
templum sanctum e contra, iura, ut libet. Nam calcare limen sacrum non permitteris". Ad ille, elevatis manibus, ait: „Per omnipotentem Deum et virtutem beati
Martini antestitis eius, quia hoc incendium non admisi". Data itaque sacramenta, dum recederet, visum est ei quasi ab igne circumdare. Et statim ruens in terra,
clamare coepit, se a beato antestite vehementer exuri. Aiebat enim miser: „Testor Deum, quia ego vidi ignem de caelo cadere, qui me circumdans validis vaporibus
conflat". Et dum haec diceret, spiritum exalavit. Multis haec causa documentum fuit, ne in hoc loco auderent ulterius periurare'. Plurima quidem de his
virtutibus hic diaconus retulit, quae sequi longum potavi.

## 17. De signis quae apparuerunt.

**[017]** Dum autem in loco illo commoraremur, vidimus per duas noctes signa in caelo, id est radius a parte aquilonis tam clare splendidus, ut prius sic
apparuisse non fuerent visi; et ab utraque quidem parte, id est ab euro et zephero, nubes sanguineae. Tertia vero nocte quasi hora secunda apparuerunt hii
radii. Et ecce! dum eos miraremur attoniti, surrexerunt a quatuor plagis mundi alii horum similes; vidimusque totum caelum ab his operire. Et erat nubes in
medio caeli splendida, ad quam se hi radii collegebant in modum tenturii, quod ab imo ex amplioribus incoeptum fasceis, angustatis in altum, in uno cuculli
capite saepe collegitur. Erantque in medio radiorum et aliae nubes, ceu coruscum valide fulgorantes. Quod signum magnum nobis ingessit metum. Operiebamur enim,
super nos aliquam plagam de caelo transmitti.

## 18. Quod Childeberthus in Italiam direxit exercitum.

**[018]** Childebertus vero rex, inpellentibus missis imperialibus, qui aurum, quod anno superiore datum fuerat, requirebat, exercitum in Italia diregit. Sonus
