Bourges, where his relatives lived, because it lay in King Guntram’s kingdom. Sichar’s wife Tranquilla left his sons and property in Tours and Poitiers and went
to her relatives at the village of Mauriops, where she married again. Sichar was about twenty years old when he died. In life he had been frivolous, drunken,
and murderous, injuring many while drunk. Chramnesind went again to the king, and judgment required him to prove that Sichar had deserved death. He did so. But
because Brunhild had placed Sichar under her protection, she ordered his property confiscated; it was later restored by Flavian, a member of the royal
household. Chramnesind also hastened to Agen and obtained a letter from her ordering that no one molest him, for his property had been granted to him by the
queen.

### 20. My embassy to King Guntram to preserve the peace

**[020]** In King Childebert’s thirteenth year, after hastening to meet him at Metz, I was ordered to go as an envoy to King Guntram. I found him at Chalon and
said: ‘Your most glorious nephew Childebert sends you abundant greeting, renowned king, and gives immense thanks for your kindness in continually admonishing
him to do what pleases God, is acceptable to you, and benefits the people. He promises to fulfil everything you discussed together and declares that he will
violate none of the written agreements between you.’ The king replied: ‘I cannot likewise thank him, for what was promised me is being violated. My share of
Senlis is not restored, and I was not permitted to remove men hostile to me whose departure I desired for my own welfare. How can you say that my dearest nephew
wishes to transgress none of the written agreements?’ I answered: ‘He wishes to do nothing against those agreements but promises to fulfil them all. If you wish
to send men now to divide Senlis, there will be no delay and you shall immediately receive your share. As for the men you mention, let their names be supplied
in writing, and every promise shall be fulfilled.’ As I spoke, the king ordered the agreement read before the bystanders.

COPY OF THE AGREEMENT. When in Christ’s name the most excellent lords Kings Guntram and Childebert and the most glorious lady Queen Brunhild met at Andelot in a
spirit of charity to settle by fuller counsel everything which might cause scandal among them, it was agreed between them through the mediation of bishops and
nobles, with God as witness and in a spirit of charity, that as long as almighty God permits them to remain in this world they shall preserve pure and sincere
faith and charity towards one another. Whereas Lord Guntram claimed under his agreement with Lord Sigibert of good memory that the whole share of Charibert’s
kingdom which Sigibert had obtained should be restored to him, while Lord Childebert’s party wished to recover everything his father had possessed, it was
firmly decided that the third share of Paris with its territory and people which had come to Sigibert from Charibert’s kingdom by written agreement, including
the fortresses of Dunum and Vendôme and whatever the king had received in the districts of Étampes and Chartres in that third with their territories and
peoples, together with what he had previously held from Charibert’s kingdom during Sigibert’s lifetime, shall remain perpetually under Lord Guntram’s right and
dominion. On the same condition King Childebert shall claim under his authority from this day the cities of Meaux, two shares of Senlis, Tours, Poitiers,
Avranches, Vic, Consorans, Labourd, and Albi with their territories. It was further agreed that whichever king God commands to survive shall recover in
perpetuity the entire kingdom of the other if he departs this life without sons and leave it to his own posterity with the Lord’s help. It was specially decided
to preserve inviolably whatever King Guntram has granted or may yet grant his daughter Chlothild, in all property and possessions, cities, lands, or revenues;
these shall remain under her right and dominion. Whatever she wishes to do with fiscal lands, valuables, or resources, or confer upon anyone at her own
discretion, shall be preserved for ever with the Lord’s help and never overturned by anyone. Under Childebert’s protection and defence she shall securely
possess in all honour and dignity both these and everything she possessed at her father’s death. Lord Guntram likewise promises that if, through human
frailty—which divine mercy forbid and he does not desire to see—Childebert should die during his lifetime, he will receive as a loving father under his
protection and defence Childebert’s sons Kings Theudebert and Theuderic and any others God may yet grant, so that they may securely possess their father’s
kingdom. He will also receive under his protection and spiritual love Childebert’s mother Queen Brunhild, his sister Clodosind as long as she remains in
Frankish territory, and his queen Faileuba, as a good sister and daughters. They shall possess in all honour, dignity, security, and quiet all their property,
cities, lands, revenues, titles, and possessions, both what they now hold and what they may yet justly acquire with Christ’s favour. Whatever they wish to do
with fiscal lands, valuables, or resources or confer upon anyone at their discretion shall remain fixed for ever, and their wishes shall never be overturned by
anyone. Concerning Bordeaux, Limoges, Cahors, Béarn, and Bigorre, which Brunhild’s sister Gailswintha is known to have acquired on coming to Francia as dowry
and morning gift, and which Brunhild is known to have acquired by judgment of the glorious King Guntram and the Franks while Kings Chilperic and Sigibert were
alive, it is agreed that Brunhild shall immediately receive Cahors with its territory and people as her own property. Guntram shall possess the other cities
named above for his lifetime; after his death they shall revert with God’s favour to the dominion of Brunhild and her heirs in full security, and during
Guntram’s lifetime neither Brunhild nor her son King Childebert and his sons shall reclaim them by any device or at any time. It is likewise agreed that
Childebert shall hold Senlis in full, and Guntram’s third share due from it shall be compensated to Guntram’s party from Childebert’s third in the district of
Rouen. According to the agreements between Guntram and Sigibert of good memory, leudes who first swore to Guntram after Chlothar’s death and are later proved to
have transferred to another party shall be removed from the places where they live. Similarly those proved to have first sworn to Sigibert after Chlothar’s
death and then transferred to another party shall likewise be removed. Whatever these kings have granted to churches or their faithful men, or may yet justly
grant with God’s favour, shall be preserved securely. Whatever is owed by law and justice to each faithful man in either kingdom shall suffer no prejudice; he
may possess and recover what is owed. If anything was taken from anyone without fault during the interregna, it shall be restored after a hearing. Each shall
securely possess what he held through earlier kings’ generosity until the death of King Chlothar of glorious memory, and shall now recover whatever was taken
from faithful persons thereafter. Because pure and sincere concord between these kings is bound in God’s name, any faithful man of either kingdom wishing to
travel in the other on public or private business shall never be denied passage. Neither party shall solicit the other’s leudes or receive those who come. If
either party believes a claim should be made for some offence, those involved shall make amends according to the nature of the fault after excuses have been
heard. It was added that if either party ever violates these provisions by any craft, it shall lose all benefits both promised and presently granted, which
shall accrue to the party that has inviolably kept everything written above, and the violating party shall be wholly released from the obligation of its oaths.
Having settled all these matters, the parties swore by the name of almighty God, the inseparable Trinity, all divine things, and the dreadful Day of Judgment to
keep everything written above inviolably without evil deceit or fraud. This agreement was made on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the
twenty-sixth year of Lord King Guntram and the twelfth of Lord Childebert.

When the agreement had been read, the king said: ‘May God’s judgment strike me if I violate anything contained here.’ Turning to Felix, who had come with me as
an envoy, he said: ‘Tell me, Felix, have you now fully established friendship between my sister Brunhild and Fredegund, that enemy of God and men?’ When Felix
denied it, I said: ‘The king need not doubt that the friendship between them established by envoys many years ago is still maintained. But know that the hatred
formerly fixed between them still grows and does not wither. Would that you, most glorious king, had less friendship with her! As I have often learned, you
receive her envoys more honourably than ours.’ He replied: ‘Know, priest of God, that I receive her envoys without abandoning the friendship of my nephew King
Childebert. I cannot bind myself in friendship with a woman from whom men have often come to take my life.’ Felix then said: ‘I believe your majesty has learned
that Reccared sent envoys to your nephew asking for your niece Clodosind, your brother’s daughter, in marriage. Childebert wished to promise nothing without
your counsel.’ The king said: ‘It is not fitting for my niece to go where her sister was killed, nor is it reasonable that my niece Ingund’s death should remain
unavenged.’ Felix answered: ‘Reccared wishes to clear himself fully by oaths or any other conditions you command; only consent that Clodosind be betrothed to
him as he asks.’ The king said: ‘If my nephew fulfils what he wished written in the agreements, I shall grant his wish in this too.’ When I promised full
fulfilment, Felix added: ‘He also begs your kindness to give him help against the Lombards, so that they may be expelled from Italy, the part his father
acquired during his lifetime may return to him, and the rest may be restored through your joint assistance to the emperor’s authority.’ The king replied: ‘I
cannot send my army into Italy and voluntarily deliver it to death, for a most severe plague is now devastating Italy.’ I said: ‘You told your nephew to
assemble all the bishops of his kingdom because many matters require investigation. But according to canonical custom your glorious nephew wished each
metropolitan to meet with his own provincial bishops and correct by episcopal decree whatever was unreasonably done in his own region. Why should so great a
multitude assemble in one place? The Church’s faith is not shaken by any danger, and no new heresy has arisen. What necessity requires so many lord bishops to
meet together?’ He answered: ‘Many unjust acts require judgment, including incest and the matters between us. Above all, the greatest matter of God requires you
to investigate why Bishop Praetextatus was killed by the sword in church. Those accused of immorality must also be examined, so that the guilty may be corrected
by episcopal sanction or, if found innocent, the public error of the charge removed.’ He ordered the synod postponed until the Kalends of the fourth month.
After this I went to church, for it was the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. After Mass he invited me to a banquet as rich in dishes as in joy. The king
continually spoke of God, building churches, and defending the poor; he sometimes laughed, delighting in spiritual jest and adding things for my enjoyment. He
said: ‘Would that my nephew kept his promises! Everything I have is his. If he is offended because I receive envoys of my nephew Chlothar, am I so foolish that
I cannot moderate between them and prevent scandal spreading? I know how to restrain it rather than extend it. If I recognize Chlothar as my nephew, I shall
give him two or three cities in some region, so that he may not seem disinherited from my kingdom and what I leave him may cause no trouble to Childebert.’
Saying these and other things, cherishing me with sweet affection and loading me with gifts, he ordered me to depart, instructing me always to communicate to
King Childebert whatever would benefit his life.

### 21. The king’s almsgiving and goodness

**[021]** As I have often said, this king was great in almsgiving and ready for vigils and fasts. It was then reported that bubonic plague was severely
devastating Marseilles and that the disease had quickly spread as far as the village called Octavus near Lyons. Like a good bishop providing remedies to heal
the wounds of a sinful people, the king ordered everyone to assemble in church, celebrate Rogations with utmost devotion, consume nothing but barley bread and
clean water, and attend vigils diligently. This was done. For three days his almsgiving exceeded its usual abundance, and he showed such concern for all the
people that he seemed not only a king but also a priest of the Lord. He placed all his hope in the Lord’s mercy and cast upon Him his anxious thoughts, trusting
with complete faith that God would bring them to effect. The faithful then commonly reported that a woman whose son lay anxiously in bed afflicted by quartan
fever approached the king through the crowd, secretly tore threads from the fringe of his royal garment, placed them in water, and gave it to her son to drink.
His fever was immediately extinguished and he was healed. I do not doubt this, for I myself have often heard possessing spirits invoke Guntram’s name while
tormenting a servant and, through his power, confess their own evil deeds.

### 22. The plague at Marseille

**[022]** I said above how much Marseilles suffered from a most terrible contagion, and I have decided to repeat the account more fully. In those days Bishop
Theodore had gone to the king intending to make some charge against the patrician Nicetius. When King Childebert would not hear him on this matter, he prepared
to return home. Meanwhile a ship from Spain arrived at Marseilles with its usual merchandise and wickedly carried the seed of this disease. Many citizens bought
various goods from it. Immediately one household of eight persons was left empty, all its inhabitants killed by the contagion. The plague did not immediately
spread its fire through every house; after a fixed interval, like a flame catching a crop, it burned through the whole city with the conflagration of disease.
The bishop came to the place and confined himself within Saint Victor’s basilica with the few who remained with him. Throughout the city’s destruction he
devoted himself to prayers and vigils, imploring the Lord’s mercy that the destruction might cease and the people rest in peace. The plague raged fiercely for
two months. When the people returned securely to the city, the disease came again and those who returned died. Marseilles was subsequently afflicted by this
destruction many times.

### 23. The death of Bishop Agericus and his successor

**[023]** Bishop Ageric of Verdun fell gravely ill from the gall of prolonged bitterness because Guntram Boso, for whom he had stood surety, had been killed,
and still more because Berthefred had been killed within the oratory of the church house. Guntram’s son, detained with him, daily wept and said: ‘You have been
left orphans through hatred of me.’ Inflamed by these causes and burdened by gall and especially by want of food, Ageric died and was placed in a tomb. His
abbot Bucciovald sought the bishopric but obtained nothing. Royal authority decreed that the referendary Charimer should become bishop with the citizens’
consent, setting Abbot Bucciovald aside. Bucciovald was said to be proud, and some therefore called him Buccus Valens. Licerius, bishop of Arles, also died;
Virgil, abbot of Autun, was appointed to his church with Bishop Siagrius’s assistance.

### 24. The bishopric of Fronimius

**[024]** Deotherius, bishop of Vence, also died, and Fronimius succeeded him. Fronimius had been an inhabitant of Bourges but went for some unknown reason to
Septimania. After King Athanagild’s death his successor Liuva received Fronimius magnificently and he was ordained bishop of Agde. After Liuva’s death, while
Leovigild raged in the perfidy of heretical depravity and Ingund, King Sigibert’s daughter mentioned above, was brought to Spain for marriage, Leovigild heard
that Fronimius had advised her never to defile herself with the poison of heretical belief. He therefore continually laid snares of injury for him until he
expelled him from the bishopric. Unable to find a trap in which to catch him, Leovigild finally sent a man to attack him with a sword. Warned by intermediaries,
Fronimius left Agde and came to Gaul. Received and honoured with gifts by many bishops, he went to King Childebert. The situation was revealed, and in the ninth
year of his expulsion the king granted him episcopal authority over Vence. That year the Bretons severely plundered the territories of Nantes and Rennes,
harvesting vineyards, devastating cultivated fields, and carrying off the people of the estates captive. They kept none of their earlier promises and even spoke
disparagingly of our kings.

### 25. Childebert’s army goes into Italy

**[025]** When the Lombards asked King Childebert for his sister as their king’s wife, he accepted gifts and promised her. But when Gothic envoys arrived and he
learned that their people had been converted to the Catholic faith, he promised her to them instead. He also sent an embassy to the emperor so that, having
previously failed to act, he might now make war with imperial counsel and expel the Lombards from Italy. He likewise sent his own army to invade that region.
The commanders advanced with the army and battle was joined. My men were severely slaughtered: many fell, some were captured, and very many escaped by flight
and scarcely returned home. The destruction of the Frankish army was such that nothing like it is remembered from former times.

### 26. The death of Queen Ingoberg

**[026]** In King Childebert’s fourteenth year Queen Ingoberga, widow of the late Charibert, departed from this world. She was a very prudent woman endowed with
a religious life and diligent in vigils, prayers, and almsgiving. Admonished, I believe, by divine providence, she sent messengers to me so that I might assist
in carrying out her intentions for the remedy of her soul, on condition that I visit her and record in writing what she decided after taking counsel. I confess
that I went and found a woman who feared God. She received me kindly, called a notary, took counsel with me, and assigned certain property to the church of
Tours and Saint Martin’s basilica and other property to the church of Le Mans. A few months later she was worn down by sudden illness and departed this world,
leaving many people freed by written charters. She was, I think, in her seventieth year and left an only daughter, whom a son of a king in Kent took in
marriage.

### 27. The death of Amalo

**[027]** Duke Amalo sent his wife to another estate to attend to business and fell in love with a freeborn girl. One night, drunk with wine, he sent servants
to drag the girl to his bed. She resisted and was forcibly brought to his lodging. While they struck her, a stream of blood ran from her nostrils and covered
the duke’s bed. He beat her with fists, cuffs, and other blows, then took her in his arms and immediately fell asleep. Stretching her hand across the man’s
head, she found a sword, drew it, and struck the duke’s head with a manly blow, as Judith struck Holofernes. He cried out and the servants ran in. When they
wished to kill her, he exclaimed: ‘Do not, I beg you. I sinned by trying to violate her chastity. Let her who sought to preserve her purity by no means perish.’
With these words he died. While the assembled household lamented over him, the girl was rescued by God’s aid, left the house, and travelled by night to Chalon,
about thirty-five miles away. Entering Saint Marcellus’s basilica, she prostrated herself at the king’s feet and revealed all she had suffered. The most
merciful king not only spared her life but ordered a decree issued placing her under his protection so that none of the dead man’s relatives could ever molest
her. I learned that, by God’s gift, the girl’s chastity had not been violated in any way by the savage ravisher.

### 28. The gifts sent by Queen Brunhild

**[028]** Queen Brunhild ordered a wonderfully large shield made of gold and gems and sent it to the king in Spain together with two wooden dishes commonly
called bacchinons, likewise made with gems and gold. She sent Ebregisel, who had often gone to that region as an envoy. After his departure someone told King
Guntram that Queen Brunhild was sending gifts to Gundovald’s sons. Hearing this, the king ordered strict guards along the roads of his kingdom so that no one
could pass without examination. Men’s clothing, shoes, and other possessions were searched for hidden letters. Ebregisel arrived at Paris with these gifts and
was arrested by Duke Ebrecharius and brought before Guntram. The king said: ‘Most wretched of men, was it not enough that by shameful counsel you invited that
Ballomer you call Gundovald to a marriage, though my hand overcame him when he sought to surpass the power of my kingdom? Now you send gifts to his sons so that
you may again summon him to Gaul to be slaughtered. You shall not proceed where you wish but shall die, because your embassy is hostile to my people.’ Ebregisel
denied involvement in these matters and said the gifts were being sent to Reccared, who was to marry Childebert’s sister Clodosind. The king believed him and
released him, and he continued his appointed journey with the gifts.

### 29. The Lombards seek peace from King Childebert

**[029]** At the invitation of Sigismund, bishop of Momotiacum, King Childebert decided to celebrate Easter in that city. His elder son Theudebert was then
seriously afflicted by a swelling of the throat but recovered. Meanwhile Childebert assembled an army and prepared to go with it into Italy to attack the
Lombards. Hearing this, the Lombards sent envoys with gifts, saying: ‘Let there be friendship between us; let us not perish, and we shall pay a fixed tribute to
your authority. Wherever you need help against enemies, we shall not refuse it.’ Childebert sent envoys to King Guntram to communicate these offers. Guntram was
not opposed to this understanding and advised confirming peace. Childebert ordered the army to remain where it was and sent envoys to the Lombards so that, if
they confirmed their promises, the army could return home. But nothing was fulfilled.

### 30. The tax assessors at Poitiers and Tours

**[030]** At Bishop Maroveus’s invitation King Childebert sent assessors to Poitiers, namely Florentian, the queen’s major-domo, and Romulf, count of his
palace. The people were to render after reassessment the tax they had paid in his father’s time. Many taxpayers had died, and the burden had fallen upon widows,
orphans, and the infirm. Examining the rolls in order, they relieved the poor and infirm and subjected to public tax those whom justice made liable. They then
came to Tours. When they wished to impose taxation upon the people, saying they had a book showing how taxes had been paid under earlier kings, I replied: ‘It
is well known that Tours was assessed in King Chlothar’s time and that the books were taken to the king; but he was moved by fear of Bishop Saint Martin and
burned them. After Chlothar’s death this people swore allegiance to King Charibert, and he likewise promised on oath not to impose new laws and customs but to
maintain them in the condition in which they had lived under his father’s dominion, and promised no new ordinance despoiling them. Gaiso, count at that time,
obtained the capitulary which the earlier assessors were said to have made and began to exact tribute. Forbidden by Bishop Euphronius, he took the little he had
collected to the king and displayed the capitulary containing the tribute. The king sighed, feared Saint Martin’s power, and burned it. He sent the exacted gold
back to Saint Martin’s basilica, adjuring that no one of Tours should pay any public tribute. After his death King Sigibert held this city and imposed no
tribute. Now Childebert, reigning in the fourteenth year after his father’s death, has likewise exacted nothing, and this city has never groaned under any
burden of tribute. It is now within your power to assess tribute or not, but take care not to do harm if you intend to act contrary to his oath.’ They answered:
‘We have here a book in which tribute is imposed upon this people.’ I said: ‘This book was not brought from the king’s treasury and has had no force through so
many years. It is no wonder if it was kept in someone’s house through enmity towards these citizens. God has judged those who, after so long, produced it to
despoil our citizens.’ While this was happening, Audinus’s son, who had produced the book, was seized by fever that day and died on the third day. I then sent
messengers to the king to obtain his command. They immediately brought back an authoritative letter ordering that, in reverence for Saint Martin, the people of
Tours should not be assessed. The men sent for this purpose abandoned the matter and returned home.

### 31. King Guntram sends an army into Septimania

**[031]** King Guntram assembled an army for Septimania. Duke Austrovald first approached Carcassonne, received oaths, and subjected its people to royal
authority. The king sent Boso and Antestius to capture the other cities. Boso advanced arrogantly, despised and condemned Duke Austrovald for entering
Carcassonne without him, and directed there the men of Saintes, Périgueux, Bordeaux, Agen, and Toulouse. While he was borne along in this pride, the Goths were
informed and prepared an ambush. He pitched camp beside a small river near the city, sat down to feast, indulged in drunkenness, and heaped insults and
blasphemies upon the Goths. They rushed upon the army and found it feasting and unsuspecting. The soldiers shouted and rose against them. The Goths resisted
briefly, then pretended flight. As the Franks pursued, the men prepared in ambush rose, surrounded them, and slaughtered them almost to extermination. Those who
escaped scarcely got away on horseback, leaving all their equipment on the plain and taking none of their possessions, counting it enough if their lives were
spared. The pursuing Goths recovered and plundered all their property and carried off all the foot-soldiers captive. About five thousand men fell there, and
more than two thousand were captured, though many were later released and returned home.

### 32. The enmity between Childebert and Guntram

**[032]** The angered king ordered the roads of his kingdom closed so that no one from Childebert’s kingdom could pass through his territory, saying: ‘My army
has fallen through the wickedness of the man who made a treaty with the king of Spain, and his intervention causes those cities not to submit to my authority.’
Another fire of bitterness was added because King Childebert intended to send his elder son Theudebert to Soissons. This made Guntram suspicious, and he said:
‘My nephew is sending his son to Soissons so that he may enter Paris and seek to take my kingdom.’ Childebert could never, if it is right to say so, have
entertained such a thought. Guntram also cast many reproaches at Queen Brunhild, saying these things were done on her advice and adding that she wished to marry
the son of the late Gundovald after inviting him to wed. He therefore ordered a synod of bishops assembled on the Kalends of November. Many hastening from the
farthest parts of Gaul turned back on the road because Queen Brunhild cleared herself of this charge by oaths. The roads were then reopened and passage granted
to those wishing to go to King Childebert.

### 33. The religious woman Ingtrud goes to Childebert to accuse her daughter

**[033]** In those days Ingitrude, who had founded a monastery in Saint Martin’s courtyard, went to the king intending to accuse her daughter. Berthefled,
daughter of the late King Charibert, had been living in that monastery, but when she left, Ingitrude returned to Le Mans. She was devoted to gluttony and sleep
and took no care for God’s service. I think the affair of Ingitrude and her daughter should be traced from an earlier point. Some years before, when Ingitrude
began establishing a convent of women in Saint Martin’s courtyard, she sent word to her daughter: ‘Leave your husband and come, so that I may make you abbess
over the flock I have gathered.’ Hearing this foolish counsel, Berthegund came to Tours with her husband. Entering her mother’s monastery, she told him: ‘Go
back and govern our property and children, for I shall not return with you. One joined in marriage will not see God’s kingdom.’ Her husband came to me and
reported all she had said. I went to the monastery and read the decrees of the Nicene canons, which state: ‘If anyone leaves her husband and rejects the bed in
which she has lived well, saying that one joined in marriage has no share in the glory of the heavenly kingdom, let her be anathema.’ Hearing this, Berthegund
feared exclusion from communion by God’s bishops, left the monastery, and returned with her husband. Three or four years later her mother again sent for her and
begged her to come. Berthegund loaded ships with her own and her husband’s property and, taking one son, came to Tours in her husband’s absence. Her mother
could not keep her because of the husband’s accusations and wished not to incur the charge he had maliciously devised, so she sent her to her brother Bertram,
Ingitrude’s son and bishop of Bordeaux. When her husband followed, Bertram said: ‘You married her without her parents’ consent; she shall not be your wife.’
They had by then lived together for nearly thirty years. The husband often went to Bordeaux, but the bishop would not restore her. When King Guntram came to
Orléans, as I mentioned in the previous book, the husband attacked the bishop sharply, saying: ‘You took my wife with her servants. Committing an adulterous
disgrace unworthy of a bishop, you have been with my maidservants and she with your menservants.’ Enraged, the king pressed the bishop to promise to restore
her, saying: ‘She is my kinswoman. If she has done any wrong in her husband’s house, I shall punish her; otherwise why is the husband, reduced to every
humiliation, deprived of his wife?’ Bishop Bertram promised: ‘I confess that my sister came to me after many years and I kept her with me as I wished out of
charity and affection. She has now left me; let her husband seek her and take her where he wishes without opposition from me.’ But he secretly sent messengers
instructing her to change her clothing, accept penance, and seek Saint Martin’s basilica. She did so at once. Her husband came with many followers to remove her
from the holy place. She wore religious clothing and claimed to have accepted penance, but refused to follow her husband. When Bishop Bertram died at Bordeaux,
she returned to herself and said: ‘Woe to me for following my wicked mother’s counsel! My brother is dead; I am abandoned by my husband and separated from my
children. Where shall wretched I go, and what shall I do?’ Taking counsel, she went to Poitiers. Her mother wished to keep her but could not. Enmity arose, and
both frequently went before the king, the mother seeking to retain her father’s property and the daughter her husband’s. Berthegund produced a donation from her
brother Bertram, saying: ‘My brother granted me these things.’ Her mother rejected the donation and sought to claim everything. She sent men who broke into
Berthegund’s house and stole all her property together with the donation. The mother thus proved her own guilt when, under constraint, she later restored some
property to her daughter’s renewed claim. Although Maroveus and I repeatedly received royal letters requiring us to make peace, and Berthegund came to Tours and
appeared before the tribunal, I pressed her as far as possible to accept a settlement, but her mother could not be moved. Inflamed with gall, Ingitrude went to
the king intending to disinherit her daughter from her father’s property. She pleaded in the king’s presence in her daughter’s absence, and it was judged that a
fourth share should be restored to the daughter, while Ingitrude and her grandchildren by one son should receive three shares. The priest Theutharius, recently
converted from being King Sigibert’s referendary and admitted to the priesthood, came to carry out this division by royal command. But the daughter resisted,
and neither the division was made nor the scandal settled.

### 34. Fredegund’s enmity with her daughter

**[034]** Rigunthis, Chilperic’s daughter, often insulted her mother, saying that she herself was the mistress and her mother owed her service. She frequently
attacked her with reproaches, and they sometimes struck one another with fists and slaps. Her mother said: ‘Why do you trouble me, daughter? Here are your
father’s possessions in my custody; take them and use them as you wish.’ Entering the treasury, she opened a chest filled with necklaces and precious ornaments.
For a long time she took out various objects and handed them to her daughter standing beside her, then said: ‘I am tired. Put in your hand and take out what you
find.’ As Rigunthis put in her arm and drew things from the chest, her mother seized the lid and slammed it upon her neck. She pressed it down violently, and
the lower edge so crushed her throat that her eyes seemed ready to burst. One of the girls inside cried loudly: ‘Run, I beg you, run! My mistress is being
brutally choked by her mother!’ Those waiting outside the doors burst into the chamber and led the girl outside, rescued from imminent death. Afterwards enmity
grew still more violently between them, chiefly because Rigunthis pursued adulteries, and quarrels and blows were continual.

### 35. The death of Waddo

**[035]** When Beretrudis died she made her daughter her heir, leaving property to convents of women she had founded and to churches and basilicas of holy
confessors. Waddo, mentioned in the previous book, complained that his horses had been stolen by her son-in-law. He thought of going to an estate in Poitou
which Beretrudis had left her daughter, saying: ‘This man came from another king’s realm and stole my horses, and I shall take his estate.’ He sent word to the
steward to prepare everything needed for his arrival. Hearing this, the steward gathered the household and prepared for battle, saying: ‘Unless I die, Waddo
shall not enter my lord’s house.’ Waddo’s wife heard of these preparations and said: ‘Do not go there, dear husband; you will die, and I and the children will
be wretched.’ She tried to hold him back, and his son said: ‘If you go we shall die together, and you will leave my mother a widow and your other son
fatherless.’ When these words could not restrain him, he raged at his son, calling him cowardly and weak, and hurled an axe which nearly struck his brain; but
the boy moved aside and escaped. Waddo and his men mounted and departed, again instructing the steward to sweep the house and cover the benches with rugs.
Disregarding the command, the steward stood with crowds of men and women before his lord’s doors awaiting Waddo. Waddo came, immediately entered, and said: ‘Why
are these benches not covered with rugs and the house not swept?’ Raising his hand with a dagger, he struck the steward’s head; he fell dead. The dead man’s son
hurled a lance from opposite at Waddo; it pierced his belly and came out through his back. As Waddo fell, the assembled crowd began to overwhelm his party with
stones. Some of his companions approached through the showers of stones, covered him with a cloak, calmed the people while his son lamented, lifted him still
living onto a horse, and brought him home. He immediately died amid his wife’s and sons’ tears. After this miserable end his son went to the king and obtained
his property.

### 36. Childebert sends his son Theudebert to Soissons

**[036]** In the year of his reign mentioned above King Childebert stayed with his wife and mother in the territory of Strasbourg. The leading men of Soissons
and Meaux came to him and said: ‘Give us one of your sons to serve, so that, keeping a pledge of your stock with us, we may more easily resist your enemies and
defend your cities’ frontiers.’ Delighted, he resolved to send his elder son Theudebert. He assigned counts, household officers, major-domos, nurses, and all
necessary for royal service, and sent him in the sixth month as the men had requested. The people received him joyfully and prayed that divine goodness would
grant longer life to him and his father.

### 37. Bishop Droctegisil

**[037]** Droctigisel was bishop of Soissons in those days. In the fourth year of an illness caused, it is said, by excessive drinking, he lost his reason. Many
citizens asserted that this had been brought upon him by sorcery through the agency of an archdeacon whom he had removed from office. His madness was worse
within the city walls, but when he left the city he was better. When King Childebert came to the city and Droctigisel was better, he was not permitted to enter
because the king had arrived. Although he was gluttonous and drank wine immoderately, unbecoming episcopal restraint, no one ever accused him of adultery.
Afterwards, when a synod of bishops assembled at the estate of Sauriciacum, it was decreed that he might enter his own city.

### 38. The plot against Brunhild

**[038]** When Queen Faileuba, Childebert’s wife, was ill after bearing a child which soon died, word reached her that certain men were plotting against her and
Queen Brunhild. When she recovered and came before the king, she revealed to him and his mother everything she had heard. The report was that Septimina, nurse
of his infants, wished to persuade the king to cast off his mother, abandon his wife, and take another, after which they could do whatever they wished with him
or obtain by requests. If the king refused her advice, they would kill him by sorcery, elevate his sons to the throne, expel their mother and grandmother, and
govern the kingdom themselves. She named as associates Sunnegisel, count of the stable, Gallomagnus the referendary, and Droctulf, who had been assigned to
assist Septimina in nursing the king’s little children. Septimina and Droctulf were arrested, stretched between stakes, and severely beaten. Septimina confessed
that she had killed her husband Jovius by sorcery for love of Droctulf and committed adultery with him. They confessed the charges mentioned above and named the
men as participants in the plot. Those men were sought but, terrified by conscience, sought hiding within church precincts. The king himself went to them and
said: ‘Come out for judgment, so that we may learn whether the charges against you are true or false. I do not think you would have fled into this church unless
your consciences terrified you. Nevertheless, you have a promise of life even if found guilty. We are Christians, and it would be wrong for a criminal brought
out of church to be punished.’ They came out and accompanied the king to judgment. Questioned, they protested: ‘Septimina and Droctulf revealed this plot to us,
but we abhorred and shunned it and would never consent to the crime.’ The king said: ‘If you gave no consent, you would certainly have brought it to our ears.
Is it then true that you consented, since you wished to hide it from my knowledge?’ They were immediately expelled and again sought the church. Septimina and
Droctulf were severely beaten and wounded on the face with hot cauteries. Deprived of all her property, Septimina was taken to the estate of Marilegio to turn a
mill and prepare flour daily for the needs of those in the royal kitchen. Droctulf’s hair and ears were cut off and he was sent to cultivate a vineyard, but
escaped after a few days. Recaptured by the steward and brought again to the king, he was severely beaten and sent back to the vineyard. Sunnegisel and
Gallomagnus were deprived of property acquired from the fisc and driven into exile. Envoys including bishops came from King Guntram and pleaded for them, and
they were recalled but left with nothing except what appeared to be their own property.

### 39. The scandal in the convent of Poitiers stirred up by Chrodield and Basina

**[039]** In the monastery at Poitiers the devil sowed rebellion in the heart of Chrodield, who claimed to be a daughter of the late King Charibert. Trusting in
royal ancestry, she exacted oaths from the nuns that they would bring charges against Abbess Leubovera, expel her, and put Chrodield in her place. She then left
with forty or more women and her cousin Basina, Chilperic’s daughter, saying: ‘I am going to my royal kinsmen to make my disgrace known, for we are humiliated
here not as kings’ daughters but as children of wretched maidservants.’ Unhappy and fickle, she forgot the humility shown by blessed Radegund, who founded the
monastery. Coming to Tours, she greeted me and said: ‘Holy bishop, deign to shelter and feed these women, reduced to great humiliation by the abbess of
Poitiers, while I go to my royal kinsmen, report our sufferings, and return.’ I answered: ‘If the abbess has offended or violated the canonical rule, let us go
to my brother Bishop Maroveus and jointly charge her. When matters have been corrected, you shall return to your monastery, lest the community which holy
Radegund gathered by fasts, prayers, and frequent alms be scattered in wantonness.’ She replied: ‘No; we shall go to the kings.’ I said: ‘Why do you resist
reason and refuse episcopal counsel? I fear the assembled bishops will exclude you from communion.’ This is contained in the letter my predecessors wrote to
blessed Radegund at the foundation of her congregation, whose text I have decided to insert here.

COPY OF THE LETTER. To the most blessed lady Radegund, daughter of the Church in Christ, from Bishops Euphronius, Praetextatus, Germanus, Felix, Domitian,
Victorius, and Domnolus. The remedies of immense divinity are continually solicitous for the human race and never seem separated in any place or time from the
constancy of their benefits, since the merciful ruler of things everywhere scatters such persons into the inheritance of ecclesiastical cultivation that,
tilling His field with the rake of faith in intent labour, Christ’s crop may reach a happy hundredfold yield through divine moderation. His beneficent
dispensation spreads so widely for future profit that He nowhere denies what He knows benefits many; by their most holy example He may have much to crown when
He comes in judgment. When with the dawn of Catholic religion the beginnings of venerable faith first breathed in Gaul and the ineffable mysteries of the divine
Trinity had then reached the knowledge of only a few, God deigned to send blessed Martin, of foreign stock, to enlighten this country, consulting its mercy,
lest it acquire less than the circle of cities obtained through apostolic preaching. Though Martin did not live in the apostles’ time, he did not lack apostolic
grace: what was absent in order was supplied in reward, for subsequent rank takes nothing from one who excels in merit. I congratulate you, most reverend
daughter, that examples of heavenly love rise again in you by divine favour. As worldly time declines in age, faith flourishes anew through the contest of your
mind, and what had grown lukewarm in the cold lethargy of old age now burns again with ardent spirit. Since you came from almost the same region from which
blessed Martin came here, it is no wonder that you imitate in works the man I believe guided your journey. Following his footsteps, fulfil his examples with a
happy vow, and make the most blessed man your companion in proportion as you flee association with the world. By the shining ray of his teaching you fill your
hearers’ hearts with heavenly light, so that women’s minds, kindled by divine fire, hasten eagerly to be watered from the fountain of your breast in Christ’s
charity. Abandoning their parents, they choose you as a mother made by grace rather than nature. Seeing the vows of this zeal, we thank heavenly clemency, who
joins human wills to His own, for we trust that He wishes to keep in His embrace those He commands to be gathered with you. Since we learn that by divine favour
some women from our territories have eagerly come to be instructed in your rule, and having willingly received your letter of petition, we establish this with
Christ as author and healer. Although all assembled there in the Lord’s charity must inviolably preserve what they once freely accepted—for it is wrong to
defile faith promised to Christ with heaven as witness, and no light crime to pollute God’s temple and be destroyed by His anger—we specially decree that if any
woman from places committed to our episcopal government by the Lord is admitted to your monastery at Poitiers, she shall have no further permission to depart,
according to the constitutions of Lord Caesarius of Arles of blessed memory. Having entered by a declared will according to the rule, she must remain, lest one
woman’s shameful disgrace bring crime upon what shines in honour among all. Therefore, if—God forbid—any woman, inflamed by insane enticement, wishes to cast
her discipline, glory, and crown into the stain of such disgrace and, like Eve cast from paradise by the enemy’s counsel, endures leaving the monastery’s
enclosure—indeed the kingdom of heaven—let her be plunged and trampled in the vile mud of the streets, separated from my communion, and struck by the wound of
dread anathema. If, abandoning Christ and captured by the devil, she wishes to marry a man, not only she who flees but also the man who joins her, a foul
adulterer and sacrilegious rather than husband, and whoever supplies poison rather than counsel for this, shall be struck by the same vengeance in heavenly
judgment at my desire, until, after separation and fitting penance for the execrable crime, she merits to be received back and rejoined to the place from which
she departed. I add that bishops who succeed me shall be bound by the guilt of similar condemnation if—which I do not believe—they relax anything contrary to
this decision. Let them know that they will plead with me before the eternal Judge, for instruction in common salvation requires inviolable observance of what
is promised to Christ. I have thought fit to strengthen this decree of my determination by my own signatures, to be perpetually observed by me under Christ’s
guidance.

When this letter was read, Chrodield said: ‘No delay shall ever detain us until we go to the kings whom we know to be our kinsmen.’ They had come on foot from
Poitiers without the use of any horse and were weary and very weak. No one had provided them food on the journey. They reached my city on the first day of the
first month amid great rains, and the roads were dissolved by the immense quantity of water.

### 40. The origin of the first scandal

**[040]** They also disparaged the bishop, saying that the women had been disturbed and the monastery abandoned through his deceit, but I have decided to trace
the origin of this scandal further back. When blessed Radegund founded this monastery in King Chlothar’s time, she and her whole congregation were always
subject and obedient to the earlier bishops. In Sigibert’s time, after Maroveus obtained the city’s bishopric, blessed Radegund received letters from King
Sigibert and, because of her faith and devotion, sent clerics to the East for wood of the Lord’s cross and relics of the holy apostles and other martyrs. They
brought back these sacred pledges. The queen asked the bishop to deposit them in the monastery with due honour and great psalmody. Despising her request, he
mounted his horse and went to his estate. The queen again wrote to King Sigibert, begging him to command some bishop to place these pledges in the monastery
with the honour and ceremony she desired. Blessed Euphronius, bishop of Tours, was assigned the task. Coming to Poitiers with his clerics, he brought the holy
pledges into the monastery in the local bishop’s absence with a great company of psalm-singers, shining candles, and incense. Afterwards Radegund repeatedly
sought her bishop’s favour without obtaining it. Necessity therefore drove her and the abbess she had appointed to Arles. Having received there the rule of
Saint Caesarius and blessed Caesaria, they secured the kings’ protection because they could find no care for their defence in the man who ought to have been
their pastor. Scandal grew daily until blessed Radegund’s death. After her death the abbess again asked to live under her own bishop’s authority. Though at
first he wished to refuse, on his advisers’ counsel he promised to be their father as was fitting and defend them when necessary. He therefore obtained a
command from King Childebert permitting him to govern this monastery canonically like his other parishes. But something, I believe, still remained in their
minds which, as these women assert, stirred up scandal. While they prepared to hasten before the kings, I advised them: ‘Your intention is unreasonable, and no
account can be inserted into it which removes the scandal. But if you reject reason and refuse salutary counsel, at least consider waiting until this winter,
now approaching spring, has passed and the weather is more favourable before going where you wish.’ Basina accepted this advice. In the following summer she
left the others at Tours, entrusted the nuns to her cousin Chrodield, and went to King Guntram. Received and honoured with gifts, she returned to Tours, leaving
Constantina, Burgolin’s daughter, in the monastery at Autun, and awaited the bishops whom the king had ordered to hear their case against the abbess. Meanwhile
many of the women were overcome by various suitors and married before Basina returned from the king. When the waiting women perceived that no bishop came, they
returned to Poitiers and took refuge in Saint Hilary’s basilica. Gathering thieves, murderers, adulterers, and men guilty of every crime, they prepared for
battle, saying: ‘We are queens and shall not enter our monastery until the abbess is expelled.’ A certain recluse was there who a few years earlier had thrown
herself over the wall and fled to Saint Hilary’s basilica, uttering many charges against the abbess which I knew to be false. After she was drawn back into the
monastery by ropes at the place where she had jumped, she asked to be enclosed in a private cell, saying: ‘I have greatly sinned against the Lord and my lady
Radegund,’ who was still alive then. ‘I wish to withdraw from the whole congregation’s company and do penance for my negligence. I know the Lord is merciful and
forgives those who confess their sins.’ She entered a cell. When this revolt arose and Chrodield returned from King Guntram, the recluse broke the cell door at
night, left the monastery, and went to Chrodield, again uttering many charges against the abbess as before.

### 41. The bloodshed in Saint Hilary’s church

**[041]** While this was happening, Gundegisil of Bordeaux, joined by Nicasius of Eauze, Saffarius of Périgueux, and Maroveus of Poitiers because Bordeaux was
the city’s metropolitan see, came to Saint Hilary’s basilica to rebuke the women and return them to the monastery. They obstinately resisted, and when
Gundegisil and the others pronounced excommunication according to the letter quoted above, the crowd of criminals arose and inflicted such slaughter within
Saint Hilary’s basilica that the bishops fell upon the pavement and could scarcely rise. The deacons and other clerics left the basilica covered in blood with
broken heads. So immense a terror, aided I believe by the devil, seized them that they left the holy place without saying farewell and each returned by whatever
road he could. Desiderius, a deacon of Bishop Siagrius of Autun, was also involved in this calamity. Without seeking a ford in the Clain, he entered where he
first reached the bank and, his horse swimming, was carried to the field on the farther bank. Chrodield then appointed managers, seized the monastery’s estates,
and subjected to her service anyone from the monastery she could capture, beating and striking them. She threatened that if she could enter the monastery she
would throw the abbess from the wall. When this was reported to King Childebert, he immediately sent an order to Count Macco to suppress it with all
determination. After Gundegisil and the other bishops had suspended the women from communion, he wrote in his own and his companions’ names to the bishops then
assembled with King Guntram. He received this reply:

COPY OF THE REPLY. To their always honoured lords, most worthy of the apostolic see, Gundegisil, Nicasius, and Saffarius, from Bishops Aetherius, Siagrius,
Aunacharius, Isychius, Agricola, Urbicus, Felix, Veranus, another Felix, and Bertram. As greatly as we rejoiced at your safety when the messenger opened your
holiness’s letter, so greatly are we grieved by the injury you report suffering, since the rule is transgressed and no reverence shown to religion. You report
that the nuns who left blessed Radegund’s monastery at the devil’s instigation would hear no correction from you or return within its enclosure, and moreover
inflicted injury upon Lord Hilary’s basilica by attacking you and your men, for which you suspended them from communion and chose to consult my humble selves.
Since I know you have examined the excellent canonical decrees and possess the fullness of the rule, so that those detected in such excesses deserve not only
excommunication but penitential satisfaction, I declare with reverence and eager charity that I agree with your sentence, until I may consider together at the
synodal council on the Kalends of November how such rashness may receive the bridle of discipline, so that none may afterwards delight in committing similar
offences through pride. Yet because the Lord’s Apostle Paul continually admonishes me to correct transgressors by assiduous preaching ‘in season and out of
season’ and declares piety useful for all things, I suggest that you continue earnestly imploring the Lord’s mercy, that He may kindle them with a spirit of
compunction so that they may make worthy satisfaction for their offence and return to their monastery through your preaching, with Christ’s favour, as souls in
some manner lost. May He who carried one straying sheep upon His shoulders back to the fold deign to rejoice over these women’s return as over a recovered
flock. I specially ask that you continually grant me the support of your intercessions, as I trust. Your own Aetherius, a sinner, presumes to greet you. Your
client Isychius reverently dares to greet you. Your lover Siagrius reverently greets you. Your worshipper Urbicus, a sinner, greets you as a servant. Your
venerator Bishop Veranus reverently greets you. Your servant Felix presumes to greet you. Your humble lover Felix dares to greet you. Your humble and obedient
Bishop Bertram presumes to greet you.

### 42. Copy of the letter sent by Saint Radegund

**[042]** The abbess also recited the letter which blessed Radegund had wished to send to the bishops of her time, and now sent copies again to the bishops of
neighbouring cities. Its text is as follows:

COPY OF THE LETTER. To the holy lords and fathers in Christ, most worthy of the apostolic see, all the bishops, from Radegund, a sinner. The beginning of
fitting provision advances effectively when a cause is entrusted to the ears and understanding of the universal fathers, physicians, and pastors of the flock
committed to them; their participation can furnish counsel through charity, support through authority, and intervention through prayer. Long ago freed from lay
bonds by divine providence and inspiration, I seemed voluntarily brought under the rule of religion with Christ as leader. Considering with eager mind the
progress of other women, so that with the Lord’s favour my desires might benefit others, I founded a convent of women at Poitiers under the institution and
generosity of the most excellent lord King Chlothar and endowed it by donation with all that royal munificence granted me. I also adopted for the congregation
gathered through me by Christ’s gift the rule under which holy Caesaria lived, which blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, fittingly compiled from the holy
fathers’ institutions. With the consent of the most blessed bishops of this and other cities and by my congregation’s election, I appointed my lady and sister
Agnes as abbess. I had cherished and educated her from childhood as a daughter and committed myself after God to obey her direction according to the rule.
Observing apostolic form, the sisters and I transferred to her by written deeds the earthly substance we appeared to possess, reserving nothing as our own in
the monastery for fear of Ananias and Sapphira. Because human conditions and times are uncertain and the world hastens to its end, when some desire to serve
their own rather than the divine will, I, moved by zeal for God, offer this petition in Christ’s name to the merit of your apostolic office. Unable to be
present, I prostrate myself by this letter’s proxy as though at your feet, adjuring you by Father, Son, Holy Spirit, and the dreadful Day of Judgment—so
presented, may no tyrant attack you but a lawful king crown you—that if after my death any person, the local bishop, a prince’s authority, or anyone else should
attempt, which I do not believe, to disturb the congregation by evil persuasion or judicial pressure, break the rule, appoint an abbess other than my sister
Agnes whom blessed Germanus’s blessing consecrated in the presence of his brothers, or if the congregation itself should attempt by murmuring to change her, or
if any person or local bishop should seek by new privilege any dominion over the monastery or its property beyond that held by my episcopal predecessors or
others during my lifetime, or anyone attempt to depart contrary to the rule; or if any prince, bishop, powerful man, or sister of any rank should sacrilegiously
attempt to diminish or appropriate property granted me by the most excellent Lord Chlothar or his most excellent royal sons and transferred by me with his
permission to the monastery’s possession, confirmed by the most excellent Kings Charibert, Guntram, Chilperic, and Sigibert with oaths and their own signatures,
or property given by others for their souls’ remedy or by the sisters from their own possessions—then may your holiness and your successors after God so act at
my supplication and by Christ’s will that such persons be held outside your grace as robbers and despoilers of the poor, and with your opposition may never
diminish or change anything in my rule or the monastery’s property. I further ask that when God calls my sister Agnes from this world, she whom God and Agnes
choose from my congregation, keeping the rule and diminishing nothing of its holy purpose, be ordained abbess in her place; let neither her own nor anyone’s
arbitrary will prevail. If—God forbid—anyone acts against these conditions commended to you before the Lord and His saints, contrary to God’s command and the
kings’ authority, or seeks to diminish Agnes’s person or substance or trouble my sister Abbess Agnes, may he incur the judgment of God, the Holy Cross, and
blessed Mary, and have the blessed confessors Hilary and Martin, to whom after God I committed my sisters’ defence, as opponents and persecutors. And you,
blessed bishop, and your successors, whom I diligently adopt as patrons in God’s cause, if anyone—God forbid—attempts anything against these provisions, do not
hesitate to hasten to the king who then rules this place or to Poitiers for the cause commended to you before the Lord. Labour as executors against others’
injustice and defenders of justice, so that the Catholic king permits no such crime in his times and does not allow what has been established by God’s, my, and
the kings’ will to be overturned. I likewise adjure the princes whom God commands to survive me for the people’s government, by the King ‘whose kingdom shall
have no end’ and at whose nod kingdoms stand, who granted them life and rule, to order the monastery which I am seen to have founded, canonically organized, and
endowed with the permission and support of their royal fathers or grandfathers to be governed under their protection and direction together with Abbess Agnes.
Let them permit no one to molest my abbess or anything belonging to my monastery, nor to diminish or change it. Rather, for God’s sake and at my supplication
before the Redeemer of nations, let them together with the lord bishops defend and protect it as I commend, so that in honour of Him whose handmaids they
protect they may be joined eternally in the everlasting kingdom with the Defender of the poor and Bridegroom of virgins. I also adjure you holy bishops, most
excellent lord kings, and all Christian people by the Catholic faith in which you were baptized and preserve the churches, that in the basilica I began building
in honour of Saint Mary, the Lord’s Mother, where many of my sisters are laid to rest, whether completed or unfinished, my body be buried when God commands me
to depart this light. If anyone wishes or attempts otherwise, may he incur divine vengeance through the victory of Christ’s cross and blessed Mary, and through
your intervention may I merit a burial place in that basilica with my sisters’ congregation. With tears I pray that this my petition, signed with my own hand,
be kept in the universal Church’s archive, so that if necessity arises against wicked men, your defence and merciful consolation may supply my sister Abbess
Agnes and her congregation with pastoral help wherever they ask aid, and those for whom God prepared your grace’s protection may not despair of being abandoned
by me. Recalling all this before your eyes, by Him who from the cross commended the glorious Virgin His mother to blessed John the Apostle, I ask that, as John
fulfilled the Lord’s command, so may my unworthy and humble charge be fulfilled by my lords the Church’s fathers and apostolic men. When you worthily preserve
this deposit, you shall worthily show apostolic example and share in the merit of Him whose command you fulfil.

### 43. Theuthar comes to settle the scandal

**[043]** Afterwards Bishop Maroveus, hearing various reproaches from the women, sent Porcarius, abbot of Saint Hilary’s basilica, to Bishop Gundegisil and his
other provincial bishops, asking them to grant the women communion and permission to come to a hearing. He obtained nothing. King Childebert, continually
troubled by both the monastery and the women who had left, sent the priest Theutharius to settle their disputes. When he summoned Chrodield and the other women
to a hearing, they said: ‘We shall not come because we are suspended from communion. If we are reconciled, we shall not delay attending.’ Hearing this, he went
to the bishops, but after discussing the matter obtained no decision on their communion and returned to Poitiers. The women separated: some went to relatives,
some to their own houses, and some returned to their former monasteries, because together they could not endure the severe winter for lack of firewood. Only a
few remained with Chrodield and Basina, between whom there was also great discord because each wished to take precedence over the other.

### 44. The weather of the present year

**[044]** After Easter that year such immense rain with hail fell that within two or three hours great rivers were seen running even through the smaller
valleys’ channels. Trees flowered in autumn and produced fruit a second time. Roses appeared in the ninth month. Rivers rose immoderately, overflowed their
banks, covered places they had never reached, and caused no small damage to the crops.

# LATIN TEXT

---

*IN CHRISTI NOMINE INCIPIT LIBER VIIII. IN ANNO XII. CHILDEBERTHI REGES.*

## 1. De Richaredo et legatis eius.

**[001]** Igitur post mortem Leuvigilde Hispanorum regis Richaredus, filius eius, foedus iniit cum Goesintha, relicta patris sui, eamque ut matrem suscepit.
Haec enim erat mater Brunechildis reginae, matris Childeberthi iunioris. Richaredus vero de alia uxore erat filius Leuvigildi. Denique, cum noverca habitu
consilio, legatus ad Gunthramno rege adque ad Childebertum dirigit, dicens: 'Pacem habete nobiscum, et ineamus foedus, ut adiutus praesidio vestro, cum
necessitas poposcerit, simile nos condicione, intercedente caritate, muniamus'. Venientes vero legati, qui ad Guntchramnum regem directi erant, apud Matascensem
oppidum iussi sunt residere, ibique, transmissis viris, rex causas cognovit, sed recipere noluit verba eorum. Unde talis postmodum inter eos inimicitia
pullulavit, ut ad civitates Septemaniae nullum de regno eius transire permitterent. Hi vero qui ad Childeberthum regem venerunt cum caritate recepti sunt,
datisque muneribus, accepta pace, cum muneribus sunt regressi.

## 2. De obito beatae Radegundae.

**[002]** Eo anno beatissima Radegundis ab hoc mundo migravit. Quae magnum planctum in monasterio, quem constituerat, dereliquid. Fuique et ego praesens ad eam
sepiliendam. Obiit autem mense sexto, tertia decima die mensis, sepulta post triduum. Quae autem ibi ipsa die virtutes apparuerunt, vel qualiter fuerit
funerata, in libro Miraculorum plenius scribere studui.

## 3. De eo, qui cum cultro ad Gunthchramno rege venit.

**[003]** Interia advenit festivitas sancti Marcelli, quae apud urbem Cavillonensim mense septimo caelebratur, et Gunthchramnus rex adfuit. Verum ubi, peracta
solemnia, ad sacrosanctum altarium communicandi gratia accessisset, venit quidam quasi aliquid suggesturus. Qui dum properat contra regem, cultei ei de manu
dilabitur; adpraehensumque repente, alium cultrum evaginatum in manu eius repperierunt. Nec mora, eductus a basilica sancta, vinctus et tormentis addictus,
confitetur se emissum ad interficiendum regem, dicens: 'Sic enim tractavit, qui me misit, quia: „Cognovit rex multorum in se odia adgregata, et suspectus, ne
percutiatur, omnino se a suis vallari praecipit; nec repperitur aditus, qualiter ad eum cum gladiis possimus accedere, nisi in aeclesia, in qua securus et nihil
metuens stare denuscitur, verberitur"'. Sed et his de quibus locutus fuit adpraehensis, multis interemptis, hunc verberatum plagis demisit vivum, quia nefas
potavit, si his qui ab eclesia eductus fuerat truncaretur.

## 4. Quod Childebertho alius natus est filius.

**[004]** Eo anno Childebertho rege alius filius natus est, quem Veranus Cavelonensis episcopus suscipiens a lavacro, Theodorici nomen inposuit. Erat enim eo
tempore ipsi pontifex magnis virtutibus praeditus, ita ut plerumque infirmis signum crucis inponens, statim sanitate, tribuenti Domino, restauraret.

## 5. De prodigiis.

**[005]** Prodigia quoque multa dehinc apparuerunt. Nam vasa per domus diversorum signis, nescio quibus, caraxata sunt, quae res nullo umquam modo aut eradi
potuit aut deleri. Inceptum est autem hoc prodigium ab urbis Carnotinae territurio; et veniens per Aurilianensem, usque Burdegalensem terminum peraccessit, non
praetermittens ullam urbem, quae fuit in medio. In vineis vero mense octavo, transacta vindimia, palmites novos cum uvis deformatis aspeximus. In aliis
arboribus frondes novi et nova visa sunt poma. Radii a parte aquilonis apparuerunt. Adserebant nonnulli, vidisse se serpentes ex nube delapsos. Alii
adfirmabant, villam cum casis et hominibus subitania internicione evanuisse. Et multa alia signa apparuerunt, quae aut regis obitum adnunciare solent aut
regiones excidium. Vindimia eo anno tenuis, aquae validae, pluviae inmensae, flumina quoque granditer adaucta fuerunt.

## 6. De seductoribus et ariolis.

**[006]** Fuit eo anno in urbe Thoronica Desiderius nomine, qui se magnum quendam esse dicebat, adserens se multa posse facere signa. Nam et nuntius inter se
atque Petrum Paulumque apostolos discurrere iactitabat. Ad quem, quia praesens non eram, rusticitas populi multa confluxerat, deferentes secum caecos et
debiles, quos non sanctitate sanare, sed errore nigromantici ingenii quaerebat inludere. Nam hos, qui erant paralitici aut alia inpediti debilitate, iubebat
valide extendi, ut, quos virtutis divinae largitione diregere non poterat, quasi per industriam restauraret. Denique adpraehendebant pueri eius manus hominis,
alii vero pedes, tractumque diversis in partibus, ita ut nervi potarentur abrumpi, cum non sanarentur, demittebantur exanimis. Unde factum est, ut in hoc
supplicio multi spiritum exalarent. Tantoque miser elatus erat, ut iuniorem sibi beatum Martinum esse diceret, se vero apostolis coaequaret. Nec mirum, si hic
similem se dicat apostolis, cum ille auctor nequitiae, a quo ista procedunt, Christum se esse in fine saeculi fateatur. Nam de hoc animadversum est, ut superius
diximus, errore nigromantiae artis fuisse inbutum, quia, ut adserunt qui eum viderunt, cum quisque de eo procul et abditae quicquam locutus fuisset mali, coram
populo adstante inproperabat, dicens, quia: 'Hoc et illud de me effatus es, quae sanctitate meae erant indigna'. Et quid aliud nisi nuntiantibus daemoniis
cognoscebat? Habebat autem cucullam ac tonicam de pilis caprarum, et in praesente quidem abstinens erat a cybis et potu, clam autem, cum in diversurio venisset,
ita infercibat in ore, ut minister non occurrerit tantum poscenti porregere. Sed detecta dolositas eius et a nostris depraehensa, eiectus est extra urbis
terminum. Nec cognovimus deinceps, quo abisset; dicebat tamen civem se esse Burdegalensem. Nam et ante hos septem annos fuit et alius valde seductur, qui multos
decepit dolositate sua. Hic enim colobio indutus erat, amictus desuper sindonem, crucem ferens, de qua dependebant ampullulae, quas dicebat oleum sanctum
habere. Aiebat enim se de Hispaniis adventare ac reliquias beatissimorum martyrum Vincenti levitae Felicisque martyris exhibere. Sed cum iam vespere ad
basilicam sancti Martini Thoronus advenisset et nos convivio resederemus, mandatum misit, dicens: 'Occurrant reliquiis sanctis'. Cui nos, quia hora iam
praeterierat, dixemus: 'Requiescant beatae reliquiae super altarium, donec mane procedemus ad occursum earum'. Sed hic primum diluculo consurgens, nec
expectatis nobis, advenit cum cruce sua et in cellola nostra adfuit. Stupefactus ego et admirans levitatem, interrogo, quid sibi haec vellent. Respondit quasi
superbus et inflata voce: 'Meliorem', inquid, 'occursum nobis exhibere debueras. Sed haec ego in auribus Chilperici reges ingeram; ille autem ulciscitur
dispectionem meam'. Et ingressus in oraturio, me postposito, ipse capitellum unum adque alterum ac tertium dicit, ipse orationem profert et ipse consumat,
elevataque iterum cruce, abiit. Erat enim ei et sermo rusticus et ipsius linguae latitudo turpis atque obscoena; sed nec de eo sermo rationabilis procedebat.
Qui usque Pariseus accessit. His enim diebus rogationes publicae caelebrabantur, quae ante sanctum dominicae ascensiones diem agi solent. Factum est autem, ut,
procedente Ragnemodo pontifice cum populo suo et loca sancta circumeunte, ut et hic cum cruce sua adveniens, inusitato populis exhibens indumento, adiunctis
publicanis ac rusticis mulieribus, et iste chorum suum faceret, et quasi cum sua multitudine loca sancta circuire temptat. Haec cernens episcopus, misit
archidiaconum, dicens: 'Si reliquias sanctorum exhibes, pone eas paululum in basilica et nobiscum caelebra dies sanctos; decursa autem sollemnitatem,
profecisceris in viam tuam'. At ille parvi pendens, quae ab archidiaconum dicebantur, coepit episcopum conviciis ac maledictionibus prosequi. Sacerdos vero
intellegens eum seductorem, iussit eum recludi in cellolam. Perscrutatisque cunctis quae habebat, invenit cum eo sacculum magnum plenum de radicibus diversarum
herbarum, ibique et dentes talpae et ossa murium et ungues atque adipes ursinos. Vidensque haec maleficia esse, cuncta iussit in flumine proici; ablataque ei
cruce, iussit eum a termino Parisiacae urbis excludi. Sed hic iterum, facta sibi altera cruce, coepit quae prius gesserat exercere; captusque ab archidiacono et
catenis vinctus, iussus est costodire. His diebus Parisius adveneram et ad basilicam beati Iuliani marthyris metatum habebam. Nocte igitur insequenti erumpens
miser iste de custodia, cum ipsis quibus erat nexus catenis ad antedictam basilicam sancti Iuliani properat atque in pavimento, in loco quo ego stare eram
solitus, ruit ac sopore vinoque obpressus obdormivit. Nos vero ignari facto, media surgentes nocte ad reddendas? Domino gratias, invenimus eum dormientem. De
quo tantus fetor egrediebatur, ut omnium cloacarum adque secessorum fetores fetor ille devinceret. Sed nec nos prae hoc fetore in basilicam ingredi potueramus.
Accedens vero unus clericorum, clausis naribus, eum excitare nititur nec potuit; ita enim erat miser madefactus vino. Tunc quattuor accedentes clerici, levantes
eum inter manus, in uno angulo basilicae proiecerunt; et exhibentes aquas, abluto pavimento, resperso etiam herbolis odoratis, sic ingressi sumus explere
cursum. Numquam tamen nobis psallentibus potuit excitare, donec, dato terris diae, altius solis lampas ascenderet. Dehinc excusatum reddidi sacerdotem.
Convenientibus autem episcopis apud urbem Parisiacam, dum haec in convivio narravimus, ipsum pro castigationis gratia adesse praecipimus. Quo adstante, elevatis
Amelius Beorretanae urbis episcopus oculis, cognoscit eum suum esse famulum sibique per fugam dilapsum; et sic excusatum receptum reduxit in patriam. Multi enim
sunt, qui, has seductiones exercentes, populum rusticum in errore ponere non desistunt, de quibus, ut opinor, et Dominus in euangelio ait, consurgere in
novissimis temporibus pseudochristus et pseudoprophetas, qui, dantes signa et prodigia, etiam electos in errore inducant. De his ista sufficiant; nos potius ad
propositum rediamus.

## 7. De remotione Ennodi ducis et de Wasconibus.

**[007]** Ennodius cum ducatum urbium Thoronicae atque Pectavae ministraret, adhuc et Vice Iuliensis atque Benarnae urbium principatum accipit. Sed euntibus
comitibus Thoronicae atque Pectavae urbis ad regem Childeberthum, obtenuerunt, eum a se removere. Ille vero, ubi se remotum de his sensit, ad civitates superius
memoratas properat; sed dum in illis commoraretur, mandatum accepit, ut se ab eisdem removerit; et sic accepto otio, ad domum suam reversus, privati operis
curam gerit. Wascones vero de montibus prorumpentes, in plana descendunt, vineas agrosque depopulantes, domus tradentes incendio, nonnullus abducentes captivos
cum pecoribus. Contra quos saepius Austrovaldus dux processit, sed parvam ultionem exegit ab eis. Gothi vero propter superiores anni devastationem, quam in
Septimaniam regis Gunthramni exercitus fecit, in Arelatense provinciam proruperunt, egeruntque praedas atque captivos abduxerunt usque decimo ab urbe miliario.
Unum etiam castro Ugernum nomen cum rebus atque habitatoribus desolantes, nullo resistenti, regressi sunt.

## 8. De praesentia Gunthchramni Bosonis.

**[008]** Gunthchramnus vero Boso, cum exosus reginae haberetur, coepit per episcopus ac proceres discurrere et veniam sero praecare, quam ante dispexerat. Nam
cum rex Childeberthus esset iunior, Brunechildem reginam saepe conviciis atque inproperiis lacessibat; sed et iniuriis, quae ei ab adversis inferebantur, fautor
exteterat. Sed et rex ad ulciscendam iniuriam genetricis iussit eum persequi atque interfici. Ille vero cum se cerneret positum in discrimine, Veredunensem
eclesiam petiit, per Agericum prorsus episcopum, qui erat regis pater ex lavacro, veniam inpetrare confidens. Tunc pontifex ad regem properat depraecaturque pro
eo; cui rex cum negare nequiret quae petebat, ait: 'Veniat coram nobis, et datis fideiussoribus in praesentia patrui mei, quicquid illius iudicium decreverit,
exsequamur'. Tunc adductus ad locum ubi rex morabatur, nudatus armis ac per manicas tentus, ab episcopo repraesentatur rege. Ad cuius provolutus pedes, ait:
'Peccavi tibi ac genetrice tuae, non oboediendo praeceptionibus vestris, sed agendo contra voluntate vestram atque utilitatem publicam; nunc autem rogo, ut
indulgeatis malis meis, quae in vobis gessi'. Rex autem iussit eum elevari a terra et posuit in manu episcopi, dicens: 'Sit penes te, sanctae sacerdos, donec in
praesentia Gunthchramni regis adveniat'. Et iussit eum discidere.

## 9. De interitu Rauchingi.

**[009]** Post haec Rauchingus cuniunctus cum prioribus regni Chlothari, fili Chilperici, confingens se quasi tractaturus de pace, ut inter terminum utriusque
regni nulla intentio aut dereptio gereretur, consilium habuerunt, ut scilicet, interfecto Childebertho rege, Rauchingus cum Theodobertho, seniore eius filio,
Campaniae regnum teneret, Ursio vero ac Berthefredus, iuniorem filium nuper genitum, qui Theodoricus cognominatur, in se susceptum, excluso Gunthchramno rege,
reliquum regni teneret, multa etiam contra Brunechilde reginam frementes, ut eam in contumiliam redigerent, sicut prius fecerant in viduetate sua. Rauchingus
ergo, summa elatus potentiam et, ut ita dicam, ad ipsius regalis sceptri se iactans gloriam, iter praeparat ad Childeberthum regem accidendi, ut consilium quod
inierat possit explere. Sed pietas Domini haec verba in aures Gunthchramni regis prius inposuit, qui, missis nuntiis clam ad Childeberthum regem, omnes ei
molitiones has in notitiam posuit, dicens: 'Accelera velociter, ut videamur a nobis; sunt enim causae, quae agi debeant'. At ille diligenter inquirens, quae ei
nuntiata fuerant, veraque esse cognuscens, arcessiri Rauchingum iussit. Qui cum adfuisset, priusquam eum rex suo iussisset adstare conspectui, datis litteris et
pueris distinatis cum evectione publica, qui res eius per loca singula deberent capere, iussit eum in cubiculo intromitti; locutusque cum eo alia ex aliis,
egredi iterum de cubiculo iubet. Cumque egredieretur, a duobus ostiariis pedibus adpraehensus, ruit in gradibus ostei, ita ut pars corpori eius esset
intrinsecus, pars vero extrinsecus extenderetur. Tunc hi, qui iussi ad haec explenda parati erant, cum gladiis super eum ruunt atque ita minutatim caput eius
conliserunt, ut simile totum cerebro potaretur; statimque mortuus est. Tunc denudatus et per fenestram eiectus, sepulturae mandatus est. Erat autem levis in
moribus, ultra humanum genus cupiditate ac facultatibus inhians alienis et ex ipsis divitiis valde superbus, in tantum ut iam in ipso interitus sui tempore
