consilio pare tractare, qualiter talium temiretas frenum districtionis possit accipere, ut deinceps nulli libeat sub hunc lapsum, faciente iactantia, similia
perpetrare. Attamen, quia nos sua dictione domnus Paulus apostolus indesinenter videtur monere, ut 'oportune inportune' debeamus quoscumque excedentes sidola
praedicatione corregere, et pietatem protestatur ad omnia utilem esse, adeo suggerimus, ut adhuc et oratione assidua Domini misericordiam depraecimini, ut ipse
spiritu conpunctionis ipsas inflammare dignetur, ut id, quod per delictum visae sunt contraxisse, digna satisfactione paeneteant. ut in monastirio suo vestra
praedicatione animas, quae quodammodo perierunt, propitio Christo revertantur, ut ille, qui unam humeris inlatam ovem errantem ad ovilem reduxit, et de istarum
transgressionem quasi adquisitum gregem congaudere dignetur, hoc specialius postulantes, ut pro nobis intercessionum vestrarum suffragia indesinenter, ut
confidemus, tribuatis. Peculiares vester Aetherius peccator salutare praesumo. Cliens vester Isychius reverenter audeo salutare. Amatur vester Siagrius
reverenter saluto. Cultor vester Urbecus peccator famulanter saluto. Veneratur vester Veranus episcopus reverenter saluto. Famulus vester Filex salutare
praesumo. Humilis vester atque amator Felix audeo salutare. Humilis atque oboediens vester Berthramnus episcopus salutare praesumo.

## 42. Exemplare epistolae, quam sancta Radegundis direxit.

**[042]** Sed et abbatissa recitavit epistulam, quam beata Radegundis episcopis, qui suo tempore erant, diregi voluit. Cuius nunc iterum ipsa abbatissa
exemplaria ad vicinarum urbium sacerdotes direxit. Cuius haec est exemplar: EXEMPLAR EPISTULAE. Dominis sanctis et apostolica sede dignissimis in Christo
patribus, omnibus episcopis Radegundis peccatrix. Congruae provisionis tunc roborabiliter ad effectum tendit exordium, cum generalibus patribus, medicis ac
pastoribus ovilis sibi conmissi causa auribus traditur, cuius sensibus conmendatur; quorum participatio de caritate consilium, de potestate suffragium, de
oratione ministrare poterit interventum. Et quoniam olim vinclis laicalibus absoluta, divina providente et inspirante clementia, ad relegionis normam visa sum
voluntariae duce Christo translata, ac pronae mentis studio cogitans etiam de aliarum profectibus, ut, annuente Domino, mea desideria efficerentur reliquis
profutura, instituente atque remunerante praecellentissimo domno rege Chlothario, monastirium puellarum Pectava urbe constitui conditumque, quantum mihi
munificentia regalis est largita, facta donatione, dotavi; insuper congregationem per me, Christo praestante, collectae regulam, sub qua sancta Casaria deguit,
quam sollicitudo beati Caesarii antestites Arelatensis ex institutione sanctorum patrum convenienter collegit, adscivi. Cui, consentientibus beatissimis vel
huius civitatis vel reliquis pontificibus, electione etiam nostrae congregationis, domnam et sororem meam Agnitem, quam ab ineunte aetate loco filiae colui et
eduxi, abbatissam institui ac me post Deum eius ordinatione regulariter oboedituram conmisi. Cuique, formam apostolicam observantes, tam ego quam sorores de
substantia terrena quae possedere videbamur, factis cartis, tradedimus, metu Annaniae et Saffirae in monastirio positae nihil proprium reservantes. Sed quoniam
incerta sunt humanae conditionis momenta vel tempora, quippe mundo in fine currente, cum aliqui magis propriae quam divinae cupiant voluntate servire, zelo
ducta Dei, hanc suggestionis meae paginam mereto apostulatus vestri in Christi nomen supraestis porrego vel devota. Et quia praesens non valui, quasi vestris
provoluta vestigiis, epistulae vicarietate prosternor, coniurans per Patrem et Filium et Spiritum sanctum ac diem tremendi iudicii, sic repraesentatos vos non
tyrannus obpugnit, sed legitimus rex coronet, ut, si casu post meum obitum, si quaecumque persona vel loci eiusdem pontifex seu potestas principis vel alius
aliquis, quod nec fieri credimus, congregationem vel suasu malivolo vel inpulsu iudiciario perturbare temptaverit aut regulam frangere seu abbatissam alteram
quam sororem meam Agnitem, quam beatissimi Germani praesentibus suis fratribus benedictio consecravit, aut ipsa congregatio, quod fieri non potest, habita
murmoratione, mutare contenderit, vel quasdam dominationes in monasterio vel rebus monastirii quaecumque persona vel pontifex loci, praeter quas antecessores
episcopi aut alii, me superstete, habuerunt, novo privilegio quicumque affectare voluerit, aut extra regulam exinde egredi quis temptaverit; seu de rebus, quas
in me praecellentissimus domnus Chlotharius vel praecellentissimi domni reges, filii sui, contulerunt et ego ex eius praeceptiones permisso monastirio tradidi
possedendum et per auctoritates praecellentissimorum domnorum regum Chariberthi, Guntchramni, Chilperici et Sigiberthi cum sacramenti interpositione et suarum
manuum subscriptionibus obtenui confirmari; aut ex his, quae alii pro animarum suarum remedio vel sorores ibidem de rebus propriis contulerunt, aliquis princeps
aut pontifex aut potens aut de sororibus cuiuslibet personae aut minuere aut sibimet ad proprietatem revocare sacrilego voto contenderit, ita vestra sanctitatem
successorumque vestrorum post Deum pro mea supplicatione et Christi voluntate incurrat, ut, sicut praedones et spoliatores pauperum extra gratiam vestram
habeantur. numquam de nostra regula vel de rebus monasterii, obsistentibus vobis, inmenuere valeat aliquid aut mutare. Hoc etiam depraecans, ut, cum Deus
praedictam domnam sororem nostram Agnitem de saeculo migrare voluerit, illa in loco eius abbatissa de nostra congregatione debeat ordinare, quae Deo et ipsi
placuerit, custodiens regulam, et nihil de proposito sanctitatis imminuat; nam numquam propria aut cuiuscumque voluntas praecipitat. Quod si, quod absit, contra
Dei mandatum et auctoritatem regum aliquis de suprascriptis condicionibus vobis coram Domino et sanctis eius praecabiliter conmendatis agere aut de persona aut
substantiam minuenda voluerit aut memoratae sorore meae Agnite abbatissae molestias aliquas inferre temptaverit, Dei et sanctae Crucis et beatae Mariae incurrat
iudicium, et beatus confessores Helarium et Martinum, quibus post Deum sorores meas tradidi defendendas, ipsos habeat contradictores et persecutores. Te quoque,
beati pontifex, successoresque vestros, quos patronos in causa Dei diligenter adscisco, si, quod absit, exteterit, qui contra haec aliquid moliri temptaverit,
pro repellendo et confutando Dei hoste non pigeat ad regem, quem eo tempore locus iste respexerit, vel ad Pectavam civitatem pro re vobis ante Dominum
conmendatam percurrere et contra aliorum iniustitia exsecutores et defensores iustitiae laborare, ut tale nefas ullo modo suis admitti temporibus rex patiatur
catholicus, ne convelli permittant, quod Dei et mea et regum ipsorum voluntate firmatum est. Simul etiam principes, quos Deus pro gubernatione populi post
discessum meum superesse praeceperit, coniuro per Regem, 'cuius non erit finis' et ad cuius nutum regna consistunt, qui eis donavit ipsum vivere vel regnare, ut
monasterium, quod ex permisso et solatio domnorum regum patres vel avi eorum construxisse visa sum et ordinasse regulariter vel dotasse, sub sua tuitione et
sermone una cum Agne abbatissa iubeant gubernare; et a nullo neque saepe dictam abbatissam nostram neque aliquid ad nostrum monasterium pertenentem molestari
aut inquietari vel exinde imminui aut aliquid mutari permittat; sed magis pro Dei intuitu una cum domnis episcopis ipsi, me supplecante coram Redemptorem
gentium, sicut eis conmendo, defensari iubeant et muniri, ut, in cuius honore Dei famulas protegunt, cum defensore pauperum et sponso virginum perpetualiter
aeterno socientur in regno. Illud quoque vos sanctos pontifices et praecellentissimos domnos reges et universum populum christianum coniuro per fidem
catholicam, in qua baptizati estis et ecclesias conservatis, ut in basilica, quam in sanctae Mariae dominicae genetrices honore coepimus aedificare, ubi etiam
multae sorores nostrae conditae sunt in requie, sive perfecta sive inperfecta, cum me Deus de hac luce migrare praeceperit, corpuscolum meum ibi debeat
sepeliri. Quod si quis aliud inde voluerit aut fieri temptaverit, obtenente cruce Christi et beata? Maria, divinam ultionem incurrat, et, vobis
intercurrentibus, in loco ipsius basilicae merear cum sororum congregationem obtenere loculum sepulturae. Et ut haec supplicatio mea, quam manu propria
subscripsi, ut in universalis aeclesiae archevo servetur, effusis cum lacrimis depraecor, quatinus, si contra inprobos aliquos necessitas exerit, ut vestra
defensione soror mea Agnis abbatissa vel congregatio eius, quo succurri sibi poposcerint, vestrae misericordiae pia consolatio opem pastorali sollicitudine
subministret, nec de me distitutas se prodament, quibus Deus praesidium vestrae gratiae praeparavit. Illud vobis in omnibus ante oculos revocantes, per ipsum,
qui de cruce gloriosam virginem, suam genetricem, beato Iohanni apostolo commendavit, ut, qualiter ab illo conpletum est Domini de mandato, sic sit apud vos
indigna et humilis dominis meis aeclesiae patribus et viris apostolicis quod commendo; quod cum dignanter servaveritis deposito, meretis participes, cuius
impletis mandatum, apostolicum digne reparetis exemplum.

## 43. Quod Teutarius ad hoc scandalum mitigando venit.

**[043]** Post haec Maroveus episcopus, cum diversa inproperia ab his audiret, Porcarium abbatem basilicae beati Helari ad Gundegysilum episcopum vel reliquos
conprovincialis eius distinat, ut, data conmunione puellis, ad audientiam veniendi licentiam indulgere dignarentur. Sed nequaquam potuit obtenere. Childeberthus
autem rex, cum assiduas de utraque parte, monasterii scilicet vel puellarum, quae egressae fuerant, molestias patiretur, Theutharium presbiterum ad dirimandas
quaeremunias, quae inter easdem agebantur, distinat. Qui, provocatis Chrodieldem cum reliquis puellis ad audientiam, dixerunt: 'Non venimus, quia a communione
suspensae sumus. Si reconciliare merimur, tunc ad audientiam venire non differimus'. Haec audiens ille, ad episcopos abiit. Cumque cum his de hac causa locutus
fuisset, nullum effectum obtenere potuit de communione earum; et sic ad urbem Pectavam regressus est. Puellae vero separatae ab invicem, aliae ad parentes,
aliae ad domus proprias, nonnullae in his monasteriis, in quibus prius fuerant, sunt regressae, quia hiemem validum simul positae propter penuriam ligni
tollerare non poterant. Pauci tamen cum Chrodieldae et Basina remanserunt. Erat enim tunc et inter eas magna discordia, pro eo quod alia aliae se praeponire
cupiebat.

## 44. De temperiae anni praesentis.

**[044]** Eo anno post clausum pascha tam inmensa cum grandine pluvia fuit, ut infra duarum aut trium horarum spatium etiam per minores vallium meatus ingentia
currere flumina viderentur. Arbores in autumno floruerunt et poma, sicut prius dederant, ediderunt. Mense nono rosae apparuerunt. Flumina vero ultra modum
excreverunt, ita ut excedentes litoribus loca, quae numquam contingere consuetae fuerant, operirent, non minimum de sationibus inferentes damnum. EXPLICIT LIBER
NONUS.

---

# BOOK TEN

# ENGLISH TRANSLATION

---

### 1. Of Gregory, pope of Rome

**[001]** In King Childebert’s fifteenth year my deacon returned from Rome with saints’ relics and reported that in the ninth month of the previous year the
Tiber had flooded Rome so greatly that ancient buildings collapsed and church granaries containing many thousand measures of wheat were destroyed. A multitude
of serpents, including a great dragon as large as a massive beam, descended the riverbed into the sea; the beasts were suffocated in the turbulent salt waves
and cast ashore. The disaster called bubonic plague followed immediately. Arriving in the middle of the eleventh month, it first struck Pope Pelagius, according
to Ezekiel’s words, ‘Begin at my sanctuary,’ and killed him without delay. After his death the disease caused a great slaughter of the people. Because God’s
Church could not be without a ruler, all the people elected the deacon Gregory. Of foremost senatorial birth and devoted to God from youth, he founded six
monasteries on his own property in Sicily and a seventh within Rome’s walls. Assigning them only enough land for daily sustenance, he sold the rest with all his
house’s resources and distributed it to the poor. He who had formerly gone through the city in robes of silk interwoven with gleaming gems now consecrated
himself to the Lord’s altar in humble clothing and was chosen as seventh deacon to assist the pope. His abstinence in food, wakefulness in prayer, and severity
in fasting so weakened his stomach that he could scarcely stand. He was so instructed in grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric that he was considered second to none
in the City. Yet he tried carefully to avoid this eminence, lest worldly pride in attained honour steal back what he had previously cast away. He therefore
wrote to the Emperor Maurice, whose son he had received from the holy font, adjuring and earnestly begging him never to consent to the people’s desire to
elevate Gregory to this glorious office. But Germanus, prefect of Rome, intercepted his messenger, seized and destroyed the letter, and sent the emperor the
people’s consent. Thanking God that his friend the deacon had found a place of honour, the emperor commanded his appointment. While his consecration was delayed
and plague devastated the people, he addressed them for penance as follows:

POPE GREGORY’S ADDRESS TO THE PEOPLE. Dearest brothers, I ought at least to fear God’s scourges, which I deserved to fear before they came, now that I
experience them. Let sorrow open the way of conversion, and let the punishment I suffer dissolve my hearts’ hardness. As the prophet foretold, ‘The sword has
reached the soul.’ Behold, all the people are struck by the sword of heavenly wrath and each is destroyed by sudden death. Sickness does not precede death;
rather, as you see, death outruns the delays of sickness. Each stricken person is snatched away before turning to penitential lament. Consider how he appears
before the severe Judge who has no time to weep for his deeds. Households are not diminished in part but fall together; houses are left empty, parents see their
children’s funerals, and their heirs precede them in death. Let each of us flee to penitential lament while there is time to weep before being struck. Recall
before my mind’s eyes whatever I have done in error and punish by tears what I have wickedly done. ‘Let me come before His presence with confession,’ and as the
prophet admonishes, ‘Lift up my hearts with my hands to God.’ To lift hearts with hands to God is to raise the zeal of my prayer with the merit of good works.
He who cries through the prophet, ‘I do not desire the sinner’s death, but that he turn and live,’ surely gives confidence to my fear. Let no one despair
because of the enormity of his iniquities: three days’ penance wiped away the ancient sins of the Ninevites, and the converted thief obtained life’s reward even
while sentenced to death. Let us change our hearts and presume that we have already obtained what we ask. The judge is more quickly moved by prayer if the
petitioner corrects his own depravity. With the sword of so great a judgment hanging over me, let me persist in urgent tears. Importunity, usually unwelcome
among men, pleases the judgment of truth, because merciful and compassionate God wishes pardon to be won from Him by prayers and does not wish to be angry as
much as I deserve. Through the psalmist He says: ‘Call upon Me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you shall magnify Me.’ He who admonishes
me to call is Himself witness that He desires to pity those who call. Therefore, dearest brothers, with contrite hearts and corrected works, let us come with
devout, tearful minds at dawn on Wednesday for the sevenfold litany distributed below, so that when the severe Judge sees me punishing my own sins He may spare
me from His proposed condemnation. Let the clergy set out from the church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian with the priests of the sixth region; all abbots
with their monks from the church of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius with the priests of the fourth region; all abbesses with their congregations from
the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter with the priests of the first region; all children from the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul with
the priests of the second region; all laymen from the church of the holy protomartyr Stephen with the priests of the seventh region; all widows from the church
of Saint Euphemia with the priests of the fifth region; and all married women from the church of the holy martyr Clement with the priests of the third region.
Going out from the individual churches with prayers and tears, let us assemble at the basilica of blessed Mary, ever Virgin and Mother of my Lord Jesus Christ,
so that by long supplication with tears and groans I may merit pardon for my sins. After this address he assembled the clergy and ordered psalmody and prayers
for the Lord’s mercy for three days. From the third hour both choirs of singers came to church crying Kyrie eleison through the city’s streets. My deacon, who
was present, asserted that within one hour, while the people uttered their supplications, eighty persons fell to the ground and died. But the bishop did not
cease preaching that they should not stop praying. My deacon also obtained the saints’ relics from Gregory while he was still a deacon. When Gregory prepared a
secret flight, he was captured, dragged to blessed Peter the Apostle’s basilica, consecrated to episcopal grace, and made pope of the City. My deacon did not
depart until Gregory returned from Porto to his bishopric and he himself saw how he had been ordained.

### 2. Of the return of Grippo the legate from the emperor Maurice

**[002]** Grippo, returning from the Emperor Maurice, reported that the previous year he and his companions had landed in Africa and entered Carthage. While
waiting for instructions from the prefect about approaching the emperor, a servant of Evantius who had accompanied them stole an object from a merchant and
brought it to their lodging. The owner pursued him and demanded its return. He delayed, and the quarrel grew daily. One day the merchant found the servant in
the street, seized his clothing, and said: ‘You shall not be released until you restore to my possession what you violently stole.’ Trying to free himself, the
servant did not hesitate to draw his sword and kill the man, then returned to the lodging without telling his companions. The envoys were Bodigisel, son of
Mummolin of Soissons, Evantius, son of Dynamius of Arles, and Grippo, a Frank by birth. They had risen from a meal and lain down to rest. When the city’s
magistrates learned what their servant had done, they collected soldiers and armed the whole population and surrounded the envoys’ lodging. Awakened
unexpectedly, the envoys were astonished. The commander cried: ‘Lay down your arms and come out so that we may peacefully learn how the murder occurred.’
Terrified and still ignorant, they requested an oath of safe conduct before coming out unarmed. The men swore, but their violence did not keep the oath. As soon
as Bodigisel came out they struck him with swords, and Evantius likewise. When they lay before the lodging’s door, Grippo seized arms and advanced with his
servants, saying: ‘We did not know what had happened, and behold, my travelling companions sent to the emperor have been struck down. God shall judge my injury
and their deaths by your destruction, because you slaughter us though innocent and coming in peace. There shall no longer be peace between my kings and your
emperor. We came for peace and to furnish aid to the republic. I call God as witness today that your offence has broken the promised peace between the rulers.’
As Grippo spoke these and similar words, the Carthaginian force dispersed and everyone went home. The prefect approached Grippo and soothed his anger, arranging
how he should appear before the emperor. Grippo went, delivered his embassy, and described his companions’ deaths. Greatly displeased, the emperor promised to
avenge them according to King Childebert’s judgment. Honoured with gifts, Grippo returned in peace.

### 3. That King Childebert's army went into Italy

**[003]** When Grippo reported this to King Childebert, the king immediately assembled an army for Italy and sent twenty dukes against the Lombards; I have not
thought it necessary to insert their names in order. Duke Audovald and Wintrjo assembled the people of Champagne. Coming to Metz on their route, they committed
such plunder, murder, and slaughter that they seemed to bring an enemy into their own region. The other dukes and their companies did likewise, afflicting their
own region and people before gaining any victory over the enemy. Approaching Italy, Audovald and six dukes went right and came to Milan, camping at a distance
in the plain. Duke Olo rashly approached Billitio, a fortress of that city situated in the Canine Fields, was wounded by a javelin beneath the nipple, and fell
dead. Others who went out for plunder and provisions were scattered and killed by Lombard attacks. In Milan’s territory is a lake called Ceresium, from which a
small but deep river flows. They heard that the Lombards were stationed on its bank. Before crossing the river, a Lombard stood on the opposite bank protected
by hauberk and helmet and carrying a spear, and cried to the Frankish army: ‘Today it shall appear to whom Divinity grants victory.’ This was evidently a
prearranged signal. A few Franks crossed, fought, and killed him; behold, the entire Lombard army turned and fled. Crossing the river, the Franks found none of
them, only camp arrangements, fireplaces, and tent sites. Returning to camp, they received imperial envoys announcing an army to assist them: ‘We shall come
with it in three days, and this shall be your sign. When you see houses burning in the village on the mountain and smoke rising to heaven, know that we are
present with the promised army.’ They waited six days as agreed, but none came. Chedinus entered the left side of Italy with thirteen dukes, captured five
fortresses, and exacted oaths. Dysentery severely afflicted the army because the unfamiliar air disagreed with them, and many died. When wind arose and rain
fell and the air cooled slightly, health returned to the sick. After wandering through Italy for nearly three months without accomplishing anything, unable to
avenge themselves upon enemies sheltered in strong places or capture their king, who had fortified himself in Pavia, the army, weakened by the air and worn by
hunger, decided to return home. After receiving oaths, they subjected to the king’s authority the territory his father had previously held and carried off
captives and other plunder. Returning, they were so starved that they sold their arms and clothing to buy food before reaching home. Authari, king of the
Lombards, sent envoys to King Guntram, saying: ‘Most pious king, we desire to be subject and faithful to you and your people as we were to your fathers, and we
do not depart from the oath my predecessors swore to yours. Cease persecuting me; let there be peace and concord, so that I may aid you against enemies when
necessary. When my peoples are preserved and you recognize my peacefulness, the adversaries clamouring around may be terrified rather than rejoice at my
discord.’ Guntram received these words peacefully and sent them to his nephew Childebert. While they remained there after delivering this message, others
arrived announcing King Authari’s death and Paul’s succession and repeating the same proposals. Childebert arranged a conference at which they would state
future terms and dismissed them.

### 4. That Maurice sent the slayers

**[004]** Maurice sent to Childebert twelve men from Carthage with bound hands and chains, alleged to have killed the king’s envoys the previous year.
Childebert might execute them or release them for ransom at three hundred gold pieces each, whichever he chose, so that the scandal might be ended and no enmity
arise. Childebert refused to receive the prisoners, saying: ‘It is uncertain whether these are the murderers or other men, perhaps someone’s slaves, whereas my
men who were killed among you were freeborn.’ Grippo, who had accompanied the murdered envoys, was present and said: ‘The city prefect attacked me with two or
three thousand assembled men and killed my companions. I too would have died had I not defended myself courageously. If I go there I can identify the men. If
your emperor wishes to keep peace with my lord as you say, he ought to exact vengeance upon them.’ The king arranged to send the prisoners later to the emperor
and dismissed them.

### 5. That Chuppa burst into the border of Tours

**[005]** In those days Chuppa, formerly King Chilperic’s count of the stable, invaded Tours’s territory and attempted to carry off cattle and other property as
plunder. The inhabitants perceived it, gathered a crowd, and pursued him. They recovered the plunder, killed two servants, and captured two others, while Chuppa
escaped naked. The prisoners were sent to King Childebert, who imprisoned and questioned them about who had helped Chuppa escape capture. They answered that it
was done through the deceit of Animodus, the deputy who governed that district with judicial authority. The king immediately wrote ordering the city count to
send Animodus bound before him or, if he resisted, overpower and kill him if he wished to gain royal favour. Animodus did not resist but gave sureties and went
as commanded. He found Flavian, a royal household officer, pleaded his case with his associate, and was found innocent. Reconciled with Flavian after giving him
gifts, he was permitted to return home. Chuppa later assembled some of his men and attempted to abduct the daughter of the late Badegisel, bishop of Le Mans,
for marriage. He attacked the estate of Mareuil at night with a company of associates, but the matron Magnatrudis, the girl’s mother, perceived his plot. She
went out with her servants, violently repelled him, and killed many of his men, so that he departed in shame.

### 6. Of the Prisoners of the Auvergne

**[006]** At Clermont prisoners escaped at night when their bonds were broken and the prison doors opened by God’s will, and entered a church. Count Eulalius
ordered weights of chains added, but when placed upon them they were immediately shattered like fragile glass. Through Bishop Avitus’s intervention they were
rescued and restored to their own liberty.

### 7. That King Childebert granted to the clergy in that city that they should not render tribute

**[007]** In Clermont King Childebert in generous piety remitted all tribute from churches, monasteries, and other clergy belonging to or serving the Church.
The collectors had long been despoiled because, over long years and succeeding generations and with the possessions divided into many parts, the tax could
scarcely be collected. By God’s inspiration he corrected this so that the fiscal debt no longer injured the collectors and no delay called the Church’s
ministers away from their duties.

### 8. Of Eulalius and Tetradia, who was his wife

**[008]** A synod of bishops was held on the common border of Auvergne, Gévaudan, and Rouergue concerning Tetradi, widow of the late Desiderius, because Count
Eulalius sought from her property she had taken when fleeing from him. I think the cause, her departure from Eulalius, and her flight to Desiderius should be
traced from an earlier point. Eulalius acted unreasonably as young men do; frequently rebuked by his mother, he hated her instead of loving her. She often
devoted herself to prayer in his house’s oratory and, while the servants slept, passed nocturnal vigils in tearful prayer, but was found strangled on the
hair-shirt where she prayed. No one knew who had done it, but the crime of parricide was attributed to her son. When Cautinus, bishop of Clermont, learned this,
he excluded Eulalius from communion. At the feast of the blessed martyr Julian, Eulalius prostrated himself at the bishop’s feet before the assembled citizens,
protesting that he had been excluded unheard. The bishop allowed him to attend Mass with the others. When communion came and Eulalius approached the altar, the
bishop said: ‘Public rumour proclaims you a parricide. I do not know whether you committed the crime, so I place judgment in God’s and blessed Julian’s hands.
If you are innocent as you claim, approach, take a particle of the Eucharist, and put it in your mouth. God shall behold your conscience.’ He received the
Eucharist, communicated, and departed. His wife Tetradi was noble through her mother but of inferior birth through her father. While Eulalius slept with
maidservants he neglected his wife and often severely beat her when returning from fornication. He incurred debts through many crimes and often disposed of her
ornaments and gold. Amid these troubles she lost all honour in his house. While he was away at court, his nephew Virus, who had lost his own wife, desired her
in marriage. Fearing his uncle’s enmity, Virus sent her to Duke Desiderius so that she might later marry him. She took all her husband’s movable substance in
gold, silver, and clothing and her elder son, leaving the younger at home. Returning, Eulalius learned what had happened. After his grief subsided he attacked
his nephew Virus and killed him among Auvergne’s narrow valleys. Desiderius, whose own wife had recently died, heard of Virus’s death and married Tetradi.
Eulalius abducted a girl from a monastery at Lyons and married her, but his concubines, instigated by envy as some assert, obstructed his reason by sorcery.
Much later he secretly attacked and killed Emerius, this girl’s cousin. He likewise killed Socratius, his mother-in-law’s brother, whom her father had by a
concubine, and committed many other evils too lengthy to recount. His son John, who had left with his mother, fled Desiderius’s house and came to Clermont. When
Innocentius obtained the bishopric of Rodez, Eulalius asked him to help recover property owed him in that city’s territory. Innocentius replied: ‘If you give me
one of your sons to keep as a cleric in my service, I shall do as you ask.’ Eulalius sent the boy John and recovered his property. Bishop Innocentius tonsured
him and appointed him his church’s archdeacon. John devoted himself to such abstinence that he ate barley instead of wheat, drank water instead of wine, rode an
ass instead of a horse, and wore the humblest clothing. When the bishops and nobles assembled on the border of the cities named above, Tetradi was brought from
Agen and Eulalius appeared to plead against her. He sought the property she took from his house when leaving for Desiderius. Judgment required Tetradi to
restore the property with fourfold satisfaction and declared her sons by Desiderius illegitimate. It was also decreed that if she paid Eulalius she might enter
Clermont and enjoy without challenge the property inherited from her father. This was done.

### 9. Of King Guntram's army which went into Brittany

**[009]** While the Bretons were fiercely ravaging Nantes and Rennes, King Guntram ordered an army assembled under Dukes Beppolen and Ebracharius. Ebracharius
suspected that if Beppolen gained victory he would acquire his own dukedom, and hostility grew between them; along the whole march they attacked each other with
blasphemies, insults, and curses. They committed burnings, murders, robberies, and many crimes along the way. They crossed the Vilaine and reached the Oust,
destroyed nearby cottages, built bridges, and crossed with the whole army. A priest attached to Beppolen said: ‘Follow me and I shall lead you to Waroch and
show you the Bretons gathered together.’ When Fredegund heard that Beppolen, already hated by her, was marching, she ordered the Saxons of Bayeux, tonsured and
clothed in Breton fashion, to aid Waroch. Beppolen and his followers engaged them and killed many Bretons and Saxons over two days. Ebracharius had withdrawn
with the larger force and would not approach until he heard Beppolen was dead. On the third day Beppolen’s men were killed and he fought on wounded by a lance
until Waroch and his men rushed and killed him. They had been trapped between narrow roads and marshes, where more were stuck in mud than slaughtered by the
sword. Ebracharius went as far as Vannes. Bishop Regalis sent clergy with crosses and psalmody to meet and conduct him into the city. Some reported that Waroch
tried to flee to the islands in ships laden with gold, silver, and other goods, but when they reached the open sea a wind sank them and he lost the cargo.
Nevertheless he came to Ebracharius, sought peace, and gave hostages and many gifts, promising never to act against Guntram’s interests. When he withdrew,
Bishop Regalis, his clergy, and the citizens likewise swore: ‘We are in no way guilty towards my lord kings and have never proudly opposed their interests, but
we lie under the heavy yoke of Breton captivity.’ After peace was made Waroch said: ‘Depart and report that I shall willingly fulfil all the king’s commands.
That you may believe more fully, I shall give my nephew as hostage.’ He did so and the war ceased, though great multitudes of the royal army and the Bretons had
been killed. When the army left Brittany and the stronger crossed the river, the weaker and poorer could not cross with them. While they remained on the
Vilaine’s bank, Waroch forgot his oath and hostages and sent his son Canaon with an army. They bound the men found there, killed those resisting, and some
attempting to cross with horses were swept by the torrent into the sea. Many were later released by Waroch’s wife with wax and tablets as though free and
returned home. The army which had already crossed feared returning by the same road lest it suffer for its deeds and made for Angers, seeking a bridge over the
Maine. The small advance party reaching that bridge was robbed, beaten, and utterly disgraced. Passing through Tours they plundered and despoiled many,
surprising the inhabitants. Many soldiers told King Guntram that Duke Ebracharius and Count Wiliacharius had taken money from Waroch and caused the army’s
destruction. Ebracharius was presented, severely reproached, and dismissed from the king’s presence, while Wiliacharius hid in flight.

### 10. Of the death of Chundo, his chamberlain

**[010]** In Childebert’s fifteenth year, Guntram’s twenty-ninth, while Guntram hunted in the Vosges forest he discovered the tracks of a slaughtered wild ox.
Closely questioning the forest guard about who had dared do this in the royal forest, he learned that the king’s chamberlain Chundo was responsible. He ordered
Chundo arrested and brought bound to Chalon. When both pleaded before the king and Chundo denied the charge, the king decreed trial by combat. The chamberlain
provided his nephew as champion. The young man hurled a lance at the forest guard and transfixed his foot, and the guard fell on his back. The youth drew the
knife hanging from his belt and tried to cut the fallen man’s throat, but the wounded guard pierced his belly with a knife. Both fell dead. Seeing this, Chundo
fled to Saint Marcellus’s basilica. At the king’s cry he was seized before reaching the sacred threshold, bound to a stake, and overwhelmed with stones. The
king afterwards greatly repented that precipitate anger had made him so quickly kill a faithful and useful man for a trifling offence.

### 11. Of the sickness of Chlothar the younger

**[011]** Chlothar, son of the late King Chilperic, became gravely ill and was so despaired of that his death was reported to King Guntram. Guntram left Chalon
intending to go to Paris and reached the territory of Sens, but returned when he heard the boy had recovered. His mother Fredegund, seeing him despaired of,
vowed much money to Saint Martin’s basilica, and he seemed to improve. She also sent messengers to Waroch asking that Guntram’s soldiers still captive in
Brittany be released for the boy’s life, and Waroch did so. Thus it was evident that this woman’s collusion had caused Beppolen’s death and the army’s
destruction.

### 12. Of the malice of Bertegundis

**[012]** When the religious Ingitrude, who founded a convent of women in Saint Martin’s courtyard as related above, fell ill, she appointed her granddaughter
abbess, at which the rest of the congregation greatly murmured; but they ceased quarrelling when I rebuked them. At enmity with her daughter because she had
taken her property, Ingitrude adjured that Berthegund should never be permitted to pray in the monastery she founded or over her tomb. She died, I think, in her
eightieth year and was buried on the seventh day before the Ides of the first month. Her daughter Berthegund came to Tours and, not being received, went to King
Childebert requesting authority to govern the monastery in her mother’s place. Forgetting the judgment he had given her mother, the king granted a new decree
signed by himself, placing all her mother’s and father’s property under her authority and removing whatever Ingitrude had left the monastery. Coming with this
command, Berthegund stripped all the monastery’s furnishings until only bare walls remained. She gathered men guilty of various crimes, prepared for
disturbances, to seize the produce of any remaining estates given by the devout. She committed so many evils there that they can scarcely be narrated in order.
Taking the property, she returned to Poitiers, uttering many false charges against the abbess, her close relative.

### 13. The altercation concerning the resurrection

**[013]** At this time one of our priests, infected with the Sadducees’ malicious poison, said there would be no future resurrection. When I affirmed that it
was foretold in sacred Scripture and demonstrated by apostolic tradition, he answered: ‘It is well known that this is commonly proclaimed, but we are not
certain whether it is true, especially since the angry Lord said to the first man whom he formed with his sacred hand: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat
bread, till thou return unto the ground from which thou wast taken; for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return. What will you who preach a future
resurrection answer to this, when Divinity does not promise that man reduced to dust will rise again?’ I said: ‘I think no Catholic is ignorant of what the
words of our Lord and Redeemer and of the fathers before us say on this. In Genesis, when the fathers died, the Lord said: Thou shalt be gathered unto thy
people, being buried in a good old age. And to Cain it is said: The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground. Thus it plainly appears that
souls live after leaving the body and await the future resurrection with expectant faces. It is written of Job that he will rise in the resurrection of the
dead. The prophet David, though speaking in the Lord’s person and foreseeing the resurrection, says: Shall he that sleepeth not rise again? That is, shall he
overcome by the sleep of death not come to resurrection? Isaiah teaches that the dead will rise from their tombs. When the prophet Ezekiel describes man
reformed—dry bones covered with skin, bound with sinews, threaded with veins, and animated by the breathing spirit—he most plainly teaches the future
resurrection. Another manifest indication was that a dead corpse touching Elisha’s bones revived by the power’s effect; this revealed the resurrection of the
Lord himself, the firstborn of the dead, who brought death upon death and restored life to the dead from the tomb.’ The priest said: ‘I do not doubt that the
Lord died and rose in the man he assumed, but I do not accept that other dead people will rise.’ I said: ‘What necessity was there for God’s Son to descend from
heaven, assume flesh, undergo death, and penetrate hell, except that the man he formed should not be left abandoned in perpetual death? The souls of the just
confined in hell’s prison until his passion were released at his coming. Descending into hell and flooding its darkness with new light, he led their souls out
with him so they would no longer be tormented at that exit, according to: And in his tomb the dead rise.’ The priest said: ‘Can bones reduced to ashes be
animated again and produce a living man?’ I answered: ‘I believe that however much man is reduced to dust and scattered by water and earth under the violent
force of wind, it is not difficult for God to restore him to life.’ He answered: ‘I think you chiefly err in trying with smooth words to assert this bitter
deception, saying that one seized by beasts, submerged in water, devoured by fishes, reduced to dung and expelled through the bowel’s private passage, or cast
into flowing water or destroyed in putrefying earth, will come to resurrection.’ I answered: ‘I think you have forgotten what John the evangelist, reclining on
the Lord’s breast and searching the mysteries’ divine secrets, says in Revelation: Then the sea gave up its dead. Thus whatever fish, bird, or beast has
swallowed of the human body will be reunited by the Lord and restored in resurrection; it will not be difficult for him who created things not born from nothing
to repair what is lost. He will restore the body to the same solid integrity it had before, so that the body which was in the world may receive punishment or
glory according to merit. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: The Son of man shall come in his Father’s glory with his angels, to render to every man according
to his works. When Martha doubted her brother Lazarus’s present resurrection, she said: I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day. The
Lord said: I am the resurrection, the way, the truth, and the life.’ The priest said: ‘How then is it said in the psalm: The ungodly shall not rise in
judgment?’ I answered: ‘They do not rise to judge, but to be judged; the Judge cannot sit with the ungodly when rendering the causes of his own acts.’ He said:
‘The Lord says in the Gospel: He that believeth not is condemned already, surely because he will perish in resurrection.’ I answered: ‘He is condemned to come
to eternal punishment because he did not believe in God’s only-begotten Son, yet he will rise in the body to suffer in it the punishment for the sin he
committed in it. Judgment cannot occur unless the dead first rise. As I believe heaven holds the saints who have died—from whose tombs that power often proceeds
so the blind are illuminated, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and other benefits of healing are granted to sick petitioners—so I believe the sinner is held
in hell’s prison until judgment.’ The priest said: ‘In the psalm we read: The spirit hath passed away from man, and he shall not be; neither shall he know his
place any more.’ I said: ‘This is what the Lord himself says in the parable to the rich man tormented in hell’s flames: Thou receivedst good things in thy
lifetime, and likewise Lazarus evil things. That rich man did not then know his purple and fine linen or the banquet’s luxuries which air, earth, or sea had
produced for him, just as Lazarus did not know the wounds and sores he endured lying at his gate, while Lazarus rested in Abraham’s bosom and the other was
tormented in flames.’ The priest said: ‘In another psalm we read: Their spirit goeth forth, and they return to their earth; in that day all their thoughts
perish.’ I answered: ‘You speak well. When the spirit has left man and the body lies dead, it does not think of what it leaves in the world. As an example: it
does not think of building, planting, or cultivating a field, or of gathering gold, silver, or the world’s other riches. That thought has perished from the dead
body because there is no spirit in it. Why do you doubt the resurrection which the apostle Paul, in whom Christ himself spoke, plainly expounds: We are buried
with Christ by baptism into death, that as he died and rose, so we should walk in newness of life? Again: We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.
The trumpet shall sound, the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. Again: Star differeth from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of
the dead. And there: It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption, and so forth. Again: We must all appear before Christ’s judgment seat, that
everyone may receive the things proper to his body, according to what he hath done, whether good or evil. To the Thessalonians he most plainly describes the
future resurrection: I would not have you ignorant concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. For if we believe
that Jesus died and rose again, even so God also bringeth with him them which sleep in Jesus. For this we say unto you by the Lord’s word, that we which are
alive and remain unto the Lord’s coming shall not precede them which are asleep. For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the
archangel’s voice and God’s trumpet, and the dead in Christ shall rise first; then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the
clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words. Many testimonies confirm this cause.
I do not know why you doubt the resurrection which saints expect for merit and sinners fear for guilt. The elements I observe demonstrate it: trees covered with
leaves in summer are stripped when winter comes, but with returning spring they are clothed again as though rising in the foliage they had before. Seeds cast
into the earth also show this; committed to furrows, if they die they rise with manifold fruit, as Paul says: Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened
unless it first die. All these are manifest to the world for faith in resurrection. If there is no future resurrection, what profit will the just have from
doing good, and what harm will sinners have from doing evil? Let all depart into their pleasures and each do as he pleases if there will be no future judgment.
Do you not fear, impudent man, what the Lord himself said to the blessed apostles: When the Son of man shall come in the seat of his majesty, all nations shall
be gathered before him, and he shall separate them one from another as a shepherd divideth lambs from kids; he shall set the sheep on his right and the goats on
his left. To these he says: Come, ye blessed, receive the kingdom; to those: Depart from me, ye workers of iniquity. As Scripture teaches, these shall go into
everlasting punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. Do you think there will be no resurrection of the dead or judgment of works when the Lord does
this? Let Paul answer you as he answered other unbelievers: If Christ be not risen, my preaching is vain, and your faith is vain.’ The priest, saddened, left my
presence and promised to believe in the resurrection according to the sequence of sacred Scriptures I have recalled above.

### 14. Of the death of Theudulf the deacon

**[014]** At that time Theudulf, a deacon of Paris, fancied himself somewhat learned and often raised disputes on this question. Leaving Paris he came to Angers
and attached himself to Bishop Audoveus because of their old friendship while living together in Paris; Bishop Ragnemod of Paris often excommunicated him for
delaying his return to the church where he had been ordained deacon. He became so intimate with the bishop that Audoveus, being good-mannered and pious, could
not shake off his importunity. The bishop built an upper room on the city walls. Descending from it after a banquet, he supported his hand on Theudulf, who was
so drunk with wine that he could scarcely even feign a step. Moved by some impulse, he struck with his fist the neck of the boy carrying a light before them.
When the boy was pushed, Theudulf could not restrain himself and was hurled from the wall with that momentum, seizing the bishop’s napkin hanging from his belt;
the bishop would nearly have fallen with him had the abbot not quickly clasped his feet. Theudulf fell upon a stone, broke his bones and rib cage, vomited blood
with his gall burst, and expired. He was addicted to wine and dissolute in adulteries.

### 15. The scandal of the monastery of Poitiers

**[015]** When the scandal sown by the devil in Poitiers’ convent daily grew in greater iniquity and Chrodield sat prepared for sedition with the murderers,
sorcerers, adulterers, fugitives, and other criminals she had gathered, she ordered them to rush into the convent at night and drag the abbess out. Feeling the
tumult coming, the abbess, suffering from gout, asked to be carried to the ark of the Holy Cross for its help. The armed men entered and wandered through the
convent by candlelight searching for her; entering the oratory they found her lying on the ground before the ark. One fiercer than the rest, who had undertaken
the crime to cut the abbess down with a sword, was struck by another with a knife, through divine providence, I believe. He fell bleeding to the ground and did
not fulfil the vow he had lightly conceived. Meanwhile the prioress Justina and other sisters put out the candle and covered the abbess with the altar cloth
before the Lord’s cross. The attackers came with drawn swords and lances, tore the clothing, nearly tore the nuns’ hands, and seized the prioress for the abbess
in the darkness. Shaking off the coverings and loosing her hair, they dragged her to Saint Hilary’s basilica to imprison her. Approaching it as the sky
lightened, they recognized she was not the abbess and ordered the girl back to the convent. Returning, they seized and dragged out the abbess and shut her in
custody near Saint Hilary’s basilica where Basina was lodged, stationing guards at the door so no one could help the captive. Then, approaching the convent in
dark night without any light, they pulled a cask once smeared with pitch from the storehouse, set it afire, made a great torch, and stole all the convent’s
furnishings, leaving only what they could not carry. This happened seven days before Easter. The bishop, taking it grievously but unable to calm the diabolical
sedition, sent to Chrodield: ‘Release the abbess so she is not held in prison these days; otherwise I shall not celebrate the Lord’s Easter, nor shall any
catechumen receive baptism in this city unless she is freed. If you refuse, I shall gather the citizens and take her away.’ Chrodield immediately assigned
assassins: ‘If anyone tries to take her by force, strike her with the sword at once.’ Flavian, recently appointed domesticus, was present, and by his help the
abbess entered Saint Hilary’s basilica and was released. Meanwhile murders were committed at Saint Radegund’s tomb and men were maimed in the sedition before
the blessed cross’s ark. As this fury increased daily through Chrodield’s pride and the rebels committed constant slaughter and the other outrages mentioned,
her boasting swelled until she looked down haughtily on her cousin Basina. Basina began penance, saying: ‘I erred in following Chrodield’s boasting. Now she
despises me and I am insubordinate to my abbess.’ Turning, she humbled herself before the abbess and sought peace; they were of one mind and will. After the
scandal began, the abbess’s servants resisted Chrodield’s faction and struck Basina’s servant, who fell and died. They fled after the abbess to the confessor’s
basilica, so Basina left the abbess; but when the servants again escaped by flight, they returned to their former peace. Many enmities arose between these
factions. Who could explain in words so many wounds, slaughters, and evils? Scarcely a day passed without murder, an hour without quarrelling, or a moment
without tears. Hearing this, King Childebert sent an embassy to King Guntram so bishops joined from both kingdoms could correct events by canonical sanction.
Childebert ordered me, Eberegisil of Cologne, and Maroveus of Poitiers to attend; Guntram sent Gundegisel of Bordeaux and his provincials because Bordeaux was
Poitiers’ metropolis. I objected: ‘We shall not go unless the savage sedition raised by Chrodield is first suppressed by the judge’s severity.’ A decree was
therefore issued to Count Macco ordering him to suppress resistance by force. Hearing this, Chrodield stationed her armed assassins before the oratory door to
resist the judge if he used force. The count had to advance armed and suppress them: some were beaten with clubs, others pierced with missiles, and the fiercer
resisters struck with swords. Seeing this, Chrodield took the Lord’s cross whose power she had despised and came out: ‘Do not use force against me, I beg, for I
am a queen, a king’s daughter and another king’s cousin. Do not do this, lest a time come when I take vengeance on you.’ The crowd disregarded her words, rushed
upon the resisters, bound and dragged them from the convent, stretched them on stakes, and beat them severely; some had their hair cut off, others their hands,
others their ears and noses, and the sedition was suppressed. Then the bishops sat on the church tribunal. Chrodield appeared, heaping insults and accusations
on the abbess, asserting that she kept a man in the convent dressed as a woman who served her constantly, pointing with her finger: ‘There he is.’ Standing
before all in women’s clothing, he said he could do no man’s work and therefore changed his dress; he knew the abbess only by name and had never seen or spoken
with her, especially as he lived more than forty miles from Poitiers. Unable to convict the abbess on this charge, Chrodield added: ‘What holiness is there in
an abbess who makes men eunuchs and orders them to live with her in imperial fashion?’ Questioned, the abbess said she knew nothing of it. When Chrodield named
the eunuch servant, the chief physician Reoval appeared: ‘When this boy was small and suffering from a thigh disease, he was despaired of. His mother went to
Saint Radegund asking that care be given him. She called me and ordered me to help if I could. As I had once seen physicians do at Constantinople, I cut away
his testicles and restored the boy healthy to his grieving mother; I know the abbess knew nothing of it.’ Unable to find the abbess guilty here either,
Chrodield brought other savage calumnies. Since her assertions and the answers are included in the written judgment against them, I have preferred to insert its
text for reading.

### 16. The judgment pronounced against Chrodield and Basina

**[016]** COPY OF THE JUDGMENT. To the most glorious lord kings, from the bishops present. By propitious Divinity, religion has most rightly made its causes
known to the pious and Catholic princes given to the people, to whom rule is granted, understanding through the Holy Spirit’s participation that it is
associated with and established by the decree of those who govern. At your authority’s command we met at Poitiers concerning conditions in the convent of
Radegund of holy memory, to hear the disputing parties and determine the quarrels between its abbess and the nuns who unwisely left that flock. Summoning the
parties, we asked Chrodield and Basina why they so audaciously broke the convent doors and left contrary to their rule, causing the gathered congregation to
disperse. They answered that they could no longer bear the danger of famine, nakedness, and murder, adding that various persons bathed unsuitably, that the
abbess played at tables, dined with secular persons, held betrothals in the convent, rashly made a garment for her niece from a silk altar cloth,
inconsiderately removed the gold leaves around it and criminally hung them around her niece’s neck, unnecessarily made her a gold-embroidered fillet, and
celebrated drinking parties within. Asked for her answer, the abbess said of the famine that, as the time’s scarcity permitted, the nuns never suffered
excessive want. Of clothing she said that if anyone searched their little chests, they had more than necessity required. Of the bath she related that it
happened during Lent; because of the lime’s harshness and lest the new building harm bathers, Lady Radegund ordered the convent servants to use it publicly
until every harmful smell departed, which the servants did from Lent to Pentecost. Chrodield answered: ‘Afterwards many likewise bathed for a long time.’ The
abbess said she could neither approve their statement nor knew whether it happened, blaming them for not reporting it to her if they saw it. Of playing tables
she said that even if she had played while Lady Radegund lived, she considered it a small fault, and related that neither rule nor canons forbade it in writing.
At the bishops’ command she promised with bowed neck to perform whatever penance was ordered. Of banquets she said she introduced no new custom beyond what
occurred under Radegund, offering eulogiae to Christian faithful, and it was not proved she ever banqueted with them. Of the betrothal she confessed receiving
the pledge for her orphan niece before the bishop, clergy, and elders, asking pardon before all if this was a fault, but she held no banquet in the convent
then. Of the altar cloth she produced the noble nun Didimia, who had given her the silk robe brought from her parents as a gift; she cut part for her purpose
and gave the rest, as much as suitable, for an altar cloth, putting the surplus purple cutting on her niece’s tunic, saying she gave it there for the convent’s
benefit. Didimia confirmed all this. Of the gold leaves and gold-embroidered fillet she called your servant Macco as witness, since through his hand she
received twenty solidi from her niece’s betrothed, with which this was publicly made, no convent property being mixed in. Chrodield and Basina were asked
whether they charged the abbess with adultery, murder, sorcery, or any capital crime deserving a blow. They answered that they had nothing except to proclaim
that she acted against the rule in these matters. Finally, for the sins whereby the cloister was broken and for so many months the wretched women, whom we
believed innocent nuns, could do whatever they wished without their abbess’s discipline, they presented them pregnant to us. Discussing everything in order and
finding no crime overthrowing the abbess, we warned her with fatherly admonition concerning the lesser charges never to repeat them for reproach. Then we
examined the adverse parties who committed greater crimes: despising their bishop’s preaching within the convent lest they go outside, trampling him and leaving
him in utmost contempt, breaking locks and doors, making his command void, departing, and drawing others into transgression. Moreover, when Bishop Gundegisel
and his provincials, summoned on this matter, came to Poitiers by royal command and called them to a hearing at the convent, they despised the admonition. When
the bishops, with pastoral solicitude, came to them at Saint Hilary’s basilica where they lodged and admonished them, they raised sedition, beat bishops and
ministers with clubs, and shed the deacons’ blood in the basilica. Then, by the princes’ command, the venerable priest Theutharius was sent on the case and a
judgment date fixed. Not awaiting it, they most seditiously burned casks in the convent courtyard, broke the doorposts with crowbars and axes, set fire, beat
and wounded nuns in the oratories, stripped the convent, tore the abbess’s clothing and hair, dragged her grievously in ridicule through the crossroads, and
confined her, if not bound, not free. When Easter’s festival arrived, the bishop offered payment for the condemned woman so she might await baptism, but no
suppliant voice obtained it. Chrodield answered that they neither knew of nor ordered such a crime, yet asserted that she had given a sign to her men that she
not be killed. Thus it is certain what may be understood from the added cruelty: they killed a convent servant fleeing to blessed Radegund’s tomb and healed no
one, seeking nothing as the crime grew. They entered the convent by themselves afterwards, refused the lords’ command to present the seditious men publicly,
bore arms against royal commands, and indignantly raised arrows and lances against the count and people. Coming again to the public hearing, they secretly and
injuriously took out the most sacred Holy Cross, to their guilt, which they were afterwards compelled to restore in church. Recognizing so many unrestrained and
continually increased capital crimes, we told them to ask the abbess’s pardon and amend what was wrongly plundered. Refusing and instead discussing her murder,
which they publicly confessed, we opened and reviewed the canons and judged it most equitable to deprive them of communion until worthy penance and restore the
abbess to remain in her place. At your command, having examined the canons, we report completing what pertained to ecclesiastical order without respect of
persons. Concerning the convent property and your royal parents’ charters stolen from the place, which they confess having but disobediently refuse voluntarily
to return, your piety and authority must compel restoration by royal power for the place’s repair, that your and earlier princes’ eternal reward may remain. Do
not permit them to return or aspire again to the place they so impiously and profanely destroyed, lest worse occur. When all is restored entire by the Lord’s
help, may everything be gained for God under Catholic kings and religion lose nothing; may the preserved state of fathers and canons profit us for worship and
be propagated to you for fruit. May Christ the Lord nourish and rule you, granting a lasting kingdom and conferring a blessed life.

### 17. Of their excommunication

**[017]** After this judgment they were suspended from communion and the abbess restored to the convent. They went to King Childebert, adding evil to evil and
naming persons who, they alleged, not only committed adultery with the abbess but carried messages daily to her enemy Fredegund. Hearing this, the king sent men
to bring the accused in chains, but when examination found no crime in them, they were allowed to depart.

### 18. Of the slayers sent against King Childebert

**[018]** Before these days, when the king entered the oratory of the house at Marilac, his servants saw an unknown man standing at a distance and said: ‘Who
are you, whence do you come, and what is your business? We do not know you.’ He answered: ‘I am one of you.’ Quickly expelled from the oratory and questioned,
he immediately confessed that Queen Fredegund had sent him to kill the king, saying: ‘We are twelve men sent by her; six came here and six remained at Soissons
to deceive the king’s son. I was awaiting a place where I could strike King Childebert in the oratory, but terrified by fear I did not resolve to fulfil my
wish.’ Given over at once to savage tortures, he named various accomplices. Sought in different places, some were imprisoned, others released with hands cut
off, and others freed in ridicule with noses and ears amputated. Many prisoners, fearing kinds of torture, stabbed themselves with their own swords, and some
died under torture, so the king’s vengeance was accomplished.

### 19. Of the expulsion of Egidius, bishop of Reims

**[019]** Sunnigisil was again given to torments and beaten daily with rods and thongs; when his putrefying wounds first began closing as matter ran off, they
were renewed for punishment. Under these torments he confessed not only King Chilperic’s death but various other crimes. Among these confessions he added that
Egidius, bishop of Reims, had participated in Rauching, Ursio, and Berthefred’s plot to kill King Childebert. The bishop was immediately seized and brought to
Metz, greatly exhausted by long illness. While he was held in custody, the king ordered bishops summoned for his examination at Verdun at the beginning of the
eighth month. Rebuked by other bishops for ordering a man seized and imprisoned without a hearing, he allowed Egidius to return to his city and sent letters, as
said above, to all his kingdom’s bishops to meet at that city in mid-ninth month for examination. There were heavy rains, immense waters, intolerable cold,
roads dissolved in mud, and rivers overflowing their banks, but they could not resist the royal command. Meeting, they were conducted to Metz, where Egidius
appeared. The king declared him his enemy and betrayer of the kingdom and sent Duke Ennodius to prosecute the case. His first proposition was: ‘Tell me, bishop,
why did you leave the king in whose city you enjoyed episcopal honour and submit to King Chilperic’s friendship, proved always my lord king’s enemy, who killed
his father, exiled his mother, and seized his kingdom? And in those cities unjustly subjugated, you obtained fiscal estates from him.’ He answered: ‘I cannot
deny being King Chilperic’s friend, but this friendship did not grow against King Childebert’s interest. I bought the estates you mention by that king’s
charters.’ Producing them publicly, the king denied granting them. Otto, then referendary, whose subscription appeared, was summoned and denied signing; his
hand was forged in the document. Here the bishop was first found false. Letters were then produced containing many insults against Brunhild, written to
Chilperic, and Chilperic’s answers to the bishop, including: ‘Unless the root of a thing is cut, the stalk grown from the earth does not wither.’ It is manifest
this was written so Brunhild might be overthrown and her son destroyed. The bishop denied sending or receiving these letters, but his familiar servant appeared
with them in his notebooks among bundles of papyrus, leaving the assembly no doubt they came from him. Then agreements purportedly between Childebert and
Chilperic were produced, stipulating that after expelling Guntram the two would divide his kingdom and cities. The king denied making them with his counsel:
‘You set my uncles against each other so civil war arose; the army devastated Bourges, the Étampes district, and Meulan castle, and many were killed, whose
souls, I think, God’s judgment will require at your hands.’ The bishop could not deny this. These writings were found together in one of Chilperic’s archive
chests and reached Childebert when, after Chilperic’s murder, his treasures were taken from the villa of Chelles near Paris. As the dispute continued, Abbot
Epiphanius of Saint Remigius’s basilica appeared, saying Egidius received two thousand gold pieces and many valuables to preserve Chilperic’s friendship. Envoys
who had accompanied him to that king said: ‘Leaving us, he spoke alone with Chilperic for a long time; we understood none of the words, but afterwards
recognized the prosecution of the aforesaid destruction.’ When he denied it, the abbot, always privy to these secret counsels, named the place and man who
brought the gold and narrated in order how the kingdom’s and King Guntram’s destruction was agreed. Convicted, Egidius confessed. The summoned bishops, hearing
this and seeing the Lord’s priest an accomplice in such evils, sighed and requested three days for discussion, hoping he might recover and find some excuse. On
the third day, meeting in church, they asked whether he had any excuse. Confused, he said: ‘Do not delay sentence on the guilty; I know I deserve death for
treason, having always acted against this king’s and his mother’s interest, and by my counsel many conflicts occurred in which parts of Gaul were devastated.’
The bishops, hearing and lamenting their brother’s disgrace, spared his life but removed him from the priestly order after reading the canons. He was taken at
once to Argentorate, now called Strasbourg, and condemned to exile. Romulf, Duke Lupus’s son, already honoured with the priesthood, replaced him, and Abbot
Epiphanius was removed from office at Saint Remigius’s basilica. Many weights of gold and silver were found in the bishop’s archive. What came from iniquitous
warfare was placed in the royal treasury; what came from church tribute or other church accounts was left there.

### 20. Of the girls mentioned above reconciled in this synod

**[020]** At this synod Basina, King Chilperic’s daughter, whom I said was excluded from communion with Chrodield, prostrated herself before the bishops and
asked pardon, promising to enter the convent in charity with the abbess and transgress nothing of the rule. Chrodield protested that she would never enter while
Leubovera remained abbess. The king asked pardon for both; received into communion, they were ordered back to Poitiers, Basina returning to the convent as
stated, and Chrodield residing on the estate formerly belonging to Waddo mentioned above, which the king granted her.

### 21. Of the death of the sons of Waddo

**[021]** Waddo’s sons wandered through Poitiers committing various crimes, murders, and thefts. Earlier they rushed upon merchants in the night’s darkness,
slaughtered them with swords, and took their goods; they also treacherously surrounded and killed a man of tribunitian authority and plundered his property.
When Count Macco tried to suppress them, they sought the king’s presence. When the count went to pay the customary service due the fisc, they too appeared
before the king, offering a great belt ornamented with gold and precious stones and a wonderful sword whose hilt was set with Spanish gems and gold. When the
king clearly learned from them that the crimes he had heard of were committed, he ordered them bound and tortured. Under torture they began revealing their
father’s hidden treasure, taken from the property of Gundovald mentioned above. Men sent to search immediately found an immense quantity of gold, silver, and
various objects ornamented with gold and gems, which they placed in the royal treasury. Afterwards the elder was beheaded and the younger condemned to exile.

### 22. Of the death of Chulderic the Saxon

**[022]** Childeric the Saxon, after various crimes, murders, seditions, and many other shameful acts, went to Auch, where his wife had property. When the king
heard of his wickedness and ordered him killed, one night he became so drunk with wine that he was found dead in bed, suffocated by it. Men asserted he had been
standard-bearer in the crime named above, when the Lord’s priests were struck down in Saint Hilary’s basilica through Chrodield; if so, God avenged the injury
to his servants.

### 23. Of the signs and the doubt concerning Easter

**[023]** This year such splendour shone upon the lands at night that you would think it midday; fiery globes were also often seen running through the sky at
night and illuminating the world. There was doubt about Easter because Victorius’s cycle fixed it on the fifteenth moon. Lest Christians celebrate these
solemnities like Jews under that moon, he added: But the Latins on the twenty-second moon. Many in Gaul celebrated on the fifteenth moon, but I on the
twenty-second. I investigated carefully, and the springs in Spain which are divinely filled were filled at my Easter. A great earthquake occurred on the
eighteenth day before the Kalends of the fifth month, the fourth day of the week, early in the first hour as light began returning. The sun suffered an eclipse
in the middle of the eighth month, and its light so diminished that scarcely as much remained for shining as the horns of a five-day moon retain. There were
heavy rains, severe autumn thunder, and waters rose excessively. An inguinal plague grievously devastated Viviers and Avignon.

### 24. Of the overthrow of the city of Antioch

**[024]** In Childebert’s sixteenth and Guntram’s thirtieth year, a bishop named Simon came to Tours from overseas and told me of Antioch’s destruction,
asserting he had been taken captive from Armenia into Persia. The Persian king invaded Armenia’s border, took plunder, burned churches, and carried this bishop
and his people captive. They also tried to burn the basilica of the forty-eight martyrs mentioned in my Book of Miracles who suffered in that region,
surrounding it with piles of wood mixed with pitch and pigs’ hides and applying burning torches; but the fire did not catch the prepared pyre. Seeing God’s
wonders, they withdrew. A bishop who heard of this priest’s capture sent ransom through his men to the Persian king, who accepted it and freed him from
servitude. Leaving those regions, Simon came to Gaul to receive consolation from the devout and told me this: There was at Antioch a man very devout in
almsgiving, with a wife and children. From the time he first possessed anything, no day of his life passed without his tasting food with a poor man. One day he
went around the city until evening but could find no needy person with whom to eat. Going outside the gate as night fell, he found a man in white clothing
standing with two others. Looking at him like Lot in ancient history, overcome with terror he said: ‘Perhaps my lord is a stranger; deign to come to your
servant’s house, take food, and rest in bed; in the morning go the way you wish.’ The elder, holding a handkerchief, said: ‘Man of God, could you not save this
city with your Simeon from overthrow?’ Raising his hand, he shook the handkerchief over half the city, and immediately every building and structure fell; old
men and infants, men and women, both sexes were crushed and died. Seeing this, stupefied by the man’s appearance and the ruin’s sound, he fell to the ground
like one dead. The man raised his hand with the handkerchief over the city’s other half, but his two companions seized and entreated him with terrible oaths to
spare it. Calmed from fury, he restrained his hand and raised the fallen man: ‘Go home. Do not fear! Your sons, wife, and whole household are safe; none has
perished. Your constant prayer and daily alms to the poor protected you.’ Saying this, they vanished from his eyes and appeared no more. Returning to the city,
he found half destroyed with men and cattle; some extracted from ruins were dead, few found alive were disabled. Yet what the angel of the Lord, so to speak,
told him was not void: he found his whole household safe, lamenting only relatives’ deaths in other houses. The Lord’s right hand protected him and his house
amid the wicked, and he was saved from death’s dangers like Lot in Sodom.

### 25. Of the death of the man who said he was Christ

**[025]** In Gaul the often-mentioned disease invaded the province of Marseille. Severe famine oppressed Angers, Nantes, and Le Mans. These are the beginnings
of sorrows according to the Lord’s Gospel: There shall be pestilences, famines, and earthquakes in places; false Christs and false prophets shall arise and give
signs and wonders in heaven so as to lead the elect into error, as happened now. A man from Bourges, as he later confessed, entered a forest to cut wood for
some work when a swarm of flies surrounded him, causing him to be considered mad for two years; this shows it was a diabolical emission’s wickedness. Afterwards
passing neighbouring cities, he entered Provence and prayed dressed in skins like a religious. The adverse party, to mock him, gave him power of divination. To
advance in greater crime, he left that province and entered the Gévaudan, proclaiming himself great and fearlessly professing himself Christ, taking a woman as
his sister whom he called Mary. A multitude brought sick people whom he restored to health by touch. Those meeting him gave gold, silver, and clothing, which he
distributed to the poor to seduce more easily. Prostrating himself and praying with the woman, he rose and ordered those around to adore him. He foretold the
future, announcing disease to some, losses to others, and future salvation to a few; he did all this through diabolical arts and I know not what delusions. An
immense multitude was seduced, not only rustics but ecclesiastical priests. More than three thousand followed him. He began robbing and plundering those met on
the road, giving the spoil to those who had none. He threatened bishops and citizens with death because they disdained to adore him. Entering Le Puy’s territory
he approached Anicium and halted with his whole army near the basilicas, drawing up a line to war upon Bishop Aurelius, then residing there, sending before him
naked dancing and playing messengers to announce his coming. Astonished, the bishop sent vigorous men asking what he meant. One, their leader, bent as if to
kiss his knees and discuss his way, then ordered him seized and stripped. Immediately drawing his sword, he cut him to pieces. That Christ, who should rather be
called Antichrist, fell dead, and all with him dispersed. Mary was tortured and revealed all his phantasms and delusions. The men whom diabolical deception had
disturbed into believing him never returned to full sense, always professing him Christ and Mary a part of deity. Many others arose throughout Gaul, attaching
little women by such delusions who in frenzy confessed them saints, and presented themselves as great among the people. I saw many and tried by rebuke to recall
them from error.

### 26. Of the death of the bishops Ragnimodus and Sulpicius

**[026]** Ragnemod, bishop of Paris, also died. When his brother, the priest Faramod, sought the episcopate, a merchant named Eusebius, Syrian by race, was
substituted by giving many gifts. On obtaining the episcopate he expelled all his predecessor’s household and appointed Syrians of his own race as ministers of
the church house. Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, also died, and Eustasius, a deacon of Autun, obtained his see.

### 27. Of those whom Fredegund commanded to be slain

**[027]** A considerable dispute arose among the Franks of Tournai because one man’s son often angrily rebuked another’s son, who had married his sister, for
leaving his wife to visit a prostitute. As the offender did not amend, this anger rose so high that the young man rushed upon his relative and killed him and
his companions, but was himself struck down by those with whom the other had come; of both parties only one remained, for whom no assailant was left. The raging
relatives were often urged by Queen Fredegund to abandon enmity and become concordant lest persistent litigation grow into greater scandal. Unable to placate
them with gentle words, she restrained both with the axe. Inviting many to a feast, she made these three sit on one bench. When the meal lasted until night
covered the world and the table was removed according to Frankish custom, they remained seated as placed. Drinking much wine, they became so drunk that their
servants, soaked, slept in corners wherever each fell. Men appointed by the woman stood behind the three with three axes; while they talked, the servants’ hands
