failing from fasting, a thumb of marvelous whiteness appeared above the altar, shining with light. Recognizing the woman’s gift from God, she rose from the
pavement, had a little golden reliquary made, placed within it what she had been found worthy to receive through the Lord’s generosity, and returned joyfully to
her own home. In her was fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen I say to you, though he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet
because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs.” After this, three bishops came from their cities to venerate at this place and wished
to obtain a portion of this sacred pledge. Although it was placed in their midst, they could take nothing at all from it. Then, keeping vigil for one night,
they prayed that they might merit something from the thumb. A linen cloth was placed beneath it, and while they were trying to remove a portion, one drop of
blood fell from it onto the linen. Seeing this, they kept vigil for two more nights. Then, prostrate before the holy altar, they prayed that they might merit
something still greater from the thumb, and two more drops flowed from it. Rejoicing, they devoutly collected what the Lord had given and divided the linen with
its drops according to the number of his servants; they carried these into their cities, to great amazement. Because that place at Maurienne formerly belonged
to the city of Turin, at the time when Rufus was bishop his archdeacon said to him: “It is not right for this sacred pledge to be kept in a less important
place. Rise, take it, and carry it to the church of Turin, which is more populous.” Rufus replied that he did not dare do this. The archdeacon said: “I will
carry it, if you permit.” The bishop said: “Do as you please.” Then the archdeacon went to the place and, while celebrating vigils, put out his hand toward the
reliquary. Immediately driven out of his mind and seized by fever, he breathed his last on the third day. Great fear came upon everyone, and no one afterward
dared to move the blessed relics.

## 14

**[014]** In the city of Tours, while we were placing relics of the Precursor himself in the oratory of the forecourt of blessed Martin, a blind man received
his sight as someone led him by the hand. A possessed man who invoked the power of blessed John and of Bishop Martin was purified when the demon was expelled.
One of the girls whose duty it was to prepare the fuel for the lamp entered this oratory carrying a wax candle in order to perform her task. After arranging and
lighting the lamp, she drew the rope toward herself, raised the lamp high, tied the loops into a knot around a nail in the wall, and went away. When she
returned, the candle she carried in her hand went out. Going quickly back to the hanging lamp, she could neither reach the lamp to light the candle nor untie
the knot of the rope. While she stood perplexed about what to do, a flame suddenly dropped from the hanging lamp and lit the candle in her hand. Thus, with the
service of light going before her, she went where she wished. People also report that oil bubbles up from the lamp in this oratory, for relics of the holy cross
are kept there as well.

## 15

**[015]** Within the territory of this city, in the village of Langeais, a certain woman among the inhabitants sprinkled flour with water on the Lord’s day and
formed a loaf. She drew aside the hot coals and covered the loaf with glowing ashes to bake. As soon as she had done this, her right hand was kindled by divine
fire and began to be consumed. Crying out and lamenting, she sought the basilica of this village, in which relics of blessed John are kept. Pouring out prayer,
she vowed to perform no work on this day consecrated to the divine name, but only to devote herself to prayer. On the following night she made a wax candle
equal to her own height. Remaining in prayer throughout the night and holding the candle in her own hand the whole time, she came forth unharmed, the burning
having been extinguished.

## 16

**[016]** Since I have mentioned John the Baptist, it is fitting that I should also record something about the Jordan. Two springs rise from Mount Paneas, one
called Jor and the other Dan. Descending on either side of the city of Paneas, formerly called Caesarea Philippi, they join both their streams and their names
beneath the city itself and form the single Jordan, which flows as far as the city of Jericho and beyond. In it is the place where the Lord was baptized. At one
bend the water turns back upon itself, and there lepers are now cleansed. When they arrive, they wash repeatedly in the river until they are purified of their
disease. While they remain there, they receive food at public expense; once healed, they return to their own homes. Five miles from that place the Jordan itself
mingles with the sea and loses its name. It is called the Dead Sea because it was transformed by the fiery destruction of Sodom and the other cities, and its
water is mixed with bitumen; for this reason some call it the Sea of Bitumen. Anyone who does not know how to swim is borne upon its water, and sulfur adheres
around him.

## 17

**[017]** There are also hot waters near the city of Livias, in which Joshua son of Nun used to bathe, and there likewise lepers are cleansed. The place is
twelve miles from Jericho. Near Jericho there are trees that produce wool. They bear fruit shaped like gourds, with a hard shell around them, and inside they
are full of wool. People say that garments for Joshua son of Nun himself used to be made from these. Even today such trees yield wool; some was brought to us by
certain people, and we saw it and marveled at both its whiteness and fineness.

## 18

**[018]** Before this time I saw a man named John who had gone from Gaul suffering from leprosy. He said that he had remained for a whole year at the very place
where I have said the Lord was baptized. He washed continually in the river; restored to his former health, with his skin renewed for the better, he was healed.
Receiving relics of blessed Mary from Jerusalem, he was returning to his homeland, but first decided to go to Rome. When he entered the lonely wilderness of
Italy, he fell among robbers. Without delay he was stripped of his clothing, and the reliquary in which he carried the blessed pledges was also taken. Those
enemies supposed that a sum of gold sesterces had been gathered inside. Breaking its lock, they searched everything intently. Finding no money in it, they drew
out the relics and threw them into the fire, killed the man, and departed. But he rose half alive and, seeking at least to gather the ashes of the burned
relics, found them lying unharmed upon the glowing coals. He marveled that the very linen in which they had been wrapped was so intact that it seemed not to
have been cast upon the coals but taken out of water. He collected everything with joy, resumed the journey on which he had set out, and reached Gaul unharmed.
I have seen many who were cleansed of this disease after being immersed either in the Jordan or in the waters of the city of Livias.

## 19

**[019]** In the city of Tours there is a church consecrated in the name of Saint Mary the Virgin and John the Baptist, in which divine vengeance has appeared
against perjurers. A certain man entered this church intending to commit perjury. When he stood before the altar and raised his hand to utter the false oath, he
immediately fell backward and struck his head against the pavement so violently that he could scarcely be raised alive. Returning to his senses, he publicly
revealed the deceit of the perjury he had concealed. We ourselves have also seen certain people of Tours commit perjury in the same place who were so condemned
by divine judgment that within the course of that very year they departed from this world.

## 20

**[020]** As I have said, the city of Paneas is situated at the very first outflow of the Jordan. In it is a statue made of the purest metal, in which the form
of our Redeemer is said to be represented. As I have heard from many who have beheld it, a marvelous brightness is present in its face. Lest this seem absurd to
anyone, I will not hesitate to relate what Eusebius of Caesarea reports about it. He says: “It is established that the woman whom the Gospels record as having
been cured by the Savior while suffering from a flow of blood was a citizen of this city, and her house is still shown there. Before the doors of her house, on
a raised place, a certain base is displayed, upon which is seen a bronze image of the woman herself, as though fallen to her knees and extending her hands in
supplication. Beside it stands another statue, likewise cast in bronze, representing a man decorously wrapped in a robe and extending his right hand to the
woman. At the foot of this statue, on the base, a plant of a strange kind grows. When it has sprung up, it usually grows as far as the fringe of the garment on
that bronze robe. When the growing plant touches that fringe with its highest tip, it acquires power to drive away all diseases and infirmities. Whatever bodily
illness there may be, it is expelled by taking a small draft moistened with this healing herb. But it possesses no power at all if it is plucked before its
growth has touched the top of the bronze fringe. They reported that this statue was formed in the likeness of Jesus’ face. It remained even to my own times, as
I myself inspected with my own eyes. Nor is it surprising if those from the Gentiles who believed seemed to offer a gift of this kind to him in return for the
benefits they had received from the Savior, since even now I see images of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the Savior himself being drawn and pictures
painted.” So Eusebius reported.

## 21

**[021]** In my own time Christ is loved with such great love through undivided faith that believing people who keep his law upon the tablets of their hearts
also fasten his image, painted on visible tablets in commemoration of his power, throughout churches and houses. But in this matter too the enemy, always
jealous of the human race, is at work. A certain Jew had often seen an image of this kind painted on a wooden panel and fixed to a church wall. He said: “Behold
that deceiver who humbled me and my race!” Coming by night, he struck the image itself with a weapon. He knocked it from the wall, covered it with a cloth,
carried it to his house, and prepared to burn it in the flames. But a wonderful thing happened, one in which the power of God cannot be doubted: blood flowed
from the wound where the image had been pierced. The wicked attacker himself, overcome by fury, did not notice it. When he entered his house through the
darkness of the obscure night and brought a light, he saw himself entirely stained with blood. Fearing that his crime would be exposed, he hid the panel he had
thrown down in a dark place and did not dare touch again what he had wickedly presumed to carry away. When the Christians came to the house of God at dawn, they
did not find the image. Astonished and asking what had happened, they discovered traces of blood. Following these, they came to the Jew’s house. When they
questioned him about the panel, they learned nothing certain. But searching for it carefully, they found it in a corner of the Jew’s room. They restored it to
the church and overwhelmed the thief with stones.

## 22

**[022]** In the city of Narbonne, in the older church which glories in the relics of the blessed martyr Genesius, there is a painting that represents my
crucified Lord girded, as it were, with a linen cloth. While this painting was continually being viewed by the people, a terrible figure appeared in a vision to
a certain priest named Basil, saying: “All of you are covered with various garments, yet you continually look upon me naked. Go as quickly as possible and cover
me with clothing!” The priest did not understand the vision and, when day came, gave no thought to the matter. It appeared to him again, but he treated that
also as of little importance. Three days after the second vision, the figure afflicted him with severe blows and said: “Did I not tell you to cover me with
clothing so that I would not be seen naked? And you have done nothing about it. Go,” it said, “and cover with linen that painting in which I appear crucified,
lest swift destruction come upon you.” Shaken and greatly afraid, he related these things to the bishop, who immediately ordered a veil to be spread over it.
Thus the painting is now viewed covered. Even if it is uncovered briefly for contemplation, the veil is soon let down and covers it again, so that it is not
seen exposed.

## 23

**[023]** There is also that famous miracle of the springs of Spain which the province of Lusitania displays. At the field of Osen there is a pool carved in
ancient times and wonderfully constructed of variegated marble in the form of a cross. A building of great brilliance and height has also been constructed over
it by Christians. When the sacred day has arrived after the course of the departing year—the day on which the Lord, having confounded the betrayer, offered the
mystical supper to his disciples—the citizens gather at that place with the bishop, already perceiving the scent of the sacred perfume. After the priest has
offered prayer, they order the doors of the church to be secured with seals, awaiting the coming of the Lord’s power. On the third day, that is, the Sabbath,
when the people assemble for baptism, the bishop comes with his citizens, inspects the seals, and unlocks the closed doors. Wonderful to relate, they find full
the pool they had left empty. Indeed, it is filled to a higher heap, just as wheat is customarily piled above the rim of a measure. One may see the waters surge
this way and that without flowing off in any direction. Then, when the water has been sanctified with exorcism and chrism sprinkled over it, all the people draw
from it out of devotion and carry home a full vessel for their salvation, intending to protect their fields and vineyards with its most health-giving
sprinkling. Although a countless multitude of jars is filled from it, the heap is never diminished. But as soon as the first infant has been immersed, the water
immediately recedes; when everyone has been baptized and the waters have returned into themselves, they conclude with an unknown ending just as, I do not know
how, they begin from an unknown source.

## 24

**[024]** I will not remain silent about a certain heretic who neither feared God nor showed reverence for this holy place nor believed in his heart the miracle
that the Lord deigns to perform there to strengthen the faith of his people. He came with a troop of horses and ordered their baggage to be untied and placed in
the basilica and mangers to be prepared in it for the cavalry, wretchedly mocking what the inhabitants related about this place. As midnight passed, he was
seized by fever. Nearly lifeless and repenting too late, he cried out for the horses to be driven from the building. Although subject to the king, he
nevertheless possessed great power in that region. When the horses had been driven from the holy basilica, he turned upon himself and began to tear his own body
with his teeth. Because of his excessive raging, his attendants could not restrain him at all. At last, overwhelmed, he breathed out his spirit in their hands.
Theodigisilus, king of this region, saw this miracle performed at these springs consecrated to God and thought within himself: “It is a device of the
Romans”—for my people call those of my religion Romans—“that this should happen, and it is not the power of God.” Coming the following year, he secured the door
with his own seals together with the bishop’s seal and placed guards around the church, in case he might detect anyone involved in a deception by whose device
the water came into the springs. He did the same in another year. In the third year he assembled a multitude of men and ordered ditches to be dug around the
basilica, lest water be conducted into the spring through hidden channels. The ditches were nearly five feet deep and fifteen feet wide, but nothing concealed
could be found. Nevertheless, as he came to the end of his life—and I believe it was because of the rashness of this investigation—he was not found worthy to
see the day of the following year on which this mystery was celebrated, because he had presumed to investigate the secret of divine power. Relics of Saint
Stephen the Levite are kept there.

## 25

**[025]** Since, as I said above, that spring is filled by divine will for the ministry of baptism, and since, once it has been filled, the people eagerly
hasten to draw from it, a certain man took a small vessel and handed it to the priest who was distributing this water to be filled. While the elder was filling
it, the man stretched out his hand amid the pressing crowd toward another man’s belt and stole his knife. He put it back in its sheath and extended his hand to
receive the flask he had given the priest. When he had accepted it and moved to another place, he could not find even one drop of water in it. Greatly
confounded and recognizing that this had happened to him because of the theft, he returned the knife he had stolen to its owner. Then, when the flask was again
held out, he received it full of water. That people is heretical: seeing these mighty works, it is not moved to believe, but always craftily continues to attack
the mysteries of the divine commandments with the most wicked chatter of interpretations. Yet the power of the Lord destroys and confounds the opposing side.

## 26

**[026]** The apostle James, who is also called the brother of the Lord, is said to have been ordained bishop by my Lord Jesus Christ himself. After the Lord’s
glorious ascension, while James was attempting to open the way of justice to the erring Jews, he was thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple and dashed
against the ground. His brain was beaten out with a fuller’s club, and he yielded up his spirit. He was buried on the Mount of Olives, in the memorial that he
had built for himself earlier and in which he had buried Zechariah and Simeon. So much concerning the apostle James.

## 27

**[027]** The apostle Peter instituted the tonsure of the upper head to teach humility. Ordained bishop by the other apostles, he established his see at Rome.
Through his prayer and Paul’s, the cunning of Simon Magus was both exposed and overwhelmed. Even today in the city of Rome there are two hollows in a stone upon
which the blessed apostles, bending their knees, poured out prayer to the Lord against Simon Magus himself. When rainwater has collected in them, the sick seek
it, and drinking it immediately brings them health. As I said before, after the Neronian and Simonian conflicts the holy apostle Peter came to the cross. Having
completed the contest of the blessed trophy, he asked to be crucified with his feet turned upward toward heaven, crying out that he was unworthy to be exalted
in the same manner as the Lord. Thus directing his living spirit to the stars, he was buried in the temple formerly called the Vatican, which has four rows of
exceedingly admirable columns, ninety-six in number. It also has four at the altar, making one hundred altogether, besides those that support the canopy over
the tomb. This tomb, placed beneath the altar, is considered very remarkable. Anyone who wishes to pray opens the screens surrounding the place and approaches
above the tomb. Then, opening a small window and putting his head inside, he earnestly asks for whatever his need suggests. The result is not delayed, provided
only that the prayer offered is just. If someone wishes to obtain blessed relics, a small cloth that has just been weighed is placed inside. Then, keeping vigil
and fasting, the person prays most devoutly that the apostolic power will support his devotion. Wonderful to relate, if the person’s faith has prevailed, the
little cloth raised from the tomb is so filled with divine power that it weighs much more than it did when previously weighed. Then the one who raised it knows
that he has received with the apostle’s favor what he sought. Many also make golden keys to unlock the screens of the blessed tomb and bring earlier keys for a
blessing; with these the illnesses of the afflicted are cured. Undivided faith accomplishes all things. There are also four columns of marvelous elegance and
snow-white brilliance, which are said to support the canopy over the tomb.

## 28

**[028]** After a full year’s cycle had revolved, on the very day on which the apostle Peter suffered, the apostle Paul died at Rome, struck by the sword. Milk
and water flowed from his sacred body. Nor is it surprising that milk flowed from his body, for he both labored with and brought forth unbelieving nations and,
nourishing them with spiritual milk, led them to the solid food of the Holy Scriptures by unlocking their obscurities. I have heard many things about his
miracles, but from the great number I have undertaken to declare only one. It happened in a certain place that, at the devil’s instigation, a man prepared a
noose to take his own life. Finding a secluded room in which to do this, he passed a rope over a beam and began to tie a noose, yet he continually invoked the
name of the apostle Paul, saying: “Help me, Saint Paul!” Behold, a foul and deadly shade, whose countenance resembled nothing so much as the devil, appeared to
him and urged him: “Come, act, do not delay! Complete more quickly what you have begun.” While he prepared this deed—the taking of his own life—he kept saying:
“Most blessed Paul, be my helper!” At last, when the noose was ready and the shade was pressing him more violently to put in his neck, another shade suddenly
appeared, similar to the first, and said to the one that was with the man: “Flee, most wretched one! Behold, the apostle Paul is coming here! He has been
invoked by this man, and behold, he is present!” Then the shades vanished. The man returned to his senses and marked the cross of the Lord’s power upon his
faltering breast. With his cheeks drenched in a shower of tears, he did penance for having attempted this. It is therefore clear that this same man was saved
from this precipice of savage death through the power of the blessed apostle.

## 29

**[029]** John, apostle and evangelist of God, after completing the course both of his lawful contest and of his most salutary preaching, descended alive into a
tomb and ordered himself to be covered with earth. His sepulcher even now exudes manna like flour. Blessed relics made from it have been carried throughout the
whole world and bring health to the sick. This is the John whom the Lord loved more than the other apostles and who was distinguished by so great a love of
charity that, reclining upon the very breast of the sacred body, he drank in the secrets of the heavenly mysteries. To him also, as to a specially chosen
disciple, my Lord entrusted his glorious mother at the very hour of the Passion, when he was placed upon the cross for the salvation of the world. Concerning
him, after the resurrection, the Lord also said: “So I will him to remain until I come.” At Ephesus the place is shown where this apostle wrote the Gospel that
is read in church under his name. At the summit of that mountain there are four adjoining walls without a roof. He used to remain there devoting himself to
prayer and continually beseeching the Lord for the sins of the people. He obtained the favor that no rain should fall in that place until he had completed the
Gospel. Even to this day the Lord grants this: no rain falls there, nor does a violent shower come. In that city Mary Magdalene rests, with no covering above
her. In it also are the Seven Sleepers, about whom, God willing, I shall relate something later. There too the idol of Diana was destroyed by the apostle Paul.
But let me return to what I began.

## 30

**[030]** On the day of his solemnity the apostle Andrew produces a great miracle: manna like flour and oil with a nectar-like fragrance overflow from his tomb.
By this the fertility of the following year is shown. If only a little flows out, the earth yields little fruit; if it is abundant, it signifies that the fields
will have a great produce of fruits. People say that in some years so much oil overflows from the tomb that the stream runs as far as the middle of the
basilica. These things occur in the province of Achaia, in the city of Patras, where the blessed apostle and martyr, crucified for the Redeemer’s name, ended
this present life by a glorious death. When the oil flows down, it gives off such a fragrance that one would think a heap of many spices had been scattered
there. It is regarded among the people as a miracle and benefit, for anointings made with it or drinks given from it often bring relief to the sick. After his
glorious assumption, many miracles are said to have been shown both at this tomb and in various places where his relics have been deposited. I have not thought
it absurd to record a few of them, because the glory of the martyrs and the power of the saints are an edification of the Church. At the time when, after
Chlodomer king of the Franks had been killed, the army regrouped and devastated Burgundy, relics of the aforementioned apostle together with those of the martyr
Saturninus were kept in a certain basilica. The basilica was set on fire, and when the mass of its roof was already collapsing, the poor and elderly whom the
barbarians had left behind wept, saying: “Woe to us, who today are deprived of the aid of such great relics! No hope of the present life will remain for us if
these perish.” While they were weeping thus, a man of Tours arrived by God’s will. Sympathizing with their lamentations and knowing the power of the martyrs,
protected no less by faith than by a shield, he entered through the midst of the flames, seized the holy relics from the altar, and carried them outside without
being harmed by the fire. But immediately he was so constricted that he could not take another step forward. Judging himself unworthy to carry them, he selected
from among the captives a little girl who was a virgin, hung the reliquary around her neck, and thus returned safely to his homeland. He placed the relics on
the altar of the church of Neuilly, where no relics of saints had previously been kept, and each year celebrated their solemnities most devoutly. When his son
failed to do this after his father’s death, he suffered from quartan fever for a whole year and vowed to build a new basilica in their honor. When he had done
so, the fever departed and he was healed. Nor do I think it happened without divine providence that on the very day the blessed relics were transferred to
another basilica, men who had lost their way while carrying relics of blessed Vincent were brought to that village. At the priest’s request, they divided with
him a small portion of the relics, which he placed on the holy altar from which he had removed the others. When Mummolus, in the time of King Theudebert, was
traveling to the Emperor Justinian and furrowing the route to Constantinople by ship, he put in at the city of Patras, where this apostle is kept. While he
remained there with his attendants, his bladder became diseased and he developed stones. Then, afflicted by various pains, he was consumed by fever. Deprived of
pleasure in eating and drinking, he awaited only the approach of death. Seeing himself thus exhausted and without hope of life, he asked for his will to be
written. When it had been secured with signatures and seals, he ordered inquiry to be made whether anyone could be found in the city skilled in the art of
medicine who might help one about to die. When this was suggested to the bishop then presiding, he said: “How long, dearest friends, will you exhaust yourselves
with useless labor and seek medicine among men, when the heavenly physician is present here, one who often drives away the illnesses of the sick by the
operation of his own power without the aid of herbs?” “Who is he?” they asked. “Andrew,” he said, “the apostle of Christ.” When they reported this to the sick
man, he asked to be carried to the blessed tomb. Prostrate on the pavement, he faithfully prayed for what his need demanded. About the middle of the night sleep
overcame all who were present. Immediately the sick man felt the need to pass urine. Touching one of the boys, he asked in a faint voice for a small vessel to
be brought. When it was brought, as he tried to pass urine he emitted a large stone, so solid that as it fell it made a sound in the basin that had been
prepared. Then the fever departed with every pain, and he was restored unharmed to his ship.

## 31

**[031]** According to the history of his Passion, the apostle Thomas is recorded as having suffered in India. After a long time his blessed body was taken up
and transferred to the city the Syrians call Edessa, and was buried there. In the region of India, at the place where he first rested, there is a monastery and
a church of marvelous size, carefully decorated and furnished. God displays a great miracle in this building. A lamp placed there and lit shines perpetually day
and night by divine will before the site of his burial, receiving no fuel of oil or rush. It is neither extinguished by wind nor destroyed by accident nor
diminished by burning. It possesses an increase through the apostle’s power which is not known by man but is known only to the divine power. Theodore, who
visited that very place, explained this to us.

## 32

**[032]** In the aforementioned city, where I have said the blessed limbs are buried, a great assembly of people gathers when the feast arrives. People coming
from various regions with prayers and merchandise are granted permission to sell and buy for thirty days without any collection of tolls. During these days,
which fall in the fifth month, great and unusual benefits are granted to the people. No quarrel arises among the crowd, no fly touches slaughtered flesh, and no
water is lacking to the thirsty. On other days water must be drawn there from wells more than one hundred feet deep, but now one need dig only a little to find
waters overflowing in abundance. There is no doubt that these things are bestowed through the apostle’s power. When the days of the festival have ended, tolls
are paid to the public treasury, the flies that had been absent return, and the nearness of the water disappears. Then rain sent from heaven washes the entire
forecourt of the church so thoroughly of the filth and various refuse produced during those solemnities that one would think it had never been trodden upon.

## 33

**[033]** As the sacred history of the apostles relates, Stephen, the first deacon of the Holy Church and its first martyr, was overwhelmed with stones at
Jerusalem for the holy name of Christ, whom he beheld at the right hand of the Power in spiritual contemplation, and he prayed to that Majesty for his
persecutors. There was an oratory in the city of Tours dedicated by the ancients in his name, which I ordered to be extended a little. When this had been done,
I moved the altar forward, still intact as it was. Searching in its cavity, I found none of the holy relics that report said were there. Then I sent one of the
abbots to bring me relics of Stephen from the oratory of the cathedral house, but I forgot to hand him the key to the reliquary, which hung from my belt. When
the abbot arrived, he took the seal from the cupboard but found the reliquary locked. He hung in uncertainty about what to do. If he returned to me, it was a
long journey there and back. If he brought the reliquary itself, he knew it would trouble me because relics of many saints were kept there. If he did not do so,
he would not fulfill the order he had received. What more need be said? While he held the reliquary doubtfully in his hand, the fastenings sprang open with a
sound, and he saw the reliquary unlocked. Then, giving thanks, he took the relics and brought them to me amid great amazement. After Mass had been said, I
deposited them, with the Lord’s guidance. When I returned to the city many days later, I found the reliquary locked with its bolt pushed back, just as I had
left it. A portion of the blessed blood of this most holy Levite, as is widely reported, is kept on the altar of the church of Bourges. In the time of Bishop
Felix, a certain man accused his neighbors of some crime. He frequently provoked them with insolent words and summoned them before the public tribunal, until
the leading men of the city decreed that those who had been accused should clear themselves of this charge by oath. They entered the sanctuary of the
aforementioned church and raised their hands to utter their oaths, but the prosecutor declared in a loud voice that they were committing perjury. Immediately
his feet were lifted into the air and he was dashed down, striking his head on the pavement; the surrounding crowd saw him nearly lifeless. After almost two
hours, when it was thought that he would breathe out his spirit, he opened his eyes and confessed his crime, declaring that he had unjustly harassed the men and
falsely proclaimed them guilty. Thus the innocent were released, the guilty man exposed, and the power of the blessed saint made manifest. In the city of
Bordeaux there was an old woman burdened with age but sustained by integrity of faith. It was her custom to enter the basilicas of the saints, supply oil, and
light the lamps. To perform this task she entered the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on Saturday night. The pulpit of this altar is set on high; its
lower part is closed by a door like a crypt and likewise contains its own altar with relics of the saints. The venerable woman devoutly descended into it to
light the lamp, as I have said, accompanied by only one little girl. While she was doing this work and approaching night covered the world in darkness, clerics
came, said the appointed psalms, locked the door of the crypt, and departed, unaware that the woman was inside. Having lit the lamp, she hurried to the door to
go out. Finding it closed, she cried out and called by name the person who ought to open it for her. But because of her age her voice was not strong enough to
penetrate these barriers. Realizing that no one heard her, she lay prostrate on the pavement and said: “I will pray for my sins and for the people to the Lord,
creator of all, until someone comes who can unlock the entrance to this building.” Remaining awake in prayer, she saw, about the middle of the night, the doors
opened and the whole basilica shining with immense light. Behold, a choir of psalm-singers entered the basilica! After they had sung the Gloria to the Trinity
and their psalmody had fallen silent, she heard men speaking among themselves: “The holy Levite Stephen is delaying me. I ought already to have visited other
basilicas, and I cannot unless he who is expected arrives first.” While they repeated this frequently, a man in a white garment suddenly arrived. All that
venerating multitude humbly greeted him, saying: “Bless me, sacred and holy Levite Stephen.” Greeting them in turn and offering prayer, he was asked why he had
delayed a little in visiting the holy places. He replied: “A ship at sea was in danger of sinking. I was invoked there and stood by it; having rescued it,
behold, I am here. And so that you may prove that what I say is true, you can see that the garment I wear is still wet with the sea waves and dripping with
drops of water.” The woman, pressing the pavement with great trembling, watched intently. When they departed and the doors were again divinely locked, she went
to the place where the saint had stood and carefully collected with a handkerchief the drops that had fallen on the pavement. She revealed this to Bertram, who
then governed the city as bishop. Receiving it with joy and great amazement, he kept it with him. Many sick people experienced healing through this
handkerchief, and the bishop himself often took relics from it and faithfully deposited them when he consecrated churches. I learned these things from the
bishop’s own account.

## 34

**[034]** The history of his contest relates that the apostle Bartholomew suffered in Asia. Many years after his Passion, when persecution again came upon the
Christians, the pagans saw all the people flocking to his tomb and continually bringing prayers and incense. Incited by envy, they took away his body, placed it
in a lead coffin, and threw it into the sea, saying: “You will no longer deceive my people.” But through the cooperation of God’s providence in the secret
working of his purpose, the lead coffin was lifted from that place and borne by the waters to the island called Lipari. It was revealed to the Christians that
they should collect him. They gathered and buried him and built a great church over him. Invoked there now, he shows that he benefits the people through many
miracles and favors.

## 35

**[035]** As is read in his Passion, the martyr Clement was cast into the sea with an anchor suspended from his neck. Now, on the day of his solemnity, the sea
recedes for three miles. Offering a dry path to those who walk, it allows them to reach the martyr’s tomb. There the people pay their vows and pray, then return
to the shore. It happened that at one celebration a woman came to the place with her little son. After the solemnities had been performed, while she was
feasting, the infant fell asleep. Meanwhile the sound of the approaching sea was suddenly heard. Forgetting her child, the woman began hurriedly to seek the
shore with the rest of the people. When she had reached the shore as the sea came in behind her, she remembered that she had left her son. Cast down upon the
ground with great weeping, crying out that she was wretched, she filled the shores with her cries and ran around the banks in case anyone had seen her drowned
child cast up on the shore. Finding no trace, she was at last comforted by her relatives and taken home, spending the whole year in grief and lamentation. When
the cycle of the year returned, she came again to await the martyr’s solemnity, hoping perhaps to find some trace of her little child. What more need be said?
As the sea receded, she went ahead of everyone entering and was herself the first to reach the tomb. Prostrate on the ground, she completed her prayer and rose,
her cheeks abundantly wet with showers of tears. Turning her face to one side, she saw her son still held in sleep in the very place where she had left him
sleeping. Thinking he was dead, she came nearer as though to gather up a lifeless corpse. But recognizing that he was asleep, she quickly roused him and, while
the people looked on, lifted him unharmed in her arms. Amid kisses she asked where he had been during the space of the year. He said he did not know that a
whole year had passed; he thought he had slept in pleasant slumber for the space of only one night.

## 36

**[036]** There was an abundant spring on an estate within the territory of the city of Limoges. Its water both refreshed the produce of gardens and the
cultivation of fields by its approach and made them fertile by its force. Channels were made to conduct it through necessary places, so that human effort might
supply what nature did not provide. With its vein overflowing, it had such sweet streams that you would see a vegetable or shrub rejoice if it had been
irrigated by it. The grace of the divine Majesty also assisted it, so that wherever its stream was directed, shoots quickly received increase. While the
inhabitants were directing it through every place as though in play, the ground opened—as I believe, through the envy of the Adversary—and the spring issued
forth, scattering its waters, about twelve stades away in the middle of a marsh where it could accomplish no useful work at all. Fear immediately seized
everyone’s mind, for something strange had come upon the region. The inhabitants awaited its destruction and at the same time lamented with continual weeping
the benefit they had been accustomed to enjoy. The course of one year and then another passed in this dryness. Everything in that place which the spring had
been accustomed to irrigate dried up with thirst. In the third year it happened that a traveler brought relics of the blessed martyr Clement, whom I have
already mentioned, and delivered them to Aridius, a priest of that city and a man religious in all holiness. The grieving neighborhood looked to him day and
night, trusting in his prayer that, if he petitioned the Lord, he could restore the spring to its place. He said: “Let us go, dearest friends. If what my bearer
asserted is true—that these are relics of the martyr Clement—it will now appear when his power has been manifested.” He went with psalm-singing to the site of
the spring. After the psalms had been said, he prostrated himself in prayer. Placing the holy relics at the very entrance of the spring, he asked that he who
once had opened an abundant stream for the condemned in the desert to cut through rock would, through Clement’s intercession, again recall to this place the
waters that his merciful kindness had formerly bestowed. Immediately the vein rushed back to its entrance, vomiting forth great waters, and flowing along it
filled the channel it had formerly occupied. While the people marveled, immense thanks were rendered to the Lord, who both revealed the martyr’s power and
deigned to fulfill the prayer of his faithful servant.

## 37

**[037]** As the history of his Passion declares, after receiving the crown of martyrdom together with the virgin Daria, the martyr Chrysanthus bestowed many
benefits of healing upon the people. For this reason a crypt of wonderful workmanship was built over them, vaulted in the form of arches and standing with the
greatest stability. When a crowd of people had gathered for their feast, a most wicked emperor ordered a wall to be erected at the entrance to the crypt,
shutting in the multitude, and commanded the building to be covered with sand and stones. A great mound arose above it. The written account of their contest
most certainly testifies that this was done. The crypt long remained covered beneath this shroud, until the city of Rome abandoned its idols and submitted to
Christ the Lord. As time went on, the place of this burial was known to no one, until it was revealed and disclosed by the Lord Jesus. On one side of the place,
separated by an intervening wall, are the tombs of the martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria; on the other side the bodies of the remaining saints have been gathered
together. The builder left an open window in the wall placed between them, so that an entrance for viewing might lie open to those contemplating the saints’
bodies. People also say that when those who had come to the sacred solemnities were shut in, the men had brought with them silver pitchers fashioned from metal,
containing wine offered for the sacrifice of the divine oblation. It is evident that the silver remained there, and it can still be seen today by those who
look. But because the human mind continually gapes after base and shameful desires, a certain subdeacon saw the silver through the window and thought to himself
what, driven by avarice, he later carried out. Rising by night, he entered the basilica of the saints, then went through the window into the chamber. Feeling
with his hands in the darkness, he took some of the pitchers. Wishing to leave with his plunder, he circled throughout the entire night but could never find the
entrance by which he had come in. When day came, wishing to conceal his deed because he was conscious of his guilt, according to the Lord’s saying, “Everyone
who does evil hates the light, lest his works be exposed,” he hid himself in a corner of the chamber all day so as not to be seen. On the following night he
again sought the entrance but could not find it; he did this through the course of three nights. On the third day, tormented by hunger, he approached the window
before the people, abandoned the silver, confessed his deed, and came outside in great shame. The crime he had committed was not hidden from the people who were
present. Much later, when Damasus, bishop of the holy apostolic see, learned what had happened, he ordered the window to be more carefully covered and adorned
the place with verses. There my Lord Jesus Christ is blessed in praise of his name to this day.

## 38

**[038]** Not far from the wall of this city is also the martyr Pancras, a mighty avenger against perjurers. If anyone’s insane mind wishes to utter an empty
oath at his tomb, before he reaches the tomb—that is, before he comes as far as the screens beneath the arch where the clerics customarily stand singing
psalms—he is immediately either seized by a demon or falls upon the pavement and loses his spirit. Therefore, whenever anyone wishes to elicit from another an
assurance of good faith concerning any matter, so as to know the truth, he sends him nowhere else than to this basilica. They say that many people living near
the basilicas of the apostles or other martyrs seek no other church for this purpose than that of blessed Pancras, so that, with the judgment of his severity
making a public distinction, hearers may either believe the truth or experience the blessed martyr’s judgment for deceit.

## 39

**[039]** There are many martyrs in the city of Rome whose complete histories of their Passions have not been brought to me. Concerning Bishop John, however,
since no written account of his contest has reached me, I could not remain silent about what I learned from faithful people. When he came to the episcopate, he
detested heretics with the greatest zeal and dedicated their churches to Catholic worship. When King Theodoric learned this, he was inflamed with fury because
he was devoted to the Arian sect. He ordered gladiators to be sent throughout Italy to slaughter the entire Catholic population, however many they found.
Hearing this, blessed John approached the king to entreat him not to do these things. The king received him deceitfully, bound him, and placed him in prison,
saying: “I will make sure that you no longer dare to mutter against my sect.” The saint of God was so worn down by injuries in prison that not long afterward he
breathed out his spirit. He died gloriously in prison in the city of Ravenna. The mercy of the Lord immediately brought vengeance upon the wicked king. Suddenly
struck by God and exhausted by great blows, he perished and at once received the perpetual burning of flaming Gehenna.

## 40

**[040]** Great is the dignity of the Christian name, if you pursue in deed what you confess in faith. As the apostle says: “Faith without works is dead in
itself.” Just as it is not carnal descent but faith that makes the sons of Abraham, so works, not merely the grace of the name, make true Christians. Through
this name darkness is illuminated, serpents flee, idols are overthrown, the soothsayer ceases, the diviner wastes away, and worshipers of demons are driven off.
My Prudentius mentions in his book against the Jews that an emperor proceeding to the foul sacrifice of demons adored the gods, prostrated himself before their
images, and awaited the priests of the idols as they slaughtered herds of cattle whose foreheads, bound with laurel, were struck with axes. While the elders
handled the portions of the internal organs with bloody hands and attempted to discover something divine by examining the lobes of the liver and the entrails
among the vital organs, he saw that everything was disturbed and could not recognize with certainty what he wished to know. Troubled, he exclaimed: “Alas, alas!
I do not know what is happening here, but it is thought to be contrary to my gods. I see my gods departing far away and tasting nothing of the sacrifices
prepared. As the matter itself shows, there is present here someone from the service of certain gods who are accustomed to oppose me. It will be astonishing if
some worshiper of the Christians’ God, whom they declare was crucified, does not drive my gods to this flight. The censers of incense grow cold, the fire on the
altars cools, and the very blade applied to the victims is seen to become blunt. Inquire now, most sacred Augustus, who stands here washed with water and
anointed with balsam, and let him depart immediately, so that the gods I invoke may approach.” Saying this, as though he beheld Christ himself, the avenger of
these things, he fell lifeless to the ground and proclaimed that the deities had been offended. Then the emperor himself put aside his diadem and said: “Who
here is hostile to my deities and an associate of the Christian religion, who bears his forehead marked with the sign of chrism and adores the wood of the
cross? Let him declare it without delay.” Then one of the emperor’s bodyguards, placed in their midst, threw his weapons to the ground and said: “I am he whose
God is Christ, washed in his baptism and redeemed by his cross. I continually invoked his name while your priests were consecrating to demons these things set
before them. Your gods flee his name, nor can they stand in a place where the name of such great Majesty has been invoked.” As the youth spoke, the astonished
and trembling emperor left the temple of demons. So great a fear of God kindled all who stood there that no one followed Augustus to the palace. Instead, all
raised their hands and eyes to heaven and with one mouth and one accord praised Christ the Lord, invoking him with suppliant voices to be their helper. Lest
this account seem incredible to anyone, I will append a few of Prudentius’s verses:

“Yet among all the princes there was one—not he whom I remember from the boy’s story—the strongest leader in arms, founder and most renowned maker of laws,
counselor of his country in speech and hand, but not a counselor for adopting religion, a lover of three hundred thousand gods. He bent his Augustan head before
the feet of image-made Minerva, licked the sandals of Juno, threw himself at the feet of Hercules, and covered Diana’s knees with wax. Then, sacrificing at the
gate, the old man, customarily crowned with fillets, appeased Achates with much blood. With bloody hands he handled the throbbing organs, cold with mortal
chill, and, a skilled interpreter, marked the last pulses of life in the warm heart with measures and an end. Suddenly, amid the sacrifices, the pale priest
cried out: ‘Behold, what am I doing? Something greater, best of kings, something greater—I know not what divinity—comes between me and my altars. I see the
summoned shades scattering far away. Certainly some one of the Christian youths has stolen in here. The fillet and every couch of the gods tremble at this race
of men. Let the washed and anointed man depart far away, so that fair Proserpina may return to the restored rites.’ He spoke and fell down bloodless, as though
he beheld Christ himself threatening with a drawn thunderbolt. The prince also, lifeless, put aside his diadem, grew pale, and looked around at those standing
by to see whether any nursling of chrism had marked his temples with the signed wood and with his forehead disturbed the Zoroastrian whispers. One bodyguard
from the troop of golden-haired boys, keeper of the purple, is discovered in hiding. He does not deny it; he throws down his gemmed spears with their twin
blades and confesses that he bears the sign of Christ. The prince sprang up, the terrified priest having fallen, and fled the marble shrine with no companion,
while the trembling cohort, forgetting its master, raised upturned faces to heaven and called upon Jesus.”

I have inserted only these verses into my reading to confirm what I have related, showing of what benefit the Christian name and the standard of the cross are
to those who, believing in faith, accomplish in deed what they have believed, as was said above.

## 41

**[041]** In a certain place there was a church consecrated to blessed Lawrence both by relics and by name, which through the neglect of a long period had
become badly unroofed. When the inhabitants wished to restore it, they went to the forests, cut and smoothed timber, made beams, placed them on wagons, and
brought them to the site. When these were laid out on the ground to begin the work, one was found to be too short. Great grief immediately seized the priest
overseeing the work. Weeping bitterly, he did not know what to do or where to turn. Then, looking at the shorter oak beam, he said: “O most blessed Lawrence,
glorified when placed upon the fire, always cherishing and refreshing the poor, consider my poverty. My resources are too small for me to provide another here.”
Immediately, while all were astounded, the beam grew to so great a length that a large part had to be cut off. The people, thinking it wrong to lose such
benefits and believing that the beam had been touched and lengthened by the martyr’s hand, broke off the surplus piece by piece and often drove away various
illnesses with it. The priest Fortunatus described this in these verses:

“Lawrence, deservedly burned with life-giving flames, who return from the fire a victor through fervent faith: while the people renewed the church with too
short an oak, the beams grew, and nourishing faith grew also. When the timber was too short, it stretched itself by your reward; how small it was before,
afterward it had to be cut. The tree deserved to grow more when cut by axes, and with dry foliage it learned to be longer. The people obtain health from the
part cut off; if the blind man comes fearless, he receives sight.”

He wrote many more verses about this, which I have omitted, writing only these as testimony to the man. These events occurred at Briona, a fortress in Italy. I
myself saw a man suffering severely from toothache receive a little piece of this wood from a priest. As soon as he touched the tooth, he was immediately free
of pain. Nor did I think I should remain silent about relics of Lawrence rescued from an enemy fire and brought into the Limousin by a certain man. Although he
was repeatedly admonished in visions to deliver them to Abbot Aridius, he did not fulfill the command. He himself, his wife, and his whole household began to
fall ill. Compelled by necessity, he delivered them to the holy man and immediately departed restored to health.

## 42

**[042]** Cassian, martyr of Italy and a distinguished teacher of boys, was handed over by the persecutors’ judgment, when persecution arrived, to his own young
and tender flock. Thirsting for their master’s blood, they struck his head with their waxed tablets, cut him with the broad ends of their styli, and pierced his
limbs with their small points. Thus they made their master a martyr worthy of God. Such fear is observed in his honor to this day that no one has dared to touch
any of his belongings. If anyone does so, he is either seized by a demon or consumed by sudden death; in either case he does not escape vengeance unpunished.

## 43

**[043]** Agricola and Vitalis were crucified for Christ’s name at Bologna, a city of Italy. As I have learned through revelations made to faithful people—for
the history of their Passion has not yet reached me—their tombs are placed above the ground. When many people, as usually happens, touched them with their hands
or kissed them with their mouths, the custodian of the church was admonished to keep the unclean away from them. A certain bold and criminal man removed the
covering of one tomb in order to take some of the sacred ashes. Putting his head inside, he was pressed down by it and, scarcely freed by others, went away
confounded. He was not found worthy to receive what he had presumed to take by rash daring, and thereafter approached the saints’ tombs with greater reverence.
Another man, transporting public taxes, negligently lost a bag of money while traveling. Approaching the city, he realized that he had lost the public funds he
was carrying. Prostrate before the tombs of the blessed martyrs, he prayed with tears that through their power he might recover what was lost, so that he, his
wife, and his children would not be reduced to captivity because of it. Going outside into the forecourt, he met the man who had found the money lying in the
road. Upon careful inquiry, the man said that he had found the bag at the very hour when this man had implored the martyrs’ aid. Namatius, bishop of the
Auvergne, devoutly sought their relics in order to place them in the church he had built. He sent a priest there, who departed with God’s grace and brought back
what he had sought. Returning with his companions, he took quarters five miles from the city of Clermont and sent messengers to the bishop to direct what they
should do. When morning came, the bishop admonished the citizens and hurried most devoutly with crosses and wax candles to meet the holy relics. When the priest
offered to let him see the blessed relics if he commanded, he said: “It is better for me to believe these things than to see them. I read in the Holy
Scriptures, and the Lord himself declared blessed those who believed in him although they had not seen him.” With the bishop’s faith prevailing, the Lord
glorified his saints by a miracle. As they came on, the sky suddenly darkened and a dark and dreadful rain fell upon them. Such a quantity of rain poured down
there that rivers could be seen running along the roads. Yet around the holy relics, over an area of fully one iugerum, not even one drop was seen to fall. As
they proceeded, the rain followed them at a distance as though rendering service, refreshing the people but not touching the bearers of the relics. Seeing this,
the bishop magnified the Lord, who, thus favoring his faith, deigned to work such things for the glory of the saints. Assembling the citizens, he dedicated the
holy church, now illumined by these relics, with great joy and devotion.

## 44

**[044]** The illustrious martyr Victor is also magnified in the city of Milan because he often releases the bound from prisons and permits captives to depart
free. At one time Apollinaris went to Italy with Duke Victorius, who is reported to have been killed at Rome. The inhabitants held Apollinaris as a captive,
saying: “You will not see your homeland; as his attendant, you will pay a deserved penalty.” After uttering these threats, they sent him into exile in Milan.
When the feast of Saint Victor arrived and the people assembled, Apollinaris attended the vigils, for he was being watched under a form of free custody.
Prostrate before the saint’s sacred tomb, he began to pray even more earnestly than usual that the martyr’s power would free him from this exile. About the
middle of the night he went out of the building and heard one poor man say to another: “What do you think, fellow pauper, is the power of this martyr? I speak
truly and am not deceived: tonight any captive who slips away by flight will depart released to his homeland and will never be found again.” Apollinaris
received these words as an omen sent by God’s will. Again and again prostrating himself at the martyr’s tomb, he prayed that, aided by the martyr’s power, he
might depart without hindrance. Soon calling a boy, he ordered a horse to be saddled, saying: “Today I am to be released from this bond of custody.” They
mounted and crossed the Alpine ridges, which were filled with a multitude of drifts, and were carried to the Auvergne. The blessed martyr’s power went before
them so that no one asked where they were going or whence they had come. It is clear that they were saved from this affliction by the blessed martyr’s
protection.

## 45

**[045]** In this same city is the basilica of Saint Lawrence the Levite, whom I mentioned above. There a crystal chalice of admirable beauty was kept. During a
certain solemnity, while it was being carried by a deacon to the holy altar, it slipped from his hand, fell to the ground, and was shattered into fragments.
Pale and bloodless, the deacon carefully gathered the fragments of the vessel and placed them on the altar, not doubting that the martyr’s power could make it
whole. After spending the night in vigils, tears, and prayer, he looked for the chalice and found it restored whole upon the altar. When this miracle was
announced to the people, it kindled their spirits with such devotion that they asked the bishop to celebrate a new annual solemnity to God in the martyr’s
honor. Then the bishop of the place suspended the chalice above the altar and instituted a most devout celebration both then and for each year thereafter.

## 46

**[046]** In this city are kept the victorious bodies of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which, as the history of their Passion itself relates,
long lay hidden in a pit. Revealed to blessed Ambrose and found by him, they were buried, with miracles displayed, in the basilica he had built at his own
initiative. Relics of them especially illumine the older churches of Tours and, with God’s favor, have been spread throughout the whole compass of Gaul. On one
occasion certain religious men discussed why the aforementioned relics had been distributed so densely through individual places. What I heard someone relate
about them I have not thought absurd to insert in my reading, because it is not contained in the history of their Passion. He said that when these glorious
bodies were transferred into that church and the solemnity of Mass was being celebrated in the martyrs’ honor, a panel fell from the ceiling, struck the
martyrs’ heads, and drew out a stream of blood. Linen cloths, small garments, and church veils were stained with it, and the blessed blood was collected. It is
said to have flowed until enough linens were found to receive it. From this an abundance of their relics was collected and spread throughout all Italy and Gaul.
Saint Martin received many of them, as the letter of the most blessed Paulinus relates. As for the limbs of Saint Nazarius and the boy Celsus, whose suffering
at Embrun, a city of Gaul, is related by the account of their contest, these too were buried secretly because of pagan persecution, so that they might be
consigned to oblivion in later times. The man who related what I have just told about the aforementioned saints used to say that a pear tree had grown over
these tombs and that a poor man had made a little garden on this site which enclosed the tree. When it bore fruit in due season according to its nature, any
sick person held by any illness who bit off a fruit immediately recovered as the disease departed. The poor man derived great profit from this. But when the
martyrs revealed themselves and ordered the tree to be cut down, the poor man broke into loud weeping and would not allow it. After he had been removed and the
pear tree cut down, a basilica of wonderful workmanship was built. Relics of blessed Genesius, martyr of Arles, are also venerated on its altar. The poor man
was so distinguished by faith that he was thereafter found worthy of the priesthood in this church.

## 47

**[047]** The martyr Saturninus, as is reported, was ordained by disciples of the apostles and sent to the city of Toulouse. At the pagans’ instigation he was
bound to the feet of a wild bull, thrown down the steps of the Capitol, and ended his present life with the structure of his skull shattered. When certain
religious people were transferring his relics to another region, the course of their journey brought them past the boundary of the district of Brivat in the
territory of the Auvergne. As the sun was setting, they turned aside to the lodging of a certain poor man and asked for the accommodation they needed. Received
by the man, they told him what they were carrying. Moved by regard for hospitality and by fear of God, he placed the reliquary in his store chamber and set it
on top of the grain kept in a vessel. When morning came, the men took the relics, thanked the man, and went on the journey they had begun. On the following
night the man was admonished in a vision, someone saying to him: “Do not remain in this place, for it has been sanctified by the relics of the martyr
Saturninus.” Thinking little of the vision, he gave no further consideration, as a rustic would, to what he had been admonished about. Without delay he fell
into misfortune. His small resources gradually began to diminish, and his wife to waste away from another disease. What more need be said? Within one year he
was reduced to such poverty that nothing remained with which he could feed or clothe himself, as human necessity demands. At last coming to his senses, he said
to his wife: “I have sinned before God and his saints by not departing from this little lodging as I was admonished. I know that the evils I suffer have come
upon me for this reason. Now let me obey the vision I saw and remove this little lodging from the place, so that I may be saved.” He removed the hut and erected
an oratory formed of wooden boards. Pouring out prayer there daily, he implored the blessed martyr’s help. At last the blows ceased. When he put his hand to
work, such an abundance of produce followed that within a short time he recovered more than he had lost. These events occurred within my own territory. Nor will
I remain silent about this, to crush the pride of the wicked: in the time of King Chlothar, a certain Plato came to the monastery of Pauliac, in whose oratory
relics of this saint are kept. Because he had not received some gift from the abbot, he is reported to have said: “I will make this church a house of the king,
in one corner of which his horses will be fed.” Departing in fury and preparing to go to the prince, he was seized by fever and breathed out his spirit on the
third day. Descending swiftly to hell, he left the house of God to the worship of him whose name it had previously been consecrated to bear.

## 48

**[048]** These are the names of the forty-eight martyrs said to have suffered at Lyons: Vettius Epagathus, Zacharias, Macharius, Alcibiades, Silvius, Primus,
Alpius, Vitalis, Comminius, October, Philominus, Geminus, Julia, Albina, Grata, Aemilia, Postumiana, Pompeia, Rhodona, Biblis, Quarta, Materna, Elpenipsa, and
Stamas. These were given over to beasts: Sanctus, Maturus, Alexander, Ponticus, and Blandina. These yielded up their spirits in prison: Arescius, Photinus,
Cornelius, Zotimus, Titus, Zoticus, Julius, Aemilia, Gamnitae, Pompeia, Alumna, Mamilia, Justa, Trifima, Antonia, and blessed Bishop Photinus. The wicked judge
ordered their holy bodies to be committed to the fire and their burned ashes to be scattered in the Rhône. After these things had been done, while the
Christians were in deepest grief, thinking that the blessed relics had perished, the martyrs appeared by night to faithful men, standing whole and unharmed in
the place where they had been committed to the flames. Turning to the men, they said: “Let my relics be collected from this place, because none of me has
perished. From here I have been translated to the rest promised me by Christ, king of heaven, for whose name I suffered.” Those men reported this to the other
Christians, who gave thanks to God and were strengthened in faith. Gathering the sacred ashes, they built a basilica of marvelous size in their honor and buried
the blessed relics beneath the holy altar, where they continually declared by manifest miracles that they dwell with God. The place where they suffered is
called Ainay, and for that reason the martyrs themselves are called by some the Martyrs of Ainay.

## 49

**[049]** The glorious Bishop Photinus, who presided as priest over the city of Lyons, was consummated in martyrdom and carried into heaven through the merit of
his noble contest. Bishop Irenaeus, worthy of him both in merit and holiness, succeeded him and himself also ended in martyrdom. He is buried beneath the altar
in the crypt of the basilica of blessed John. The martyr Epipodius is buried on one side and Alexander on the other. If dust is collected from their tombs with
faith, it immediately heals the sick. Great brightness is present in that crypt, which, I believe, marks the merit of the martyrs.

## 50

**[050]** Benignus, witness to the Lord’s name, was consummated in martyrdom at the fortress of Dijon. Because he was placed in a large stone coffin after his
martyrdom, people of my time, especially blessed Bishop Gregory, thought that some pagan had been buried there. Rustics made vows there and quickly obtained
what they sought. A certain man who received many benefits from the blessed tomb brought a wax candle, lit it, and returned home. A very small boy watching this
went down to the tomb after the man had left, intending to extinguish and carry away the burning candle. As he descended, behold, a serpent of marvelous size
came from the other side and coiled around the candle. The frightened boy went back up and tried two or three times to take the candle, but the snake prevented
him. When these and similar things were reported to the blessed bishop, he did not believe them at all; rather, he strongly protested against their worshiping
there. At last God’s martyr revealed himself to the blessed confessor and said: “What are you doing? Not only do you despise me, but you also reject those who
honor me. Please do not do so; quickly prepare a covering over me.” Shaken by this vision, the bishop visited the blessed tomb and there, weeping, long begged
pardon for his ignorance. Because the ancient vaulted crypt there had fallen into ruin, the blessed bishop rebuilt it, covering it with an elegant vault. But
for some reason the holy tomb ended up outside. Wishing to transfer it inside, he assembled abbots and other religious men for this service. At this gathering
the blessed martyr performed a great miracle for the people and his confessor. As I said above, that stone coffin was so heavy that in my time even three pairs
of oxen could not drag such a weight. While they delayed for a long time and could not discover how to carry it inside, Saint Gregory, with wax candles lit and
loud psalm-singing, took hold of the coffin at the martyr’s head. Two priests moved it at the feet, and they carried it into the crypt with the greatest ease
and placed it where they wished. It was no small spectacle for the people. A few years later the blessed confessor received the history of Benignus’s Passion
brought by travelers to Italy. The holy martyr afterward manifested himself to the people through many miracles. Without delay Gregory ordered a great basilica
to be built over that crypt. Nearby is another basilica in which a certain religious woman named Paschasia is venerated. At that time the builders saw an old
woman come out of this basilica, beautiful in her black clothing, swan-white hair, and countenance. She addressed the builders: “Come, dearest friends, complete
the good work. Let the machines by which this structure is raised be lifted. It is rightly hastened, for it has such an executor. If the keenness of your eyes
were permitted to behold it, you would indeed see Saint Benignus going before you as you work.” Having spoken, she entered the basilica from which she had come
and appeared to no one afterward. People of that time believed that blessed Paschasia had appeared there. Into hollows made in the stone upon which Benignus’s
feet were fixed when the lead was poured back, many people pour wine or cider. If eyes afflicted with inflammation or any wounds are anointed with it, the
illness is immediately put to flight and they are healed. I myself clearly experienced this. When my eyes were severely afflicted with inflammation, I was
touched with this sacred liquid and immediately lost the pain. When the bubonic plague came to the region of the Auvergne—the plague driven away by the prayer
of Saint Bishop Gallus—and the walls of houses and churches were marked and scored in sudden appearances, my mother saw in a dream that the wine kept in my
storerooms had become blood. As she lamented and said, “Woe to me, for my house has been marked for the plague,” a man said to her: “Do you know that the day
after tomorrow, the Kalends of November, the Passion of the martyr Benignus will be celebrated?” “I know,” she said. “Go,” he said, “keep vigil all night in his
honor and have Masses celebrated, and you will be freed from the plague.” Waking from sleep, she fulfilled what had been commanded her. Although the neighbors’
houses were marked, my house remained untouched.

## 51

**[051]** The martyr Symphorian consummated his martyrdom in the city of Autun. From the place where he was struck by the sword and his blood flowed, a certain
religious man took up three pebbles together with the blood itself. Enclosed in a silver reliquary, he placed them on the holy altar of a church constructed of
wooden boards at the fortress of Thiers in the Auvergne. At the time when Theodoric king of the Franks devastated that region, this fortress was consumed by
enemy fire. While the house of God, made of wooden boards as I have said, was seized by the flames and consumed along with the burning of the other houses, the
lamenting people said: “If only at least the blessed relics had not perished!” Meanwhile, when a great heap of glowing coals had been formed from the fire and
the north wind was blowing and blazing, the sparks left by the conflagration were violently scattered in all directions. Behold, that silver reliquary appeared
shining unharmed in the midst of the immense fire like a brilliant star. The clerics present collected it and, examining it, found none of the blessed relics
diminished. That so delicate an object had been preserved amid such violent flames—in which, so to speak, not only this but even a thousand pounds of silver or
iron could have melted without delay—truly manifested great power there and strengthened the people in the worship of God and the honor of his name. Afterward
they built another basilica on the same site and placed the holy relics on the altar.

## 52

**[052]** Only a few written records concerning the miracles of blessed Marcellus, martyr of Chalon, have come to me to be committed to memory. However small
they may be considered as accounts, they must be referred to him who works these things in individual cases. A certain matter had caused Fedamius, son of
Eunomius, formerly a priest of the Auvergne, to visit the city of Chalon. He had lodging at the basilica of the holy martyr Marcellus and received provisions
from the abbot of the place. He himself related what I am setting out: “A dispute arose between two men. As they litigated, the suit reached the point of being
settled by oath. They entered the basilica of the holy martyr. When the man raised his hands to commit perjury and wished to name the saint with open mouth, his
voice stuck in his throat and his tongue could not be turned to its office. Nor did this seem too little for the glory of the blessed athlete: with his hands
raised, the man himself became entirely rigid as though made of bronze. Then prayer offered for him obtained the release of one bound by the devil’s art. After
his release he confessed his deed in his own words and amended what he had negligently done.”

## 53

**[053]** Joined to this martyr by blood and by his contest is the blessed athlete Valerian, who, having completed his contest, was buried at the fortress of
Tournus, forty miles from Chalon. Gallus, count of that city, was afflicted by the pain of colic, which had so inflamed his whole abdomen not only with twisting
pain but also with swelling that he seemed dropsical. He could take neither food nor drink and, because of this affliction, was beginning to fail from the
disease of starvation. Nearly lifeless and seeing himself despaired of, he asked to be carried to the blessed martyr’s tomb. When he had been laid there, the
priest Epyrechius, who then governed that church, approached him—a man of miracles and pure mind, as I myself inspected with my own eyes—and said: “If you wish
to be healed, trust in the power of the glorious martyr and vow to send one beam with its fittings for restoring the roof of this church. It will be your
protection if you devoutly fulfill what you promise.” Attentive and praying, Gallus vowed what the priest indicated. Immediately healed, he ordered the beam to
be delivered to the saint’s basilica without anyone reminding him. Behold what the Lord Jesus Christ bestows on earth through the holy martyrs whom he has
glorified and taken into the heavenly kingdom! Rightly so: believing his sacred name in their hearts, invoking it in their works, confessing it in temptations,
they not only followed the Lord as faithful servants but also encouraged others by their examples to follow him.

## 54

**[054]** Timothy and Apollinaris, having consummated their martyrdom in the city of Reims, merited the heavenly kingdom. A devout man sought their relics after
building a basilica in their honor. The bishop who was present sent them with honor through a priest. While he was traveling, an importunate woman—and, I
believe, one unworthy of the favor—came forward on the road. Greeting the priest, she kissed the linen with which the sacred ashes were covered and asked that
some of them be granted to her. The priest long hesitated and put off giving them, but at last overcome by her persistence, he divided off a small portion for
her. Mounting his horse, he began to complete the journey assigned him, but though he struck both the horse’s flanks, he could in no way make it move forward.
He himself was so weighed down that he could scarcely raise his head. Understanding that he was being held by the martyrs’ power, moved by penitence he usefully
recovered what, through intervening negligence, he had presumed to give away. When he had restored to the reliquary what he had taken, he was permitted to
depart.

## 55

**[055]** Eutropis, martyr of the city of Saintes, is said to have been sent into Gaul by blessed Bishop Clement and also to have been consecrated by him with
the grace of the episcopal order. Having fulfilled the course of this office and completed his preaching to unbelievers, he fell as a victor with his head
crushed when the pagans rose up, men whom the author of envy had not permitted to believe. But because persecution was then raging and he was neither buried in
a worthy place nor venerated by Christians with due honor, the fact that he was a martyr was consigned to deep oblivion. It is recorded that this was revealed
in the following manner. After the space of many years a basilica was built in his honor. When the work was completed, Palladius, who then governed the chair of
