the priestly order, assembled the abbots and took care to transfer the sacred ashes to the place he had prepared. When this had been done, two of the abbots
opened the covering and beheld the holy body. They contemplated the scar on the head where the sharp edge of the axe had been fixed. Lest the present vision be
rendered void, spiritual instruction also admonished them: when the priests had given their limbs to rest on the following night, he appeared to these two in a
vision and said: “Know that I consummated my martyrdom through the scar you beheld on my head.” From this it became known to the people that he was a martyr,
because no history of his Passion was available.

## 56

**[056]** The martyr Amaranthus, having completed the course of his faithful contest at the city of Albi, lives buried in glory. As the history of his Passion
declares, his tomb long lay hidden, covered with brambles and thorns. But at the Lord’s command it was revealed to the Christian people, and the crypt in which
he rested was opened and shone brightly. When the place had been emptied of inhabitants under pressure from enemies, people coming from afar endeavored to
render honor to the blessed martyr as their own guardian. Since Christian devotion frequently brought wax candles, it happened one day that someone, because of
the length of the journey, had brought no additional fire with which to light a candle. He seized a flint and struck it with iron as though to elicit fire.
While he was doing this and shaking the stone with repeated blows without being able to strike out any spark, the candle already fixed to the blessed tomb was
lit by a heavenly lamp. What human effort had not accomplished was performed by the majesty of the divine name. When human endeavor ceased, heavenly services
were ministered, and the kindled candle was glorified by the brilliance of a new light. When this had been revealed to the people, no one afterward presumed to
bring additional fire for lighting a lamp. But after the place began to be continually inhabited and houses in which fire could be kindled were present there,
this miracle was no longer granted to the people, although the place is more frequently illumined by other miracles.

## 57

**[057]** Associated with this crypt is Eugenius, martyr of the Honorian persecution and the greatest ornament of the priestly fillet. His own Passion or that
of his companions relates that he was driven into exile in this city. Although he had possessed great powers in the world and had already emerged victorious
from martyr’s torments, through the Lord’s revelation he learned the time of his calling, when he would be summoned to glory. Knowing as manifest what had been
hidden from the people—that he would be a companion of the martyr Amaranthus—he was directed to Amaranthus’s tomb. Prostrate on the ground, he poured out prayer
to the Lord for a very long time. Then, stretching his arms across the pavement, he directed his spirit to heaven. Gathered up by Christians, he was committed
to burial in the very crypt I have mentioned. When on one occasion innumerable people assembled for his feast, they brought much merchandise into the forecourt.
One of the girls living in the place went to a stall as though to buy something. Seeing an article suited to her, she accepted it from the merchant.
Immediately, quicker than speech, she handed it to another person and denied having received it. The merchant insisted: “I held it out to you with my own hand,
and you accepted it to examine it carefully.” When she denied it, the merchant said: “If avarice prompts you to such obstinacy in denial, let the blessed martyr
Eugenius judge it. If you go to his tomb and say with an oath that you did not receive it, I will consider as nothing the loss I have suffered.” She promised
that she could clear herself by an oath and went boldly to the tomb. Raising her hands to swear, she immediately became rigid with her limbs loosened, her feet
were fixed to the pavement, and her voice stuck in her throat. Only her open mouth gaped, bare of speech. Seeing this, the merchant said before the rest of the
people: “May this article you took from me be of benefit to you, girl. The vengeance administered through the martyr is enough.” Saying this, he left the place.
Held in this torment for a very long time, she at last spoke at the martyr’s command and publicly confessed what she had wished to remain hidden. What are you
doing, O wretched avarice? Why does a woman’s mind, not a man’s, succumb to the desire for other people’s property? Why do you pierce the strong breastplate of
the mind with the small arrow of cupidity? Why, O man, do you gather talents of rusting gold when you will burn with them in Gehenna? What benefit are
perishable gains to you when they produce the loss of eternal life, according to the Lord’s word: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but
suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?”

## 58

**[058]** There is a church in the village of Yzeures within the boundary of the city of Tours which is often illumined by sacred miracles. As is customary, it
has windows closed with glass enclosed in wood, so that they may more splendidly supply the light the world has merited to the sacred building. An importunate
thief approached this church. Entering by night and seeing that the custodians’ care protected everything and noticing nothing among the sacred furnishings that
he could carry off, he said to himself: “If I can find nothing else, at least I will take these glass panes I see; by melting down the metal, I may obtain some
gold for myself.” Removing and scattering the glass, he took the metal and carried it into a district in the territory of Bourges. He boiled the glass in a
furnace for three days but could produce no work from it. Overcome by his crime and seeing divine judgment upon himself, he nevertheless was unmoved and
persisted in evil. He sold the glass taken from the cauldron, now transformed into I know not what little lumps, to merchants who came by, so that, having
received money, like a new Gehazi he might acquire perpetual leprosy. When the day came after the year’s course on which he had committed this theft, his head
was given over to swelling. His eyes also became so inflamed that they seemed to be bursting from their places. These things happen to him every year on the day
he committed the theft. The wretch laments the glass he cannot recall from the journey to which he sent it.

## 59

**[059]** In the city of Nantes two martyrs were slaughtered for Christ’s name, one called Rogatian and the other Donatus. The great confessor Similian is also
there. When the aforementioned city was surrounded by a barbarian siege in the time of King Clovis and sixty days had already passed in this affliction, about
the middle of the night men in white garments carrying shining wax candles appeared to the people coming out of the basilica of the blessed martyrs. Behold,
another choir like this one proceeded from the basilica of Bishop Similian. Joining together and exchanging greetings, they devoted themselves to prayer. Then
each withdrew to the place from which he had come. Immediately the entire hostile phalanx, terrified by immense fear, departed from the place in so sudden an
onrush that when daylight came none of them could be found. The aforementioned miracle appeared to a certain Chillo, who then commanded the army. He had not yet
been reborn by water and the Holy Spirit. Immediately pierced to the heart and converted to the Lord, born again by a second birth, he testified in a clear
voice that Christ is the Son of the living God.

## 60

**[060]** In the territory of this same city, in a village above the bed of the Loire, relics of blessed Nazarius are kept. At one time a devout man placed upon
the altar of that basilica a belt most carefully fashioned of the purest gold with all its fittings, praying that the martyr’s power would deign to assist him
in his affairs. After he departed, a certain Breton, one of the attendants of Waroch, count of the Bretons, and the first man with him, arrived. He violently
took away the belt’s fittings and then demanded the belt itself. The priest resisted, saying: “These are God’s property and were given to the holy martyr to
refresh the poor, so that those who faithfully and devoutly serve this church may not suffer dreadful famine. You ought rather to bring something here than take
it away.” The abbot’s preaching did not soften the greedy man’s mind. Instead, inflamed, he began to threaten him: “Unless you surrender the belt without delay,
you will be killed by my hand.” Overcome, the abbot placed the object upon the altar where the holy relics are covered, saying: “Here is the little article you
seek. If you have no fear of the martyr’s power, take it. As I trust, he will be an immediate judge if you presume to take it.” Fearing nothing, the man took it
and ordered his horse to be prepared before the very portico of the basilica. The priest said to him: “No one has ever presumed to mount a horse in this place.
Please give glory to God and honor the martyr, lest you suffer some evil.” Neglecting the priest’s commands, he mounted the horse in the sacred forecourt. As he
came out, his head struck the upper lintel of the gate and he fell to the ground with his skull shattered. Carried by his attendants’ hands into a certain poor
man’s nearby hut, he immediately breathed out his spirit. When Waroch heard this, terrified by fear, he both restored what the man had taken and contributed
much from his own property.

## 61

**[061]** In the city of Cologne there is a basilica in which fifty men of that sacred Theban Legion are said to have consummated martyrdom for Christ’s name.
Because it gleams with wonderful workmanship, gilded as it were with mosaic, the inhabitants have chosen to call the basilica the Golden Saints. At one time
half the head of Bishop Ebergisil, who was then bishop of this city, was shaken by severe pains. He was at that time on an estate very near the town. Greatly
weakened by the pain, he sent his deacon to the basilica of the saints. Because a well is said to be in the middle of that church into which the saints were
thrown together after their martyrdom, the deacon collected dust from it and brought it to the bishop. As soon as he touched his head with it, he was
immediately delivered from all pain.

## 62

**[062]** The body of the holy martyr Mallosus was discovered by this bishop in the following way. Report said that he had consummated his martyrdom at the town
of Birten, but the place where he rested was hidden from the people. There was an oratory there in which his name was invoked. The aforementioned bishop built a
basilica in his honor so that, when he received some revelation concerning the martyr, he might transfer the blessed limbs into it with the Lord’s consent. He
assembled materials in the side of the basilica—that is, in the wall on the oratory’s side, in the apse—awaiting the Lord’s mercy to reveal what he should
command concerning the martyr. After this a certain deacon of Metz was guided in a vision and taught where the martyr rested. A short time later he came to the
bishop and, rehearsing as certain signs what he had seen in the vision although he had never been there before, said: “Dig here, and you will find the saint’s
body,” meaning in the middle of the apse. When the bishop had dug to a depth of about seven feet, the fragrance of an immense perfume reached his nostrils. He
said: “I believe in Christ that he has shown me his martyr, since this sweetness has surrounded me.” Digging on, he found the holy body unharmed. Crying out in
a loud voice, he made all the clergy sing together, “Glory to God in the highest.” After the hymn had been sung, he transferred the holy body into the basilica
and buried it with due praise. People say that the martyr Victor is also buried there, but I have not yet learned of his being revealed.

## 63

**[063]** The martyr Patroclus, buried in the city of Troyes, often showed himself a friend of God through many miracles. There was a small oratory over him in
which only one cleric served. The people of the place rendered little service to the martyr because no history of his Passion was readily available. Rustics
customarily venerate more attentively those saints of God whose contests they read. A certain man coming from a distant journey brought the little book of this
contest and handed it to the lector whom I said served in that place to be read. Greatly rejoicing after the reading, he quickly copied it by night with the
help of a lamp. When the people had departed, he presented his discovery to his bishop, thinking that through it he would obtain the bishop’s favor. But the
bishop did not believe him and, regarding it as fabricated, ordered the cleric to be beaten, rebuked, and sent away, saying: “It is clear that you composed
these things according to your own desire. You never found them with anyone.” Much later, so that the martyr’s power would not remain hidden, an army went into
Italy and brought back the history of this Passion just as it had been written down by the cleric. Greatly confounded, the bishop recognized that what the
cleric had said was true. From then on the people began to honor the martyr more. Building a basilica over him, they devoutly celebrate his feast together every
year.

## 64

**[064]** The martyr Antolian consummated his martyrdom in the city of Clermont. In his honor Alchima, the sister, and Placidina, the wife of Bishop
Apollinaris, desired to build a church. While laying the foundations they removed many saints’ bodies, not knowing the merit of those whose tombs they had
found. Because of the multitude of other tombs that had filled the place from antiquity, they could not bury them individually. Throwing the gathered mass of
bones into one pit, they covered them with earth. That this was not acceptable to God or the holy martyr appeared to someone in a vision. The man saw blessed
Antolian with the other saints lamenting and saying: “Woe to me, because many of my brothers have been injured on my account. Nevertheless, I declare that those
who began these things cannot bring them to completion.” And so it happened. They erected walls above the altar of that building and raised a tower and columns
with Pharian and Heraclean ornamentation, vaulting arches and applying a painting to the ceiling remarkable for the diversity of its colors. The work was so
elegant and delicate that over a long period it was divided by frequent cracks and seemed almost to hang in ruin. Bishop Avitus saw this danger and,
anticipating the future collapse of the columns, ordered the roofs, beams, and tiles to be removed. These were taken away, and no supports were placed against
the columns. By God’s will, when the builders descended from the scaffolding to take food and everyone else withdrew from the basilica, the columns fell with
their immense weight and a great sound upon and around the altar. The building was filled with a cloud of dust from the shattered lime. The bloodless bishop,
sighing over the prospect of two losses, did not know what damage had occurred—whether they had broken the marble and anyone from the people had perished. No
one could approach because of the cloud of dust. After two hours, when the cloud had receded, they entered either to gather the bodies of the dead or examine
the fragments of columns. They learned that no one had perished. They marveled that the altar was unharmed: the columns, falling from so great a height, had
caused it no injury. What more need be said? They found everything intact and beheld everything preserved. They glorified the martyr and beheld God’s power,
which had thus preserved the altar and columns unharmed. In the territory of this city the martyr Julian also merited the palm of his contest by striving
lawfully. I have declared the miracles of his that have come down to me in the book I undertook to write separately about them.

## 65

**[065]** In this same territory, at the time when Chramn went into the Auvergne and his servants were committing various crimes, five men secretly attacked the
most sacred oratory of the estate at Issoire, in which relics of Saint Saturninus are kept. Breaking in, they took small cloths and the other ornaments of the
ministry and departed under cover of night. The priest discovered the theft and searched among the neighbors but could find no trace of what had been taken. The
robbers who had committed the deed immediately crossed into the territory of Aurillac. Dividing the goods, each received his share. Divine vengeance quickly
followed: four were killed in seditions. The fifth, remaining alive, claimed for himself the whole inheritance of this theft. But when he brought these things
into his house, his eyes were immediately covered with blood and he was blinded. Pierced both by pains and by divine inspiration, he vowed: “If God looks upon
my misery and restores my sight, I will return to that holy place what I took.” Praying this with tears, he received his sight. Coming to the town of Aurillac,
by God’s providence he found a deacon of Clermont. He handed the objects over to him and suppliantly begged him to restore them to the oratory. The devout
deacon did so.

## 66

**[066]** Very recently, in the territory of this city of Clermont adjoining the fortress of Thiers, Saint Genesius of that place revealed himself in the
following manner. A poor man lost the oxen he kept for cultivating his land when they happened to slip from his sight. Though he sought them with anxious
inquiry, he could not find them. On the following night a man appeared to him in a vision and said: “Go along the road that leads to the forest, and you will
find the oxen you anxiously seek beside a marble stone, cropping an abundance of grass. Yoke them to a wagon, bring the marble, and place it over the burial
near the road. I who speak to you am Genesius. That tomb is mine; clothed in white, I departed from this world through martyrdom.” Rising at dawn, the man found
the oxen beside the stone and did as he had been commanded in the vision. Nor was the miracle absent in this: the immense stone, which many pairs of oxen could
scarcely move, was transported by only two. Since then many sick people coming there, paying the promises of their vows, receive health. Hearing this, Avitus,
bishop of that city, built a great basilica over the saint’s tomb. When it had been dedicated, he ordered the feast to be observed there. Now a great multitude
of people comes with vows, as I have said, and returns with health. He also illumined this basilica with relics of Saint Genesius of Arles.

## 67

**[067]** This martyr Genesius consummated his contest by the cutting off of his neck for Christ’s name in this same city, Arles, prevailing through fervor of
faith. There is a tree where he is said to have been beheaded, a mulberry by species, from which many benefits have often been granted to the sick through the
martyr’s bestowal. As time passed and many people stripped away its branches and bark for healing, it dried up. Nevertheless, what remains of the trunk still
lives for those who faithfully ask and provides similar remedies.

## 68

**[068]** A bridge once stood over the river Rhône where the blessed martyr is said to have swum. On the day of his solemnity its chains broke, and because it
was set upon boats it began to sway. The boats themselves opened under the excessive weight of the people and submerged the crowd in the riverbed. All placed
together in this danger cried out with one voice: “Most blessed Genesius, rescue us by the power of your own holiness, lest the people perish who have
faithfully come devoutly to celebrate your solemnity.” Soon a wind blew and the whole crowd was brought back to shore, marveling that it had been saved by the
martyr’s power. The screens of the blessed tomb were also often broken by Lombards or other enemies. But the men, seized by a demon or overcome by madness,
raged or tore themselves with their own teeth and carried away none of the things they had violently begun to take. People also say that there was a woman in
this city against whom her husband alleged a crime that was in no way proved. A judge sentenced her to be immersed in water. An immense stone was tied to her
neck with ropes, and she was thrown from a boat into the Rhône. She prayed for the blessed martyr’s aid and, invoking his name, said: “Saint Genesius, glorious
martyr, who sanctified these waters by the stroke of your swimming, rescue me according to my innocence!” Immediately she began to be borne upon the waters.
Seeing this, the people took her into a boat and led her unharmed to the saint’s basilica. Neither her husband nor the judge sought her any further.

## 69

**[069]** Oh, how much innocence avails, how much a pure mind merits! Another woman in a similar situation was accused of adultery by her husband. She denied it
at length before the judge, and since she could not be overcome by her own confession, she was sentenced to be immersed. While the people ran to the spectacle,
she was led to the bridge over the river Arar. They tied a millstone to her neck with a rope and threw her into the river, while her husband shouted above her:
“Now wash away with abundant waters your fornications and impurities with which you often stained my bed!” But the mercy of the Lord, who does not permit the
innocent to perish, provided a post beneath the waters which no one could see. It caught the rope and held the woman up so that she did not reach the bottom of
the river. Both were beneath the water—the woman and the stone—balanced on the point of that post. When the sun was already seeking its setting, the woman’s
relatives asked the judge for permission to search the riverbed for their kinswoman’s corpse. Receiving this indulgence, they descended to the place where she
had been thrown. They saw her hanging with the stone. Throwing in a hook, they drew her out. Realizing she was alive, they quickly transferred her to the
basilica nearest the river, fearing that the judge would order her immersed again. They asked the woman how she had been able to live beneath the flood. She
replied: “It seemed to me no different from a dream. I felt the waters only when I was thrown into them and descended, and when I was taken from them again and
rose.” Everyone marveled that she could not die in such danger. The faith of a pure conscience saved her, together with the Lord whom she continually invoked.
She was then handed over to her relatives, and neither judge nor husband investigated her further. But let me return to the miracles of the martyrs.

## 70

**[070]** The city of Besançon, illumined by its own martyrs, often rejoices in present miracles. As their Passion declares, the two martyrs Ferreolus and
Ferrutio are buried in a hidden crypt. At one time my sister’s husband became gravely ill with an increasing fever. When he had lain gasping on his bed for four
months and his grieving wife could think of nothing but what was necessary for burial, she went weeping and sorrowful to the basilica of the saints. Prostrate
before the tombs, she pressed the cold pavement with her palms and face. It happened by chance that the extended palm of her right hand covered a sage leaf that
had been scattered in the crypt in honor of the martyrs. After pouring out prayer, she rose from the tombs with tears. Thinking she had taken in her hand
something from the linens she was wearing, as usually happens, she kept her palm closed. Leaving the basilica and opening her hand, she marveled at the herb
leaf. Astonished at what this was, she recognized that a heavenly gift had been divinely granted her, so that through it the martyrs’ power might aid the sick
man. Returning home more joyful, she diluted the leaf with water and gave it to her husband to drink. Full of faith, as soon as he drank it he immediately
merited to obtain the completest health.

## 71

**[071]** Bishop Dionysius was given as a martyr to the city of Paris. At the time when King Sigebert came with his army to that city and burned the greatest
part of its villages, one of his leading men hurried to the basilica of the aforementioned martyr, not out of devotion to prayer but solely to steal something
from the building. Finding the doors unlocked and the church empty of custodians, he rashly tore away the all-silk cloth adorned with gold and gems that covered
the holy tomb and carried it off with him. Coming to the camp, he needed to travel by ship. His boy, whom he then had in his charge, boarded the ship with him
wearing two hundred gold pieces suspended from his neck. Suddenly, touched by no one, the boy fell from the ship. Submerged by the waters, he could never be
found. The man, seeing God’s judgment upon himself in the loss of the boy and the gold, quickly returned to the shore from which he had departed and restored
the tomb cloth with the greatest speed. Although he did this, when the cycle of the year returned he did not live to reach the day on which he had committed the
crime. Another man, not fearing to tread upon the holy tomb, sought to strike down a golden dove with a spear. His feet slipped on either side because the tomb
was raised high. His testicles were crushed, the spear was fixed in his side, and he was found lifeless. Let no one doubt that this did not happen by chance but
was done by God’s judgment.

## 72

**[072]** The martyr Quentin rests at the town of Vermand in Gaul. His blessed body was found by a religious woman who had formerly been blinded. As soon as it
was raised from the riverbed, it produced a miracle: where it first shone upon the woman’s face, it restored her blinded eyes. In this city one of the robbers
secretly stole a priest’s horse. Found by the priest, he was reported to the judge. Without delay he was seized, bound in chains, and subjected to torture.
Confessing his deed with his own mouth, he was sentenced to the gallows. But the priest feared that a man’s soul would be taken away because of his loss. He
begged the judge that the guilty man’s life be granted and he be released from punishment, saying that it was already enough for him that through so many kinds
of torments the robber had declared what he had done. Since the judge’s severity could not be bent by any prayers, he condemned the accused to the gallows. Then
the priest prostrated himself with tears at the blessed martyr’s tomb and suppliantly prayed: “I beseech you, most glorious athlete of Christ, rescue this poor
man from the hand of unjust death, lest it become a reproach to me if this man dies through my accusation. Show your power, I pray: release with the gentle
governance of mercy him whom human harshness could not absolve.” While the priest prayed with tears, the bonds of the gallows broke apart and the accused fell
to the ground. Hearing this, the terrified judge, marveling at the divine power, presumed to harm him no further.

## 73

**[073]** Within the boundary of the city of Bazas is another martyr adorned with the honor of the priesthood, whose Passion history is read among the
inhabitants of the place. While he was in the body, he long obtained by his prayers that a dry chestnut tree return to greenness. Although miracles are often
shown over the sick in his basilica, this is admirable above the rest: a lily formerly gathered and dried becomes green anew at his solemnity, so that on that
day the people behold as new flowers those they had previously seen dried. At his tomb a false oath uttered by the faithless is often refuted by the martyr’s
power, so that one who came elated with rashness departs corrected.

## 74

**[074]** The Lord often weakens the arrogance of a stubborn mind with the rod of correction in order to restore it to the veneration of his worship, as
trustworthy report declares was once done with King Sigismund. After his son had been killed through his wicked wife’s counsel, Sigismund was pierced to the
heart. He went to Agaune and, prostrate before the tombs of the most blessed martyrs of the fortunate legion, did penance. He prayed that divine vengeance would
repay him in this world for whatever sins he had committed, so that he might be found absolved at the Judgment if the evils he had done were repaid before he
departed from the world. There he established daily psalm-singing and enriched the place most abundantly both with territories and other property. Later he was
captured by King Chlodomer together with his sons and killed at Chlodomer’s command. Brought back to this place, he was committed to burial. What now occurs
shows that he has been taken into the company of the saints. Those who suffer from chills and devoutly celebrate Masses in his honor and offer an oblation to
God for his rest are immediately restored to their former health, their trembling suppressed and their fevers extinguished.

## 75

**[075]** Great is the power at the tombs of the aforementioned martyrs. I have chosen to touch upon only a few, leaving many aside. A certain woman brought her
only son to this monastery and handed him to the abbot to be educated, so that, having become a cleric, he might be assigned to the holy offices. When he had
already been instructed in spiritual letters and was singing psalms with the other clerics in the choir, he was struck by a slight fever and breathed out his
spirit. His bereaved mother ran to the funeral rites lamenting and buried her son. But the tears poured out at the funeral were not enough for her grief. She
came every day and wailed over her child’s tomb, sending her cries aloft. At last blessed Maurice appeared to her in a vision by night and said: “Woman, why do
you continually lament your son’s death and never desist from mourning?” She replied: “The days of my life will not exhaust this lamentation. As long as I live,
I will always weep for my only son. I will never be relieved of tears until owed death closes the eyes of this body.” He said: “Do not weep for him as though
dead, but bear yourself calmly. Know that he dwells with me and enjoys the abode of perennial life in my company. And so that you may truly believe that what I
say is certain, rise tomorrow for matins and you will hear his voice among the choirs of psalm-singing monks. Not only tomorrow, but on all the days of your
life when you come, you will hear his voice in the psalmody. Therefore do not weep, because you ought rather to rejoice than mourn.” The woman rose and drew
long sighs. She did not sleep on her bed until the monks sounded the signal to rise. When it sounded, she went to the church to test something of the vision she
had seen. Nothing of the holy promise failed; what had been divinely announced was immediately known to be fulfilled. When the cantor gave the response and the
company of monks took up the antiphon, the mother heard and recognized her little child’s voice and gave thanks to God. What had been promised by the martyr’s
mouth was also completely fulfilled: on all the days of her life, whenever the woman came to the psalm-singing, she heard this little child’s voice among the
other modulations of voices. When King Guntram had so devoted himself to spiritual actions that, abandoning worldly pomp, he distributed his treasures to
churches and the poor, he sent a priest to transmit gifts by vow to the brothers serving the Saints of Agaune. He instructed the priest to bring him relics of
the saints on his return. Having fulfilled the king’s command, the priest was returning with these relics and sought a boat on Lake Geneva, into which the Rhône
flows. That lake extends about four hundred stades in length and one hundred fifty in width. When the returning priest had boarded the boat, a sudden tempest
arose and lifted the waves. Mountains of water rose to the stars. Now, as the prow opened, the stern of the little ship was borne aloft; now, with the stern
submerged, the prow was raised high. The sailors were thrown into confusion, and nothing but death alone was awaited in the danger. When the priest saw himself
overwhelmed by these waves and heavily covered by their foam, he drew from his neck the reliquary containing the saints’ relics and faithfully held it out
against the swelling waves. Invoking the saints’ protection in a clear voice, he said: “Glorious martyrs, I pray your power that I may not perish in these
waves. Rather, you who continually give aid to the perishing, deign, I beseech you, to extend to me the right hand of salvation. Suppress the waves and bring me
back to the desired shore by the help of your aid.” As he spoke, the wind ceased, the waves subsided, and they were carried to shore. I learned this from the
priest himself. They say that trout in this lake are weighed at sizes up to one hundred pounds.

## 76

**[076]** There is also marvelous power at the tomb of Saint Victor, martyr of Marseille. Sick people who come to him are often healed, and the possessed,
although they violently dash themselves about and cry out to the martyr, are liberated when the demons are expelled. A servant of Patrician Aurelian was seized
by a demon and tormented with a painful condition, so that he often tore himself with his own teeth. Brought to the saint’s basilica, he confessed that he was
being burned by the saint’s power and raged through the whole building. On the third day he departed cleansed. He was so strengthened by the merit of faith that
afterward, with his hair humbled, he received the rank of abbot and was placed in charge of a monastery.

## 77

**[077]** At the town of Nîmes is the glorious tomb of the blessed martyr Baudilius, from which many miracles are often manifested. A laurel sprang from the
tomb, passed through the wall, and formed a tree outside with health-giving foliage flourishing. The inhabitants often experienced it as a heavenly remedy for
many illnesses. Because it was frequently stripped of its leaves and even its bark for these benefits of healing, it dried up. Since I have said that it drives
away the diseases of many illnesses, it would take long to record each one. I therefore thought it sufficient to say that it dried up from bestowing remedies. A
report is current that a merchant carried a relic made from these leaves into the East. Before the merchant reached the gate, a possessed man in the church
cried out, to the people’s amazement, that the martyr Baudilius was approaching the eastern region. The blessed martyr also displayed his power in other
matters. While Ara, duke of King Theodoric of Italy, resided in the city of Arles, a certain archpriest of the diocese of Nîmes was hateful to him. Boiling with
bile, Ara sent his servants against him, saying: “Go as quickly as possible, bind his feet and hands, and bring him by force, so that he may know that I am lord
of this region.” Not understanding “archpriest,” they thought he had ordered the archdeacon brought. Mounting their horses, they came to the city and asked
about the archdeacon, who was pointed out to them. His name was John; he was very religious and, in his archdiaconate, devoted himself to teaching little
children. The duke’s servants seized him, bound his hands and feet beneath a horse’s belly, and brought him. But the martyr’s power did not cease to assist his
own foster son. The servants took quarters with him near the gate itself because, the gate valves having been locked for the night, they could not enter. That
night, while the duke slept, the archdeacon stood before him in a vision and said: “Man, what guilt have I incurred toward you that you ordered me summoned with
such injury and reduced to this humiliation? Truly I tell you, you will not escape God’s judgment.” Awaking and dismayed by fear, Ara cried to his attendants:
“Inquire whether the servants I sent to Nîmes have already come.” Asking from the city wall, they replied that they were present with the man. The messengers
reported what they had heard. The duke immediately said: “Bring me the man you have brought.” When this had been done, the duke looked at him and, terrified,
said: “I ordered the archpriest brought, not the archdeacon.” Prostrate at his feet, he said: “Please pardon this offense. It was not in my intention that you
should suffer these things.” He immediately sent him back to the city honored with worthy gifts. Out of reverence for the martyr he afterward loved him with
such affection that, when the bishop of that city died, he ordered John himself to be appointed bishop. Nor did he order the archpriest sought any further. O
great power of the martyr, which through an innocent man’s injury released a guilty man from punishment! The apostle’s word was fulfilled: “All things work
together for good to those who love God,” since this injury constructed for John the step by which he climbed to govern God’s Church.

## 78

**[078]** The church of the city of Agde, which glories in relics of Saint Andrew the Apostle, is often illumined by glorious miracles and frequently convicts
those who seize its property. Count Gomacharius seized a field belonging to this church. Leo, bishop of the church, ran to him in great distress and said: “My
son, relinquish the property of the poor which the Lord entrusted to my administration. Do not let it harm you or be destroyed by the tears of the needy who
were accustomed to be fed by its fruits.” Because Gomacharius was a heretic, he thought little of what the bishop said and retained the property under his
control. As the day advanced, he was seized by fever. Afflicted not only by bodily burning but also by distress of soul, he sent messengers to the bishop: “Let
the priest deign to pour out prayer to the Lord for me, and I will relinquish his field.” While Leo prayed, Gomacharius recovered from the illness oppressing
him. Once healed, he said to his men: “What do you think these Romans will say now? They will claim I was afflicted with fever because I took their field,
whereas it happened to me according to the customary condition of the human body. Nevertheless, they will not have it while I live.” Quicker than speech, he
sent someone to seize it again. When the bishop learned this, he came and said: “Do you repent of having previously done well, that you now try to overturn it
again? Please do not, lest you be subjected to divine vengeance.” Gomacharius said: “Be silent, be silent, decrepit old man! I will make you ride unrestrained
around the city on an ass with reins, so that you are ridiculous to everyone who sees you.” Leo silently returned to his customary defenses. He prostrated
himself in prayer, celebrated vigils, and spent the entire night in tears and psalm-singing. When morning came, he approached the lamps hanging from the church
ceiling, extended the rod in his hand, and broke them all, saying: “No light will be kindled here until God takes vengeance on his enemies and restores his
house’s property.” As he said this, the heretic immediately collapsed in a renewed fever. At the point of death, he sent to the bishop: “Let the priest pray to
the Lord for me, that I may live. I will restore the field and confer another like it upon his dominion.” The bishop replied: “I have already prayed to the
Lord, and he has heard me.” Gomacharius sent second and third messengers, but the bishop persisted in one answer and was not moved to offer prayer to the Lord
for him. Seeing this, the heretic ordered himself placed on a wagon and carried to the bishop, to entreat him personally: “I will restore the field I wickedly
seized with double satisfaction, provided only that your holiness pray for me.” When Leo also refused, Gomacharius compelled him by force to go to the church.
Leo dismounted and entered, and Gomacharius immediately breathed out his spirit. The church at once recovered its property.

## 79

**[079]** Heresy is always hostile to Catholics and never omits to lay snares wherever it can, as widespread report declares happened in a certain place. There
was a Catholic woman with a heretical husband. When a very Catholic priest of my religion came to her, the woman said to her husband: “I ask your charity that,
because of the arrival of this priest who has deigned to visit me, there be rejoicing in my house and that, having prepared a dinner with worthy expense, I
feast with him.” Her husband promised to do as she asked. Another priest, one of the heretics, also arrived. The husband said to his wife: “Today’s joy is
doubled, because priests of both religions are in my house.” When they reclined at the banquet, the husband occupied the right-hand corner with the heretical
priest and stationed the Catholic on the left, placing a little chair at his left where his wife might sit. The husband said to the heretical priest: “If you
agree with my words, today I will make sport of this priest of the Romans. When a dish is served, hasten to make the sign more quickly. When he has not put out
his hand, he will be sad while I eat the food with joy.” The priest replied: “I will do as you direct.” When a plate of vegetables came, the heretic made the
sign and put out his hand first. Seeing this, the woman said: “Do not do this; I bear the priest’s injury with displeasure.” When another food was served, the
Catholic took some. At the second and third dishes the heretic did likewise. A fourth was served, with a hot frying pan placed in its center containing the food
customarily made from beaten eggs with a little flour mixed in and decorated with pieces of dates and round olives. Before that dish even touched the table, the
heretic hastened to raise his hand toward it and make the sign. Immediately setting down his spoon, he took the food, not realizing whether it was hot, and
quickly gulped down the burning morsel. His chest immediately kindled and he began to burn. Emitting his wicked spirit with an immense groan and rumbling of his
belly, he was carried from the banquet, laid in a tomb, and covered with a heap of earthly mass. Then the priest of my religion exulted: “Truly God has avenged
his servants.” Turning to the husband whose banquet it was, he said: “His memory has perished with a sound, and the Lord remains forever. Now serve me what I
may eat.” Terrified, the man, after the banquet was finished, fell at the priest’s feet. He who had been held in this perfidy was converted to the Catholic
faith and believed with his household. Joy was multiplied, just as the woman had previously asked.

## 80

**[080]** An Arian priest was disputing with a deacon of my religion and, as is that people’s custom, putting forward venomous assertions against the Son of God
and the Holy Spirit. After the deacon had discussed at great length certain points concerning the rationale of my faith, and the heretic, blinded by the
darkness of perfidy, rejected what was true—according to the saying, “Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul”—the deacon added: “Why exhaust ourselves with
long-drawn-out speeches? Let the truth of the matter be proved by deeds. Let a bronze vessel be heated over a fire and someone’s ring thrown into boiling water.
Whoever lifts it from the boiling water will be proved to have attained justice. When this has been done, let the opposing party be converted to recognition of
this justice. Understand therefore, heretic, that if my party, assisted by the Holy Spirit, accomplishes this, you will confess that there is nothing discordant
and nothing dissimilar in the Holy Trinity.” The heretic agreed to this test, and, having entered into an agreement until morning, they departed. But the fervor
of faith through which the deacon had first proposed this began to cool as the enemy laid snares. Rising at dawn, he poured oil on his arm and sprinkled it with
ointment. Nevertheless, he went around the holy places and prayed to the Lord. What more need be said? About the third hour they assembled in the forum. The
people ran to the spectacle. A fire was lit, the bronze vessel was placed over it and boiled fiercely, and the ring was thrown into the boiling water. The
deacon first invited the heretic to remove it from the heat. The heretic immediately refused, saying: “You who proposed this test ought to remove it.” Although
trembling, the deacon bared his arm. When the heretical priest saw it smeared with ointments, he exclaimed: “You thought you would be burned, so you spread
these ointments by magic arts. What you are doing will not avail.” While they disputed, a deacon from the city of Ravenna named Hyacinth arrived. Asking what
the dispute was and learning the truth, he did not delay. Drawing his arm from his garments, he plunged his right hand into the bronze vessel. The ring that had
been thrown in was very light and small and was borne along by the water no less than chaff can be carried by the wind. He searched for it for a long time and
found it within the space of one hour. Meanwhile the fire beneath the cauldron was being kindled more violently, so that, boiling more fiercely, the ring could
not easily be reached by the searching hand. When he finally drew it out, the deacon felt nothing in his flesh. Rather, he testified that the bottom of the
bronze vessel was cold, while at the surface there was a heat of moderate warmth. Seeing this, the greatly confounded heretic boldly thrust his hand into the
vessel, saying: “My faith will provide this for me.” As soon as his hand entered, all his flesh immediately melted and flowed off down to the very joints of his
bones. Thus the dispute ended.

## 81

**[081]** In my own time also, when the unbelief and wicked Arian sect had been disseminated in parts of Spain through the worst assertions of evil men, a
certain cleric was seized and confessed himself a Christian, asserting that the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father. The king then ruling offered
him gifts and suppliantly begged him as though he were the king’s superior, asking him to suppress his confession of the equality of the Holy Trinity and
declare the Son and Holy Spirit inferior to the Father. If he did this, he would be enriched with resources and considered great among the people. The cleric
fled this counsel like a viper’s bite and rejected the deadly poison of the wicked serpent. The king added: “I see the hard intention of an insane mind, but I
know how to moderate you. He whom gifts do not deflect, torments will easily subdue.” The cleric replied: “Would that I were considered worthy to be slaughtered
in this confession! I abhor your gifts like dung.” Enraged, the king ordered him stretched on pulleys and severely beaten, asking: “What do you believe?” He
answered: “I have already told you: I believe in God the Father Almighty and his Son Jesus Christ.” After this he was severely beaten but always persisted in
confession. This torture could never deflect him from the line of faith. When he was first beaten, he felt only three blows, which, as he later related,
penetrated his very soul. He felt the remaining lashes no more than if some covering had been laid over his back. Placed amid torments, he proclaimed even more
the faith he had begun to confess. When the king was satisfied with his beating, the cleric was released, with the protestation that he must never be found
within the boundaries of Spain. Departing joyfully, he returned to Gaul. To give credibility to my account, I saw the man who related what he had heard from the
cleric’s own mouth.

## 82

**[082]** Through this confession the glorious martyrs have always merited ineffable benefits of saving gifts and have granted to those who ask, by their power,
what has been bestowed on them by the Lord Creator. I learned that the following recently happened, as related by my deacon. Having received relics of certain
martyrs and confessors from Pelagius, pope of Rome, this deacon was escorted as far as Portus with loud psalm-singing, the service of the clergy, and the
attendance of an immense crowd. Boarding a ship, they raised the sails, extended the tackle along the yardarm that bears the form of a cross, and, with the wind
blowing, took to the deep sea. While sailing to reach the port of Marseille, they began to approach a place where a rocky mountain rises from the seashore and
gradually descends, extending beneath the surface into the sea. Driven by the wind, the keel was borne headlong with great force, so that it would be shattered
by striking the rock. Seeing the danger of death, the sailors cried out. The deacon raised the reliquary with the holy relics and began with groaning and a very
loud voice to invoke each saint’s name, praying that those about to perish would be freed from this danger by their power. The ship was now, now approaching the
rock, as I said. Immediately, in the presence of the holy relics, a wind contrary to this wind was stirred from that very place with greater violence. It struck
back the wave, repelled the opposing wind, recalled the ship to the deep sea, and freed everyone from the danger of death. Thus the mass of danger turned aside,
and they reached the desired port with the Lord’s grace and the saints’ protection. There were relics of saints whose sacred footsteps were washed by the Lord’s
hands, together with relics of Paul and Lawrence and Pancras, Chrysanthus and the virgin Daria, John and the other Paul, his brother, whose contests and palms
of victory Rome herself, head of the world, devoutly celebrates.

## 83

**[083]** I will also declare what happened concerning the relics my father once kept with him. At the time when Theudebert ordered the sons of the Auvergne to
be taken as hostages, my father, recently joined in marriage, wished to fortify himself with relics of the saints. He asked a certain priest to grant him some
of them so that, setting out on a long journey, he might be protected by such a defense. The priest placed the sacred ashes enclosed in a golden locket around
him, though my father did not know the blessed saints’ names. He used to relate that he was then rescued from many dangers. He testified that through their
power he often escaped the violence of robbers, the perils of rivers, the outrages of seditious men, and attacks of swords. I will not remain silent about what
I myself saw concerning them. After my father’s death my mother carried these relics on her person. The time for reaping the crops had arrived, and great heaps
of grain had been gathered on the threshing floors. In those days, when the seeds were being threshed, the threshers had made themselves fires from the chaff
because, although Le Mans lies open to the crops and bare of forests, there was an intervening frost and no other source from which to kindle fire. Meanwhile
everyone withdrew to take food. Behold, fire began gradually to spread through the chaff amid its own increase. Without delay, with the south wind blowing, the
heaps were seized by the flames. A great conflagration arose, followed by men’s shouts, women’s uproar, and children’s wailing. These things were happening on
my land. Sensing this, my mother, who wore these relics hanging from her neck, sprang from the banquet. Raising the sacred relics against the balls of fire, she
caused the whole conflagration to yield so instantly that scarcely any seeds of fire could be found among the masses of burned chaff. Yet it did not harm the
grain it had seized. Many years later I received these relics from my mother. While I was traveling from Burgundy to the Auvergne, a great storm arose against
me. The sky began to flash with frequent fires and resound with violent crashes of thunder. Then I drew the blessed relics from my bosom and raised my hand
against the cloud. It immediately divided into two parts, passing to right and left, and harmed neither me nor anyone afterward. But I, as youthful fervor often
does, began to be inflated with the arrogance of vainglory and silently to think that these things had been granted not so much to the saints’ merits as to me
personally. Boasting to my traveling companions, I began to declare what God had granted to my innocence so that I merited this. Without delay my horse suddenly
slipped beneath me and dashed me to the ground. I was so severely injured by this fall that I could scarcely rise. I understood that this had happened to me
because of vanity, and it was enough thereafter to take care that the sting of vainglory never goaded me again. If it happened afterward that I was found worthy
to behold any of the saints’ miracles, I proclaimed that they were bestowed by God’s gift through faith in the saints.

## 84

**[084]** Rashness is useful in nothing when anyone seeks what he is not permitted to practice. Thus a count of the Bretons was severely afflicted by pains in
his feet. Spending his substance on physicians, he obtained no relief. One of his men said to him: “If some vessel of the ministry that is placed on the altar
were brought to you from the church and you washed your feet in it, this could bring you healing.” Foolish and ignorant, they did not recognize that vessels
consecrated to God ought not be adapted to human uses. The count quickly sent to the church and received a silver paten of the most sacred altar from the
sanctuary. He washed his feet in it, but immediately additional pains completely disabled him, and he could never afterward take a step. I have also learned
that a duke of the Lombards did likewise.

## 85

**[085]** I bewail my sins and lament because I do not know myself to be clean. Approaching the Lord’s altar, although polluted in deed, I boldly take his holy
body and blood rather for judgment than to obtain pardon. I recall what I heard happened in my youth. It was the day of the Passion of the great martyr
Polycarp, and his solemnity was being celebrated in the village of Riom in the Auvergne. After the Passion had been read together with the other lessons brought
in by the priestly canon, the time came to offer the sacrifice. Taking the tower-shaped vessel in which the mystery of the Lord’s body was kept, the deacon
began to carry it to the entrance. Entering the church to place it upon the altar, he let it slip from his hand, and it was borne into the air. Moving toward
the altar itself, it could never be reached by the deacon’s hand. I believe this happened for no other reason than that he was polluted in conscience, for
adulteries were often reported to have been committed by him. Only one priest and three women, of whom my mother was one, were permitted to see this; the others
did not. I confess that I myself was present at this festival at that time, but I was not found worthy to see it.

## 86

**[086]** Likewise the priest Epachius, when he rashly presumed to do what he was unworthy of, fell prostrate to the ground by divine judgment. Seeking the
church to celebrate the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity, he went out of God’s temple at each successive hour and in his own house drank wanton cups from foaming
goblets. Many affirmed that they had seen him drinking that night after cockcrow. But because he was of senatorial rank and no one in the aforementioned village
of Riom was considered nobler in worldly dignity, he was asked to celebrate the solemnity of Mass. Soaked in wine, the wretch did not hesitate to undertake what
anyone fasting, with conscience afraid, cannot accomplish without fear. When the sacred words had been spoken and the sacrament of the Lord’s body broken, he
himself partook and distributed it to others to eat. Immediately emitting a sound like a horse’s neigh, he fell to the ground. Foaming at the mouth and spitting
out the particle of the sacred mystery itself, which he had been unable to crush with his teeth, he was carried from the church in his attendants’ hands. He was
never afterward free of this infirmity of epilepsy but continually suffered it through the increases and decreases of every lunar course, because the unhappy
man did not abstain at all from drinking wine excessively. What honor and reverence this night ought to be celebrated with, the present example teaches. At one
time during this solemnity, when I had left the vigil and slept a little, a man came to me and said: “Rise and return to the church.” Awaking, I opposed him
with the sign of the cross and fell asleep again. The same figure did not desist but repeated the earlier words. When, admonished a second time, I still did not
rise but slept again, he came a third time, struck my cheek, and said: “Behold, you ought to admonish the others to vigil, and are you still weighed down by
sleep?” Terrified by fear, I returned to the church with great speed. Let this suffice concerning the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. Now let me return to the
rash.

## 87

**[087]** There was an adulterous woman from the city of Jericho whose most loathsome custom was that whenever she conceived by a paramour and gave birth, she
immediately suffocated the child and hid it in the earth. Thus she made hidden from men what was not concealed from God and his angels. When the holy day of
Epiphany arrived and everyone went down into the Jordan to wash both the wounds of the body and the scars of the soul, she approached the bank with the rest of
the people. Raising her garments to her knees to enter the river—wonderful to relate—the water fled before her feet. As she pursued it, the river was forced
back to the other bank. Seeing this, the people marveled that such a thing had happened on this most celebrated day. Recognizing that the woman was criminal,
they asked what evil she had done that this should happen to her amid such a gathering. Turning to the people, she confessed her crime: “I have already killed
seven little children born to me. Conceiving them in incest, I feared to make them public. Yesterday I suffocated an eighth. I beg you to pour out prayer to the
Lord for me, so that, my iniquity remitted, I may now cease from sin and heavenly wrath may not consume me.” As she spoke, all the people prostrated themselves
on the ground and poured out prayer to the Lord that he would mercifully pardon what she had done wrong through the assistance of weakness. After the prayer,
the woman stretched her arms upon the ground and breathed out her spirit. I think this happened so that the pardoned crime would not be repeated further. The
people recognized the offense for which the river waters had receded before the woman’s face. Solomon’s proverb was fulfilled: “The Spirit of the Lord flees the
deceitful.” I learned that this miracle happened from the mouth of Deacon John, who asserted that he was present at the time.

## 88

**[088]** In the city of Toulouse there is said to have been a man named Antoninus, wicked toward God and hateful to all men because he committed many crimes.
When his days were completed and he departed from the world, he was buried in the basilica of blessed Vincent, in which he had deposited a coffin for himself
while alive. When deep silence seized everyone in the high night and all had given their limbs to rest as sleep caressed them, that coffin was thrown out of the
holy basilica through a window and deposited in the middle of the forecourt. When morning came, it was found there with the covering above it broken. His
relatives, not understanding God’s power or perceiving the injury to the saint in whose church they had rashly buried an unworthy man, again lowered the coffin
and dug it deeper into the place where it had been before. When another day dawned, they found it again thrown outside into the middle of the forecourt. Thus
they understood the mighty works of God. Touched by no one since then, it is preserved to this day in the place where it was thrown as a testimony. Let this
suffice concerning the rash.

## 89

**[089]** Vincent, both Levite and martyr, consummated his martyrdom in Spain. Within the boundary of Poitiers there is a village in the Arbatilicus district
called Becciaco, where his relics are kept. His solemnity is celebrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of the eleventh month. But the inhabitants,
especially the archpriest, fell into I know not what error and wished to celebrate it a day early. After Mass had been said and they sat down to the banquet,
one of the possessed began to cry out: “Run, citizens! Leave the village! Go out to meet blessed Vincent! Behold, he comes to the vigils! Behold, tomorrow you
will celebrate his feast!” At these words they renewed the solemnities and remained awake in vigils all night. When morning came and the mysteries of Mass were
being celebrated, the possessed man who had predicted the saint’s arrival and two others with him were cleansed. Two paralytics were also made upright that day.
Thus they departed from the festival with joy. When certain pilgrims were carrying his relics, they came to the village of Céré in the city of Tours. Bringing
them to a poor man’s hut, they were received. On the following day two paralytics received the ability to walk through these relics, and one blind man received
sight. Not far from that village is another called Orbigny, in whose church relics of this saint are kept. When they had been taken by thieves and the thief
left them with a certain abbot in Bourges after receiving payment, it was revealed to the abbot that he must restore them to the place from which they had been
removed. It was likewise revealed in a vision to the archpriest near this monastery that he must not delay their restoration. As he brought them back with
psalm-singing, a man who had lain for a whole year oppressed by grave illness was carried in his attendants’ hands. Venerating and suppliantly kissing the veil
covering the sacred ashes, his illness was immediately suppressed and he was healed. He followed the martyr’s procession with the others.

## 90

**[090]** Glorious Eulalia, who suffered in the city of Mérida, presents a great miracle to the people on the day of her immolation. Before her altar, where her
holy members are covered, stand three trees; I do not know of what species. Although by the middle of the tenth month, when her Passion is celebrated, they have
been stripped of all the beauty of their leaves, on that day, as heaven brightens, they put forth flowers in the form of the dove, a bird of sweetness. This
signifies that her holy spirit penetrated the heavens in the form of a dove and that snow falling from heaven covered her blessed little body, already lifeless
and stripped of clothing, with a soft fleece. If the trees freely produce this miracle as usual, the people know that their year will be free from afflictions
or full of fruits. If the flowers appear later than customary, the people recognize that this happens because of their own fault. Before the flowers burst
forth, the people lie complaining and sorrowful at the martyr’s tomb, praying to be found worthy to behold the accustomed grace. Nor does the procession proceed
with psalm-singing unless these things have been manifested. If the martyr is appeased by the people’s tears, budding flowers immediately emerge from the trees.
Breathing a nectar-like fragrance, they both gladden the mind’s sadness by their arrival and refresh it by their sweetness. Carefully collected and brought to
the bishop in the basilica, the procession is then celebrated with joy. I have also often known these flowers to benefit the sick.

## 91

**[091]** At one time the basilica of the martyr Felix was broken into by thieves. This martyr suffered in the city of Girona in Spain. Taking silk cloths woven
with gold and adorned with necklaces, together with the other ornaments, the thief departed. As he went, an unknown man joined him and asked where he was going.
The thief replied: “If my words were concealed with you, I would show you a great treasure.” The stranger said: “Show whatever you wish; I will conceal it with
all my strength.” The thief showed him the objects and said: “If these are sold in other regions, they will bring great profit to both of me.” The stranger
said: “I am a man with many friends in various regions, and I have a large and secluded house. If you put these things in it, you can sell them afterward
whenever you please.” He went ahead, and the man with the burden followed, thinking he was being led to another city. God had closed his eyes, and he did not
recognize that he was returning by the road he had come. What more need be said? They arrived at the saint’s basilica, and the man said: “Behold the house of
which I spoke! Enter and lay down your burden.” The thief entered. When he had deposited the burden and began to look around, coming to his senses he recognized
the saint’s basilica from which he had taken those things. The man had already withdrawn from him. He related to the people everything he had done with that
man. It is therefore beyond doubt that the blessed martyr himself had appeared to him. His relics are kept in the basilica of Narbonne. Because the height of
this building obstructed the view of Liguria, a most pleasant place, from the king’s palace, King Alaric consulted his counselor Leo. Leo said: “Let one course
of the structure be removed from this building; the king will contemplate more freely what pleases him.” Immediately calling the workmen, the counselor lowered
the saint’s basilica by buildings it did not deserve. He immediately lost the sight of his eyes.

## 92

**[092]** The Spanish city of Calahorra possesses the martyrs Emeterius and Celedonius. Through the blessed saints’ power it often receives remedies for various
illnesses, a miracle to behold. When these martyrs were seized by the persecutor and dragged to punishment, they were afflicted with various torments for
confessing the divine name. After the sentence of final condemnation had been pronounced, they were led away to be beheaded. As the executioner cut off their
heads, a great miracle appeared to the people. The ring of one and the handkerchief of the other were received by a cloud and carried into the heavens. All
present saw this. As far as the keenness of their eyes could reach, they followed in astonishment the gleam of the gold and the whiteness of the linen. Aurelius
Clemens testifies to this event in his book of Crowns in these verses:

“That event is not hidden and does not grow old with time: gifts flew upward through the air and by shining showed that the way of heaven lay open. The ring is
borne by a cloud, figuring that one’s faith; this one gives his handkerchief as a pledge of his mouth, as they say. Snatched by a heavenly breeze, they enter
the inmost part of light. The gleam of gold is hidden through the axis of the liquid sky, and the textile’s whiteness long eludes the pursuing sight. They are
carried up to the stars and are seen no more.”

## 93

**[093]** Most blessed Cyprian, both bishop and martyr of Carthage, often grants health to sick suppliants. In his basilica the lectern, upon which a book is
placed for singing or reading, is reported to be wonderfully constructed. It is said to have been carved entirely from one marble stone: the table above,
reached by four steps, the screens around it, and the columns beneath. It also has a pulpit under which eight persons can be accommodated. It could never have
been installed there by any human device unless the martyr’s power had provided it.

## 94

**[094]** This is the account of the Seven Brothers who rest at Ephesus. In the time of Emperor Decius, when persecution was being waged against Christians,
seven men were seized and brought before the prince. Their names are Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Constantine, Dionysius, John, and Serapion. Tempted with
various words to yield, they in no way acquiesced. Because of their nobility, the emperor granted them time for deliberation so that they would not perish
immediately. They shut themselves in a cave and lived there for many days. One of them would go out, buy food, and supply what was necessary. When the emperor
returned to the same city, they petitioned the Lord to deign to rescue them from this danger. Having prayed, they fell asleep prostrate on the ground. When the
emperor learned that they were remaining in this cave, by God’s will he ordered the mouth of the cave blocked with great stones, saying: “Let them perish there,
since they refused to sacrifice to my gods.” While this was being done, a Christian wrote their names and martyrdom on a lead tablet and secretly enclosed it at
the cave’s entrance before it was blocked. After the course of many years, when peace had been given to the churches and the Christian Theodosius had obtained
the empire, the foul heresy of the Sadducees arose, denying the future resurrection. A citizen of Ephesus intended to make sheepfolds for his sheep on the
mountain. Rolling stones away to fit together their enclosures, unaware of what was within, he opened the cave’s entrance but did not discover the secret kept
inside. The Lord put the spirit of life into the seven men, and they arose. Thinking they had slept for only one night, they sent one youth from among
themselves to buy food. Coming above the city gate, he saw the sign of the glorious cross and heard the people swearing by Christ’s name. He was astounded.
Producing the coins he had from Decius’s time, he was seized by a merchant, who said: “You have found treasures hidden in antiquity.” Denying this, he was led
to the bishop and the city judge. When they pressed him, compelled by necessity he revealed the hidden mystery and led them to the cave where the men were.
Entering, the bishop found the lead tablet on which everything they had suffered was written. He spoke with them, and they quickly sent news to Emperor
Theodosius. The emperor came and adored them, prone on the ground. They addressed the prince thus: “Glorious Augustus, a heresy has arisen which attempts to
turn the Christian people away from God’s promises by saying that the resurrection of the dead will not occur. Therefore, so that you may know that according to
the apostle Paul we will all be presented before Christ’s tribunal, the Lord commanded me to be raised and to say these things to you. See therefore that you
are not deceived and excluded from God’s kingdom.” Hearing this, Emperor Theodosius glorified the Lord, who had not permitted his people to perish. The men
again prostrated themselves on the ground and fell asleep. When Emperor Theodosius wished to make golden tombs for them, he was prohibited in a vision from
doing so. To this day the men rest in that place covered with little silk or fine linen cloths. Their Passion, which I translated into Latin with a certain
Syrian interpreting, explains this more fully.

## 95

**[095]** They say that there were forty-eight men in Armenia who suffered in the mountains of Armenia, where water and earth are bound by great cold because of
the excessive height. The Lawgiver shows that the height of these mountains is not small when he says that the ark made by Noah rested upon them. The persecutor
dug out the earth there and made a great cistern, ordering it filled with water. The men were stripped, their hands bound behind their backs, and he commanded
them placed in the lake bound by ice. A bath was heated opposite, and he said: “Choose one of two things. Either confess your Christ and fail in this cold, or
deny him, offer sacrifice to the gods, and fly to the bath so that you may live and not die wretchedly because of a crucified man.” When all refused to
sacrifice to demons, their guard saw forty-eight most precious crowns fall from heaven and descend upon the men’s heads, with one of them being withdrawn. The
faith of one man had failed. Leaving his companions, he immediately flew quickly to the bath. Sacrificing victims and being honored by the governor, he washed
in the warm bath, only to receive afterward the punishment of perpetual fire. Seeing this, the guard, as I said, proclaimed in a loud voice that he was a
Christian, saying: “I desire to die with these men.” Without delay afflicted with various torments, he was stripped of his clothing but not his faith and placed
in the lake to endure the cold with the rest and obtain the crown the wretch had lost. The men’s little bodies had already died from the cold, their teeth
clenched together, and the sound of their voices was shut off. Only a murmur of prayer glided from the secret places of their breasts to heaven, known to God
alone, who knows the heart’s secrets. Their exhausted limbs trembled from both fasting and frost. Their hope was fixed on heaven, though their flesh was already
dead. Meanwhile the wicked judge ordered the waters removed and the bath heated sevenfold, so that savage flames might dissolve those whom cold had not
released. The men were brought from the lake confessing Christ and cast amid the burning vapors of fire. They patiently endured the torments inflicted so as to
receive a greater palm. Leaving their bodies in these flames and committing their souls to Christ, they consummated their martyrdom in peace. Then the governor,
seeing himself conquered by their constancy and thinking he could at least defeat the dead whom he had been unable to overcome alive, ordered their little
bodies burned and thrown into a nearby river. When this had been done, a new miracle appeared to the weeping Christians. The water stood still and did not
absorb the half-burned bones but supported them upon itself as though entrusted to it. Gathered by rejoicing Christians, they were buried with the most worthy
honor.

## 96

**[096]** The martyr Sergius also performs many signs among the people, curing illnesses and healing the diseases of those who faithfully pray. Therefore
immense vows are promised to his basilica and gifts brought, from which nothing at all may be subtracted or taken. If anyone does so, he immediately incurs
judgment of disgrace or death. Because of this defense many consecrate their property to the saint so that, protected by his power, it will not be plundered by
the wicked. There was a poor old woman, similar, I believe, to that evangelical pauper who once devotedly threw two mites into the treasury when she had nothing
else. This woman had a few chicks which by vow she had subjected to the basilica’s authority, intending to give them to its house when necessity demanded. When
many people came to the saint’s feast, two men who had formerly seen these chicks conspired and stole one. Cutting off its head, pulling out its feathers, and
cutting off its feet, they placed it in a vessel with water over the fire and eagerly kindled the flames. The water boiled most violently, but the stolen flesh
was not cooked. Even as the water was consumed by boiling, the chick did not soften at all. They repeatedly tested it with their hands and tried to insert a
fingernail, but found it harder than when they had put it in. Meanwhile invited guests arrived for the feast but would in no way partake of the preparation. The
table stood veiled in snow-white napkins adorned with embroidered work. The food remained in its new hardness. The dish was repeatedly diluted with water, but
nothing cooked was found to serve. Thus by a new miracle the feast was reduced to stone. With the hosts confounded and the guests embarrassed, they departed
from dinner in shame.

## 97

**[097]** The twins Cosmas and Damian, physicians by art, after becoming Christians drove away the illnesses of the sick solely through the merit of their
miracles and the intervention of their prayers. Consummated by various torments, they are united in heaven and show many miracles to the inhabitants. If any
sick person full of faith prays at their tomb, he immediately obtains medicine. Many also report that they appear to the sick in visions and indicate what they
should do; when they do it, they depart healed. I have heard many such accounts, which I thought too long to pursue, judging what I have said sufficient. All
who faithfully prayed departed healed.

## 98

**[098]** The martyr Phocas also rests in Syria, joined by region to these martyrs. After the many injuries he suffered for the Redeemer’s name, the way in
which he triumphed over that ancient serpent is still declared to the people today. If a serpent in those places tightens its bite on anyone and diffuses its
poisons, as soon as the stricken person touches the gate of the forecourt where the martyr rests, the swelling is suppressed, the poison’s power evacuated, and
he is saved. As is widely reported, some already swollen by the evil beast’s bite, their whole bodies inflated as the poison thickened in them so that they were
breathing out their spirits, were carried in attendants’ hands, placed in the forecourt, and healed. It is never permitted for a person to die from this venom
if, full of faith, he touches the sacred threshold.

## 99

**[099]** Another martyr, Domitius, is present in this region. Although he bestows many benefits on the inhabitants, he heals sciatica with especially swift
power. It is said that the saint himself was afflicted by this pain while in the body. While he was healing many laboring under this affliction, as I said, a
certain Jew seized by the same infirmity devoutly sought the saint’s basilica although he did not believe in Christ. He ordered himself laid at the gate of the
forecourt, crying out that he was unworthy to enter the sacred threshold. He said: “Glorious martyr, I know that I am blinded by the veil of the Law and that
you might disdain to bestow mercy on me. But now I flee to you and as a suppliant ask your mercy: first turn aside my bodily infirmity and then tear away the
disease of unbelief.” After he made this confession before the courtyard gate, night came and he slept. The blessed martyr did not delay long to have mercy.
Visiting the sick man in a dream that night, he commanded him to depart healed. Awaking, the Jew felt himself restored to health. Confessing that Christ the Son
of God is the Savior of the world, he departed healed. Seeing this, Christians held by the same infirmity brought complaints to the saint: “Behold, I have
confessed God rightly and have not yet merited liberation, while this unbeliever in Christ the King, circumcised in flesh but not in heart, departs healed!”
Saying this, they angrily began to break the basilica’s lamps hanging from the ceiling. Nor did they lack the mercy they sought: healed that very day, they
returned home.

## 100

**[100]** I have learned of many miracles performed by the martyr George, of which I will relate a few. Certain people were carrying his relics together with
those of other saints. When the bearers arrived at a place within the boundary of Limoges where a few clerics continually prayed to the Lord in an oratory
joined together from wooden boards, they asked for lodging. Kindly received, they spent the night singing psalms with the other brothers. When morning came,
