When his attendants saw him lying down longer than usual, they approached and said: “Why are you weighed down for so long? Such prolonged devotion in prayer was
never your custom.” They said of him that whenever he entered a church, he would mutter briefly and leave again without even bowing his head. When the servants
questioned him and he could make no answer, they lifted him in their hands from the place and laid him on a bed in the nearest cell. As the fever grew stronger,
the wretch cried out that the martyr was burning him. What he had at first kept silent he now confessed as the torches of the soul’s judgment were applied: his
crimes. He begged as loudly as he could that water be poured over him. Water was brought in a vessel and repeatedly thrown over him, and smoke issued from his
body as from a furnace. Meanwhile the wretch’s limbs turned black as though burned, and such a stench came from them that hardly any of those standing by could
endure it. Then he motioned with his hand to indicate that he felt lighter. Soon afterwards, as they withdrew, he breathed out his spirit. There is no doubt
what place he holds in the other world, since he departed this one under such a judgment.

## 18. The Man Who Stole a Horse during the Saint’s Vigil

**[018]** On another occasion, during the vigil of the festival, a man stole a horse belonging to someone who had happened to come to that solemnity. He mounted
it and hastened swiftly away. One who had lost the light of truth was not to be found by the light, and night was to conceal the thievish deceit of one whose
breast was possessed by the darkness of greed. The Lord said of such people in the Gospel: *Everyone who does evil hates the light*. When the sky grew light, he
said: “Now I am safe, for I am thirty leagues away from the saint’s basilica; now I believe myself near my own house.” While he silently turned these thoughts
over within himself, the darkness was driven from the sky, and he realized that he was wandering among the people near the same village. Fearing that his crime
would be publicly exposed, he very cautiously restored the horse to the place from which he had taken it. Thus the wretch was held by the martyr’s power all
night in a circuit around the village and, as I believe, was deluded by the author of evil who possessed him, so that he could not take the road he wished. O
wicked greed, what are you doing? You always cast your lovers down into confusion.

## 19. The Man Who Swore Falsely over a Triens

**[019]** A certain man had lent another a *triens*, which he received back a few days later. A year afterwards he met the man in the courtyard of the sanctuary
and demanded that his property be returned to him, as though he had not received it. The other protested and maintained that he had returned what he had
received. When they had argued for a very long time, the man who had made the repayment said to his companion: “How long shall we both contend? Let us place
this matter under the judgment of almighty God. Let us go to the martyr’s tomb, and let the holy patron’s power decide what you say under oath.” The other did
not hesitate. He entered the tomb chamber and boldly raised his hands to swear falsely, but the unhappy wretch immediately became rigid. His voice stuck in his
throat, his tongue was constricted in his jaws, and his empty lips quivered without speech. He was also quite unable to draw back the arms he had raised in aid
of his frustrated oath. While the crowd marvelled and the crime was made public, the whole multitude of people broke out with one voice, imploring the Lord’s
mercy and the blessed martyr’s help. After four hours or more he returned to his senses and publicly confessed that he had been making an unjust demand. He then
departed healed.

## 20. The Man Who Despoiled the Holy Basilica by Theft

**[020]** The man who did violence to the holy basilica had often heard these stories, but kindness could not soften a wicked mind once possessed by vice, as
Solomon testifies: *Wisdom does not enter a malicious soul*. The saint’s festival had come, and a certain man among the people saw the blessed basilica gleaming
with magnificent ornaments. He coveted in his wicked mind what he could not conceal once he had obtained it. When the people left the basilica after the evening
office, he hid himself by shrinking into a corner of the building. When nocturnal silence had been granted to all and shadowy darkness covered the world, he
arose from the corner. Without hesitation, since he was impelled by Satan as his attendant, he leapt swiftly over the railing of the blessed tomb, tore down
from above a cross flashing with gems, and threw it to the ground. He gathered the small curtains and hangings suspended around the walls, made them into one
bundle, and put it on his shoulders. Raising the cross in his hand, he returned to the place from which he had set out. He placed the bundle at his head and,
overcome by the sleep of sin, fell asleep. At midnight the guards making their rounds of the holy basilica saw in a corner one gem of the cross shining like a
heavenly beam. Astonished, they approached fearfully. Bringing a candle near, they found the man lying there with the stolen things that he had been unable to
carry away. They held him in custody that night. When morning came, he revealed everything he had done, maintaining that he had fallen asleep from exhaustion
because, after going around the basilica for a very long time with his load, he had been unable to find a door by which to leave.

## 21. The Man Who Lost His Horse at the Festival

**[021]** The martyr displayed many other signs against transgressors, but let these suffice to restrain their negligence. Now let me return to the joys of the
benefits that he bestows upon the people with generous compassion. But first I think I should not omit something I know very well from experience: what faithful
prayer to this patron obtains when property has been lost. I have chosen to relate only one instance. A devout poor man had come to the blessed martyr’s
festival. He let his horse loose and entered the sacred building; standing motionless at the vigils, he passed the night in prayer with the others. When the sky
grew light, he returned to his lodging and did not find the horse he had left. He searched for a very long time, but did not discover even tracks showing in
which direction it had gone. After two days he again ran through the woodland pastures, questioning the inhabitants to see whether anyone had captured it or had
seen it captured by someone. Finding no clue of any kind, anxious and sorrowful he returned to the holy tomb. There he explained the cause of his pain and
grief, saying: “Holy one, I came to your threshold bringing nothing but the prayers of my littleness. I have taken nothing unjustly and done nothing unworthy of
your solemnity. Why, then, have I lost my property? I ask you to restore what has been lost and return what I need.” After offering this approach with tears, he
left the church and saw his horse in the distance, held by a certain man. He went up to him and questioned him about where he came from, where he had been, and
how long he had possessed the horse. He learned that it had been found at the very hour when he had implored the blessed martyr’s help.

## 22. A Blind Man Given Sight

**[022]** A certain man had lost an eye through a diabolical attack and was sitting miserably in his little lodging, deprived of light. Unable to work with his
own hands, he had no hope of obtaining food. A man appeared to him in a vision of the night and advised him to walk to the blessed basilica, promising that if
he prayed devoutly there, help would be found. He delayed not at all. Taking his staff and supported by a boy, he entered the holy place. After completing his
prayer, he approached Publianus, the chief priest who then governed the place, and begged him to place Christ’s cross upon his blind eyes. Publianus was a very
religious man. Wishing to avoid hardness and pride, he tried to escape the request, but the blind man held fast to him and would not let him go at all until he
fulfilled what was asked. Publianus then prostrated himself before the tomb and for a very long time implored the martyr’s intercession. Then he brought his
hand to the blind eyes. As soon as he made the sign of the cross, the man received his sight. Marvel, I beg you, at the martyr’s power: it is not enough for him
to work miracles himself; now, with the favour of his power concurring, he also works publicly through the hands of his disciples. Nor was the disciple’s merit
small, to whom these gifts are seen to have been granted.

## 23. The Healing of the Foot of Gallus, Afterwards Bishop

**[023]** At that time my uncle Gallus, afterwards bishop, was in the city of Clermont. It seems right not to omit how he was helped by the saint’s power in his
youth. I have often related what destruction King Theuderic inflicted upon the Auvergne, when neither old nor young were left any of their possessions except
the empty land, which the barbarians could not carry away with them. In those days my uncle, of glorious memory, who later, as I have said, governed the church
of Clermont in the episcopal office, was an orphan. His possessions were so plundered by the army that nothing whatever remained in store. With only one small
boy, he often travelled on foot as far as the village of Brioude. Once, while he was making this journey, he loosened his shoes because of the heat of the sun
and walked with bare soles. He trod upon a thorny stake which, perhaps recently cut, was still fixed in the earth, its upright point hidden among the green
grass. It was driven into his sole, projected beyond it, and was broken off below, so that it could not be pulled out. A stream of blood flowed. Unable to walk,
he implored the blessed martyr’s help. The pain was somewhat suppressed, and he completed the journey he had begun, although limping. On the third night, as the
wound festered, very great pain arose. He fled for refuge to the help he had already proved and prostrated himself gloriously at the tomb. When the vigils were
complete, he returned to his bed. While awaiting the martyr’s power, he was overcome by sleep. On rising, he felt no pain. He looked at his sole, and the part
of the stake that had entered was not visible; yet he felt that it had been pulled from his foot. Searching carefully for the wood, he found it on his bed and
marvelled at how it had come out. In his episcopate he used to show the site of the wound, where a great hollow could still be seen, and testify that the
blessed martyr’s power had been at work in it.

## 24. The Fever of His Nephew Peter

**[024]** After a long time, the blessed martyr’s festival came again, and my father was hastening with his whole household to the joys of this solemnity. As we
were travelling, my elder brother Peter was seized by a burning fever and became so gravely ill that he could neither thrive nor take food. That whole journey
was made with great grief, and the issue hung in the balance: would he recover or die? At last we reached the place in this distress. We entered the basilica
and venerated the tomb of the sacrosanct martyr. The sick boy also prostrated himself on the pavement, praying the glorious martyr for healing. When the prayer
was complete, he returned to the lodging, and the fever subsided a little. When night came and we were hastening to the vigils, he asked to be carried there
too. Lying before the tomb, he implored the martyr’s intercession throughout the whole night. When the nocturnal watch was finished, he asked that dust gathered
around the blessed tomb either be given him to drink or hung around his neck. When this was done, all the burning fever subsided so completely that on that very
day he took food in health and walked wherever his inclination led him.

## 25. My Headache

**[025]** At the following festival, while we were again hastening with great joy to the holy basilica, my head, struck by the sun, began to ache severely. As
the pain increased, it generated an inward fever, so that it allowed me neither to take food nor to speak. When I had been consumed by this pain for two days,
on the third day we came to the basilica of Saint Ferreolus, beside which is the spring I mentioned above. This basilica is about ten stades from the village of
Brioude. When we reached the place, I decided to go as far as the spring, trusting in the martyr’s power that if a little of its water were poured over me, I
would soon be healed. On arriving, I poured out prayer, drew water, cooled my mouth, and poured it over my head. Immediately, as the water ran off, the pain was
driven away, and I departed healed. I went joyfully all the way to the tomb of the glorious martyr, marvelling and thanking him because he had deigned to visit
me with his power before I was privileged to behold his tomb.

## 26. A Fevered Man Healed at the Spring

**[026]** Because the martyr was struck down there, this spring possesses exceptional power. A certain man seized by fever and in extremity desired to draw
water from the spring, and faithfully begged to be carried to it. His people lifted him in their arms and laid him by the place. As soon as he received a
draught of the water and bathed his face and head, he was granted health. He had been carried there by other people’s hands, but returned by his own steps. He
was an inhabitant of this village, but his name has been lost.

## 27. Thunder and Lightning in the Basilica

**[027]** One day a storm arose and descended rapidly upon the village of Brioude with a great rush of wind. Lightning flashed from the clouds and thunder gave
forth terrible sounds. The earth shook with the crash, and it seemed that almost everything would be burned by the lightning. Their only hope lay in the
glorious martyr’s power. Without delay, with a flash and a heavy thunderclap, a fiery bolt entered through the opening from which the bell rope hangs. It struck
two columns and shook fragments from them. Rebounding from there, it went out through the window above the holy tomb; yet no one among the people was injured,
thanks to the blessed martyr’s protection. How great is the blessed martyr’s love for his own foster-children! He allowed columns to be struck, not the throng;
glass to be shattered, not the congregation; lightning to pass over his own tomb, rather than the destruction of the whole multitude. When the bolt had been
expelled from the holy martyr’s basilica, it burned a heap of hay, killed sheep, and destroyed beasts of burden. If anyone thinks this happened by chance, let
him rather marvel and be astonished at the renowned martyr’s power: fire passing through the midst of the people harmed no one, but fulfilled its course only
where it knew it had permission.

## 28. The Man Who Could Not Reach the Tomb because of the Crowd

**[028]** A cleric of Aredius, abbot of Limoges, came to the festival. Because of the multitude of people, he could not only fail to reach the holy tomb, but
could not even enter the basilica itself. He returned sorrowfully to his lodging, lay down on his bed, and fell asleep. Immediately a man stood beside him in a
vision and said: “Why are you overcome by sleep? Go quickly to the martyr’s church, and you will find everything open.” He rose terrified and, believing what
had been said, hastened quickly to test whether what had been revealed to him was true. When he came to the door, he found that the people had withdrawn on
every side and that a way had been made all the way to the holy altar and the tomb itself, with no one obstructing him. Thus he approached without any pressure,
poured out his prayer, and returned with joy. Lest anyone doubt this, I call almighty God to witness that I learned it from the mouth of the abbot himself, in
whose monk it occurred.

## 29. His Festival

**[029]** The people, ignorant of the time of his festival, hung in sorrowful suspense, not knowing the day on which the blessed martyr ought to be honoured for
the glory of his power and passion. This ignorance persisted until the time of blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre. It happened that the aforesaid bishop came
to Brioude. When he asked the inhabitants when these sacred rites were celebrated, they answered that they did not know. He said: “Let us pray, and perhaps the
Lord’s power will reveal it to us.” When they had done so, morning came. Calling together the elders of the place, he said that the festival should be
celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of the seventh month. From that time the devout people who come there, paying their vows to the bishop, carry
back healing for both soul and body.

## 30. The Demoniacs

**[030]** When demoniacs come, they often vomit forth reproaches against the saint of God, asking why the saint summons others to his festivals. They confess
them by name and declare their powers and merits. They say: “Julian, let it suffice you to torment us by your own power. Why do you summon the others? Why do
you invite strangers? Here is Martin of Pannonia, our perpetual enemy, who drove three dead men out of our caverns. Here is Privatus of the Gabali, who refused
to surrender his sheep to the barbarians when they were stirred up at our instigation. Your colleague Ferreolus has come from Vienne; through you he has sent
punishment upon us and protection to the inhabitants. Why do you call Symphorian of Autun and Saturninus of Toulouse? You have assembled a council to inflict
infernal torment upon us.” By saying these and similar things, they present the saints of God to human minds so clearly that no one can doubt that the saints
dwell there. Many sick people are healed by them and depart in health.

## 31. The Gentleness of the Animals

**[031]** It is also most worthy of record how gentle the animals offered in fulfilment of vows become in this basilica: how playful calves, kicking horses, and
grunting pigs grow quiet when they have crossed the holy threshold. I have often seen powerful bulls, tied and led with ropes by fifteen men or more, make such
a violent charge at the men that you would think they would break the ropes themselves. Yet when they entered the holy building, they became so quiet that you
would think you were leading them like gentle lambs. I have also seen many of them enter through the midst of the crowds, moving the people aside with their
muzzles and bowed heads rather than their horns. As though approaching a judge’s tribunal, they displayed a certain feeling of fear. They did not kick, gore
anyone, or look fiercely about, but hastened in complete gentleness to the holy altar and kissed it; then they returned with the same patience with which they
had entered. So too the wildness of other beasts of burden, when they come there, lays aside all fury and becomes gentle, so that you behold them with great
astonishment as mild as doves. No one at all is permitted to remove anything from animals offered in fulfilment of vows; no one presumes to exchange or buy them
before they reach the basilica. Those who have done so have often been severely shaken by divine vengeance. Fever threatens them, some evil creeps upon them,
heavy loss follows, or disease carries off the animal that was withheld. The matter seldom passes without immediate vengeance.

## 32. His Relics Carried into the Countryside of Reims

**[032]** Let it suffice to have spoken of the miracles that have been or are being performed around the holy basilica. Now, prompted by devotion, I wish to say
a little about those places where his relics are kept and so bring this little book to an end. A certain man in the province of Belgica Secunda, in the district
around the city of Reims, zealously built a basilica in honour of the blessed martyr. When the building was complete, he faithfully and devoutly sought his
relics. Having received them, he was returning along the road with psalmody when he entered the countryside of Reims. Not far from the road was the field of a
certain wealthy man of that region, and a great multitude had gathered to cut it. As the traveller approached with these relics, one of the ploughmen began to
be violently tormented and, as though beside himself, said: “See, most blessed Julian is approaching! Behold his power! Behold his glory! Run, men; leave the
oxen, abandon the ploughs, let the whole company go to meet him!” They stood astonished and did not know what he was saying. While they were dazed and wondering
at both the cries and the words of the man, the wretch immediately left his ploughshare in the field. Throwing himself to the ground and beating his hands, he
rushed swiftly to the side by which the man bearing the blessed martyr’s relics was coming, crying: “Holy one, why do you torment me so? Glorious martyr, why do
you burn me? Why do you enter a region not owed to you? Why do you search through our dwellings?” While he was saying this, he came turbulently to the place
where the priest had already erected a canopy. Prostrating himself before the holy relics, he lay on the ground for a very long time. When the priest placed the
holy reliquary upon him, blood immediately burst from his mouth, and he was cleansed of the assault of diabolical error. Afterwards he proclaimed the saint’s
power and became a companion on that journey.

## 33. His Relics Also Displayed in the East

**[033]** I shall now tell what the report of faithful brethren indicates concerning his relics in the East. In a certain eastern city, while a man was being
tormented by a demon in church, he declared that the blessed martyr’s relics were on a ship. When the ship reached port, the man leapt toward it and threw
himself on the ground before it. Corrupt matter burst from his mouth and nostrils, and the man was cleansed. When this was reported to the bishop, he stirred
the people to proceed to the port with lighted candles. The shipmaster heard of it and, weeping for joy, hastened to meet the bishop. He maintained that he had
taken nothing else from the blessed martyr’s basilica except a little of the dust lying around the holy tomb. Almighty God confirmed the man’s faith and did not
permit the martyr’s power to be hidden. The bishop then took up the relics and carried them with great honour to the holy church. The merchant, seeing such
great wonders, built a basilica in the martyr’s honour. He placed the blessed relics in it and afterwards saw many miracles performed.

## 34. Gregory’s Own Experience of the Relics

**[034]** I myself experienced these things long ago. After my ordination I happened to go to the Auvergne. On my journey I visited the blessed basilica. When
the festival was complete, I tore off fringes from the pall that covers the holy tomb. Believing that I would carry protection for myself in them, I finished my
prayer and departed. At the city of Tours, monks had built a basilica in honour of this martyr, as well as their means allowed, desiring that it be consecrated
with his powers. Hearing that I had brought these relics, they asked that the building be dedicated and enriched with these same safeguards. I quietly took up
the reliquary and, as night was beginning, hastened to the basilica of blessed Martin. A faithful man who was then standing some distance away told me that when
we entered the basilica, he saw a beacon of immense light fall from heaven and descend upon the blessed basilica, and then it seemed to enter inside.

## 35. How His Relics Were Placed in His Basilica at Tours

**[035]** When faithful people related these things to us on the following day, we concluded that the light had proceeded from the blessed martyr’s power. The
sacrosanct relics were therefore placed upon the altar. After a night of vigil, they were carried with great psalmody to the aforesaid basilica. And behold, one
of the demoniacs, wringing his hands, his mouth gaping and spitting bloody spittle, said: “Martin, why have you joined yourself to Julian? Why do you summon him
to this place? Your presence alone was torment enough for us; you have called one like yourself to increase our torments. Why are you doing this? Why do you
torture us together with Julian?” While the wretch uttered these and other cries, and after the solemnities of mass had been completed, he dashed himself
repeatedly before the holy altar for a very long time. Corrupt matter flowed from his mouth, and he was freed from the infestation of diabolical madness.

## 36. The Wine Increased on That Night

**[036]** I do not think I should pass over in silence what happened on that night before the holy relics were placed there. A monk of that place, rejoicing at
the coming of the solemnity and most generously inviting everyone to the basilica’s little cellar, urged them all to keep faithful vigil in the basilica.
Drawing wine from a vessel, he began joyfully to offer it to them as an act of devotion, saying: “Divine compassion is granting us great patronage in the
blessed martyr. I therefore ask your charity to keep vigil unanimously with me, for tomorrow his holy relics are to be placed in this place.” They passed the
night with sacred hymns and heavenly melodies and also celebrated the solemnities of mass. The cleric, exulting in the festival, again began to invite those
whom he had previously invited to take refreshment, saying: “I thank you for remaining so steadfast in keeping vigil.” Nor did the martyr long delay rewarding
their good will with the grace of his power. When the cleric entered the storeroom, he found that the small cask, which he had left almost half empty, was
overflowing through its upper opening. The abundance of flowing wine made a stream across the ground all the way to the door. Astonished, he repeatedly drew out
the vessel placed below, full. Even after a very great quantity had been dispensed, nothing whatever was lacking; it remained continually full until the next
day, while everyone marvelled. It was the third day before the Kalends of the fifth month. O wonderful power of the martyr! It produced wine from a vessel
without the flower of the vine. Whereas harvested wines are usually stored in vessels, here the cask poured forth new wine in which no grape had flowed, but
power alone. The little vessel swelled with liquid; the fruit was not brought in but created. The Lord did this to glorify the martyr—he who filled the Virgin’s
womb without seed and caused her to remain a mother in chastity. Here May overflows with a new fruit, offering Falernian wine to drink without vines. In other
vineyards the buds were scarcely breaking forth, but in this vessel wine flowed from power. May was made equal to October, since it offered new cups; indeed, it
had more than October, for no vineyard was shown in store, yet Falernian wine was generated in the house. A rough vintage came without a winepress, found not on
vine-branches but in hidden mysteries. No heap of grapes was pressed from the tree, yet waves of wine flowed. Falernian was drawn when no footprints were seen
in the winepress; behold, no vine was visible, and the cups were abundantly filled. But what am I saying? That heavenly power is never lacking to the faithful.
He who once provided wine from water at a wedding now generously offers the same to his own people without the substance of any element. He who satisfied five
thousand men with two fish now restores multiplied gifts to good will. At the time of his own birth the angelic voice testified, saying: *Glory to God in the
highest, and on earth peace to people of good will*. But now let us come to the subsequent works of power.

## 37. A Crippled Man Healed in the Same Place

**[037]** A servant of this monastery had long been miserably crippled and dragged himself along. He came to this basilica of the saint and kept the vigils.
When they were complete, he returned to his bed in the morning; while being carried in the bearers’ hands, his sinews were loosened and he was healed.

## 38. A Blind Girl Given Sight

**[038]** A certain girl had sore eyes and was almost blinded by an excessive stream of tears. Her father heard of the glorious martyr’s power and hastened with
her to the holy basilica. After the vigils had been celebrated, in the morning he brought food and drink to the poor who belonged to that register. While they
were feasting, the girl suddenly cried out that she was tormented by a headache and begged to be allowed a little sleep. While she rested and the guests applied
themselves to the feast, she rose and asked to be led to the holy altar. Before she had prostrated herself on the ground and earnestly implored the Lord’s
mercy, her tears were checked and her eyes were cleansed of their soreness; she rose joyful. Then, to her father’s joy, she was returned home healed.

## 39. Another Crippled Child

**[039]** There was another very small boy whose parents lived not far from this basilica. In the second year after his birth, all his limbs became contracted,
and he was reared without hope of any improvement. He was so contracted that his knees could not be separated from his mouth at all. His parents kept vigil at
the holy basilica and laid the little child before the sacrosanct relics. A little afterwards they found him sitting, with all his limbs straightened. They then
poured out prayer and returned to their home rejoicing.

## 40. Perjurers

**[040]** In the territory of Tours there is a village called Gaudiacum, where relics of the blessed martyr are kept. Although it is frequently illuminated by
great miracles, vengeance is most often active there against perjurers. When anyone swears falsely there, as though at the instigation of the enemy of the human
race, divine vengeance follows so swiftly that he immediately suffers openly, either in a succession of losses, in the loss of a kinsman, or in being consumed
by disease. The martyr by no means permits the offence to remain unpunished; nor does the crude rusticity of the barbarians dare to swear falsely there with
such rash daring. Let these examples concerning this matter suffice, for it would take long to recount in order everything that has happened there.

## 41. The Relics That the Priest Aridius Took

**[041]** When the priest Aridius, a very religious man whom I also mentioned in the second book of the miracles of blessed Martin, came to me from Limoges, I
carefully examined his life and conduct and began to ask what the most blessed martyr had revealed in miracles there. Aridius had built a basilica in the
blessed martyr’s honour and enriched it with his relics. Being very modest, he hesitated for a long time, but at last and most unwillingly disclosed these
things: “When I first visited the blessed Julian’s basilica, I took a little wax from the tomb. Then I came to the spring in which the blessed martyr’s blood
was shed. I washed my face in its water and filled a small ampulla from it as a blessing. I call almighty God to witness that before I reached home it had
changed into balsam in colour, thickness, and fragrance. When the bishop came to dedicate the building and I had related this, he wished to place nothing else
as relics upon the holy altar except the little vessel whose water had been changed into balsam, saying: ‘These are genuine relics, which the martyr has
enriched with the powers of paradise.’”

## 42. A Paralytic Healed

**[042]** There are indeed many other stories; I omit most of them and disclose a few. A certain sick man, weak in all his limbs, was placed on a wagon and
brought to his monastery. While he lay in this vehicle before the basilica at night, he suddenly saw it shining with great splendour and heard within it the
voices of people singing psalms, as though there were many of them. While this was happening and he was pouring out prayer, he became as though stupified and
forgetful of his pains. As he approached, the splendour he had seen passed before his eyes. When the radiance was withdrawn, he returned to himself and
perceived that he had been restored to his former health.

## 43. A Blind Man Given Sight

**[043]** A blind man also approached his sacrosanct altar, led by a guide. When he touched his eyes to the covering of the holy relics, he received the light.
Demoniacs covered with this pall have also often been cleansed. Whenever the power of judges acted excessively in that place, it departed confounded.

## 44. The Cross Stolen from the Altar

**[044]** Above this altar hung a cross of solid gold, made with elegant workmanship. It was so brilliant to behold that you would think it was made of the
purest gold. When barbarians came, someone judged it to be golden, tore it down, and hid it in his bosom. But the man who had taken it was immediately burdened
by such a great weight that he could not support it at all. Immediately pierced by the martyr’s power and moved to repentance, he sent it back from his journey
and restored it to the holy place.

## 45. How His Relics Were Sought

**[045]** After these things had happened, Aridius sent his cleric, saying: “Go to the blessed Julian’s basilica. Pour out prayer and ask the custodians to be
so kind as to grant you some wax or dust from the tomb where he lies, so that when it has been brought back I may receive it from you with a blessing.” The
cleric went, requested what had been commanded, and received it. When he wished to carry what he had received, he was burdened by such a great weight that he
could scarcely raise his neck. Shaken by great trembling, he fell to the pavement. Pouring out prayer again with tears, he arose unharmed and perceived that he
had received freedom to depart. He therefore set out on his journey. As the sun was burning excessively, he was seized by thirst. Coming to a villa near the
road, he approached a little cottage and asked for water. A young man coming out of it to give an answer saw them and fell to the ground as though dead. His
parents ran together and accused the travellers, maintaining that their kinsman had been killed by their magic arts. They seized the boy and lifted him up half
alive. But he escaped from their hands, clapped his palms, and began to rage and cry out that he was being burned by the power of the martyr Julian. Hearing
this, the cleric placed the reliquary containing the holy relics upon his head and, full of faith, began to pray most earnestly. The young man vomited up blood
and the demon, and departed cleansed. Afterwards the bearer, strengthened in faith, completed the whole journey with psalms and thanksgivings and reached the
desired place with the martyr as his guide. From that time onward, so many demoniacs, sufferers from chills, and people afflicted by various diseases were
healed there by the martyr’s power that neither their names nor their number could be collected.

## 46a. The Boy Taken to a Diviner, and Another Healed by the Saint’s Power

**[046a]** Among the other remarkable miracles that ought to be recorded, I include this one, that it may correct the foolish and strengthen the wise. In the
time of Bishop Cautinus, when the plague called the inguinal pestilence was devastating the Auvergne for its destruction because the people’s sins had
multiplied, I sought the village of Brioude, so that I who could not be protected by my own merits might be saved by the protection of the blessed martyr
Julian. While I was staying in that village, one of our boys was seized by this disease. He laid his head upon his little bed and began to suffer gravely. He
had a continual fever together with phlegm in the stomach, so that if he took anything he immediately vomited it back. Food gave him no strength but was rather
thought to be his death. When my people saw him afflicted to the point of extremity, they called in a certain diviner. He came without delay, approached the
sick boy, and tried to practise his art. He muttered incantations, cast lots, hung amulets around his neck, and promised life to one whom he himself had
delivered over to death. These things were done without my knowledge. When they were reported to me, I was filled with bitterness and recalled with a heavy sigh
what the Lord declared to King Ahaziah through the prophet Elijah: *Because you have abandoned the Lord God of Israel and consulted the god of Ekron, you shall
not rise from the bed to which you have gone up, but shall surely die*. After the diviner’s arrival, the boy was more violently inflamed by fever and breathed
out his spirit. A few days after his death, another boy began to suffer from a similar affliction. Then I said to my people: “Go to the martyr’s tomb and bring
something from it to the sick boy. You will see the mighty works of God and learn the difference between the righteous and the unrighteous, between one who
fears God and one who does not serve him.” They went and took a little dust from around the tomb where he lay. As soon as the sick boy drank some of it with
water, he immediately obtained healing; his strength returned, the fever was extinguished, and he recovered. Understand now, all you who are foolish among the
people; after you have examined these things, know that the works the devil performs to seduce the human race are nothing. I therefore admonish everyone who has
been signed with the banner of the cross, everyone who has been cleansed by the washing of baptism, everyone who has put off the old nature and now lives as a
new person, to set such things aside and disregard them. Let him seek the patronage of the martyrs, through whom miracles of healing are celebrated; let him ask
the help of the confessors, who are deservedly called friends of the Lord; and he will obtain whatever he wishes.

## 46b. Roses Divinely Revealed at His Tomb

**[046b]** At that time, after the death of the custodian Proserius, the deacon Urbanus was appointed custodian of this basilica, and a wonderful thing appeared
at the holy tomb. While the deacon was keeping vigil on his little bed, a sound was heard as though the door of the basilica were being opened. After an
interval of many hours, he heard it closed again. He then rose from his bed and, with a light going before him, approached the holy tomb. Wonderful to tell! He
saw the pavement strewn with glowing roses. They were very large and had a fragrance of immense sweetness. [He also marvelled at roses within the very carvings
of the railing, for it was the ninth month.] They were as fresh as though you would think they had been plucked from green branches at that very moment. He
gathered them with great reverence and put them away privately, distributing remedies from them to many sick people. A certain demoniac who came from the
territory of Tours drank a potion infused with them; the demon was cast out, and he departed cleansed.

## 47. A Woman Given Sight

**[047]** There was a woman blind from birth who asked her parents to bring her to blessed Martin’s tomb. When she arrived, she prostrated herself for three
days at the railings outside the tomb of the holy bishop. In a dream she received an answer from the holy man: “If you desire to receive the light, seek the
basilica of Saint Julian. When you seek the martyr’s protection there, he and Martin together will restore the sight you need by the united intercession of
their prayers.” The woman arose but, not knowing that relics of this martyr were kept in the territory of Tours, directed her steps to the city of Saintes.
Victorina, a mistress of a household descended from noble stock, had built a basilica on the territory of her villa and placed relics of the blessed martyr in
it. The woman approached this building and prayed for three days. On the third day came the feast of the Lord’s Baptist. While the people stood and listened to
the teaching of the readings, a great murmur suddenly arose. The priest celebrating the solemnity wished to suppress the voices and asked what it was. One of
those standing by said: “The murmur cannot be quieted, for the Lord’s power has revealed a miracle. Behold, that woman who was declared blind has received her
sight, and blood has burst from her eyes.” Then all blessed God, recognizing alike what had been done.

## 48. The Relics Brought by the Priest Nanninus

**[048]** The priest Nanninus of the house of Vibriacum sought relics of this glorious martyr. He obtained them by order of the blessed bishop Avitus and came
with psalmody as far as the basilica of Saint Ferreolus, which is situated far from the village itself; there one demoniac was cleansed. As he proceeded singing
psalms and reached the midpoint, another girl departed cleansed, the wicked enemy having been driven away by the saint’s power before her.

## 49. Many Sick People Saved by the Same Relics

**[049]** When he came to the place where he had built an oratory in the saint’s honour, he placed these relics upon the altar. One man who had lost his eyes
approached him, and another whose hand was powerless. When their prayer was complete, the former received light after darkness, and the latter the use of his
hand after long inactivity. A woman named Aeterna, who was tormented together with her daughter by the wicked enemy, was healed at this altar and departed safe
with her child. Several sufferers from chills were also cured in that place.

## 50. Another Blind Man Given Sight

**[050]** Since it is not unreasonable that blessed Julian should bestow gifts of healing together with John or Martin, with whom he exults as a victor over the
world in heaven, I shall also relate how he flourished with similar power together with Nicetius of Lyon. Within the boundary of the territory of Tours, a
certain Litomeris built a basilica in honour of the holy martyr. When we were invited according to custom to bless it, we placed in it relics of the holy martyr
Julian together with those of Nicetius of Lyon. Not long afterwards a blind man came, poured out a faithful prayer, and was granted the recovery of his sight. I
have mentioned this blind man in the book of the life of Saint Nicetius, for it is fitting that writing should join together the shared power of both saints.
Let the attentive reader therefore understand from these miracles that he can be saved only by the help of the martyrs and of the other friends of God. I
implore the Lord’s mercy through the patronage of the blessed martyr Julian, that, standing as an advocate before the Lord in the causes of his own foster-son,
he may obtain for me that I complete the course of this life without the impediment of any stain, and that I blamelessly hold, faithfully practise, and manfully
guard until the consummation of this life those things which I confessed in baptism. Amen.

*Here ends the book of the glory of Saint Julian.*

# LATIN TEXT

---

## 1. De passione eius.

**[001]** Magnum in nobis quodam modo igniculum ad iustitiae suae adipiscendam semitam pietas divina succendit, cum dicit: Oculi Domini super iustos, et aures
eine ad preces eorum; ostendens, quod qui iustitiam ex toto corde dilexerit, cum deprecatus fuerit, audiatur a Domino. Utinam quisque nostrum, cum haec cantare
coeperit, statim spraetis mundi scandalis, neglectis concupiscentiis vanis, derelictisque semitis pravis, iustitiae viam expeditus et sine inpedimento
saecularium actionum conaretur inrepere. Per hanc enim viam Abel iustus suscipitur, Enoch beatus adsumitur, Noe reservatur, Abraham elegitur, Isaac benedicitur,
Iacob dilatatur, Ioseph custoditur, Moyses sanctificatur, David praedestinatur, Salomon ditatur, tres pueri inter incendia rorolenta vaticinantur, Danihel inter
innocuas bestias pascitur. Per hanc viam apostoli diriguntur, martyres beati glorificantur. 'Et qualiter?' inquis. Scilicet dum infirma curant, mortua
suscitant, praesentia contemnunt, futura desiderant, tortores dispiciunt, poenas non sentiunt, ad caelestia regna contendunt. Quod procul dubio virtute propria
non obtenerent, nisi per viam iustitiae rectissime incedentes a Domino audirentur. Sic et inclitus martyr Iulianus, qui Viennensi ortus urbe Arvernus datus est
martyr, ab hoc igne succensus, haec concupivit ac mente tota desideravit. Quia cum esset apud beatissimum Ferreolum, iam tunc martyrii odoro flagrabat. Qui,
relictis divitiis ac propinquis, tantum ob solius amorem martyrii Arvernus advenit. Sed nec hoc sine divino mandato peregit, cum tunc persecutio in Viennensi
urbe ferveret. Legerat enim, Dominum praedixisse: Si vos persecuti fuerint in istam civitatem, fugite in aliam. Contulit ergo se hic in Arverno territurio non
metu mortis, sed ut relinquens propria facilius perveniret ad palmam; metuebat enim, ne ei parentes essent obvii, si inter eos hoc certamen inisset; et perderet
miles Christi coronam gloriae, si legitime non certasset. Igitur instante persecutione ad Brivatinsim vicum, in quo fanatici erroris neniae colebantur, advenit.
Et cum insequi adversarios nutu Dei sensisset, a vidua quadam se occultari deprecatur. Quem illa tegens, ilico, martyre poscente, detexit; qui suis
insecutoribus ita infit: 'Nolo', inquit, 'diutius commorari in hoc saeculo, quia sitio tota animi aviditate iam Christum'. At illi eductam vibranti dextera
frameam, deciso capite, in tribus, ut ita dicam, partibus gloriosus dividitur martyr. Nam caput Viennae defertur, artus Brivate reconduntur; felix anima Christo
conditore suscipitur. Senes quoque, qui sacrosanctum corpus mancipaverant sepulturae, ita redintegrati sunt, ut in senectute summa positi tamquam iuvenes
haberentur. Caput quoque eius Ferreolus martyr accepit, conpletoque certamine, tam illius membra quam istius caput in unius tumuli receptaculo collocantur. Quod
ne cuiquam fortassis videatur incredibilis esse narratio, quae audivi gesta fideliter prodam.

## 2. De revelatione capitis eius.

**[002]** Quodam autem tempore dum ad occursum beati Niceti antestitis usque Lugduno processissem, libuit animo non aliter nisi orationis causa Viennam adire et
praecipue sepulchrum visitare Ferreoli martyris gloriosi; insederat enim menti propter antiquam dilectionem eorum, me sic esse eius alumnum ut Iuliani. Denique,
oratione facta, erigo oculorum aciem ad tribunal conspicioque in eo versiculos hoc modo conscriptos: Heroas Christi geminos haec contenit aula: Iulianum capite,
corpore Ferreolum. Cumque haec legens aedituum consulerem, cur haec scripta sic fuerint, respondit: 'Basilica sancti martyris Ferreoli super ipsum Rhodani litus
ab antiquis fuerat collocata. Denique cum, inpulsante violentia amnis, porticus, quae ab ea parte erat locata, corrueret, providens sacerdos Mamertus nomine,
qui tunc Viennensim regebat eclesiam, ruinam futuram praeveniens, aliam basilicam eleganti opere et in ipsa mensura sagaci intentione construxit, illuc sanctum
martyris transferre cupiens corpus. Advenit autem ad hoc opus abbatum atque monachorum magnus numerus, vigilataque nocte, accepto sarculo fodere coeperunt.
Cumque in profunde discenderent, tria sepulchra repperiunt, at confestim stupor mentes spectantium invadit. Nec quisquam erat certus, quisnam esset beati
martyris tumulus. Igitur cum starent omnes in hebitate mentis attoniti, inspirante, ut credo, Divinitate, unus ex circumstantibus exclamat, dicens: „Antiquitus
referri solitum erat, et celebri per populos sermone vulgatum, caput Iuliani confessoris in sepulchro retenere martyris Ferreoli. Si, operturio amoto,
unusquisque consideretur, potest, quae sint membra Ferreoli martyris, protenus inveniri". Haec audiens sacerdos, cunctos iubet in oratione prosterni. Qua
inpleta, procedit ad tumulos, detectosque duos, singulos in his quiescentes invenit viros. Cumque aperuisset et tertium, invenit in eo virum iacentem inlaeso
corpore, integro vestimento, qui, deciso capite, caput amplexus aliud brachio retenebat. Erat enim acsi nuper sepultus neque pallore faciei demutatus neque
capillorum decisione turpatus neque ulla putredine resolutus, sed ita integer, inlaesus, ut putares eum adhuc sopore corporeo detenere. Tunc antistis gaudio
magno repletus, ait: 'Hoc esse cadaver Ferreoli, hoc esse caput Iuliani martyris, dubium non habetur'. Tunc cum magno psallentio, plaudente populo, in loco ubi
nunc adoratur, Domino annuente, perducitur'. Haec autem, ut ad sepulchrum martyris ab ipso aedituo cognovi, fideliter retuli. Praebet tamen huic operi
testimonium Sollius noster, ipsi Mamerto scribens his verbis: Tibi soli concessa est in partes orbis occidui martyris Ferreoli solida translatio, adiecto nostri
capite Iuliani. Unde pro conpensatione deposcimus, ut nobis inde veniat pars patrocinii, quia vobis hinc rediit pars patroni.

## 3. De virtute fontis, ubi caput eius ablutum est.

**[003]** In loco autem illo quo beatus martyr percussus est fons habetur splendidus, lenis, dulcibus aquis uberrimus, in quo et a persecutoribus caput
amputatum ablutum est, de quibus aquis multae sanitates tribuuntur infirmis. Nam saepe caecorum oculi ab his tacti inluminati sunt; tertianorum, quartanariorum
febrium accensi, ut potati qui patiuntur fuerint, conquiescunt. Nam et si quis gravi laborans incommodo, inspirante martyre, desiderium habuerit hauriendi,
protinus ut hauserit convalescit; et ita velociter extinguitur vis febrium, ceu si videas, super inmensum rogum proiectis undis incendia universa restingui.

## 4. De senibus et matrona, cuius vir tenebatur.

**[004]** Post passionem vero beati martyris, ac fama praeeunte de senibus, quos, dum sanctos artus sepulturae mandarent, fortitudini pristinae fuerint
restituti, multa ibi beneficia expetentes credentesque, indulgente martyre, consecuntur. De quibus pauca perstringenti deprecor veniam condonari, quod me minus
vel idoneum vel peritum ad haec narranda cognosco, nec inbutum grammaticis artibus nec litteris liberalibus eruditum; sed quid facio, quod inpellit me amor
patroni, ut nequeam haec silere? Vinctus ab Hispaniis et carceri deditus, apud imperatorem Trevericum capitali diiudicatus sententia tenebatur. Quod coniux
illius cognitum, dum tumulare viri membra festinat, ad Brivatinsim vicum pervenit, repertosque viros, dum diversa studio intento rimaretur, cognoscit, quid in
eo loco vel de martyre vel de senibus fuerit gestum; fidelique insinuatione credens, ad sepulchrum beati martyris deliberat properare, ut causas suggerat, casus
reseret vel cunctum laborem sui doloris exponat, adserentibus tum praeterea hominibus: 'Absque dubio pollicemur, domina, tibi a martyre reddi laetitiam, qui
senum quondam decrepitae aetatis membra rigentia antiquo vigore restituit'. Impletaque haec oratione, promittit, ut, si sospitem reciperet coniugem, martyris
sepulchrum, in quo possit spatio, cimento contegerit. Fide plena et de martyris pietate secura Treverus est ingressa, inventumque virum gratia imperiali
receptum, laeta regreditur; inquisitumque tempus, quo vir relaxatus esset e carcere, haec fuit absolutionis hora, qua illa martyris est auxilium inprecata;
dehinc pollicitationem quam promiserat cum inmensis muneribus adimplevit.

## 5. De eo qui alium in basilica occidere voluit.

**[005]** Erat autem haud procul a cellula, quam supra sepulchrum martyris haec matrona construxerat, grande delubrum, ubi in colomnam altissimam simulachrum
Martis Mercuriique colebatur. Cumque delubri illius festa a gentilibus agerentur, ac mortui mortuis thura deferrent, medio e vulgo commoventur pueri duo in
scandalum, nudatoque unus gladio alterum appetit trucidandum. At ille cernens, nihil veniae reservari, cum a diis suis non defensaretur, nostrae religionis
custodiam, nostrae confessionis veniam, nostri contagionis medellam, cellulam expetiit martyris gloriosi. Tunc ille qui sequebatur, cum in adsultu gladii eum
non potuisset attingere, et hic super se ostium reserasset, atque ille, arreptam utramque postem, ostium conaretur infringere: ilico adhaerentes manus tabulis,
dolore maximo quatiuntur, et tanta afflictione miser torquetur, ut ubertim fluentes lacrimae, qualis esset dolor intrinsecus, extrinsecus nuntiarent. Interea,
stupente vulgo, inclusus qui fuerat progreditur liber; parentes quoque illius qui virtute sancti retenebatur, cognoscentes martyris sepulturam, devotis multis
muneribus pro filio exorabant.

## 6. De conversione incolarum.

**[006]** Factum est autem, dum haec agerentur, ut presbiter quidam via illa discenderet. Qui cum didicisset quae acta fuerant, pollicetur parentibus, si a
gentilitate discederent, filium reciperent sanum. Ipse quoque sacerdos sequenti nocte videt per somnium, simulachra illa quae a gentilibus colebantur nomine
divino comminui atque in pulvere redacta solo prosterni. Quarta autem die cum gentilitas vellet iterum diis exhibere libamina, maestus presbiter ad sepulchrum
sancti prosternitur et cum lacrimis exorat, ut tandem gentilitatem hanc, quae iacebat in tenebris, splendor divinae potentiae visitaret, nec sineret ultra
martyr beatus, alumnos proprios ista caligine deteneri, cum ille perennis claritatis gaudia possideret. Confestim ad eius oratione commoventur tonitrua,
renident fulgora, discendit imber igne mixtus et grandine, turbantur omnia. Concurrit vulgus ad cellulam, prosternitur coram sacerdote omnis caterva gentilium,
et mixto cum lacrimis cuncti ululatu Domini misericordia deprecantur, pollicenturque sacerdoti, si grando recederet, et martyrem patronum expeterent et ad Deum
eius, relictis simulachrorum cultibus, integro de corde transirent. Porro ille, fusa oratione, cuncta quae petiit meruit obtenere. Recedente autem tempestate,
puer cum parentibus credens, ipsa die a doloribus liberatur; gentiles in Trinitatis nomine baptizati, statuas quas coluerant confringentes, in lacum vico
amnique proximum proiecerunt. Ab eo enim terapore in loco illo et fides catholica et martyris virtus est amplius declarata.

## 7. Qualiter Hillidius populum ab hostilitate liberavit.

**[007]** Post haec venientes quidam de Burgundionibus ad Brivatinsim vicum, eum cum armorum multitudine copiosa circumdant, captoque populo, direpto
sacrosancto ministerio, ultra amnem transeunt, et viros gladio interficere, reliquum vulgus sorte dividere parant. Tunc Hillidius quidam a Vellavo veniens et,
ut aiunt, commonitione columbae alitis incitatus, super eos inruit. Hortatosque socios, ita hostes ad internitionem caecidit, ut, captivis laxatis, triumphans
in lande martyris, amne transmisso, ad beatam cellulam tamquam novus Moyses cum omni populo canendo revertitur; nec minor, ut arbitror, exultatio fuit ereptis,
quam quondam Israhelitis dimersis fuit Aegyptiis. Quod ne quis dubitet hanc beati martyris fuisse victoriam, sed insinuatio columbae aliquod misterium fuisse
creditur virtutis divinae. Nam, veniente Hillidio, haec in obviam venit; cum ille, ut adsolet, aliquid demoraretur, haec in circuitu illius volitabat; illoque
progrediente, ista praecedebat et revertebatur in obviam, quasi accelerare deprecans iter. Dum haec agerentur, adveniens puer captivitatem adnuntiat, et sic
iste viam acceleravit. Sed et, ipso pugnante, columba semper circa eum est visa decurrere. Quod ne quis invideat confictum de columba et homini praestitum
christiano, cum Horosius consolem Romanum, id est Marcum Valerium, a corvo alite scribat adiutum.

## 8. De interitu corum qui ministerium basilicae portaverunt.

**[008]** Prostratis ergo Hillidius hostibus, quattuor ex his per fugam lapsi, patenam et urceum, qui anax dicitur, in patriam deferunt, et divisam in tantis ut
erant partibus patenam, urceum regi Gundobaldo ob gratiam exhibent conquirendam. Reliquum vero argentum reginae sagacitas repperit; cui additis multis
muneribus, loco illi sancto restituit, fideliter insinuans regi, non oportere eum, ut gratiam martyris sancti propter argenti parvitatem amitteret.

## 9. De Fedamia paralytica.

**[009]** Pro quibus ac talibus virtutum ornamentis magna ibi basilica fabricata a fidelibus, virtutibus, ut praefati sumus, martyris beati refulget, in qua
paralyticorum, clodorum, caecorum et aliorum quoque morborum saepius petita remedia conquiruntur. Fedamia quaedam mulier paralysi humore constricta, quae nullum
corporis membrum sine dolore vigebat, exhibita est, deferentibus propinquis, ad beatam basilicam, ut vel stipem a largientibus mereretur. Quae dum in porticu
illa, quae sanctae basilicae coniungitur, decubaret noctem dominicam, dum sacrosanctis vigiliis populi fides devota concelebrat, et illa quiescens lectulo
paululum obdormisset, a viro quodam per visum correpta atque increpita est, dicente sibi, cur, reliquis excubias nocturnas Deo exhibentibus, illa deesset.
Respondit, se ab omni membrorum parte debilem nec penitus gressum agere posse. Tunc quasi sustentata a viro qui loquebatur ei et ad sepulchrum usque deducta,
dum in sopore fundit orationem, visum est ei, quasi multitudo catenarum ab eius membris solo decidere. A quo etiam sonitu expergefacta, sensit omnium artuum
recepisse plenissimam sanitatem. Protinus surrexit a lectulo, et stupentibus cunctis, cum gratiarum actione vociferans, sanctam est ingressa basilicam. Ferunt
etiam quidam, solitam fuisse eam referre habitum viri qui cara fuerat adlocutus. Dicebat, eum statura esse procerum, veste nitidum, elegantia eximium, vultu
hilarem, flava caesariae, inmixtis canis, incessu expeditum, voce liberum, allocutione blandissimum, candoremque cutis illius ultra lilii nitorem fulgere, ita
ut de multis milibus hominum, quae saepe vidisset, nullum similem conspicaret. Unde multis non absurde videtur, ei beatum martyrem apparuisse. Quae mulier post
decim et octo annos sanata est.

## 10. De eo qui perenssorem suum de basilica conabatur extrahere.

**[010]** Quidam dum in seditione, quam commoverat, cum oculum amisisset, hominem qui ictum intulerat de basilica conabatur extrahere; quod dum agit, non modo
amissi oculi non recepit lumen, verum etiam sentit, alium, quem sanum habuerat, obcaecari. Porro, cum peccata sua confiteretur, dicens: 'Merito mihi evenit
iudicium sine misericordia, qui non feci misericordiam', prostratus coram sancto sepulchro cum populo, qui tunc ad festivitatem advenerant, indulgens laedenti,
et visum recepit et gratiam. Sicque factum est, ut is qui sancti auxilium expetierat tutaretur, et ille vero qui non credebat argueretur; et sic uterque laetus
emendatusque discessit.

## 11. De contracto, qui die dominica boves iunxit.

**[011]** Alius quoque ausu temerario die dominica iungens boves, agro sulcare coepit, adprehensamque securim, ut aliquid emendaret in vomere, protinus
contractis digitis manubrium in dextera eius adhaesit. Cumque prae dolore nimio cruciaretur, post duos annos veniens ad beati martyris basilicam, vigilias
fideliter celebravit. Statim in ipsa die dominica reserata manus lignum, quod invitus tenebat, amisit; magnam inferens populo disciplinam, ut quod die dominica
fuerat perpetratum ipsa quoque die dominica purgaretur. At ille magnificans gloriam martyris, recessit incolomis, nec ultra die resurrectionis dominicae
quicquam ausus est operare.

## 12. De Anagildo muto et surdo vel caeco.

**[012]** Sic et Anagildus quidam mutus et surdus et caecus vel omnium membrorum conpagem debilitatus ad limina sacrosancta proiectus est, scilicet ut vel ab
stipe pasceretur devotorum, qui victus alimoniam propriis manibus laborare non poterat. Igitur cum per annum integrum ante sanctam aedem decubasset, tandem
visitatus a virtute beati martyris, ab omni infirmitate sanatus est.

## 13. De his qui Theodorici regis tempore basilicam inruperunt.

**[013]** Videtur mihi, ut, sicut sancti virtute curata morbida retexuntur, ita et infidelium pravitates oratione illius confutatae ad emendationem aliorum, ne
similia appetant, declarentur, quia utraque sancti gloria praestat, ut et hos sanitati reddat, ne amplius crucientur, et illos arguat, ne in futuro iudicio
condemnentur. Et quia nulli latere credo aliquid de hostilitate Theodorici regis ac infirmitatibus Sigivaldi, quae ei in Arverno posito contigerunt, propter
virtutem tamen beati martyris est diligentius exponendum, quo facilius fides dictis adhibeatur. Igitur, cum ad direptionem Arvernorum rex antedictus festinaret,
et ingrediens terminum, vastationi cuncta subigeret, pars aliqua ab exercitu separata ad Brivatinsim vicum infesta proripuit, fama vulgante, quod in basilica
essent incolae cum multis thesauris adunati. Cumque pervenissent ad locum, inveniunt multitudinem promiscui sexus, obseratis ostiis, in templo ipso cum propriis
facultatibus resedere. Cumque intrare non possint, unus, effractam ceu fur in altari sancto fenestram vitream, ingreditur, quia qui non intrat per ianuam hic
latro est. Dehinc, reseratis aedis illius valvis, exercitum intromittit. At illi, direpta cuncta, pauperum supellectilem cum ministris ipsius basilicae
reliquumque populum qui infra erat eductum foris diviserunt haud procul a vico. Quae cum ad regem delata fuissent, conprehensos ex his aliquos diversis mortibus
condemnavit. Fugiens vero ille qui, inrupta aede, caput fuit huius sceleris, igne de caelo dilapso consumptus interiit. Super quem cum multi acervum lapidum
congregassent, a tonitruis et corruscationibus detectus, terrenam caruit sepulturam. Qui vero de consentaneis latentes regi in patriam eunt regressi, correpti a
daemone, diversis exitibus hanc vitam crudeliter finierunt. Haec audiens rex, omnia quae exinde sunt ablata reddidit. Praeceperat enim, ne in septimo a basilica
miliario quis vim inferret.

## 14. De Sigivaldo pervasore.

**[014]** Tunc Sigivaldus cum rege praepotens cum omni familia sua in Arverna regione ex regis iussu migravit. Ubi dum multorum res iniuste conpeteret, villam
quandam, quam gloriosae memoriae Tetradius episcopus Biturigensis basilicae sancti Iuliani reliquerat, sub specie obumbratae commutationis avidus pervadit; sed
mense tertio, postquam adgressus est, correptus a febre et sine sensu effectus, declinavit capud ad lectulum. Cuius uxor dum de hoc exitu maesta penderet, a
quodam sacerdote commonita est, ut eum si videre vellet incolomem auferret a villa. At illa haec audiens, praeparatis carrucis conpositoque plaustro, quo eum
eveheret, mox ut praedium sunt egressi, protinus divina sunt pariter gratia munerati. Nam iste sospitate, illa meruit ex huius incolomitate laetitiam. Ferunt
etiam in oratorium praedii illius sanctum Iulianum martyrem cum Tetradio episcopo conloquentem cuidam religioso revelatum fuisse, promittentem se episcopo
villam, quam pro animae suae remedium sibi reliquerat, recepturum. Sed et habitum beati martyris in eodem modo esse, ut quondam paralytica exposuerat,
referebat.

## 15. De pastoris malitia.

**[015]** Pastor vero quidam non strinuitate, sed nomine Ingenuus genere, dum in multis rebus contra basilicam sancti martyris iniuste ageret, ad hoc levitas
eius, inimico incrassante, convaluit, ut colonicas basilicae concupiscens, quae agro eius erant proximae, pervadere non timeret Ad quem sacerdos loci cum
aliquos de clericis quasi legatus mitteret, ut, accepta ratione, quod male pervaserat relaxaret; ille quasi contra iniquum hostem, tela correpta, prosiluit,
fugatosque sagittis clericos, res sancti in sua dominatione retenuit. Factum est autem, ut in proximo adveniret dies passionis martyris gloriosi; ad quam ille
inmemor pervasionis suae atque iniuriae, quam intulerat clericis, ante quinque dies solemnitatis ad vicum Brivatinsim advenit. Qui cum in domo hospitalitatis
suae convivium laetitia et exultatione fungeretur, subito corruscatione facta tonitruum sonuit; rursumque iteratum, iaculo igneo de caelis elapso percussus est,
nullo tamen de reliquis pereunte. Deinde ad exemplum omnium, tamquam rogus flammeus ardens, paulatim consumebatur. Ad quod miraculum populus, qui ad beati festa
convenerat, haec cernens cum admiratione, metuebat; satisque illi fuit, ne de rebus sancti aliquid ultra contingere. Quod ne fortuitu actum quis putet, cernat
inter multos innoxius unum interisse sacrilegum.

## 16. De contumacia Becconis.

**[016]** Quid etiam ad Becconis comitis confutandam superbiam beatus martyr sit operatus, evolvam. Hic cum actiones ageret publicas et elatus iactantia multos
contra iustitiam adgravaret, casu contigit, ut dimissum accipitrem diu per diversa vacantem perderet; similiter, ut unus de servientibus basilicae sancti
Iuliani accipitrem alium, dum per viam ambularet, quasi vagum invenit. Erat enim puer ille pincerna in domo basilicae. Quod cum ad Becconem pervenisset, quod
scilicet puer repertum teneret accipitrem, calumniari coepit ac dicere: 'Meus ille erat', inquit, 'et hic furto eum sustulit'. Deinde succendente avaritia misit
illum vinctum in carcere, deliberans eum in sequenti patibulo condemnare. Tunc sacerdos maestus valde ad sepulchrum sancti properat, reseratisque cum gemitu
causis, adprehensis decim aureis, per fideles amicos Becconi obtulit. Quod ille pro nihilo respuens, cum iuramento adseruit, numquam se puerum dimissurum, nisi
exinde aureos triginta acciperet. Quod presbiter desuper sepulchro sancti accipiens, Becconi transmisit; quos acceptos, satiata auri cupiditate, puerum
restauravit incolomem. Sed Deus omnipotens, qui permanet ante solem, secundum bonitatis suae divitias humiliavit calumniatorem. Nam ipsius anni transacto
curriculo, veniens ad sancti festivitatem cum caterva satellitum, ingressus est limen sanctum. Procedente vero lectore, qui beatae passionis recenseret
historiam, ut revolvit librum et in principio lectionis sancti Iuliani protulit nomen, confestim Becco voce nescio qua teterrima ad terram corruit, cruenteque
spumans, dare voces diversas coepit. Inde inter suorum manus sublatus, a basilica domi reducitur. Nec fuit dubium pueris eius, haec ob iniuriam basilicaris
famuli evenisse. Omnem quoque ornatum, quod super se tunc habuit, tam in auro quam in vestimentis, basilicae contulit et multa deinceps munera misit; sed usque
ad diem obitus sui sine sensu duravit.

## 17. De diacono, qui oves basilicae abstulit.

**[017]** Fuit etiam quidam diaconus, qui, relictam eclesiam, fisco se publice iunxit, acceptaque a patronis potestate, tanta perpetrabat scelera, ut vix possit
a vicinis circumpositis sustinere. Accidit autem quadam vice, ut saltus montenses, ubi ad aestivandum oves abierant, circumiret atque pascuaria quae fisco
debebantur inquereret. Cumque diversos spoliaret iniuste, conspicit eminus greges, qui tunc sub nomine martyris tuebantur, ad quos levi cursu evolans, tamquam
lupus rapax diripit arietes. Conturbati atque exterriti pastores ovium, dicunt ei: 'Ne, quaesumus, contingas hos arietes, quia beati martyris Iuliani dominio
subiugati sunt'. Quibus ille haec inridens respondisse fertur: 'Putasne, quia Iulianus commedit arietes?' Dehinc ipsos verberibus adfectos, quae voluit
abstulit; ignorans miser, quod, qui de domibus sanctorum aliquid aufert, ipsis sanctis iniuriam facit, ipso sic Domino protestante: Qui vos spernit, me spernit,
et qui recipit iustum, mercedem iusti accipiet. Contigit autem, ut post dies multos, non religione sed casu conferente, ad vicum Brivatinsim properaret,
proiectusque humo ante sepulchrum, mox a febre corripitur et tanta vi caloris obprimitur, ut neque consurgere neque puerum evocare possit. Famuli vero cum
vidissent eum extra solito plus occumbere, accedentes: 'Quid tu', inquiunt, 'in tanta diuturnitate depraemeris? Non enim tibi tam longa mos erat orandi
devotio'. Ferebant autem de eo, quod quandoquidem in eclesia fuisset ingressus, parumper inmurmurans, nec capite inclinato, regrediebatur. Tunc interpellantibus
pueris, cum responsum reddere non valeret, ablatus manibus e loco, in cellam, qui erat proxima, lectulo collocatur. Igitur, invalescente febre, proclamat se
miser incendi per martyrem, et quod primo siluerat, admotis animae iudicii facibus, crimina confitetur, iactarique super se aquam, voce qua poterat
deprecabatur. Delatis quoque cum vasculo limphis et in eum saepe deiectis, tamquam de fornace ita fumus egrediebatur e corpore. Interea miseri artus ceu
conbusti in nigridine convertuntur, unde tantus procedebat fetor, ut vix de adstantibus possint aliqui tolerare. Innuens enim dehinc manu, indicat, se esse
leviorem; mox, illis recedentibus, hic spiritum exalavit. De quo haud dubium est, qualem illuc teneat locum, qui hinc cum tali discessit iudicio.

## 18. De eo qui caballum in vigilia sancti furavit.

**[018]** Alias autem per vigiliam festivitatis equum alicuius, qui tunc forte ad eandem solemnitatem venerat, furto prehendit, ascensumque, velociter properat;
scilicet ut qui lumen perdiderat veritatis, non inveniretur a luce, et cuius pectus cupiditatis tenebrae obsederant, eius et furtivam fraudulentiam nox celaret.
De talibus enim Dominus dicebat in euangelio: Omnis qui male agit odit lucem. Albiscente igitur caelo, dicebat: 'Iam securus sum; nam triginta leugas a sancti
basilica elongatus sum; iam secus propriam domum esse me credo'. Dum haec tacitus revolveret infra se, demotis ex axe tenebris, cognoscit, se ipsi vico
propinquum inter populos devagare; timensque, ne scelus suum patefieret publico, cum cautela grandi caballum in loco unde digressus fuerat reformavit. Sic miser
virtute martyris tota nocte detentus in circuitu vici et, ut ego credo, ab auctore qui eum obsederat est delusus, ut viam quam adprehendere voluit non valeret.
O scelerata cupiditas, quid agis! Semper amatores tuos in confusione praecipitas.

## 19. De eo qui propter treantem periuravit.

**[019]** Quidam alteri triantem praestiterat, quem, interpositis paucis diebus, recepit. Post annum vero in atrio sancti conventum hominem, rem suam, quasi non
recepisset, sibi reddi deposcebat. At ille detestans adserebat, se reddidisse susceptum. Cumque diutissime altercarentur, ille qui reddiderat ait ad socium:
'Usquequo uterque contendimus? Sub iudicio hoc omnipotentis Dei ponamus. Eamus ad tumulum martyris, et quod sub sacramenti interpositione dixeris discernat
virtus sancta patroni'. At ille nec dubitans ingressusque sepulchrum, dum audacter elevat manus, ut periuret, infeliciter miser inriguit. Haeret vox in gutture,
lingua coartatur in fauce, vibrant labia vacua a sermone; ipsa quoque brachia, quae ad adiutorium frustrati sacramenti erexerat, prorsus retrahere non valebat.
Ad haec vulgo admirante, publicato scelere, multitudo cuncta populi una voce prorumpens, Domini misericordia ac beati martyris auxilium deprecatur. Post
quattuor vero aut eo amplius horas ad sensum regressus, quod iniuste repetebat publica confessione patefecit, et sic sanus abscessit.

## 20. De eo qui basilicam sanctam furtu spoliavit.

**[020]** Saepe haec ille audierat qui basilicae sanctae violentiam intulit; sed iniquam mentem semel obsessam vitio bonitas mollire non potuit, Salamone
obtestante: In malivola anima non ingreditur sapientia. Advenerat festivitas sancti, et ecce quidam e populo conspicatur ornamentis inmensis beatam basilicam
effulgere. Concupescit iniqua mente, quod adipiscens non poterat occultare. Igitur discedente populo a basilica post gratiam vespertinam, hic se in angulo
basilicae repraemens latitavit, ac datum cunctis nocturna quiete silentium vel operiente umbrosa caligine mundum, consurgit ab angulo, et nihil dubitans, utique
quia satellite Satanan inpellebatur, super cancellum beati sepulchri cursu prosilit rapido, detractamque a summo unam gemmis corruscantibus crucem ad terram
deiecit, collectisque villolis ac palliolis de circuitu parietum pendentibus, unum voluculum facit, inpositumque umeris, ac elevatam crucem manu, ad locum unde
discesserat repetit, ac positam capiti sarcinam, peccati sopore conpraessus, obdormivit Media vero nocte circumeuntes custodes sanctam basilicam, aspiciunt in
angulo unam gemmam crucis tamquam iubar caeleste refulgere; obstupefacti accedunt comminus cum timore, admotoque cereo, inveniunt personam cum rebus furatis,
quas auferre non potuerat, inibi decubare. Denique, sub custodia eum illa nocte detentum, mane facto cuncta quae fecerat patefecit, adserens se lassum
obdormisse, eo quod diutissime circuiens cum fasce basilicam, ostium unde egrederetur repperire non poterat.

## 21. De eo qui caballum in festivitate perdidit.

**[021]** Multa quidem et alia in praevaricatoribus ostendit, sed satis sint ista ad cohercendam desidiam eorum. Nunc vero ad gaudia prosperitatum, qua larga
pietate praestat populis, revertamur. Sed prius illud non arbitror postponendum, quod expertum valde cognovimus, quid in rebus perditis apud hunc patronum
fidelis deprecatio consequatur; ex quibus unum tantum commemorare studui. Ad festivitatem beati martyris devotus pauper advenerat, laxatoque equite, sacram
ingressus est aedem, ac vigiliis inmobilis instans, noctem cum ceteris orando deduxit. Inlucescente vero caelo ad metatum regressus, caballum quem reliquerat
non invenit; quaesitumque diutissime, nec signa quidem, qua in parte discessisset, agnovit. Transacto igitur biduo, recurrit iterum per saltus, perscrutans
locorum incolas, si forte aliquis aut teneret captum aut capi vidisset ab aliquo. Nullum dehinc indicii genus repperiens, anxius atque maestus ad sepulchrum
sancti regreditur, ibique causas doloris ac meroris exponens, aiebat: 'Ad tua, sanctae, limina veni, nihil aliud quam parvitatis meae vota deferre; nihil
iniuste abstuli, nihil gessi indignum tuae solemnitati. Cur, inquam, perdidi rem meam? Rogo, ut restituas amissum, ut necessarium reddas'. Hoc fletu aditus
agens, ut egressus est templum, conspicit eminus a quodam viro suum equitem reteneri. Ad quem accedens, dum discutit, unde sit, aut unde venerit, vel ex quo
tempore hunc habeat equum, didicit, ipsa hora eum fuisse repertum, qua ille beati martyris inploravit auxilium.

## 22. De caeco inluminato.

**[022]** Cum autem quidam ab eo loco per incursum diabolicum oculum perdidisset et ad hospitiolum suum viduatus lumine infeliciter resederet, ac manibus
propriis nihil laborare praevalens, spem ullam alimonii non haberet, apparuit ei vir in visu noctis, commonens, ut ad beati basilicam ambularet; ibique, si
devote suggerat, promittit auxilium inveniri. At ille nihil moratus, arrepto bacello, adminiculante puero, sanctum ingressus est locum. Qui post conpleta
oratione archipresbiterum, qui tunc locum ipsum regebat, nomine Publianum adivit, supplicans, ut oculis caecis Christi crucem inponeret. Erat enim valde
religiosus. Quod ille, dura iactantiam evadere cupit, evitans, tenetur a caeco, nec omnino dimittitur, nisi quae petebat adimpleret. Tunc ille prostratus ante
sepulchrum, diutissime martyris est suffragium inprecatus; deinde admotam oculis caecis manum, protinus ut signum crucis inposuit, visum iste recepit.
Admiramini, quaeso, virtutem martyris, cum parum sit exercere miracula, nunc etiam per manus discipulorum, adstipulante virtutis suae favore, publice operatur.
Sed nec meritum discipuli fuit exiguum, cui haec praestita esse cernuntur.

## 23. De pede Galli postmodum episcopi sanato.

**[023]** Erat enim tunc temporis apud urbem Arvernam patruus meus Gallus episcopus, de quo non videtur omitti, qualiter in adolescentia sua fuerit a sancti
virtute iuvatus. Et quia saepius commemoravi, quale excidium Arvernae regioni rex Theodoricus intulerit, cum neque maioribus neque minoribus natu aliquid de
rebus propriis est relictum praeter terram vacuam, quam secum barbari ferre non poterant. His ergo temporibus gloriosae memoriae patruus meus, qui postea, ut
dixi, sacerdotale fasce Arvernae rexit eclesiam, pupillus erat; cuius facultates ita direptae sunt ab exercitu, ut nihil prorsus remaneret in promtu; ipse
quoque cum uno tantum puerulo usque Brivatinsim vicum plerumque itinere pedestri discurrebat. Accedit autem quodam tempore, dum hoc iter tereret, ut, laxatis
prae calore solis calciamentis, nuda incedens planta, sudem calcaret spineum. Qui tunc fortassis incisus adhuc terrae haerens, erecto acumine inter herbas
virides latitabat. Qui defixus plantae et superegressus effractusque deorsum extrahi nequebatur. Igitur defluente sanguinis rivo, cum gressum facere non
valeret, beati martyris inplorat auxilium, paululumque dolore conpraesso, licet claudicando, iter quod coeperat expedivit. Tertia vero nocte, conputrescente
vulnere, dolor maximus incitatur. Ille vero ad experta dudum praesidia confugiens, sepulchro gloriose prosternitur; expletisque vigiliis, regressus ad lectulum,
dum virtutem martyris praestolatur, somno incumbente depraemitur. Deinde consurgens, nullam doloris sentit iniuriam, aspectaque planta, pars sudis, quae
ingressa fuerat, non videtur; evulsam tamen sentiebat a pede. Quod lignum diligenter inquirens, in stratu suo repperit, admirans, qualiter fuisset egressum.
Solitus namque erat in episcopatu suo locum vulneris ostendere, in quo magna adhuc fossa conspiciebatur, obtestans, in hoc beati martyris fuisse virtutem.

## 24. De febre Petri nepotis eius.

**[024]** Post multum vero tempus advenerat festivitas beati martyris, et pater meus cum omni domo sua ad huius solemnitatis gaudia properabat. Nobis vero iter
agentibus, Petrus, frater meus senior, ab ardore febrium occupatur et tam graviter agit, ut neque vigere neque cibum sumere possit. Totumque illud iter cum
grandi agitur maerore, et in discrimine res vertitur, utrum convalescat aut pereat. Denique cum isto labore pervenitur ad locum; ingredimur basilicam, adoramus
sacrosancti martyris sepulturam. Prosternitur et aegrotus in pavimento, deprecans medellam a martyre gloriose. Post conpleta vero oratione ad metatum regressus,
febris paululum conquievit. Veniente autem nocte, nobis ad vigilias properantibus, rogat se et ille deferri, incumbensque ante sepulchrum, tota nocte martyris
suffragium deprecatur. Exactis deinde nocturnis excubiis, rogat, ut de pulvere, quod circa beatum erat tumulum, collecto vel potui darent vel collo
suspenderent. Quo facto, ita omnis ardor febrium conquievit, ut ipsa die et cibum caperet incolomis et, ubi delectatio vertisset animum, ambularet.

## 25. De mei capitis dolore.

**[025]** Sequenti vero festivitate, dum iterum cum magno gaudio ad sanctam properaremus basilicam, mihi caput a sole percussum graviter dolere coepit. Qui
dolor adcrescens, febrem intrinsecus generabat, ita ut nec cibum me capere nec loqui permitteret. Cumque per duos dies ab hoc dolore consumerer, die tertia ad
basilicam sancti Ferreoli, cui fons ille de quo superius meminimus est contiguus, advenimus. Distat autem basilica haec a Brivatinsi vico quasi stadiis decim.
Cumque in loco illo venissemus, libuit animo ad fontem usque procedere, confidens de virtute martyris, quod, si me exinde levis unda perfunderet, mox sanarem.
Adveniens vero orationem fundo, aquam haurio, os refrigero, caput infundo; statimque decedentibus limphis, fugato dolore, sanus abscedo et usque ad sepulchrum
martyris gloriosi laetus ingredior, admirans et gratias agens martyri, quod prius me virtute sua dignatus fuerit visitare, quam ipsius mererer cernere
sepulchrum.

## 26. De febricitante ad fontem sanato.

**[026]** Est enim ad hunc fontem, quia ibidem martyr percussus est, virtus eximia. Quidam a febre correptus, dum in extremis ageret, desiderium habuit de aqua
fontis haurire, ad quam etiam se deportari fideliter exoravit. Quem sui inter manus adprehensum et in loco depositum, protinus ut aquae haustum accepit et
