faciem caputque perfudit, recipere meruit sanitatem, et aliorum manibus inlatus, propriis gressibus est regressus. Fuit autem incola huius vici, sed excidit
nomen eius.

## 27. De tonitruo in basilica facto cum corruscatione.

**[027]** Quadam autem die orta tempestas cum magno venti impetu super vicum Brivatinsim rapide discendebat. Micabant enim de nubibus fulgora, ac tonitrua
terribiliter voces dabant. Quatitur terra fragore, et exuri a corruscatione pene omnia putabantur; sola erat expectatio in virtute martyris gloriosi. Nec mora,
dato cum fulgore gravi sono tonitrui, iaculum igneum per aditum, quo funes ille signi dependit, ingreditur, perculsisque duabus columnis, frustas excussit Inde
repercutiens, per fenestram, quae super sanctam habetur tumulum, est egressum; nullum tamen per beati custodiam de populo laesum. O quam magnus circa alumnos
proprios beati martyris [affectus]! Sustulit columnas percuti, non falangas; confringi passus est vitreum, non catervam; permisit super sepulchrum proprium
praeterire corruscum, ne fieret multitudinis totius interitum. Igitur expulsum a basilica sancti martyris iaculum, acervus feni conbussit, interfecit pecora,
iumenta delevit. Quod si haec fortuitu quis putat, admiretur magis et stupeat incliti potentiam martyris, quod praeteriens ignis per medium populi neminem
nocuit, sed ibi tantum explevit vota, ubi se cognovit habere licentiam.

## 28. De eo qui prae multitudine populi ad sepulchrum non valebat accedere.

**[028]** Clericus autem Aredii Lemovicini abbatis ad festivitatem veniens, prae multitudine populi non modo ad sanctum tumulum accedere, verum etiam nec in
ipsam basilicam potuit introire. Cumque maestus metatu se reddidisset, recubans in lectulo obdormivit. Protinus adstetit ei vir in visu, dicens: 'Quid tu',
inquid, 'sopore depraemeris? Vade celerius ad templum martyris, et omnia invenies reserata'. At ille metu territus exsurgens, credulus dictioni properat
velociter experire, si vera essent quae sibi fuerant indicata. Cumque venisset ad ostium, repperit, remotos undique populos, usque sanctum altare vel ipsum
tumulum via facta nullum obsistere. Et sic sine ulla inpraessione accedens, fusa oratione, cum gaudio est regressus. Quod ne quis dubitet, testor omnipotentem
Deum, quia ab ipsius abbatis haec ore cognovi, apud cuius monachum gesta sunt.

## 29. De festivitate eius.

**[029]** Huius festivitatis tempus ignara plebs maesta pendebat, nesciens diem, in quo martyr beatus deberet pro virtutis ac passionis gloria honorari. Et haec
ignorantia usque ad beatum Germanum Autissiodorensim antestitem est protracta. Factum est autem, ut antedictus pontifex Brivatem adveniret, sciscitatusque ab
incolis, quo tempore huius sacra celebrarentur, se nescire respondent. Tunc ille: 'Oremus', inquit, 'et fortassis nobis haec Domini potentia revelabit'. Quod
cum fecissent, mane orto, convocatis senioribus loci, ait, quinto Kalendarum mensis septimi caelebrandam esse festivitatem. Ex hoc nunc devotus adveniens
populus, vota praesoli reddens, refert et animae et corporis medicinam.

## 30. De inerguminis.

**[030]** Inergumini vero cum advenerint, plerumque evoment in sanctum Dei convitia, cur sanctus alios ad suam convocat festa, ipsosque nominatim confitentes,
eorum fatentur virtutes et merita. Aiunt enim: 'Sufficiat tibi, Iuliane, nos propria virtute torquere; ut quid reliquos provocas? quid invitas extraneos? Ecce
Martinum Pannonicum inimicum iugiter nostrum, qui tres a nostris cavernis repulit mortuos. Adest Privatus ex Gabalis, qui oves suas barbaris, nostra
instigatione commotis, tradere noluit. Advenit Ferreolus collega tuus ex Viennensibus, qui nobis in te supplicium, incolis praesidium misit. Quid Sinphorianum
Aeduum, quid Saturninum vocas Tholosanum? Adgregasti concilium, ut nobis ingeras infernale tormentum'. Haec et his similia dicentibus, ita sanctos Dei humanis
mentibus repraesentant, ut nulli sit dubium, cos inibi commorari; multi tamen ab his infirmi curantur et sani recedunt.

## 31. De mansuetudine pecorum.

**[031]** Sed et illud est memoratu dignissimam, quae sit mansuetudo pecorum in hac basilica votivorum; qualiter vituli petulantes, calcitrantes equi,
grunnientes suillae, cum limen sanctum ingressi fuerint, conquiescunt. Nam vidimus saepe cuturnosos tauros, qui a quindecim aut eo amplius viris alligati,
funibus ducebantur, talem in hominibus impetum dare, ut putaris, eos ipsos quoque disrumpere funes, sed, cum aedem sanctam ingressi sunt, ita quieverunt, ut
arbitraris, illos tamquam agnos mansuetos haben. Vidimus et nunc per medias turmas multos ingredi, inclinato capite populos amoventes rostro, non cornibus et,
tamquam tribunal adire iudicis, aliquod sensum habere timoris; non calcem mittere, non aliquem cornu petere, non oculis torvis aspicere, sed in omni
mansuetudine usque ad sanctum properantes altare osculantesque, rursus in ipsa qua ingressi fuerant patientia repedare. Sic et reliquorum iumentorum petulantia,
cum illic accesserit, deposito cuncto furore, mitescit, ut ea in mansuetudine columbarum cum grandi admiratione conspicias. De his vero quae votiva eunt nullo
paenitus quempiam subtrahere licet; nullus, priusquam ad basilicam veniat, aut commutare praesumit aut emere. Nam qui fecerint saepius ultione divina graviter
quatiuntur. Nam aut febris inminet, aut malum aliquod obrepit, aut damnum grave succedit, aut hoc quod abstulit morbus aufert. Difficile tamen sine praesenti
ultione res praeterit.

## 32. De reliquiis eius in Campaniam translatis.

**[032]** De illis dixisse virtutibus [sufficiat], quae circa sanctam basilicam aut gesta eunt aut geruntur; nunc pauca de locis illis, in quibus eius habentur
reliquiae, disserentes, finem huius libelli facere placet, devotione commonente. Quidam apud Belgicae secundae provintiam, id est suburbano Remensis urbis,
basilicam in honore beati martyris studiose construxit, cuius reliquias post perfectam fabricam expetiit fideliter ac devote. Quas acceptas, dum via cum
psallendo regreditur, Remensim est ingressus campaniam. Erat enim haud procul a via ager cuiusdam divitis campanensis, ad quem scindendum multitudo magna
convenerat. Igitur adpropinquante viatore cum his pignoribus, coepit quidam de aratoribus male torqueri et quasi in excessu mentis dicere: 'En', inquit,
'beatissimum Iulianum adpropinquantem! Ecce virtutem eius! Ecce gloriam eius! Currite viri, relinquite boves, dimittite aratra, caterva omnis eat in obviam!'
Stupentes illi et quid narraret ignoti, dum hebetati admirantesque tam voces quam dicta personae, protinus miser, relicto arvis vomere, elidens se in terram
verberansque palmas, in parte qua vir ille beati martyris veniebat cursu celeri capitur, clamans: 'Ut quid me, sancte, sic crucias? Ut quid me, gloriose martyr,
incendis? Cur regionem tibi non debitam adgrederis? Cur habitacula nostra perlustras? Talia eo dicente, ad locum, ubi iam sacerdos tabernaculum erexerat,
turbolentus advenit, prostratusque coram sanctis reliquiis, diutissime humo incubuit. Tunc presbiter capsulam illam sanctam super eum ut posuit, ilico erumpente
ex ore eius sanguine, ab incursione diabolicae erroris mundatus est; deinceps virtutem sancti praedicans, comes fuit huius itineris.

## 33. Item de reliquiis eius in Oriente exhibitis.

**[033]** Quid de eius reliquiis in Oriente fidelium fratrum relatio signat, edicam. In quadam Orientis civitate, dum in eclesia quidam a daemonio torqueretur,
in navi beati martyris praedixit esse reliquias. Cumque navis portum fuisset adepta, hic ad eam saltuatim prosilit, ac provolutus solo coram navi, erumpente ab
ore et naribus tabe, persona purgata est. Quae cum episcopo nuntiata fuissent, commovet populum cum accensis cereis ad portum usque procedere. Igitur nauclerius
audiens flensque prae gaudio, in occursum episcopi properat, nihil se aliud adserens de beati sustulisse basilicam, nisi parumper pulveris, qui circa sanctum
iacebat tumulum; sed Deus omnipotens conprobans fidem viri, oculi virtutem martyris non permisit. Dehinc episcopus sublatas reliquias usque ad sanctam eclesiam
cum magno honore deportat. Negotiator vero tanta cernens mirabilia, basilicam in honore martyris aedificavit, in qua beatas reliquias collocans, multa deinceps
miracula vidit operari.

## 34. Sine titulo in capitulis

**[034]** Haec ego dudum experta. Contigit, ut post ordinationem meam Arvernus accederem; profectusque, beati basilicam adivi. Expletaque festivitate, disruptis
a palla quae sanctum tegit tumulum fimbriis, in his mihi ferre praesidium credens, impleta oratione, discessi. Apud Turonicam vero urbem monachi in honore
ipsius martyris basilicam, qualem possibilitas eorum habuit, aedificaverunt, cupientes, eam eius virtutibus consecrari. Audientes autem, Haec pignora a me
fuisse delata, rogabant, ut dedicata aedes hisdem augeretur exubiis. At ego, adpraehensam secretius capsam, ad basilicam beati Martini, incipiente nocte,
propero. Referebat autem mihi vir fidelis, qui tunc eminus adstabat, cum nos basilicam sumus ingressi, vidisse se pharum inmensi luminis e caelo dilapsam super
beatam basilicam discendisse, et deinceps quasi intro ingressa fuisset.

## 35. Qualiter Turonus in basilica eius reliquiae sunt locatae.

**[035]** Cum enim nobis haec in crastinum a fidelibus relata fuissent, conicimus, eam a virtute beati martyris processisse. Depositis ergo super altare
sacrosanctis reliquiis, vigilata nocte, cum grande psallentio ad antedictam deferebantur basilicam; et ecce unus ex inerguminis, manibus in se conlisis, ore
patulo, cruentus proiciens sputos, aiebat: 'Ut quid te, Martine, Iuliano iunxisti? Quid eum in his provocas locis? Sat nobis erat praesentia tua supplicium;
similem tui ad augenda tormenta vocasti. Cur haec agis? Quare nos cum Iuliano sic crucias?' Haec et alia misero declamante, expletis missarum solemnitatibus,
dum se ante sanctum altare diutissime conlidit, profluente sanie ex ore eius, ab infestatione furoris diabolici liberatos est.

## 36. Quod vinum ea nocte aderevit.

**[036]** Sed nec hoc silere puto, quod in nocte illa, priusquam sanctae reliquiae ibidem collocarentur, sit gestum. Monachus ipsius loci, dum de adventu
solemnitatis gauderet et singulos quosque ad cellariolum basilicae prumptissimus invitaret, hortans, ut omnes in basilicam fideliter vigilarent, extracto a vase
vino, coepit eos causa devotionis cum gaudio propinare, dicens: 'Magnum nobis patrocinium in beatam martyrem pietas divina largitur. Idcirco rogo caritatem
vestram, ut unianimiter vigiletis mecum. Cras enim sanctae eius reliquiae in hoc loco sunt collocandae'. Exacta quoque cum sacris hymnis modolisque caelestibus
noctem, caelebrata etiam missarum solemnia, ovans festivitate clericus, coepit eos iterum quos prius invitaverat rogare ad refectionem, dicens: 'Gratias vobis
ago, quod sic ad vigilandum immobiles perstitistis'. Sed nec martyr diu distulit bonam voluntatem virtutis suae gratia munerare. Nam ingressus prumptuarium
clericus, repperit cupellam, quam pene mediam reliquerat, per superiorem aditum redundare, in fantum ut copia defluentis vini rivum per terram ad ostium usque
duceret. Quod ille admirans, positum deorsum vas, saepius extulit plenum; sed et de ipso, cum satis abundeque fuisset expensum, nihil prorsus defuit, sed usque
in crastinum, mirantibus cunctis, semper stetit plenum. Erat autem tertio Kal. mensis quinti. O admirabilis virtus martyris! Cum produxit de vase sine flore
vindemiam, cum sit solitum, ut collecta vina condantur in vascula, protulit doleum musta, in quo non uva, sed virtus sola defluxit. Turgescit vasculum a
liquore, fructus non inlatus est, sed creatus. Agit hoc ille Dominus ad glorificandum martyrem, qui inplens uterum Virginis sine semine, et permanere praestitit
matrem in castitate. Sed tamen hic novo Maius exuberat fructu, cum sine codicibus Falerna porregit ad bibendum. In aliis vineis vix adhuc erumpunt gemmae, in
hoc vero vase vinum defluit a virtute. Aequatur Maius Octobri, cum nova porregit pocula; plus habet quam ille, cum in prumtu non ostenditur vinea et in domo
gignuntur Falerna. Rudis etenim venit sine torculare vindemia, quae non in palmitibus, sed in occultis mysteriis est reperta. Acervus acenorum non premitur ab
arbore, et vini defluunt undae. Hauriuntur Falerna, cum in torculari non cernuntur inpraessa; vitis, ecce, non aspicitur, et pocula large conplentur. Sed quid
inquam? Non enim deest fidelibus virtus illa caelestis. Nam qui quondam nuptiis de aquis praestetit vina, nunc suis eadem large porregit sine ullius elimenti
natura; et geminis piscibus quinque milia hominum satiavit, nunc bonae voluntati multiplicata restituit. In ipsius enim ortus tempore angelica vox testata est,
dicens: Gloria in excelsis Deo et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis. Sed iam ad sequentia virtutum opera veniamus.

## 37. De contracto in eodem loco sanato.

**[037]** Serviens huius monasterii diu contractus infeliciter trahebatur. Adveniens autem ad ipsam sancti basilicam, vigilias celebrat Quibus expletis, mane
dum ad stratum suum regreditur, inter portantium manus resolutis sanatus est nervis.

## 38. De caeco inluminato.

**[038]** Puella quaedam lippis oculis et, nimio imbre lacrimarum profluente, pene caecata. Cuius pater, audita virtute martyris gloriosi, cum ea ad basilicam
sanctam properat, celebratisque vigiliis, mane pauperibus qui ad matriculam illam erant cibum potumque protulit. Aepulantibus vero illis, subito puella capitis
dolore se [torqueri] proclamat et, ut modico sopori indulgeator, inplorat. Qua quiescente, cum convivae aepulum adplicarent, illa surrexit et ad sanctum se
altare ducere poscit. Antequam solo prostrata fuisset et adtente Domini misericordia deprecaretur, restrictis lacrimis, purgatis lippitudine oculis, laeta
surrexit. Tunc, patre gaudente, domi redditur sana.

## 39. De alio contracto.

**[039]** Alius quidam puerulus parvulus, cuius parentes haud procul ab ipsa basilica conmanebant, in secundo ortus sui anno membris totis contractus, sine spe
alicuius boni nutriebatur. Qui ita contraxerat, ut genua ab eius ore penitus separari non possent. Cuius parentes, cum ad sanctam basilicam vigilassent, et
proiectum infantulum coram sacrosanctis reliquiis, post paululum repperiunt eum sedentem, membris omnibus esse directum. Dehinc, fusa oratione, gaudentes ad
domum suam regressi sunt.

## 40. De periuribus.

**[040]** Est autem in Turonico vicus cui Gaudiaco nomen est, in quo beati martyris reliquiae contenentur, qui cum magnis virtutibus crebro inlustretur, in
periuribus tamen plerumque agitata ultione. Nam cum ibidem, quasi inimico humani generis suadente, periuraverit, ita ultio divina prosequitur, ut protinus aut
in successione damni aut in amissione proximi aut in consumptione morbi manifesta patiscat; non tamen causam remanere inultam, martyr prorsus indulget, sed nec
inibi tam ausu temerario periurat barbarorum cruda rusticitas. De quo negotio ista sufficiant, quia longum est singula quae de his acta sunt per ordinem
memorare.

## 41. De reliquias eius, quod Aridius presbiter sustulit.

**[041]** Cum autem ad me Aridius presbiter ex Lemovicino venisset, vir valde religiosus, cui etiam in secundo virtutum beati Martini libro memini, dum
sollicite vitam eius perscrutarer et actionem, inquirere coepi, quae ibidem beatissimus in miraculis prodidisset; in honore enim beati martyris basilicam
aedificavit, quam et eius reliquiis inlustravit. Sicut ergo est verecundissimus, diu cunctatus, tandem haec et valde invitus exposuit. 'Quando', inquit, 'primum
beati Iuliani adivi basilicam, parumper cerae a sepulchro sustuli. Inde veniens ad fontem, in quo beati sanguis effusus est, abluta aquis facie, parvam ab his
pro benedictione conplevi ampullam. Testor omnipotentem Deum, quia, antequam ad domum accederem, colore, spissitudine atque odore in balsamo conmutata est.
Veniens vero sacerdos ad dedicandam aedem, cum haec exposuissem, nihil aliud pro reliquiis in sanctum altare condere voloit nisi vasculum, cuius aqua in balsamo
conmutata fuerat, dicens: „Haec sont certae reliquiae, quas martyr paradisiacis virtutibus inlustravit".

## 42. De paralytico sanato.

**[042]** Malta quidem et alia sunt, de quibus, plurima praetermittens, aliqua pando. Infirmus quidam omnibus membris debilis, plaustro inpositus, ad eius
monasterium est adductos. Qui cum ante ipsam basilicam in hoc vehiculo nocte iaceret, videt eam subito magno splendore fulgente vocesque in ea psallentium
tamquam multorum hominum audiebat. Dum haec agerentur, et ille orationem funderet, quasi stupens factus nec memor dolorum, eo adpropinquante, splendor quem
viderat praeteriit ante oculos eius. At ille, fulgore demoto, in se reversus, sensit se pristinae saluti recuperatum.

## 43. De caeco inluminato.

**[043]** Caecus quoque adminiculo deducente ad sacrosanctum altare eius accedens, dum de operturio sanctarum reliquiarum oculos adtigit, lumen recepit. Sed et
inergumini ab hac palla cooperti, saepe mundati sunt; et potestas iudicum, quotienscumque in eo loco superflue egit, confusa discessit.

## 44. De cruce altaris furata.

**[044]** Pendebat autem super ipsum altare crux holocrysa, eleganti opere facta, et erat tam praeclara visu, ut eam putares ex auro esse mundissimo.
Advenientibus vero barbaris, a quodam esse aurea aestimata direpta est et sinu recondita. At is qui eam sustulerat tanto subito pondere praegravatur, ut eam
penitus sustenere non possit, statimque conpunctus virtute martyris ac paenitentia motus, de itinere transmissam loco sancto restituit.

## 45. Qualiter expetita sunt eius pignora.

**[045]** Quae postquam gesta sunt, misit clericum suum, dicens: 'Vade', inquit, 'ad beati Iuliani basilicam, et fundens orationem, supplica, ut tibi aliquid
cerae vel pulveris de sepulchro iacentis largire dignentur aeditui, ut delatum a me cum benedictione suscipiatur'. Ille vero veniens, quae sibi fuerant imperata
flagitat ac suscipit. Et cum suscepta ferre vellet, tanto gravatur pondere, ut vix cervicem possit engere. Unde tremore magno concussus, pavimento prosternitur,
et iterum cum lacrimis orationem fundens, surrexit incolomes et acceptam sensit abeundi habere libertatem. Igitur arrepto itinere, incandescente nimium sole,
siti corripitur. Veniens autem ad villam viae proximam, unam casolam adit, aqua deposcens; de qua egrediens iuvenis dare responsum, ut eos vidit, in terram
corruit, factusque est sicut mortuus. Concurrentes autem parentes eius, calumniabant hominibus, adserentes, parentem suum eorum magicis artibus fuisse
peremptum, et adpraehensum puerum, levaverunt eum semivivum. At ille de manibus eorum elapsus, percussis palmis, coepit debachando clamare vel dicere, quod
martyris Iuliani virtute exuriretur. Clericus vero haec audiens, positam super caput eius capsulam cum pignoribus sanctis, fide plenus orare coepit attentius;
ipse quoque cum vomitu sanguinem daemoniumque proiciens, purgatus abscessit. Dehinc firmatus in fide portitor, iter totum cum psalmis et gratiarum actionibus
carpens, ad locum praeoptatum, martyre ducente, pervenit. Iam exinde tempere procedente quanti ibi inergumini, frigoritici vel diversis morbis obpraessi
martyris virtute sanati sunt, nec nomina reteneri nec numerus potuit collegi.

## 46a. De puero ad ariolos ducto et alio per virtutem sancti sanato.

**[046a]** Inter reliquas vero insignia suscipiendorum miraculorum ponimus et istud, quod insipientes corrigat et roboret sapientes. Igitur Cautini episcopi
tempore, quo, ingruentibus peccatis populi, Arverna regio ab excidio lues quam inguinariam vocant devastabatur, ego Brivatinsim vicum expetii, scilicet ut, qui
meritis tutari nequibam, beati martyris Iuliani salvarer praesidio. In quo dum commorarer vico, unus puer ex nostris ab hoc morbo corripitur, reclinatoque ad
lectulum capite, graviter agere coepit. Erat autem febris assidua cum stomachi pituita, ita ut, si aliquid acciperet, confestim reiceret; nec erat ei cibus
confortatio, sed magis exitus putabatur. Denique mei cum viderent eum in extrema vexari, hariolum quendam invocant. Ille vero venire non differens, accessit ad
aegrotum et artem suam exercere conatur. Incantationes inmurmurat, sortes iactat, ligaturas collo suspendit, promittit vivere quem ipse mancipaverat morti. Haec
autem me nescio agebantur; quae cum mihi delata fuissent, amarissime reddor et cum gravi suspirio illud conmemoro, quod Dominus per Heliam prophetam Oziae regi
pronuntiat, dicens: Quia dereliquisti dominum Deum Israel et consoluisti deum Acharon, ideo de lectulo, in quo ascendisti, non consurges, sed morte morieris.
Nam iste post adventum harioli validius febre succensus, spiritum exalavit; cuius post obitum interpositis paucis diebus, puer alius simili laborare coepit
incommodo. Tum ego eis inquio: 'Accedite ad martyris tumulum et aliquid exinde ad aegrotum deportate, et videbitis magnalia Dei atque cognoscetis, quid sit
inter iustum et iniustum et inter timentem Deum et non servientem illi'. Accedentes autem, parumper pulveris circa sepulchrum iacentis sustulerunt. De quo ut
hausit infirmus cum aqua, protinus adsecutus est medicinam, recuperatusque viribus ac restincta febre, convaluit. Intellegite ergo nunc, o omnes qui insipientes
estis in populo, et post ista discusseritis, scitote, quia nihil sunt quae ad seducendum humanum genus diabolus operatur. Ideo moneo, ut, si quis vixillo crucis
signatus, si quis baptismi ablutione mundatus, si quis, vetustate deposita, in novo nunc homine viget, talia postponat ac neglegat; quaerat autem patrocinia
martyrum, per quos sanitatum miracula celebrantur, postolet adiutoria confessorum, qui merito amici sunt dominici nuncupati, et quae voluerit obtenebit.

## 46b. De rosis ad sepulchrum eius divinitus ostensis.

**[046b]** Eo tempore, cum post obitum Proserii martyrarii Urbanus diaconus huius basilicae ordinatur aedituus, mira res ad sepulchrum sancti apparuit. Nam,
vigilante diacono in lectulo suo, auditus est sonitus, quasi ostium basilicae panderetur. Post multarum vero horarum spatium audivit eum iterum claudi. Post
haec surgens de stratu, praecedente lumine accedit ad tumulum sancti. Mirum dictu! Vidit pavimentum rosis rutilantibus esse respersum. Erant autem magnae valde
cum flagrantia odoris inmensi. [In ipsas quoque cancelli celaturas mirabatur rosas intus, nonas enim erat mensis]; et haec ita erant virides, acsi easdem ipsius
putaris horae momento ramis virentibus esse discerptas. Tunc cum grandi reverentia collectas secretius posuit, multis exinde infirmis medicamenta distribuens.
Nam inerguminus quidam ex Turonico veniens, ut exinde delibuto potum sumpsit, eiecto daemone, purgatus abscessit.

## 47. De muliere inluminata.

**[047]** Mulier erat a nativitate caeca, quae se exhiberi a parentibus ad beati Martini tumulum deprecata est. Ubi cum venisset, prostrata per triduum ad
cancellos, qui ante sepulchrum sancti antistitis habentur extrinsecus, responsum accepit per somnium, dicente sibi sancto viro: 'Si lumen recipere desideras,
require basilicam sancti Iuliani, in qua dum praesidium martyris expetis, ille coniunctus Martine visum tibi necessarium simul orationum suarum suffragiis
revocabunt'. Exsurgens autem mulier, ignorans, quod in Turonico huius martyris reliquiae tenerentur, ad Sanctonicam urbem dirigit. Victurina etenim
matrisfamilias ex nobili stirpe progenita in villae suae territurio basilicam construxerat reliquiasque martyris beati condiderat. Ad hanc ergo aedem mulier
accedens, orat per triduum. Die autem tertia advenit natalis baptistae dominici; stante autem populo et lectionum dogmata auscultante, subito murmur magnus
oritur. Presbiter vero qui solemnia caelebrabat conpraemere voces cupiens, interrogat, quid hoc esset. Cui unus ex adstantibus ait: 'Murmur mitiscere non
potest, quia virtus Domini miraculum prodidit. Ecce enim mulier illa, quae caeca testabatur, erumpente ab oculis sanguine, visum recepit'. Tunc omnes
benedixerunt Deum, cognoscentes pariter quae fuerant gesta.

## 48. De reliquiis, quae Nanninus presbiter detulit.

**[048]** Nanninus igitur presbiter domus Vibriacensis martyris huius gloriosi reliquias expetivit Quae ex iussu beati Aviti pontificis sumptas, cum psallentio
usque ad basilicam sancti Ferreoli – procul ab ipso vico sita est – pervenisset, unus ex inerguminis est mundatus. Procedens autem psallendo, cum ad medianam
pervenisset, coram hoste inprobo virtute sancti depulso, puella alia purgata discessit.

## 49. De eiusdem reliquiis multis infirmis salvatis.

**[049]** Accedens autem ad locum, ubi oratorium quod in honore sancti construxerat, posuit haec pignora in altare. Accedens autem ad eum unus cum amissis
oculis, alias manu debilis, impleta oratione, hic lucem recepit post tenebras, manus ille usum post otia diuturna. Mulier etiam nomine Aeterna cum filia ab
hoste iniquo vexata, ad hoc altare curata, cum prole sospis abscessit. Frigoritici etiam in illo loco nonnulli salvati sunt.

## 50. De alio caeco inluminato.

**[050]** Sed quoniam non est absurdum, si beatus Iulianus cum Iohanne aut Martino dona sanitatum inpertiat, cum quibus victor saeculi in caelo trepudiat,
referam adhuc, qualiter cum Nicetio Lugdunense simili virtute floruerit. Igitur infra terminum territurii Turonici Litomeris quidam in honore sancti martyris
basilicam aedificavit, in qua nos ex more ad benedicendum evocati, sancti Iuliani martyris cum Niceti Lugdunensis reliquias collocavimus. Sed non multum post
tempore caecus adveniens, fideliter orationem fudit, visum recipere meruit. Memini huic caeco in libro vitae sancti Niceti, quia dignam est, ut communis virtus
utriusque sancti scripta connectat. Ergo his miraculis lector intendens intellegat, non aliter nisi martyrum reliquorumque amicorum Dei adiutoriis se posse
salvari. Ego autem Domini misericordiam per beati martyris Iuliani patrocinia deprecor, ut advocatus in causis alumni proprii coram Domino adsistens obteneat,
ut absque inpedimento maculae ullius huius vitae cursum peragam atque illa quae confessus sum in baptismum inreprehensibiliter teneam, fideliter exerceam,
viriliter usque ad consummationem huius vitae custodiam. Amen.

---

*Explicit liber de gloria sancti Iuliani.*
# THE MIRACLES OF SAINT MARTIN

**Source.** Latin controlled throughout against *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum*, 1,2, *Miracula et opera minora*, edited by
Bruno Krusch, second edition (1969), from the official openMGH TEI transcription. The English is the project's complete translation of that control text.

**Scene.** Gregory wrote these books successively at Tours, recording Martin's continuing miracles at the tomb, at Marmoutier and Condat, and wherever Martin's
relics, oil, wax, water, or invocation traveled. The narrative moves from earlier testimony to Gregory's own episcopate and finally to his latest journeys and
contemporaries.

**Kinship and same-name fence.** Gregory names his mother, his sister and her husband Iustinus, and his niece Eustenia. Martin, bishop of Tours, is
distinguished from the Bishop Martin who meets the relics arriving in Galicia in I.11; identical names elsewhere do not establish identical persons.

**Recension note.** MGH prints the chapter marker at I.25 as “2).” between chapters 24 and 26; the chapter is numbered 25 here. The transmitted chapter
inventories are otherwise I: 40, II: 60, III: 60, and IV: 47. Book IV closes with MGH's bracketed explicit.

# ENGLISH TRANSLATION

## BOOK I

### EPISCOPAL PREFACE

**[000]** To the holy lords and brothers, most sweet in the love of Christ, and to the sons of the church of Tours entrusted to me by God, Gregory, a sinner.
The miracles which our Lord God deigned to work through his blessed bishop Martin while he was in the body, he deigns daily to confirm in order to strengthen
the faith of believers. He who worked through Martin when he was in the world now adorns his tomb with miracles; and he who then sent him as a daystar to
perishing nations now bestows benefits upon Christians through him. Let no one therefore doubt the earlier miracles, when he sees the gifts of present signs
being dispensed, when he sees the lame made straight, the blind illuminated, demons put to flight, and every other kind of disease cured through Martin's
healing. For my part, putting faith in that book about his life written by earlier authors, I shall commit to memory for posterity, as far as I can recall them
and at the Lord's command, the miracles of the present. I would not presume to do this had I not been admonished two and three times in a vision. I call
almighty God to witness that once in a dream at midday I saw in the basilica of lord Martin many weak people afflicted with various diseases being healed; and I
saw this while my mother looked on. She said to me, "Why are you sluggish about writing what you see?" And I said, "You know well that I am destitute of
learning, and that I, foolish and uneducated, would not dare to publish such admirable miracles. Would that Severus or Paulinus were alive, or at least that
Fortunatus were here to describe them! For I, being incapable of this, shall incur reproach if I attempt to record it." She said to me, "Do you not know that,
because of the people's understanding, the way you are able to speak is considered more illustrious among us? Therefore do not doubt, and do not cease doing
this, because it will be a crime for you if you keep silent about it." Wishing to do this, I am afflicted by the torment of a twofold distress, of grief and
terror alike: grief because such great miracles performed under our predecessors have not been written down; terror at approaching an outstanding work as an
unpolished rustic. But drawn on by hope in divine goodness, I shall approach what I am advised to do. For he who brought water from dry rock in the desert and
quenched the thirst of a thirsty people can, I believe, utter these things through my tongue; or at least it will be clear that he can again open the mouth of
an ass, if, opening my lips, he deigns to expound these things through my unlearned self. But why should I fear my rusticity, when the Lord our Redeemer and
God, to destroy the vanity of worldly wisdom, chose beforehand not orators but fishermen, not philosophers but rustics? With your prayers, therefore, we trust
that, even if uncultivated speech cannot adorn the page, the glorious bishop will make it shine with his illustrious miracles.

### 1

**[001]** Many have written about the miracles of Saint Martin, either in verse or in prose. First among them was Sulpicius Severus, who had such an ardent love
for the holy man of God that, while Martin still lived in this world, he wrote one book about the wonders of his life; then, after the blessed man's death, he
wrote two more, which he wished to be called dialogues. In these he included, on Postumianus's report, some things about the miracles of hermits and anchorites.
But in none of them could he find our Martin inferior; he made him equal to the apostles and holy men of old, even saying: "Fortunate Greece, which deserved to
hear the apostle preach; but Gaul has not been abandoned by Christ either, for he granted it to have Martin."

### 2

**[002]** The blessed Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, after writing verses about Martin's miracles which Severus had covered, included in five books the
miracles performed after his death—that is, in the sixth book of his work. For he says: "When demoniacs were carried through the screens of the basilica in a
whirlwind of air and were often thrown into the well by the demon's assault, they were taken out unharmed before the watching people." We too have seen this
happen in our own times. "At another time a demon drove a vessel it had seized headlong toward the river, as though intending to drown the prize it had taken.
But the help of the blessed confessor did not fail the perishing man. Entering the river and making for the farther bank, he emerged unharmed, even his clothes
dry. When he reached the cell of Marmoutier, he appeared cleansed." Paulinus also testifies that the man had often uttered many cries, frequently spoken in
unknown languages, foretold future events, and confessed crimes. But, as we said, when he touched the holy threshold he departed healed. "When Egidius was
besieged by enemies and, cut off from help, was assailed in distress, he was delivered through invocation of the blessed man, and his enemies fled. A demoniac
declared in the middle of the basilica, at the very hour when it happened, that this had been granted through Saint Martin's intercession. A girl afflicted by
paralysis and, what is worse, entangled in the error of pagan worship sought the blessed tomb; after vigils were celebrated, she was restored to health. When
she was later drawn back to the vomit of idolatry, she again incurred the illness from which she had been freed through the bishop's intercession. A certain
Chunus, driven by the swift prompting of a demon, violently tore away the crown from the tomb which proclaimed the saint's merit. Immediately deprived of sight,
he restored his plunder under the compulsion of pain and recovered his vision. A man moved by the tempter drew his sword and tried to strike someone in the
confessor's portico; immediately, by God's swift judgment, his wrath turned back upon him and he stabbed himself with his own blade. Finally, when the people
joyfully wished to bring columns to adorn the blessed church, a man hostile and opposed to the work made many threats to shut them out of the channel because
they would provide no assistance to those seeking wagons. While he was proudly striking his horse and it had plunged into a small stream, he died in the heart
of the swirling waters, suffocated by his own blows. Then, with the young man leading, the columns were brought all the way to the blessed church. They also
report that whenever oil was placed at the blessed tomb, he saw that it had increased. The holy bishop Perpetuus, who must be proclaimed a worthy disciple of
the blessed man, brought a flask of oil to the holy tomb so that the power of the righteous man might sanctify it when poured in. He mixed with the liquid dust
scraped from the marble covering the holy limbs, and the oil overflowed so abundantly that it drenched the bishop's garments, an oily wave fragrant with
nectar-like odor. Many sick people obtained healing from it. Storms were also often kept from fields purified with this liquid. When a devout man full of faith
approached the holy church and, thirsting for the saint's grace, considered what he might take from the blessed building for his health, he went near the tomb
and begged the sacristan to give him a little blessed wax from it. He received it joyfully and departed; trusting in it, he placed it in a field where he had
sown grain. A most savage storm, which had often devastated the neighborhood in preceding years, was kept away by this blessing and did no further harm there as
it had usually done. When the magnificent and longed-for Easter festival arrived, the people devoutly came to the blessed cell where he had often dwelt and
conversed with angels. Kissing each place and watering it with tears—the place where the blessed man had sat or prayed, where he had eaten or granted his body
rest after many labors—they prepared a fleet of boats to cross the river, intending to reach the blessed tomb and prostrate themselves before the confessor,
begging pardon with tears. As they sailed, the wind was stirred by the tempter's assault; a boat sank in the deep, and both sexes were swept away by the river.
While they were tossed among the stormy waves and all hope of escape had perished, one cry arose from them all: "Merciful Martin, rescue your servants and
handmaids from present destruction!" As soon as this was said, a calm breeze lifted the limbs of the drowning unharmed from the waves, and the water, serving
them, restored them all to the bank they desired. None perished; all were saved and celebrated the Easter festival with the greatest exultation. For that power
was not absent which divided the Jordan and led the people through on dry ground beneath masses of water, when Joshua took twelve stones from the riverbed and
consecrated on the bank where he had arrived the signs which the apostles would bear; nor that power which, embracing Peter with a merciful right hand as he was
perishing, rescued him from death; nor that which drew from the depths of the sea to the desired shore a sailor about to drown who invoked Martin's Lord. A man
asking to take something from the holy building as a blessing received wax from the holy tomb and stored it in the inner rooms of his house like a heavenly
treasure. Through the tempter's envy a fire was sent upon the house; the devouring flame surrounded it and, spreading through the dry timbers, destroyed
everything. Meanwhile a cry was raised to heaven and blessed Martin's help implored. They remembered the piece of wax brought from the saint's church. When it
was found and thrown into the fire, it immediately extinguished the whole blaze; by a new miracle, wax which had usually fed fire suppressed its violence by the
power of holiness." Paulinus wrote these things in verse in the sixth book of his work, having received an account of them from the holy bishop Perpetuus. When
the document containing this account reached him, his nephew was suffering from a serious illness. Trusting in the saint's power, he said, "If it pleases you,
blessed Martin, that I should write anything in your praise, let your power appear over this sick man." He placed the document on the man's chest, and
immediately the fever departed and the sick man was healed. The priest Fortunatus also wrote the whole work of Martin's life in verse in four books.

### 3

**[003]** Attracted by these examples, though unskilled, we nevertheless attempt to recall for memory, as far as we can discover them, some of the miracles of
the holy and most blessed Martin performed after his death; for this labor of writing will contain what is not found inserted in the work of Severus or
Paulinus. The glorious lord Martin, shining and resplendent throughout the world, arose like a new sun as the world was already declining. As the earlier
history relates, he was born at Sabaria in Pannonia and was directed with God's help to the salvation of Gaul. Illuminating it with miracles and signs, he
unwillingly accepted the honor of the episcopate in the city of Tours under pressure from the people. Leading a glorious and almost inimitable life in that
office for twenty-five years, two months, and ten days, he rested in peace at midnight in the eighty-first year of his age, when Caesarius and Atticus were
consuls. It is most clear that his glorious departure, praiseworthy throughout the world, occurred on the Lord's day, and we confirm this by certain testimonies
in what follows. It is considered no small merit that the Lord received him into paradise on the same day on which the Redeemer and Lord himself rose victorious
from hell, so that he who had always kept the Lord's solemnities undefiled should, after the afflictions of the world, be placed at rest on the Lord's day.

### 4

**[004]** The blessed Severinus, bishop of the city of Cologne, a man of honorable life and praiseworthy in all things, was making his customary circuit of the
holy places with his clergy on the Lord's day when, at the very hour the blessed man died, he heard a choir singing on high. He called his archdeacon and asked
whether the voices he himself heard attentively were also striking the archdeacon's ears. The man answered, "Not at all." Severinus said, "Listen carefully."
The archdeacon began to stretch his neck upward, prick up his ears, and stand on tiptoe, supported by his staff. But I believe he was not of equal merit and
therefore did not deserve to hear these things. Then both he and the blessed bishop prostrated themselves on the ground and prayed that divine goodness would
permit him to hear. When they rose, the old man asked again, "What do you hear?" He said, "I hear voices singing as though in heaven, but I have no idea what it
means." Severinus replied, "I shall tell you what it means. My lord Bishop Martin has departed from this world, and the angels are now carrying him on high with
song. For a little while, so that these voices could be heard, the devil tried to detain him with his wicked angels; but finding nothing of his own in Martin,
he departed confounded. What then will become of us sinners, if the wicked host wished to harm so great a bishop?" While the bishop was speaking, the archdeacon
noted the time and quickly sent to Tours someone to inquire carefully into these things. On his arrival, the messenger ascertained most clearly that the blessed
man had died on the very day and at the very hour when Saint Severinus heard the choir singing. If we return to Severus's history, he wrote that at that same
hour Martin was revealed to him with the book of his life.

### 5

**[005]** At that time the blessed Ambrose, the flowers of whose eloquence are fragrant throughout the whole church today, presided as bishop over the city of
Milan. When he celebrated the Lord's-day rites, it was his custom that a reader coming with a book would not presume to read before the saint had given the
command with a nod. On that Lord's day, after the prophetic lesson had been read and the man who was to deliver the lesson from the blessed Paul stood before
the altar, the most blessed bishop Ambrose fell asleep over the holy altar. Many saw this, but no one presumed to wake him. After nearly two or three hours had
passed, they roused him, saying, "The hour has already passed. Let the lord order the reader to read the lesson, for the waiting people are now very weary." The
blessed Ambrose answered, "Do not be disturbed. It has been greatly to my benefit to sleep, since the Lord deigned to show me such a miracle. Know that my
brother Martin the bishop has departed from the body, and that I have attended his funeral; after completing the customary service, I had only the concluding
prayer left when you woke me." Astonished and amazed, they noted the day and time and inquired carefully. They found that it was on that very day and at that
very time that the blessed confessor had said he attended Martin's funeral. O blessed man, at whose departure the company of saints sings, the choir of angels
exults, and the host of all heavenly powers runs to meet him; at whose departure the devil is confounded in his presumption, the church is strengthened in
power, and bishops are glorified by revelation; whom Michael took up with the angels, whom Mary received with choirs of virgins, and whom paradise holds joyful
with the saints! But why do we attempt praise of him which we cannot fulfill? He himself is the praise of him from whose lips praise never departed. Would that
we could at least relate the simple history!

### 6

**[006]** It is also worthwhile to include in this account how, with an angel's approval, his holy little body was translated to the place where it is now
venerated. In the sixty-fourth year after the death of the glorious lord Martin, the blessed Perpetuus received the dignity of the episcopal throne of Tours.
Having attained this eminence, with the people greatly united in their prayers he resolved to lay over the blessed limbs the foundations of a larger church than
had stood there before. Applying diligent effort, he brought the project wonderfully to completion. There would be much to say about this building, but because
it is still standing I thought it better to say nothing. When the longed-for time came for the bishop to dedicate the church and transfer the holy little body
from the place where it had been buried, blessed Perpetuus summoned the neighboring bishops to the feast, together with no small crowd of abbots and clergy of
every rank. Wishing to do this on the Kalends of July, they kept vigil through one night; in the morning they took mattocks and began to dig away the earth
above the holy tomb. Once it was uncovered, they put their hands to it to move it, but though the whole multitude labored all day, they accomplished nothing.
After keeping vigil through another night, they tried again in the morning but again could do nothing at all. Troubled and terrified, they did not know what to
do. One of the clergy said to them, "You know that the anniversary of his episcopal consecration usually falls after these three days; perhaps he is directing
you to transfer him on that day." Devoting themselves day and night to fasting, prayer, and continual psalmody, they spent those three days in unbroken
observance. On the fourth day they approached and laid hands on the tomb, but still could not move it at all. Everyone was terrified; they were already
preparing to cover with earth the vessel they had uncovered, when there appeared to them the venerable white hair of an old man, snow-white in its radiance.
Saying that he was an abbot, he told them, "How long will you remain troubled and delay? Do you not see lord Martin standing ready to help you if you lay hands
on it?" Throwing off the cloak he wore, he put his hand to the sarcophagus with the other bishops. Crosses and candles were prepared, an antiphon was begun, and
they all lifted their voices in psalmody on high. Immediately, through the old man's effort, the sarcophagus moved with the greatest lightness and, by the
Lord's approval, was brought to the place where it is now venerated. When it had been set according to the bishop's wish and mass had also been celebrated, they
went to the banquet and looked carefully for the old man but could not find him anywhere. No one came forward who had seen him leave the basilica. I believe it
was some angelic power which declared that it had seen the blessed man and thereafter appeared to no one. Many miracles have been performed in that place since
that day, but through negligence they have not been written down. For my part, I could not keep silent about what I either saw happen in my own time or learned
with certainty had happened.

### 7

**[007]** A man named Theodomundus, whose pathways of hearing and speech were blocked, came daily to the holy basilica and bowed in prayer, moving only his
lips. He could not produce any sound with full meaning, being deprived of the function of speech. He seemed to pray so earnestly that he was often seen weeping
amid his silent words. If anyone gave him alms in consideration of his need, he immediately distributed it to other poor people like himself; asking by gestures
for contributions from others, he extended support to the needy. After he had lived in that holy place in such devotion for three years, one day, admonished by
divine goodness, he came before the holy altar. Standing with eyes and hands raised to heaven, a stream of blood mixed with putrid matter burst from his mouth.
Spitting on the ground, he began to groan heavily and cough up with blood some unknown fragments, so that one would think someone had cut his throat with an
iron instrument. Corrupt matter also hung from his mouth like bloody threads. Then, when the bonds of his ears and throat were broken, he lifted himself up and
again raised his eyes and hands to heaven; with his mouth still bloody, he broke out in these first words: "I give you great thanks, most blessed lord Martin,
because by opening my mouth you have enabled me after a long time to utter words in your praise." While all the people wondered and were astonished at such a
miracle, they asked whether he had also recovered his hearing. He replied in everyone's hearing that he heard everything clearly. Restored to health in this
way, he was taken in by Queen Chrodechildis in recognition of Saint Martin's power and out of reverence for him. Placed in a school, he committed the whole
sequence of the Psalms to memory. God made him a perfect cleric and permitted him to remain in the church's service for many years afterward.

### 8

**[008]** A woman named Chainemunda was deprived of the light of her eyes and could not find her way by sight unless someone led her. Very devout and full of
faith, she came to the venerable church of the blessed bishop Martin. She was not only blind, as I have said, but also full of wounds over her whole body.
Putrid sores had covered all her limbs; her face was pitiable and horrible to look upon, so that the people thought her a leper. She felt her way daily to the
building of the glorious daystar; after nearly three years, while she stood before the tomb, her eyes were opened so that she saw everything clearly. All
illness was removed from her limbs, the fluid flowing from her body dried up, and new skin grew over her. She was restored to her former health so completely
that no trace of illness remained in her body. Living for many years afterward, she continually gave thanks to almighty God because through his blessed
confessor he had thus restored her to soundness.

### 9

**[009]** I shall not omit how present was the invocation of his name when it calmed a stormy sea. The blessed Baudenus, bishop of the city of Tours, was
crossing an estate by boat when a sudden, terrible tempest with violent wind arose. The calm sea was stirred by the blast, and the boat was tossed by masses of
waves. First its prow rose on the billows, then it plunged between the gaps in the waters. Some hung as though on the stage of a watery mountain; others, as the
waves opened, gaped down into the depths. Not even the yardarm remained which bore the sign of the blessed cross. Their limbs were loosened by fear, and all
were prepared to die without hope of life. The elder prostrated himself in tearful prayer, stretched both palms toward the stars, implored blessed Martin's
help, and repeatedly cried out that he should deign quickly to come to him. One of the faithless men said, "That Martin whom you invoke has already abandoned
you and will not help you in this necessity." I truly believe this utterance came from the adversary to disturb the blessed bishop's prayer. But Baudenus
repelled this dart with the breastplate of faith and more and more urgently begged the holy man's protection, at the same time urging everyone to pray. While
this was happening, a very sweet odor like balsam suddenly filled the ship; it smelled of incense as though someone were going around with a thurible. When the
fragrance arrived, the savage violence of the winds subsided; the masses of water standing around them collapsed, and the sea became calm. All who had already
been given over to death marveled at the peace of the waves; serenity returned immediately, and they were brought to shore. No one doubted that this storm had
been stilled by the blessed man's arrival. Then all together thanked the Lord because he had deigned to deliver them from this danger through the invocation of
his bishop.

### 10

**[010]** At that time a man from Cambrai sought relics of blessed Martin. Having received them toward evening, he set out singing psalms. As he was crossing
the river Loire, it became late; the sky suddenly darkened, and great flashes of lightning and peals of thunder descended. While this was happening, two boys'
spears, sending forth fiery flames, gave light to the travelers. The shining spears went before them, bringing no less miracle than benefit to the wayfarers and
displaying the power of the blessed bishop.

### 11

**[011]** My barren tongue fails, though desiring to recount such great miracles. The son of Chararic, king of Galicia, was gravely ill and had fallen into such
exhaustion that he barely breathed. His father, together with the inhabitants of the place, had subjected himself to the foul Arian sect. That region was also
more defiled by leprosy than other provinces usually were. When the king saw his son sinking toward the end, he said to his men, "Tell me, I beg you, of what
religion was that Martin who they say shines forth in Gaul with many miracles?" They replied, "While in the body, he governed the people of the catholic faith
with pastoral care, declaring that the Son is to be venerated with the Father and the Holy Spirit in equal substance and omnipotence. Even now, seated in
heaven, he does not cease to provide continual benefits for his own people." Chararic said, "If what you say is true, let faithful friends hasten to his church
carrying many gifts. If they obtain healing for my little son, I shall inquire into the catholic faith which he believed and shall believe it." He weighed out
gold and silver equal to his son's weight and sent it to the venerable place of the tomb. When the envoys arrived, they offered their gifts and prayed at the
blessed tomb for the sick boy. But because the sect still occupied his father's heart, the boy did not immediately deserve to receive complete healing. The
returning messengers told the king that they had seen many miracles at the blessed tomb, saying, "We do not know why your son was not healed." Understanding
that his son could not be healed unless he believed Christ equal with the Father, he built a church of wonderful workmanship in blessed Martin's honor. When it
was finished, he declared, "If I deserve to receive relics of the righteous man, I shall believe whatever the bishops preach." He again sent his men with
greater gifts. Arriving at the blessed place, they requested relics. When these were offered to them according to custom, they said, "We shall not do it that
way; rather, we ask permission to deposit gifts from which we may afterward take something." They placed a weighed piece of silk cloth over the blessed tomb,
saying, "If we find favor before the patron we seek, what we have deposited will afterward weigh more, and we shall have the blessing sought through faith."
After keeping vigil for one night, in the morning they weighed what they had deposited. So much of the blessed man's grace was poured into them that they kept
the balance beam raised in the air as long as it could possibly remain suspended. When the relics were raised with great triumph, the envoys heard the voices of
people singing psalms who had been imprisoned in the city. Marveling at the sweetness of the sound, they asked the guards what it meant. The guards said,
"Relics of lord Martin are being sent to Galicia, and that is why the singing is taking place." Weeping, the prisoners invoked Saint Martin to free them by his
visitation. The guards were terrified and fled; the bars of their restraints were broken, and the people rose free from bondage. With the populace watching,
they came to the holy pledges, kissing the blessed relics with tears and thanking blessed Martin for their release because he had deigned to save them by his
mercy. The bishop obtained pardon for their offenses from the judge, and they were released unharmed. Seeing this, the bearers of the relics rejoiced greatly,
saying, "Now we know that the blessed bishop deigns to show himself merciful to us sinners." Giving thanks, with a prosperous voyage and the patron's protection
attending them, over gentle waves with moderated breezes, the sail hanging and the sea calm, they quickly reached a port in Galicia. Then the blessed Martin,
now regarded as bishop in a distant region, came there admonished by God. I do not believe it was without divine providence that he set out from his homeland on
the very day the blessed relics were taken from their place, and so entered the port of Galicia together with those pledges. Receiving the pledges with the
greatest veneration, the people strengthened their faith by miracles. The king's son, all illness gone, hastened in health to meet them. The blessed Martin
received the office of priestly grace. The king confessed the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and was anointed with his whole household. The foulness
of leprosy was driven from the people, and all the sick were healed; from then until now the disease of leprosy has never appeared in anyone there. The Lord
bestowed such grace there at the arrival of the blessed patron's pledges that it would take very long to recount the miracles performed that day. That people is
now so inflamed with the love of Christ that all would most willingly undergo martyrdom if a time of persecution were at hand.

### 12

**[012]** Queen Ultrogotha, hearing of the miracles performed at the place where the holy limbs rest, devoutly sought to see them as though she were going to
hear the wisdom of Solomon. Abstaining from food and sleep and sending abundant alms ahead of her, she reached the holy place. Entering the basilica in fear and
trembling, she did not dare approach the tomb, declaring herself unworthy and unable to come near because her sins stood in the way. After spending one night in
vigils, prayers, and flowing tears, in the morning she offered many gifts and asked that masses be celebrated in honor of the blessed confessor. While they were
being celebrated, three blind men who had sat for a long time without sight at the feet of the blessed bishop were suddenly surrounded by a great radiance and
recovered the light they had lost long before. When this happened, a cry of people glorifying God rose to heaven. The queen ran to the miracle, and the people
ran too. Everyone marveled at the woman's faith and at the confessor's glory; but above all our God was praised, who grants such power to his saints that he
deigns to work these things through them, bestowing upon this world, among its other lights, the immense star of blessed Martin so that its darkness might shine
through him. Truly, like a fruitful olive tree, he daily offers the Lord the fruit of the conversion of the wretched.

### 13

**[013]** Nor shall I pass over what I recall my venerable fellow servant, the priest Fortunatus, reported. A man in Italy was so attacked by the poison of a
pustule and brought into such danger that he despaired of living. He asked some people which of them had been to blessed Martin's church, and one of those
present declared that he had. The sick man asked what he had brought from there as a blessing. The man denied that he had presumed to take anything. The sick
man asked again what clothing he had worn when he visited the holy church. He answered that it was the same clothing he was wearing at that moment. The sick man
faithfully cut off a piece of the garment and placed it on the pustule. As soon as it touched his limbs, the pustule's wound lost the force of its poison;
through this medicine and the saint's power, he brought the sick man back to health. Fortunatus declared that this remedy was especially effective among the
Italians: if anyone was struck by the wound of a pustule, he should take refuge at the nearest oratory of blessed Martin; and whatever was first snatched,
either from the veil at the door or from the cloths hanging on the walls, if placed on the sick man and adhering to him, would restore health. He declared, as a
witness concerning his own father, that this remedy had saved his carnal parent from death by a pustule.

### 14

**[014]** Fortunatus also reported this: "An oratory of blessed Martin has been founded on the summit of a fortress in a region of Italy called Tertium.
Whenever barbarians treacherously approached a neighboring tower in a night attack, if any of the watchmen in the tower held a lance, sword, knife, or stylus
and drew it from its sheath, for nearly an hour such light shone from the whole blade as if the iron had turned into a wax candle. Immediately warned by this
sign, the guards became more attentive to their watch and drove off the lurking enemies with stones. He judges by sure indication that this occurred through
Saint Martin's help, since by his nearness the saint showed constant and present protection to peoples devoted to him." I learned of this miracle from the man
named above.

### 15

**[015]** He also declared that, at Ravenna, he and his companion Felix in rhetoric touched their eyes with oil from a lamp burning beneath a painted image of
blessed Martin, and their sight was restored.

### 16

**[016]** Likewise, in the city just mentioned, when the procurator Placidus had been given up by the doctors, he fled to another nearby oratory of holy virgins
and lay down in its portico. At night blessed Martin came in a dream to the abbess and asked what she was doing. She said she was resting. The saint told her,
"I was about to return to Gaul, but I declare that I have delayed because of this man lying outside in the portico." The abbess arose and related the vision,
giving the man faith that he would be freed from danger, which he certainly deserved to obtain. As the priest mentioned above declares, Martin's glory is
venerated in the places of Italy much more ardently than, if it may be said, where his holy limbs lie buried—so much so that frequent miracles cannot be
gathered into scattered words, nor can such an infinite number be contained on pages.

### 17

**[017]** At the gate of Amiens where the blessed man once cut his cloak and covered a freezing poor man, the faithful built an oratory in which religious
virgins now serve. In honor of the holy bishop they possess only a small means of support, except that the devotion of the devout often feeds them. At one time
they had a few beehives. A malicious man saw them and said to himself, "If only I could carry off some of those hives!" The following night, incited by a demon,
he loaded a boat with three stolen hives so that, after crossing the river, he could more easily claim what he had taken. But I believe this theft was an
impediment to him, as was afterward clearly proved. When at sunrise people hurried to the riverbank to cross, they saw a boat at the shore, bees emerging in
swarms from the hives, and a man lying prostrate apart. Thinking him overcome by sleep, but having already learned from the virgins that a theft had occurred,
they hurried to bind him. Approaching, they found him dead. The virgins were informed at once and restored to the cell what had been stolen, marveling that the
sentence of divine vengeance had fallen upon the man so swiftly.

### 18

**[018]** Likewise, at the oratory of Siroiale, whose altar the kindly hands of the holy confessor consecrated, many obtained the benefits they sought. A
paralyzed man came there and, keeping vigil all night, held a wax candle as tall as himself. In the morning, when light returned to the world, he leapt up
healed before the people, his steps freed.

### 19

**[019]** Nor shall I be silent about what he bestowed upon blindness when a devout woman sought his blessed tomb. A woman from the territory of Tours named
Bella, having lost her eyesight, was gravely afflicted. Tormented day and night by unceasing pains, she said to her people, "If I had been led to lord Martin's
basilica, I would immediately have recovered my health. I trust that he who could heal a poor man's leprosy by touching him with a kiss can pour light into my
eyes." Then, with someone leading and supporting her, she came to the holy place. Devoting herself there to frequent fasting and prayer, she deserved to recover
the sight she had lost. She was so healed that she who had come blind, led by another, returned ready to be a guide for many blind people. She later married,
bore sons, and in sound health repaid thanks to the one who had restored her.

### 20

**[020]** Since I have already related two or three times how miracles were performed and dangers calmed by invocation of the glorious name alone, I shall now
unfold how the blessed bishop, when invoked, supported a man perishing at the very precipice of death. A certain Ammonius, an official of the holy basilica, was
coming from dinner soaked with wine when, driven by the enemy, he was thrown from a high rock adjoining the road. The depth of the place was nearly two hundred
feet. As he spun through the depth of that precipice and flew downward without the help of wings, at every moment of his descent he cried out for Saint Martin's
help. Then, as if shaken from his mount by other hands, he was thrown onto trees growing in the valley. Descending gradually from branch to branch, he reached
the ground without danger of death. Yet, so that the adversary's work once begun should not seem wholly frustrated, his foot was slightly injured. But he came
to the glorious lord's church, applied himself to prayer, and lost all force of pain.

### 21

**[021]** I do not think it superfluous to include in this account how invocation of his name gave life to a man about to die. In a certain place a man was
arrested for crimes of theft and severely flogged, then led to the gallows to be condemned to hanging. When he had reached this end and death was near, he asked
for time to pray. With his hands still tied behind his back, he threw himself face down on the ground and began with tears to invoke blessed Martin's name,
asking that, even if Martin would not help him in this necessity, he would at least absolve him of his sins hereafter. When the prayer was finished, he was
hanged and the soldiers left the place. With his mouth half open and his lips moving slightly, he kept striving to implore Saint Martin's help. As soon as the
soldiers departed, his hands and feet were released. He hung there for two days, until it was revealed to a religious woman that she should take him down. She
came and found him still alive. With blessed Martin's help, she took him from the gallows and brought him unharmed to the church. Those who saw him there were
dumbfounded and amazed, saying, "How is he alive?" They asked how he had been delivered. He said, "Blessed Martin delivered me from present death and brought me
here." Truly, according to my understanding, I consider this miracle no less than the raising of a dead man; for the blessed confessor, so to speak, broke open
the jaws of death, drew him back from its mouth, and restored him to life. He is still alive in the world today as testimony to the blessed man's power.

### 22

**[022]** I shall not pass over what happened in the diocese of Condat, a place illuminated by frequent miracles. For the blessed man cast off the burden of the
flesh there and departed to the Lord. A man named Leomeris, a servant of a man from Angers, was stricken with a hemorrhage; his hand was contracted and his
tongue bound. Held in this weakness for a long time, he performed no work for his master. Admonished by faith, he kept vigil at the blessed basilica; his hand
was straightened and his tongue freed from every impediment, and he testified before the people to blessed Martin's miracle, saying, "Behold, let me be your
witness and prove what the holy man of God has done this night!" Returning to his master, he told him everything that had happened. But the master, not
believing in the glorious bishop's power, assigned him to his usual service. When Leomeris began to work, he was again reduced to weakness. His master
understood that this was a mystery of God and sent him back to the holy place he had visited before. Spending the night there with the greatest devotion, when
day came he was restored to the health he had previously obtained.

### 23

**[023]** I thought it right not to omit from this account what I heard the priest Wiliacharius relate. At the time when he had incurred King Chlothar's
hostility because of Chramn's treachery, he fled for refuge to Saint Martin's basilica. He was kept there in chains, but by the power of the blessed daystar the
chains could not remain intact and were shattered. Through some negligence or other he was caught outside the portico. Loaded with iron and with his hands tied
behind his back, he was led to the king. He began to cry aloud and pray that blessed Martin would have mercy on him and not allow him to go into captivity, he
who had devoutly sought Martin's church. Immediately, as he spoke and while the blessed bishop Eufronius prayed on the city wall opposite the basilica, his
hands were released and all the links of his chains broke and fell. When he was brought to the king, he was again held bound in fetters and chains. But when he
invoked the name of the patron just mentioned, all the iron on him was shattered as though he were a potter breaking clay. There was only this interval: he was
not released from a bond until he invoked that most sacred name; once invoked, everything was loosed. Then the king, a man of superior understanding, saw Saint
Martin's power at work there, freed Wiliacharius from the burden of bonds, and restored him to his former liberty. I learned from the mouth of the priest
Wiliacharius himself, before many witnesses, that this happened. Would that the blessed confessor would deign to manifest himself to me in such power, to loose
the bonds of my sins as he crushed the vast weights of chains upon that man!

### 24

**[024]** Alpinus, count of the city of Tours, was gravely consumed for a whole year by pain in one foot. He had no rest day or night and continually implored
blessed Martin's help amid his cries of torment. The blessed confessor appeared to him in a night vision, smiling with a cheerful face and wearing his customary
armor. He placed the blessed sign of the holy cross on the sick foot; immediately all pain fled, and Alpinus rose healed from his bed.

### 25

**[025]** Charigisilus, referendary of King Chlothar, experienced the same grace. His hands and feet had been contracted by a fluid. He came to the holy
basilica and devoted himself to prayer for two or three months. Visited by the blessed bishop, he deserved to obtain health in his weak limbs. He later became a
household official of the king just named and bestowed many benefits on the people of Tours and those serving the blessed basilica.

### 26

**[026]** I shall also relate how the madness of diabolical arts is stripped bare at his basilica. A man named Aquilinus, while hunting with his father in the
forests of Francia, incurred a terrible panic through the enemy's ambush. His heart trembled and at times he seemed out of his mind. His parents understood that
he was afflicted by a demonic attack and, following rustic custom, brought him amulets and potions from soothsayers and diviners. When these customary remedies
did no good, inflamed by pain they sought Saint Martin's help, saying, "He can expose malicious snares; as we have heard, he uncovered the shade worshipped
under a false name of religion." They roused Aquilinus from the region and sent him to the holy basilica. There, restraining himself with the greatest
abstinence in prayer, he continually asked for the saint's help. After he had remained in this faith for a considerable time, all fear was removed and he
recovered the sanity he had previously possessed. Forgetting his parents, he serves in that place to this day in gratitude for the benefit received.

### 27

**[027]** A man named Charivaldus met a similar ambush while hunting and had lost the use of one side, his hand and foot disabled. Carried by his servants to
the glorious church, he subjected himself to continual fasting and prayer for nearly a whole year. Recovering health in all his limbs, he joyfully returned
home. We therefore warn that no one should consult diviners, because they will never help the sick. A little dust from the basilica is more effective than their
insane medicines.

### 28

**[028]** Who could ever discover or know how many miracles occur continually or have occurred through the dust or wax of that place, or through whatever one
can take from the tomb? Yet I considered it a crime to keep silent about one manifest miracle which I learned from the faithful. A man full of faith wished to
carry away some pledge secretly from the saint's basilica. Though he tried many times, he never succeeded, since he did not presume to do so openly. Wishing to
return, he came at night to the rope by which the bell is sounded and cut off a piece with a knife to take with him. Returning home, he provided healing to many
sick people through it, so that there was no doubt that a sick person would recover if he deserved faithfully to kiss that pledge. Behold, O saint, what you
bestow on the faithful who come to your own walls! Through you those who devoutly carry away pledges are saved; when your help follows, they are delivered. But
vigorous faith accomplishes all these things, as the Lord says: "Your faith has saved you."

### 29

**[029]** It seems that I should also not keep silent about how the blessed man grants his servants protection to defend their property wherever he commands.
King Charibert hated the clergy, neglected God's churches, despised the bishops, and inclined rather toward luxury. It was suggested to him that a certain
property which Saint Martin's basilica had held for a long time was owed to the rights of his treasury. Ancient usage had given that place the name Navicellae.
Accepting this wicked advice, he quickly sent boys to subject that estate to his own lordship. When he seemed not to possess what he held, he ordered grooms
with cavalrymen sent to the place and commanded, without regard for justice, that the horses be fed there. The boys came and took the hay that had been gathered
to feed the horses. While the enjoined service was being carried out and the cavalrymen stationed there began to use the hay, the horses were seized by madness.
Neighing at one another and breaking their halters, they leapt across the plains and fled. Badly scattered, some were blinded, some hurled over rocks, and
others rushing into hedges were impaled on the points of stakes. The grooms understood God's wrath; they drove beyond the boundary of the property the few
horses they could catch and received them back healthy. They told the king that the property was being held most unjustly and that this was why they had
suffered these things, adding, "Give it up, and you will have peace." Filled with fury, he is said to have replied, "Whether it is owed justly or unjustly,
while I reign the basilica shall not have it." Immediately, by divine command, he died and departed. When the most glorious King Sigibert succeeded to his
kingdom, at the suggestion of the blessed bishop Eufronius he restored the property to Saint Martin's lordship, and the basilica possesses it to this day. Hear
this, all who hold power! Clothe others in such a way that you do not strip others; add to your riches only that by which you do no harm to churches! For God is
a swift avenger of his servants. I therefore warn anyone who reads this about the powerful not to become angry; for if he becomes angry, he will confess that it
was said about himself.

### 30

**[030]** The blessed confessor appeared similarly in the matter of property unjustly taken from him. A man named Eustochius often harassed the holy bishop
Eufronius unjustly over the inheritance of his kinsman Baudulf, who had made Saint Martin's basilica his heir. Moved by these continual injuries, the blessed
bishop returned some of the property to Eustochius. While Eustochius was carrying it home, his only son immediately fell into a fever; burning gravely for one
night and day, he died. Death came to meet him as swiftly as his father had become master of property not owed to him. Following Gehazi's example, Eustochius
possessed gold and silver, but he acquired what was more costly to him, leprosy of the soul, and lost his son; nor did he ever deserve to have another
afterward.

### 31

**[031]** To restrain the audacity of the faithless, I shall not keep silent about how present divine vengeance was against another man who swore falsely in the
holy portico. Every day the faithful provide necessities to the almshouse which the saint feeds by his generosity from the alms of the devout. The blessed poor
have the custom that, when many of them go away to different places, they leave a custodian there to receive whatever is offered. A devout man once brought a
triens as an act of charity. The custodian of the place took it and did not fear to hide it from the brothers. When the poor assembled at the sixth hour, they
asked the custodian what the blessed shepherd, looking upon them with his usual kindness, had sent. They had heard that something had been given there. He
answered with an oath: "By this holy place and the power of lord Martin, nothing more than one silver coin has come here." He had not finished the words; the
speech still hung on his lips when he immediately fell trembling to the ground. Other hands returned him to his bed, and he began to sob violently. Asked by
those standing around what was wrong, he answered, "I swore falsely about the triens the poor were asking for, and therefore present vengeance is scourging me.
I beg you to take it and return it to the almshouse." When it was returned, he immediately breathed his last. O wretched man, so overtaken by wicked greed that
he perished, losing the profit of life and failing to possess the gain of the cursed money! "To what do you not drive mortal hearts, accursed greed?" You who
once envied the widow buying the heavenly kingdom with two mites now plunge this man into the depths over one triens. You who tied Judas with a noose over the
price of the Master now drown this man in hell over a small coin. Let these words suffice to restrain the rashness of the wicked.

### 32

**[032]** Now that I have finished what happened to others, I shall approach what the power of the present patron has worked around my unworthy self. In the one
hundred and sixty-third year after the death of the holy and praiseworthy blessed bishop Martin, while the holy bishop Eufronius was governing the church of
Tours in his seventh year and the most glorious King Sigibert was in his second year, I fell into an illness with malignant pustules and fever. Denied the use
of drink and food, I was so afflicted that, all hope of present life lost, I thought only of what was necessary for burial. Continual death with burning fever
beset me, desiring to expel my soul from my body. Already almost lifeless, I invoked the name of the blessed bishop Martin and recovered a little strength.
Though still attempting it feebly, I began to prepare a journey, for it had entered my mind that I ought to visit the place of his venerable tomb. I was seized
by such longing that I thought I ought not to live if I delayed setting out. I had barely escaped the burning of that affliction when I began again to burn with
the fever of longing. Without delay, though still weak, I undertook the journey with my companions. After two or three stages, I entered some woods and again
collapsed with fever. I became so gravely ill that everyone thought I would lose my life. My friends approached and, seeing me very weak, said, "Let us return
home; if God wishes to call you, die in your own house. If you recover, you will more easily complete your votive journey. It is better to return home than to
die in the wilderness." Hearing this, I wept bitterly and lamented my misfortune, saying, "I adjure you by almighty God and the day of judgment feared by all
