the guilty to consent to what I ask. Do not abandon the journey we have begun. If I deserve to see Saint Martin's basilica, I thank my God; if not, carry my
lifeless body there and bury it. My resolve is not to return home if I have not deserved to be presented at his tomb." Then, all weeping together, we resumed
the journey we had begun. With the glorious lord's protection going before us, we reached his basilica.

### 33

**[033]** At that time one of my clergy named Armentarius, well instructed in spiritual writings, was so quick to grasp musical modulations that you would think
he was not studying but writing them down. Very energetic in service and faithful in what was entrusted to him, he had been infected by poison and malignant
pustules and had lost all understanding; he had been reduced to such a state that he could neither comprehend nor do anything. On the third night after we
arrived at the holy basilica, we resolved to keep vigil, and we did so. In the morning, when the signal called us to the morning office, we returned to our
lodging. Resting on our beds, we slept until nearly the second hour. I awoke with all the bitterness of weakness and heart removed and felt that I had recovered
my former health. Rejoicing, I called a familiar servant to attend me. Armentarius quickly arose, stood before me, and said, "Lord, I shall obey whatever you
command." Still thinking him out of his mind, I said, "If you can, call the servant." He replied, "I shall fulfill whatever you order." Astonished, I asked what
this meant. He said, "I know that I am very well, but one error remains in my mind: I do not know from what direction I came here." He began to attend me
exactly as he had been accustomed to do before his illness. Exulting and weeping for joy, I thanked almighty God for both of us, because through the patron's
intercession he had restored me in body and Armentarius in mind; one act of assistance arising from faith had also benefited another man who was out of his mind
and had not known how to ask. Nor shall I pass over this: forty days later, on the first day of the same month, I delighted to drink wine, which my illness had
caused me to detest until then.

### 34

**[034]** When we returned, we carried three wax candles as a blessing from the blessed tomb. It would take long to recount how many miracles were performed
through that wax upon sufferers from chills and other sick people. But I shall relate one miracle among many. Hail had been accustomed to devastate a field of
our property every year; it raged so severely that when it came it left nothing. I chose a tree in those vineyards taller than the rest and placed some of the
holy wax on it. From that day to the present, no storm has ever fallen there; approaching, it has passed the place by as though afraid.

### 35

**[035]** At the prompting of faith, one of our people, unknown to me, had taken a venerable piece of wood from the screen of the bed at the holy lord's
monastery and kept it in his lodging for his salvation. But—I believe because it was not honored or cherished as it should have been—his household began to
suffer grave illness. No one knew what was wrong; nothing improved, and each day conditions grew worse. In a night vision he saw a terrible figure who said to
him, "Why are you suffering like this?" He replied, "I have no idea how this happened." The figure said, "You are keeping carelessly with you the wood which you
took from lord Martin's bed; that is why you have incurred these things. Go now, take it to the deacon Gregory, and let him keep it with him." Without delay the
man brought it to me. I received it with the greatest veneration and placed it in a worthy location. His whole household was healed, so that no one there
suffered any further harm.

### 36

**[036]** Once, out of a desire to visit, I was traveling to my venerable mother in Burgundy. As I was passing the woods situated beyond the river Berbera, I
encountered robbers. Surrounding me, they intended to rob and kill me. Taking refuge in my customary help, I implored Saint Martin's protection. Immediately and
graciously coming to my aid, he so terrified them that they could do nothing against me. Instead, those who had come to be feared began themselves to fear and
fled at full speed. Mindful of the apostle's teaching that I should give my enemies food and drink, I ordered drink offered to them. They did not wait but fled
as fast as they could. You would have thought they were being driven with cudgels or forced to run against their will despite their horses' limitations. Thus,
with the Lord granting it and the patron helping, I arrived at my destination. It would take too long not only to write but even to relate from how many
tribulations and hardships he rescued me, in how many necessities his mercy stood beside me, and how many bitter trials his power restrained in me.

### 37

**[037]** What shall I say about sufferers from dysentery, among whom a remedy is found as swiftly as it is faithfully sought? I saw a woman gravely afflicted
by dysentery for five months. Whenever necessity moved her, she had to be carried in others' hands to the necessary place; by excessive evacuation she had lost
both the strengthening effect of food and the strength of her little body. At my direction she kept vigil at the basilica. When day returned after the night's
darkness, she scraped dust from the blessed tomb and drank both remedy and cup together. She returned home on her own feet, though on coming she had been
supported by others.

### 38

**[038]** What shall I relate about demoniacs and sufferers from chills? If abstinence and faith are truly joined in them, every snare is quickly removed with
the patron's help. Many sufferers from chills, shaken by the force of a severe fever, lie all day between the altar and the holy tomb; toward evening they drink
dust from the blessed sepulchre and immediately deserve to receive health. A demoniac named Paul, who was said to have a legion of demons, climbed a machine
near the holy chamber at the enemy's urging and is said to have declared, "A little vessel which I, a burned creature, inhabit." He threw himself down, but by
the blessed man's power was laid so gently on the pavement that he injured no limb of his doomed little body.

### 39

**[039]** A blind and crippled woman named Leomeria had lived wretchedly for a long time. Others' hands carried her again and again along the road leading to
the blessed basilica. At last regarded by his mercy, as she lay at the holy doorway she received both sight and the ability to walk. If only everything were
made public which individuals secretly receive when they ask faithfully, and which the conscience of many keeps hidden after health secretly sought has been
faithfully obtained! If all these things were made public, as I have said, I think not only books but the world itself could not contain them, as the evangelist
says of the Lord.

### 40

**[040]** Since this account seeks its conclusion, I shall relate one more illustrious miracle before the book ends. A young man named Securus came from his
mother's womb with a withered hand and foot; the dried structure of all his limbs had become so rigid that he looked like some monster. He was also bound under
the yoke of servitude. When his masters saw that for seven years he had been wholly unable to work, they carried him in their hands and placed him before the
blessed tomb so that he who could not be fed by his own labor might at least be fed by passersby. After he had lain there for many days, his disabled foot was
straightened; his dry hand was healed as its veins filled with blood. Receiving the blessed confessor's help, he was so formed in his whole body that you would
think he had been born anew. Count Iustinus redeemed the boy and set him free. He later received baptism and remains in health under the holy church's
protection to this day. Who could ever investigate or relate these things in such order as to praise them sufficiently? Nevertheless, I have faithfully
endeavored to write what I could discover, hoping to receive this reward: that when these things are read in praise of the most holy bishop, refreshment for my
sins may perhaps be granted to me. As the poet says: "Perhaps one day it will be pleasant to remember even these things."

HERE ENDS BOOK I.

## BOOK II

### PREFACE

**[000]** Having written down the miracles of Saint Martin which I saw or could discover from faithful men concerning earlier times, and burning greatly with
the thirst that what the Lord deigned to accomplish in praise of his bishop should not be handed over to oblivion, I also wish to relate the things I marvel at
seeing done in my own time. I leave little material to more eloquent writers but take up the mighty deeds of his miracles in my own works, so that what skill
does not spread out on pages, the multitude of miracles may extend in heaps.

### 1

**[001]** In the one hundred and seventy-second year after the death of the blessed bishop Martin, when the most glorious King Sigibert was reigning in his
twelfth year, after the death of the holy bishop Eufronius I unworthily received the burden of the episcopate—not by my own merit, since my conscience is most
foul and I am wrapped in sins, but by the gift of faithful God, who calls things that are not as though they were. In the second month after my ordination,
while I was on an estate, I contracted dysentery with a violent fever and became so ill that, with death threatening, I despaired of living in any way. The
continual operations of evacuation discharged whatever they could receive undigested, and food inspired horror. As the strength of my stomach failed from not
eating, fever alone fed my body, for no strengthening nourishment could be taken. There was also severe pain penetrating my whole bowel and descending into my
groin, consuming me with its torment no less than the fever had exhausted me. When I was so afflicted that no hope of life remained and everything was
considered in terms of funeral arrangements, and the doctor's antidote could do nothing for me whom death had taken possession of to destroy, despairing of
myself I called the chief physician Armentarius and said, "You have employed all the ingenuity of your art and tested the force of every medication, but worldly
things do nothing for one who is perishing. One thing remains for me to do. I shall show you a great antidote. Let them bring dust from the most sacred lord's
tomb and make me a drink from it. If this does not work, every refuge of escape is lost." He sent a deacon to the aforementioned tomb of the blessed daystar,
who brought some of the sacrosanct dust. They diluted it and gave it to me to drink. As soon as I drank it, all pain subsided and I received health from the
tomb. The benefit was so immediate that, though this happened at the third hour, I went healed to dinner that same day at the sixth hour. It also seemed right
to include how God rebuked me so that I would not permit foolish and thoughtless people to disparage the blessed solemnities before me. On the next day after I
recovered, I came to mass on the Lord's day and, not wishing to tire myself, ordered one of the priests to celebrate the glorious solemnities. When that priest
delivered the festive words in some rustic manner, many of my people began to ridicule him, saying, "It would have been better to keep silent than to speak so
uncouthly." The following night I saw a man saying to me, "There must be no dispute about the mysteries of God." I call God to witness that I have not invented
this; I have set before you the very words I heard. Therefore, most beloved, let no one presume to dispute about this mystery, even if it seems to be spoken
rustically, because before God's majesty pure simplicity avails more than philosophers' cleverness.

### 2

**[002]** I thought it pleasing not to omit what escaped me in the preceding book. I related that I kept with me the candles I had taken from the blessed
bishop's tomb, by which I said storms had been calmed and other illnesses driven away. My sister's husband Iustinus fell ill and, as fever grew stronger with
pain in all his limbs, began to sink gravely toward the end. A messenger brought me this news, urgently asking me to send whatever medicine I could find for the
dying man so that he would not die. Trusting in the blessed bishop's power, I sent one of the candles by a servant, saying, "Light it before him; let him pour
out prayer to the Lord while contemplating the light and implore the bishop's omnipotence to help him." The servant carried what I had given. When it was lit
before the sick man's bed, they scraped with a knife the ash of the wick already consumed by fire, diluted it with water, and gave it to the sick man to drink.
As soon as he drank, he immediately recovered his health. Restored to soundness, he later explained to me how the blessed bishop's power had helped him. He used
to relate that as soon as the beam of light proceeding from the candle struck his eyes and drove away the night's darkness, the fever immediately left his body
while he contemplated the flame. His stomach, long weakened by fasting, demanded strengthening food; and he who had been accustomed to drink only plain water to
quench the fever's burning now desired wine. The bishop's power did this, often granting help to the wretched with overflowing compassion and bestowing
medicines on the sick.

### 3

**[003]** I fear that if I presume to go too far, an increasingly rustic style will make the page contemptible. A woman named Maurusa had been gravely afflicted
by arthritic pain; her feet were twisted back toward her legs so that she could not raise herself at all. She was also deprived of the light of her eyes.
Suffering gravely for a long time, she was thought dead though still alive, and had no hope of nourishment unless someone extended a merciful hand. Every day,
watching for the regard of the devout, the feeble woman begged for necessities. Once she was suffering more severely than usual; she could not move any limb,
and only the breath of respiration moved in her chest. Now nearly lifeless, she asked to be carried to Saint Martin's feet. When faithful hands brought her
there, compelled by pain she cried out for the blessed man's help and prayed that he would have mercy on her. At last that mercy which never sends the poor away
empty looked upon her. On his festival the threads of her withered sinews were loosened; making the sign of the blessed cross to her mouth with the right hand
she had not moved for six years, she was restored to her feet and returned to her lodging without anyone's assistance, though she had not recovered her
eyesight. Two years later she came again to the blessed patron's tomb and began to pray more attentively, as was fitting. Her eyes were soon opened and she rose
into renewed light. I have written this miracle here because she received her sight after my arrival; she had previously been healed of her disability.

### 4

**[004]** A servant named Veranus belonging to our most faithful fellow priest Symon had been assigned to him as steward of entrusted provisions. While he sat
at the guard post appointed for him, gouty fluid came upon him and deprived him of the use of his feet. Tormented by such pains for a whole year so that even
the nearby neighborhood was disturbed, his sinews suddenly contracted and he became completely disabled. His master, grieving at the ruin of his faithful
household servant, ordered him carried to the blessed bishop's feet. Making a vow, he said, "If you restore him to health, most merciful lord Martin, on that
day I shall free him from the bond of my service; his hair shall be cut and he shall be assigned to your service." Placed at the feet of the most precious lord,
he lay motionless there for five days. On the sixth day he was overcome by sleep; while sleeping, he dreamed that a man was accustomed to stretch his foot on
the bed. Awakening, he rose healed of all disability. His head was tonsured, he received freedom, and he now serves the blessed lord's needs. O admirable
redemption by the blessed man! Who could ever redeem with a thousand talents as our present intercessor for crimes does? In one blow and one moment, without a
gold coin, he both frees a body from disability and releases a condition from its burden.

### 5

**[005]** A man from Auxerre named Mallulfus was carried by supporting hands and laid at blessed Martin's tomb. Devoting himself to unceasing prayer and
fasting, he suddenly received health and brought back to their customary use the feet he had displayed twisted. He was so re-formed by the saint's power that he
who had been carried by others' hands rose in sound health on his own footsteps while I watched.

### 6

**[006]** Another paralyzed man from the territory of Orléans was conveyed by wagon to the holy basilica. Lying for many days at the door near the baptistery
which opens a passage at midday, he implored the blessed bishop's help. One day as he lay there he was tormented more severely than usual, so that the neighbors
ran together at his cries. The bonds of his sinews were being loosened and straightened, which caused unbearable pain. Thus, by the patron's gift, he was raised
onto the soles of his feet and stood up weeping for joy before the people. He was immediately made a cleric and, confirmed in health, returned home.

### 7

**[007]** Another man named Leuboveus, already a cleric and disabled in walking, came dragging himself along the ground because poverty meant he had no one to
carry him. Day after day he sought blessed Martin's threshold. One day, while he was weeping outside at the saint's feet, his knees and feet were straightened
and he received health before the watching people. It is established that these three miracles occurred on the very day when the most glorious King Sigibert
crossed the Seine and made peace with his brothers without a clash of armies. No one should doubt that this too was the blessed bishop's victory.

### 8

**[008]** At that time a blind man begged alms from charitable people. He had no other means of subsistence unless someone extended a hand out of compassion,
nor any support at home except the pity of the devout. One day, while he stood with feet planted before the holy tomb, pain suddenly seized his eyes. As he was
severely afflicted by it, his eyes began to emit foam. Blood burst from his eyelids; born again into renewed light, he deserved to see the light he had long ago
lost.

### 9

**[009]** A woman from the territory of Vermandois named Gunthedrudis had lost her eyesight. Leaving home and country at the prompting of faith, she came to the
holy basilica. Serving there for many days, she deserved to recover sight in one eye. Soon forgetting husband and sons, she changed her clothing and, by the
Lord's inspiration, passed into the religious life of the church.

### 10

**[010]** Nor shall I be silent about how a flow of blood was dried at the blessed tomb as though by the garment of our Redeemer. A woman from Auvergne came
with her husband from the district of Trasalis, suffering from a hemorrhage; she lodged beside the basilica's portico. Every day she lay prostrate at the holy
confessor's threshold and begged for the help of health. One day she approached the holy tomb, praying and kissing it, and touched her ears and eyes with the
pall spread over it. Immediately the stream of blood dried and she was so healed that she thought she had touched the Redeemer's fringe. Her husband fell ill
and was laid by others' hands at the basilica door. Praying faithfully, his fever was quenched and he recovered. Thus he was healed of his affliction and she of
her hemorrhage; glorifying God, they returned together to their own home.

### 11

**[011]** Mummola, wife of the tribune Animus, was terrified by panic at night and lost the use of one foot. She had fallen into such weakness that she had to
be supported and carried by others' hands wherever she intended to go. She was laid at blessed Martin's feet and held a wax candle in her hand all night as a
votive offering while I kept vigil in the basilica. In the morning, when the signal for matins sounded, she stood on the disabled foot. All weakness was calmed,
and she returned freely to her lodging on her own feet with no one supporting her.

### 12

**[012]** Once, when the blessed Germanus, bishop of the city of Paris, was coming to the glorious bishop's festival, Ragnimod—then a deacon, now a
bishop—joined his retinue while gravely suffering from dysentery. But blessed Germanus first came to an estate of his church situated in this territory. When he
was about to arrive at Tours before the night of the vigils of Martin's solemnity, he ordered the deacon to remain at the estate, saying, "Lest you become
exhausted by traveling and something worse happen to you." Ragnimod replied, "It is God's power which commands us to suffer according to our merit. I shall not
leave except to go to the blessed bishop's basilica; for I trust that if I touch his tomb, I shall be healed." He immediately mounted a horse and came to the
basilica. In the morning he took a drink made from the tomb's dust; his illness subsided at once and he recovered.

### 13

**[013]** A blind man named Ursulfus from a district across the Loire in the city of Tours devoutly sought blessed Martin's intercession. Serving continually at
his church for two months, he persevered in fasting and prayer. On a Sunday of the Lord's resurrection, while he was at the lord's feet watching the solemnity
of mass with the rest of the people, his eyes were suddenly opened and he began to see everything clearly, so that he came to the holy altar to receive
communion without anyone leading him. I shall explain the cause of his blindness. On the first day of Easter his master ordered him to go around a field.
Finding an opening through which cattle entered, he tried to close it and was blinded. Then, as I said, he came to the blessed tomb and, weeping and wailing,
begged for the sight he had lost. On that day, while the grace of the Lord's body was being given to the people, the blessed bishop deigned to restore light to
him; as the sun shone, the stars of his own lights gleamed. Where, I ask, can such a physician be found who brings two medicines to one illness? Behold, two
miracles shown to one blind man: Martin first opened his bodily eyes to contemplate earthly things, then illuminated the eyes of his heart so that he would not
desire them; he deigned to dedicate to his own service the man whom, so to speak, he caused to be born anew into the world.

### 14

**[014]** Nor shall I keep silent about what this patron accomplished on his festival. A girl from the palace named Palatina was struck by a paralyzing fluid
and, badly afflicted, lost the use of her steps; the sinews in her knees contracted so that her heels joined her legs. Her father carried her to Tours and
devoutly laid her before blessed Martin's feet. Lying there for three months, she begged alms from passersby. On the day of the blessed man's illustrious
solemnity, while I was saying mass, she prayed faithfully in the place named above. As I duly celebrated the sacrosanct rites and related the declaration
concerning the holy lord's miracles, she suddenly began to cry out and weep, indicating that she was in torment. When the declaration was finished and all the
people cried "Holy" in praise of the Lord, immediately the sinews which had been bound were released. She stood on her feet before all the people and, by the
Lord's favor, reached the holy altar to receive communion on her own feet with no one supporting her. She remains in health to this day.

### 15

**[015]** A man named Merobaudis from the district of Poitiers was struck by a terrible blindness sent by the adversary while he was laboring at his work.
Suffering wretchedly in this affliction for six years, he came to Saint Martin's holy church. Devoting himself constantly to prayer there, on the day after the
holy festival, while he stood at Saint Martin's feet, he suddenly saw what seemed like lightning shining around him. His eyes opened immediately and he saw
everything. He was at once made a cleric in that place and departed healed.

### 16

**[016]** There was also this illustrious miracle: on the day of Epiphany, through the blessed bishop's intercession, the Lord brought forth Falernian wine from
water and drew wine from the riverbed for a poor man—he who once changed water into wine. Once while I was traveling in the district of Balbiacum, I came to the
river Loire. When I carefully asked the boatman who was to carry me to the other bank where I should proceed to fish, he indicated a place, saying, "May blessed
Martin be your help." My people received this ungratefully, saying that no catch had ever been known to occur in his name. He replied, "There is no doubt that
his power grants it. I shall tell you what happened to me this year and how, with the Lord helping through invocation of his name, I obtained what I desired. It
was the day of Epiphany. I entered my storeroom and could find nothing to drink. I went out and prayed, 'Most blessed Martin, send me some wine on this holy
solemnity, so that I do not remain fasting while others feast.' While I prayed silently, I heard a voice from the farther bank calling me to bring my boat
across for a traveler. Taking the poles and with the rowers' strokes beginning to cut the waves, I reached what seemed the middle of the river. Suddenly a great
fish, thrown from the depths, fell into the boat. I caught it at once, carried the man across, and returned home. I sold the fish for one measure of wine and
was refreshed with the others. Know therefore how quickly he will appear for whatever he is invoked, if he is asked faithfully." I call God to witness that I
learned this from the boatman's own mouth.

### 17

**[017]** One day Guntramn Boso was crossing the river Loire opposite the village of Amboise. Darkness had fallen and dreadful night held the world. Suddenly
the wind turned against them and the boatmen were thrown into confusion on the water. The boats supporting the bridge separated; filled with water to the top,
everyone sank with the boats into the deep up to their belts, though the boats were not pulled from beneath their feet. Everyone was terrified. Boso cried out
loudly for blessed Martin's help and prayed that he would hasten to deliver them, saying confidently to his companions, "Do not be afraid. I know that the holy
man's right hand is ready to extend help especially in necessities." As he spoke, God righted the boats and changed the opposing wind to a favorable one. With
no one lost, they reached the bank. The blessed confessor's intercession came so presently that they even recovered the silver they had lost to the river's
current, the river itself finally restoring it to the shore.

### 18

**[018]** A man from the territory of Vienne named Landulfus was gravely troubled by the attacks of a lunar demon. Often thinking himself surrounded by the
enemy, he fell to the ground and emitted bloody foam from his mouth, and was considered dead. Skilled physicians called this kind of disease epilepsy; rustics
called it the falling sickness because he fell. Seeing himself afflicted in this condition, Landulfus heard the fame of the blessed daystar and visited his holy
basilica so that his present intercession might help him above all. Though he came to that place full of faith, the audacity of the savage demon assailed him
more ardently. He could not leave the portico because of the public attacks of demons, though in the portico he was not harmed. They came visibly with a great
clashing of arms and tried to pierce him with the empty points of missiles. If he lay down on the ground, a horrible multitude of frogs seemed to leap upon him.
Voices were also publicly heard from him, taunting and saying, "Martin, whom you have sought, can do nothing to help you, because you are assigned to our
dominion." But he remained confidently immovable against these attacks, opposing them with the sign of the cross and terribly putting them to flight through the
soft air. After these empty and vain assaults, when the enemy saw that he could not claim Landulfus, he tried to mock him with tricks. Taking the appearance of
a veteran, he came and said, "I am Martin whom you invoke. Arise and adore before me if you wish to receive health." Landulfus replied, "If you are lord Martin,
make the sign of the cross over me and I shall believe." Hearing the name of the sign always opposed to him, the demon vanished like smoke. After this, standing
at the glorious lord's feet, Landulfus became entranced and saw the blessed basilica shining with new light. The saint came out and said to him, "Your prayer
has been heard; behold, you shall be healed of the illness from which you suffer!" Making the sign of the blessed cross over his head, Martin departed.
Returning to himself, Landulfus felt that every snare had been removed and that he had received complete health. Yet after recovering, he began to drink wine
excessively. When his body, long abstinent, became soaked with the fluid, one side with a foot and hand was contracted. He again devoted himself to abstinence
and had his head tonsured; by the blessed man's power he was once more restored to health.

### 19

**[019]** While I write each of the blessed man's miracles briefly and do not expand them in longer discourse, I pursue the journey I have begun with great awe
and fear, lest the more prudent say, "A skilled writer could have extended this greatly." But it seems to me, engaged in ecclesiastical teaching, that a history
pertaining to the church's edification should be woven in brief and simple speech, verbosity set aside, so that it may reveal the blessed bishop's power without
imposing tedium on the wise. Thus the reader may be drawn to the reading and the saint revealed in the work. The deacon Theudomeris had the passages of his eyes
gravely obstructed for four years by a fluid of the head as cataracts descended. He came to the cell at Condat where the blessed man died. Prostrating himself
at Martin's bed, he spent the whole night motionless in tears and prayers and wet the earth with weeping; his sighs warmed the venerable wood of the screen.
When day dawned, the cataracts of his eyes were opened and he deserved to see light. Have doctors with their instruments ever done anything like this? They
cause more pain than healing; distending and transfixing the eye with needles, they first produce the torments of death before opening sight. If care fails,
they prepare eternal blindness for the wretched patient. For this blessed confessor, his will is the instrument and his power alone the ointment.

### 20

**[020]** A demoniac named Desiderius came from Auvergne and raved in that cell throughout the night. In the morning he began to declare that blessed Martin was
burning him. While uttering these cries, he vomited some unknown purulent matter with blood. The demon was cast out and he was cleansed; leaving the dust
infected with corruption, he departed the cell healed.

### 21

**[021]** A man brought to the same place a disabled hand with contracted fingers. His nails were fixed into his palm, and blood sometimes flowed, causing him
extreme pain. Weeping and praying under the stimulus of both pain and faith, he threw himself at the glorious lord's aforementioned bed. The next day his
fingers straightened and he recovered his hand unharmed.

### 22

**[022]** A matron named Remigia incurred a similar illness and came very devoutly to the blessed cell. Devoting herself to vigils and prayers and feeding the
almshouse community assembled there, she lifted her withered arm with its contracted fingers, now healed, to do the mixing. Serving the blessed poor all day,
she returned home in sound health. In subsequent years she annually provided sufficient food for the brothers just mentioned. Once one of her servant girls was
severely shaken by a quartan fever. Coming according to custom and providing food for those poor people, she implored the holy man's help. For four days she lay
at the blessed cell in unbroken prayer and fasting. Healed of all fever, she returned home with her servant, glorifying God.

### 23

**[023]** A man named Vinastis performed similar works and received sight while providing the necessities of life to those poor people. Burdened by very great
blindness for many years, he had the custom of coming from his own region to the saint's aforementioned cell and providing abundant food for the poor. After
most devoutly celebrating vigils, he refreshed them to satiety, serving them like a servant according to his ability. After he had done this for many years, on
one occasion, his vow and service fulfilled, he prostrated himself at the screen of the holy bed. Praying and saying farewell, he wished to return. Rising after
prayer, his eyes opened a little and he saw a silk curtain hanging from the screen. He said, "I see what looks like a silk cloth hanging here." His people
replied, "I know that you see truly." He began again to weep and pray that the blessed confessor would graciously complete the work begun. While he prayed more
attentively, he fell asleep. A man appeared to him in a vision, saying, "Go to lord Martin's basilica, and there you will obtain complete health." Without
delay, led by his servants' hands, he touched the blessed confessor's threshold and, with faith assisting, received complete sight.

### 24

**[024]** In Berry there was a woman who conceived and bore a son whose knees were contracted toward his stomach and his heels toward his legs; his hands
adhered to his chest and his eyes were closed. He resembled some monster more than a human being. Many looked at him with derision, and his mother was
reproached for having produced such a child. She confessed with tears that he had been conceived on the Lord's night. Not daring to kill him, she nursed him
like a healthy boy, as mothers do. When he grew older, she handed him over to beggars. They took him, placed him in a wagon, and pulled him about showing him to
the people, receiving much alms through him. This continued for a long time. In the eleventh year of his age he came to blessed Martin's festival and, thrown
outside before the tomb, lay there wretchedly. After the festival he received sight and hearing. Taken back to his customary way of life, he begged for alms.
About a year or more later he came again to the solemnity and was placed where he had previously lain. When the festive rites were over, all his limbs were
straightened and he obtained the fullest health. Though these things may seem unbelievable, I saw him in sound health; I learned the story not from someone
else's report but from his own mouth. Since I have said that this happened to his parents because of sin through violating the Lord's night, beware, you men who
are joined in marriage! It is enough to devote other days to pleasure; spend this day undefiled in God's praises. When this happens, children are born crippled,
epileptic, or leprous. Let it be a lesson that an evil committed in one night may be suffered for many years.

### 25

**[025]** With your prayers I shall explain a miracle admirable above the rest. After an immense heap of grief it disclosed great joy to me: it revealed the
blessed man's power, averted what was tottering, and fortified the wavering hearts of the people with abundant firmness and stability. After I had spent the
venerable night of the Lord's nativity in sacrosanct watches and was leaving the church intending to go to the saint's basilica, one demoniac more savage than
the rest began to rave violently. Tearing and striking himself, he cried, "You seek Martin's threshold in vain; you approach his building to no purpose. He has
abandoned you because of your many sins. Behold, he abhors you and is performing wonders in Rome. He pours light into blind eyes there and straightens the steps
of the paralyzed; his power puts an end to other diseases too." At this diabolical voice all the people were thrown into confusion; not only the dull hearts of
lesser folk but I myself was shaken with fear. Entering the basilica with great weeping, I all prostrated myself on the pavement, praying to deserve the holy
man's presence. Behold, a man named Bonulfus, whose two hands and one foot had been contracted three years earlier by a fever of extreme illness, and who still
limped on a disabled foot after his hands had been straightened at the blessed man's festival, prostrated himself before the holy altar. He prayed that he who
had restored his withered hands would also straighten his contracted foot by the same power. During this prayer he was surrounded by extreme fever and tormented
with pain in his sinews as though stretched on a rack. Meanwhile pain provoked the suppliant to insolence; he who had come seeking medicine began to utter
reproach: "O lord Martin, I sought health from you, not torments. If I do not deserve it, at least let me not be afflicted with pains." While I stood around
weeping and awaiting the blessed man's arrival and the holy rites proceeded, the sacred gifts were placed on the altar and the mystery of Christ's body and
blood was covered with a pall according to custom. The contractions of his sinews relaxed; the skin behind the sick man's knee burst, a stream of blood flowed,
and he extended his foot healed. Seeing this, I thanked almighty God and, my eyes wet with tears, broke out before the people: "Let all fear depart from your
hearts, because the blessed confessor dwells with me. Do not believe the devil at all; he has never uttered anything true. He was a liar from the beginning and
has not stood in the truth." As I spoke, everyone's grief loosened into joy. The sick man himself rose before me and stood free upon his feet. All the people
saw this and, lifting a cry to heaven, rejoiced: "Glory to God in the highest, who, as he once glorified the shepherds with angelic light, so today has
glorified me with the blessed confessor's presence and shown by present power that he is with me." Thus all were rescued from fear of the enemy and strengthened
by Christ's protection.

### 26

**[026]** The blessed man appeared with no less power on the holy day of Epiphany when he opened before the people the obstructed mouth of a mute man. A cleric
of Condat named Piolus came from birth into this laborious world with closed hands, useless for work. Whether this happened because he or his parents sinned, so
that he was born maimed, is not for my judgment to resolve. One thing I know: the bishop's grace was shown to him as to other sick people. When he was ten years
old and suffered severe pains in his hands as his nails grew, unable to endure them he visited the blessed confessor's threshold. Remaining there many days in
the greatest abstinence, he brought back straightened fingers and healthy hands. About five years later he incurred a severe affliction. Worn down by violent
fever, he was deprived of spoken utterance; rescued from the fever, he remained without the faculty of speech. The passage of his mouth was so obstructed that
he could not emit even a groan. He carried in his hand three boards tied with a strap; striking them together, he produced with boards the sound he could not
make with his mouth. This device is useful to vine-dressers defending vineyards from flocks of attacking birds. The man came to the saint's basilica on the
night when the Lord Jesus Christ drew streams of water and offered Falernian wine, and resolved to keep vigil at the blessed man's feet. After midnight he fell
asleep. Seeing in a vision some unknown danger, he was terrified and first opened his closed mouth with these words: "Lord Martin, deliver me!" Blood burst from
his mouth and throat, and he received both hearing and speech.

### 27

**[027]** When King Sigibert had been killed and Chilperic, delivered from imminent death, began to reign, Ruccolenus with the men of Le Mans gravely oppressed
the city of Tours. Devastating everything, he left no hope of sustenance in the church's houses or the poor's lodgings. The next day he sent envoys to the city
demanding that the clergy drag out the men who, because of an offense not unknown to you, had taken residence in the saint's basilica. If this was delayed, he
promised that everything would be consumed by fire. Hearing this and deeply grieved, I went to the holy basilica and implored the blessed man's help.
Immediately a paralyzed woman who had been contracted for twelve years was straightened. Ruccolenus himself approached the farther bank and was at once struck
by the king's disease. Afflicted by Herodian illnesses which would take long to recount, he melted like wax dripping before a fire and died of dropsy, swollen
up, on the fiftieth day. Nor shall I be silent about this: at that time the riverbed, by God's will or the blessed man's power, filled without an inundation of
rain and prevented the enemy from crossing to harm the city.

### 28

**[028]** On the recurring solemnity when the Lord suffered for the world's salvation and, his traitorous disciple confounded, served the apostles a banquet,
everyone was hurrying to church to offer their longed-for vows to the Lord. A woman burdened by longstanding blindness was on an estate and began to weep: "Woe
to me, blinded by sins, who do not deserve to watch this festival with the rest of the people!" Prostrating herself on the ground with great weeping, she
invoked the blessed confessor's name. When her prayer was finished, she was restored to her former sight. Having received light, she came to the blessed
basilica to give thanks to God with admirable clarity of eyes. A demoniac was also cured that day by the saint's power.

### 29

**[029]** Two blind men from Berry came with dried eyelids joined together by sticky matter and lay praying at the blessed lord's feet. On his festival, while
the people stood by and miracles from his life were being read, a radiance like lightning came over them. The bonds which had sealed their eyelids were broken,
blood flowed from their eyes, and with vision opened wide they deserved to see everything.

### 30

**[030]** A woman whose gaping mouth had been bound by excessive fluid with fever could not control her tongue and could emit only a groan like an animal, not a
voice like a human being. At the prompting of faith she entered the blessed confessor's porticoes with great confidence of mind. Remaining there many days and
begging both alms and the opening of her mouth, she was at last regarded by the saint's power. On a Lord's day while mass was celebrated, she stood in the holy
basilica with the rest of the people. When the Lord's Prayer was said, she too opened her mouth and began to chant the holy prayer with the others. Though held
bound under the yoke of servitude, she was redeemed from the blessed confessor's property and now remains free with the faculty of speech.

### 31

**[031]** The blessed man showed himself present when invoked by no lesser miracle. A religious woman named Apra, overwhelmed by violent fevers, had lost all
use of her limbs except that her tongue alone still served. She lay with hands and feet contracted and begged the blessed man's help day and night. One night
she dreamed that an old man came to her and touched all her limbs with a gentle touch. Waking in the morning, she felt her feet and one hand restored to health.
Astonished, she did not know what had caused this. Admonished in sleep on another day, she set out without delay for the blessed basilica. That night was the
vigil of the confessor's death. When midnight had passed, while keeping vigil she was shaken by some terror, and suddenly her contracted hand was straightened.
While the people marveled, she recounted all she had previously suffered, recognizing that the power now shining in the straightening of her hand was the same
which had earlier raised her feet.

### 32

**[032]** Since I daily see such miracles as I have written, what will those wretched men say who declare that Severus lied in his life of the holy bishop? I
heard one man, filled I believe with a wicked spirit, assert that oil could not have increased under Martin's blessing and that a flask which slipped and fell
onto a marble pavement could not have remained unharmed. I shall therefore declare what recently happened, presenting many as witnesses. One of my deacons was
severely tormented by a quartan fever. I often reproached him for being sluggish about going to the saint's basilica and not praying from the heart so that the
bishop's power might help him. At last moved by my words, he fell trembling before the blessed tomb. When the fire of the fever had quieted a little, he asked
for a flask half full of liquid oil—he had already spent a great deal on that fever, although it had helped little—and it was half empty. He anointed his
forehead and temples with this liquid and asked that the little vessel be placed beside the blessed tomb. On the fourth day, when the fever assailed him, he
went to the basilica, fell down, and prayed for a very long time. Taking up the flask he had left half full, he found it full. Marveling at the blessed bishop's
power, he carried it home with fear and veneration. Anointed again from it, all the burning of his illness immediately subsided and he was never again afflicted
by it. I recall with a deep sigh and amazement what later happened to the same flask. It hung on the wall in the deacon's lodging when, by the enemy's
approaching malice, it was struck and fell shattered into pieces; the spilled oil was quickly absorbed by the earth. A servant present took the broken vessel,
squeezed the very earth, and extracted a little oil. Gathering the spilled liquid with the broken glass, he brought it to me. I carefully transferred it to
another vessel. The measure of oil was about half a small cup, yet it stood only two fingers high in the vessel. Looking the next day, I found the oil about
four fingers deep. Astonished at the holy liquid's power, I left it secured and covered with my seal. Looking again after seven days, I found more than a sixth
of a gallon there. Calling the deacon and showing him, he affirmed on oath that as much had then been lost in the broken flask as he now saw in this one. To
this day it bestows benefits in God's name on those who ask. The deacon himself later anointed another person suffering from the same illness with this
ointment; the oil increased, the man was healed, and he afterward restored many others to health through it.

### 33

**[033]** Let the region of Angers also produce its miracle. A man named Allomeris came from there with contracted feet and hands and a disabled tongue and
sought the blessed confessor's church. He remained there all through Lent, constantly praying and imploring the holy bishop's power to visit him. That Lord's
day before holy Easter arrived on which my Lord entered Jerusalem along roads strewn with spoil from trees, while the crowd followed crying, "Hosanna! Blessed
is he who comes in the name of the Lord." Late that day, as Allomeris lay alone outside before the tomb, he suddenly fell into ecstasy and lay terrified as
though dead. As he himself reports, after being overwhelmed for two hours or more, he suddenly returned to his senses as if waking from sleep. Lifted up, he
marveled that he was healed. Keeping vigil all night, in the morning he disclosed to me in his own words what had happened. Made a cleric, he returned healed to
his lodging.

### 34

**[034]** That same year, when the summer festival longed for by the people arrived, a cleric whose eye had been covered by a foul cloud preventing him from
seeing light visited the blessed confessor's building. After keeping vigil through the night with the others, as the sky grew light and he was leaving the
basilica, he deserved to recover the sight he had long lost. At the same festival three demoniacs struck themselves repeatedly and called upon the blessed
bishop, confessing their sins and begging the saint to spare them. At last they threw up some unknown purulent matter from their mouths and were cleansed by the
saint's power.

### 35

**[035]** Soon afterward, on the third day after the festival, four prisoners were bound in jail. The judge's cruelty constrained them so severely that no one
was permitted to provide the necessities of life. They prayed with pure hearts for the blessed bishop's protection. While they were devoutly doing this, at
midday the beam confining their enclosed feet suddenly split; their chains broke and they felt themselves freed. Without delay they went to the door. It opened,
and with no one preventing them they entered the holy church. The guards were so dumbfounded that they did not presume even to rebuke them with words; following
them, they hid themselves with the prisoners in the church. The prisoners gave greatest thanks to God because he had deigned to free them through the bishop's
intercession.

### 36

**[036]** Many people full of faith who carry the blessed man's relics experience many miracles. Leodovaldus, bishop of the city of Avranches, devoutly sought
the holy lord's relics through his priest. Having received them and entered the boundary of that city, he was met while still in a deserted place by a paralyzed
man carried by supporting hands. The man faithfully kissed the veil covering the case of holy pledges; he immediately stood on his feet and returned home on his
own. You do these things, most blessed confessor, and it is not enough for you to adorn your own building with prodigies unless you also illuminate various
remote places you never visited on foot with awe-inspiring miracles. Next a blind man hurried quickly to meet the relics, led by a support. Arriving as the
blessed pledges were being placed on the altar and the solemnity completed, he deserved to receive his eyesight. Another woman who had long been mute likewise
received the use of speech.

### 37

**[037]** In those days a demoniac came to the blessed man's basilica declaring that the demon was subjecting him to many torments and confessing that the
blessed bishop was forcibly casting it from the vessel it had acquired. Rolling on the ground, he began to eject foul-smelling blood through his mouth. After
lying there for nearly two hours, the demon was expelled and he arose cleansed.

### 38

**[038]** A little native girl of the city of Tours came from her mother's womb mute. Her mouth was so closed that she could not even make the sounds expected
from the time of the cradle. Her mother, anxious about so sad an offspring and continually grieving, was admonished in a vision to visit the blessed daystar's
tomb. Taking the girl with her, she went without fear. She laid her before the saint's tomb, prayed for a very long time, and took her up again. She lit incense
and held the girl above it, asking whether it smelled good to her. The girl answered, "Good." The sorrowing mother recognized her daughter's first word. She put
in the girl's mouth water she had once received from blessed springs and asked again what taste it had. The girl answered, "Good." The mother joyfully brought
her home healed, she whom in sadness but with trusting faith she had carried to the blessed tomb.

### 39

**[039]** A religious man named Aridius came from Limoges to Tours solely out of devotion. Kissing the blessed tomb in prayer, he crossed the river and reached
the holy monastery. Visiting each place where the blessed man had bowed in prayer or sanctified by singing psalms, where he had given sleep to his tired body or
food when failing from hunger, going around and through everything, Aridius came to the well which the holy man of God had opened by his own labor. He prayed,
drew water, put it in a little flask, and carried it home. He gave healing from it to many sick people. Once his brother Renosindus, driven by violent fevers,
lay in bed. On the eighth day he lay with eyes closed, about to breathe out his spirit; the whole household was in uproar, grieving the patron's death and
preparing funeral necessities. It occurred to the priest to put a drop of water from the blessed well into the dying man's mouth. When the drop touched his
mouth, the sick man immediately opened his eyes; his tongue was also freed and he asked for more. Taking the cup and drinking, all his fever immediately fled.
To his household's amazement, he rose healed from the bed where he had lain.

### 40

**[040]** What can my littleness recount about these miracles, when the holy man of God taken up from the world is still regarded as a preacher in the world?
Though he cannot show himself openly to the people, he continually manifests himself by miracles revealed: he gives light to the blind, heals the paralyzed, and
restores other sick people to their former health. But as I have often testified, I consider myself unworthy to set forth the signs of so great a man.
Nevertheless, because I am daring enough to dare, I ask the reader's pardon. Love for the patron drives me forcibly, and because I have declared him still a
preacher, I shall tell what recently happened. A poor man from Le Mans named Sisulfus fell asleep in his little garden at midday. Suffering some wicked attack,
he leapt from sleep and, his fingers contracted into his palms, raised his disabled hands with great pain. Overcome by pain, he again fell asleep and saw in a
vision a man standing before him in black garments with white hair. Turning to him, the man said, "Why are you so moved by tears?" Sisulfus replied, "Behold,
venerable lord, I fell asleep briefly and awoke in pain; I have lost the work of my hands, and I do not know what sin I committed." As the Lord said to his
disciples about the man born blind—that neither he nor his parents had sinned, but God's work was to be manifested in him—the man said, "Your disability reveals
the torment of a sinning people. Go now through villages and fortresses and as far as the city; preach that everyone should abstain from perjury and usury and
do no work on the Lord's day except the mystical solemnities. Behold, I shall lie in tears before the Lord, begging pardon for the people. There is still hope
of obtaining it if amendment follows among the people. The Lord's indignation causes the hostilities, illnesses, and other evils the people suffer. Therefore
announce quickly that they must amend, lest they perish cruelly in their sin. When you have done what I commanded, hasten to the basilica at Tours. Visiting you
there, I shall obtain from the Lord your healing." Sisulfus said, "Tell me, I beg you, lord, who you are and what your name is." The man replied, "I am Martin,
bishop of Tours." At these holy words the poor man awoke, took a little staff, undertook the commanded journey, and announced to the people what had been
commanded. In the seventh month after these events he visited the blessed basilica and lay prostrate for three days. On the fourth day he was visited by the
saint's power. The flesh of his closed palms had already putrefied. When his fingers were straightened, blood burst from them. All these things were healed, and
he recounted in his own words what I have related.

### 41

**[041]** You act according to your custom, most blessed confessor: you are merciful to the people's iniquities, heal everyone's diseases, and illuminate with
your medicines all who faithfully invoke you; you do not withhold from strangers what you gladly grant your own. A twenty-five-year-old inhabitant of the
territory of Tours was burdened by an inflammation of the eyes. Cataracts descended and his eyelids constricted, leaving him very blind. Added to this evil, he
was struck by a cudgel; his sight was destroyed and one eye burst. He had lived in this blindness for twenty-five years. Admonished in a vision, he came to the
blessed tomb and devoted himself to prayer. On the third day he received light in one eye. Encouraged by this cure, he began to pray more attentively. On the
fourth day the eye which had burst was re-formed and opened to sight. Though it does not see as clearly as the other, it provides the benefit of light.

### 42

**[042]** A disabled man whose contracted hand had become rigid prayed attentively in the portico before the blessed tomb. Visited on Martin's holy vigil, his
fingers straightened and his hand recovered, restored to its former use.

### 43

**[043]** How often I marvel that the miracles of the prophets and exalted men which I read were performed long ago are renewed here! What shall I say? What
many of them did while living in the world, this one man renews daily even after burial. What then am I doing? Why do I, few in number, keep silent and conceal
what many peoples proclaim? I must not linger longer at this point. I shall bring before my age a new Elisha who sent a dead corpse living from the tomb; the
blessed confessor did this while I was present. Imploring the help of the undivided Trinity, I shall explain the occasion. A newborn boy, his mother's milk
failing, was given to a nurse to rear. She was barren of this fluid and did not supply milk abundantly enough for his little age. He who should have grown began
to shrink as days passed, becoming so emaciated that only thin skin remained to cover his little bones. His mother died, and he spent nearly a year in this
condition. He was his father's only memorial of his beloved wife. As his food diminished and he failed from starvation, fever came upon him. When the burning
touched him, his father ran to church so that his offspring would not die unbaptized. The boy was baptized but received no bodily strengthening besides that
spiritual remedy. His eyes were already sunken, his eyelids loose and lowered, and he had no breath. With his father wailing, he was laid on the blessed tomb.
That heavenly power which once brought a little boy to life in the confessor's hands did not fail. As soon as his clothing touched the tomb's covering, the
child breathed again. What a miracle! You could see his pale cheeks gradually redden as divine power worked, and his sleeping eyes open in renewed light.
Brought to life by the saint and received back by his father, he remains in health today as testimony to Martin's power.

### 44

**[044]** A blind man from Poitiers deprived of light for six years prayed in prostration at the blessed tomb for three days and, through the accustomed power
at work, received the light he lacked. This happened during the holy patron's festival at which Maroveus, bishop of Poitiers, was present, rightly to be
proclaimed a disciple of the most blessed Hilary. When the solemnity ended, Maroveus joyfully returned to his own city with his fellow citizen who had received
sight.

### 45

**[045]** At the village of Vultaco in Poitou, two boys were resting in one bed on the Lord's night. They dreamed that they heard the bell usually rung for
matins. Rising from bed, they went toward the church. Reaching its portico, they found choirs of women singing there. Greatly terrified and recognizing a throng
of demons, they fell to the ground. Because of the weakness of their age they did not protect themselves with the saving sign; one was deprived of sight, the
other of both sight and walking. Burdened by these infirmities for many years, the one who had lost only sight came devoutly to blessed Martin's basilica. As
soon as he finished prayer, he immediately received sight. The other received sight in the same holy place but returned home still limping. He came to the cell
at Condat containing the blessed man's bed. While vigils were celebrated there on the Lord's night, he suddenly felt divine power present as the people prayed.
Before the watching people he dragged himself along the ground and raised himself against the wall containing the window which had once been the passage for the
blessed body. Praying and weeping for joy, he was restored to complete health and never afterward suffered any burden of evil infirmity.

### 46

**[046]** A boy named Leodulfus, disabled in his left foot, came to Tours while going around with other petitioners seeking alms. After a brief stay he tried to
complete the journey he had begun. Limping along with his companions, he was overcome by pain at the tenth milestone from the city. Abandoned by his companions,
he wailed alone on the riverbank as many hurried to the festival, crying, "Woe to me! Because I refused to watch the glorious man's solemnity, his power strikes
me. I beg you, most faithful Christians who fear God, help my ignorance, help me oppressed and disabled; if fear of God remains in you, carry me to the holy
place." As he implored many passersby, a man put him on his wagon and brought him to the holy basilica. Continuing in prayer for three days, his feet were
restored and he departed healed.

### 47

**[047]** A crippled man, resembling the hermit whose ox was once his comfort, had one ox. Joined to a wagon, it pulled him from house to house as he begged
alms from the devout. When the bishop's festival approached, he came to Tours, prostrated himself before the tomb, and most devoutly implored the blessed
bishop's help. His people carried him again and placed him before the holy apse of the tomb. When mass was finished and the people began to receive the
Redeemer's sacrosanct body, the knots binding his knees immediately loosened and he was raised to his feet. Everyone marveled. Giving thanks, he proceeded on
his own feet to the blessed altar with no one supporting him, and lived in health thereafter.

### 48

**[048]** From the district of Carnon, situated in the territory of Angers, a man named Floridus with contracted hands and feet was brought to the holy cell at
Condat from which the blessed confessor departed to Christ. Devoting a few days there to vigils and prayer, all illness fled from his body. His limbs
straightened, and he returned home healed.

### 49

**[049]** The feast day of the blessed solemnity arrived and many throngs gathered. A disabled man with a contracted arm appeared. He kissed the blessed tomb
with his lips, watered it with tears, and implored the blessed confessor's help aloud. Not doubting in faith, he awaited the accustomed help. When the bishops
who had come to perform the rites proceeded and the reader whose duty it was to read arrived, took the book, and began to read the holy confessor's life, the
man's arm immediately straightened and he rose healed before everyone, obtaining the protection he had faithfully sought.

### 50

**[050]** Likewise at the same festival a blind man prayed as a suppliant for sight. When he touched the little pall hanging on the wall outside at the saint's
feet, blood immediately burst from his eyelids and he received sight before the people.

### 51

**[051]** When dysentery with hidden pustules was wearing down many cities and Tours suffered more gravely than other places, many who scraped and drank dust
from the blessed tomb were healed. Many anointed with the oil kept there were delivered; for some the remedy was the water used to wash the tomb before Easter.
While benefits of many kinds were granted to many, I saw one man lying in despair with dysentery. Brought to the basilica, he spent a restless night while
others celebrated vigils. At dawn he approached the tomb, drank the dust with wine, and returned healed from the sepulchre.

### 52

**[052]** Another man seized by a violent fever lay in bed, vomiting poison from his mouth and excessively loose in his bowels. As the poison spread, a wound
appeared in the sufferer's groin and moved visibly in an incredible way down to the sole of his foot; it was the size of a goose egg. Returning upward with
extreme pain, it ran through his sides and arms and advanced to his neck; then it was led down the other side to his foot. Turning back, it came to the place
where it had first arisen. While it wandered thus through the sick man's limbs, the wretch did not know where to turn or what to do, but only cried out with
tears. Pain forced groans from him because so many pains rushed upon one little body. When this was reported to me, I directed that the customary antidote be
sought from the true physician and that the dying man be given something from the tomb to give him life. His attendants ran with great haste, lifted dust from
the monument, and brought it to the sick man; diluted with wine, they gave it to him to drink. When he drank, all pain fled so completely that he was restored
to health that very hour.

### 53

**[053]** Countless peoples hearing such things seek the blessed confessor's protection from distant regions. Among these it is especially admirable how he
restores human understanding stolen by the devil's art. A citizen of Bayeux, disturbed by drinking too much wine, was walking along a road when winds blowing
from different directions suddenly stirred the dust of the field. Mixed with stubble as usual, it rose on high and the whole air became one cloud of dust.
Covered by it, he lost his senses and fell from his horse. Soon found by his people, he was brought home delirious. Becoming ungovernable, he tried to flee with
no one pursuing him. What more? He was bound with ropes, heaped with chains, and kept in custody. Grinding his teeth because denied freedom to flee, he tore
himself with his own bites. While this was happening, his parents were admonished and brought him to the blessed basilica. After long prayer there he departed
healed, vowing to come every year and pay his vows to the holy confessor. Then, his hair cut at the monastery nearest him and ordained a priest, he began to
serve God energetically, but did not pay what he had promised the blessed bishop. In the fourth year, power was again given to the enemy, I believe; he fell
once more into renewed madness. Bound in chains as before, he was brought back to the holy building. Remaining there in vigils and prayers for six months or
more and paying what he had previously withheld through sloth, he returned home healed. But because of his sins, again frequently soaked with wine, he died in
the same tribulation.

### 54

**[054]** If I pursued everything that is being done or has been done, I would heap up a great pile of the confessor's wonders. Paula of Lexovia, now grown,
lost her eyesight. Devoutly visiting the saint's threshold, she lay prostrate on the ground praying throughout the festival. On the third day after the holy
festival, when her people urged her to return, she asked to be led to the blessed tomb. Prostrating herself again and again, she wiped her eyes with the pall
covering the holy tomb, said farewell, and departed. As she boarded a boat, she said, "I thank you, blessed confessor, because although I did not deserve to
see, I was present at least by touch at your holy threshold." After saying this with tears, she wiped her eyes and received sight. Turning, she asked, "Is that
the blessed basilica?" Those nearby said it was. She replied, "I shall not return until I have given thanks to the patron for the health received." Many saw her
return and proclaim the bishop's praise. When she finished praying, she departed rejoicing.

### 55

**[055]** At the same festival a boy from Sens brought a withered hand. On the fourth day of the blessed solemnity, while he stood at Martin's feet praying, his
fingers straightened before the watching people. The whole assembly saw God's mighty deeds: his hand was suffused with blood, which gradually ascended through
the dry veins. The hand was so absorbent that you would think a sponge long dry had been plunged into water and was thirstily drinking liquid. His veins filled,
his sinews strengthened, and his skin reddened; he raised his formerly pale hand healed.

### 56

**[056]** In a similar sequence a woman of Poitiers deserved to obtain healing. Her fingers were contracted into her palm, the nails fixed into the very bones,
so to speak, and her whole hand had putrefied. She came devoutly to the saint's festival seeking the longed-for cure. After the customary solemnities were
awaited, she told her people, "I came with an undivided heart to ask the blessed man's protection, but my sins stood in the way and I did not deserve to receive
what I sought. Now that prayer is complete, let us return to our country, trusting in the daystar's goodness that faithful prayer will benefit the soul while
the body is weak." Saying this and similar things as though bidding the saint farewell, she departed. As the day turned toward evening, she took lodging near
the bank of the river Caris. Awaking near midnight, she thanked God for her existence, life, strength, and for having touched the blessed bishop's tomb. After
saying this with great weeping, she fell asleep again. Behold, a man with swan-white hair and a purple garment stood before her holding a cross and said, "Now
you shall be healed in the name of Christ our Redeemer." Taking her hand, he put his finger between her fingers which had closed her palm and, moving it a
little, straightened them. Seeing this in a vision, she awoke and, blood still flowing, raised her hand healed in praise of God. Returning to the basilica, she
completed her thanksgiving and went back rejoicing.

### 57

**[057]** On the festival of blessed John, while the people gathered for mass, a woman took a hoe and went into a field, intending to clear the crop by herself
of tares pulled up among the good seed. She could not be surrounded by assistance because of reverence for the Lord's precursor. As soon as she began working,
her hands were seized by divine fire; her whole face, seeming to emit flames, broke out in blisters and pustules. The wretched woman burned no less from the
pain of shame than of body, since she unwillingly revealed what she had secretly done. Crying and wailing, she quickly sought blessed Martin's basilica.
Prostrated before his tomb in this torment for four months, all the burning was quenched and she was restored to bodily integrity. She was the maidservant of a
man of Tours who, granting half her price, sought another.

### 58

**[058]** A boy of Paris whose trade was making clothes became a quartan fever patient as melancholy—that is, the dregs of cooked blood—increased. As the fluid
seethed, his whole body was covered with tiny pustules so that some thought him a leper. He endured terrible pains throughout his limbs and was deprived of
sight in both eyes. Hearing the blessed bishop's fame and his miracles reported everywhere, he sought the city of Tours. Coming to the saint's basilica, he
fasted and prayed for many days. Receiving sight, he was restored to his former health. He was freeborn. When Leodastis, then governing the county of Tours,
heard that he was such a craftsman, he began to harass him, saying, "You are a runaway from your masters and shall no longer be allowed to wander about." He
sent him bound to his house for custody. But even there the angelic confessor's power did not fail. As soon as the boy was seized, he was afflicted by the
illness from which he had been freed. When he became gravely ill, the count saw that he could gain nothing over him, released him from bonds, and ordered him to
depart freely. Returning to the basilica, the boy was healed again.

### 59

**[059]** Similar is the case of a woman who, after obtaining freedom, was sold again by the patron's barbarian sons. By the saint's power, so that she might
more easily be defended, all her limbs were contracted and disabled. The sinews of her knees were twisted so that her calves touched her thighs. Abandoned by
the masters to whom she had been unjustly sold, she sought the blessed confessor's protection. After remaining at his building for only a short time, she was
granted both liberty and health.

### 60

**[060]** Because the former little book began where Paulinus left off and was completed in forty chapters, I resolved to complete this one I began in sixty.
Blessed Martin, who, though bereaved of this world, preserved the intact glory of virginity and triumphantly fulfilled martyrdom in hidden snares and public
injuries, and who bears the crown of thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit, was to be magnified in these one hundred miracles. I hoped not to be
disappointed in the vow which I completed in eight years at the Lord's command. Having begun with the miracle performed upon myself, I have returned to myself
again. I think this happened by divine providence, so that the book should end with him with whom it is read to have begun. When I had described fifty-nine
miracles and was still attentively awaiting the sixtieth, the left temple of my head was suddenly seized by pains. My veins throbbed, tears flowed, and such
torment threatened that I pressed my eye forcibly to keep it from bursting. After suffering this severely for a day and night, I came to the saint's basilica in
the morning and prostrated myself in prayer. When finished, I touched the place of pain with the veil hanging before the blessed tomb. At that touch the
throbbing of veins and flow of tears immediately stopped. Three days later a similar pain struck the right side of my head. My veins throbbed and tears flowed
abundantly. Rising again in the morning, I touched my head to the veil as before and departed healed. After ten days I decided to have blood let. On the third
day after the bloodletting, a thought entered me—injected, I believe, by the adversary—that what I had suffered had come from blood and would immediately have
ceased if a vein had been cut at once. While I considered and turned this over, the veins of both temples leapt out. The former pain returned and now seized not
one side but my whole head. Moved by the pains, I hurried to the basilica. Begging pardon for the wicked thought, I touched my head to the pall covering the
blessed tomb. The pain immediately subsided and I left the tomb healed. There are many other things the blessed man does daily which would take long to pursue.
If I still deserve to see miracles, I intend to join them to another little book. As I said, let these two books remain at this number. I also give greatest
thanks to the Lord's goodness because through the glorious bishop's intercession I was granted the ability to bring to completion what I undertook at the
beginning. I pray that the generous confessor who often gives to the people will grant me, a sinner, that he cleanse me from the diseases he often looks upon
and considers, restore to me the light of truth, rescue me from the fall of unfaithfulness, cleanse my heart and mind of the foul leprosy of luxury, purge my
thoughts of evil desires, and wash away and cast down the whole mass of my misdeeds. When I am placed on the left in judgment, may he deign to draw me from
among the goats with his sacrosanct right hand and, holding me behind his back, await the judge's sentence. When at that judgment I am assigned to hell's
flames, may he cover me with the sacrosanct cloak with which he is covered by glory and excuse me from punishment. May the angels say to the King what they once
said of the monk raised from the dead: "This is he for whom Martin prays." Since I do not deserve to be clothed in that brightness, may I at least deserve to be
freed from the attacking ministers of hell. May guilt not prevail so far over me that I am separated from the kingdom of him whom I have faithfully confessed in
the world.

HERE ENDS BOOK II.

## BOOK III

### PREFACE

**[000]** Beginning by Christ's ordinance to write a third little book about blessed Martin's miracles, I thank almighty God, who deigned to grant me such a
physician to purge my illnesses, wash my wounds, and provide health-giving medicines. At his blessed tomb the mind is humbled and prayer exalted. If tears flow
and true compunction follows, if sighs are sent from the depths of the heart and sinful breasts are beaten, weeping finds joy, guilt pardon, and pain of heart
reaches healing. The touch of the blessed sepulchre has often commanded discharges to stop, the blind to see, the paralyzed to rise, and even bitterness of
heart to depart far away. Having often experienced this myself, I judge myself unworthy to insert here among such masses of miracles what he deigned to work
upon me. Yet I fear appearing guilty if I fraudulently hide them. I call God and the hope I have placed in his power to witness, trusting that his mercy will
not disappoint me. Whenever pain has struck my head, throbbing has beaten my temples, heaviness has burdened my hearing, darkness has covered the sharpness of
my eyes, or pain has settled in other limbs, as soon as I touched the painful place to the tomb or hanging veil, I immediately received health, silently
marveling that pain departed with speed at the very touch.

### 1

**[001]** I shall insert first in this little book a miracle I recently experienced. While I sat at dinner eating after a fast, a fish was brought in a dish. I
made the Lord's cross over it and ate, but one of its bones adhered most injuriously in my throat. Causing severe pains, it cut my throat with its point and
obstructed my gullet along its length. It impeded the sound of my voice and did not allow even saliva, which often flows from the palate, to pass. On the third
day, when neither coughing nor spitting could expel it, I took refuge in my accustomed protection. I approached the tomb, fell on the pavement, and with
groaning and abundant tears implored the confessor's help. Rising, I touched my gullet, throat, and the rest of my head to the hanging veil. Without delay I
received health; before I left the holy threshold, I felt no fatigue. What became of the evil little bone I do not know. I did not expel it by vomiting or feel
it pass into my bowel. I know only that I felt healed so quickly that I thought someone had put in a hand and removed what had injured my throat.

### 2

**[002]** A twelve-year-old girl disabled in every limb lay in bed at her parents' home for six years as if dead, not walking, not working with her hands, not
seeing light, not speaking, and not hearing speech. Her parents poured out prayers for their daughter at the blessed tomb, offered gifts, and made further vows.
The people assembled for the rites and the holy festival was celebrated joyfully. On the third day of the festival the girl called her father, saying, "I am
thirsty." Rejoicing that he had deserved to hear his daughter's voice, which he had never heard, he ran quickly and brought her a little water to drink. When
she drank, she said, "Give me your hand." Her father took her right hand and lifted her. Standing on her feet and raising hands and eyes to heaven, she said, "I
