thank you, almighty God, who, regarding my humility, have deigned to save me through your holy bishop." Her limbs were restored, she received sight and hearing,
and returned home rejoicing.

### 3

**[003]** Two years before these events, a man neither fearing nor honoring the holy day of the Lord's resurrection took grain and went to a mill. He put in
wheat and began to turn the mill by hand. When the work was done, he could not open his palm; with severe pain he unwillingly held the handle he had grasped.
Seeing that he was not released, he cut away the handle on both sides and came to the saint's basilica. After prayer and vigils, his fingers were loosened and
his hand restored to its former use. In another year he undertook on this holy day the same work for which God had previously rebuked him, and the wood again
adhered to his hand. Weeping in pain, he returned to the saint's basilica but did not immediately deserve to be heard. Two years later, at the same festival
where I related that the girl was healed, he too was freed from the burden of the wood.

### 4

**[004]** A crippled man from Limoges who could neither walk nor see was carried by devout hands and laid before the holy sepulchre. He implored the blessed
bishop's mercy; his weak limbs were straightened and he was granted health.

### 5

**[005]** A blind man who had long lacked eyesight came to the same festival. After praying, while he stood before the holy sepulchre, his eyes suddenly opened
and he rejoiced at receiving light.

### 6

**[006]** A boy native to Tours was consumed by a severe and lengthy illness. All his limbs were disabled and fever left him without hope of walking; his
twisted shins could not be separated, like ropes. After the fever departed, he asked his parents to carry him to the holy basilica. When he was brought, they
laid him at the saint's feet and prayed that the accustomed power would help him. On the third day, while he and his parents persevered in prayer and fasting,
the light of mercy arose; his twisted shins were corrected and his parents received him back healed.

### 7

**[007]** Another man named Senator from Cracatonnus, a village of Angers, was making a key on the Lord's day when the fingers of both hands contracted. His
nails fixed into his palms, he who had wished to open a door could not open his hands. After four months his nails were embedded in the flesh and his palms
putrefied. He sought the confessor's help. Devoting four days to prayer and fasting, he raised his hands healed and returned in sound health, praising the
bishop's power and preaching that no one should undertake what he had presumed to do.

### 8

**[008]** While these things were happening at Tours, envoys from Spain, Florentius and Exsuperius, came to King Chilperic. I received them at the church's
banquet. As I dined, because they declared themselves catholics, Florentius, the elder, earnestly asked to learn something about the blessed man's power.
Thanking God, I asked whether even Martin's name was heard in those regions or his life read by anyone. Florentius replied that his name was magnificently
honored there. He also said he was a special nursling of the bishop and that great power had been shown upon himself. "His grandfather," he said, "many years
ago built a basilica in honor of the blessed bishop Martin. When it was completed and elegantly decorated, he sent religious clergy to Tours seeking the
bishop's relics, so that he might consecrate with Martin's relics the place he had built in his name. After doing so, he came every day and prostrated himself
on the ground with his wife, imploring the holy bishop's help. Much later this child was born. At three months old he was assailed by fever and so weakened that
he could not suck the breast or take any nourishment. As the disease continued and food was refused, only his breath fluttered and death alone was awaited. Soon
he breathed out his spirit. His grieving mother and grandmother took in their arms the little lifeless body of their only firstborn offspring and laid it before
blessed Martin's altar with hope not uncertain. As if they saw the saint with physical eyes, the grandfather addressed him: 'I had the greatest hope, most
blessed confessor, of bringing your pledges here so that diseases would be driven away, fevers extinguished, darkness scattered, and other illnesses cleansed,
because very many things are read about what you did while alive and accomplish after death. I have heard that by prayer you raised the dead, drove away leprosy
with a kiss, cured demoniacs with a word, stopped poison with a finger, and did many other things. Your power will appear here if now, according to my faith,
you raise this little child. If you do not, I shall no longer bend my necks here, light a lamp, or show any honor.' Saying this, they left the infant before the
altar and departed. Coming in the morning, they found him turned toward the altar. Marveling, his mother took him in her arms. Recognizing that he had resumed
breathing, she put him to her breast; he immediately sucked milk and was strengthened. Then his mother, father, and whole household raised their voices to
heaven and blessed God: 'Now I know that you are a great God and alone do wonders, restoring my little child through your confessor's prayer.' They showed
greater reverence to that place than before." I learned from Florentius's own mouth that these things happened.

### 9

**[009]** There was a cleric from an estate near Poitiers belonging to the holy basilica, disabled in the use of one foot which, as he declared, he had lost
through an attack of the noonday demon. He cut a stick to the length of his knee, put leather on top, and stretched his knee backward on it; with the stick
supporting him, he accomplished the walking he could not do with his foot. Nine years later he came to the basilica and prayed for three days. Before the third
day of the festival his knee straightened and he rose. He explained to the people arriving for the saint's rites how he had been healed by Martin's power.

### 10

**[010]** The saint's power helped my mother in this way. After she had given birth and the pains of labor were over, she incurred pain in a muscle of one shin.
It was sudden, as if a nail were being driven in, causing such a heavy piercing that it often produced fainting. Nothing could ease it unless the shin was held
before a fire for a very long time and became numb from the hearth's heat; it also quieted if a little ointment was poured on. What more? After my ordination
she came to Tours both to meet the holy bishop and from desire to see me. Remaining there two or three months, she continually implored the blessed bishop's
help. At last his accustomed compassion looked upon her: the pain departed from the shin which had troubled the woman for thirty-four years.

### 11

**[011]** Another woman from the territory of Angers had her fingers fixed into her palm. When she poured out prayers at the holy place, her fingers
straightened and she departed with her hand healed.

### 12

**[012]** A servant of my household was seized by fever and gravely burned. His limbs burned outwardly and a powerful thirst burned within. If he took any
drink, he immediately vomited it from his stomach, and he took no food. When he was exhausted by this suffering on the fourth or fifth day, he asked to be given
a little dust from the sepulchre to drink. It was brought and diluted with wine. Drinking faithfully, he received health and recovered.

### 13

**[013]** Theoda, daughter of the former priest Wiliacharius, frequently suffered from fluid in her feet and lost the use of one foot which had become disabled.
She came to the blessed basilica and poured out frequent prayers. Her disability was removed and she was granted sound health.

### 14

**[014]** At that time a man lived on an estate under the protection of the saint's almshouse who walked bent over as if his kidneys were broken. Like the woman
in the Gospel account, he leaned forward and could not raise himself upward. With two sticks placed under his armpits, he walked bent over. He came to the
festival and on the third day after the rites was raised up. Cleansed of every diabolical assault, he departed healed.

### 15

**[015]** Gundulfus, a citizen of Tours, lived from childhood with Guntharius, King Chlothar's son. While in Guntharius's service, he climbed a tree at the
king's command to pick ripe apples. A branch broke and he fell; striking his foot against a stone, he was disabled. Many years later, while still disabled, he
mounted a horse and urged it quickly forward. His step slipped and he was thrown; his other foot, previously healthy, was crushed and gravely injured. He asked
to be carried to the blessed basilica. Thrown onto the pavement, he faithfully poured out prayer. The mercy which always helps the afflicted did not delay: all
pain was immediately removed and he rose healed from the pavement. For about thirty years, as I said, he had continually limped on the other foot. At last,
examining the offenses of his own conscience, he resolved to convert by cutting his hair and serving the holy bishop himself. First he obtained a command from
the king to transfer all his property to the basilica while alive. When this was done and his head tonsured, fulfilling his vow of good resolve, his foot,
shortened by broken bones, was lengthened. He who had formerly walked supported by two servants now runs wherever he wishes without anyone's help or any
impediment of disability.

### 16

**[016]** Afterward a blind boy from Limoges received his eyesight in this way. In the third year after his birth, as he was beginning to walk and his tongue
was breaking into words, he played lovingly with his mother, kissed her, hung on her neck, and was carried in her arms. A force of wind stirred by a diabolical
assault lifted dust and chaff from the ground and carried it in a great whirlwind over the boy and his mother. The rustic and incautious woman did not protect
herself and her son with the saving banner; the snare prevailed and the child's eyes were filled with dust and sealed. He cried out for a long time and, though
at last soothed by his mother, remained blind. When grown he was handed over to beggars so that by walking with them he might receive some alms. His parents
were very poor. In the twelfth year of his blindness he came to Tours before the solemnity when the Father joined the Word to flesh and brought salvation into
the world. When the festival vigil had passed and the others withdrew, he lay motionless at the saint's feet. He felt as if someone had pricked his eyes with a
needle; blood immediately burst from them and flowed down his cheeks. Turning his face upward, he saw a candle shining above him. Crying aloud, he said, "I
thank you, holy confessor of God, because by your power I have deserved to receive light." O admirable grace! O immense power! You scatter your gifts among the
peoples with many kinds of affection. He who sought alms received light; long without external light, his face is adorned with the light of your power. If the
darkness of many sins did not keep you from my sight, surely you would come visibly and cry to the sick in Peter's words: "Gold and silver I do not have, but
what I have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ, depart healed."

### 17

**[017]** I had occasion to visit the town of Reims and was kindly received by Bishop Egidius, then governing the church. As the Lord's day dawned the next
morning, I went to church and sat in the sanctuary awaiting the bishop's arrival. At that time I carried Saint Martin's relics on me, though in a rash manner.
Siggo, formerly King Sigibert's referendary, came to meet me. I kissed him and asked him to sit beside me. One of his ears was blocked and he could barely hear
what I said with the other. After sufficient conversation, he was called into the church house. As soon as he left me, the barriers of his deaf ear broke open;
feeling as if a great wind had gone out of it, he recovered his hearing. Returning at once, he began to thank me, saying, "This is the third day since I lost
hearing in this ear, but while speaking with you I felt it quickly opened." Confused lest this be attributed to me, I said, "Do not give thanks to me, sweetest
son, but to him whose power restored your hearing. Know that I carry blessed Martin's pledges with me; his might has driven away the heaviness of your hearing."

### 18

**[018]** Once a savage plague raged so severely among cattle that none were expected to survive to restore the breed. One of my people went to the holy
basilica and received in a little vessel oil from the lamps hanging in the chamber together with their water. Carrying it home, he dipped his finger in the
liquid and marked with the Lord's cross the foreheads and backs of cattle not yet touched by the disease. Full of faith, he threw the animals to the ground on
their backs and poured some of this ointment into their mouths. Quicker than speech, the hidden plague was driven away and the cattle delivered.

### 19

**[019]** An inhabitant of Avranches, denied the use of sight for six years, sought to be saved by the blessed confessor's protection. Coming to his basilica
and devoting much time to fasting and prayer, he implored the blessed bishop's help. When the sacrosanct festival arrived and the people watched the solemnity
of mass, his sight was restored. He returned to his country seeing, though another had led him to the holy basilica. In joy at such mercy he vowed to be
tonsured there, a vow he later devoutly fulfilled on returning.

### 20

**[020]** A man from overseas was working in a field when a violent wind with dust suddenly arose over him and he lost his eyesight. He who had long been a
guide for the blind was himself led home by another. He remained in this blindness for three years. Afterward he sought the blessed confessor's basilica.
Devoting himself to prayer there for four years, he was visited by divine power; his eyes opened and he deserved to see light.

### 21

**[021]** As I have often said, this fame spread not only through his own city but also in other cities and almost throughout the world. A man named Julian came
from Spain and devoutly brought his disabled hands and feet to this physician, saying, "I believe, most holy bishop, that you can provide me the assistance of
healing which you are not accustomed to deny to others who hope in you." Constantly attending prayer in this belief and not doubting the Lord's mercy, his feet
and hands were straightened and he was restored to health.

### 22

**[022]** Since I have often said in earlier books that miracles are frequently celebrated in the place from which he departed to heaven, I shall reveal what
recently happened. A native of Tours, deprived of clarity of sight, sought the cell at Condat containing the blessed bishop's bed, thinking she would have
protection if she touched the screen of that bed. It is called a bed only because he lay on that pavement with ashes spread beneath and a stone placed at his
head, the Israel of my time, his neck bowed. The woman was led to this shrine by her husband and, moved with compunction, poured out prayer there for many days.
At last the mercy so often poured out in pity looked upon her and restored her lost sight. Faith so inflamed her that she never left the place until the day of
her death.

### 23

**[023]** An inhabitant of Angers whose limbs were disordered by disease turned his head toward the bed. As fever increased daily and every skill failed, he was
deprived of hearing and speech. After a few days he recovered from the fever but remained voiceless. His brothers took away his share of the property and threw
him from his father's house, saying, "He has become mad. God forbid that he should share our property or acquire part of the inheritance." They were freeborn
and occupied their own possession; thinking nothing of what belonged to God, they cast out the mute and deaf man whom they ought rather to have cherished.
Though without those faculties, he retained understanding in his heart. Taking boards in his hand and striking them together, he imitated the voice of one
asking. With this device he came to the village mentioned above and joined others begging alms. Six years had passed since this poor man began feeding on the
riches of the holy cell. On a Sunday night, while lying at his host's house, the place was suddenly filled with immense light. Terrified, he fell prostrate.
Immediately he saw a man adorned in priestly dress touch him and place Christ's cross on his forehead, saying, "The Lord has healed you. Arise, hasten to
church, and thank your God." Raising his voice in thanksgiving, he filled the neighborhood with cries. Everyone ran to the sight and marveled at hearing speak
the man they had seen mute the day before. The bell was rung for matins, the people assembled, vigils were celebrated, and the saint's glorified power was
revealed. In those days two demoniacs were cleansed in that place when the demons were cast out.

### 24

**[024]** But let us return to Aridius, or rather, so to speak, the blessed confessor's special nursling, to whom Martin often grants the sight of miracles
through his pledges. Aridius came to the saint's festival with his customary kindness, humility, and charity. Returning, he carried a little flask full of oil
from the holy sepulchre, saying, "Perhaps there is some sick person on the road who, moved in heart, desires to receive a blessing from blessed Martin's
building." In one place a devout woman approached with another flask of oil, saying, "I beg you, servant of Christ, sanctify this oil with your blessing." Lest
he seem given to vanity, he said, "My power is small; but if you wish, I have oil from blessed Martin's sepulchre with which this oil may be filled. If you
believe his power is great, you will draw health from it." Rejoicing, she asked him to do as the priest said. Her vessel was half empty. When the liquid taken
from the saint's basilica was poured in, the oil immediately bubbled and filled the flask to the top. Seeing this and marveling at the blessed confessor's
power, the matron returned home rejoicing.

### 25

**[025]** Another woman whose fingers were contracted and fixed into her palm sought the basilica of the blessed bishop Martin. After a few days of pouring out
prayer and imploring the saint's help, her fingers straightened and she received her hand unharmed.

### 26

**[026]** Before these years a girl fell into a severe illness and all her limbs were contracted with disability. Hearing of the miracles the glorious bishop
performs in individuals, she devoutly invoked his name. A few days later she asked to be carried to his basilica. Lying in its portico for many days and
frequently pouring out tearful prayer, she was visited by the bishop's power. Divine mercy helped her and she departed healed.

### 27

**[027]** A boy from the territory of Angers, while staying at his parents' house, lost the use of his hands and feet through an assault of diabolical art, as
he declared. His fingers contracted inward and his nails were fixed into his palms; the sinews of his knees withered and drew his heels toward his thighs.
Carried wretchedly by his parents for six years, he was brought to the holy bishop's church. Persevering in prayer, his limbs were restored and, in accordance
with his name, Floridus flourished as if new.

### 28

**[028]** A cleric, by birth a servant of the holy basilica itself, was deprived of sight by the adversary's attack. Unable to work, he remained sick in his own
lodging. After enduring this blindness for nearly three years, he sought the blessed bishop's building. Imploring his accustomed mercy, he returned home with
sight restored.

### 29

**[029]** A servant from the territory of Tours was making a hedge on the Lord's day when his hands began to adhere to the wood. He quickly pulled out his right
hand; while astonished and wondering what had happened, that hand contracted with great pain and its nails were fixed into the palm. With all the fingers of his
right hand contracted, he returned grieving to his lodging. Four years later he came to the saint's basilica and was healed after prayer. He preached to the
people that no one should consider doing the deed, lest a greedy farmer stain the solemnity of so great a day and weak humanity, performing earthly works,
dissolve the heavenly mystery of my sacred redemption and restoration.

### 30

**[030]** A boy from Albi, his stomach wasting away with various diseases, shrank from food and drink. Tormented by this suffering for many days, he vomited
with severe bitterness even what he seemed able to take. Full of faith, he desired to come to the blessed confessor's basilica. Fasting and praying there for
three days, on the fourth day he conceived a desire to take food. Tasting wine, he was strengthened. Giving thanks, he departed healed.

### 31

**[031]** A woman, also said to come from Angers, was withered in all her limbs but especially carried her right hand and fingers more withered than the rest.
She prostrated herself at the saint's tomb. After leaving, she remained briefly in the portico. Through the glorious bishop's intercession coming to her aid,
her veins received blood, her skin strength, and the rest of her body vigor, and she was restored. The cause of her suffering was that after sunset on the
Sabbath, adjoining the Lord's night, she had wished to shape bread.

### 32

**[032]** Another woman suffered similarly: her hands contracted inward and, joined together, adhered to each other. Tormented by the greatest pains, she set
out, saying, "If I go to Saint Martin's basilica, this illness will immediately depart. I trust that he who has often had mercy on those suffering such things
will help me too." While she spoke and pursued the journey she had begun as best she could, her hands separated, though her fingers did not straighten. When she
reached the holy place and prayed, all pain was immediately removed, her fingers straightened, and she raised her freed hands in thanksgiving.

### 33

**[033]** This year a serious disease of horses appeared in the region of Bordeaux. At the estate of Marciacum in that territory, subject to blessed Martin's
lordship, there is an oratory consecrated in his name and power. When the calamity arrived, people came to the oratory making vows for their horses: if they
escaped, the owners would give tithes to the place. When this cause benefited them, they added the practice of marking the horses with impressions from the iron
key which unlocked the oratory door. The saint's power so prevailed that both horses already sick were healed and those not yet infected suffered nothing
further.

### 34

**[034]** The previous year the people of Tours were most gravely devastated by an epidemic. The illness was such that a person seized by violent fever became
covered with blisters and tiny pustules. The blisters were white and hard, without softness, causing only extreme pain. When they matured, burst, and began to
discharge, clothing adhered to the body and the pain increased more strongly. In this sickness the physicians' art could do nothing unless the Lord's help
arrived. Many seeking a blessing from the holy basilica obtained help. But why must I mention many, when the rest obtained what I saw one woman obtain? The wife
of Count Eborinus was held by this plague and so covered with blisters that neither hands nor soles nor any part of her body remained free; even her eyes were
covered and obstructed. When she was in danger of death, she sought a blessing from the saint's sepulchre. Some of the water used to wash the blessed tomb at
the Lord's Easter was sent to her. Her wounds were moistened with it and she was able to drink from it. The fever was soon quenched, the blisters discharged
without pain, and she was healed.

### 35

**[035]** Since the whole world experiences many miracles of which, I think, not the smallest part reaches me, I report what the neighborhood experiences.
Badegyselus, bishop of Le Mans, was invited to a place in his diocese to consecrate a basilica in the blessed man's name and with his relics. When the rites
were celebrated and Saint Martin's name invoked, two paralyzed people received the ability to walk and one blind person received sight.

### 36

**[036]** A citizen of Tours named Agustus suffered from extreme pain in his kidneys. His feet contracted and his kidneys were drawn nearly down to them,
leaving him severely disabled. He suffered this illness for two years. Admonished by his people, he sought the saint's basilica. Fasting and praying there for
seven days, his pain was removed, his feet straightened, and he departed healed.

### 37

**[037]** At that time a woman remained alone at the loom when her companions left. A most foul shadow appeared to her as she sat and, seizing the girl, began
to drag her. She cried out and lamented; seeing no help, she nevertheless tried to resist bravely. After two or three hours the other women returned and found
her lying half-alive on the ground, wholly unable to speak. She gestured with her hand, but since they understood nothing she remained mute. The shadow which
had appeared to her laid such snares for the people of that house that they left and moved elsewhere. After two or three months the girl came to the basilica
and deserved to recover speech. She recounted in her own words everything she had suffered.

### 38

**[038]** A deacon of Châlons, following the custom of his people, drank while others celebrated the morning thanksgiving. He was deprived of his eyesight.
Recognizing his guilt and that he had done something unworthy of his calling, he abstained from food and drink, spending nights in vigils and attending prayer.
Meanwhile the fame embracing the whole wide world reached his ears: Bishop Martin was at Tours, and at his tomb the destruction of such illnesses had often been
driven away and stilled. The deacon did not delay. Ordering a journey prepared, he came to the holy basilica with no doubt about the blessed man's power.
Prostrating himself on the ground and devoting himself to prayer, on the third day his eyes opened and he received light. Seeking carefully to elicit the truth
about why this had happened, I learned from him: "Seven months ago, when the morning bell sounded and I was going to church, I met one of my friends. Rushing to
embrace and kiss him, I asked whether he had left everything at home prosperous. Called back from the road, I began to drink with him. When I seemed to have
fulfilled friendship with cups, I said farewell and departed. As he left, my eyes adhered with eyelids joined by such sticky matter that I could not open them.
Going away sad in this illness, I desired to visit the blessed bishop's tomb. On the third day after arriving, as I stood at his sepulchre, a great fever
suddenly seized my eyes. I began to groan violently and implore the saint's help strongly. Blood immediately burst from my eyes, drove away night, and brought
back day." After saying this, the deacon returned home healed.

### 39

**[039]** A blind woman with hands and feet contracted backward sought with her parents' assistance to celebrate the glorious bishop's blessed festival. On the
third day after the festival, wishing to return home, she prostrated herself in the holy basilica and prayed that the Lord would deign to show her the customary
help of his mercy. As she asked with tears, her hands and feet were immediately straightened and made firm. Brought to the holy sepulchre, she gave thanks for
the health received. She then asked to be led to the door, where she prostrated herself again and told her people, "I shall not rise from here until he who
restored the use of my feet and hands first restores the light of my eyes." As she spoke, demoniacs suddenly cried out that they were being tormented and
confessed Martin's presence. But because the devil, a liar from the beginning, was not to be believed, the man's presence was declared by the facts themselves:
the woman who had just been straightened was now given sight, proving that the blessed bishop was present.

### 40

**[040]** A little later a paralyzed man lay on a cot; he had come from Berry conveyed by wagon. Visited in the same way by the blessed bishop's power, he rose
healed. Restored to his own steps, he was received in health by the watching crowd of relatives.

### 41

**[041]** In those days a girl born of freed parents was condemned by the patron's sons to the yoke of servitude, her liberty broken. Because she refused to
perform any work for her unjust masters, she was bound with chains and fetters. While others sought the blessed festival, she remained in custody, weeping and
wailing because she could not attend. Suddenly the beam confining her feet split. As though already free, though still bound with chains, she slipped away and
sought the blessed basilica. As soon as her feet touched the sacred threshold, the chains broke and fell from her neck. She was granted both health and liberty.

### 42

**[042]** What if I return to the writings of his blessed life? Is it not admirable that the sacred book of this history, surrounded by flames, was neither
consumed nor burned? A monk of Marmoutier went by his abbot's command to another cell to perform some work and took with him the book of the blessed bishop's
life for his soul's salvation and correction of life. When night came, he lay on a bed filled with straw accumulated over a long time and placed the book at his
head. While he slept, a man appeared in a dream saying, "Do not sleep in this straw, for it is sprinkled with blood." I believe, as mortality happens, that some
crime had been committed there and that the blessed man would not allow words of his praise to be turned over in it. The first vision seemed trivial to the man
and the second admonition did not prevail; the third shook the monk terribly. He arose and went out to work at dawn, ordering a servant to remove the straw from
the bed and burn it, saying nothing about the book. The ignorant servant found it among the straw, threw it outside, and lit the fire. When the straw was
reduced to embers and only ashes remained, the book appeared unharmed; neither its sides nor a single leaf, in truth, had been consumed. Divine power deigned to
guard the praises of its own nursling so that flame did not burn the book of him whom the fire of lust did not burn in this world. Lest anyone find it
incredible, that very codex is kept with me today.

### 43

**[043]** Once while I was traveling, two servants guarding the horses became sick, one with illness and the other with dysentery. Violent fever held them both,
and they were so exhausted that they could not be supported even when placed on horses' backs. I took out dust from the saint's sepulchre which I had carried
away in a little case, diluted it with water, and ordered them to drink. Fever and pain were immediately suppressed and both recovered.

### 44

**[044]** Glorious are the miracles the Lord deigns to work daily in his bishop's praise. As I have often testified, my unskilled self cannot recount them, but
as that lack of skill permits they shall be studied out lest eyes seem to see nothing. A citizen of Tours named Malulfus, seized by a savage illness, lay
panting in bed. Wasting away from the affliction, his hands and feet contracted. He endured this disability for five years. In the sixth year he asked to be
carried to the saint's basilica. Lying in prayer there, he lost his disability and deserved to obtain health.

### 45

**[045]** Lest what I report seem incredible because individuals' names are not recorded on the pages, the reason is that when they are restored to health by
the holy man of God, they immediately leave and sometimes return so secretly that, if it is right to say, no one sees them. When rumor arises that the blessed
bishop's power has appeared, I call the custodians of the building and learn what happened, but I do not always learn names from them. I generally write by name
those I have seen or questioned myself. A man from Berry with disabled hands came to the festival. His fingers were so fixed into his palms that his hands
seemed to swarm with worms. When the solemnity was celebrated, the fingers of both hands straightened and he was granted health. All the people saw him
returning in sound health. His disability had occurred because he had wished to build a hedge around a crop on the Lord's day.

### 46

**[046]** A woman from the territory of Poitiers whose arm had withered with contracted sinews came to the blessed man's tomb. Spending the night in prayer and
vigils, she brought back her arm healed. Immediately assigned to service by her masters, she incurred the same condition. She returned and was healed. Her
masters then came and tried to take her away, but accepted a price from the saint's property and desisted; thus she was granted freedom.

### 47

**[047]** In those days a man was summoned to pay a debt contracted in his necessities. Lacking the strength and means to repay what he had borrowed, he was
confined in prison. When the creditor saw that nothing could be extracted because he had nothing and no one extended a merciful hand, he bound him more tightly
in chains. Denying him food and drink, he said, "I shall make you waste away with hunger as a lesson to everyone until you repay everything." While this was
happening, relics of the holy bishop carried in the district of Sessionicum passed through the street. Hearing the singers' voices, the prisoner prayed that the
holy bishop's power would visit him. His bonds immediately loosened and, with no one restraining him, he entered the holy basilica. Redeemed by the devout, he
was freed from the bond of debt.

### 48

**[048]** At one festival a woman who continued in blindness after losing her sight heard of the holy man's miracles and eagerly sought his basilica.
Prostrating herself on the dry ground before the sepulchre, as soon as she poured out prayer she deserved to receive light.

### 49

**[049]** At this solemnity came a boy with eyes closed, ears blocked, mouth obstructed, hands useless, and feet unable to walk. What more? He was so
prematurely dead to the use of all limbs that only his breath fluttered. When he touched the holy place, every disability was removed and he departed healed
with thanksgiving.

### 50

**[050]** Lupus, a priest of Bordeaux, was once gravely troubled by quartan fever; when the fever came he could take neither food nor drink. Meanwhile Saint
Martin's festival arrived. After celebrating vigils with the other clergy, in the morning he went ahead of everyone and hastened to the saint's basilica. On the
way he met a Jew who asked where he was going. He replied, "I have contracted quartan fever and am hurrying to the saint's basilica so that his power may drive
away this illness." The Jew said, "Martin, whom the earth covers and has made earthy, will do you no good. You seek his building in vain; a dead man cannot give
medicine to the living." Despising the ancient serpent's words, Lupus went where he had begun. Prostrating himself before the holy pledges, he prayed and found
two little candles made of wax and papyrus. Taking them home, he lit them and drank the papyrus ash with clean water. He immediately received health. The Jew
was seized by the same illness and shaken for a year, but his wicked mind could never be changed even by torments.

### 51

**[051]** Chardegysilus, a citizen of Saintes surnamed Gyso, received me at his house and invited me to an oratory which his mother had built and consecrated
with blessed Martin's relics. After prayer, when I asked attentively whether the bishop's power had been shown there, he replied, "Three years ago this little
son of mine whom you see before me, while still hanging at his mother's breast, began to suffer illness. For thirty days or more he was carried laboriously in
my hands until he became so weak that he could suck neither breast nor other food. As he failed, on the sixth day after he became more gravely ill I laid him
before the altar, weeping and awaiting his death. Unable to bear the grief, I left the house and ordered my wife to bury him as soon as he died. While his
mother wept, the infant lay until evening. At sunset he raised his voice, saying, 'Sweetest sister, where are you?' He used to call his mother this in infant
endearment. She ran to him saying, 'I am here, sweetest son.' Taking him in her arms, she offered her breast; he sucked milk and recovered."

### 52

**[052]** In the days when this was reported to me, one of my clergy incurred a flux of the bowel with fever and extreme stomach failure; most of what he
discharged from below was blood. He was more afflicted because increasing nausea made him immediately vomit any food he took. As soon as he drank dust from the
sepulchre, every illness was removed and he was strengthened.

### 53

**[053]** I thought I should also not keep silent about how he has often raised those falling headlong into death by extending the right hand of mercy. A
servant of my citizen Genitor was arrested by a judge for theft and condemned to the gallows. While being led away, he invoked the blessed bishop's name:
"Deliver me, holy confessor Martin, from imminent danger." Hanged and left alone, he suddenly heard a voice in a stirring wind say, "Let us free him." Behold,
shaken from the four quarters of heaven, the stake supporting him was torn from the earth with an immense clod like an uprooted tree. The man given over to
death rose alive again. Another man who had committed many sins and, moved by God, was doing penance for his evils, was arrested without cause and condemned to
a similar death, continually invoking the blessed confessor's help. When he was hanged, his bonds broke and he fell unharmed to the ground. But wicked human
minds hanged again the man whom God rescued. The abbot of a nearby monastery heard and ran about three miles to the count to plead for him. Obtaining the man's
life, he returned and found him alive. Taking him down from hanging, he brought him to the monastery confessing, "I felt Saint Martin's power, which rescued
me."

### 54

**[054]** Within the boundary of Tours there was a man from the village of Mons Laudiacensis, simple by nature and bound in marriage. While resting with his
wife at midnight, panic arose. Terrified and leaping from bed, he wandered anxiously through his lodging and lost the service of his voice. Without delay he
indicated by gestures that his wife should bring him to the saint's basilica. He lay continually in prayer before the blessed sepulchre for six months. His
tongue was freed and by the blessed man's power he deserved to recover the speech he had previously possessed.

### 55

**[055]** A woman from across the Loire worked on the Lord's day, though the authority of the fathers forbade work on that day. Her hand contracted and became
rigid, her fingers fixed into her palm. Tormented by pain, she approached the holy confessor's building and vowed that if healed she would never again do on the
day of the Lord's resurrection any work unsuitable to it. Her fingers were immediately removed from her palm and she departed with her hand straightened.

### 56

**[056]** Great is the confessor's mercy: he rebukes the foolish in such a way that, placing their vice before their eyes, he returns them amended thereafter.
Another woman was disabled for this reason. On the Sabbath after sunset, adjoining the night of the Lord's resurrection, she put bread in the oven and her arm
was shaken with pain. Putting in a second and third loaf, her hand unwillingly began to grip the wood it held. Understanding that she was condemned by divine
power's judgment, she quickly threw away the peel she held, but could not escape punishment. Her hands contracted with such severe pain that the nails were
fixed into her palms. Believing no physician's compress could heal her, she sought the blessed basilica. Praying faithfully, her hands straightened and she
departed healed. She vowed to serve at the holy church one week each month. It is most clearly known that she observed this for one year. After that year she
omitted one month's week and did not come to the holy basilica. While sitting in her lodging, one eye was pierced by pain. Pressing it, the other immediately
began to hurt. Within one hour she became blind in both eyes. Without delay she confessed and fled to her accustomed protection. Humbly pouring out prayer and
doing penance with compunction for her negligence, on the eighth day blood flowed from her eyes and she received sight.

### 57

**[057]** A man's eyes were covered by a thick cloud of darkness and sealed by eyelids joined with sticky matter; in addition, he was held by great pains. What
more? He devoutly sought the saint's festival with the others, earnestly praying to deserve visitation by the blessed bishop's power on the solemn day. But the
confessor's might preceded the sacred rites, showing himself present to the people by driving away darkness and pouring back light. Three days before the
festival, while the man prayed in the portico surrounding the apse of the body, his eyes suddenly opened and looking up he deserved to see light. When he
related this with thanksgiving to those present, they told him to be silent and pray instead so that the blessed bishop would more quickly complete the power
begun. Prostrating himself on the ground and bursting into tears, his eyes were strengthened and he rose healed from the ground.

### 58

**[058]** Three days after this solemnity a paralyzed man was praying in that place. As he related, his disability had occurred for this reason. When he was a
little boy guarding animals in a field with others, he fell asleep over a spring. The others withdrew at midday and he remained alone. At last released from
sleep, he tried to rise and was seized by pains. Soon all his limbs contracted, his arms twisted outward, the sinews of his knees contracted, and his heels were
drawn toward his thighs. Unable to walk, immense tears and loud cries flowed from him. His companions returned to see the animals and found him wailing. Carried
in his parents' arms, he was restored to his home. A few days later, when the pains eased a little, he was assigned to beggars. Going around regions and cities
with them for ten years or more, he came to this festival and all his limbs were strengthened. Two blind people received sight that day; two demoniacs were
cleansed at the bishop's sepulchre.

### 59

**[059]** One of my young men was so troubled by nightly fevers that from the eighth hour until the second hour of the next day he could obtain no rest from
burning. All food was horrible to him and he took nothing to strengthen himself. Savage pain shook all his limbs and pallor occupied his cheeks. While he was
carried sick in his parents' hands, I could scarcely obtain his being brought to the blessed bishop's sepulchre. At last brought, he took a drink of the tomb's
sacrosanct dust diluted in water. By this blessing all pain was immediately put to flight and the fever extinguished. Without delay the boy sought a private
place for evacuation and was led into a corner to purge his bowel. When he discharged his bowel's contents under the impulse of wind, two worms like serpents
immediately came out, moving before human eyes as though alive. After they were evacuated, he was completely healed. He took food and drink as usual; pallor
fled and redness returned to his cheeks, and all his limbs were strengthened.

### 60

**[060]** An opportunity recently arose for me to visit my mother in the territory of Cavaillon. Fearing illnesses that might occur, I presumed to take with me
dust from the blessed bishop's sepulchre so that if disease attacked any of my people, the saint's power would help with its customary aid. When I reached my
mother, fever with dysentery immediately seized, wore down, and consumed one servant. Denied the use of food, he was nourished only by fevers. On the third day,
hearing this, I gave the dying man diluted dust to drink. The fever immediately fled, the pain subsided, and he recovered. In those days I heard from Bishop
Veranus that once, burning with the heat of quartan fever, he sought the basilica of blessed Martin in that place and was healed after keeping vigil. Returning
from this journey to Auvergne, I found Bishop Avitus so gravely shaken by tertian fever that if he took any food he immediately vomited it. Taking a drink from
this pledge, he trampled the fever and was strengthened. An epidemic fever attacked two of my servants; as often happens with this contagion, savage pain seized
the joints of all their limbs. Drinking this blessing, they were healed. On this journey I myself felt severe toothache; not only the teeth but my whole head
was pierced by throbbing veins and darts of pain, and my temples throbbed violently. I sought this protection and, the pain immediately suppressed, recovered. O
indescribable antidote! O ineffable medication! O praiseworthy remedy! O heavenly purgatory, so to speak! It conquers physicians' subtleties, surpasses the
sweetness of aromatics, and exceeds the strength of all ointments. It cleanses the bowel like scammony, the lung like hyssop, and purges the head itself like
pellitory. Not only does it strengthen weak limbs but, greater than all these, it wipes away and smooths the very stains of consciences. Let what has been
inserted suffice for this little book. If I still deserve to see miracles, I intend to insert them in another little book, so that what is shown may not be
hidden from eyes but rather made public. For the rest, I implore his power: may he who grants such things from a tomb deign to raise me, already dead to God
through sins, from the sepulchre of this death, so that in the resurrection of the flesh he may obtain indulgence for me for all time when he himself is carried
to his crown.

HERE ENDS BOOK III.

## BOOK IV

### PREFACE

**[000]** The prophet admonishes us with most salutary exhortation, saying, "Your friends are to be honored, O God." Likewise in another psalm: "He magnifies
those who fear the Lord," and is joined to the blessedness of the eternal house. It is therefore clearly evident to human understanding that everyone is
admonished—not only those free from crime but those given to the evil of deadly sin—to render reverent worship to God's friends. This not only bestows benefit
in the present world but provides refreshment in the future. When I often see the marks of miracles proceeding from the blessed ones' tombs, I am rightly moved
to pay them the reverence due, for I do not cease to implore from them remedies for illnesses. I do not doubt that through their prayers I obtain even the
remission of sins and deserve not only this but salvation from infernal punishments by their intervention. I trust that just as here they cut away kinds of
diseases, there they avert savage pains of torment; just as here they mitigate bodily fevers, there they extinguish eternal ones; just as here they cleanse the
foul ulcers of lurid leprosy, there by their intervention they obtain healing for the stains of sins; and just as here they raise dead corpses to life, there
they restore to eternal life those buried in sin, drawing them out with an inserted hand from the Acherontic pools. Therefore, when each person rejoices in his
own joy under a patron, he pays the due honor more earnestly when he feels himself cleansed by the patron's power of the illness which held him, as I and
innumerable peoples have now experienced with the blessed bishop Martin, the special patron of the whole world. Would that the sloth of my mind would permit me
to venerate him as befits God's friend, who often restores me to health when oppressed by so many kinds of diseases!

### 1

**[001]** Recently I incurred pain in my bowel. Though it did not produce complete evacuation, the evil of pain wandered through the winding recesses of my
intestines. I confess I often used baths and had warm things bound over the tortures of my bowel, but nothing could cure the illness. The sixth day had dawned
and the pain was increasing more and more when I remembered that, as written in the second book of this work, I had been healed of this pain by the saint's
power a few years earlier. I rashly approached the place of the sepulchre, threw myself on the ground, and prayed. Taking one of the hanging veils secretly
under my clothing, I traced the sign of the cross with it on my bowel. The pain immediately subsided and I departed healed.

### 2

**[002]** Once my tongue became severely swollen so that often when I wished to speak it made me stutter, which brought reproach upon me. I approached the
saint's tomb and drew my impeded tongue along the wood of the screen. The swelling was immediately suppressed and I recovered. It had swollen violently and
filled the whole cavity of my palate. Then after the third day my lip began to swell severely. I again approached the tomb seeking health. Touching my lip with
the hanging veils, the throbbing of the vein immediately stopped. I believe these things happened to me from an abundance of blood, but I did not try to have
blood let because of the saint's power. This condition caused me no further trouble.

### 3

**[003]** A little boy was burdened by fever; his limbs wasted away and, taking no food, he was about to breathe out his spirit. His father ran to me in tears.
I directed him to carry the boy to the basilica and keep vigil all night. When he did so, he immediately received his son back healed through the holy bishop's
power.

### 4

**[004]** A man whose fingers had contracted into his palm came to the festival celebrated in the fifth month. After praying, his fingers straightened and he
departed. A woman blind for eight years prostrated herself on the ground before the holy sepulchre; her eyes were illuminated and she returned to her place.
Three demoniacs were then cleansed by the saint's power.

### 5

**[005]** That year, the thirteenth of King Childebert, at the festival celebrating Martin's blessed death, a swineherd servant of Theudulf, a citizen of Tours,
kept watch at night around the herd entrusted to him so that no beast would seize any of it or a thief's deceit carry it off. A sudden darkness spread over his
eyes and he lost the light. Remaining blind for six years, he came to this festival. After the third day he was illuminated by the saint's power and set free by
his master.

### 6

**[006]** In the fourteenth year of the king named above, when the saint's solemnity arrived, twelve paralyzed people were straightened, three blind people
illuminated, and five demoniacs cleansed. Aridius, abbot of Limoges, mentioned in earlier books, attended this festival. Through him the Lord restored a
paralyzed woman who had lain for eight years on a wagon in the blessed confessor's portico; her steps were straightened. The man of God himself declared that he
felt as though blessed Martin's hand were present when, placing the sign of the cross, he touched the sick woman's limbs with a healing touch. Florentianus the
maior and Romulf, count of the palace, also attended this festival. They greatly admired the confessor's glory, through whom the Lord then deigned to work such
miracles.

### 7

**[007]** Since I have mentioned Florentianus the maior, I think it wicked to keep silent about what I learned from him. Once he went to Galicia on an embassy.
Coming into King Miro's presence, he disclosed the business entrusted to him. At that time King Miro was in the city where his predecessor had built Saint
Martin's basilica, as I explained in the first book. Before this building's portico a vine-covered chamber extended with hanging clusters of grapes, flourishing
as though painted. Beneath it was the path leading the visitor on foot to the sacred building's doors. As the king passed beneath it to enter the church to
pray, he told his men, "Take care not to touch any of these grape clusters, lest you incur the holy bishop's offense. Everything in this portico is consecrated
to him." Hearing this, one servant said to himself, "I do not know whether these things are consecrated to this saint. One thing I know: my mind is resolved to
eat them." He immediately put in his hand and began to cut a cluster's stem. His right hand immediately adhered to the chamber; his upper arm withered and
became rigid. He was the king's jester, accustomed to provoke his mirth with playful words. But no laughter or trick of his art helped him. Compelled by pain,
he began to cry: "Help me, men, in my misery; help me oppressed; relieve me suspended; implore the holy bishop Martin's power for me, tormented by such an end,
afflicted by such a blow, severed by such a cut." When the king came out and learned what had happened, he burned with such fury against the servant that he
wished to cut off his hand and would have done so had his people not prevented him. His servants said, "Do not add your vengeance to God's judgment, O king,
lest you turn back upon yourself the injury you threaten the servant." Moved in heart, the king entered the basilica, prostrated himself before the holy altar,
and poured out prayer to the Lord with tears. He did not rise from the pavement until the river of his eyes had washed away the page of his chosen sin. When the
servant was released from the bond by which he had been bound and entered the basilica, the king rose from the ground, received his servant healed, and returned
to the palace. The maior mentioned above testified that he learned this from the king's own account, as I have related. The glorious bishop so illuminates his
own city with miracles that he is not felt to be absent from foreign places.

### 8

**[008]** In the present year Palladius, bishop of Saintes, sought this holy confessor's relics. He had built a basilica in Martin's honor and consecrated it
with these pledges. He deserved to receive miracles there which his own city has often experienced. After two or three months I received his letter indicating
that three paralyzed people with contracted feet had come; as soon as they entered the basilica and prayed, their steps straightened and they were restored to
health. Two blind people deserved to receive light there after prayer, and more than twelve recovered from chill fever when their trembling was driven away.

### 9

**[009]** Two of my servants, the cleric Dagobaldus and the layman Theodorus, suffered dysentery with fever. They were so weakened that when the necessity of
evacuation came they could be raised from bed only by others' hands. Drinking dust from the sepulchre, they immediately recovered.

### 10

**[010]** I have a sapphire-colored dish which the saint is said to have brought from the Emperor Maximus's treasury; power often proceeds from it upon
sufferers from chills. If anyone comes while fever is mounting with its customary trembling and drinks water from it, he is immediately healed. At the village
of Condat there is another dish likewise presented by the saint, made of crystal, offering a similar benefit to the sick if faithfully sought. One of my
notaries, Bodilo, was troubled in mind by stomach weakness so that he could neither write nor take dictation as usual and could barely review what was dictated.
Frequently reproached, he poured water over the blessed man's dish which I said was with me and drank it. Immediately restored to his senses, he performed the
work of his office more keenly than usual.

### 11

**[011]** Why is it wonderful that he restores to men senses disturbed by adversity, when he often converts sterility to fruitfulness? Blidericus, a citizen of
Chartres, married and prayed to be enriched by God's gift with offspring of his own, but he could obtain no progeny from his wife. Thirty years passed with his
wife remaining sterile. Considering most salutarily for his soul's benefit, the man said to her, "Behold, the world I use is passing away, and no offspring is
born between us to possess the accumulated fruits of my labor when I am gone. I shall go to Saint Martin's basilica and make it my heir so that, denied
children, I may possess in the future with it what I can have." The wise woman consented to her prudent husband's counsel. Without delay he went to the holy
basilica and prayed. He invited the abbot to come home with him. When he came, Blidericus handed over all his possessions, saying, "Let everything I seem to
have be under Saint Martin's lordship; I shall use it only to be fed from it while I live." The property was conveyed and he urged the abbot to remain there.
Wonderful to tell! After thirty years, on the very night he transferred his property to the basilica, he knew his wife. She conceived and bore a son, and
afterward he had others. No one doubts that this was granted to the man by the saint's power. Nevertheless, having received sons, he did not oppose his promise;
giving them other properties, he confirmed what he had first bestowed on the saint.

### 12

**[012]** At the villa of Turnacum in the territory of Le Mans, now held under the holy basilica's lordship, a woman held by longstanding blindness and burdened
by old age sat at the villa's oratory. While begging alms and continually invoking Saint Martin's name, on a Sunday night her eyes began to be pierced by pain.
Prostrating herself before the holy altar, blood burst out and she received light. Relics of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul are kept in that place,
but she declared that she had been healed by the holy bishop's power. My faith holds that one Lord works in the miracles of many saints; those whom the Lord
makes equal in miracles on earth are not separated in power, being equal in heaven.

### 13

**[013]** At the festival attended by Aunacharius, bishop of Auxerre, a man brought a withered and contracted hand. After the third day of the festival he carried it home restored.

### 14

**[014]** Baudegisilus, son of Baudulf and an inhabitant of the village of Geinum in the territory of Angers, was wounded by the dart of a savage fluid and lay
disabled. While his poor father fed him without benefit of work, he begged his father with rising tears to let him kiss Saint Martin's basilica threshold.
Without delay his father placed him in a boat, since he could not be carried otherwise, and devoutly laid his son at the saint's feet outside the sepulchre.
Devoting several days to prayer and asking the saint's help, his disability was removed and he was restored to health. He was returned home healed with his
father.

### 15

**[015]** In the territory of Auch lived a man named Caelestis who had many beehives. A swarm came out, climbed high, and traveled far. He followed but could
obtain no success in catching it. Prostrating himself on the ground, he invoked Saint Martin's name: "If your power, most blessed confessor, will restrain this
swarm and return it to my lordship, I shall take for my own uses the honey later produced from it, but I shall send all the wax intact for the lights of your
basilica." While he still lay on the ground after saying this, the swarm immediately descended and settled on a small tree nearest him. He collected it, put it
in a hive, and brought it home. Within two or three years he gathered many swarms from it. When he had accumulated more than two hundred pounds of wax, rumor of
hostilities arose. Lest his vow perish, he buried the wax in a ditch in the ground. When peace returned, he summoned my deacon to fetch it. A servant with him
was suffering severe kidney pain. Approaching Caelestis and learning from his mouth what had happened, the deacon ordered the wax hidden in the earth uncovered.
The suffering servant took a hoe to dig and said, "If you are merciful, Saint Martin, in looking upon this man's gift, let your power touch my kidneys and be my
salvation when I uncover this wax." Striking the earth with the hoe, the little bones of his kidneys cracked and immediately all pain was removed. He was
presented healed with the wax at the blessed basilica.

### 16

**[016]** A man of Tours appeared guilty before a judge, who ordered him bound and guarded. When the holy days of the Lord's resurrection approached, the judge
ordered him confined in another custody on the farther bank of the Loire. He was led not only with his neck bound in chains but also with his hands tied behind
his back. Arriving at the riverbank and awaiting the boat to cross, he continually implored Saint Martin's help. The guards suddenly seemed to have been struck
on the head by someone. They immediately fell to the ground; the chains holding the prisoner broke and the straps on his hands loosened. Feeling himself free
while the men still lay on the ground, he withdrew and entered the holy church's threshold. He was released by the judge. Some reported that in those days
prisoners at Poitiers were also released from the penitentiary. There can be no doubt that the power of each confessor could illuminate each city with sacred
miracles.

### 17

**[017]** A little boy named Leodoaldus, servant of Baudeleifus from a village of Angers to which antiquity gave the name Crovium, had been reborn by water and
the Holy Spirit. While playing in the street with other infants and running here and there as that age permits, a wind suddenly arose violently, lifted dust,
and filled the child's eyes. Stricken blind and tormented by pain, the boy had a certain man appear to his grandmother in a dream and say, "Go to Saint Martin's
basilica and this boy will receive sight." The woman did not delay. Full of faith, she came to the festival and received her grandson illuminated by the
bishop's power.

### 18

**[018]** A girl of this city's territory named Viliogundis was blinded in similar circumstances. Running through the village streets playing with other girls,
the violence of the wind lifted dust and filled her eyes. Immediately tormented by pain, she asked her parents to lead her to Saint Martin's basilica. As soon
as they prayed for her, she received sight. The boy and girl just mentioned met me together as I left the holy solemnity of mass, saying that at that very hour
they had received light through the blessed bishop's power. This brought great joy to me, believing that the blessed confessor's power had deigned to visit me.

### 19

**[019]** Litoveus, disabled in his limbs from infancy, was blinded when fever came upon him. Coming to the previous festival, his limbs were straightened but
he departed still deprived of light. Returning again to this solemnity, the darkness was removed and he arose given over to light.

### 20

**[020]** At this festival Leudardus, servant of Eumerius, deacon of Nantes, had been bound by the chain of blindness for six years. Approaching the basilica,
he was illuminated by the blessed confessor's power. He had been admonished in a dream vision to implore this holy bishop's help.

### 21

**[021]** A citizen of Tours hurrying to meet the king deposited at the sepulchre for one night a vessel of wine and one loaf, so that on his journey he would
have this protection of health. Taking them from there, he began his journey. Seeking lodging, he entered a man's house and put down his baggage. A woman with
an unclean spirit began with immense cries to announce blessed Martin's arrival: "Why do you persecute me, holy one? Why do you torment me, servant of God?" The
visitor took a cup, poured in a little wine from the vessel, and put in it a broken fragment of the blessed bread. When the raving woman received it, the demon
was immediately cast out with blood and she was saved. Another woman there had long suffered from chills; taking a little of this blessing, she was healed.

### 22

**[022]** Silluvius, an inhabitant of Bayeux, was working in the countryside when the wind stirred. Struck by panic, he began to tremble and all his limbs
failed; he cried out and testified that death threatened him. Neighbors ran to the sight. Amid cries and howls his sinews contracted and he became wholly
disabled. Not only was he denied the use of his ears, but he also lost his eyesight. After fifteen years in this misfortune, he came to Saint Martin's festival;
his limbs strengthened and his eyes recovered, he departed.

### 23

**[023]** By no different power Ermegundis, a citizen of Angers and inhabitant of Crovium, crippled and blind, departed this festival straightened and
illuminated. Charimundus also came disabled from Bricilonnus and was restored by the blessed bishop's power.

### 24

**[024]** Many experienced the power of this solemnity with Christ's grace cooperating. Leodomundus, blind for seven years, Domnitta for three, and three other
blind people received sight at this festival through the blessed bishop's help; many demoniacs were cleansed.

### 25

**[025]** A household servant of my priest Leo was carried in her parents' arms to a little villa near the city. Violent fever overwhelmed her and day and night
she seemed in danger of death. Seeing her rendered lifeless by the disease's violence, the priest mounted a horse at night and came to the holy confessor's
basilica. Knocking at the cell where the sacristan slept, he could not wake the man. Unable to enter the holy basilica, he prayed before the apse of the
sepulchre and collected a little earthly dust, which he carried away full of faith. He diluted it and gave it to the little girl to drink; the fever immediately
departed.

### 26

**[026]** I had occasion to visit King Childebert. Traveling through the district of Reims, I found a man who reported that Martin's power had opened a worldly
prison in which the king's servant was held among other prisoners; released from the penitentiary, the prisoners departed free. The prison was constructed with
strong planks laid over a pile of timbers, with massive stones placed on top to weigh them down. The prison door, furnished with an iron bolt, was shut with a
locking bar. But as the reporter declared, the bishop's power moved the stones, threw down the planks, broke the chains, and opened the beam confining the
prisoners' feet. Without opening the door, it lifted the men through the air and brought them outside through the open roof, saying, "I am Martin, a soldier of
Christ, your deliverer. Depart in peace and go securely!" When I reached the king and spread abroad this miracle, he affirmed that some of the released men had
come to him and that he had pardoned the guilty men the composition owed to the treasury which they call fredum. This happened four days before the festival in
that king's sixteenth year.

### 27

**[027]** When the blessed man's feast arrived, Nonnichius, bishop of Nantes, came to the saint's basilica bringing a boy named Baudegisillus disabled in his
limbs. After celebrating the saint's rites, he took him back healed, his limbs restored.

### 28

**[028]** While I was staying with the king, a royal chancellor named Claudius was seized by fever. Overwhelmed by severe fever, he shrank from food and drink
and complained to me about his suffering. He drank the diluted dust I had taken from the saint's holy sepulchre for salvation; the fever was immediately
suppressed and he was healed.

### 29

**[029]** The venerable Agnes, abbess of the holy virgins of Poitiers, related a miracle reported to her by the merchant of Trier to whom it happened: "When I
came to Metz, a merchant asked where I was from. I said, 'From Poitiers.' He asked whether I had ever visited blessed Martin's basilica at Tours. I said that
whenever I traveled in Austrasia I presented myself there. He told me what benefit he had experienced from lord Martin. While trading salt at Metz and mooring
at the bridge, he said, 'Lord Martin, I commend to you myself, the servants I have, and my little boat.' While I lay in the boat, I all fell asleep. Waking in
the morning with my servants, I found myself before the gate of Trier, not knowing how I had come, though I still believed myself at Metz. Whether it was
sailing or flying, by blessed Martin's commendation alone I did not feel the river and avoided the shipwrecking swelling waves of the Moselle. Best of all, I
passed unharmed among rocks at night without a watchful boatman, a blowing wind, or a moving oar."

### 30

**[030]** Later, when I came to Poitiers, I wished solely for prayer to visit the monastery of Ligugé, where the blessed man had settled an assembled community
of monks. There he is read to have raised his first dead man and from there he is written to have been led to the episcopate. Seeking the desired place, I
prostrated myself at the screens of the corner where he is said to have brought back the dead man's spirit. After pouring out tears with prayer and solemnly
celebrating mass, I asked the abbot whether the Lord had shown any miracle there. Before the brothers present he declared that the blind were frequently
illuminated and the disabled made whole there. "What happened recently I shall unfold to you, lord, since you inquire carefully. A woman living near this place,
struck by a paralyzing fluid, had completely lost the use of all her limbs. Placed on a wagon drawn by oxen, she was carried around the houses of the rich to
supply the necessities of her poverty. Brought to this place and prostrated on the pavement, she slowly approached and devoutly kissed the veil covering the
holy screen, saying, 'I believe you are present here, blessed confessor; I testify that here you raised the dead. I trust that if you wish you can save and
restore me to health, just as you once broke hell's jaws and brought back a dead man's soul.' Saying this, she abundantly watered her cheeks with tears. As soon
as her prayer was finished, everything withered, contracted, or loosened in the woman's body was restored by the blessed bishop's power." Similarly another
paralyzed man came to this monastery; when he touched the veil of that screen, all disability was removed and he departed healed. It is about forty stades from
Poitiers.

### 31

**[031]** Leaving there, I entered the territory of Saintes. While speaking about blessed Martin's miracles at a banquet, one citizen faithfully related this,
with others affirming its truth. Naiogialo is a villa in that territory. While Saint Martin was still living in the body and going there, he met a man carrying
water in a vessel. The well from which he carried it was in a valley about a thousand paces from the villa; the inhabitants brought drawn water from it. The man
of God said to the water-carrier, "I beg you, beloved, hold your hand and grant a little water for this ass I am riding to drink." The man replied, "If you
think it necessary to water your animal, go to the well, draw water, and give it. I shall not provide what I have carried with labor." Saying this, he passed
by. As he departed, a woman came also carrying water in a basin. The man of God spoke similarly to her. Like Rebecca hearing God's messenger long ago, she said,
"I offer drink both to you and your ass; it is no labor for me to draw again. Only let your will be done, you who suffer necessity while traveling." Setting
down the vessel, she gave his ass drink. Drawing water again and filling the vessel, she returned to the villa. Following her, the saint said, "I shall repay
you a benefit as a reward because you watered my ass." Kneeling on the ground, he prayed the Lord to reveal a vein of spring water in that place. As soon as the
prayer was finished, the earth split and revealed an immense spring before the wondering people. To this day it benefits the people living in that field. At the
spring's mouth is a stone as testimony which retains the footprint of the ass on which the holy bishop sat.

### 32

**[032]** I think I should also not keep silent about the saint's power shown when Plato obtained the episcopate of Poitiers. A house adjoining the church house
was burning in a great fire, and wind drove sparks and coals onto the church buildings. Plato had dust from the blessed sepulchre with him and raised the
chrismal vessel against the fire. A wind suddenly arose contrary to the first; defending the church roof from the flames, it drove them in another direction and
the church house was delivered.

### 33

**[033]** When Plato's son lay in bed consumed by a most bitter fever and was considered nearly lifeless, Plato gave the sick boy a drink of this diluted dust.
The fever immediately fled and the boy recovered from his suffering. But let us return to the saint's basilica.

### 34

**[034]** Some years ago a great earthquake shook the land and everything was so violently moved that it seemed about to collapse in a moment. A man named
Leodulfus was vehemently shaken by it and not only lost his senses but became disabled in all his limbs. Coming to the saint's basilica at Tours and devoting a
few days to prayer, he was restored to voice, understanding, and all his limbs, returning healed as if alive again.

### 35

**[035]** I think I should not pass over an innocent man accused through the calumnies of the wicked who was being brought to the city bound with a strap to be
thrown into prison. When he was brought in public before the basilica of Saint Peter the apostle and reached a field, his hands were released. He told the
guards, "It is evident that I am innocent of the offense you allege, since my hands have been divinely released." Indignant, they bound him more tightly and
added another strap, so to speak binding the bonds themselves. At that time I happened to come through the street from Saint Martin's basilica. As they
approached me, as soon as the bound man saw the saint's basilica his hands were immediately released. Leaping from the horse on which he sat, he seized my feet
and explained that he was being unjustly condemned. After I spoke with the judge, he departed without further trouble.

### 36

**[036]** The wife of my man Serenatus was returning from cultivation after her husband had gone ahead. Suddenly slipping from her companions' hands, she fell
to the ground. Her tongue was bound and, unable to utter any word, she became mute. Soothsayers approached and, saying she suffered an attack of the noonday
demon, offered bonds of herbs and words of incantation. But as usual they could provide no medicine to the dying woman. While the household raised a mixed
uproar of wailing, her son ran panting to my niece Eustenia, announcing that his mother had reached the boundary of life. Eustenia came to visit the sick woman,
removed the bonds the fools had imposed, poured oil from the blessed sepulchre into her mouth, and rubbed her with wax. Speech immediately returned; the wicked
deceit was broken and the sick woman recovered.

### 37

**[037]** After the death of the most glorious King Guntramn, when King Childebert visited Orléans, one of the palace servants was gravely shaken by tertian
fever as fevers came and went with trembling. He complained to me and I gave him dust from the holy sepulchre. Drinking it, his trembling was suppressed and he
recovered. The following night, when the day on which he customarily suffered arrived, he saw in a vision a most foul figure approaching and saying, "Behold,
the time of your trembling has come; why do you delay? Do what you are accustomed!" As it spoke, a man arrived with a shining face, snow-white hair, and
beautiful countenance, saying, "Do not tremble; make the sign of the venerable cross on your forehead and you will immediately be healed." Awaking from this
vision and protected by the commanded sign, he never again suffered what he had endured. A servant girl of the queen, exhausted by this fever, drank the same
holy medicine and was healed.

### 38

**[038]** Not many days later the yearly day returned the saint's solemnity. Returning from the king, I attended the festival. Four blind people departed having
received light, two demoniacs were cleansed, and two contracted paralytics returned healed with their steps restored.

### 39

**[039]** A few days later the judge's sentence confined certain guilty people of Tours in prison. While the prisoners lamented, the blessed confessor's power
appeared: breaking the fetters' bonds, it permitted them to go free into the basilica. Released by the judge, they departed home.

### 40

**[040]** In Cantabria a man named Mauranus rose from bed one morning and left the house. He seemed to have been struck on the neck by someone. Immediately
falling to the ground, he became like a dead man. For three days only his breath lived and he was thought dead. On the fourth day he opened his eyes but could
say nothing; the faculty of speech had been taken away. Hearing blessed Martin's miracles, he gave a triens to sailors, gesturing a request that they carry him
to the blessed bishop's church. After they left, he returned home and saw before his feet a gold piece resembling a triens. Taking and weighing it, it was the
weight of one solidus. Seeing this, he said to himself, "Blessed Martin's power has repaid me with interest the merit I sent to his church." Inflamed with
desire, he wished to board one ship and then another but was held back by his parents. Finding a third ship, he could not be restrained at all. Boarding, they
entered the high sea under a driving wind, and the holy bishop's power opened his mouth. Stretching his hands to heaven, he said, "I thank you, almighty God,
who commanded me to furrow this journey. Before I see your saint's church, I am filled with his benefits." Sailing on, they were driven to Bordeaux. Leaving the
ship, he approached the saint's basilica and paid his vow. I learned from his own mouth the account I have written.

### 41

**[041]** At another festival celebrated in winter came Maurellus from the house of Pontico, a servant of Duke Aginus. In March he had lost the use of one knee
through some attack and, unable to take a step, had applied a stick to his knee as is the custom of the lame. After praying to the Lord for three days, on the
fourth day, the day after the festival, his knee straightened and he departed healed. A few days later men held in prison bonds were divinely released, entered
the saint's basilica, and were freed from harm by the judge.

### 42

**[042]** A boy with contracted hands and feet from the villa of Themellus in the district of the village of Amboise in Tours came to the saint's basilica.
While begging alms for food among other petitioners, he was visited by the saint's power and departed straightened.

### 43
