This confessor’s blessed body had been buried by the ancients in a crypt. Because the building was narrow and difficult to enter, Saint Avitus, bishop of the
city, constructed around it an apse of marvellous workmanship. He searched for the blessed limbs and found them in a reliquary formed of wooden boards. Taking
them up, he wrapped them in fitting linens and enclosed them in a sarcophagus according to custom; he then raised the crypt and filled it in. In this place
Justus also rests, alike in merit and in name, who is said to have been this glorious bishop’s archdeacon.

### 5

**[013]** Many other miracles concerning this saint have been reported, but I have thought it lengthy to write them down. I consider what has been said
sufficient for perfect faith, because more will not profit those for whom a few things are not enough. At this tomb the blind receive sight, demons are put to
flight, the deaf recover hearing, and the lame recover the power to walk. Our Lord Jesus Christ grants these things; he promised to bestow without uncertainty
whatever believers asked of him.

## III. Abbot Abraham

### Prologue

**[014]** I think it is hidden from no Catholic that the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, if you have complete faith and do not hesitate, if you
say to this mountain, ‘Remove yourself,’ it will remove itself”; and: “Whatever you ask in my name, believe that you will receive it, and it will come to you.”
There can therefore be no doubt that the saints can obtain from the Lord what they ask, because their faith, with its foundation set in him, is not shaken by
any waves of hesitation. For the sake of this faith they have become exiles not only within the territory of their own country when they desire to lead the
heavenly life, but they have also sought places across the sea and in foreign lands, so that they might please more fully him to whom they had devoted
themselves. So it is now with the blessed Abbot Abraham, who after many temptations entered the territory of Clermont. For the greatness of his faith he is
rightly compared to that elder Abraham, to whom God once said: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and go into the land that I will show you.” This
Abraham left not only his own land but also the conduct of the old man, and put on the new man who is formed according to God in righteousness, holiness, and
truth. Therefore, when he perceived that he was perfect in God’s work, he did not hesitate to ask in faith for what he trusted to obtain through his holy life.
Through him the Maker of heaven, sea, and earth deigned to work miracles small in number but wonderful.

### 1

**[015]** This Abraham arose on the bank of the river Euphrates. Advancing there in God’s work, he desired to go into the solitudes of Egypt to visit the
hermits. While he was making that journey, pagans captured him, inflicted many blows upon him for Christ’s name, and threw him into chains. After living in
exile in them for five years, he was released when an angel loosed him. Wishing also to visit the western region, he came to Clermont and established a
monastery there at the basilica of Saint Cyricus. He was a man of wonderful power, one who put demons to flight and gave light to the blind, and a most mighty
healer of other diseases as well.

When the feast of the aforesaid basilica arrived, he called the cellarer and directed him, according to custom, to place vessels full of wine in the courtyard
to refresh the people attending the solemnity. The monk objected, “You have invited the bishop, together with the duke and the citizens, and we have scarcely
four amphorae of wine left. How will you fill all these vessels?” Abraham said, “Open the storeroom for me.” When it was opened, he entered and prayed. Like a
new Elijah, he raised his hands to heaven, his eyes streaming with tears, and said, “I ask you, Lord, let the wine in this vessel not fail until it has been
ministered to everyone in abundance.” The Holy Spirit rushed upon him, and he said, “Thus says the Lord: The wine in the vessel will not fail, but will be given
in full measure to all who ask, and there will be an abundance.” At his word and with the cheerfulness of his distribution, the whole people were served
abundantly, and wine remained. The diligent cellarer had previously measured the vessel, which held fifty measures, and had found a depth of only four palms.
Seeing what had happened, he measured it again the next day and found as much in the vessel as he had left there on the preceding day.

The saint’s power was thus made known among the people. Full of days, he died in that monastery and was buried there with honour. At that time Saint Sidonius
was bishop, and Victorius was duke, who had received authority over seven cities through the favour of Euric, king of the Goths. The blessed Sidonius wrote this
saint’s epitaph, in which he mentioned certain of the things I have related. Those suffering from fevers often lie at this blessed Abraham’s tomb and are raised
up by the aid of heavenly medicine.

## IV. Saint Quintianus

### Prologue

**[016]** Everyone who knows that he bears a body of earthly matter ought to take care not to sink into those things which are known to be earthly and friendly
to this flesh. According to the apostle Paul, the works of the flesh are manifest, full of uncleanness and iniquity; they render the person who follows them
polluted and foul, and in the end consign him to eternal weeping. But the fruit of the Spirit is everything that is strong and radiant in God. In this world,
when the flesh has been mortified, it makes the soul exult; in the world to come it bestows eternal joys. We who are now placed in the body ought therefore to
behold what God has wrought in his saints. Dwelling in them as in a tabernacle splendid, white, polished by their merits, and adorned with the various flowers
of virtue, he stretched out the right hand of his majesty and deigned through them, in his own compassion, to accomplish what they asked. So now, through the
blessed Quintianus, of whom we are about to speak, he often completed a work of righteousness radiant with the generosity of a noble mind. Let not the pursuit
of the flesh plunge and press us down into earthly things after the manner of cattle. Rather, attracted by the examples of the saints and prudently
understanding the things of God, let spiritual work raise us to heavenly and eternal things. Let not our mind, overcome by shameless actions, run riot within
us; let victorious wisdom reign, claiming the throne of eternity according to our merits.

### 1

**[017]** The most blessed Quintianus was an African by birth and, as some say, a nephew of Bishop Faustus, who is reported to have raised his own mother.
Endowed with holiness, radiant with the gift of virtues, ardent with the fire of charity, and pre-eminent in the flower of chastity, he was chosen, sought, and
ordained for the episcopate of the church of Rodez. While his virtues continued to increase in that office and he was always growing in God’s works, he enlarged
the basilica of the blessed Bishop Amantius and transferred the holy body further forward. This work was not acceptable to the saint. He appeared to Quintianus
in a vision and said, “Because you have been seen in rash daring to remove limbs that were resting in peace, behold, I will remove you from this city, and you
will be an exile in another region; nevertheless, you will not be deprived of the honour you enjoy.”

Not long afterwards, a scandal arose between the citizens and the bishop. Suspicion touched the Goths who were then dwelling in that city that the bishop wished
to submit himself to the rule of the Franks. Taking counsel, they planned to run him through with the sword. When this was reported to the holy man, he rose at
night, left the city with his most faithful servants, and came to Clermont. There he was received by Saint Bishop Eufrasius, who had succeeded the former bishop
Abrunculus. Eufrasius and the prelate of the city of Lyon gave him houses, fields, and vineyards, and cared for him with the greatest attention. He was by then
an old man and a true worshipper of God.

When Saint Eufrasius departed from this world, Apollinaris administered the priesthood for three months and then died. When these events were reported to King
Theodoric, he ordered Saint Quintianus to be established there and all authority over the church to be handed to him, saying, “This man was cast out of his city
because of his zeal for our love.” When Saint Quintianus had obtained the episcopate of the aforesaid city, a certain Proculus, a priest ordained from the
treasury, inflicted many injuries upon him. Taking from him all authority over the church’s affairs, Proculus ordered that scarcely enough food for each day,
and very meagre food at that, be supplied to him. But through Quintianus’s prayer, Proculus was reproved by the more prudent citizens; when all authority had
been restored, he withdrew from his plots against him. The aforesaid bishop, however, did not forget the injury. As the apostle Paul once spoke of Alexander, so
he often chanted of Proculus: “Proculus the treasurer has done me many evils; may the Lord repay him according to his works.” It is manifest that this later
happened to him.

### 2

**[018]** The blessed man was constant in prayer and loved his people so greatly that, when Theodoric came and surrounded the city with his army, God’s saint
walked around its walls at night singing psalms. Afflicting himself with fasting and vigils, he prayed urgently that the Lord would deign quickly to aid the
region and its people. When King Theodoric was even considering overthrowing the city walls, the Lord’s mercy and the prayer of his priest softened him; he had
been intending to drive Quintianus back into exile. At night he was struck with terror, leapt from his bed, and tried to flee alone along the public road. He
had lost his senses and did not know what he was doing. His men noticed and tried to restrain him, but could scarcely do so; they urged him to protect himself
with the saving sign. Then Hilpingus, his duke, approached the king and said, “Most glorious king, hear the counsel of my littleness. The walls of this city are
very strong, and huge ramparts surround it. That your magnificence may understand more fully, I speak of the saints whose basilicas surround the walls of that
city; moreover, the bishop of that place is held in great esteem before God. Do not do what you are considering. Do not injure the bishop or overthrow the
city.” The king mercifully accepted his counsel and issued an order that no one should be harmed within eight miles of the city. Let no one doubt that this was
granted through the bishop’s intercession. Then that priest Proculus, when the walls of the fortress of Lovolautre were breached, was cut to pieces by sword
blows from the entering enemies before the very altar of the church. As the bishop had often sung, the Lord repaid him according to his works.

### 3

**[019]** After the slaughter of the Auvergne disaster had been completed, Hortensius, one of the senators who held the countship of that city, wickedly ordered
a certain relative of the saint, named Honoratus, to be detained in the city square. This was quickly reported to the blessed man. Through his friends he began
to ask Hortensius to grant a hearing and order Honoratus’s release, but Hortensius refused entirely. The blessed old man then ordered himself to be carried to
the square where Honoratus was held. When he arrived, he asked the soldiers to release him. They were afraid and did not dare obey the bishop. The bishop said,
“Carry me quickly to Hortensius’s house.” He was very old and could not walk on his own feet. When his servants had carried him to Hortensius’s house, he shook
the dust from his shoe upon it and said, “Cursed be this house, and cursed be its inhabitants forever. Let it become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell
in it.” All the people said, “Amen.” He added, “I ask you, Lord, let no one from this family ever be advanced to the episcopal priesthood who does not obey a
bishop.” As soon as the bishop left, all the households in that house were seized by fever; groaning briefly, they breathed out their spirits. When this had
continued until the third day, Hortensius saw that none of his servants were being left to him. Fearing that he too would perish with them, he went sorrowfully
to the holy man, threw himself at his feet, and with tears begged pardon. Quintianus most kindly granted it and sent blessed water to the house. When it had
been sprinkled over the walls, every illness was immediately driven away, and a great miracle appeared there. Those who had fallen ill were healed, and those
who were well did not fall ill again.

### 4

**[020]** This bishop was regarded as learned in the ecclesiastical Scriptures, and he was also magnificent in almsgiving. Whenever he saw a poor man crying
out, he would say, “Help him, I beg you, help him, and supply the poor man with the necessities of life! You are ignorant, sluggards; perhaps it is he himself
who, throughout the course of the Gospel reading, commanded that he should be fed in the least of the poor.” He also cast out demons that confessed him. Coming
to the monastery of Cambidobre, he found a possessed man raging horribly. He sent priests to lay hands on him, but when the evil spirit had not been expelled by
their exorcism, God’s saint drew near, put his fingers into the man’s mouth, and restored the person delivered.

The blessed man performed many other miracles and, after praying, often obtained from the Lord whatever he had asked. On one occasion in Auvergne, a great
drought was consuming everything; the grass was dry, and no fodder at all remained for the animals. God’s saint was devoutly celebrating the rogations held
before the Lord’s Ascension. On the third day, as they were approaching the city gate, the people urged him to deign to begin the antiphon himself, saying, “If
you, blessed bishop, devoutly begin the antiphon, we trust in your holiness that the Lord will immediately deign in his kindly mercy to grant us rain.” He
prostrated himself upon his hair shirt in the street itself and prayed with tears for a very long time. Rising, he began the antiphon they had requested, as was
his power. Its words were taken from Solomon’s prayer: “If heaven is shut and there is no rain because of the people’s sins, and they turn and entreat your
face, hear, Lord, forgive the sins of your people, and give rain to the land which you gave your people to possess.” When they had begun to sing most devoutly,
the confessor’s humble prayer penetrated the ears of the Power on high. Behold, heaven grew dark and was covered with clouds. Before they reached the city gate,
violent rain fell upon that whole land, so that everyone marvelled and said it had been granted through the blessed man’s prayers.

### 5

**[021]** God’s bishop grew old and advanced so far in age that he could not spit upon the ground, but had a small vessel held to his lips into which he
discharged the saliva of his mouth. His eye did not grow dim, nor was his heart turned away from God’s ways. He did not turn his face from the poor or fear the
person of the powerful. One and the same holy freedom was his in all things: he accepted a poor man’s cloak as though he were venerating the toga of a renowned
senator. He died perfect in holiness and was buried in the basilica of Saint Stephen to the left of the altar. At his tomb the fever of quartan patients,
oppressed by melancholy, is often extinguished even now.

## V. The Holy Abbot Portianus

### Prologue

**[022]** How much Almighty God grants to those dedicated to his name, and how much he repays them with the help of his kindness for faithful service! He
promises that he will render great things in heaven, but in this world he often reveals what they are to receive. He frequently makes free people from servants,
and from free people he makes the glorious, according to the psalmist’s saying: “Raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dungheap, that
he may place him with the princes of his people.” Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, also says of this: “Those who were full before hired themselves out for bread,
and the hungry are filled.” Concerning this also the Virgin Mary herself, the mother of our Redeemer, said: “He has put down the mighty from their seat and
exalted the humble.” So the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The first will be last, and the last first.” Divine mercy therefore draws the hearts of the needy
with its love, so that it may make the small great and make co-heirs of his Only-Begotten from the lowest. From this worldly poverty God has appointed him over
heaven, to which earthly dominion could not ascend; thus the rustic goes where the wearer of purple did not deserve to go. So it is now with the blessed Abbot
Portianus: God not only rescued him from the burden of worldly servitude but exalted him with great miracles and, after the world and the afflictions of this
age, established him in eternal rest. He placed him among the choirs of angels, from which that earthly master was excluded.

### 1

**[023]** From his earliest years the most blessed Portianus strove always to seek the God of heaven, even amid earthly servitude. He is said to have been the
slave of a certain barbarian. He often took refuge at a monastery so that the abbot might return him to his master with an excuse. At last he fled, and his
master followed on his heels and began to accuse the abbot, reckoning that the abbot was enticing him away so that his slave would not serve him. When the
master persisted in accusing the abbot and demanding, according to custom, that he return the slave, the abbot said to Portianus, “What do you want me to do?”
He replied, “Return me with an excuse.” After he had been returned with an excuse and his master wished to take him home, the master was so blinded that he
could recognize nothing at all. Perceiving that he was afflicted with severe pain, he called the abbot and said, “Entreat the Lord for me, I beg you, and accept
this slave into his service; perhaps I shall deserve to recover the light I have lost.” Then the abbot called the blessed man and said, “Lay your hands upon his
eyes, I ask you.” Portianus refused, but at last, overcome by the abbot’s entreaties, he placed the sign of the blessed cross over his master’s eyes.
Immediately the darkness was broken, the pain subsided, and the master was restored to his former health.

The blessed Portianus was then made a cleric. He was so distinguished by an accumulation of virtue that, when the abbot died, he succeeded him. It is said that
in summer, when the sun’s heat consumed everything with the force of its warmth and wearied with its burning even the stronger bodies that were refreshed by
food and drink, every trace of moisture was lost from his mouth through fasting. Burning with thirst, he chewed salt and then took a little liquid with which he
briefly moistened his dry gums. Although this moistened his dry palate, it caused greater torment by increasing his body’s thirst. As is hidden from no one,
salt provokes the heat of thirst more than it extinguishes it; but in his case, by the Lord’s gift, thirst was driven away from him.

### 2

**[024]** In those days Theodoric entered the territory of Auvergne, exterminating and devastating everything. When he pitched camp in the meadows of the
village of Artonne, the aforesaid old man hastened to meet him as though to intercede for the people. He entered the camp in the morning while the king was
still sleeping in his tent, and approached the pavilion of Sigivald, who was then held in first place with him. While Portianus complained about this captivity,
Sigivald begged him to deign to take unmixed wine after washing his hands with water, saying, “Divine goodness grants me great joy and advantage today if, after
prayer, you deign to accept a drink within the enclosure of my tent.” He had heard the report of Portianus’s holiness and therefore paid him honour out of
reverence for God. Portianus excused himself in various ways, asserting that it could not be done: the proper hour had not come, he had not yet paid his
respects to the king, and—most important of all—he had not yet rendered to the Lord the psalmody due to him. Setting these objections aside, Sigivald compelled
him by force. When the vessel containing the drink had been brought, he asked the saint to sanctify it by first laying his hand upon it. Portianus raised his
right hand and made the sign of the cross. The vessel split down the middle, and the wine within it poured onto the ground together with an enormous serpent.
Those present were terrified by the sight and fell at the blessed man’s feet; they kissed his footprints and the soles of his feet. All marvelled at the old
man’s power and marvelled that they had been divinely saved from the wicked serpent’s venom. The whole army rushed together at this miracle. The entire
multitude surrounded the blessed man, seizing the fringes of his garment and touching his hand, even if they could not honour him with a kiss. The king also
leapt from his bed and ran to meet the blessed confessor. Without Portianus speaking, he released all the captives for whom the saint was interceding and
afterwards recovered the rest as he wished. With the Lord’s cooperation, Portianus bestowed a double benefit there: he rescued some from death and freed others
from the yoke of captivity. Truly, as I believe—and this is my faith—those saved from this danger were as it were raised from the dead.

### 3

**[025]** I did not wish to pass over the fact that the devil tried to mock him with various devices. Seeing that he could do him no harm, he attacked him in
visible combat. One night, after Portianus had given himself to sleep, he suddenly awoke and saw his cell as though consumed by fire. Terrified, he rose and
went to the door. When he could not unbar it, he prostrated himself in prayer. Making the saving sign before and around himself, he immediately saw the phantom
flames that had appeared vanish, and he knew that this had been the devil’s deception. It was at once revealed to the blessed Protasius, who was then a recluse
in the monastery of Cambidobre. With the greatest haste he sent a monk from his cell to his brother, encouraging him: “Dearest brother, you must resist the
devil’s snares manfully. Fear none of his deceit, but overcome everything he inflicts by constant prayer and by opposing the sign of the cross against it, for
he always strives to assail God’s servants with such temptations.” The blessed man grew old and, having completed the course of good work, departed to the Lord.
His tomb is now often glorified by divine miracles. We have learned only these things about the holy man; we do not criticize others who know greater things
about him if they wish to write anything in his praise.

## VI. Saint Gallus The Bishop

### Prologue

**[026]** The height of worldly nobility always gapes after desires, rejoices in honours, is puffed up by public greetings, pounds the forum with lawsuits,
feeds on plunder, delights in calumnies, and covets talents of tarnished gold. When it seems to possess little, it burns all the more to amass a great deal; the
heaped-up mass of gold brings with it a burning thirst to possess more, as Prudentius says: “For the hunger for gold grows greater from the gold acquired.”
Thus, while nobility rejoices in the pomps of the world and takes pleasure in vain honours, it recalls nothing of the dignities that endure. It does not look to
things unseen, provided only that it possesses at the wrong time those things by which it thinks to satisfy the mind.

But there are those who free themselves from these bonds like birds flying from snares and striving toward higher things by the vigour of an eager mind.
Abandoning and renouncing earthly possessions, they direct all their strength toward heavenly things. Such was Saint Gallus, an inhabitant of the city of
Clermont. Neither splendour of birth, nor the loftiness of senatorial rank, nor abundance of wealth could draw him away from the worship of God. Neither his
father’s affection, nor his mother’s blandishments, nor the love of nurses, nor the compliance of attendants could separate him from the love of God. Counting
all these as nothing and loathing them like dung, he vowed himself to God’s love and service and subjected himself to monastic discipline. He knew that he could
not otherwise overcome the flames of youthful ardour unless he submitted to canonical censure and the severest discipline. He knew that he would raise himself
from worldly humility to higher things and, through patient endurance, be carried to the glory of that lofty summit. The outcome later proved it.

### 1

**[027]** Saint Gallus began to devote himself to God from adolescence. Loving the Lord with his whole soul, he also loved the things he knew were beloved by
God. His father was named Georgius; his mother Leucadia descended from the stock of Vettius Epagathus, whose martyrdom at Lyon Eusebius’s history attests. They
belonged to the foremost senators, so that nothing more well-born or noble could be found in Gaul. When his father wished to seek for him the daughter of a
certain senator, Gallus took one small servant with him and sought the monastery of Cournon, situated six miles from the city of Clermont. He humbly entreated
the abbot to deign to cut the hair of his head. The abbot saw the boy’s prudence and refinement and asked his name, family, and country. Gallus declared that he
was called Gallus, a citizen of Clermont and the son of Georgius the senator. When the abbot learned that he was born of the foremost lineage, he said, “Your
desire is good, my son, but first these things must be brought to your father’s knowledge. If he wishes it, I will do what you ask.” The abbot therefore sent
messengers to the father about this matter to ask what he ordered to be done concerning the boy. Somewhat saddened, the father said, “He was my firstborn, and
for that reason I wished to join him in marriage. But if the Lord deigns to enrol him in his service, let his will rather than ours be done.” He added,
“Whatever the child suggests to you by God’s inspiration, carry it out.”

### 2

**[028]** When the messengers reported this, the abbot made the boy a cleric. Gallus was of remarkable chastity; like an elder, he desired nothing perverse and
even refrained from youthful games. He had a voice of wonderful sweetness and pleasing modulation, devoted himself constantly to reading, delighted in fasting,
and abstained greatly from food. When the blessed Bishop Quintianus came to that monastery and heard him singing, he would no longer allow him to remain there
but brought him to the city and nourished him in spiritual sweetness like a heavenly father. After his father’s death, his voice grew ever more harmonious as
the days passed, and he had the greatest love among the people. These things were reported to King Theodoric, who immediately summoned him and cherished him
with such affection that he loved him more than his own son. The queen also loved him with similar affection, not only for the beauty of his voice but also for
the chastity of his body. King Theodoric then brought many clerics from the citizens of Clermont and ordered them to serve the church of Trier in rendering
service to the Lord, but he would by no means allow the blessed Gallus to be separated from him. Thus, when the king went to the city of Cologne, Gallus went
with him.

There was a certain shrine there filled with various ornaments. The neighbouring barbarians offered libations in it and gorged themselves with food and drink to
the point of vomiting. Worshipping the images there as God, each carved a limb in wood according to the part afflicted by pain. When Saint Gallus heard of this,
he immediately hastened there with only one cleric. When none of the foolish pagans was present, he kindled a fire, applied it to the shrine, and burned it.
Seeing the smoke of the temple rise to heaven, the pagans sought the author of the fire; when they found him, they pursued him with drawn swords. Turning in
flight, he hid himself in the royal hall. After the king learned what had happened, while the pagans uttered threats, he soothed them with gentle words and thus
calmed their wicked fury. The blessed man often used to relate these events with tears and say, “Woe to me, because I did not stand firm so as to be finished in
this cause!” He was then performing the office of deacon.

### 3

**[029]** When the blessed Bishop Quintianus passed from this world at the Lord’s command, Saint Gallus was then residing in the city of Clermont. The citizens
of Clermont gathered at the house of the priest Inpetratus, Gallus’s maternal uncle. They discussed the bishop’s death and asked who ought to be appointed in
his place. After deliberating for a very long time, each returned to his own affairs. After their departure Saint Gallus called one of the clerics and, with the
Holy Spirit rushing upon him, said, “What are these men whispering? Why are they running about? What are they debating? Their work is empty! I shall be bishop;
the Lord will deign to grant me this honour! When you hear that I am returning from the king’s presence, take my predecessor’s saddled horse, go out to meet me,
and present it to me. If you disdain to hear this, take care that you do not regret it later.” He was lying on a small bed as he spoke. The cleric became angry
with him, uttered many reproaches, and struck his side against the rail of the bed, injuring him; then he departed in confusion. When he had gone, the priest
Inpetratus said to the blessed Gallus, “Hear my counsel, my son. Do not delay at all; go to the king and tell him what has happened here. If the Lord inspires
him to grant you this priesthood, we will give great thanks to God. If not, at least you will be commended to the man who has been ordained.” Gallus went and
reported to the king what had happened to the blessed Quintianus.

At that time Aprunculus, bishop of Trier, also died. The clerics of that city assembled and asked King Theodoric for Saint Gallus as bishop. He answered, “Go
away and seek another; I have destined Deacon Gallus for elsewhere.” They then chose and accepted Saint Nicetius as bishop. The clerics of Clermont came to the
king with the consent of foolish men and with many gifts. That wicked seed had already begun to bear fruit: the priesthood was either sold by kings or purchased
by clerics. They then heard from the king that they were to have Saint Gallus as bishop. The king ordered that, after Gallus had been ordained priest and
expenses had been provided from public funds, the citizens should be invited to a banquet and rejoice over the honour of their future bishop Gallus. This was
done. Gallus used to relate that he had given no more for his episcopate than one triens to the cook who served the meal. Afterwards the king gave him two
bishops as companions and sent him to Clermont. That cleric named Viventius, who had injured his side against the bedrail, hastened according to Gallus’s word
to meet the bishop, not without great shame, and presented both himself and the horse Gallus had ordered. When both entered the bath, the cleric concealed his
pain; Gallus gently teased him about the injury he had incurred from the impulse of the cleric’s pride, causing him great embarrassment, but without anger,
taking pleasure only in spiritual jest. Gallus was then received into the city with much psalmody and ordained bishop in his church.

### 4

**[030]** Once he had assumed the episcopate, he treated everyone with such humility and charity that he was loved by all. He possessed patience beyond human
custom, so that, if it is permissible to say so, he could be compared to Moses in enduring various injuries. Thus, when his own priest struck him on the head at
a banquet, he remained so quiet that he did not return even a harsh word. Bearing patiently everything that happened to him, he cast it upon God’s judgment, by
whom he asked to be nurtured. A certain Evodius, a priest from the senatorial order, also attacked him with many calumnies and insults at a church banquet. The
bishop rose and went around the precincts of the holy basilicas. When this was reported to Evodius, he sent runners quickly after Gallus and, throwing himself
at his feet in the street itself, begged pardon, entreating that Gallus’s prayer with the Almighty Judge would not condemn him. Gallus kindly raised him and
mercifully forgave everything he had said. He admonished him never again to dare to attack the Lord’s bishops in this way, because he himself would never
deserve to receive the episcopate. The outcome later proved this. In the Gévaudan, when Evodius had already been elected to the episcopate, had already been
placed on the throne, and everything was prepared for him to be blessed as bishop, the whole people suddenly rose against him so violently that he could
scarcely escape alive. He later died a priest.

### 5

**[031]** In the city of Orléans, after Bishop Marcus had been accused by wicked men and driven into exile, a great assembly of bishops was gathered at King
Childebert’s command. In that synod the blessed bishops recognized that the whispered charge against him was empty and restored him to his city and his throne.
On that occasion the deacon Valentinianus, who is now a priest and singer, went in the service of Saint Gallus. While another bishop was celebrating Mass, this
deacon wished to sing more out of vainglory than from fear of God, but Saint Gallus prevented him, saying, “Allow it, my son: when we celebrate the solemnities
at the Lord’s command, then you too should sing. Now let the clerics of the bishop who is consecrating the Mass sing together.” Valentinianus declared that he
could sing even then. The bishop answered, “Do as you please; you will not accomplish what you wish.” Disregarding the bishop’s command, he went and sang so
badly that everyone ridiculed him. On another Sunday, when the oft-mentioned bishop was celebrating Mass, he ordered him to go: “Now, in the Lord’s name, you
will perform what you wish.” When he did so, his voice was so splendid that everyone praised him. O blessed man, to whom such grace was granted that, like
souls, human voices also were under his authority when they were with him: he prevented them from singing when he wished and permitted them to sing when it
pleased him.

### 6

**[032]** God performed other great miracles through him. Julian the defender, afterwards a priest and a man of the sweetest disposition, was seized by a
quartan fever and grievously tormented. He sought the holy bishop’s bed. Lying in it, covered by the bishop’s own bedclothes, he slept briefly and was so healed
that he was never again shaken by that infirmity.

When the city of Clermont was being consumed by a very great fire and the saint learned of it, he entered the church and entreated the Lord for a very long time
with tears before the holy altar. Rising, he took up the Gospels, opened them, and went to meet the fire. At the sight of him and of what had been prepared
against it, the whole conflagration was immediately extinguished so completely that not even fiery embers remained in it. In his time the city of Clermont was
also shaken by a great earthquake. We do not know why this happened, but we know that it injured none of the people.

When the plague called the inguinal pestilence was raging through various regions and was then devastating most severely the province of Arles, Saint Gallus was
afraid not so much for himself as for his people. Day and night he entreated the Lord not to let him see his people laid waste while he lived. An angel of the
Lord appeared to him in a vision at night, with both hair and clothing as white as snow, and said, “Divine goodness looks favourably upon you, O bishop, as you
intercede for your people. Do not be afraid, for your prayer has been heard. Behold, you and your people will be delivered from this disease; while you live, no
one in this region will perish from this destruction. Do not fear now, but after eight years, be afraid.” It was later manifest that, after those years had
passed, he departed from the world. He awoke and gave thanks to God for this consolation, because God had deigned to strengthen him through a heavenly
messenger. He instituted those rogations in which, at mid-Lent, the people were to come on foot singing psalms to the basilica of the blessed martyr Julian. The
journey is about 360 stades. While that plague consumed other regions, as we have said, it did not touch the city of Clermont because Saint Gallus’s prayer
interceded. I therefore consider it no small grace that he, placed as a shepherd, deserved not to see his sheep devoured while the Lord defended them.

### 7

**[033]** Let us come to the time when the Lord commanded him to be taken from this world. As he lay oppressed by illness, an internal fever so consumed all his
members that he lost both hair and beard. Knowing by the Lord’s revelation that he would depart after three days, he called the people together and, breaking
bread, distributed communion to everyone with holy and loving intent. When the third day came—it was the Lord’s Day, which brought immense grief to the citizens
of Clermont—he asked, as heaven was already growing light, what they were singing in church. They said that they were singing the blessing. He then completed
matins with the fiftieth psalm, the sung blessing, and an alleluia with its little chapter. When that office had been performed, he said, “We bid you farewell,
brothers.” Saying this, he stretched out his limbs and sent his spirit, fixed upon heaven, ahead to the Lord. He died in the sixty-fifth year of his age and the
twenty-seventh year of his episcopate. He was then washed, clothed, and carried into the church until the bishops of the province could gather to bury him.

A great miracle was shown to the people there: God’s saint drew his right foot toward himself on the bier and turned onto his other side, toward the altar.
While these things were happening, the rogations held after Easter were being celebrated. He lay in the church for three days amid continuous psalmody and a
great crowd of people. When the bishops arrived on the fourth day, they lifted him from the church, carried him to the basilica of Saint Lawrence, and buried
him. The number of mourners and the size of the lamentation at his funeral can scarcely be described. Women in dark garments, as though they had lost their
husbands, and likewise men with covered heads, as is customary at wives’ funerals, followed in mourning. The Jews themselves also followed, lamenting with
lighted lamps. All the people said with one voice, “Woe to us! After this day we shall never deserve to have another bishop like him.” Because the provincial
bishops were far away, as we have said, and could not come sooner, the faithful placed a sod of earth over the blessed body, as is the custom of rustics, so
that it would not swell from the heat. After his funeral a certain woman named Meratina—truly, as I carefully ascertained, a most pure virgin devoted to
God—gathered the sod after it had been thrown away by others and placed it in her garden. She often watered it, and with the Lord giving increase, she made it
live. Sick people not only took grass from this sod and drank it and were healed, but the faithful prayer offered over it also obtained aid. Later, when the
virgin departed, it perished through neglect.

Many miracles were shown at his tomb. Those with quartan or various other fevers, as soon as they faithfully approach the blessed tomb, immediately receive
health. Valentinianus the singer, mentioned above, who is now a priest, was seized by a quartan fever while he was performing the office of deacon and suffered
for many days in great weakness. On a day when this fever attacked him, he resolved to go around the holy places praying. Coming to this saint’s tomb, he
prostrated himself and said, “Remember me, most blessed and holy bishop. I was instructed, taught, and encouraged by you. Remember your own pupil, whom you
loved with singular affection, and rescue me from this fever by which I am held.” Having spoken, he gathered the little herbs which devout people had scattered
over the tomb in the bishop’s honour. Because they were green, he put them in his mouth, chewed them with his teeth, and swallowed their juice. That day passed
without an attack of the illness, and thereafter he was so restored to health that he no longer suffered what the common people call relapses. I learned that
this happened just as I have related from the priest’s own mouth. There is no doubt that he who called Lazarus from the tomb displays miracles from the tombs of
his servants through his own power.

## VII. Saint Gregory The Bishop

### Prologue

**[034]** Men of outstanding holiness, whom the palm of perfect blessedness has raised from the earth and carried to heaven, are those whom either the bond of
unfeigned charity binds, or the fruit of almsgiving enriches, or the flower of chastity adorns, or the certain struggle of martyrdom crowns. Their zeal for
beginning the work of perfect justice was above all to prepare the body without stain and offer it as a dwelling for the Holy Spirit, and thus to strive toward
the heights of the other virtues. Becoming persecutors of themselves, they slaughtered their own vices within themselves and, like proven martyrs, triumphed
after completing the course of their lawful contest. No one can accomplish this without God’s help unless protected by the shield or helmet of the Lord’s aid;
whatever he achieves, he must ascribe not to himself but to the glory of the divine name, according to the apostle’s saying: “Let him who glories glory in the
Lord.” The blessed Gregory also brought all glory to this rule. From the lofty power of senatorial rank he subjected himself to such humility that, casting away
all worldly cares, he dedicated himself solely to the work of God, whom he kept in his heart.

### 1

**[035]** Saint Gregory, one of the foremost senators and well instructed in letters, sought the countship of the city of Autun. Holding the countship, he
governed that region for forty years with justice as his companion. He was so severe and strict toward evildoers that scarcely any guilty person could escape
him. He had a wife of senatorial birth named Armentaria, whom he is said to have known only for the procreation of children; by the Lord’s gift he had sons by
her. It never happened that he burned with desire for another woman, as youthful ardour often does.

### 2

**[036]** After his wife’s death he turned to the Lord. Chosen by the people, he was ordained bishop of the city of Langres. His abstinence was great, but so
that it would not be thought vainglory, he secretly placed other thin loaves of barley beneath wheaten loaves. Breaking the wheat bread, he distributed it to
others, while he himself ate the barley in secret without anyone knowing. He acted similarly with wine: when the cupbearer offered him wine, he ordered water to
be poured over it to disguise the water, choosing a glass that concealed the water’s clearness. In fasting, almsgiving, prayer, and vigils he was so effective
and devout that, though placed in the midst of the world, he shone like a new hermit.

When he was staying constantly at the fortress of Dijon, his house adjoined the baptistery in which relics of many saints were kept. At night, without anyone
noticing, he rose from his bed and went to pray with God alone as witness. The door was divinely unbarred, and he sang psalms intently in the baptistery. After
he had done this for a long time, the matter was at last discovered and disclosed by one deacon. When the deacon learned that these things were happening, he
followed at a distance so that the blessed man could not perceive him, and waited to see what he did. He observed that when God’s saint came to the door of the
baptistery and knocked with his own hand, the door opened with no one appearing. After Gregory entered, there was silence for a very long time. Afterwards the
singing of what sounded like many voices was heard for three hours and almost longer. I believe that, because the relics of great saints were kept in that
place, they revealed themselves to the blessed man and joined with him in rendering psalmody to the Lord. When the course was completed and he returned to his
bed, he laid himself so cautiously upon the bedding that absolutely no one noticed. The attendants found the baptistery door barred and opened it with their own
key as usual. When the signal sounded, God’s saint rose for the Lord’s office like the others, as though newly awakened.

On the first day of his episcopate, possessed people confessed him. The priests asked him to deign to bless them. He manfully refused so as not to incur vain
glory, crying out that he was an unworthy minister for revealing the Lord’s miracles. But because he could no longer conceal it, he ordered them brought to him.
Without any touch, merely making the sign of the cross against them, he commanded the demons by his word to depart. Hearing this, they immediately released the
bodies their wickedness had bound. Even in his absence, many possessed people who were suspended and marked with the rod he used to carry in his hand were
delivered. If any sick person took something from his bed, it was an immediate remedy.

His granddaughter Armentaria was once grievously afflicted in adolescence by a quartan fever. Though often treated by the care of physicians, she could feel no
relief. The blessed confessor himself often urged her to persevere in prayer. One day she sought his bed; lying in it, every fever was so extinguished that she
was never again ill with it.

### 3

**[037]** Saint Gregory travelled to the city of Langres for the holy day of Epiphany. Stricken by a slight fever, he left the world and departed to Christ.
After his passing his blessed face was so glorified that it looked like roses. His face appeared red, while the rest of his body shone like a gleaming white
lily, so that you would think he had already then been prepared for the glory of the future resurrection. When they were carrying him to the fortress of Dijon,
where he had ordered himself to be buried, he became heavy in that open country not far from the fortress on the northern side. The bearers, unable to sustain
the bier, set it on the ground. After briefly recovering their strength and lifting it again a little later, they carried him to the church within the walls.
When the bishops arrived on the fifth day, he was carried from the church to the basilica of the blessed John. Behold, the prisoners in chains began to cry out
to the blessed body, saying, “Have mercy on us, most merciful lord. Deign to release us, whom you did not release while living in the world, now that you are
dead and possess the heavenly kingdom. Visit us, we beg you, and have mercy on us.” As they cried these and other things, the body became so heavy that the
bearers could not sustain it at all. Setting the bier on the ground, they waited for the blessed bishop’s power. While they waited, the prison doors suddenly
opened. The beam by which the prisoners’ feet were confined drove back its bolts and split down the middle; the chains were broken, and all were released
together. With no one restraining them, they came to the blessed body. The bearers then lifted the bier, and these men served among the rest; afterwards they
were dismissed by the judge without any penalty.

### 4

**[038]** Afterwards the blessed confessor was buried and manifested himself by many miracles. A certain religious man declared that on the day of his burial he
had seen the heavens opened. There is no doubt that, after the angelic acts, Gregory was gathered into the starry companies. A prisoner was being led along the
road by which the blessed body had been brought from Langres to the aforesaid fortress. Soldiers on horseback went ahead, dragging the bound man behind them.
They came to the place where the blessed confessor’s limbs had rested. As they passed it, the prisoner invoked the blessed bishop’s name and asked that his
mercy would free him. While he prayed, the nooses on his hands loosened. Feeling himself released, he remained quiet and kept his hands covered, so that he was
still thought to be bound. When they entered the gate of the fortress and came before the church courtyard, he leapt forward, threw the strap of the bonds into
the faces of those dragging him, and sought the church, through which he was freed with the help of Almighty God and by the blessed bishop’s intercession.

Another admirable miracle showed how glorious his blessed body appeared when it was transferred after a long time. The blessed bishop had been buried in a
corner of the basilica. That place was small, and the people could not approach it as devotion required. His son and successor Saint Tetricus saw this and
observed that miracles were continually performed there. He laid foundations before the altar of the basilica, erected an apse, and constructed and vaulted it
with marvellous workmanship. When the vault was finished and the wall broken through, he built an arch. After this work had been completed and adorned, he dug a
burial place in the middle of the apse. Wishing to transfer his blessed father’s body there, he called together priests and abbots for that office. Watching,
they prayed that the blessed confessor would permit himself to be transferred to this prepared dwelling. At daybreak, with choirs singing psalms, they took up
the sarcophagus and carried it before the altar into the apse which the blessed bishop had built. While they were carefully arranging the tomb, suddenly—and, I
believe, at God’s command—the lid of the sarcophagus moved on one side. Behold, his blessed face appeared so whole and unharmed that you would think he was not
dead but sleeping. Nothing of the very garment placed with him was shown to have decayed. He rightly appeared glorious after his passing, for his flesh had not
been corrupted in mockery. Great is the integrity of body and heart which bestows grace in the present world and grants eternal life in the world to come; of it
the apostle Paul says: “Follow peace and sanctification, without which no one will see the kingdom of God.”

### 5

**[039]** On the Lord’s Day a certain girl was arranging her hair. She took up a comb, and—I believe because of an offence against the holy day—it adhered to
her hands. Its fixed teeth caused her great pain in both fingers and palms. Weeping and entreating, she went around the basilicas of the saints; trusting in the
power of the blessed Bishop Gregory, she prostrated herself at his tomb. After she had implored the blessed confessor’s aid for a very long time, her hand was
restored to its former use, and the comb fell away. Possessed people confessing him are also often cleansed at his tomb. After his passing we often saw them
fastened to the walls by the little rod mentioned above, which he used to carry in his hand, as though they were held by strong and very sharp stakes.

### 6

**[040]** We know many other deeds concerning him, but lest they provoke weariness, we have touched briefly upon a few out of many. He died in the thirty-third
year of his episcopate, at ninety years of age, and has often manifested himself by evident miracles.

## VIII. Saint Nicetius, Bishop Of Lyon

### Prologue

**[041]** The oracles of sacred Scripture often bear witness to the good of the divine foreknowledge, by which God frequently provides for his kingdom those
whom he will adopt. So the mystical utterances of the heavenly mouth were brought to Jeremiah, that excellent prophet: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew
you; and before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you.” What does the Lord himself, the founder of both Testaments, say when he places at his right hand
those whom his generous bounty has adorned with the lamb’s fleece? “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”
The blessed apostle, that vessel of election, likewise says: “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” Concerning
Isaac and John also, God foretold both name and work and merit: how they would be born and what they would do. So now, concerning the blessed Nicetius, that
ancient compassion of mercy itself—which enriches the undeserving, sanctifies the unborn, and arranges and orders all things before they are brought
forth—wished to reveal beforehand to his mother with what insignia of priestly grace he would flourish on earth.

A small book about his life, composed by I know not whom, is preserved with me. It discloses many of his miracles, but does not clearly set forth either the
beginning of his birth and conversion or the sequence of his miracles. Although I have not discovered all his miracles which the Lord deigned to perform through
him either secretly or publicly, I have nevertheless taken care to set forth, though in a rather rustic style, those which did not reach the earlier author.

### 1

**[042]** A certain Florentinus, one of the senators, had taken Artemia as his wife and already had two children when he was sought for the episcopate of the
city of Geneva. Having obtained the consent of the prince, he returned home and told his wife what he had done. Hearing this, she answered her husband, “I beg
you, sweetest husband, desist from this course and do not seek the episcopate of the city, for I carry in my womb a bishop conceived from the seed taken from
you.” The wise man listened to his wife and desisted, remembering what the divine voice had once commanded the blessed Abraham at the beginning of our faith:
“Whatever Sarah says to you, hear her voice.” When the days of her delivery were completed, the woman gave birth to a boy. At baptism she called him Nicetius,
as one who would be a future conqueror of the world. She had him reared with the greatest diligence and instructed in ecclesiastical letters.

After his father’s death, Nicetius, now a cleric, remained with his mother in his paternal home and worked with his own hands among the other servants,
understanding that bodily disturbances could only be suppressed by labour and hardship. Once, while he was still living in that house, a malignant pustule arose
on his face. The poison grew stronger and consumed him until the boy was despaired of. His mother continually invoked the name of the blessed Martin more
particularly than the many names of the saints for his recovery. The boy lay in bed for two days with closed eyes and offered no word of consolation to his
lamenting mother. His mother, wavering between hope and fear, prepared the necessities for his funeral according to the rite of burial. On the second day toward
evening he opened his eyes and said, “Where has my mother gone?” She came at once and said, “Here I am; what do you want, my son?” He said, “Do not be afraid,
mother. The blessed Martin made the cross of Christ over me and commanded me to rise unharmed.” As soon as he had spoken, he rose from the bed. Divine power
doubled the grace of this miracle, both revealing Martin’s merit and saving from the contagion one who was to be a bishop. The scar visible on his face was a
witness to this event.

### 2

**[043]** At thirty years of age he was honoured with the priesthood. He by no means refrained from the labour he had previously undertaken, but always worked
with his own hands among the servants, fulfilling the apostle’s command: “Labour with your own hands, so that you may have something to give to those suffering
need.” He took particular care that all the boys born in his house, as soon as they left the cries of infancy and began to speak, should immediately be taught
letters and imbued with the psalms. Thus, when he entered the oratory to complete the course, he would be joined by such psalm-singers that he could fulfil both
the antiphons and the various meditations as the devotion of his mind required. He not only preserved his own chastity but continually preached to others the
grace of preserving it, teaching them to abstain from polluted touch and obscene words.

I recall that in my adolescence, when I had first begun to recognize the elements of letters and was about eight years old, he ordered unworthy me to be placed
on his bed and received me in his arms with the sweetness of paternal affection. Taking the edge of his garment in his fingers, he wrapped himself in his tunic
so carefully that my limbs never touched his blessed members. Observe, I beg you, and consider the caution of this man of God! If he kept himself from being
touched by the limbs of a little boy in whom there could as yet be no stings of concupiscence or incitements to wantonness, how did he flee from a place where
suspicion of wantonness could exist? As we have said, he was chaste in body and pure in heart. He uttered no scurrilous words but always spoke the things of
God. Although he loved all people with that bond of heavenly charity, he was so obedient to his mother that he obeyed her as a servant obeys a burden laid upon
him.

### 3

**[044]** When Sacerdos, bishop of Lyon, fell ill in the city of Paris, he was loved with great affection by Childebert the elder. The king wished to go to his
bedside and visit the sick man. When he came, the bishop said, “Most merciful king, you know very well that I have served you faithfully in all your necessities
and have devoutly fulfilled whatever you commanded. Now, because the time of my dissolution is at hand, I beg you not to let me depart from this world in
sorrow, but willingly to grant one petition that I ask.” The king said, “Ask; you will obtain whatever you wish.” Sacerdos said, “I ask that my nephew, the
priest Nicetius, be appointed bishop of the church of Lyon. As the words of my testimony declare, he is a lover of chastity and of churches, very devoted to
almsgiving, and whatever belongs to God’s servants he carries out both in works and in conduct.” The king answered, “Let God’s will be done” . . . and a lover
of peace. If anyone injured him, he either immediately granted pardon himself or sent word through another person to beg pardon.

I once saw him send the priest Basilius to Count Armentarius, who in those days governed the city of Lyon with judicial authority. He said to him, “Our bishop
brought this case, which is being attacked afresh, to an end by giving judgment; he therefore warns you not to presume to reopen it.” Inflamed with fury,
Armentarius answered the priest, “Go and tell him that many cases placed before him will have to be ended by another’s judgment.” The priest returned and simply
reported what he had heard. Saint Nicetius was angered against him and said, “Truly I say, you will not receive the blessing from my hand, because you have
brought to my ears words extorted by fury.” He was reclining at a banquet, and I, who was then performing the office of deacon, had reclined close to his left.
He said to me privately, “Speak to the priests, so that they may intercede for him.” When I had spoken, they did not understand the saint’s wish and remained
silent. Seeing this, he said, “You rise and intercede for him.” I rose trembling, kissed his holy knees, and prayed for the priest. Nicetius relented and
offered the blessing, saying, “Dearest brothers, I ask that useless words, idly whispered, may not beat upon my ears. It is not right for rational people to
entertain the insolent words of irrational people. You ought to take care only that those who wish to contrive anything against the church’s interests are
confounded by your proposals. I desire not only not to admire irrational things but not even to hear them.” O blessed man, who wished with every intention to
avoid scandal!

Let those hear this who, when offended, refuse to forgive. Calling together the whole city to avenge themselves, they do not fear even to bring forward
witnesses who say with wicked voices, “We heard this and that from him speaking against you.” Thus Christ’s poor are oppressed by such accusations while mercy
is set aside.

### 4

**[045]** One morning Saint Nicetius rose for matins. After two antiphons had been sung, he entered the sanctuary. While he was seated there, a deacon began to
sing a responsorial psalm. Nicetius was moved and said, “Let him be silent, be silent! Let not the enemy of justice presume to sing.” Faster than it takes to
tell, the deacon’s mouth was stopped and he fell silent. The saint ordered him to be called and said, “Had I not commanded you not to enter God’s church? Why
have you presumed to enter with rash daring? Why did you dare to raise your voice in the Lord’s songs?” All present were astonished and knew no evil about the
deacon. Then the demon in him cried out and confessed that it was being tormented by the saint with immense agonies. The deacon had presumed to sing in church;
though the people did not know his voice, the saint recognized it and execrated him with the sharpest words. The saint then laid hands on the deacon, cast out
the demon, and restored the man to a sound mind.

### 5

**[046]** Having manifested himself among the people by these and other signs, he departed to Christ in the twenty-second year of his episcopate, at sixty years
of age. While he was being carried for burial, a certain blind man asked to be brought beneath the bier. As soon as he entered under it, his face, long deprived
of light, was adorned with opened eyes. Divine goodness did not delay to glorify his blessed limbs with signs while it received his blessed soul among the stars
with the angelic choirs.

After the days established by Roman law for the public reading of a deceased person’s will, this bishop’s testament was brought into the forum and, with crowds
standing around, was unsealed and read by the judge. A priest of the basilica, swelling with bile because Nicetius had left nothing to the place where he had
been buried, said, “Many people always claimed that Nicetius was stupid. Now it is plainly shown to be true, since he bequeathed nothing to the basilica in
which he is buried.” The following night Nicetius appeared to the priest with two bishops, Justus and Eucherius, in shining vesture. He said to them, “Holiest
brothers, this priest overwhelms me with blasphemies, saying that I left no property to this church where I rest. He does not know that I left there whatever
most precious thing I had: the clod of my body.” They said, “He acted unjustly in disparaging God’s servant.” The saint turned to the priest and struck his
throat with fists and palms, saying, “Sinner who must be crushed, cease speaking foolishly!” The priest awoke with swollen jaws and was so constricted by pain
that he could swallow even the saliva of his mouth only with the greatest difficulty. He lay in bed for forty days in grievous torment. But after invoking the
confessor’s name, he was restored to health and never again dared to utter the words he had previously presumed to speak.

Because I know that Bishop Priscus was always hostile to this saint, he gave this man’s chasuble to a certain deacon. It was very large because the man of God
himself had been robust in body. The hood of this garment was widened and sewn as is usually done with the white vestments placed on bishops’ shoulders during
the Easter feasts. The deacon went about wearing this garment and cared little to whom it had belonged. He kept it on his bed and used it in the forum; if firm
faith had been present, health could have been restored to the sick from its fringes. Someone said to him, “Deacon, if you knew God’s power and who he was whose
garment you use, you ought to conduct yourself more cautiously with it.” He replied, “Truly I tell you, I use this chasuble as a blanket, and from the longer
part of its hood I shall cut a covering for my feet.” The wretch immediately did as he had promised, and at once received the vengeance of divine judgment. When
he had cut the hood and fitted coverings over his feet, he was immediately seized by a demon and fell onto the pavement. He was alone in the house, and there
was no one to help the wretch. As he spat bloody foam from his mouth, his feet stretched toward the hearth, and the fire devoured his feet together with the
coverings. So much for acts of vengeance.

### 6

**[047]** Our deacon Agiulfus also came from Rome bringing me blessed pledges of the saints. Solely for the sake of prayer, he visited the place where the saint
rests. Entering the shrine and considering the illustrious work of various miracles, he saw an immense crowd streaming to his tomb like swarms of happy bees
gathering at their accustomed hive. Some, served by the priest who was present, took little particles of wax for a blessing; others took a little dust; some
took threads torn from its covering and departed, all bearing away one grace of healing for different needs. Struck with faith at this sight, Agiulfus said
tearfully, “If devotion to the deed of my own bishop caused me to furrow the mass of sea waves with oars, so that, after visiting the tombs of the eastern
martyrs, I ought to bring back some pledge from them, why should I not take pledges of my own Gallic confessor, through which complete health may be restored to
me and mine?” He immediately approached and, with hands covered by a cloth, received from the offering priest certain little herbs which the people’s devotion
had cast onto the sacred tomb. He stored them away and carefully carried them home. The working of miracles immediately confirmed the man’s faith. Leaves torn
from these herbs were offered to fever patients with a drink of water; as soon as they drank, it brought health, and it did so for many afterwards. When he told
me these things, he reported that four people had already been cured of this infirmity by them.

My priest John, returning from the city of Marseille with him in the course of his business, prostrated himself in prayer at this saint’s tomb. Rising, he saw
broken fetters and broken links of chains which had bound the necks of guilty people or rubbed their legs raw, and he marvelled. This sight was not devoid of
miracles. When the priest returned to me, he asserted under oath that in his presence three blind people there had been restored to sight and had returned home
healed. In the Gallic city of Orléans also, while his relics were being carried with honour and psalmody, the Lord deigned to bestow such grace that those who
humbly worshipped, both blind and lame, recovered sight and the power to walk. No one could doubt that the confessor was present when they saw such gifts of
healing ministered to the sick.

### 7

**[048]** A sedition arose in a certain place. As the mob raged and stones and firebrands flew, fury supplied no ordinary weapons. One man struck another with
the point of a raised sword in a violent assault. A few days later the slain man’s brother caught the assailant and slaughtered him in a similar death. When the
judge of that place learned of it, he ordered the man to be bound, beaten, and thrust back into prison, saying, “This criminal deserves to perish by death,
because by the decision of his own will, without awaiting a judge, he rashly dared to avenge his brother’s death.” While he was held in custody, he invoked the
names of many saints and prayed for mercy. Then, turning as it were directly to God’s saint, he said, “I have heard of you, Saint Nicetius, that you are
powerful in the work of mercy and merciful in releasing prisoners who weep. I now entreat you to deign to visit me with that surpassing mercy by which you have
often become renowned for releasing other prisoners.” Soon he fell asleep, and the blessed man appeared to him, saying, “Who are you who invoke the name of
Nicetius? How do you know who he was, that you do not cease to entreat him?” The prisoner explained the cause of his offence in order and added, “Have mercy on
me, I beg you, if you are the man of God whom I invoke.” The saint said, “Rise in Christ’s name and walk free; no one will seize you.” Awaking at this voice, he
marvelled to find himself released, his chains broken and the beam shattered. Without delay and with no one restraining him, he went fearlessly to Nicetius’s
tomb. The judge then remitted the condemnation for his fatal offence, and he departed free to his own home.

### 8

**[049]** It is pleasing to add to these miracles what kindled lamps have done at his bed, because the things this saint, dwelling in heaven, performs on earth
are immense. The little bed on which the saint used to rest is often adorned with illustrious miracles. Bishop Aetherius has now had it made with great care,
and he worships it most devoutly, and rightly so. Fever patients often lie beneath it; when heat and chill are suppressed, they are healed, and other sick
people laid there are immediately raised up. It is covered by a beautiful pall, and wooden lamps are continually kindled upon it. One of these, as the sacristan
himself asserted, remained shining for forty days and as many nights without the help of any fuel. No papyrus was added, nor was a drop of oil poured in; it
remained in brilliant light in the same arrangement in which it had first been set.

Gallomagnus, bishop of Troyes, devoutly sought this saint’s relics. As they were brought away with psalmody, the eyes of the blind were enlightened by their
power, and other kinds of disease also deserved to receive medicine. A face-cloth woven with hanging tufts of wool, which the saint had on his head on the day
of his death, was also brought to me; I received it as a heavenly gift.

After many days it happened that I was invited to bless a church in the parish of Paternacum in the city of Tours. I confess that I went, consecrated the altar,
tore threads from the linen cloth, and placed them in the church. After Mass had been said and prayer offered, I departed. A few days later the man who had
invited me came and said, “Rejoice in the Lord’s name, bishop of God, at the power of the blessed Bishop Nicetius. Know that he has shown a great miracle in the
church you consecrated. There was a blind man in my district held in lasting darkness. A man appeared to him in a vision at night and said, ‘If you wish to
become well, prostrate yourself in prayer before the altar in the basilica of Saint Nicetius, and you will recover your sight.’ When he did this, the darkness
was broken and divine power opened the light to him.” I confess that I placed pledges from these relics on the altars of other basilicas as well. Possessed
people confess the saint in them, and faithful prayer often obtains its effect.

A servant of Bishop Phronimius of Agde was afflicted by attacks of epilepsy, so that he often fell and foamed, lacerating his tongue with his own teeth.
Physicians did many things for him, and it happened that, after a few months, the disease did not touch him; but falling again into renewed torment, he suffered
worse than before. When his master saw that such great miracles were occurring at the blessed Nicetius’s tomb, he said to him, “Go and prostrate yourself before
the saint’s tomb, praying that he deign to help you.” When the servant had carried out these instructions, he returned healed, and the disease never touched him
again. It was the seventh year of the boy’s good health when the bishop presented him to me.

### 9

**[050]** While the saint was alive, a certain poor man obtained from him a letter signed in his own hand, authorizing him to beg alms through the houses of
devout people. After Nicetius’s death the poor man still went around with this letter and received no small gifts from almsgivers in memory of the saint.
Everyone who saw the saint’s signature desired to offer something to the needy man. A certain Burgundio saw this. Without honouring or venerating the saint, he
began to watch the poor man from a distance. Seeing him enter the woods, Burgundio attacked him, took six gold pieces together with the letter, and left him
half dead after kicking him. Amid the kicks and other blows the poor man cried, “I adjure you by the living God and the power of Saint Nicetius to have at least
his letter returned to me, for I shall have no more life if I lose it.” Burgundio threw it on the ground and went away. The poor man picked it up and came to
the city. Bishop Phronimius, mentioned above, was there at that time. The poor man approached him and said, “There is the man who beat me severely and robbed
me; he took six gold pieces which I had received because of my regard for Saint Nicetius’s letter.” The bishop reported this to the count. The judge called
Burgundio and began to question him about what he would say. He denied it before everyone, saying, “I have never seen this man or taken his property.” The
bishop looked at the letter and saw the saint’s signature. Turning to Burgundio, he said, “Behold, the signature of Saint Nicetius is contained in this letter!
If you are innocent, come closer and swear while touching with your hand the writing he himself traced. We trust in his power that he will either prove you
guilty of this crime today or certainly allow you to depart innocent.” Without delay Burgundio approached the bishop’s hands as he held the letter extended.
Raising his hands to take the oath, he fell backward on his back. With eyes closed and foam coming from his mouth, he was thought to be dead. After about two
hours he opened his eyes and said, “Woe to me! I have sinned by taking this poor man’s property!” He immediately related in order how he had injured the man.
The bishop then obtained the count’s pardon for the offence; Burgundio returned to the needy man only what he had taken and added two solidi for the beating.
Both then departed from the judge’s presence.

### 10

**[051]** How many bound in prison chains have been released through this saint, and how many prisoners’ chains or fetters have been broken, is witnessed today
by that mass of iron gathered from the aforesaid punishments and seen in his basilica. Recently, in the presence of King Guntram, I heard Siagrius, bishop of
Autun, tell the king that the blessed man appeared in prisons in seven cities in one night, released them from confinement, and allowed them to depart free. The
judges did not afterwards dare to take any action against them. If a person suffering fever, chills, or various diseases takes dust from his tomb and receives
it mixed with water, he soon recovers health. There is no doubt that he grants this who said to his saints: “Whatever you ask in my name, believe that you will
receive it, and it will come to you.”

### 11

**[052]** In the village of Prisciniacum in the city of Tours, a church built long ago was without pledges of the saints. When the inhabitants of the place
often asked me to consecrate it with the ashes of certain saints, I placed some of the aforesaid relics on the holy altar. The Lord’s power is often manifested
in that church through the blessed bishop. Most recently three women from the territory of Bourges, tormented by a demon, were being led to the basilica of
Saint Martin and entered this church. Striking their palms against themselves and confessing that they were being tormented by Saint Nicetius’s miracles, they
spat from their mouths something purulent mixed with blood and were immediately cleansed of the possessing spirits.

One of these rustics, named Dado, went to the battle fought at Convenues and often rushed into mortal dangers. He vowed that if he returned home unharmed, he
would give some of what he had acquired to adorn the aforesaid church in honour of the blessed Nicetius. On his return he brought two silver chalices and vowed
again on the journey that he would present them to the church if he reached his own home safely. When he arrived home, he gave only one and tried to withhold
the other, giving instead a Sarmatian covering with which the Lord’s altar and the offerings might be covered. The blessed man appeared to him in a dream and
said, “How long will you hesitate and pretend to fulfil your vow? Go, then, and return to the church the other chalice you vowed, lest you and your house
perish! As for the covering, because it is rare, it is not to be placed over the gifts of the altar, since it does not fully cover the mystery of the Lord’s
body and blood.” Terrified, he delayed nothing and quickly fulfilled the vow he had made.

This man’s brother came to the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity and advised the priest, “Let us keep watch together with one accord in God’s church and devoutly
entreat the blessed Nicetius’s power, so that by his intercession we may pass the course of this year in peace.” The priest heard this with joy and ordered the
signal for vigils to be sounded. When it sounded and the priest came with the clerics and the rest of the people, this man, gaping after gluttony, kept delaying
his arrival. The priest repeatedly sent for him. He answered, “Wait a little, and I will come.” Why say more? The vigils passed, daylight came, and the man who
had first urged the vigils did not come. After completing the office, the priest, angered with the man, hurried to his lodging as though to suspend him from
communion. The man had been seized by fever: as wine had inflamed him, so now a divine fire burned him. Without delay, on seeing the priest, he cried out and
tearfully begged that penance be imposed on him. While the priest rebuked him, saying, “You deserve to be burned by Saint Nicetius’s power, because you
neglected to come to vigils at his church,” the man breathed out his spirit in the midst of their conversation. At the third hour, when the people gathered for
the solemn Mass, he was carried dead to the church. No one can doubt that this happened by the holy bishop’s power. The priest himself related these things to
me. I have either experienced very many of these events myself or learned them through faithful report; I have thought it too long to recount them all.

### 12

**[053]** Since I have decided to bring this little book to a close, I will mention one more admirable miracle concerning the book of his life which I said
above had been written by someone. Divine power proceeding from it did not leave it inglorious but revealed it as glorious to many, confirming the truth of what
was said. A deacon of Autun, afflicted by severe blindness of the eyes, heard of the things God, the glorifier of his saints, was performing at the saint’s
