tomb. He said to his companions, “If I could go to his tomb, or take some of the holy pledges, or at least deserve to touch the pall with which the saint’s
limbs are covered, I would become well.” While he was discussing these and similar words with his companions, a certain cleric suddenly stood before him and
said, “Your faith is good. But if you wish to strengthen your mind concerning these same miracles, here is a parchment volume in which these things are written,
so that you may more easily believe what has reached your hearing.” Before he sought to have it read, inspired by the regard of divine goodness, he said, “I
believe that God is powerful to work excellent deeds through his servants.” He immediately placed the volume over his eyes. At once his pain was put to flight
and his darkness broken; by the power of the volume he deserved to recover the use of sight. He was placed in such clarity that he himself could read with his
own eyes and learn the deeds of power. One and the same Lord works these things; he glories in his saints and has made glorious those raised up by illustrious
miracles. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## IX. Saint Patroclus

### Prologue

**[054]** When the excellent wisdom of the prophet Moses was preparing to construct the tabernacle conforming to the divine descent according to the command of
the Lord’s own mouth, he had been ordered to gather many things for that same furnishing, but did not have in the contents of his treasury everything the Lord
himself had shown on the summit of the high mountain. He therefore ordered the people to be admonished that each should offer God some gift according to his
ability, not from necessity but willingly. They offered gifts of gold and silver, metals of bronze and iron, the beauty of gleaming gems, and threads of
twice-dyed linen and twice-twisted scarlet; some offered reddened rams’ skins and goats’ hair. Since the teachers of the churches have handed down that all
these things are allegorical and have shown in the other gifts the kinds of graces, in those goats’ hairs they have represented words of praise. So now I
too—barren in understanding, unskilled in study, and squalid in conduct—although I do not offer gold, silver, gems, or doubled and twisted threads, nevertheless
offer in the holy church at least goats’ hairs: that is, words which disclose the miracles of the saints and friends of God. May readers be kindled by them with
the same zeal by which the saints deserved to ascend to heaven. A report recently given to me has disclosed certain things about the blessed Patroclus’s life; I
have taken care that they should not be omitted but made known. Although my speech is rustic, I have not considered it blameworthy to relate what God did
through his servant.

### 1

**[055]** The most blessed Patroclus, an inhabitant of the territory of Bourges, born of his father Aetherius, was assigned to be a shepherd of sheep when he
was ten years old, while his brother Antonius was entrusted to the study of letters. They were not exalted by nobility, but they were freeborn. One midday, when
Antonius had come from school and Patroclus from the flock entrusted to him to take food at their father’s lodging, Antonius said to his brother, “Go farther
away, rustic. Your work is to pasture sheep; mine is to be trained in letters. The care of my office makes me nobler, while the servitude of this guardianship
makes you base.” Hearing this, Patroclus regarded the rebuke as though it had been sent to him by God. He left the sheep on the level plain and sought the boys’
school with agile effort of mind and very swift running. The elements were entrusted to him, and afterwards the things necessary for a boy’s study. With memory
helping him, he was imbued so quickly that he surpassed his brother both in knowledge and in alertness of understanding, with the aid of the divine Power
consenting.

He was then commended to Nunnio for training, a man who had once been held in great esteem with Childebert, king of Paris. Nunnio nourished him with the
greatest diligence of love. Patroclus showed himself so humble and subject to everyone that all loved him like their own parent for his surpassing goodness.
Returning home after his father’s death, he found his mother still living. She said to him, “Sweetest son, your father has died, and I live without consolation.
I shall seek a beautiful, freeborn girl for you; joined to her, you may give comfort to your mother’s widowhood.” He answered, “I will not be joined to a
worldly wife, but with the Lord’s will I shall accomplish what my mind has conceived.” When his mother, not understanding, asked what this meant, he refused to
disclose it. He went to Arcadius, bishop of the city of Bourges, and asked that the hair of his head be cut and that he be enrolled in the order of clerics. By
the Lord’s will the bishop did this without delay.

Not long afterwards Patroclus took the office of deacon. He devoted himself to fasting, delighted in vigils, was trained by reading, and poured himself out
promptly in constant prayer, so that he did not even go to the common table’s meal with the other clerics. Hearing this, the archdeacon raged against him and
said, “Either take food with the rest of the brothers, or leave me. It does not seem right for you to pretend to share a way of life with those with whom you
would be expected to fulfil the ecclesiastical office.”

### 2

**[056]** God’s servant was not disturbed in mind by these words, for he already thirsted to enter the secrecy of the wilderness. He left the aforesaid city and
came to the village of Néris. There he built an oratory, consecrated it with relics of Saint Martin, and began to instruct boys in the study of letters. The
sick came to him and were healed, and possessed people who confessed his name were cleansed. He did not have the solitude he wished: his revealed power made him
known everywhere. He then wrote a short petition on a brief document and placed it on the altar, watching and praying for three days and three nights that the
Lord would deign to declare most clearly what he commanded him to do. The renowned compassion of divine goodness, which in its foreknowledge had already decreed
that he should be a hermit, ordered him to receive that document and hasten to the wilderness.

In the cell where he lived, he gathered virgins and established a monastery for girls. When he departed, he took nothing of all that he had gathered there by
his labour except one rake and one two-edged axe. Entering the deep solitudes of the forests, he came to a place called Mediocantus. There he built a cell and
devoted himself to God in the work described above. There he laid his hand on many possessed people and, putting demons to flight by the sign of the cross,
restored them to sound minds. One rabid man was brought to him who, with gaping jaws and bloody teeth, tore with his own teeth whatever he could reach.
Patroclus lay prostrate in prayer for him for three days and obtained from that power of divine compassion that, his fury mitigated, the man liable to death
should be cleansed. Putting his fingers into the man’s mouth, he drove out the spirit of savage ferocity and restored the person to safety. The phantom of
wicked persuasion could have no power before him. Just as he cleansed those who were tormented, so by the power of the most sacred cross he repelled the secret
horrors which the author of crime sent.

When the devil, falsely pretending to be Martin during that inguinal plague, had wickedly offered to a certain woman named Leubella offerings by which the
people were supposedly to be saved, these were brought to the saint. By the revelation of the Holy Spirit they not only vanished, but the very inciter of evils
appeared to the saint in most hideous form and confessed what he had wickedly done. The devil often transforms himself into an angel of light in order to
deceive the innocent by this fraud. When he laid many snares for Patroclus to prevent him from ascending to the place from which he himself had fallen, he put
into his mind the thought that he ought to leave the wilderness and return to the world. When the saint felt the poison swelling in his breast, he prostrated
himself in prayer and asked to practise nothing except what was pleasing to God. Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a vision and said, “If you wish to
see the world, behold the column; climb it and contemplate everything done in it!” In that vision a column of wonderful height stood before him. Climbing it, he
saw murders, thefts, slaughters, adulteries, fornications, and all the perverse things done in the world. Coming down, he said, “I beg you, Lord, let me not
return to these depravities which I forgot when I confessed you long ago.” The angel speaking with him said, “Then cease to seek the world, lest you perish with
it. Go instead into the oratory where you entreat the Lord; what you find there will be your consolation in your pilgrimage.” Entering the oratory cell, he
found an earthenware tile on which the sign of the Lord’s cross was impressed. Recognizing the divine gift, he understood that against all incitements of
worldly persuasion this was an impregnable defence.

### 3

**[057]** Afterwards he built the monastery of Colombier five miles from the wilderness cell in which he lived. Gathering monks there, he appointed an abbot to
preside over the monastic flock, so that he himself might enjoy solitude with freer discretion. He had completed eighteen years in that wilderness place. Then
he gathered the brothers, announced his passing, and died in a good old age and pre-eminent holiness. After his body had been washed with water and placed on a
bier, it was carried to his monastery, where while living he had directed himself to be buried.

The chief priest of the village of Néris gathered a troop of clerics and wished to take by force the clod of the holy little body, intending that it should be
buried in his village from which Patroclus had gone out. But when he came in fury and saw from a distance the pall covering the saint’s limbs gleaming white
with extraordinary brilliance, he was so terrified with fear by God’s will that with all speed he recalled from his mind what he had wrongly conceived through a
decision of levity. Joining the psalmody, he proceeded in the saint’s funeral procession and buried him with the other brothers present in the monastery of
Colombier itself.

Prudentia, a blind woman, and another girl from Limoges, likewise deprived of sight, kissed the holy tomb in prayer and deserved to receive light. Maxonidius,
after the fifth year of his blindness, visited this holy tomb and received light. The possessed persons Lupus, Theodulfus, Rucco, Scopilia, Nectariola, and
Tacihildis were cleansed at this saint’s tomb. Two girls also came from Limoges; anointed with oil which the saint himself had blessed, they were cleansed of
the wickedness by which they were possessed. Every day in that place the Lord, who perpetually glorifies his saints, works to strengthen the faith of those who
live there.

*Here ends the Life of Saint Patroclus.*

## X. Saint Friardus The Recluse

### Prologue

**[058]** There are many steps by which one ascends to the kingdom of heaven. I think David also speaks of them when he says: “He has arranged ascents in his
heart.” Let these steps, then, be understood as the advances of various works toward divine worship. No one can set foot upon them unless, as we have often
testified, he has been called by God’s help. The psalmist speaks in this way on that step of the intermediate journey: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those
who build it labour in vain.” Not only the martyrs but also those whom the authority of sacred life has strengthened sought this help continually, and thus they
came eagerly to what the thirst of spiritual desire demanded. If the mind was kindled for martyrdom, the martyr asked for the aid of this help so that he might
conquer. If he strove to practise the observance of fasting, he afflicted himself so that he might be strengthened by it. If he wished to keep his limbs
undefiled for chastity, he prayed to be fortified by it. If after ignorance he desired to turn in penitence, he begged with tears nevertheless to be raised by
it. And if any of them resolved to perform some good work, he sought to be helped by this aid. Through these ascents of this ladder—so difficult, lofty, and
steep, though they are various—one nevertheless ascends to the one Lord through the power of this help. Therefore he must always be entreated, sought, and
invoked, so that by his aid he himself may accomplish the good that the mind conceives. Of him I must also say without end: “Our help is in the name of the
Lord, who made heaven and earth.” So it was with that most blessed man of whom I am now to speak: amid the various temptations and crosses of the world he
always sought the defence of this help.

### 1

**[059]** On the island of Vindunitta in the city of Nantes there was a recluse named Friardus, a man of outstanding holiness. It delights my mind to say a
little about his life for the edification of the church, because I do not know whether it has been written by anyone. From infancy he was always devoted to God
and chaste. When he became a man, he lived always in God’s praises, always in prayer, always in vigils. He obtained the necessities of food from the earth by
his own hands. Even when he hurried among the others at work, he never ceased from prayer. To neighbours and strangers, as is the custom of rustics, this was
ridiculous.

One day, while he was gathering sheaves with the others after the stalks had been cut in the harvest, they found a swarm of wretched and savage flies which the
common people call wasps. When they stung the reapers most fiercely with their darts, the reapers ran around the harvest on every side and leapt past the place
where the wasps had gathered. They deceitfully addressed the blessed Friardus to mock him: “Let the blessed man come, let the religious man come, who never
ceases to pray, who always makes the cross over his ears and eyes, who sends the saving standards before him on the roads of his journey. Let him reap over the
swarm; let him soften it by his prayer.” Friardus accepted these words as though they were meant to bring the Lord’s power into confusion. He fell to the ground
and poured out prayer to the Lord. Approaching and making the sign of the cross over the swarm, he said, “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven
and earth.” At this prayer all the wasps immediately hid themselves in the nest from which they had emerged. Before everyone’s eyes he harvested over it
unharmed. To those mocking him this was not without miracle, because the Lord had thus deigned to strengthen one who hoped in him to their confusion.

Afterwards, when he had climbed a tree for some necessity, the branch beneath his feet suddenly broke and he began to fall. As he fell downward and struck each
branch, he invoked Christ’s most blessed name, saying, “Almighty Christ, save me.” When he reached the ground, he was unhurt, but kept saying, “Our help is in
the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

### 2

**[060]** Encouraged by these and other miracles, he began to think silently in the secrecy of his heart: “If Christ’s cross, the invocation of his name, and
the help asked from him have such power that they overcome every harsh thing in the world, overwhelm dangers, drive away the darkness of temptations, and
despise as nothing all the delights of this world, what have I to do with the world? Ought I not to abandon everything belonging to it and devote myself to the
service of him alone, by the invocation of whose name I was saved from wicked dangers?” Leaving his little dwelling, forgetting parents and country, he sought
the wilderness, lest worldly anxiety should place any hindrance to prayer in the way of one living in the world. He and Abbot Sabaudus, who had formerly been a
minister of King Chlothar, received penance and went to the island of Vindonitta in the territory of Nantes. They also had Deacon Secundellus with them. The
abbot, withdrawing his hand from the Lord’s plough, left the island and returned to the monastery; not long afterwards he was killed by the sword for hidden
reasons. Saint Friardus remained immovable on the aforesaid island with Deacon Secundellus. Each had his own cell, situated at a distance from the other.

While they persevered strenuously in prayer, the tempter appeared to Deacon Secundellus at night in the likeness of the Lord and said, “I am Christ, whom you
entreat every day. You have now become holy, and I have written your name in the book of life with my other saints. Now leave this island and go and perform
healings among the people.” Attracted by these deceptions, Secundellus left the island without telling his companion. Yet when he laid hands on the sick in
Christ’s name, they were healed. After a long time he returned to the island and came to his companion in vainglory, saying, “I went outside the island and
performed many miracles among the people.” Terrified, Friardus asked what he meant, and Secundellus simply disclosed everything he had done. The elder,
astonished, sighing and weeping, said, “Woe to me! From what I hear, you have been deceived by the tempter. Go and do penance, lest his deceits prevail over you
any longer.” Understanding this and fearing that he had perished, Secundellus fell at Friardus’s feet in tears, asking him to entreat the Lord for him. Friardus
said, “Go, and let me together ask his omnipotence for the salvation of your soul. The Lord is not slow to have mercy on those who confess him, since he himself
says through the prophet: ‘I do not desire the sinner’s death, but that he turn and live.’”

While they prayed, the tempter again came to Deacon Secundellus in a similar likeness and said, “Did I not command you, because my sheep were diseased and
needed a shepherd, to go out, visit them, and give them the help of healing?” Secundellus said, “I have truly discovered that you are a seducer, and I do not
believe you to be God, whose likeness you falsely claim to have. Nevertheless, if you are Christ, show me the cross you left behind, and I will believe you.”
When he did not show it, the deacon made the Lord’s cross on his face, and the tempter vanished in confusion. Returning again with a multitude of demons, he
beat Secundellus so severely that he was scarcely thought likely to survive. Then he departed and appeared nowhere again. Afterwards the deacon continued in
surpassing holiness and died on his appointed day.

### 3

**[061]** The blessed Friardus shone with great miracles. Once a branch broken from a tree by the wind, which he himself is said to have grafted, was gathered
up by him. He fitted it together and made from it a staff to carry in his hand. After a long time he planted the now dry rod in the ground and often watered it.
That staff put forth leaves and fruit, and within two or three years it grew extended into a great tall tree. This was held to be a great miracle by the people
who saw it. Every day an immense crowd gathered to see it, so that the revealed power made known even the remoteness of the island. God’s saint, lest he be
undermined by the stain of vainglory, took an axe and cut down the tree.

On another occasion the saint saw the ruin of another tree which, full of blossoms, had fallen under the violent force of the wind. Moved by compassion, he
prayed, “I beg you, Lord, let not the fruit of this little tree perish, which at your command produced the ornaments of flowers. Rather, granted an increase of
restoration by you, may it deserve to obtain the production of fruit.” Saying this, he took an axe and cut off the tree’s trunk. He sharpened the trunk like a
stake above the roots which still adhered to the soil and fixed it in the earth. The rootless trunk was soon joined to the roots and restored to its former
state. The flowers that had dried became green again, and that very year this tree restored fruit to its cultivator. I trust in God’s mercy that the present
miracle compels me to say that he who obtained for dry trees the power to put forth leaves in renewed greenness could obtain by his prayer from the Lord the
granting of life to the dead.

### 4

**[062]** Friardus often predicted his passing to the brothers. One day, touched by fever, he said to his companions, “Go to Bishop Felix and announce my
departure to him, saying, ‘Your brother Friardus says: Behold, having completed the course of this life, I am being released from this world. That you may be
more certain of this word, I shall pass away on the Lord’s Day and go to the rest which God, the eternal King, promised me. Come, I beg you, and let me see you
before I die.’” Felix was detained by I know not what circumstance and sent back a message: “I ask you, if it can be done, to wait for me a little until,
released from the delays of my affairs, I can come to you.” When the messengers returned and said this, Friardus was already lying in bed. He said, “Then let us
arise and wait for our brother.” O man ineffable in holiness! Although he was hastening to be dissolved and to be with Christ, he did not forget charity, but
obtained from the Lord a longer stay in the world so that he might see his brother with spiritual regard. Nor do I think Felix was of the least merit, since the
Lord deigned to postpone this saint’s days at his coming. On receiving news of the delay, Friardus’s fever immediately subsided, and he rose healed from bed.

After a long time the bishop arrived. Friardus was seized by fever. Felix entered to him, greeted and kissed him. Friardus said, “Holy bishop, you are causing
me long delays from the journey that is due.” While they watched, night passed; at daybreak, which was the Lord’s Day, he yielded up his spirit. As soon as it
departed, the whole cell was filled with an odour of sweetness and trembled all over. There is no doubt that angelic power was present there, which, marking the
saint’s merit, made the cell fragrant with divine spices. The bishop washed his glorious body and laid it in the tomb; Christ received his soul in heaven,
leaving examples of virtue to those born on earth.

## XI. Saint Caluppanus The Recluse

### Prologue

**[063]** Worldly poverty always unlocks the royal palace of heaven. It not only prepares those who follow it for heaven but also declares that, glorified by
miracles, they are illustrious in the world. Thus, while that prison-like bond of contrition opens the gate of paradise, the soul, enrolled among the angelic
choirs, exults in eternal rest. So now we cannot remain entirely silent about what we know to be true concerning the blessed recluse Caluppanus.

### 1

**[064]** From his earliest years he always sought and found the good of ecclesiastical religion. Turning to the monastic life at the monastery of Meletin in
the territory of Auvergne, he showed himself to the brothers in great humility. His abstinence was so extreme that, excessively worn down by starvation, he
could not perform the daily work with the other brothers. As is the custom of monks, they therefore heaped great reproach upon him, especially the cellarer, who
said, “He who does not resolve to labour unworthily asks to eat.”

While Caluppanus was continually burned by these words of reproach, he caught sight of a valley not far from the monastery. From its midst a rock rose by nature
and was carried aloft to about five hundred feet or more, having no connection at all with the other mountains surrounding it. A river washed the middle of this
valley and flowed gently past, touching this mountain. Into a cleft of this rock, which had once in ancient times been a refuge during the passage of enemies,
the holy hermit entered. Cutting away the rock, he established a dwelling which is now reached by a very difficult ladder. That place is so difficult to
approach that even wild beasts find it laborious to reach. There he made a tiny oratory. While he was praying, as he himself often used to tell us with tears,
serpents frequently fell upon his head. Coiling around his neck, they caused him no small horror. Because the devil is represented in the likeness of a cunning
serpent, there is no doubt that this was a snare of his assault.

Caluppanus remained immovable and was not disturbed by the attacks of the smaller snakes. One day two dragons of immense size entered toward him and stood at a
distance. One of them, whom I consider to have been the leader of the temptation, was stronger than the other. Raising its breast, it lifted its mouth toward
the blessed man’s mouth as though about to whisper something. Terrified with fear, Caluppanus became completely rigid like bronze. He could move no member at
all or raise his hand to oppose them with the sign of the blessed cross. When both had stood in silence for a very long time, it came into the saint’s mind
through the Spirit that, even if he could not move his lips, he should at least cry out the Lord’s Prayer in his heart. While he silently recited it, his
members, which had been bound by the enemy’s art, gradually began to be released. Feeling that his right hand was now free, he placed the sign of the blessed
cross upon his mouth. Turning again to the dragon, he traced Christ’s cross against it once more and said, “Are you the one who cast the first-formed man out of
the dwelling of paradise, who stained a brother’s right hand with fratricide, who armed Pharaoh to persecute God’s people, and who finally incited that Hebrew
people themselves to persecute the Lord when envy inflamed them? Depart from God’s servants, from whom you have often departed overcome and confounded. Were you
not cast down in Cain, supplanted in Esau, laid low in Goliath, and hanged in Judas the traitor? Were you not triumphed over and crushed together with your
powers and dominions in that very cross of the Lord’s might? Now hide your head, enemy, and be humbled beneath the seal of the divine cross. You have no portion
with God’s servants, whose inheritance is Christ’s kingdom.” As the saint said these and similar things and made the cross at each point, the dragon, confounded
by the power of this standard, humbled itself in turn and sank beneath the earth. While this was happening, the other serpent was coiling treacherously around
the saint’s feet and shins. When the holy hermit saw it confounded at his feet, he prayed and ordered it to depart, saying, “Go behind me, Satan; in the name of
my Christ you will be able to harm me no longer.” Going out to the threshold of the cell, it emitted a loud sound from its lower part and filled the cell with
such a stench that it could be believed to be nothing other than the devil. Neither serpent nor dragon ever again appeared before the saint.

### 2

**[065]** He was constant in God’s work and devoted himself to nothing except reading or prayer. Even when he took a little food, he always prayed. Sometimes he
took fish from the river—rarely, but whenever he wished, with the Lord’s help it was immediately at hand. He took no bread except what was sent from the
monastery. If any devout person brought bread or wine, it was assigned as food for the needy, but only for those who begged either to receive the saving sign
from him or to obtain remedies for their infirmities. Thus he cherished with the refreshment of food those to whom he gave health through prayer, recalling what
the Lord said in the Gospel about the crowds he had healed of various diseases: “I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.”

I also do not consider blameworthy the benefit which divine goodness granted him in that place. Water had to be carried from the depth of that valley for about
ten stades. He prayed to the Lord to show him a vein of spring water in the very dwelling of his cell. That heavenly power, which once brought water from flint
for a thirsty people, did not fail. Immediately at his prayer a drop of liquid burst from the rock and began to wet the ground with frequent drips. Rejoicing in
the heavenly gift, he made a small hollow in the stone like a cistern, holding about two measures, and received the waters divinely granted to him. Each day he
was supplied from them with just enough for himself and the servant who had been assigned to him.

### 3

**[066]** I myself also went to the place with the blessed Bishop Avitus. Of everything I have related, some things I learned from Caluppanus’s own account and
some I examined with my own eyes. He received the ranks of deacon and priest from the aforesaid bishop. He bestowed remedies on people afflicted by various
diseases. Yet he never left his cell to show himself to anyone. He merely stretched out his hand through a small window and made the saving sign. If anyone
visited him, he came to this little opening and offered prayer and conversation. Completing the course of his life in this religious observance, he departed to
the Lord, I believe, in the fiftieth year of his age.

## XII. Aemilianus The Hermit And Brachio The Abbot

### Prologue

**[067]** The Holy Spirit reveals through the psalmist’s mouth how much heavenly discipline offers to those who keep it and how much, if not kept, it ought to
inflict upon the negligent: “Lay hold of discipline,” he says, “lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way.” Concerning the good, Solomon says:
“The discipline of peace will be upon him.” This discipline produces the fear of the Lord; the fear of the Lord provides the beginning of wisdom; wisdom teaches
us to love God. The love of God lifts a person from earthly things, calls him to heaven, and places him in paradise, where the souls of the blessed, taking the
liquid of new wine from that life-giving vine, feast in God’s kingdom. People ought therefore to desire to drink the mystery of this vine so that they might be
able to enter that most lovely place of such delightful habitation. If the vines I now see, extended through their layers, sending out shoots and interwoven
with foliage, delight me with pleasant contemplation as their grapes hang down—not only offering an abundance of fruit but also protecting me with timely shade
from the burning sun’s heat—though I know that after the fruit of the lawful season has been gathered their falling leaves leave them seemingly dry, how much
more ought I to desire that vine which never fails and withers in no heat of temptation, where, once hope has passed, the very thing hoped for is both held and
enjoyed. Many who desired this not only left their own possessions but entered every deserted and uncultivated place, so that the consolation of solitary and
more remote prayer and streams of tears might quench the thirst of this desire. So now the blessed Aemilianus, a new hermit of my times, is shown to have done.

### 1

**[068]** Leaving parents and his own property, Aemilianus sought the deserts of the wilderness and hid himself in the secret places of the forests of
Ponticiacum in the territory of Auvergne. There he cut down the woods, levelled a small field, dug the earth with a hoe, and obtained food for life. He also had
a little garden which he watered by bringing in water. From it he took vegetables for refreshment, fattened with no grease. He had no consolation apart from
God’s help. Beasts and birds were his companions; every day they gathered around him as around God’s servant. He devoted himself to fasting and prayer, and no
occasion of worldly anxiety could hinder him from this course, because he had nothing except God.

### 2

**[069]** At that time Sigivald, a man endowed with great power, lived in the city of Clermont. In his service was a young man named Brachio, which in their
language means “bear cub.” The aforesaid man had chosen Brachio to undertake the hunting of wild pigs. Brachio went with a huge pack of Molossian hounds, going
around the forests and bringing to his master whatever he caught. One day, while pursuing an immense boar with this barking pack, the boar entered the enclosure
around the saint’s cell. The pursuing pack of dogs came barking to the entrance of the forecourt, but immediately stopped in its tracks and was not permitted to
enter after the boar. Seeing this and marvelling that it had happened by heaven’s power, Brachio went to the saint’s cell. He saw the boar standing before the
door, utterly unafraid. The old man greeted and kissed him and invited him to sit. When they were seated, the old man said, “I see you, dearest son, arrayed in
great elegance and pursuing things that prepare harm for the soul rather than salvation. Leave your earthly master, I beg you, and follow the true God, the
Maker of heaven and earth. All things are governed by his will, all subjected to his command, and by his majesty this very beast you see stands unafraid. Do not
let your master’s power, which is nothing, make you swollen or exalted. The apostle Paul says: ‘Let him who glories glory in the Lord,’ and elsewhere: ‘If I
pleased men, I would not be Christ’s servant.’ Subject yourself to the service of him who says: ‘Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will
refresh you.’ He is the Lord whose burden is light and whose yoke is sweet; his worship both bestows present things and grants eternal life. For he says: ‘If
anyone renounces everything he possesses, he will receive a hundredfold and moreover possess eternal life.’”

While the old man spoke these and similar words forcefully, the boar went unharmed into the woods. The boy departed in great wonder because the wild boar he had
begun to pursue stood before the old man as gentle as a lamb. He pondered many things and turned much over in his mind: what he should do, whether he should
leave the world or serve it. Pierced by divine goodness and, I believe, by Saint Aemilianus’s prayer, he began secretly to seek a way to become a cleric,
because he did not dare do so publicly on account of his earthly master. While still a layman, he rose from his bed two or three times in the night, prostrated
himself on the ground, and poured out prayer to the Lord. He did not know what to sing because he was ignorant of letters. Often seeing in the oratory letters
written over the images of the apostles and other saints, he copied them into a book. When clerics or abbots continually came to meet his master, Brachio would
privately call whichever of the juniors he could first reach and ask the names of the letters; thus he began to understand them. By the Lord’s inspiration he
both read and wrote before he had learned the sequence of letters.

After Sigivald died, Brachio hastened to the aforesaid old man. Spending two or three years with him, he committed the Psalter to memory. His brother often
wished to kill him because he refused to be joined in marriage. Monks were then added to them.

### 3

**[070]** When the blessed Aemilianus had completed the days of his life and departed from the body at about ninety years of age, he left Brachio as his heir.
Brachio established the monastery and obtained from Ranihildis, the daughter of the aforesaid Sigivald, a great extent of land which she left to this monastery.
It was forest land belonging to the estate of Vindiciacum.

Brachio later left this monastery and came to Tours. There he built oratories and gathered two monasteries. Once, when foreign men arrived, they brought relics
of saints with them and placed them on the altar of the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours, intending to depart the next day. Abbot Brachio was present. While
keeping watch in the basilica, around the middle of the night he saw what looked like a globe of immense fire flash from the holy pledges and rise with great
light to the ceiling of the church. There is no doubt that this was something divine, but it was shown to none of the others standing there except him.

Afterwards he returned to Auvergne, to the earlier monastery. Living there for five years, he came to Tours. When abbots had been established in the aforesaid
monasteries, he returned to Auvergne. While he was residing in the earlier cell, he was appointed over the monastery of Manat, which had grown lukewarm through
the abbot’s negligence, so that by his zeal that congregation might be governed according to the canon. He was most chaste in conduct and strenuously
disciplined others to lead a chaste life. He was gentle in conversation and kindly in affection, but was regarded as so severe toward transgressors of the rule
that he was sometimes thought cruel. Fasting, vigils, and charity had made him a perfect man.

When the time of his departure approached, he saw in a vision—as he himself related to the blessed Bishop Avitus—that he was led into the presence of the
heavenly Lord. In that presence the Seraphim, with wings outstretched, overshadowed the Majesty itself, and the prophet Isaiah, with a volume opened, cried
aloud the words he was about to prophesy. While the abbot watched in astonishment, he awoke. Carefully pondering his dream and recognizing by the Lord’s
revelation the end of his life, he said to the abbot whom he had appointed over the earlier monastery, “That place beside the river where I had intended to make
an oratory is very lovely. I therefore ask you to complete what I wished and not refuse to transfer my bones there.” He died and was buried in the oratory of
the earlier cell. When the abbot wished to complete the work enjoined upon him, by God’s will he found both lime burned in ancient times and a foundation of the
very dimensions he intended to lay. When the building was completed, he uncovered the abbot’s tomb. Opening it, he found the little body so unharmed that it
seemed to have died only the day before. Thus, after two years, with joy and attended by the troop of monks he himself had taught, Brachio was transferred to
that place.

## XIII. Saint Lupicinus

### Prologue

**[071]** Christ’s athletes and the world’s conquerors, desiring to suffer the loss of this fleeting life, wished to reach that life which remains in perpetual
exultation, is interrupted by no groaning, and is bounded by no end. Its light will never be extinguished, and its serenity is covered by no darkness of cloud.
They therefore always counted the insults of present pains as nothing, knowing that they were afflicted in a few things but would be well established in many.
Whoever contends in this struggle is not terrified by fear, dissolved by punishment, or broken by pain, so that he may deserve to enjoy with God’s elect that
loveliness of eternal delight. I know that many holy men have done this; their lives are now treated or read.

### 1

**[072]** A certain Lupicinus was a man of great holiness and very strong in God’s works. At first he begged alms through the houses of devout people and
distributed to those like himself whatever he could obtain. Finally, now in middle age, he came to the village of Berberis, now called Lipidiacum. There he
found ancient walls and was enclosed as a recluse, withdrawing himself from everyone’s sight. Through a small window he received a little bread or water;
because it was very little, it sometimes lasted him until the third day. Water was brought in through a small channel, while the window was covered with a veil.
The approach to both was so concealed that no one could look upon his blessed face. Day and night he delighted there in the melodies of psalms in God’s praise.
Mindful of the apostle’s saying, “The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which will be revealed in us,” he inflicted
torments upon himself to burden his little body further. All day, while he sang to God, he carried around the cell on his neck a great stone which two men could
scarcely lift. At night, to add to the injury, he had fixed two stakes into the rod he carried in his hand and prepared points upon them. These he placed
beneath his chin so that he would not sleep. At the end of his life his chest was corrupted by the weight of the stone, and he began to spit blood from his
mouth, casting it onto the walls around him. Often, when faithful men secretly approached the cell at night, a voice like that of many people singing psalms
resounded. He also restored many sick people to health, especially those afflicted by attacks of fever or malignant pustules, merely by touch or by making the
saving sign.

### 2

**[073]** When he was already bent with old age, he called his servant and said, “The time for hiding is past; the time for revealing has come. Know that after
three days I am to be released from this world. Now call all the faithful brothers and sons to whom I am to say farewell, so that they may come to visit me.”
When the third day dawned and the brothers streamed in, he opened the door that had been closed. Everyone present entered; he greeted and kissed them, then
poured out prayer to the Lord: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, who commanded me to be saved from the hindrances of this world and deigned to cherish me
in this world in such a way that the author of crime found nothing of his own in me.” Turning to the people, he said, “Dearest ones, magnify the Lord with me, I
beg you, and let me exalt his name together. He raised me from the dungheap, rescued me from the work of darkness, and made me a companion of his friends. He
sent his angel to call me from this worldly station and promised to lead me into eternal rest, so that, made a colleague of his friends, I might deserve to be
enrolled in his kingdom.” O blessed man, who deserved to be so consoled in this body that he knew what he would enjoy in heaven before he departed from the
world! He deserved to obtain from divine power what David often sang: “Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, so that I may know what is
wanting to me.” Then, sinking to the ground, he sent his spirit, fixed upon heaven, ahead to the Lord.

All threw themselves down in tears. Some kissed the soles of his feet, others tore fringes from his garment, and others, striving among themselves, scraped the
blessed blood that had been cast from his mouth off the wall. Each called himself wretched if he departed without a pledge from Lupicinus. To this day the wall
itself is a witness, displaying as many little holes as it received spittle from the blessed confessor’s mouth. The channel from which the blessed man took
water for his use is also a witness: those who faithfully kiss it receive health. I myself have seen many people in various infirmities who deserved to receive
medicine after scraping off spittle of the sacred mouth from the wall.

### 3

**[074]** After he had died as described, a certain noble lady was present. She washed him and clothed him in fitting garments. When she wished to carry him to
the village of Transalium, the people of the district of Lipidiacum resisted her, saying, “He cherished only my land; the clod of his body is owed to me.” The
lady answered, “If you reproach me with anything concerning the necessity of his food, I myself often sent him both wheat and barley, either for him to eat or
to distribute to others.” They said, “He has become a man of my race, drank the waters of my river, and my earth sent him to heaven. Is it right that you,
coming from a foreign land, should snatch him from my hand? Know that none of me will allow this; he will be buried here.” The lady answered, “If you ask about
the stock of his lineage, he came here from other regions. You offer him the river’s waters, but they little relieved his thirst, which that fountain flowing
from heaven instead quenched.”

While they exchanged these and similar words, the people of Lipidiacum dug the earth, set down a sarcophagus, and strove to bury him. The lady called together
supporters, drove off the villagers, seized the holy body, and began to carry it on a bier to the village of Transaliacum. Along the road she arranged troops of
psalm-singers with crosses, wax candles, and the fragrance of burning incense. Seeing this, the villagers were moved to repentance and sent after the lady,
saying, “We sinned by resisting you. We now recognize that the Lord’s will is in this. We ask not to be cast out from the services of this funeral but admitted
to its offices.” When she permitted them to follow, both peoples were joined. Coming together to the village of Transaliacum, they celebrated Masses and buried
the blessed body with the highest honour and joy. In that village the most blessed man often manifested himself in miracles. In Lipidiacum also, as I mentioned
above, his holy work is often shown. Both places are strengthened by the protection of one saint.

If the barking of certain unbelievers tries to raise a clamour against these things, let them know that I saw the priest Deodatus, who bore the summit of eighty
years of age. He related these things to me as they have been written, confirming under oath that he had recounted none of them with falsehood mixed in.

*Here ends the Life.*

## XIV. The Holy Abbot Martius

### Prologue

**[075]** Divine goodness grants me a great increase when it commands me to make pardon a refuge from my sins: if I forgive the negligent, indulge those who
injure me, and instead bestow the advantage of blessing on those who hate me. The Lord Jesus Christ says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and
pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.” Behold what a great treasure is gathered by the contempt
of anger, the reconciliation of the condemned, and the pardon of the judged! It makes you a son of God the Father, enrols you as Christ’s co-heir, and
establishes you as an inhabitant of the heavenly kingdoms. It is therefore manifest that the sins of one who bestows the benefit of pardon on an offender in
this world are blotted out in heaven. The sentence spoken by the Lord’s mouth testifies to this: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will
also forgive your sins.” When he teaches his servants to pray as suppliants, he says: “You shall say to the Father: ‘Forgive me my debts, as I also forgive my
debtors.’”

This holy man, the blessed Abbot Martius, renowned for holiness and instructed in divine studies, kept the good of this sentence in his heart so that he
willingly forgave an offender. He not only pardoned the wrong but also offered gifts of grace, lest he should in any way degrade the guilty person. But before I
come to the benefit of this grace, I shall first say a few things about his manner of life.

### 1

**[076]** The most blessed Martius is said to have been an inhabitant of the territory of the city of Clermont and its abbot. From boyhood he led a religious
life and dedicated himself entirely to God’s works. He was sparing in food, generous in almsgiving, prompt in vigils, and very devout in prayer. With all his
strength he restrained wantonness with the bridle of abstinence and the struggle of frugality so that it could not creep into him. He was rightly called
Martius: with a triumphant warfare he cut down the budding thoughts of mortal actions with the sword of the Holy Spirit at the very outset of their flashing
forth. He was not a deaf hearer, remembering the words of apostolic exhortation: “Gird yourselves with God’s armour and the sword of the Holy Spirit, so that
you may despise the devil’s fiery darts.”

When he reached the perfection of lawful age and shone like an outstanding star in this city, he withdrew not far from it, thinking that something was still
wanting to him. Taking a hoe, he began to cut a rocky mountain. Carving cells in it, he made little dwellings for himself. Bound more tightly by the chain of
sobriety, he could thus more easily offer the incense of prayers and the whole burnt offerings of praises from the altar of a pure heart to Almighty God. He
recalled that the Lord said through the Gospel: “Enter your chamber and, with the door closed, pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will
repay you.” He knew that the consolation of angelic visitation would also be present if he removed himself farther from human sight.

In this habitation of the hollowed rock of the mountain, as I have said, he prepared what was necessary. He formed in the caverns from the stone itself a bench,
a small seat, and a bed on which, after much labour, he might grant rest to his weary little body. These things were immovable because, cut from the stone
itself, they adhered to the very mass of rock. When he rested he spread nothing over them, but lay down only in the garment he was wearing. He had no other
carpets, feather cushions, or coverings to spread over them except when he himself sat upon them. He owned nothing except the worship of God, in which he
remained unfailing. The generosity of devout people sometimes supplied his food.

### 2

**[077]** The eternal Lord, who continually glorifies his saints, began to reveal to earth-dwellers his servant’s heavenly merit and to show what sort of
worshipper of his divinity he was by deigning to grant him the grace of healing. By his word he drove demons from possessed bodies in the name of Jesus Christ.
He suppressed the poison of malignant pustules with the seal of the cross. He expelled quartan and tertian fevers by pouring on the liquid of blessed oil. With
the Lord, the giver of all good things, consenting, he bestowed many other benefits on the people. At the report of so great a man, certain people began to
gather around him, rejoicing to be instructed by his teaching. Why say more? He gathered men, formed monks, and made them perfect for God’s work.

He possessed great patience and had taken up such goodness against the darts of injuries to be endured that you would think him protected by a breastplate of
sweetness. The monks had a garden filled with a great abundance of various vegetables and fruit-bearing trees, lovely to see and delightful in fertility. The
blessed old man often sat beneath the shade of these trees while their leaves whispered in the breath of the breeze. A certain shameless man without fear of
God, circumscribed by the desire of gluttony, broke through the garden hedge and entered by stealth. As the Lord reproves in the Gospel: “He who does not enter
by the door is a thief and a robber.” It was night, for these things could only be perpetrated at night because “everyone who does evil hates the light.”
Gathering vegetables, onions, garlic, and fruit, he loaded himself with the bundle of wicked theft and went to the opening by which he had entered, but could by
no means find a way out. Burdened by the weight and terrified by conscience, he drew deep sighs amid the labour of the load. Sometimes he leaned against the
trunks of trees. Again and again he went around the whole circuit of the garden; not only did he find no gate, he could not even discern the entrance he had
opened in the darkness of night. He was tormented by a double pain: fear of being held by the monks or seized by the judge. Amid these torches of thought the
night grew long for him, and the radiance of the desired light did not return. The abbot spent the night in psalmody and, I believe, learned what was happening
by God’s revelation.

When heaven was already growing light, he called the cellarer and said, “Run quickly to the garden; a mischievous ox has entered it, but has damaged nothing. Go
now, place its necessities upon it, and let it go. For it is written: ‘You shall not bind the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain.’” Not understanding
what he meant, the cellarer went to carry out the order. When the man saw him approaching, he threw on the ground what he had taken and began to flee. He
plunged his head among thorns and brambles and, like a pig, tried with an easy thrust to open an exit by which he might escape. The monk seized him and said,
“Do not be afraid, my son. My elder sent me to lead you out of this place.” The monk then gathered the fruit and vegetables the man had thrown down, placed them
on his shoulders, opened the gate, and dismissed him, saying, “Go in peace, and do not repeat what you did with cowardice as your companion.”

### 3

**[078]** This bishop also, shining in the world like the radiance of true light, continually drove away the sicknesses of infirmities by the efficacy of his
miracles. A certain Nivardus, held by a long fever, constantly drank water because he burned with heat. He swelled with dropsy until both belly and stomach
appeared stretched like a bladder. Despairing because of this infirmity, he asked to be carried to the saint by the benefit of a wagon. He was lifted from his
bed, placed on the vehicle, and brought to the saint’s cell, humbly entreating God’s bishop to lay hands on him. Martius prostrated himself in prayer before the
Lord, then turned to the sick man. Touching his limbs with the gentlest touch, he restored him to health before the eyes of those present. It is said that all
the swelling fled from the afflicted body before his fingers, so that no indication of this illness remained in him. I learned these things from my own father’s
account, because this Nivardus was bound to him in the bond of friendship.

My father also asserted that he had seen the saint, in these circumstances. When he was still a boy of about eleven, he was seized by an attack of tertian
fevers. His friends took the boy and led him to the man of God. Martius was already old and near the day of his dissolution, and his eyes were dim. He placed
his hand on the boy and said, “Who is this, and whose son is he?” They answered, “This boy Florentius is your servant, the son of the former senator Georgius.”
Martius said, “My son, may the Lord God bless you and deign to heal your sicknesses.” Florentius kissed his hand, gave thanks, and departed healed. He asserted
that in all his life he was never again attacked by this affliction.

### 4

**[079]** At ninety years of age, toiling in the good contest, completing the course of life, and keeping faith in God, Martius departed to that crown of
righteousness which the Lord will render to him on the day of recompense. He was washed with the highest honour, clothed in fitting garments, and buried within
the oratory of the monastery. The community present can testify that his blessed tomb is illuminated by divine miracles. When it sends sick people to the tomb,
it immediately sends them home unharmed. Although people streaming together from various places bring different kinds of disease and receive medicine there, the
trembling limbs of fever patients are especially often restored to complete soundness. Our Lord Jesus Christ grants this; he now glorifies the tombs of his
saints with illustrious miracles, he who once brought them back from tombs. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## XV. The Holy Abbot Senoch

### Prologue

**[080]** “Vanity of those who practise vanity,” says Ecclesiastes; “all is vanity.” Is it therefore true that everything done in the world is vanity? Thus it
happens that God’s saints, whom no heat of lust has burned, no sting of concupiscence has goaded, and no filth of wantonness has tempted even in thought, so to
speak, when heated by the proud tempter, have seemed to themselves most righteous. Puffed up by the haughty eyebrow of vainglory, they have often fallen. Those
whom the sword of greater crimes could not slaughter, the light smoke of vanity has easily ruined once they were enslaved to it. So it was with the very man of
whom I am now to speak. Although he had flourished with many miracles, he nearly perished overwhelmed in that abyss of arrogance, had not the attentive
exhortation of faithful brothers restored him.

### 1

**[081]** The most blessed Senoch was born a Taifal from the district of Poitou called Taifalia. Turning to the Lord and becoming a cleric, he established a
monastery for himself. Within the boundary of the territory of Tours he found ancient walls. Raising them from ruin, he fitted out worthy dwellings. He also
found an oratory there in which my Martin was said to have prayed. He arranged it with diligent care, erected an altar, and prepared a cavity in it to receive
the relics of saints; then he invited the bishop to bless it. The blessed Bishop Eufronius was present. After consecrating the altar, he bestowed on Senoch the
honour of the diaconate. When Masses had been celebrated and they wished to place the reliquary in the cavity, the case proved too long and could not fit. The
deacon and the bishop himself prostrated themselves in prayer and poured out petitions mingled with tears; he obtained what he asked. Wonderful to tell, the
cavity was divinely enlarged and the reliquary contracted so that, to their astonishment, it fitted inside with ample room.

In this place Senoch gathered three monks and served the Lord constantly. Above all he walked the narrow path of life, using meagre food and thin drink. During
the holy days of Lent he increased his abstinence by diminishing his food. He ate only barley bread and drank water, taking one pound of each substance each
day. He endured the rigour of winter without any covering for his feet, and his hands, feet, and neck were bound with an iron chain. He then withdrew from the
sight of the brothers and enclosed himself in a solitary cell. He prayed constantly and continued without doubt day and night in vigils and prayers. The
devotion of the faithful often brought him money, but he stored it not in hidden purses but in the pouches of the poor. He often recalled that oracle of the
Lord’s utterance: “Do not treasure up treasure for yourselves on earth, for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” What he received out of
regard for God he gave for the various needs of the indigent. Thus during his life he raised more than two hundred people from the bond of servitude and the
burden of debt.

### 2

**[082]** When I came to Tours, he left his cell and came to seek me. After greeting and kissing me, he returned again. As I have said, he was very abstinent
and healed the sicknesses of the infirm. But just as holiness arose from abstinence, so vanity began to creep in from holiness. He left his cell and went with
haughty vainglory to seek out and visit his relatives in the district of Poitou, mentioned above. Returning swollen with arrogance, he tried to please himself
alone. Rebuked by me, he accepted the reasoning that the proud are far from God’s kingdom. He cleansed himself of vainglory and made himself so humble that no
root of pride at all remained in him. He himself professed, “I now know to be true what the blessed apostle testifies by the utterance of his sacred mouth: ‘Let
him who glories glory in the Lord.’”

The Lord performed many miracles through him upon the sick. Senoch said that he would enclose himself so completely that he would never appear to human sight. I
advised him not to bind himself perpetually in this enclosure except only on the days between the deposition of Saint Martin and the solemnity of the Lord’s
Nativity, and likewise during the forty days which the authority of the fathers has ordained to be passed in the greatest abstinence before the Easter feasts.
On the other days, for the sake of the sick, he should offer himself to the people. Hearing my counsel, he willingly accepted what was said and fulfilled it
without hesitation.

### 3

**[083]** Having said a little about his manner of life, let me now come to the miracles which the healing right hand of divine power deigned to perform through
him. A certain blind man named Popusitus came to him. The blessed Senoch had by then been ordained priest. While Popusitus asked for some food, his eyes were
touched by the holy priest’s hand. As soon as he received the saving sign, he recovered his sight. Another boy from Poitou, suffering from the same disease,
heard of this confessor’s works and prayed to recover his lost sight. Senoch did not delay. Invoking Christ’s name, he made the cross over the blind eyes.
Immediately a stream of blood flowed out, light entered, and after a course of twenty years the radiance of the twin stars shone brightly on his brow, which had
been deprived of them.

Two boys, weak in all their members and contracted into a round shape like a sphere, were brought before him. He laid hands on them; their limbs were restored,
and in the space of one hour he delivered them both. He then doubled the benefit of a twin miracle. A boy and a girl stood before him with contracted hands. It
was then the middle of the Easter feast. They begged God’s servant for a remedy to straighten them. Because of the crowd of people who had gathered at the
church, he put off acting, crying out that he was unworthy to be one through whom God would deign to offer benefits to the sick. When everyone entreated him, he
took their hands in his own. After touching them and straightening their fingers, he ordered them to depart healed. So also Benaia—for that was the woman’s
name—brought closed eyes; blessed by the touch of his saving right hand, she departed enlightened.

I do not think it should be concealed that his prayer often obtained the emptying of serpents’ venom. Two men swollen from a serpent’s bite fell at his feet,
begging him to dispel by his power the poison which the evil beast’s tooth had injected into their dying limbs. He poured out prayer to the Lord: “Lord Jesus
Christ, who in the beginning created all the elements of the world and ordained that the serpent, the rival of human dignities, should be under a curse, drive
from these your servants the evil of this poison, so that the serpents may not triumph over them, but they may triumph over the serpent.” When he had said this,
he touched the whole structure of their bodies. Immediately every swelling subsided and the deadly poison lost its power to harm.

The day of the Lord’s Resurrection had arrived. A man going to church saw a multitude of cattle pasturing on his crops. He groaned and said, “Woe to me! The
work of my year’s labour perishes so completely that nothing at all remains of it.” Taking an axe and cutting branches, he began to close an opening in the
hedge. His hand immediately contracted and involuntarily retained what it had voluntarily grasped. Incited by pain, he went sorrowfully to the holy confessor,
dragging behind him the branch his hand gripped, and related everything as it had happened. Senoch sanctified oil with a blessing and anointed the hand with his
hand; drawing out the branch, he restored it. Afterwards also he restored many people to health from serpent bites and the poison of malignant pustules by
placing the sign of the cross over them. When he laid hands on some possessed by the malice of a savage demon, the demons were immediately put to flight, and he
restored minds disturbed by possession to integrity of understanding.

To all the needy whom the divine right hand saved from various infirmities through him, Senoch himself offered food and clothing with cheerful provision. His
care for the needy was so great that he even carefully constructed bridges over riverbeds, lest anyone should suffer cruel shipwreck when the waters flooded.

### 4

**[084]** Renowned among the people and made famous by these miracles, he was about forty years old when a slight fever struck him. He lay in bed for three
days. News was brought to me that he was near his passing. Hastening there quickly, I approached his bed but could elicit no conversation from him, for he was
very exhausted. After about an hour he breathed out his spirit. That multitude of redeemed people gathered for his funeral whom I mentioned above: those he had
released from the yoke of servitude or various debts, and those he had fed with food or covered with clothing. They lamented, saying, “Holy father, to whom will
you leave me?” Afterwards he was laid in his tomb and often manifested himself by evident miracles. On the thirtieth day after his death, while Mass was being
celebrated at his tomb, a certain crippled man named Chaidulfus came to his burial place begging alms. While he venerated with kisses the pall laid over it, the
bonds of his members were loosed and he was straightened. I learned of many other things done there, but have committed only these to memory.

## XVI. The Holy Abbot Venantius

### Prologue

**[085]** Heavenly power bestows a unique yet manifold gift upon the churches and the peoples of the earth when it continually grants the world not only
intercessors for sins but also teachers of eternal life. It is seen to be unique while it is bestowed as manifold by the divine Majesty, because it is lavishly
granted to all who wish to seek it, according to the saying: “Ask, and you will receive,” and so forth. The human mind ought therefore vigilantly and
unceasingly to investigate the life of the saints, so that, called forth by zeal and kindled by example, it may always be extended toward the things it knows
are acceptable to God, and may deserve to be rescued by him or be heard. The saints sought to receive these things from his Majesty, asking continually that he
himself would instill them in the heart, accomplish them in work, and speak them in the mouth. Thus the mind, more easily purified in thought, speech, and
action, might think holy things, speak just things, and do honourable things. While they served in the things pleasing to the Divinity, they obtained remission
of the debt of sin, were rescued from the contagion of foul filth, and were invited according to their merits to the heavenly kingdom. They also placed the
examples of their predecessors before their eyes and praised Almighty God for their dispositions, whose examples, as I have said, they resolved to follow.

So I also, striving to speak in praise of Venantius, God’s devoted servant and abbot, rather attribute his gifts to the Divinity. It is manifest that his right
hand accomplished what the saints are known to have done. I pray that he may open the mouth of the mute to proclaim his bishop’s works; just as I recognize by
knowledge that I am slight, so I know by conscience that I am a sinner.

### 1

**[086]** Saint Venantius was an inhabitant of the territory of Bourges, born of parents freeborn and Catholic according to the world’s dignity. While he was
flourishing in youthful age, his parents bound him in betrothal. As befits this age, he showed himself affectionate in the girl’s love and, with frequent cups,
also carried her footwear. It happened by the Lord’s inspiration that he came to the city of Tours. At that time there was a monastery near the basilica of
Saint Martin, in which Abbot Silvinus governed a flock devoted to God with the sceptre of the rule. This devout man approached it and saw the blessed Martin’s
miracles. He said within himself, “As I conjecture, it is better to serve Christ undefiled than to be involved in worldly contagion through the bond of
marriage. I shall leave a bride in the territory of Bourges and be joined by faith to the Catholic Church, so that what I believe in my heart I may deserve to
accomplish in work.” Turning these things over within himself, he came to the aforesaid abbot, fell at his feet, and with tears disclosed what he bore in his
inmost heart. The abbot gave thanks to God for the boy’s faith and, adding priestly exhortation, tonsured the young man and enrolled him in the monastic flock.
Venantius showed himself in humility to the brothers and cherished charity with everyone. He is said to have been raised to such a height of holiness that all
honoured him with the greatest zeal like a near parent. When the abbot of the aforesaid monastery died, the brothers chose Venantius to be appointed in his
place.

### 2

**[087]** One Sunday he was invited to celebrate the solemn Mass. He said to the brothers, “My eyes are covered with darkness, and I cannot see the little book.
Command another priest to do these things.” While the priest celebrated, Venantius stood nearby. The time came, according to Catholic custom, for the holy gift
to be blessed with the sign of the cross placed over it. Looking, he saw what appeared to be a ladder set at the window of the apse and an old man descending by
it, venerable in the honour of the clerical order. With outstretched right hand the old man blessed the sacrifice offered on the altar. These things happened in
the basilica of Saint Martin. No one deserved to see them except Venantius; I do not know why the others did not. He later related it to the brothers. There is
no doubt that the Lord showed these things to a faithful servant to whom he also deigned to reveal the secrets of heavenly mysteries.

On another Sunday, after prayer had been completed, Venantius was returning from the basilicas of the saints, supported by a staff. In the middle of the blessed
confessor’s courtyard he stood immovable, ears pricked and eyes fixed intently on heaven for a very long time. Then, moved from the place, he began to groan and
draw long sighs. His companions asked what this was and, if he had seen something divine, to relate it. He answered, “Woe to me, inactive and sluggish! The
solemn Masses are already being completed in heaven, and I, idle, have not yet begun the sacrament of this mystery. Truly I tell you, I heard the voices of
angels in heaven crying ‘Holy’ in praise of the Lord.” Faster than it takes to tell, he ordered the solemn Masses to be completed in the monastery.

I will not pass over another occasion when, according to the custom described above, he was returning from the basilicas he had visited for prayer. While the
words of the Lord’s Prayer were being sung at Mass in the basilica, when they said, “Deliver us from evil,” he heard a voice from a certain tomb saying
likewise, “Deliver us from evil.” It is reckoned not without the merit of perfection that he deserved to hear this. Coming also to the tomb of the priest
Paasivus, he learned from Paasivus himself what his merit was and how great his refreshment.

### 3

**[088]** Great though these things are, I wish to come to that grace of healing which the Lord offered to the sick through him. There is no doubt that God’s
right hand worked through him, as I said above, since God deigned to reveal to so great a man the things I have recorded. A little boy named Paul, afflicted by
severe pain in his legs and knees, went to the saint. Falling at his knees, he began to entreat him to obtain by his prayer the granting of medicine from the
Lord’s mercy. Venantius immediately prayed, touched the sick boy’s limbs with blessed oil, and made him rest on his own bed. After he had rested briefly,
Venantius ordered him to rise at the end of an hour. Rising, he was restored healed by the saint’s hands to his mother.

A servant of a certain Faretrius, hostile to his master, sought this bishop’s oratory. Faretrius, swollen with pride, dragged out and beat the servant in the
blessed man’s absence. Soon seized by fever, he breathed out his spirit. Venantius often mitigated attacks of quartan, tertian, and other fevers by prayer. He
extinguished the poison of malignant pustules by making the saving sign. He cleansed those possessed by demons by invoking the name of the Trinity. He himself
was also often assailed by demons, but remained victorious in the struggle. One night, when he rose from his bed to render the office, he saw two great rams
standing at his doors as though awaiting his arrival. At the sight they ran furiously toward him with a violent charge. He opposed them with the sign of the
cross; they vanished, and he entered the oratory without fear. Another night, returning from the oratory, he found his cell full of demons. He said to them,
“Where have you come from?” They said, “We left Rome yesterday and came to this place.” He said, “Depart, detestable creatures, and do not approach a place in
which the Lord’s name is invoked.” As he spoke, they vanished like smoke.

### 4

**[089]** Powerful in these and similar graces of great miracles, he completed the course of his present life and departed from the world to receive eternal
life. His blessed tomb is often made glorious by the performance of illustrious miracles. A wicked demon had occupied the mind of Mascarpio, a servant of that
monastery. For three years he was possessed; raging at the blessed man’s tomb, he was cleansed when the demon was cast out by Venantius’s power or, as I
believe, his prayer, and afterwards lived for many years with a sound mind. Julian’s wife, suffering an attack of quartan fever, came to the blessed man’s tomb.
When heat and bodily trembling subsided, she departed healed. Baudimund’s wife likewise suffered from this fever. When she prostrated herself at the holy man’s
bed and poured out prayer, she soon recovered and was restored to health. I have heard many other things about him, but think that what has been written is
sufficient for the faith of Catholics.

## XVII. Saint Nicetius, Bishop Of Trier

### Prologue

**[090]** If faith is given to words, I think that reporters of sacred works ought faithfully to be believed according to the merit of faith, because not
everything read in the Scriptures could be seen with one’s own eyes. Some things are believed because established by the report of Scripture itself, some
because confirmed by the testimony of other authors, and some on the authority of one’s own observation. But there are people—what is worse—who, perverse in
understanding, reprove attested things just as they do not believe written things, and despise things seen as though fabricated. They do not hold in their
belief what the apostle Thomas bore in his heart when he said, “Unless I see, I will not believe.” Blessed indeed are those who have not seen and have believed.
Thomas believed as soon as he saw. But, as I have said, many who see not only do not believe but even try to tear the very foundations of belief out of their
hearts by the roots. Therefore, as I am about to write certain things concerning the miracles, manliness, magnanimity, and holiness of Saint Nicetius, bishop of
Trier, I fear being reproached by some who say, “Since you are younger, how can you know the deeds of your elders? How did their acts come to you? Surely these
things written are judged to be nothing other than fabrications by you.” For this reason it is necessary to set the reporter of this work in the open, so that
those who disparage the truth may be confounded. Let them know, then, that I heard the following from the blessed Aridius, abbot of the city of Limoges, who was
nurtured by Bishop Nicetius himself and received the order of cleric from him. I do not believe Aridius deceived me in this, since at the time he related these
things to me, God through him enlightened the eyes of the blind, gave walking to the paralysed, and restored the possessed to sound minds by casting out demons.
Nor should it be believed that he could be overshadowed by a cloud of falsehood, when God often protected him under a cloud of rain in such a way that, while
his companions were soaked, he was not wetted by any shower of falling drops. If such a reporter is doubted, God’s benefits are distrusted.

The aforesaid priest therefore said of the aforesaid bishop: “Dearest brother, I have learned many things about Saint Nicetius made public by the testimony of
good men, but very many I examined with my own eyes or learned when they were reluctantly drawn from him.” When he explained to me certain things God had done
through Nicetius, he did not swell with the haughtiness of vainglory. Pierced in heart, he said with tears, “I seem to disclose these things to you, dearest
son, so that you too, living with the utmost innocence of heart, may meditate on similar things. No one can strive toward the heights of God’s miracles unless
innocent in hands and pure in heart, as the reed of David’s song sings.” The aforesaid reporter therefore began these things about him.

### 1

**[091]** Saint Bishop Nicetius was designated a cleric from the very time of his birth. When he was delivered in childbirth, his whole head, as is usual with
newborn infants, appeared bare of hair, but around it a ring of small hairs was visible, so that you would think a cleric’s crown had been marked by them.
Reared by most diligent parents and instructed in letters, he was commended to a certain abbot in a monastery. In that place he showed himself so devoted to God
that, when the abbot died, he succeeded him. After assuming the office of abbot, he showed himself such and so great in the instruction and discipline of the
brothers that no one was permitted not only to act but even to speak perversely. He said, “Dearest brothers, scurrility and every idle word must be avoided.
Just as we ought to present our whole body pure to God, so we should open our mouth for nothing except God’s praise. There are three ways in which the human
race falls: it thinks, speaks, or acts. You, dearest brothers, must avoid scurrility, malice, and every evil work.” He exhorted the brothers in many other ways
to present themselves worthy and pure before the Lord.

King Theodoric also venerated him with great honour because Nicetius often laid bare his vices and, corrected for his crimes, the king became more virtuous. For
this reason, when the bishop of the city of Trier died, Theodoric ordered Nicetius to be summoned to the episcopate. With the people’s consent and the king’s
decree, he was brought for ordination by men holding the highest honour with the king. When they approached the city at sunset and prepared lodging with tents
pitched, they immediately loosed their horses and let them into the poor people’s crops. Seeing this, the blessed Nicetius was moved by compassion and said,
“Drive your horses out of the poor man’s crop at once, or I will remove you from my communion.” Indignant, they said, “What is this cause of which you speak?
You have not yet attained the episcopal summit, and already you threaten excommunication!” He answered, “Truly I tell you, the king has determined to order me,
torn from my monastery, to be consecrated for this burden. God’s will indeed will be done, for with me resisting, the king’s will will not be fulfilled in all
evils.” He then ran quickly and drove the horses from the crop. Thus, to the astonishment of those men, he was led into the city. He did not honour the person
of the powerful but feared God alone in heart and works. Placed on the throne, while listening to the sequence of readings, he felt something heavy upon his
neck. Two or three times he secretly put his hand there to test it, but could find no object causing the weight. Turning his head to right and left, he smelled
an odour of sweetness and understood that this burden was the dignity of the priesthood itself.

### 2
