**[092]** After assuming the episcopate, he showed himself so terrible to everyone that, if they did not keep God’s commandments, he declared with a herald’s
voice that immediate death threatened them. I wish to say a few things about these matters to strengthen the censure of bishops, instruct the people, and even
correct the kings of the present day. When Theodoric died and his son Theudebert obtained the kingdom and committed many injustices, Nicetius often rebuked him
both for perpetrating them and for failing to reprove the perpetrators. The Lord’s Day came. Behold, the king entered the church with those whom the bishop had
ordered to abstain from communion. After the readings ordained by the ancient canon had been read and the gifts offered on God’s altar, the bishop said, “The
solemn Masses will not be completed here today unless those deprived of communion first depart.” The king resisted. Suddenly a young man in the crowd, seized by
a demon, cried out. Amid the torments of his torture he began in a loud voice to confess both the saint’s miracles and the king’s crimes. He declared the bishop
chaste and the king an adulterer; the former humble in fear of Christ, the latter proud in the glory of his kingdom; the bishop, undefiled in his priesthood, to
be preferred by God in the future, and the king soon to be crushed by the author of his crime. When the terrified king asked that this possessed man be cast out
of the church, the bishop said, “First let those who have followed you—the incestuous, murderers, and adulterers—be driven from this church, and God will
command this man to be silent.” The king immediately ordered all those condemned by the bishop’s sentence to leave the church. When they had been expelled, the
bishop ordered the demoniac to be taken outside. Though ten men tried to pull him away, he grasped a column and could not be torn from it. God’s saint secretly
made Christ’s cross beneath his garment against the demon and commanded it to release him. The man immediately fell together with those trying to drag him; a
little later he rose healed. After the solemnities had been performed, he was sought but could never be found. No one knew where he had come from or where he
went. Many conjectured that he had been sent by God to make known the works of king and bishop. Thus, while the bishop prayed, the king became gentler, and the
pastor, worthy to be rewarded by the Lord, rightly heard that prophetic word: “He who has restored the precious from the base will be like my mouth.”

The bishop preached to the people every day, exposing the crimes of individuals and continually interceding for the remission of those who confessed. The poison
of hatred often flared against him because he so truthfully made many people’s crimes public. He often offered himself voluntarily to persecutors and presented
his neck to the drawn sword, but the Lord did not permit them to harm him. He wished to die for justice if a persecutor became more violent. He said, “I will
gladly die for justice.” He also often excommunicated King Chlothar for unjust deeds and was never terrified when Chlothar threatened exile.

### 3

**[093]** Once, when he had been led into exile and was being removed by the other bishops who had become flatterers of the king, abandoned by all his own
people, he said to one deacon who still stood firm in faith, “What are you doing now? Why do you not follow your brothers, so that you may go where you wish, as
they have done?” The deacon answered, “As the Lord my God lives, as long as my spirit is contained within these mortal limbs, I will never abandon you.”
Nicetius said, “Because you have said this, I will tell you what I have learned by the Lord’s revelation. Today at this very hour I both recover my honour and
am restored to my church. Those who abandoned me will flee back to me in great shame.” The astonished deacon awaited the promised event, which he later
experienced. At daybreak the next day a legate of King Sigibert suddenly arrived with letters, announcing that King Chlothar had died and that Sigibert ought to
receive his rightful kingdom together with the bishop’s charity. Hearing this, Nicetius returned to the church and was restored to authority. Those who had
abandoned him were confounded, but he received them all in charity.

Who could unfold how strong he was in preaching, terrible in reproof, constant in endurance, and prudent in teaching? His rigour was always one in prosperity
and adversity. He neither feared one who threatened nor was deceived by one who flattered. As the aforesaid reporter used to say, it was little that, in the
words of the apostle Paul, he had not suffered injustice: “Dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers in the city, dangers from false brothers,” and so
forth. One day, while crossing the river Moselle by boat, he was driven by the force of the waves among the piles of a bridge. He clung to a pile only with his
palms while holding the boat with his foot. Prepared for immersion, he was rescued by those watching. He used to say that he had suffered this through the
tempter’s snare. The author of crime also often showed himself to Nicetius’s eyes as though intending to harm him. Once, while travelling, Nicetius dismounted
from his horse and entered dense brambles to relieve his belly. Behold, a most hideous shadow stood before him, tall in stature, extremely thick, foul in
colour, with immense flashing eyes like a raging bull, its mouth gaping as though ready to swallow the man of God. He made the sign of the cross against it, and
it vanished like rising smoke. There is no doubt that the prince of crime himself had been shown to him.

### 4

**[094]** As I have said, he was very strong in fasting. While the others took refreshment, he often covered his head with a hood so as not to be recognized in
public and, with only one servant, went around the basilicas of the saints. God also gave him the grace of healing. While he was going around the saints’
dwellings in that habit described above, he came to the church of the holy Bishop Maximinus. In its courtyard three possessed people, after many ravings, were
lying asleep. Seeing them given over to sleep, he made the sign of the cross against them. They immediately awoke, raised their voices on high, and, driven to
vomit, were cleansed.

When the inguinal plague was severely devastating the people of Trier around the city, God’s bishop continually implored the Lord’s mercy for the sheep
entrusted to him. At night a great sound like powerful thunder arose over the river bridge, so that the city itself seemed to split open. All the terrified
people sat up in their beds as deadly destruction covered them. Amid the noise one voice clearer than the rest was heard: “Companions, what shall we do here?
Bishop Eucharius watches at one gate, Maximinus keeps guard at another, and Nicetius moves about in the middle. We can prevail no further here unless we leave
this city to their protection.” When this voice was heard, the disease immediately ceased, and no one else died of it. There is no doubt that the aforesaid
bishop’s power defended it.

Once, when the bishop had been invited by the king, he said to his attendants, “Obtain for me an abundant multitude of fish, so that when we go to meet the
king, our work may be fulfilled and our friends served in full measure.” They answered, “Our fish trap, into which fish usually fall, is entirely deserted. The
timbers themselves have been torn from their places by the river’s force. Your command cannot be fulfilled because there is no means at hand to catch what you
order.” Hearing this, he entered his cell, called a servant, and said, “Go and tell the head cook to supply fish from the river.” The servant delivered the
order and was ridiculed by the man. When he returned, the bishop said, “I know that you spoke what I commanded, but they refused to hear. Go and tell them to
go.” When they received this order stubbornly two or three times, they finally went angrily to the fish trap. Looking, they found it so full of fish that ten
men could scarcely carry what they found. Divine power often showed him what was needful.

### 5

**[095]** I thought I should not pass over what was shown to him by the Lord concerning the kings of the Franks. In a vision at night he saw a great tower of
such height that it seemed near heaven. It had many windows; the Lord stood on its summit, and God’s angels were stationed at those openings. One of them held a
great book and said, “This king and that king will live in the world for so long.” He named each individually, both those living at that time and those born
afterwards, and described the character of their reign and the length of their lives. After each name the other angels always answered, “Amen.” These things
were later fulfilled just as the saint announced through the aforesaid revelation.

Returning from the king by boat, Nicetius fell asleep. Behold, the river, stirred by the wind, began to raise its waves high, so that the boat itself seemed
about to sink. As I have said, the sleeping bishop gave out some kind of sleep, as often happens to sleepers, as though he were oppressed by someone. Awakened
by his companions, he made the sign of the cross over the waters and the storm ceased. Sighing repeatedly, he was asked by his companions what he had seen. He
said, “I had resolved to be silent, but I will tell you. I saw myself spreading nets throughout the whole world to catch people, and I had no helper except this
boy Aridius.” The Lord rightly wished to show him as a maker of nets, for every day he caught people for the divine office.

A man with long hair and beard came to him, fell at his feet, and said, “Lord, I am the man who was saved by your help when placed in danger at sea.” Nicetius
rebuked him for offering this praise of him and said, “Tell how God rescued you from this necessity; my power can help no one.” The man said, “Recently I
boarded a ship to go to Italy. A multitude of pagans embarked with me; among that crowd of rustics I alone was a Christian. When a storm arose, I began to
invoke the Lord’s name and beg that your intercession would rescue me. The pagans invoked their gods: one cried to Jupiter, another to Mercury; one begged
Minerva’s help, another Venus’s. When I was already in danger of death, I said to them, ‘Men, do not invoke these; they are not gods but demons. If you wish to
be rescued from present destruction, invoke Saint Nicetius, that he may obtain your salvation from the Lord’s mercy.’ Raising one voice in such a cry, they
said, ‘God of Nicetius, rescue us.’ Immediately the sea was calmed, the wind fell, the sun returned, and the ship reached the place we wished. I vowed not to
cut the hair of my head before I was presented to your sight.” At the bishop’s command the man was tonsured and went to Clermont, where he confessed that he was
from. I have learned from the aforesaid abbot innumerable things related about this man, but I think I should now end the little book.

### 6

**[096]** When Nicetius recognized that the time of his departure was near, he told the brothers, “I saw the apostle Paul with John the Baptist inviting me to
eternal rest and presenting me with a crown adorned with heavenly pearls. These men said to me, ‘You will enjoy such sights with us in God’s kingdom.’” He
related this to certain faithful people. A few days later a slight fever struck him, and he sent his spirit ahead to the Lord. He was buried in the basilica of
the holy Bishop Maximinus. His tomb is now often illuminated by divine miracles.

*Here ends the Life.*

## XVIII. The Abbots Ursus And Leobatius

### Prologue

**[097]** When the lawgiving prophet’s oracle had taken its beginning from the beginning of speech and had declared that the Lord stretched out the heavens by
the right hand of his majesty, it said: “God made two great lights and the stars. He placed them in the firmament of heaven to rule day and night and to shine
in the firmament of heaven.” So now, as the authority of the ancients has ordained, he has also given great lights in that heaven of the human mind: Christ and
his church, to shine in the darkness of ignorance and enlighten the senses of my humility. As John the Evangelist says of the Lord himself: “He is the light of
the world, who enlightens every person coming into this world.” He also placed stars in it: the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, to instruct me by their
teachings or enlighten me by their wonders. As he says in the Gospel: “You are the light of this world,” and: “Let your light so shine before people that they
may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The apostles are rightly taken for the whole church, which, having neither wrinkle nor stain,
remains undefiled. As the apostle says: “He presented to himself a pure church, having neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of this kind.”

From their teaching, even down to my times, there have been those who, like the radiance of stars in this world, not only shone with the light of their merits
but also flashed with the greatness of their doctrines. They illuminated the whole world with the ray of their preaching, going through every place to preach
and establishing monasteries for divine worship. They taught people to abstain from worldly cares and, leaving the darkness of concupiscence, to follow the true
God through whom all things were made. So the account of faithful brothers indicates concerning the abbots Ursus and Leobatius.

### 1

**[098]** Abbot Ursus was an inhabitant of the city of Cahors, religious from his earliest years and devoted to the love of God. Leaving that place, he entered
the territory of Bourges. He founded monasteries—Tausiriacum, Onia, and Pontiniacum—and established superiors honoured for holiness and balanced in stewardship.
He then entered the territory of Tours and came to the place which ancient authority established to be called Senaparia. Building an oratory, he established a
monastery. Entrusting the highest responsibility of the rule to Leobatius as superior, Ursus established another monastery now called Loccis, situated on the
river Anger in the recess of a mountain above which a fortress now rises, called by the same name as the monastery. When a congregation had been gathered there,
he resolved in his mind never to go to another place, but to work with his own hands together with the whole congregation and to obtain food from the earth in
the sweat of his brow. Among the other gifts of his preaching, he commended to the brothers the apostle Paul’s saying: “Labour with your hands, so that you may
have something to give back to those suffering need,” and: “He who does not work, let him not eat.”

The Lord also gave him the grace of healing. When he breathed upon possessed people, demons were immediately cast out of the possessed bodies. The Lord deigned
to perform other miracles through him as well. He abstained from food and drink and unceasingly forbade the monks to turn either eye or thought toward any
wantonness.

### 2

**[099]** While he was doing these things and the brothers were turning a mill by hand to grind wheat for their needs, he decided, because of the brothers’
labour, to establish a mill in the very bed of the river Anger. Fixing stakes through the river and gathering heaps of great stones, he made sluices and
collected water in a channel, whose force made the wheel of the mill turn with great speed. Relieving the monks’ labour by this work and assigning it to one of
the brothers, he ensured that the necessary task was performed. A certain Goth named Silarius, greatly loved by King Alaric, coveted this mill in rivalry with
the monastery. He said to the abbot, “Give me this mill to be under my control, and I will repay whatever you wish.” Ursus answered, “My poverty established it
with great labour, and I cannot give it away now, lest my brothers perish from hunger.” Silarius said, “If you wish to grant it willingly, I thank you.
Otherwise I will take it by force, or at least make another mill, by whose sluices the water will be turned back and your wheel will no longer be allowed to
turn.” The abbot answered, “You will not do what God does not wish, and you will never receive it from me.”

Boiling with bile, Silarius constructed a similar mill below it. The water was turned backward and flooded beneath the wheel of the monastery’s work, creating a
whirlpool. The wheel stopped completely and could not turn at all as it had been accustomed. Its keeper came to the abbot in the middle of the night, as they
say, while Ursus was keeping watch in the oratory with the brothers, and said, “Rise, abbot, and entreat the Lord more intently. The mill wheel has stopped
because of the flooding from the foreign channel Silarius made.” Hearing this, Ursus immediately sent individual brothers to the monasteries he had established,
saying, “Prostrate yourselves in prayer and do no other work until I send to you again.” He himself did not leave the oratory, but intently entreated the Lord
and awaited the coming of his mercy. He did this for two whole days and as many nights. As the third day was dawning, the monk who had been keeper came again,
reporting that the wheel of their mill was turning at the highest speed according to its former custom. The abbot and brothers left the oratory and went to the
bank. Looking, they could not find the mill Silarius had made. Going to the bank and examining the bottom of the riverbed, they found no trace of it. No wood,
stone, iron, or any kind of trace could be shown. As far as could be conjectured, divine power opened the very place where it had been constructed, and it was
removed from human eyes. Ursus then sent messengers to the brothers, saying, “Rest now from your labour, for God has avenged the injury to my brothers.”

### 3

**[100]** Endowed with these and similar miracles, Ursus completed the course of life and departed to the Lord. Afterwards possessed people were healed and the
blind enlightened at his tomb. After his death the superiors throughout the monasteries received the office of abbot through the bishops’ grant. Leobatius also
was appointed abbot of the monastery at Senaparia within the territory of Tours. He continued in surpassing holiness and old age, and there he died and was
buried.

## XIX. Saint Monegundis

### Prologue

**[101]** The glorious gifts of divine benefits granted from heaven to the human race can neither be conceived by the senses, expressed in words, nor contained
in writings. From the very beginning of the rude world, the Saviour of the world allowed himself to be seen by the patriarchs and foretold by the prophets. At
last he deigned to be received in the womb of Mary, ever virgin and untouched. The almighty and immortal Creator allowed himself to be clothed in the garment of
mortal flesh, underwent death to restore humanity dead in sin, and rose again as victor. Wounded by the darts of grave crimes and afflicted by the wounds of
lurking robbers, he brought us to the shelter of heavenly medicine—that is, the teaching of the holy church—pouring in unmixed wine and the liquid of oil. He
exhorts us to live by the examples of the saints and to fortify ourselves with his unceasing commandment. He offers us as examples not only men but also the
inferior sex itself, contending not sluggishly but manfully. He shares the starry kingdoms not only with men fighting lawfully but also with women toiling
favourably in these battles. So it is now with the blessed Monegundis. Leaving her native soil like the prudent queen who went to hear Solomon’s wisdom, she
sought the basilica of the blessed Martin, to marvel at his miracles granted daily and to drink from the priestly fountain, so that she might unlock the
entrance to the grove of paradise.

### 1

**[102]** The most blessed Monegundis, a native of the city of Chartres, was joined in marriage according to her parents’ wish and had two daughters. She
rejoiced greatly over them and said, “God has propagated my lineage, so that two daughters were born to me.” But the bitterness of this world overtook this
worldly joy: the girls were stricken by a slight fever and completed the debt due to nature. Their mother sorrowfully bewailed this and mourned herself as
bereaved. Neither by day nor night did she cease weeping, and neither husband, friend, nor any relative could console her. At last, turning within herself, she
said, “If I receive no consolation for my daughters’ death, I fear that I may offend my Lord Jesus Christ. Now leaving these laments and consoled with the
blessed Job, let me sing: ‘The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord.’” Saying this,
she took off her dark garment and ordered a tiny cell to be prepared for her, with only one small window fitted through which she could see a little light.
Despising worldly ambition and rejecting her husband’s companionship, she devoted herself to God alone, in whom she trusted. She poured out prayer for her own
sins and those of the people. She had one little maid whose service supplied what necessity required. She took barley flour and ashes mixed with water, strained
them carefully, and made a dough from the water. She formed the loaves with her own hands and baked them herself, and after long fasts took refreshment. She
distributed the rest of her household’s food to the poor.

One day the aforesaid maid who usually served her—I believe she was seduced by the enemy’s cunning, whose custom is always to inflict injuries on the
good—withdrew from Monegundis’s service, saying, “I cannot remain with this mistress who lives in such abstinence. I would rather enjoy the world and take food
and drink in abundance.” It was already the fifth day since the maid’s departure, and the holy woman had received neither her accustomed flour nor water. She
remained immovable and fixed in Christ; whoever is established in him falls away neither by a whirlwind nor by the force of waves. She did not think life was
given her from mortal food but from God’s word, as it is written. She remembered that proverb of Solomon’s Wisdom: “The Lord will not kill the soul of the just
with hunger,” and: “The just person lives by faith.” Since the human body cannot be sustained without earthly food, she prostrated herself in prayer and asked
that he who gave manna from heaven to a hungry people and brought water from rock for the thirsty would also deign to grant nourishment by which her weary
little body might be strengthened a little. Immediately at her prayer snow fell from heaven and covered the ground. Seeing it with thanksgiving, she stretched
her hand through the window and gathered from the snow around the wall. Squeezing water from it, she formed bread as usual; this supplied bodily food for
another five days.

She had a little garden adjoining the cell and used to go into it for some relief. Once, as she entered and walked looking at the herbs of the place, a woman
who had put wheat to dry on her roof looked at Monegundis inopportunely, as though from a higher place, full of worldly cares. Her eyes were immediately closed
and she lost the light. Recognizing her fault, she went to Monegundis and disclosed what had happened. Monegundis threw herself into prayer and said, “Woe to
me! Because of my person, a little sinner, other people’s eyes are closed.” When she had finished praying, she laid her hand on the woman. As soon as she made
the sign of the cross, the woman recovered her sight.

A devout man from that district who had long ago lost his hearing came to this cell. His relatives entreated Monegundis to deign to lay her blessed hands on
him. Crying out that she was unworthy for Christ to work through her, she prostrated herself on the ground and, as though licking the very footprints of the
Lord’s feet, humbly implored divine clemency for him. While she still lay on the ground, the deaf man’s ears were opened. His sorrow removed, he returned home
with joy.

### 2

**[103]** Glorified by these signs among her relatives, Monegundis, lest she incur the fall of vainglory, faithfully sought the basilica of the holy Bishop
Martin, leaving her husband, household, and entire home. As she pursued the journey she had begun, she came to a village of the city of Tours named Evena, where
relics of the blessed Medard, confessor of Soissons, are kept. His vigils were being celebrated that night. She watched intently in prayer and at the appointed
hour went with the rest of the people to the solemn Mass. While God’s priests were celebrating it, a girl swollen with the poison of a malignant pustule came
and went to Monegundis’s feet, saying, “Help me, because wicked death is trying to take away my life.” Following her custom, Monegundis prostrated herself in
prayer and interceded for her with God, the Creator of all. Rising, she made the sign of the cross. The wound broke open in four places; as the pus ran out,
untimely death left the girl.

Afterwards the blessed Monegundis came to the basilica of Saint Martin. Prostrating herself before the tomb, she gave thanks that she had deserved to behold the
holy tomb with her own eyes. Settling in a tiny cell, she devoted herself daily to prayer, fasting, and vigils. That place was not inglorious because of her
power. A widow’s daughter brought contracted hands. When Monegundis, having been entreated, made the saving sign, she began to touch the girl’s fingers with her
own hands. The fingers were extended, the sinews straightened, and she released the palms unharmed.

While these things were happening, her husband heard the blessed woman’s fame. Calling his friends and neighbours, he went after her, brought her back home, and
put her in the cell where she had previously lived. She did not cease from her accustomed work but persevered in fasting and entreaties, so that she might
finally obtain the place where she wished to live. She began the desired journey again, imploring the blessed Martin’s help, that he who had given the desire
would also grant its fulfilment. She reached the basilica and returned to the cell in which she had previously stayed. From then on she remained unshaken and
was never again sought by her husband. Gathering a few nuns there, she lived in complete faith and prayer. She ate only barley bread and drank wine only a
little on feast days, and even that greatly diluted with water. She had no soft bed of hay or straw except a mat made of woven rushes, commonly called a matta.
Placing it on a frame, she spread only this over it. It was her daily bench, mattress, feather cushion, and covering—every furnishing of her bed. She taught the
women she had gathered with her to do the same. Living there in God’s praises, she bestowed saving remedies on many sick people after prayer.

### 3

**[104]** A woman brought her daughter covered with wounds; as some call it, this affliction had produced pustules. Monegundis prayed, took saliva from her
mouth, and anointed the cruel wounds. She restored the girl to health through the help of his power who formed the eyes of a man born blind with spittle.

A boy living in that place drank poison in a potion. After he had been bewitched, as they assert, serpents generated in his intestines caused great pain by
their bites, allowing him not even the smallest moment of rest. He could take neither food nor drink; if he took anything after a long interval, he immediately
rejected it. Brought to the blessed woman, he asked to be cleansed by her power. She protested that she was unworthy to do such things. Entangled by his
relatives’ entreaty, she touched the boy’s belly and soothed it with her palm. She sensed that the wickedness of venomous snakes was lurking there. Taking a
green vine leaf, she smeared it with saliva and fixed upon it the seal of the blessed cross. Placing it on the boy’s belly, she relieved the pain a little, and
he fell asleep on the bench—he who had long lacked sleep while pains pressed upon him. Rising after an hour, he went out to purge his belly and discharged the
offspring of that pestiferous generation. Giving thanks to God’s handmaid, he departed healed.

Another boy, crippled by paralysis, was carried before her in other people’s hands, begging to be healed by the blessed woman. She prostrated herself in prayer
and poured out a petition for him to the Lord. When the prayer was finished, she rose, took the boy’s hand, raised him up, and allowed him to depart safe.

A blind woman was brought to her and begged her to lay hands on her. Monegundis answered, “What have you to do with me, people of God? Does not Saint Martin
dwell here, shining daily with the work of illustrious miracles? Go there and entreat him to deign to visit you. What can I, a sinner, do?” Persisting in her
petition, the woman said, “Every day God performs excellent work through all who fear his name. I therefore flee to you as a suppliant, for the Divinity’s grace
of healing has been granted to you.” God’s handmaid was moved and laid hands on the buried lights. The cataracts were immediately opened, and she who had been
blind saw the world spread broadly around her. When many possessed people also came to her, she laid hands on them, drove away the wicked enemy, and restored
health. None of those whom the saint allowed to approach her were delayed in being cured.

### 4

**[105]** The time of her calling was approaching, and her weary body was being dissolved. When the holy virgins she had with her saw this, they wept greatly
and said, “Holy mother, to whom will you leave us? To whom do you commend the daughters you gathered in this place out of regard for God?” Weeping briefly, she
said, “If you follow peace and sanctification, God will be your protection, and you will have the holy Bishop Martin as a great shepherd. I myself will not
depart from you: when invoked, I will be present in the midst of your charity.” They begged her, “Many sick people will come to us asking to receive a blessing
from you. What shall we do when they do not see you still living? I shall send them away confounded because I do not behold your face. Since this is hidden from
our eyes, we ask that you at least deign to bless oil and salt, from which we may minister to the sick who ask a blessing.” She blessed oil and salt and gave
them to the women, who received and kept them most carefully.

The most blessed woman thus died in peace and was buried in that cell, showing herself afterwards in many miracles. After her passing many sick people
experienced healing benefits from the aforesaid blessing. One foot of Deacon Boso had swollen from a malignant pustule so that he could not walk. Carried to her
tomb, he prayed. The girls took some of the aforesaid oil the saint had left and placed it on his foot. The wound immediately burst, the poison flowed out, and
he was healed.

A blind man brought to her tomb prostrated himself in prayer. Sleep overcame him and he slept. The blessed woman appeared and said, “I judge myself unworthy to
be made equal to the saints, but here you will recover the light of one eye. Afterwards hasten as quickly as possible to the blessed Martin’s feet and prostrate
yourself before him in compunction of mind. He will restore the sight of your other eye.” The man awoke with the light of one eye restored and went where the
command of her who ordered him directed. Entreating there again, by the blessed confessor’s power the darkness of his blind eye was driven away, and he departed
seeing.

A mute man also lay prostrated at the blessed woman’s tomb. He was so pierced by faith that he wet the pavement of the cell with streams of tears. Rising with
his tongue released by divine power, he returned. Another mute man came and lay in prayer, imploring the blessed woman’s help only in his heart and not with an
articulate voice. Some of the aforesaid blessing was poured into his mouth; blood mixed with pus burst out, and he deserved to obtain the office of speech. A
fever patient approaching this monument touched the pall covering it; the fever of the affliction was extinguished, and he recovered. A crippled man named
Marcus was carried in other people’s hands to the blessed woman’s tomb and prayed there for a very long time. At the ninth hour he stood on his own feet and
returned home. The boy Leodinus fell into grave illness and had been sick for four months. As an excessive fever pressed upon him, he lost not only the power to
walk but also the ability to take food. Carried to her tomb as though dead, he received health and rose from the tomb restored to life. What shall I say of
other fever patients? Many experienced this benefit of remedy when they faithfully kissed the tomb’s pall. What of the possessed? Brought to the blessed woman’s
cell, as soon as they cross the holy threshold they are restored to sound minds. The evil spirit does not delay to leave the body when it senses this saint’s
power present. Our Lord Jesus Christ works this; he grants eternal rewards to those who fear his name.

*Here ends the account of the miracles of Saint Monegundis.*

## XX. Saint Leobardus The Recluse

### Prologue

**[106]** The faithful church is built up whenever the deeds of the saints are most devoutly read again. Although it derives the greatest joy from those who,
leading a religious life from the beginning of their lives, have deserved to reach the harbour of perfection, it also rejoices at the Lord’s command over those
who, converted from the world, have been able to bring the work begun to its fulfilment with divine mercy helping them.

### 1

**[107]** The most blessed Leobardus was a native of the territory of Auvergne. He was not of senatorial birth, but was freeborn. Holding God in his heart from
the beginning, though he did not flourish by birth, he shone brightly with glorious merits. At the proper time he was sent to school with the other boys and
committed certain psalms to memory. Not knowing that he would be a cleric, he was already being prepared in innocence for the Lord’s ministry. When he reached
the lawful age, his parents, following human custom, compelled him to give a pledge to a girl as though he were going to take her as his wife. He refused, and
his father said, “Sweetest son, why do you reject your father’s will and refuse to be joined in marriage, so that you may raise up seed from my family to profit
future generations? I labour in vain at work if there is no possessor to enjoy it. Why do I fill the house with wealth if no one from my family comes forth to
use it? Why do I subject slaves purchased for a price to my control if they must again be subject to foreign masters? The divine Scriptures testify that sons
should obey the voices of their parents. Since you are shown to be disobedient to your parents, take care lest you be unable to escape heavenly offences.”
Although the father had another son, he easily persuaded one of such tender age to comply with his own will. Leobardus gave the betrothed girl a ring, offered a
kiss, provided footwear, and celebrated the festive day of betrothal.

Meanwhile his father and mother, fallen asleep in the sleep of death, departed from the world after completing the course of their present life. When the period
of mourning with his brother had been completed, Leobardus, loaded with wedding gifts, went to his brother’s house. He found his brother so soaked with wine
that he neither recognized nor received his brother in his own house. Sighing and weeping, Leobardus withdrew and came to a hut where hay had been gathered.
Tying up his horse and giving it fodder, he lay down on the hay to rest. Awaking at midnight, he rose from his bed, lifted his hands to heaven, and began to
give thanks to Almighty God that he existed, lived, and was nourished by God’s gifts, and continued with other such things. As he drew long sighs and abundantly
wet his cheeks with frequent tears, Almighty God, who foreknew and predestined those to be conformed to the image of his Son, pierced his heart so that he left
the world and was assigned to divine worship.

### 2

**[108]** Then, as though already the priest of his own soul, he began to preach to himself: “What are you doing, soul? Why are you held suspended in
uncertainty? The world is vain, its desires are vain, the world’s glory is vain, and everything in it is vanity. It is better to leave it and follow the Lord
than to consent to its works.” When daylight began to restore day to the earth, he mounted his horse and started back to his lodging. As he went eagerly along
the road, he began to turn over within himself what he should do and where he should go. He said, “I shall seek the blessed Martin’s tomb, from which kindly
power proceeds over the sick. I believe that his prayer will also open my road to God; entreated, the Lord brought the dead back from hell.” With prayer as his
companion, he pursued the road and entered Saint Martin’s basilica. After staying near it for a few days, he crossed the river and devoutly went to a cell near
the greater monastery, from which a certain Alaricus had withdrawn. There he made parchment with his own hands and prepared himself for writing. He trained
himself to understand the Holy Scriptures and retain the psalms of David’s song, which had long passed from his memory. Instructed by readings of the divine
Scriptures, he recognized that what the Lord had previously inspired in his heart was true. Lest what I have related seem fabulous to anyone, I call God to
witness that I learned these things from the blessed man’s own mouth.

After a short time he showed himself so humble that he was honoured by everyone. Taking a hoe and cutting stone, he enlarged the cell he had entered. In that
cell he delighted in fasting, prayer, psalmody, and reading. He never ceased from the divine offices and prayer. Sometimes he wrote in order to drive noxious
thoughts from himself.

### 3

**[109]** Meanwhile the tempter showed that he is always hostile and envious toward God’s servants. When Leobardus’s little monastic cell had a certain dispute
with its neighbours, the tempter put into his mind the thought of leaving that cell and moving to another. When I had come there as usual for prayer, he
disclosed to me the deceit of the swelling poison. Sighing with no small sorrow, I began to rebuke the man, asserting that this was the devil’s cunning. As I
left him, I sent books: the Lives of the Fathers and the Institutes of the Monks, teaching both what recluses ought to be and with what caution monks ought to
live. After these had been left with him, he not only drove the perverse thought from himself but also trained his understanding with such acuteness that the
eloquence of his speech was marvellous. He was gentle in address and kindly in exhortation. He had solicitude for the peoples, inquiry for kings, and constant
prayer for all ecclesiastics who feared God. He did not, like some, take pleasure in letting lashes of hair or his beard grow loose, but cut his hair and beard
at fixed times. Living in that cell for twenty-two years in this work, he was strengthened by such grace of the Lord that he anointed malignant pustules with
the saliva of his mouth and suppressed the force of raging poison. For fever patients he sanctified a cup of wine with the character of the blessed cross,
extinguishing approaching chill and heat. He rightly drove troublesome fevers from others, for in himself he had extinguished the incitements of harmful crime.

Once a blind man came to him, humbly imploring the misery of his pain and asking the saint to touch his closed eyes with his right hand. Leobardus refused for a
very long time. At last, overcome by the man’s tears and moved by compassion, he poured out prayer to the Lord for him for three days. On the fourth day he laid
his hand on the man’s eyes and said, “Almighty Lord, only-begotten Son of God the Father, who reign with him and the Holy Spirit forever, who restored the light
of your blessed mouth’s spittle to a man blind from birth, restore the sight of light to this your servant, so that he may know that you are Almighty God.”
Saying this, he traced the cross over the blind man’s eyes. The darkness was immediately driven away, and present light was restored. Abbot Eustachius is a
witness who corroborates this miracle.

### 4

**[110]** At last, worn down by the labour of the rock beneath the mountain which he continually cut, exhausted by the austerity of fasting, and strengthened by
unceasing prayer, Leobardus gradually began to be afflicted by bodily infirmity. One day, when he was extremely weary, he ordered me to be called to him. When I
approached, after he had wept over the necessity of his funeral, he begged blessings from me, sinners. Receiving them and tasting unmixed wine, he said, “My
time is now being fulfilled; at the Lord’s command he orders me to be released from the bonds of this body. There will still be a few days, but I shall be
called before the holy day of Easter.” O blessed man, who so served the Creator of all that he knew his own death by divine revelation! It was the tenth month
when he spoke these words. In the twelfth month he again began to be gravely ill. The Lord’s Day came. He called his servant and said, “Prepare some food for me
to take, because I feel very weary.” When the servant answered, “It is ready, lord,” Leobardus said, “Go outside and see whether the people are leaving Mass now
that the solemnities have been celebrated.” He said this not because he wished to take food, but so that no one would witness his passing. The servant went out
and returned. When he entered the cell, he found the man of God with body extended, eyes closed, and spirit breathed out. It is therefore manifest that he was
received by angels, since he did not wish any person to be present at his passing. Seeing this, the servant raised his voice in weeping. The other brothers ran
together. Leobardus was washed, clothed in fitting garments, and laid in the tomb he himself had carved in the aforesaid cell. I think no faithful person should
consider it uncertain that he has been enrolled in the company of the saints.

# LATIN TEXT

## General Prologue

**[000]** Statueram quidem illa tantum scribere, quae ad sepulchra beatissimorum martyrum confessorumque divinitus gesta sunt, sed, quoniam quaedam de his nuper
repperi, quos beatae conversationis meritum evexit ad caelum, quorumque vitae tramitem certis relationibus cognitum eclesiam aedificare putavi, dicere aliqua ex
illis oportunitate cogente non differo, quia sanctorum vita non modo eorum pandit propositum, verum etiam auditorum animos incitat ad profectum. Et quaeritur a
quibusdam, utrum vita sanctorum an vitas dicere debeamus. A. Gellius quoque et conplures philosophorum vitas dicere voluerunt. Nam Plinius auctor in tertio
artis grammaticae libro ait: Vitas antiqui cuiuscumque nostrum dixerunt; sed grammatici pluralem numerum non putaverunt habere vitam. Unde manifestum est,
melius dici vitam patrum quam vitas, quia, cum sit diversitas meritorum virtutumque, una tamen omnes vita corporis alit in mundo. Et scripsi, fateor, in
inferiore confessorum libro aliqua de quorundam vitam quae in corpore operati sunt breviora, idcirco-quia, cum de Dei virtute ingentia censeantur, parva tamen
redduntur in scriptis; prolixiora quoque in hoc, quod vita· sanctorum vocitare voluimus, libro imperiti idiotaeque praesumimus propalare, orantes Dominum, ut
dignetur dare verbum in ore nostro, qui ora mutorum ad usus praestinos saepius reseravit, et quod in sanctis praecipit scribi, reputet ea suis in laudibus
declamari.

## I. INCIPIT DE SANCTIS ROMANO ATQUE LUPICINO ABBATIBUS.

### Prologus

**[001]** Series euangelicae admonet disciplinae, ut dominicae largitionis pecunia nummulariis fenerata cum digno multiplicationis fructu dispensante Domino
restauretur nec altis defossa foveis recondatur ad detrimentum; sed, rationabili dispensatione porrecta, aeternae vitae crescat ad lucrum, ut incipiens
retributionis Dominus quae commodavit inquerere cum usuris, receptis fenerationis suae duplici satisfactione talentis, dicat: Euge serve bone, quia super pauca
fuisti fidelis, super multa te constituam; intra in gaudium domini tui. Praedestinatorum est enim ista cum Dei ope perficere, qui ab ipsis cunabulorum
vagitibus, ut saepe de multis legitur, Dominum scire meruerunt, cognitumque, numquam ab eius praeceptionibus recesserunt neque post baptismi sacramentum niveam
illam pollentemque regenerationis stolam inpudicis actibus polluerunt. Qui merito sequuntur Agnum, quocumque ierit, quos ipsius Agni candor egregius liliis
decoris nullo temptationis aestu marcentibus coronavit. His denique sirtis, dextera inclitae dominationis extenta, inchoantes provocat, vincentes adiuvat,
victores adornat, quos nominis sui titulo praesignatos de terrenis gemitibus elevans, in caelorum evehit gaudia gloriosos. De quorum niveo electionis numero et
illos esse non ambigo, qui Iorensis heremi opaca lustrantes, non modo se Dei templum efficere meruerunt, verum etiam in multis mentibus Spiritus sancti gratiae
tabernacula paraverunt, id est Lupicinus Romanusque, germanus eius.

### 1

**[002]** Igitur Lupicinus ab exordio aetatis suae Deum toto requirens corde, litteris institutus, cum ad legitimam transisset aetatem, genitore cogente, cum
animi non praeberet consensum, sponsali vinculo nectitur. Romanus vero adhuc adolescentior, et ipse ad Dei opus animum extendere cupiens, nuptias refutavit.
Parentibus vero relinquentibus saeculum, hii communi consensu heremum concupescunt; et accedentes simul inter illa Iorensis deserti secreta, quae inter
Burgundiam Alamanniamque sita Aventicae adiacent civitati, tabernacula figunt, prostratique solo, Dominum diebus singolis cum psallentii modolamine deprecantur,
victum de radicibus quaerentes herbarum. Sed quoniam livor illius qui de caelo dilapsus est semper insidias humano generi consuevit intendere, contra hos Dei
servos armatur hosque per ministros suos a coepto itinere nititur revocare. Nam lapidibus urguere eos daemones per dies singulos non desinebant, et
quotienscumque genua ad orandum Dominum deflexissent, statim imber lapidum super eosdem, iacentibus daemoniis, deruebat, ita ut saepe vulnerati inmensis dolorum
cruciatibus torquerentur. Interea aetas adhuc inmatura coepit iniurias cotidiani hostis metuere, nec passa diutius sufferre dolores, relinquens heremum, ad
propriam redire deliberat. Sed quid invidia non cogat inimici Verum ubi, relinquentes hoc habitaculum quod expetierant, ad villas manentium sunt regressi, domum
cuiusdam pauperis ingrediuntur. Percunctatur mulier, de quo itinere milites Christi venirent. Respondent non sine confusione, se relinquisse heremum, et quae
eos causa a coepto distulerit opere, per ordinem pandunt At illa ait: 'Oportuerat vos, o viri Dei, contra insidias diaboli viriliter dimicare nec formidare eius
inimici tias, qui saepius ab amicis Dei superatus occubuit. Aemulus est enim sanctitati, dum metuit, ne, unde ille perfidia vilis corruit, genus humanum fide
nobilitatum ascendat'. At illi conpuncti corde, et seorsum descreti a muliere, dixerunt: 'Vae nobis, quia peccavimus in Deo dimittendo propositum nostrum. Ecce
nunc a muliere arguimur pro ignavia. Et qualis nobis in posterum erit vita, si ea, unde astu inimici expulsi fuimus, non repetamus?'

### 2

**[003]** Tunc armati vixillo crucis, sumptis in manu bacellis, regressi sunt ad heremum. Quibus venientibus, iterum eos insidia daemonis lapidibus coepit
urguere; sed persistentes in oratione, obtenuerunt a Domini misericordia, ut, remota temptatione, liberi ad illum divini cultus famulatum expeditique
perseverarent. His denique in oratione vacantibus, coeperunt ad eos turbae fratrum hinc et inde confluere et audire verbum praedicationis ab eis. Cumque iam
beati heremitae populis, ut diximus, publicati fuissent, fecerunt sibi monasterium, quod Condatiscone vocitari voluerunt, in quo, succisis silvis et in plana
redactis, de laboribus manuum propriarum victum quaerebant; tantusque fervor de Dei amore proximos locorum accenderat, ut congregata ad officium Dei multitudo
simul habitare non possit; feceruntque iterum aliud monasterium, in quo felicis alvearis examen instituerunt. Sed et his deinceps cum Dei adiutorio ampliatis,
tertium intra Alamanniae terminum monasterium locaverunt. Ibantque vicissim hi duo patres, requerentes filios, quos divinis imbuerant disciplinis, praedicantes
in singulis monasteriis ea quae ad Institutionen animae pertenebant. Lupicinus tamen abbatis super eos obtenuit monarchiam. Erat autem valde subrius et a cibo
potuque abstenens, ita ut plerumque tertia die reficerit. Cum autem eum, sicut corporis humani deposcit necessitas, sitis arriperet, vas cum aqua exhiberi
faciebat, in qua manus inmersas diutius retenebat. Mirum dictu! Ita absorbebat caro eius aquam adpositam, ut putaris eam per os eius adsumi; et sic ardor sitis
extinguebatur. Erat enim severus valde in districtione fratrum, nec quemquam non modo perverse agere, verum etiam nec loqui sinebat; mulierum quoque vel
colloquia vel occursus valde vitabat Romanus ita erat simplex, ut nihil de his penitus ad animum duceret, sed omnibus tam viris quam mulieribus aequaliter
flagitatam benedictionem, Divinitatis nomine invocato, tribueret.

### 3

**[004]** Lupicinus igitur abba cum minus haberet, unde tantam susteneret congregationem, revelavit ei Deus locum in heremo, in quo antiquitus thesauri
reconditi fuerant. Ad quem locum accedens solus, aurum argentumque, quantum levare potuerat, monasterio inferebat et, exinde coemptos cibos, reficiebat fratrum
multitudines, quos ad Dei officium congregaverat. Sicque faciebat per singulos annos. Nulli tamen fratrum patefecit locum, quod ei Dominus dignatus est
revelare. Factum est autem, ut quodam tempere visitaret fratres, quos in illis Alamanniae regionibus diximus congregatos; et accedens meridiae, cum adhuc
fratres in agro essent, ingressus est domum, in quo cibi coquebantur ad reficiendum; viditque diversorum ferculorum apparatum magnum pisciumque multitudinem
adgregatam, dixitque in corde suo: 'Non est dignum, ut monachi, quorum vita solitaria est, tam ineptis utantur sumptibus'. Et statim iussit praeparari aeneum
magnum. Cumque locatus super ignem fervere coepisset, posuit in eo cunctos simul, quos paraverant cibos, tam pisces quam holera sive legumina, vel quicquid ad
comedendum monachis distinatum fuerat, dixitque: 'De his pultibus nunc reficiantur fratres, nam non diliciis vacent, quae eos a divino inpediant opere'. Quod
illi cognoscentes, valde moleste tolerant. Tamen duodecim viri, habito consilio, iracundia inflammati, reliquerunt locum et abierunt per deserta vagantes et ea
quae erant saeculi delectabilia inquerentes. Revelatumque est statim per visum Romano, nec ei voluit divina miseratio rem actam occultare. Regresso quoque
abbate ad monasterium, dicitque ei: Si sic futurum erat, ut ad dispersionem fratrum abires, utinam nec accessisses ad eos'. Cui ille: 'Noli·', inquid, 'moleste
ferre, frater dilectissime, quae acta sunt. Nam scias, purgatam esse aream Domini, et triticum tantam reconditum in horreo, paleas autem eiectas esse foris'. Et
ille: 'Utinam nullus abscessisset ex his! Sed nunc indica, quaeso, mihi, quanti exinde abierunt'. Qui respondit: 'Duodecim viri cotornosi atque elati, in quibus
Deus non habitat'. Tunc Romanus cum lacrimis ait: 'Credo in illo divinae miserationis respectu, quia nec illos separabit a thesauro suo, sed congregabit eos et
lucri eos faciet, pro quibus pati dignatus est'. Et facta pro his oratione, obtenuit, ut reverterentur ad gratiam omnipotentis Dei. Dominus autem conpungi fecit
corda eorum; et agentes paenitentiam pro excessu suo, congregaverunt singuli congregationes suas et fecerunt sibi monasteria, quae usque hodie in Dei laudibus
perseverant. Romanus autem persistebat in simplicitate et operibus bonis, visitans infirmos et salvans eos oratione sua.

### 4

**[005]** Factum est autem quodam tempore, dum iter ageret ad visitandos fratres, ut occupante crepusculo ad hospitiolum diverteret leprosorum. Erant autem
novem viri. Susceptusque ab eis, statim plenus caritate Dei iussit, aquam calidam fieri, atque omnium pedes manu propria lavit, lectulumque spatiosum fieri
praecepit, ut omnes in uno stratu requiescerent, non abhorrens luridae maculae leprae. Quod cum factum fuisset, obdormientibus leprosis, bic inter decantationes
psalmorum vigilans, extendit manum suam et tetigit latus infirmi unius, statimque mundatus est; tactuque salubri iterum tangens alium, et ipse protinus est
mundatus. Cumque se sensissent redditos sanitati, tetigit unusquisque proximum suum, ut scilicet expergefacti rogarent sanctum pro emundatione sua. Sed cum
tacti ab invicem fuissent, et ipsi mundati sunt. Mane autem facto, aspiciens omnes nitente cute effulgere, gratias agens Deo et vale dicens ac singulorum oscula
libans, abscessit; mandans eis, ut semper ea quae Dei erant et retenerent pectore et operibus exercerent.

### 5

**[006]** Lupicinus autem iam senex factus, accessit ad Chilpericum regem, qui tunc Burgundiae praeerat. Andierat enim eum habitare apud urbem Ianubam. Cuius
ingressus portam tremuit regis cathedra, qui ea hora ad convivium resedebat. Exterritusque ait suis: 'Terrae motus factus est', inquid. Responderunt qui
aderant, nihil se sensisse commotionis. Et ille: 'Occurrite quantotius ad portam, ne forte aliquis adversari cupiens regno nostro adsit, quasi nociturus nobis;
non enim sine causa haec sella contremuit'. Qui protinus concurrentes, offenderunt senem in veste pellicia et dixerunt regi de eo. Qui ait: 'Ite, adducite eum
in conspectu meo, ut intellegam, cuius ordinis homo sit'. Et statim adductus, stetit coram rege, sicut quondam Iacob coram Pharaone. Cui ille ait: 'Quis es vel
unde venisti? Aut quod est opus tuum, vel quid necessitatis aeges, ut venias ad nos? Edicito!' Cui ille: 'Pater sum', inquid, 'dominicarum ovium, quas cum
Dominus spiritalibus cibis iugi administratione reficiat, corporalia eis interdum alimenta deficiunt. Ideo petimus potentiae vestrae, ut ad victus vestitusque
necessaria aliquid tribuatis'. Rex vero haec audiens, ait: 'Accipite agros vineasque, de quibus possetis vivere ac necessitates vestras explere'. Qui respondit:
'Agros et vineas non accipiemus, sed, si placet potestati vestrae, aliquid de fructibus deligate. Quia non decet, monachos facultatibus mundanis extolli, sed in
humilitate cordis Dei regnum iustitiamque eius exquerere'. At rex, cum audisset haec verba, dedit eis praeceptionem, ut annis singulis trecentos modios tritici
eiusdemque mensurae numero vinum accipiant et centum aureos ad conparandum fratrum indumenta. Quod usque nunc a fisci ditionibus capere referuntur.

### 6

**[007]** Post haec autem, cum iam senes profectaeque essent aetatis, Lupicinus abba scilicet et Romanus, frater eius, ait Lupicinus germano suo: 'Dic', inquid,
'mihi, in quale monasterium vis tibi parari sepulchrum, ut simul quiescamus?' Qui ait: 'Non potest fieri, ut ego in monasterio sepulchrum habeam, a quo mulierum
accessus arcetur. Nosti enim, quid· mihi indigno et non merenti dominus Deus meus gratiam ι tribuit curationum, multique per inpositionem manus meae ac virtutem
crucis dominicae a diversis langoribus sint erepti. Erit autem concursus ad tumulum meum, si ab hac luce migravero. Ideoque rogo, ut eminus a monasterio
requiescam'. Pro hac vero causa, cum obisset, in decim milibus a monasterio in monte parvulo sepultus est. Super cuius deinceps sepulchrum magnum templum
aedificatum est, in quo ingens frequentia populi diebus singulis accurrit. Multae enim virtutes ibi in Dei nomine nunc ostenduntur. Nam et caeci ibi lumen et
surdi auditum et paralytici gressum plerumque recipiunt. Lupicinus autem abba obiens, intra monasterii basilicam est sepultus, reliquitque Domino pecuniae
creditae multiplicata talenta, id est beatas monachorum congregationes in eius lande devotas. EXPLICIT DE SANCTIS ABBATIBUS LUPICINO ET ROMANO.

## II. INCIPIT DE SANCTO ILLIDIO CONFESSORE.

### Prologus

**[008]** Inter reliqua vitae perpetuae semina, quae caelestis Sator ex illo divinitatis fonte mentes incultae arvum vel inrigavit institutione vcl dogmate
fecundavit, ait: Omnis qui non accipit crucem suam et sequitur me, non est me dignus. Sed et ille nihilhominus vas electionis beatas Paulus apostolus dicit:
Semper mortificationem Christi in corpore vestro circumferentes, ut et vita Iesu manifestetur in corpore vestro mortali. Ergo confessores Christi, quos tempus
persecutionis ad martyrium non lacessivit, ipsi sibi persecutoris [Christi] modo, ut digni Deo haberentur, diversas abstinentiae cruces adhibuerunt; et ut,
mortificatis membris, soli illi viverent, de quo idem apostolus dixit: Iam non vivo ego; vivit autem in me Christus. Aspiciebant enim per illos mentis· internae
oculos Dominum caelorum discendisse ad terrae, non abiectum ad humilitatem, sed humiliatum misericorditer ad mundi redemptionem; aspiciebant pendentem in
patibulo non Deitatis gloriam, sed adsumpti corporis hostiam mundam, de qua Iohannes paulo ante praedixerat: Ecce Agnus Dei! Ecce qui tollit peccata huius
mundi! Habebant in se et clavorum adfixionem, cum a timore eius confixi atque a iudiciis divinis exterriti, nihil indignum eius omnipotentiae in cordis sui
habitatione gerebant. Fulgebat in his et illud resurrectionis lumen insigne, quo angelus refulsit, dum revolvit lapidem monumenti; quo Iesus splenduit sub illa
ostiorum obseratorum inclusione, cum inprovisus in medio [illo] apostolici senatus adstetit comitatu; quo idem Dominus eosdem verbis vitae imbuens, caelesti est
evectus in arce. Inter quos et beatus confessor Illidius ita haec omnia in cordis sui tabernaculo collocavit, ut et ipse quoque templum sancti Spiritus effici
mereretur. De cuius vita aliqua scripturus, veniam peto legentibus. Non enim me artis grammaticae studium imbuit, neque auctorum saecularium polita lectio
erudivit, sed tantum beati patris Aviti Arverni pontificis studium ad eclesiastica sollicitavit scripta; si mihi non ad iudicium contingerent, quae ipso
praedicante audivi vel cogente relegi, quiea nequeo observare; qui me post Davitici carminis cannas ad illa euangelicae praedicationis dicta atque apostolicae
virtutis historias epistolasque perduxit. De quo ea tantum capere potui, ut cognoscerem, Iesum Christum, filium Dei, ad salutem mundi venisse atque amicos eius,
qui, accepta cruce austerae observantiae, sponsum secuti sunt, dignis obsequiis honorare. Qua de re crudae rusticitatis temeritatem ostendens, quae de beato
cognovi Illidio illo quo possum proferam stilo.

### 1

**[009]** Sanctus igitur Illidius cum perfectae vitae sanctitate polleret ac diversarum in se gratiarum carismata, largiente Domino, congessisset, illud quod
adhuc sanctitatis culmini deerat, Deo inspirante ac populo elegente, promeruit, ut sacerdos Arvernae eclesiae et dominicarum ovium paetor elegeretur. Cuius
sanctitatis fama dum per diversos gratiarum evehitur ascensus, non solum ipsos Arverni terreturii terminos, verum etiam vicinarum urbium fines adivit. Unde
factum est, ut haec gloria Treverici imperatoris aures attingeret, cuius filia cum ab spiritu inmundo correpta graviter vexaretur, et non inveniretur a quo
possit erui, beatum Illidium fama detexit. Et dicto citius ab imperatore directi pueri, sanctum senem in antedicta repertum urbe potestati regiae celeriter
repraesentant. At ille, venerabiliter exceptum, de exitu infelicis conquiritur filiae. Ille vero confisus in Domino, in oratione prosternitur, noctemque cum
sacris hymnis canticisque spiritalibus ductam, inmissis in os puellae digitis, nequam spiritum a corpore abegit obsessae. Quod miraculum imperator cernens,
inmensos auri argentique cumulos sancto offert sacerdoti. Quod ille exsecrans ac refutans, hoc obtenuit, ut Arverna civitas quae tributa in specio triticea ac
vinaria dependebat in auro dissolveret, quia cum gravi labore poenu inferebantur imperiali. Sanctus vero, ut aiunt, impleto vitae praesentis tempore, in ipso
iteneris curriculo migravit ad Christum, a suisque delatus, in urbe sua sepultus est.

### 2

**[010]** Et forsitan, ut plerumque murmurare homines soliti sunt, quispiam garrulatur, dicens: 'Non potest hic habere inter sanctos pro unius tantum operatione
miraculi'. Nam, si perpenditur illud quod Dominus ait in euangelio: Multi, [inquit], dicunt mihi in illa die: 'Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo daemonia
eiecimus virtutesque multas fecimus?' Et respondebo eis, dicens, quia non novi vos, profecto intellegit, quia magis proficit ad laudem virtus egressa de tumulo,
quam ea quae quisquam vivens gessit in mundo; quia illa labem habere potuerunt per assidua mundanae occupationis impedimenta, haec vero omnem labem ad liquidum
caruerunt. Ergo quia illa, ut credimus, quae sanctus Illidius ante hoc tempus operatus est, oblivioni data sunt nec ad nostram notitiam pervenerunt, ea quae
propriis inspeximus oculis expertique sumus, vel quae a fidelibus agnita cognovimus, declaramus. Tempore, quo Gallus episcopus Arvernam regebat eclesiam, horum
scriptor in adolescentia degens graviter aegrotabat, et ab eo plerumque dilectione unica visitabatur, eo quod patruus eius esset; erat enim valitudo cum nimia
stomachi pituita ac febre valida. Interea advenit parvulo desiderium, et, credo, inspirante Deo, ut ad beati Illidii basilicam deportaretur; inlatusque manibus
puerorum ad eius tumulum, fusa oratione cum lacrimis, leviorem se sensit esse quam venerat. Reversusque ad domum, iterum a febre corripitur. Quadam vero die cum
gravius agere coepisset, eumque febris asperior solito adgravaret, et utrum evaderet, dubia sub sorte iaceret, accedens genetrix eius, ait ad eum: 'Maestum
hodie, dulcis nate, sum habitura diem, cum te talis attenet febris'. Et ille: 'Nihil', inquid, 'prorsus, obsecro, contristeris, sed ad sepulchrum [tu] me
remitte beati Illidii pontificis. Credo enim, et fides mea est, quod virtus eius et tibi laetitiam et mihi tribuat sospitatem'. Tunc sancti deportatus ad
tumulum, orationem ad Dominum fudit, spondens prostratus sponte, quod si eum obtentu antestitis sui ab hoc contagio liberaret, clericum se futurum; nec prorsus
moraretur, si deprecatio obteneret effectum'. Haec effatus, sensit protinus discedere febrem, vocatoque puero, domui se reportari deposcit Cumque in recubitu,
ubi tunc aepulabantur, fuisset inlatus, erumpente a naribus sanguinis copia, febris simul cruorque defluxit. Quod meritis beati confessoris praestitum habetur
probatum. Sed et nuper Venerandi comitis servus, cum in diuturna caecitate resederet, celebratis vigiliis, sanus abscessit.

### 3

**[011]** De reliquiis vero eius haec ipse praefatus scriptor, ut actum est, propria contemplatione prospexit Dedicaverat igitur oratorium infra domum
eclesiasticam urbis Toronicae in primo sacerdotii sui anno, in quo cum reliquorum sanctorum pignora huius autestitis reliquias collocavit. Post multos vero
dedicationis dies admonitus est ab abbate, ut reliquias, quas in altari ipso locaverat, visitaret, ne ab humore novi aedificii umectatae, aliquid in his
putredinis insederet. Quas cum requirens repperisset infectas, ablatas exi altari contra ignem siccare coepit. Verum ubi ligaturas illas singillatim conposuit,
ventum est ad reliquias beati Illidii episcopi. Denique tenens easdem contra ignem, filum quo ligatae erant, quia erat valde prolixum, super ardentes decidit
prunas et tamquam aeneum aut ferreum ab ardore ignis incanduit. Illo quoque parvi pendente, quid filum τ fieret, tantum sanctae reliquiae siccarentur, aestimans
antem, eum iam in favilla misse resolutum, dehinc sequitur et filum inlaesum. Haec videns attonitus, valde beati antistitis virtutem admiratur. Qui non sine
grandi metu unde haec abstulerat referens, gloriam eine omnibus revelavit Filum autem illud erat ex lana.

### 4

**[012]** Puer erat parvulus quasi mensium decem, qui, ut res veritatis edocuit, ipsius beati abnepos habebatur, gravissime incommodi accensu afficiebatur.
Flebat autem illa genitrix non minus obitum parvuli, quam illud quod non fuerat adhuc denuo delibutus baptismatis sacramentis. Denique, consilio habito, beati
confessoris adiit tumulum, exponit in pavimento aegrotum, qui nihil aliter quam solo spiritu palpitabat, atque in vigiliis obsecrationibusque coram sepulchro
antistitis excabat. Cumque plausum ales ille lucis nuntius, repercussis alis, altius protulisset, puer, qui valde exanimis proiectus fuerat, convaluit; et
gaudia cordis risu praecedente patefaciens, aperto divinitus ore, evocat matrem, dicens: 'Accede huc'. At illa cum tremore et gaudio accedens, quae numquam
adhuc filii vocem audierat, stupens: 'Quid vis', inquit, 'dulcissime nate?' Qui ait: 'Curre quantotius atque aquarum mini pocula defer'. At illa persistens
immobilis usque ad adventum lucis in oratione, gratias agens sancto antistiti sobolemque devovens, abscesssit ad domum; porrectaque aqua, hausit infans, atque
ab omni infirmitatis nexu absolutus, ad plenum convaluit. Deinde ad pristinos infantiae vagitus rediens, loqui ultra non potuit, nisi cum ad illam aetatis
seriem, in qua infantium lingua ad loquendum laxari solet, educatus accessit. Sed nec illud silere arbitror, quod quodam tempore, quo clibanus ad coquendas
basilicae ipsius calces succenderetur, actum est Iugum igitur, quod os fornacis validissime confirmabat, dormientibus cum ipso loci abbate qui aderant, est
effractum. Quo facto, astitit presbitero repente per visum quasi sacerdos, dicens: 'Festina velociter et excita dormientes, ne eos futurae ruinae casus
anticipet. Iam enim paratum est iugum, quod totam molem lapidum sustinet, cum ipso igne corruere'. Ille vero expergefactus, amotis ab ore fornacis omnibus,
cecidit ab utraque parte acervus lapidum aggregatus, nullum de astantibus laedens. Quod non sine antistitis intercessione praestitum reor. Tunc presbiter
memoratus, oratione facta ad sepulchrum sancti, reparatis iugis lapidibusque relatis, in clibano opus coeptum, antistite opitulante, peregit. Huius confessoris
beatum corpus ab antiquis in cripta sepultum fuit, sed quia artum erat aedificium ac difficilem habebat ingressum, sanctus Avitus pontifex urbis, constructa in
circuitu miro opere absida, beatos inquisivit artns repperitque in capsa tabulis formata ligneis. Quos assumens, involvit dignis linteis et iuxta morem
sarcofago clausit; oppletamque criptam altius collocavit. In hoc loco et meritis et nomine Iustus requiescit, qui fuisse huius gloriosi pontificis fertur
archidiaconus.

### 5

**[013]** Multa quidem et alia de hoc sancto miracula sunt relata, quae scribere longum putavi, hoc aestimans fidei perfectae sufficere, quae dicta sunt, quia
cui pauca non sufficiunt plura non proderunt. Nam ad hoc tumulum caeci inluminantur, daemones effugantur, surdi auditum et clodi recipiunt gressum, praestante
domino nostro Iesu Christo, qui credentibus repromisit a se petita sine ambiguitate largire.

## III. INCIPIT DE ABRAHAM ABBATE.

### Prologus

**[014]** Nulli catholicorum esse occultum reor, quod Dominus ait in euangelio: Amen dico vobis, si habueritis fidem integram et non haesitaveritis, si
dixeritis huic monti: 'Transfer te', et transfert se; et: 'Omnia, quaecumque petieritis in nomine meo, credite, quia accipietis, et venient vobis. Ergo non erit
dubiam, quod sancti obtenere possint a Domino quod petierint, quia in eo fides fundamine posito nullis haesitationum fluctibus vacillantur. Pro qua fide non
solum infra patriae terminum propriae, dum caelestem vitam agere cupiunt, exules facti sunt, sed etiam transmarina ac peregrina petierunt loca, ut ei cui se
devoverant plus placerent, sicut nunc beatus Abraham abba, qui post multas temptationes saeculi fines est terreturii ingressus Arverni. Qui non inmerito Abrahae
illi conparatur seni pro magnitudine fidei, cui quondam dixerat Deus: Exi de terra tua et de cognatione tua et vade in terram, quam monstravero tibi. Reliquit
autem hic non solum terram propriam, sed etiam illam veteris hominis actionem, et induit novum hominem, qui secundum Deum formatus est in iustitia, sanctitate
et veritate. Ideoque cum se perfectum in Dei opere cerneret, non fuit dubius in fide petere, quod per vitam sanctam confisus est obtenere, per quem opifex
caeli, maris ac terrae parva quidem numero, sed admiranda miracula operare dignatus est.

### 1

**[015]** Igitur Abraham iste super Eufratis fluvii litus exortus est, ubi in Dei opere proficiens ad visitandos heremitas adire Aegypti solitudines concupivit.
Quod iter dum teneret, a paganis conprehensus et multis pro Christi nomine adfectus verberibus, in vincula conicitur, in quibus per quinque annos exulans,
angelo solvente, laxatur. Occidentalem quoque plagam visitare cupiens, Arvernus advenit, ibique ad basilicam sancti Cirici monasterium collocavit Erat enim
mirae virtutis, fugator daemonum inluminatorque caecorum, aliorum quoque morborum potentissimus medicator. Igitur cum festivitas supradictae basilicae
advenisset, praepositum vocat·, ut vasa vino plena ad reficiendum populum, qui solemnitati aderat, in atrio ex more conponeret. Causatur monachus, dicens: 'Ecce
episcopum cum duce et civibus invitatum habes, et vix nobis supersunt quattuor vini amphorae, unde omnia ista conplebis?' Et ille: 'Aperite', inquid, 'mihi
poenum'. Quo aperto, ingressus est; et dans orationem, quasi novus Helias, elevatis ad caelum manibus, infusis fletu luminibus, ait: 'Ne deficiat, quaeso,
Domine, de hoc vasculo vinum, donec cunctis ministretur in abundantiam', et, inruente in se Spiritu sancto, ait: 'Haec dicit Dominus: Non deficiet vinum de
vase, sed omnibus petentibus affatim tribuetur, et abundabit'. Verumtamen ad verbum et hilaritatem dispensationis illius cuncto populo in abundantia ministratum
est, et superfuit. Sed quia strenuitas praepositi prius mensuraverat vasculum quinquagenarium et reppererat quattuor palmorum mensuram, cernens quae acta
fuerant, in crastino iterum mensurans, tantum repperit in vase, quantum in eo praęcedente reliquerat die. Ex hoc sancti virtus in populis· declarata est; in quo
monasterio plenus dierum obiit, ibique cum honore sepultus est. Erat enim eo tempore sanctus Sidonius episcopus et Victorius dux, qui super septem civitates
principatum, Eoricho Gothorum rege indulgente, susceperas. Huius vero sancti epitaphium beatus Sidonius scripsit, in quo aliqua de his quae locutus sum est
praefatus. Ad huius enim beati Abrahae sepulchrum plerumque frigoritici decubantes, medicinae caelestis praesidio sublevantur.

## IV. INCIPIT DE SANCTO QUINTIANO.

### Prologus

**[016]** Omnis, qui se terrenae materiae corpus ferre cognoscit, cogitare debet, ne in his devolvatur, quae terrena et carnis huius amica esse noscuntur, quia
iuxta apostolum Paulum manifesta sunt opera carnis, plena inmunditiae et iniquitate, pollutumque et fetidum hominem, qui ea sectatus fuerit, reddunt atque ad
extremum fletibus deputant sempiternis. Fructus autem spiritus est omne quod in Deo pollet ac nitet, quod in hoc saeculo, mortificata carne, animam exultare
facit, in futuro autem gaudiis donat aeternis. Unde nos, qui nunc sumus in corpore positi, aspicere debemus, quae operatus est Deus in sanctis suis, in quibus
tamquam in splendidum candidumque ac levigatum meritis tabernaculum diversisque virtutum floribus adornatum resedens, extensa dexterae maiestate, dignatus est
per eos miseratione propria perficere quae petissent, sicut nunc per beatum Quintianum, de quo sermo futurus est, mentis nobilis generositate fulgidum iustitiae
opus plerumque conplevit. Ergo non nos more pecorum carnis sectatio ad terrena submergat ac depremat, sed potius sanctorum exemplis inlecti, prudenter
intellegentes quae Dei sunt, spiritalis nos opera ad caelestia ac sempiterna sustollat; neque in nobis mens ab inpudicis actionibus victa luxoriet, sed
aeternitatis pro meritis vindicans solium victrix sapientia regnet.

### 1

**[017]** Igitur beatissimus Quintianus Afer natione et, ut quidam ferunt, nepus Fausti episcopi, qui genetricem suam suscitasse perhibetur, sanctitate
praeditus, virtutum dote fulgidus, caritatis igniculo fervidus, castitatis flore praecipuas, ad episcopatum Rutenae eclesiae elegitur, expetitur, ordinatur. In
quo episcopatu ampliatis adhuc virtutibus, cum in Dei semper operibus cresceret, auctam beati Amanti antestitis basilicam, sanctum corpus in antea transtulit;
sed non fuit sancto acceptabile hoc opus. Unde factam est, ut per visum apparens diceret ei: 'Quia ausu temerario artus in pace quiescentes visus es amovisse,
ecce ego removeam te ab hac urbe, et eris exul in regione altera; verumtamen non privaberis ab honore quo frueris'. Non post multum vero tempus, orto inter
cives et episcopum scandalo, Gothos, qui tunc in antedictam urbem morabantur, suspicio attigit, quod se vellit episcopus Francorum ditionibus subdere,
consilioque accepto, cogitaverunt eum perfodere gladio. Quod cum viro sancto nuntiatum fuisset, de nocte consurgens, cum fidelissimis ministris suis ab urbe
illa egrediens, Arvernus advenit. Ibique a sancto Eufrasio episcopo, qui Abrunculo quondam antestiti successerat, receptus est, largitisque ei tam domibus quam
agris et vineis, vel ille vel qui Lugdunensi urbi praeerat summa eum diligentia excolebant. Erat enim iam senex et verus Dei cultor. Decedente autem ab hoc
mundo sancto Eufrasio, Apollinaris, tribus mensibus sacerdotio subministrato, migravit. Cum autem haec Theodorico· regi nuntiata fuissent, iussit inibi sanctum
Quintianum constitui et omnem ei potestatem tradi eclesiae, dicens: 'Hic ob nostri amoris zelo ab urbe sua eiectus est'. Denique cum sanctus Quintianus in
antedicta urbe potiretur episcopatum, Proculus quidam ex aerario presbiter ordinatus, multas ei iniurias intulit, omnemque potestatem illi de rebus eclesiae
auferens, vix ei cotidianum et satis tenuem victum ministrare praecepit; sed per eius orationem a civibus correptus prudentioribus, restituta omni potestate, se
ab eius removit insidiis. Antedictus tamen sacerdos non inmemor iniuriae, sicut quondam Paulus apostolus de Alexandro, ita et hic de Proculo decantabat, dicens:
'Proculus aerarius multa mala mihi fecit, reddat illi Dominus secundum opera sua'. Quod in posterum ei evenisse manifestum est.

### 2

**[018]** Erat enim vir beatus in oratione assiduus et in tantum amator populi sui, ut, adveniente Theodorico ac vallante cum exercitu urbem, sanctus Dei muros
eius per noctem psallendo circuiret; et, ut regioni vel populo Dominus velociter succurrere dignaretur, adflictus in ieiuniis atque vigiliis instanter orabat.
Porro Theodoricus rex cum cogitaret etiam muros urbis evertere, mollivit eum misericordia Domini et oratio sacerdotis sui, quem in exilium retrudere cogitabat.
Nam nocte pavore perterritus, de stratu suo exilit ac solus per viam publicam fugire nititur. Perdiderat enim sensum, nesciens, quid ageret. Quod
animadvertentes sui eumque retenere conantes, vix potuerunt, cohortantes, ut se signo salutare muniret. Tunc Hilpingus dux eius accedens propius ad regem, ait:
'Audi, gloriosissime rex, consilium parvitatis meae. Ecce muri civitatis istius fortissimi sunt, eamque propugnacula ingentia vallant. Quod ut plenius
magnificentia vestra cognoscat, de sanctis, quorum basilicae muros [illius] urbis ambiunt, haec loquor; sed et antestis loci illius magnus apud Deum habetur.
Noli facere quod cogitas; noli episcopo iniuriam inferre aut urbem evertere'. Cuius consilium rex clementer accipiens, praeceptum posuit, ne ullus ab octavo
urbis miliario laederetur. Quod obtentu sacerdotis praestitum nullus ambigat. Tunc et Proculus ille presbiter, inruptis Lovolautrensis castri muris, ab
ingredientibus hostibus ante ipsum eclesiae altare gladiorum ictibus in frustra discerptus est, reddiditque illi Dominus, sicut sacerdos cantare consueverat,
secundum opera sua.

### 3

**[019]** Post peractam igitur stragem cladis Arvernae Hortensius unus ex senatoribus comitatum urbis illius agens, quendam de parentibus sancti, id est
Honoratum nomine, in urbis platea nequiter reteneri iussit. Quod celeriter beato viro nuntiatum est. At ille per amicos suos coepit rogare, ut eum, data
audientia, absolvi iuberet Quod ille nullatenus praestetit. Tunc beatus senex deferri se in plateam qua ille tenebatur iubet; adlatus autem rogabat milites, ut
eum dimitterent. Illi vero timentes, oboedire ausi non sunt pontifici. Et sacerdos: 'Ad domum', inquid, 'Hortensii me velociter deportate'. Erat enim senes
valde et propriis pedibus abire non poteras. Deferentes autem eum in domum Hortensii ministri eius, excutiens in eam pulverem calciamenti sui, ait: 'Maledicta
sit domus haec, et maledicti habitatores eius in sempiternum, fiatque deserta, et non sit qui inhabitet in ea'. Et dich omnis populus: 'Amen'. Et adiecit:
'Quaeso, Domine, numquam de hac generatione provehatur quisquam ad episcopale sacerdotium, qui episcopum non obaudit'. Egresso autem ex ea sacerdote, protinus
omnes familiae, quae in domum illam erant, a febre corripiuntur, et parumper ingemescentes, spiritum exalabant. Quod cum iam tertia die ageretur, videns
Hortensius, sibi nihil de suis servientibus reservari, timens, ne etiam et ipse pariter interiret, ad sanctum virum maestus ingreditur, proiectusque ad pedes
eius, cum lacrimis veniam rogat. Quam ille benignissime indulgens, benedictam aquam domui transmisit, illaque per parietes respersa, omnis aegritudo protinus
est depulsa, magnaque ibi virtus apparuit. Nam et qui incurrerant sanati sunt, et qui sani erant ultra non incurrerunt.

### 4

**[020]** In eclesiasticis vero scripturis eruditus est habitus hic sacerdos; sed et in elymosinis magnificus fuit. Nam cum pauperem quempiam clamare cerneret,
aiebat: 'Succurrite, quaeso, succurrite et pauperi victus necessaria ministrate! Ignari enim estis, o desides, et forsitan ipse est, qui se per euangelicae
lectionis seriem reficiendum in pauperibus minimis esse mandavit'. Eiciebat autem et daemonia se confitentia. In monasterio autem Cambidobrensi veniens, cum
inerguminum quendam repperisset atrocius debacchantem, misit presbiteros, nt ei manus inponerent; sed cum eorum exorcizatione larva non fuisset expulsa, sanctus
Dei comminus adpropinquans, inmissis in os eius digitis, personam reddit absolutam. Multa et alia miracula vir beatus operatus est, et oratione facta, saepius
quae petisset ad Dominum obtenebat. Porro in Arverno quodam tempore cum magna siccitas cuncta consumeret, et arentibus herbis, nulla penitus iumentis pabula
remanerent, et sanctus Dei rogationes illas, quae ante ascensionem dominicam aguntur, devotissime caelebraret, die tertia, cum iam portam civitatis
adpropinquarent, suggerunt ei, ut ipse antephonam dignaretur inponere, dicentes: 'Si tu, beate pontifex, devote antephonam inposueris, confidimus de sanctitate
tua, quod protinus nobis Dominus pluviam dignabitur benigna pietate largire'. At ille prostratus super cilicium· suum, in ipsa platea diutissime cum fletu
