beatae signaculum. Quod ponens super alvum iuvenuli, dolore paululum sedato, obdormivit in scamnum, qui olim, doloribus insistentibus, caruerat somnum. Post
unius vero horae momentum consurgens, ad purgandum ventrem egressus, pestiferae generationis germen effudit, gratiasque referens ancillae Dei, sanus abscessit.
Alius vero puer paralysi aegritudine contractus, ante eam inter manus dilatus est aliorum, deprecans a beata sanari. At illa in oratione prostrata, precem pro
eo fudit ad Dominum; consummata vero oratione, consurgens, adprehensam manum pueri, erexit eum, sospitemque abire permisit. Mulier erat caeca, quae adducta ad
eam, deprecata est, ut ei manus inponeret. At illa respondit: 'Quid vobis et mihi, homines Dei? Nonne sanctus Martinus hic habitat, qui cotidie inlustrium
virtutum opere refulget? Illuc accedite, ibi obsecramini, ut ipse vos visitare dignetur. Nam ego peccatrix quid faciam?' Illa vero in sua petitione perdurans,
aiebat: 'Deus per omnes timentes nomen suum cotidie opus exercet egregium; ideoque supplex ad te confugio, cui praestita est Divinitatis gratia curationum. Tunc
commota Dei famula, luminibus sepultis manus inposuit, statimque reseratis cataractis, mundum late patentem quae· fuerat caeca prospexit. Multisque etiam
inerguminis ad eam ingressis, ut manus inposuit, fugato hoste nequam, sospitatem restituit; nec morabantur ex his curari, quos ad se sancta permisit accedere.

### 4

**[105]** Iam enim tempus vocationis eius adpropinquabat, et defessa corpori solvebatur. Quod cum viderent sanctimoniales, quas secum habebat, flebant valde,
dicentes: 'Et cui nos, mater sancta, relinques? Vel cui conmendas filias, quas in [hoc] loco pro Dei intuitu congregasti?' At illa parumper lacrimans, ait: 'Si
pacem sanctificationemque sequamini, Deus erit protectio vestra, habebitisque sanctum Martinum antestitem pastorem magnum. Nam et ego non discedam a vobis, sed
invocata adero in medio caritatis vestrae'. At illae rogabant, dicentes: 'Venturi sunt multi infirmi ad nos, flagitantes benedictionem a te accipere; et quid
faciemus, cum te non viderint esse superstitem? Confusae enim eos foris emittimus, cum tuam faciem non contemplamur. Rogamus enim, ut, quia haec ab oculis
nostris absconditur, at saltim digneris oleum salemque benedicere, de quo possemus aegrotis benedictionem flagitantibus ministrare'. Tunc illa, benedicto oleo
ac sale, tradidit eis, qua suscipientes, diligentissime servaverunt. Sicque beatissima obiit in pace, et sepulta est in ipsa cellula, multis se in posterum
virtutibus repraesentans. Nam de memorata benedictione molti post eine transitum aegroti incolomes beneficia sunt experti. Bosonis denique diaconi pes unus a
pusula mala conflaverat, ita ut gressum facere non valeret, deportatusque ad eius tumulum, orationem fodit. Puellae vero accipientes ex oleo memorato, quem
sancta reliquerat, posuerunt super pedem eius; extemplo, erumpente vulnere, defluente veneno, sanatus est. Caecus quidam adductus ad eius tumulum, in oratione
prosternitor. Inruente autem sopore, obdormivit, apparuitque ei beata, dicens: 'Indignam quidem me iudico exaequari sanctis, sed tamen unius hic oculi recipies
lumen; deinceps autem propera quantotius ad pedes beati Martini et prosternere in conpunctione animi coram eo. Ipse enim tibi restituit alterius oculi
visionem'. Expergefactus homo, unius oculi recepto lumine, abiit quo iussio inpulit imperantis; ibique iterum obsecrans beati confessoris virtute, depulsa caeci
oculi nocte, videns abscessit. Mutus etiam ad hoc beatae tumulum prostratus occubuit, qui in tantum fide conpunctus est, ut rivis lacrimarum cellulae inficeret
pavimentum. Qui consurgens, absoluta lingua virtute divina, regressus est. Alius denique mutus veniens, in oratione decumbens, corde tantum inplorabat et non
voce solubili beatae feminae auxilium, in cuius ore de memorata benedictione parte infusa, erumpente sanguine mixto cum pure, vocis officium meruit adipisci.
Frigoriticus accedens ad hoc monumentum, pallam tegentem attegit, restincta contagionis febre, convaluit. Contractus vero Marcus nomine manibus deportatus
aliorum ad sepulchrum beatae, [ibi] orationem diutissime fodit. Hora autem nona pedibus propriis stetit, domique regressus est. Leodinus puer cum in valitudine
gravi inruens quarto aegrotaret mense et non solum gressum, verum etiam ciborum usum, insistente febre nimia, perdidisset, ad eius deportatus sepulchrum
praemortuus, accepta salute, surrexit e tumulo redivivus. Quid de frigoriticis reliquis loquar, cum plerisque hoc fuit beneficium remedii, cum pallam tumuli
sunt fideliter osculati? Quid etiam de inerguminis? Qui adducti ad cellulam beatae, com limen sanctam fuerint ingressi, integrae menti restituuntur; nec moratur
larva egredi e corpore, cum sanctae huius senserit adesse virtutem, operante hoc domino nostro Iesu Christo, qui timentibus nomen suum praemia largitur aeterna.
[FINIT DE SANCTAE MONEGUNDAE VIRTUTIBUS].

## XX. INCIPIT DE SANCTO LEOBARDO RECLAUSO.

### Prologus

**[106]** Eclesia fidelis aedificatur, quotienscumque sanctorum gesta devotissime replecantur; et licet de his teneat maximum gaudium, quod hi qui ab initio
aetatis religiosam vitam ducentes pervenire meruerunt perfectionis ad portum, tamen et de his, Domino iubente, laetatur, quod conversi a saeculo opus inchoatum
valuerunt perducere, divina opitulante misericordia, ad effectum.

### 1

**[107]** Igitur beatissimus Leobardus Arverni territurii indigena fuit, genere quidem non senatorio, ingenuo tamen, qui ab initio Deum in pectore tenens, cum
non floreret natalibus, gloriosis meritis praefulgebat. Qui tempore debito cum reliquis pueris ad scolam missus, quaepiam de psalmis memoriae conmendavit, et
nesciens se clericum esse futurum, iam ad dominicum parabatur innocens ministerium. Sed cum ad legitimam pervenisset aetatem, cogentibus iuxta consuetudinem
humanam parentibus, ut arram puellae, quasi uxorem accepturus, daret, inpellitur. Illo quoque respuente, ait pater: 'Cur, dulcissime fili, voluntatem paternam
respuis nec iungere vis conubio, ut semen excites nostro de genere saeculis sequentibus profuturum? Casso enim labore exercemur ad operandum, si possessor
deerit ad fruendum. Vel cur inplemus domum opibus, si de genere nostro non processerit qui utatur? Quid mancipia dato pretio nostris ditionibus subiugamus, si
rursum alienis debent dominationibus subiacere? Oboedire filiis voci parentum, Scripturae testantur divinae; et tu cum inoboediens esse parentibus probaris,
vide, ne te caelestibus eruere nequeas ab offensis'. Haec patre loquente, licet haberet alium filium, facile tamen tali aetatulae persuasit voluntati propriae
contraire. Denique, dato sponsae anulo, porregit osculum, praebet calciamentum, caelebrat sponsaliae diem festum. Interea genitor, genetrix mortis somno sopiti
migraverunt a saeculo, vitae praesentis curriculo iam peracto. Hic vero, cum germano tempore luctus expleto, oneratus donis nuptialibus, fratris pergit ad
domum; quem in tantum repperit vino madidum, ut nec cognoeceret nec reciperet propria in domo germanum. Ille vero suspirans et lacrimans, secessit in partem et
venit ad tugurium, in quo fenum fuerat adgregatum, ibique conligato praebens equiti pabulum, decubuit super fenum ad quiescendum. Expergefactus antem media
nocte, surgit de stratu suo, erectisque ad caelum manibus, gratias agere coepit omnipotenti Deo, quod esset, quod viveret, quod aleretur donis eius, et alia
huinscemodi prosecutus. Cum suspiria longa protraheret atque lacrimis crebris genas ubertim rigaret, Deus omnipotens, qui illos quos praescivit et
praedestinavit conformes fieri imaginis Filii sui, conpunxit cor eius, ut, relicto saeculo, manciparetur ad cultum divinum.

### 2

**[108]** Tunc ille quasi iam sacerdos animae suae, praedicare sibi ipsi exorsus est, dicens: 'Quid agis, anima? Quid in ambiguo suspensa teneris? Vanum est
enim saeculum, vanae eunt coucupiscentiae eius, vana gloria mundi, et ea quae in illo sunt omnia vanitas. Melius est enim relinquere eum et sequi Dominum, quam
ad eius opera praebere consensum'. Haec effatus, cum diem terris reddere lux diurna coepisset, ascenso equite, coepit ad hospitium suum reverti. Cumque per viam
iam alacris pergeret, volvere intra se coepit, quid ageret, quo abiret. Dixitque: 'Expetam Martini beati tumulum, unde procedit virtus alma super infirmos.
Credo enim, quod et mihi eius oratio iter reseret ad Deum, qui deprecatus Dominum mortuos reduxit a tartaro'. Et sic viam carpens oratione comite, sancti
Martini basilicam est ingressus, circa quam paucis diebus commoratus, transito amne, ad cellulam Maiori monasterio propinquam, de qua Alaricus quidam·
recesserat, devotus accessit; ibique se, propriis manibus membrana faciens, ad scribendum aptavit; ibi se, ut Scripturas Sanctas intellegeret ac Davitici
carminis psalmos, qui dudum excesserant memoriae, reteneret, exercuit. Sicque Divinarum Scripturarum lectionibus eruditus, cognovit, verum esse, quod ei Dominus
prius inspiravit in corde. Sed, ne haec cuique fabulosa videantur quae retulimus, testor Deum, quia ab ipsius benedicti haec ore cognovi. At vero, interposito
pauci temporis spatio, humilem se tantumque praebuit, ut honoraretur ab omnibus, acceptoque sarculo, cellulam, in qua ingressus fuerat, incidens lapidem,
ampliavit In qua cellula delectabatur ieiuniis, orationi, psallentio, lectioni, nec umquam a divinis officiis et oratione cessabat; scribebat interdum, ut se a
cogitationibus noxiis discuteret.

### 3

**[109]** Interea, ut se temptator manifestaret Dei servis semper inimicum esse ac invidum, cum aliquid de illius monacholi litem quandam cum vicinis habuisset,
inmisit ei cogitationem, ut, relicta cellula illa, ad aliam transmigraret. Cumque ibi ad orationem soliti evenissemus, dolum nobis veneni crassantis aperuit.
Ego vero suspirans non minimo dolore, increpare hominem coepi, asserens diaboli [haec] esse caliditatem; librosque et vita patrum ac institutione monachorum,
vel quales qui recluduntur esse debeant, vel cum quali cautela monachis vivere oporteat, abscedens ab eo, direxi. Quibus relictis, non solum cogitationem pravam
a se discussit, verum etiam tantum sensum acumine erudivit, ut miraretur facundia elocutionis eius. Erat enim dulcis alloquio, blandus hortatu, eratque ei
sollicitudo pro populis, inquesitio pro regibus, oratio assidua pro omnibus eclesiasticis Deum timentibus. Verum non ille, ut quidam, dimissis capillorum
flagellis aut barbarum dimissione plaudebat, sed certo tempore capillum tondebat et barbam. In qua cellula viginti et duos annos in hoc opere degens, tanta
Domini gratia confortatus est, ut, pusulis malis salibam oris sui perunctis, vim veneni saevientis obpraemeret, frigoriticis, vero, poculum vini caractere
crucis beatae sanctificatum, frigorem accedentem aestamque restinxit; non inmerito discutiens incommodas febres ab aliis, qui in se extinxerat incentiva
criminis noxialis. Quodam autem tempore caecus ad eum veniens, aerumnam doloris sui humiliter inplorabat ac deposcebat, ut tactu dexterae suae sanctus lumina
clausa palparet. Quod ille diutissime rennuens, tandem fletibus hominis victus, misericordia motus, cam per triduum pro eo orationem fudisset ad Dominum, quarta
die inponens manum super oculos eius, ait: 'Domine omnipotens, filins unigenite Dei patris, qui cum eo ac Spiritu sancto regnas in saecula, qui homini a
nativitate caeco reddidisti lucem beati oris ab sputo, tu redde huic famulo tuo luminis visum, ut cognoscat, quia tu es Dominus omnipotens'. Et haec dicens, ut
crucem super oculos caeci depixit, mox pulsis tenebris, lucem de praesenti restituit. Huius virtutis testimonio Eustachius abba adstipulator adsis it.

### 4

**[110]** Denique hic de labore lapidis submontani, quem assiduae caedebat, confractus, ieiunii austeritate confectus, orationi indeficienti corroboratus,
coepit paulatim corporis infirmitate distitui. Quadam autem die, dum nimium fessus haberetur, nos ad se vocari praecepit. Ad quem accedentes, postquam funeris
sui necessitate deflevit, englogias a nobis peccatoribus flagitavit. Quibus acceptis, austo mero, ait: 'Tempus meum iam impletur, iubente Domino, ut me ab huius
corporis vinculis iubeat relaxari, sed adhuc paucis diebus erit spatium. Verumtamen ante diem sanctum paschae vocandus ero'. O beatum virum, qui sic servivit
Creatori omnium, ut suum obitum revelatione divina cognosceret! Erat enim mensis decimus, quando haec est effatus. Duodecimo autem mense coepit iterum graviter
aegrotare. Advenit dies dominica, vocat ministrum suum et ait: 'Praepara quiddam cibi, quod accipiam, quia valde defessum me sentio'. Illo quoque respondente:
'Praesto est, domine', ait ad eum: 'Egredere foris et aspice, si iam, celebrata solemnia, populus de missis egreditur'. Hoc autem dicebat, non quod cibum capere
vellet, sed ut transitu suo nullus testis adesset Quo egrediente et revertente, cum ingressos fuisset cellulam, invenit virum Dei extensum corpore, clausis
oculis, spiritum exalasse. Unde manifestum est, eum ab angelis susceptum, qui homine adesse noluit suum sacer herus ad transitum. Haec cernens minister ille,
elevavit vocem in fletu. Sicque, concurrentibus reliquis fratribus, ablutus ac vestimentis dignis indutus, in sepulchro, quod ipse sibi in antedictam cellulam
sculpserat, reconditus est, quem in consortio sanctorum adscitum, nulli fidelium haberi reor incertum.
# THE GLORY OF THE CONFESSORS

## SOURCE AND CONTROL

English translation prepared for this project from the Latin control text in Bruno Krusch’s MGH *Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum*, Volume 1, Part 2, *Miracula
et opera minora* (second edition, 1969). The Latin below follows that MGH text. Gregory’s prologue and all 110 numbered chapters are included in printed order.

## SCENE AND CONTEXT

Gregory moves through Gaul and beyond it by tomb, basilica, village, monastery, and remembered journey, assembling the virtues of bishops, abbots, recluses,
consecrated women, and other confessors. The collection joins reports from local clergy and faithful witnesses to events Gregory says he witnessed himself. Its
scenes include healings at tombs, protection of church property, punishment of perjury and blasphemy, care for captives and the poor, the discovery or
translation of buried bodies, and final exhortations to almsgiving. The preface and chapters remain integral parts of the work rather than editorial additions.

## KINSHIP AND SAME-NAME FENCE

Nicetius of Lyon in chapter 60 is distinct from Nicetius of Trier in chapters 91–92. Palladius of Saintes in chapters 56 and 59 is not silently merged with
other bearers of that name. Marcellus of Die in chapter 69 is distinct from Marcellus of Paris in chapter 87. Maximus of Riez in chapter 82 is distinct from
Maximinus of Trier in chapter 91. Julian of Brioude is not a subject of this collection and is not imported into its notices. Relationships stated by the
source—such as Lusor as son of Leucadius, Pelagia as mother of Aredius, and Paulinus as husband of Therasia—are retained only in the passages that state them.

## RECENSION AND TEXT NOTE

The control text contains the prologue followed by chapters 1–110. Chapters 105–107 are represented only by rows of ellipsis points in the MGH text; they are
preserved here as explicit lacunae, not silently omitted or filled from another work. No separate continuation has been invented for those lost passages. The
closing exhortation in chapter 110 completes the transmitted collection.

# ENGLISH TRANSLATION

## PREFACE

**[000]** It shames an unwise, worthless, unskilled, and sluggish man to undertake what he cannot complete. But what am I to do? My eyes do not permit me to
pass over the miracles of the blessed which I myself have often inspected or clearly learned to have occurred through the reports of good men of certain faith.
Yet I fear that when I begin to write, because I lack rhetorical letters and grammatical art, the learned will say to me: “O rustic and unlearned man, why do
you think your name should be placed among writers? Do you think skilled people will accept a work whose author’s natural talent does not supply art and whom no
knowledge of letters assists? You have no useful argument in literature and cannot distinguish nouns. You often exchange feminine for masculine, neuter for
feminine, and masculine for neuter. You frequently fail to put in their proper places even those prepositions which the authority of noble authors has
sanctioned for observance. You use accusatives for ablatives and, in turn, ablatives for accusatives. Do you think it fitting for a lazy ox to play the game of
the wrestling school or a sluggish ass to run with swift flight among the order of ball players? Can a crow cover its blackness with the feathers of white
doves, or the darkness of pitch be changed into the color of milky liquid? Surely, just as these things are impossible, neither can you be counted among other
writers.” Nevertheless, I will answer them: “I am doing your work, and through my rusticity I will exercise your prudence. As I see it, these writings will
offer you one benefit: what I describe uncultivatedly and briefly with a blackening pen, you may expand lucidly and splendidly in polished verse on more ample
pages.” In the first little book I inserted some miracles of the Lord, the holy apostles, and the other martyrs which had hitherto lain hidden and which God
daily deigns to increase to strengthen the faith of believers, for it was very grievous that they should be consigned to oblivion. In the second I placed the
miracles of Saint Julian, and in four little books those of Saint Martin. The seventh concerned the lives of certain blessed men. I write this eighth about the
miracles of the confessors, asking the reader especially that, since, as I have often testified, neither natural art assists me nor eloquence of speech helps
me, he willingly pardon my rashness. Worldly boasting has not raised me up to write; shame weighs me down to keep silent; love and fear of Christ impel me to
relate. Since I began the first little book with the Lord’s miracles, I wish to give this little book a beginning concerning the power of the holy angels.

## 1

**[001]** While I was staying in the territory of the Auvergne, a faithful man related something to me. I know he spoke truly because I clearly learned that
what he said had happened. He ordered a drink to be prepared for the reapers from grain soaked and boiled in water. Orosius says that this boiled drink is
called caelia from the word for boiling. When it had been prepared and stored in a vessel while he delayed in the city, the servants drank most of it, as
servants do, and left only a little for their master’s uses. Trusting his order, he instructed the reapers to be invited so that, on his return from the city,
he would find them cutting the crop. When about seventy workers had been placed in the crop, the lord of the estate arrived. Examining the quality and quantity
of the drink, he found very little. Confused with shame and considering it disgraceful that the workers might lack drink—he thought there was no more than five
measures—he hung in uncertainty about what to do or where to turn. At last, inspired by the Lord, he turned to the little vessel and devoutly invoked over its
opening the names of the holy angels taught by sacred readings, praying that their power would deign to turn this small quantity into abundance so that the
workers would not lack drink. Wonderful to relate! What was drawn from it never failed the drinkers all day; until night ended the work, it was ministered
abundantly to everyone.

## 2

**[002]** Most blessed Hilary returned to his own city in the fourth year of his exile and, having completed the course of his good work, departed to the Lord.
Many miracles are said to have been shown at his blessed tomb, contained in the book of his Life. Two lepers were also cleansed in that same place. There was a
mountain in the territory of the Gabali called Hilary, with a large lake. At a fixed time a multitude of rustics, as though offering libations to the lake,
threw into it linens and cloths provided for men’s clothing. Some threw fleeces of wool, many also forms of cheese, wax, or bread, and various other offerings,
each according to his means—too many, I think, to enumerate. They came with wagons carrying drink and food, slaughtered animals, and feasted for three days.
When they were due to descend on the fourth day, an immense storm with violent thunder and lightning anticipated them. Such an immense rain with hailstones
descended in violence that each thought he would scarcely escape. This happened every year, and the foolish people remained enveloped in error. Much later a
certain bishop from that city came to the place after assuming the episcopate. He preached to the crowds to abstain from these things lest they be consumed by
heavenly wrath, but the crude rustics in no way accepted his preaching. Then, inspired by the Divinity, God’s bishop built a basilica in honor of blessed Hilary
of Poitiers at a distance from the lake’s edge and placed his relics in it, saying to the people: “Do not, little sons, do not sin before God! There is no
religion in a lake. Do not stain your souls with these vain rites. Rather acknowledge God and show veneration to his friends. Venerate Saint Hilary, God’s
bishop, whose relics are buried here! He can stand as an intercessor for you before the Lord’s mercy.” Pierced to the heart, the men were converted. Abandoning
the lake, they brought to the holy basilica everything they had customarily thrown there. Thus they were released from the error by which they had been bound.
The storm was thereafter kept from that place and no longer harmed this solemnity belonging to God after the blessed confessor’s relics were deposited there.

## 3

**[003]** Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, was a great helper to this Hilary against heresies. He shows by present miracles that he lives after the tomb. On his
birthday many sick people are saved, while the possessed rage through the whole church in violent spinning, confessing that they are tormented by immense
suffering. Raised into the air, they strike with their hands and break the lamps kindled to provide light. Drenched with their liquid, the persons are
immediately purified as the demon departs. The people then know that as many sick have been cleansed as they have seen lamps broken. He also preserves with
merciful protection everything under his basilica’s authority so that nothing may be taken by anyone. Among wicked enemies you may see herds of cattle, beasts
of burden, and flocks of sheep untouched by anyone once the cry sounds: “These belong to Confessor Eusebius.” My mother placed relics of this saint in the
oratory of her house. One winter day, while the household was already sleeping, she sat longer before the fire, which had been built from a great pile of wood,
in cheerful conversation because the night was long. Then she rose and lay down on a bed not far from the fire. While everyone slept, sparks from the flames
climbed as far as the beams. One of the beams caught and began to scatter flames violently. But I believe that through the power of that saint whose relics were
nearby, the flame was bent downward against its nature and turned back. It did not extend toward the roof, as fire usually does, but flowed downward, so that
you would think not flames but fleeces of wool hung from the beam. It did not burn the beam; the fire merely wandered along it until the mother of the household
awoke, called the servants, and extinguished the blaze with water. The whole house could easily have burned while everyone slept if the blessed saint’s power
had been absent.

## 4

**[004]** Report has informed me that Bishop Gatian was sent by Roman bishops to the city of Tours and given as the first bishop to the people of Tours. When
blessed Martin came to his tomb to pray, after pouring out prayers and saying the little chapter, he said: “Bless me, man of God.” As he spoke, a voice
descended to him and was heard saying: “Rather, servant of the Lord, I beg you to bless me.” After offering prayer again, Martin departed. Those present at the
time marveled and said that he who once called Lazarus from the tomb then dwelt in Martin.

## 5

**[005]** I have often heard old men relate an event similar to this at Artonne, a village of the Auvergne. A religious woman named Vitalina rests there.
Blessed Martin came to her tomb and gave a greeting. She begged him to deign to bless her. After they had completed prayer, the blessed man turned and said:
“Tell me, most holy virgin, have you already merited the Lord’s presence?” She replied: “One charge remains against me, which seemed trivial in the world: on
the sixth weekday, when I know the Redeemer of the world suffered, I washed my head with water.” Withdrawing from the virgin’s tomb, the blessed confessor said
to his companions: “Woe to me who live in this world! If this virgin consecrated to Christ incurred an offense because she washed her head on the sixth weekday,
what will I do, whom the deceitful world persuades to sin daily?” The blessed man performed many miracles in that village, which I thought too long to pursue.
Leaving Artonne, the man of God directed his steps toward Clermont. The city’s senators, who then gleamed there with the mark of Roman nobility, heard that the
holy man was approaching. They went out to meet him with horses, carriages, chariots, and vehicles. Martin, mounted on a little ass and seated on the meanest
saddlecloth, reached the summit of Mount Belena, from which the site of Riom can be seen. Seeing them approach with this worldly pomp, he said: “What do these
people want who approach me with this worldly display?” One who had arrived first replied: “The senators of Clermont are coming to meet you.” He said: “It is
not for me to enter their city with such ostentation.” Immediately turning the ass’s bridle back, he began to return by the way he had come. Following him, they
suppliantly begged him to come to the city: “I have heard the report of your holiness. There are many sick whom you ought to visit.” When they could not
prevail, he laid his hands on the sick who had come and restored them to health, then returned to Artonne. The screen in which the saint is said to have stood
still exists in this place. Afterward he went to the virgin’s tomb and said: “Rejoice now, Vitalina, most blessed sister; after three days you will be presented
to the Lord’s Majesty.” Then he departed. The virgin afterward appeared to many in visions, granted requested benefits, and disclosed the day of her death on
which her commemoration should be celebrated. This must be understood to mean that through the blessed bishop’s intercession she merited the Lord’s presence and
afterward did these things. At one time, after vigils had been celebrated in her honor, Eulalius, the local archpriest, invited the clergy to a banquet, while
another priest, Edatius, prepared food for widows and the remaining poor. One lacked fish and the other good wine. A fisherman was admonished in a vision by the
virgin to bring the archpriest an abundance of fish. Rising from bed, he found an immense salmon on his line and delivered it as instructed. She appeared
similarly in a vision to the priest Edatius: “Go, and beneath one tree in the forecourt you will find a triens. Give it and buy wine worthy of the poor people’s
feast.” He told no one what he had seen. He went, searched, and found it. Buying wine, he refreshed Christ’s poor. Thus the virgin’s power appeared to both and
supplied each with what was lacking.

## 6

**[006]** Martin did very many things in this world which the writers of his Life passed over, striving to avoid the disgust of detractors who often attack the
holiness of the good with venomous tongues and refuse to believe. But I, although unworthy, see his miracles daily at his tomb—for a physician is needed not by
the healthy but by the sick—and considered it absurd to remain silent about what I clearly know he did earlier. If anyone remains unbelieving and hostile enough
not to believe these things, let him go to the basilica. He will see new works done daily and former deeds repeated. Since I have written a third little book
about his works, I have undertaken to write in this one too about some things clearly known to me, so that this book also may not be without his miracles. As I
have often testified, many things have hitherto remained hidden. In the aforementioned basilica built in his honor by the faithful there is now a stone on which
the blessed man is said to have sat. Much later a priest named Leo moved the holy stone from its place to make a tomb for himself. Returning home trembling
without delay, seized by fever, he died on the third day. It was recognized that the bishop had been offended by this presumptuous act. I recall that this
happened in my own time.

## 7

**[007]** In the district of Neuilly in the city of Tours there was a tree that fell under a gust of wind and blocked the public road. When the blessed man was
traveling this way and saw the road closed by the fallen tree, moved by mercy he made the sign of the cross over it and raised it. It has been seen standing
erect beside the road to this day. Even after dying when stripped of bark, it nevertheless lived through the honor of the man of God. Many who faithfully
scraped its bark and took it diluted in water immediately received remedies. I myself also saw this tree standing erect.

## 8

**[008]** Near the town of Tours there was an oratory on the estate of Martigny where report often said Martin had prayed. When Abbot Gunthar governed the
monastic flock, if his journey happened to take him along the road not far from the oratory, he would pray before passing. After I had assumed the episcopate, I
myself was traveling past and came before the oratory but put off dismounting to pray there. Immediately my horse turned its head toward the oratory and stopped
in the middle of the road. It was struck with heels, driven with reins, and urged with goads, but did not move, as though made of bronze. Then the bishop
perceived that he was held by divine power. Dismounting and praying, he mounted the horse again and passed by. I wish, O steed, that the Lord would open your
mouth as he once opened the ass’s, so that you might say what admirable thing you saw that made you refuse to walk, what lovely thing that made you gaze at the
cell’s door, and what fearful thing that made you compel your rider to pray. Surely you would cry aloud that, seeing Martin’s brightness, you did not dare move
until your master presented the meeting owed to him.

## 9

**[009]** Aridius, a priest from Limoges and a man of the highest goodness and holiness, once sat with me in my cell. I began to ask whether any miracles were
shown in the oratory where he had deposited relics of the blessed bishop. He related that in the time of blessed Bishop Eufronius he came to Tours. Staying one
day, he took a small flask full of oil from the holy bishop’s tomb. Returning home, he sat exhausted from the journey and told his mother about its labors.
Suddenly he was struck so severely in the face that he could not recover his breath. Turning toward the oratory where the blessed bishop’s relics were kept, he
spent the night in vigil. In the morning he anointed the afflicted place with the oil he had brought. The pain subsided and he recovered. Afterward someone
brought him a hand swollen from being pierced by a thorn. As soon as it was smeared with the oil, it was restored to health. A woman who had lost her senses and
at certain hours was thought to have a demon was healed when touched with this oil. Another abbot from a nearby cell touched a blind man’s eyes with this oil,
and he immediately received sight. Although Aridius had restored many possessed people to health with it, he poured some on the head of one who had, I believe,
a more atrocious demon. The demon was immediately expelled through a flux of the bowels. In another man the demon descended into the nail of his thumb. Seeing
this, the priest poured oil over the finger. The skin immediately split, blood flowed, and the demon departed. These things he related concerning the oil.

## 10

**[010]** He added concerning a grape from the vine the saint had planted that he took it and enclosed it in a small flask filled with water. Not long afterward
a man came whose mouth was swollen by a malignant pustule and whose head and eyes were so inflamed by excessive poison that they were closed. Aridius poured
water from the grape flask into his mouth. Every swelling and pain departed as a drop fell away. He asserted that after four years the grains of that grape
still remained green in the water. Concerning wax he had taken from the tomb he added: a deaf and mute woman, who I believe had a demon, came to him. He put
some of the wax in her ear. Coming the next day, she thanked the priest for the health she had received.

## 11

**[011]** Within the boundary of the fortress of Ternod, adjoining the city of Langres, there was a priest disabled in walking. While proceeding along the road
leading to God’s church, he met an old man with a boy. Both were clerics. After exchanging greetings, the old man said to the priest: “Do you wish to be
healed?” He replied: “What more does the human race desire than to live sound in body?” Making the sign of the blessed cross over the priest’s knee, the old man
said: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, stretch out your foot.” The priest immediately stretched it out and drew it back sound. Giving thanks, he began to
continue his journey. The boy with the old man called him and said: “Priest, do you know who restored you to health?” “I do not,” he said. The boy replied:
“Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, restored you to health by his power. Build an oratory without delay where you saw the saint standing. It will be beneficial to
the people if you fulfill what I say.” Without delay the priest built an oratory on that site. Recently many paralytics there have merited to receive walking
and the blind sight.

## 12

**[012]** I recently learned of an event in Spain. When King Liuvigild marched against his son and his army, as usually happens, violently shook holy places,
there was a monastery of Saint Martin between Saguntum and Cartagena. Hearing that the army would come to that place, the monks fled and hid on an island in the
sea, leaving their aged abbot. The Goths arrived and plundered the monastery property left without a guard. They found the abbot bent by age but upright in
holiness. One drew his sword as though to cut off his neck; he fell backward and breathed out his spirit. Seeing this, the others fled in terror. When the king
was informed, he ordered with solemn attestation that everything taken from the monastery be restored.

## 13

**[013]** Seeing such great miracles performed by servants of God belonging to my religion, the aforementioned king called one of his bishops and said
privately: “Why do you not show signs among the people according to your faith, as those who call themselves Christians do?” The bishop replied: “I have often
restored sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf, and I can now do what you ask.” Secretly calling one of the heretics, he said: “Accept forty gold pieces.
Close your eyes and sit in a place along my route. When I pass with the king, cry out powerfully that through my faith I may restore your lost sight.” Having
accepted the money, the man did as commanded. The king’s new Cirula proceeded at his right, surrounded by a troop of heretics. The man blinded by money cried
out to receive his eyes through the bishop’s faith. With no small arrogance the bishop laid his hands on the man’s eyes and said: “Be it done to you according
to my faith.” As he spoke, the man’s eyes were closed with such pain that he not only lost his sight but also exposed the deceit he had contrived under
avarice’s impulse.

## 14

**[014]** A faithful man related on another occasion that he had watched a Christian contending with a heretic for my faith. After disputing at length over the
Divine Scriptures without being able to bend the heretic to recognize the truth, the man of my religion said: “If the testimonies of the Sacred Scriptures do
not move you to believe, at least experience the indivisible Trinity’s power through a miracle. I have a gold ring on my finger. I will throw it into the fire,
and you collect it glowing hot.” He threw the ring among the coals and allowed it to become so fiery that it looked like them. Turning to the heretic, he said:
“If your profession is true, take it from the fire.” When the heretic resisted, the man said: “Immeasurable Trinity, God, if I believe anything unworthy of you,
show it. Surely if my faith is right, let these savage flames have no power over me.” He took the ring from the fire and held it in his palm for a very long
time without being harmed. Rather, with the heretic confounded, the Catholic strengthened the rest by the fervor of his faith. So much for this.

## 15

**[015]** Not far from blessed Martin’s basilica rests Abbot Venantius, a man of magnificent holiness who aided many sick while in the body. Departing from the
world when his time was complete, he continually manifests by his own miracles that he lives forever. If anyone suffering attacks of fever keeps vigil and prays
at his tomb for one night, the attack is suppressed and he immediately obtains a remedy. Among the other things I saw or heard there, I beheld a woman afflicted
by quartan fever healed. Held so long by this contagion, she could take neither food nor sleep and had so declined in her whole body that scarcely the vital
breath remained. Spending the night at his tomb in groans and prayer, she remained motionless until daybreak. In the morning she gave herself to sleep. Awaking
and feeling no evil, she departed healed. I wrote this saint’s Life.

## 16

**[016]** There was also a very religious woman named Papula. She often begged her parents to place her in a monastery for girls because, impeded by worldly
cares in her parents’ house, she could not serve God. Unwilling out of love to be separated from her, they refused. She cut off her hair, put on male clothing,
went to the diocese of Tours, and joined a congregation of monks. Living there in fasts and prayers, she afterward shone with many miracles. She was as a man
among men, and no one knew her sex. Her parents searched but could never find her. When the abbot of the monastery she had entered died, the monks elected her
because of her continual miracles, unaware of her sex. She refused with all her strength. She remained in the monastery thirty years without anyone recognizing
what she was. Three days before departing this world she revealed it to the monks. After her death she was washed by other women and buried. Thereafter she
manifested herself as God’s handmaid through many miracles. Those suffering chills and afflicted by other diseases are often restored to health at her tomb.

## 17

**[017]** In another place in the district of Tours a tomb lay among thorns and brambles in which a certain bishop was said to have been buried. The inhabitants
did not know his name, and although few, they nevertheless rendered service. It happened that a poor man’s son died. When he buried him and could find no cover
for the stone coffin, he went to this place. He took the cover from this tomb—so immense that three pairs of oxen dragged it—and covered his son’s little body
with the theft from another’s tomb. When he had done this, he became deaf, mute, blind, and disabled. He remained in this punishment for nearly a whole year.
Then a bishop appeared to him in a vision: “Man, what violence did I inflict on you or yours that you uncovered me by taking the cover of my tomb? If you wish
to be healed, go now and order it quickly brought back. If you refuse, you will immediately die. I am Bishop Benignus, who came as a pilgrim to this city.”
Signaling his people, he went to his son’s monument, lifted the stone onto a wagon, and carried it back. As soon as he restored it to the coffin, he was healed.
On its return the stone was so light that two oxen brought back what three pairs had carried away.

## 18

**[018]** Within the boundary of Tours itself was a small hill filled with thorns, brambles, and wild vines, interwoven with such a density of wild growth that
scarcely anyone could break in. Report said two virgins consecrated to God rested there. The faithful often saw a divinely kindled light there during vigils on
feast days. One rather bold man, relying on his confident spirit, did not fear to approach in the dim night. He saw a wax candle of marvelous whiteness shining
with immense light. After long amazement he departed and told others what he had seen. Then the virgins showed themselves in a vision to one inhabitant. They
explained that they were buried there and could no longer endure the injury of rain without a roof. If he wished to consult his own welfare, he should cut the
thorns and provide a covering for their tombs. Awaking, as other thoughts crowded in, he consigned what he had seen to oblivion. On another night they appeared
again, threatening terribly with menacing countenance that unless he covered the place he would depart this world within the present year. Terrified, the man
took an axe, cut down the growth, and uncovered the tombs. He found thick drops of wax smelling like incense with a nectar-like fragrance. Assigning oxen and a
wagon, he gathered stones and built an oratory in summer. When the work was complete, he invited blessed Eufronius, then governing the church of Tours, to bless
it. Already exhausted by age, Eufronius excused himself: “You see, my son, that I have grown old, and winter weighs more heavily than usual. Rains descend,
winds blow everything in a whirl, rivers swell, and the roads themselves, poured over by frequent rains, have almost dissolved into mud. It is not suitable for
my age to hasten on such journeys.” Hearing this, the man departed from the bishop’s sight deeply grieved. When the bishop gave his limbs to rest, he saw two
virgins standing before him. The elder began with a sad countenance: “How have I been displeasing to you, most blessed bishop? What trouble have I brought to
the region committed to you by God? Why do you despise me? Why do you refuse to come consecrate the place a faithful man built for me? Come now; I implore you
by the name of Almighty God, whose handmaids I am.” Saying this, she wet her cheeks with tears. The old man awoke and called the rector of the cathedral house:
“I sinned by not going with the man. I saw two virgins rebuking me for it, and I fear incurring God’s offense if I delay going.” Hastening, he set out. As he
went, the rain ceased and the savage violence of the south winds subsided. Completing the journey happily, he blessed the place and returned in peace. He often
described the virgins’ faces and gait. One was taller, the other shorter in stature but not in merit; both were whiter than snow. He called one Maura and the
other Britta, saying he had learned their names from their own mouths.

## 19

**[019]** When many people repeatedly urged this bishop to go meet King Charibert and he delayed by making excuses, at last moved by his attendants he said:
“Go, prepare the journey so that I may meet the king, whom I shall not see.” Necessities were loaded on wagons and horses prepared. When everything stood ready
for departure, he said: “Let the wagons return and the horses be unharnessed. I am not making this journey now.” When his attendants asked what fickleness made
him so easily overturn what he had so insistently ordered prepared, he said privately: “The prince you compel me to visit has died. If I go, I will not find him
alive.” Astonished hearers noted the day and silently kept the saint’s words. When men arrived from Paris, they announced that the king had died at the very
hour the bishop ordered the wagons recalled from the journey.

## 20

**[020]** For believers’ instruction, I will not hesitate to relate something about my oratory, where relics of Saint Saturninus the martyr, Bishop Martin,
Illidius the confessor, and other saints are deposited: how blessed Martin’s power revealed itself by a revelation so that many saw that terrible fiery globe
which once emerged from his head while he celebrated the solemnity, visible then to only a few. Inspired by divine mercy, my mind conceived the idea of
faithfully dedicating for prayer the very elegant cell Saint Eufronius had used as a storeroom. I carefully arranged it and placed an altar as customary.
Spending one night in vigils at the holy basilica, I came to the cell in the morning and sanctified the altar I had erected. Returning to the basilica, I
solemnly brought from there his holy relics with those of the martyrs Saturninus and Julian and blessed Illidius, with shining candles and crosses. There was a
considerable choir of priests and Levites in white garments, a distinguished order of honored citizens, and a great assembly of people of the following rank. As
I carried the most sacred relics on high, adorned with cloths and napkins, I reached the oratory door. As I entered, a terrible brilliance suddenly filled the
cell, so that the bystanders’ eyes closed from fear and excessive splendor. It ran through the whole cell like lightning, causing me no small fear. No one could
know what it was; all lay prostrate on the ground in terror. Then I said: “Do not be afraid. What you see is the saints’ power. Remember especially the book of
blessed Martin’s Life and recall how, when he uttered sacred words, a globe of fire came from his head and was seen to ascend to heaven. Do not be terrified;
believe that Martin himself has visited me with the holy relics.” Setting fear aside, I magnified God: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; God the
Lord has shone upon me.” The earlier miracle was seen by few; this appeared to all the people. That was an indication of power, this an addition of grace. That
was hidden then to prevent boasting; this is manifest to all for glory. There, words faithfully spoken at a feast were announced to the Lord; here, by the
illumination of holy relics, a new oratory was consecrated to advance the Lord’s praise. I must faithfully seek and pray to him as I ought, that he may visit
this people, he who often bore the vows of prayer aloft through this sacred fire. Whether I described it when telling of the praying monk or explained that
Abbot Brachio saw fire coming from the saints’ relics, I consider this fire mystical because it does not burn but illumines. Nor can it ever be produced or
appear to anyone without the Divine Majesty’s grace.

## 21

**[021]** Although I have already written some things about Tours, since I recently beheld Saint Sollemnis’s tomb I could not remain silent about what I learned
happened at the monastery of Maillé, set on a mountain summit and fortified by ancient buildings now destroyed. They say that while the crypt was still hidden
and the place unrevealed to any Christian, inhabitants saw a light kindled there on the nights of each Sunday solemnity. No one knew the mystery’s meaning, only
suspicion held the men to believe something divine was kept there. Meanwhile two possessed men arrived from Saint Martin’s basilica. Striking their palms
together, they cried: “Most blessed Sollemnis rests here in a hidden crypt. Open the tomb of God’s friend. When you find it, cover it with veils, kindle a
light, and offer due worship. It will benefit this region if you fulfill what I say.” Saying this, they tried with loud cries to dig up the earth with their
fingernails. Seeing what was happening, the inhabitants took a hoe, dug, and opened the crypt. Descending a series of steps, they found a great tomb. The men
still infirm in mind testified that it was the tomb of most blessed Sollemnis. They soon recovered their senses. Afterward people sick with various diseases
began flocking to him and returned unharmed after receiving health. Litomeris, a native of that city, was exhausted by quartan fever. Taking wax candles from
his lodging, he rose with only one boy and went to the place. Pouring out prayer, he lit the candles and held them in his own hand all night, celebrating
vigils. When morning came he returned home and never afterward suffered the severity of chills or any collapse from this disease.

## 22

**[022]** There was a religious man, Maximus, great both in miracles and name. As the verse-written book of his Life teaches, he was my Martin’s disciple.
Wishing to conceal what he was, he sought to live as a pilgrim at Île Barbe, a monastery of Lyons. Manifested there too, he decided to return to his homeland.
While wishing to cross the river Arar, his filled ship sank and the bishop himself was covered by the flood. Around his neck he had the daily ministry with a
Gospel book—a small paten and chalice. Divine mercy, not allowing its own to perish, restored him from this danger to shore by the Lord’s command, so that he
neither suffered loss of life nor mourned loss of property. What the psalmist sang under the Holy Spirit’s influence was fulfilled: “When the just man falls, he
will not be crushed, because the Lord strengthens his hand,” and again: “The Lord will not abandon the just man’s soul.” Coming to Chinon, a fortress of Tours,
he established a monastery. When Egidius besieged this fortress and the district’s people were shut inside, the enemies blocked a well dug in the mountain’s
side which the besieged used for drinking. When the aforementioned servant of God, then enclosed with the rest within the fortress defenses, saw the people
consumed by thirst, he prayed to the Lord all night, asking him to look upon the people, put the wicked enemies to flight, and not allow them consumed by
burning thirst. With the Holy Spirit revealing to him, he said: “Whoever has a little vessel, throw it outside into the street and pray to the Lord. Today his
generosity will give you water in abundance so that you and your little children do not perish.” As he spoke, clouds suddenly covered the sky. A great rain
descended from heaven with thunder and lightning over the fortress, giving the people a double benefit: rain drove away thirst and the crashes put the enemy to
flight. Everyone’s vessels were filled and all satisfied. Thus, through the bishop’s intercession, the adversaries were put to flight and the people left the
fortress saved. Full of days, he died in that monastery and was buried there. The sick are often healed at his tomb. A little boy from the household of the
church of Tours collapsed in illness. Lying gasping and thought at the point of breathing out his spirit, he was carried to Maximus’s basilica. The fever was
immediately extinguished and he was restored to health. A girl from the same servants suffered similarly from fever. Placed before the screens of his monument,
she was restored to health that very day. When notice of these events reached me, I had the boy’s hair cut and assigned him to this monastery. Changing the
girl’s clothing, I ordered her joined to the community of nuns to serve God.

## 23

**[023]** Not far from this basilica rests a priest named John, a Breton by nation, living in the highest religion. Through his hands the Lord deigned to work
many signs of healing. Restraining himself from human sight out of divine love, he had a tiny oratory cell before the church of Chinon. In a little garden he
cultivated with his own hand he planted laurel trees, now extended with huge columnar trunks and the pleasantness of delightful foliage. Sitting beneath their
shade, the holy man read or wrote. After his death, when those trees spread with broad branches to shade the garden, one grew old with age and dried up. The
custodian dug up the trunk with its roots, cut its branches, and adapted it as a bench on which he sometimes sat when tired or cut something with an axe when
necessary. After using the bench thus for two years or more, touched, I believe, by divine inspiration and grief of heart, he said: “Woe to me! I have sinned by
using for various necessary cuttings a tree such a bishop planted with his own hand.” Taking a hoe and digging the earth, he cut off the bench’s feet, placed it
beneath the ground, and filled the hole with earth. Wonderful to relate! When spring came, just as the other trees flowered, this trunk, buried, so to speak, by
the man’s hand, grew green in restored vitality and put forth new leaves. Shoots from it remain today at a height of five or six feet or more. Growing every
year, they are raised up by the Lord.

## 24

**[024]** Blessed Monegund died in the city of Tours itself. She came from the territory of Chartres. Leaving homeland and parents, she sought Tours solely to
devote herself to prayer. God often deigned to show miracles through her. If anyone incurred a malignant pustule and came to her asking for prayer, she
immediately prostrated herself to petition the Lord. Gathering leaves of some vegetable or fruit, she smeared them with saliva, made a cross over the sore, and
applied the leaf. All the poison immediately vanished so that the sick person suffered nothing further deserving death. She also often healed those with quartan
fever and throat pain by giving blessed water. The sick now continually flock to her tomb and are healed. How many suffering chills, how many already dead from
malignant pustules as the poison thickened, and how many sick with dysentery have been healed there cannot be explained individually. Since I recorded many of
these in the book I wrote about her Life, I could not remain silent about later events. A servant of my archdeacon Probus was severely shaken by quartan fever
and had already suffered nearly a year. Placed upon the holy tomb in her relatives’ arms, she was carried home unharmed.

## 25

**[025]** I wrote Abbot Senoch’s Life long ago. After mentioning many of his miracles, I ended that little book. But since power has appeared at his tomb, it
would be absurd for me to remain silent. A boy named Nantulf, held by extreme blindness, continually lamented that this contagion had disfigured even the
adolescence of his early age. He sought the saint’s tomb and, prostrate and supported by humble prayer, begged that through Senoch’s aid his lost light be
recalled. Persisting in this prayer for four days, his eyes were opened and he departed illuminated. Even now many suffering chills and the discomfort of other
diseases are healed as soon as they pluck or touch fringes of his garment. So much for the people of Tours.

## 26

**[026]** The confessor Simeon, said to have stood on a column in the district of Antioch, frequently grants healings to the inhabitants. As is read in his
Life, after his conversion he never attentively looked upon any woman. Burning with holiness, after he mounted the higher column he allowed no strange woman,
not even his own mother, to see him. He now likewise defends that place from approach by this sex. They say a woman put on male clothing and wished to enter the
basilica of the column, wretchedly thinking she could use the garment to hide from the Most High, ignorant of the apostle’s words: “God is not mocked.” When she
came to the church and lifted her foot to enter the holy threshold, she immediately fell backward and died. It was enough for the people that no woman should
presume this again when they saw such dreadful vengeance inflicted on her.

## 27

**[027]** Saint Bishop Martial, sent by Roman bishops, began preaching in Limoges. Overthrowing idolatrous rites and filling the city with faith in God, he
departed from the world. Two priests he had brought with him from the East were then with him in Gaul. When their days were completed and they too were called
from this world, they were buried in joined stone coffins in the same crypt as the holy bishop. One was next to the wall and the other adjoining it. Both stood
above ground, but honor could not be paid to the second because of the first: no cloth could be spread there and no light kindled. The inhabitants found this
grievous. Coming to the crypt one morning, they found the tombs placed against different walls. Free access to each was thus opened, and it became clear how the
blessed bishop wished to be venerated as a worshiper of God.

## 28

**[028]** A girl came to his tomb with one hand stiffened—I do not know from what sin—and her fingers fixed to her palm. Trusting in the confessor’s power, she
believed his intercession could release her dry hand, whose preaching had released a people entangled in vain superstitious rites. Celebrating vigils on the
night of his feast, she prayed intently beside the tomb. Astonished, she marveled at her hand healed with fingers extended before the people’s testimony. At
this solemnity a mute man also merited speech. As crude rusticity does, he had uttered a false oath in church. His tongue immediately stiffened and he became
mute, seeming to imitate not a human voice but a sheep’s bleat. Coming to this confessor’s tomb, he prostrated himself in prayer. As he later asserted, he felt
as though someone touched his throat—this, I believe, was the power of the Lord’s confessor. Rising, he begged the priest present by signs to place the sign of
the cross upon his closed jaws. When the priest did so, he again prostrated himself in prayer. Immediately raised up with the office of speech restored, he
revealed in his own words everything he had suffered.

## 29

**[029]** Through Saint Stremonius, also sent by Roman bishops with most blessed Gatian and the others I have mentioned, the city of Clermont first received the
word of salvation. By his preaching it began to believe in Christ, the world’s salvation and redeemer of all, the Son of God. His tomb is in the village of
Issoire. Crude earlier rusticity, although knowing where he rested, rendered no worship of honor there. After long cycles of years, Cautinus, appointed bishop
of Clermont, governed the church of that village during his diaconate. One night as he lay on the bed of his cell adjoining the basilica, he heard psalm-singers
with voices resounding softly. Rising, he saw the church shining with great light. Astonished, he looked inside—the little cell was above, opposite the church
windows—and behold, a multitude in white garments stood around the tomb holding candles and singing psalms! Watching for a long time until they departed, at
daybreak he ordered the tomb enclosed with a screen and covered with bright cloths and instructed that reverence be paid to the place. Since then prayer has
been poured over the tomb and the bishop’s aid obtained. I heard this from the bishop’s own mouth.

## 30

**[030]** It is a great grace if the priesthood is worthily guarded in conduct. If the priesthood bestowed so much even on a wicked man and persecutor of
justice that he merited prophecy—Caiaphas, who prophesied that one ought to die for the people lest the whole nation perish—how much more can divine Majesty
bestow on those fearing God and guarding the priesthood in holiness and purity? According to James, a priest’s visitation with prayer benefits the sick, and
often the mere offering of blessed gifts from his hand provides protection. I truly learned this from an event in the Auvergne during my adolescence. A solitary
priest traveling sought lodging at a poor man’s little dwelling in Limagne. Received there, he rose from his bed at night according to priestly custom and stood
in prayer. The man, compelled by necessity to bring wood from the forest, rose very early. As rustic custom has it, even before dawn he asked his wife for food,
which she immediately offered. The man did not eat the bread until it was blessed by the priest or he received blessed gifts from him. Receiving them, he ate
and departed. Coming to the river before daylight, he placed the wagon and oxen on the bridge set over boats and began to cross to the other shore. In midstream
he heard a voice: “Sink, sink, do not delay!” Another voice replied: “Without your admonition I would already have done what you proclaim if the sacred thing
did not obstruct my efforts. Know that he is fortified by the priest’s blessed gifts; therefore I cannot harm him.” Hearing the voices, seeing no person, and
recognizing that the words concerned himself, the man signed himself with the Lord’s cross and thanked God that the opposing party could not prevail over him.
Proceeding to the farther bank, he returned home safely with the desired load.

## 31

**[031]** Antiquity reports that there were two in the Auvergne, a man and a girl, joined in marriage but not intercourse. Resting in one bed, they were not
polluted by one another in carnal pleasure. After many years of this most chaste life in secrecy, by mutual consent the man was tonsured for the clericate and
the girl put on religious clothing. When her days were complete, the girl departed from the world. Her husband prepared a burial and brought her little body to
be buried. As he enclosed her in the tomb, he raised his hands to heaven and revealed the secret agreed between them: “I thank you, maker of all things, that
just as you deigned to entrust her to me, I have returned her unpolluted by every contagion of pleasure.” Smiling, she said: “Be silent, be silent, man of God.
With no one asking, there is no need to confess our secret.” He covered her with the lid and withdrew. Not long afterward he too departed the world and was
buried in his own place. Both tombs were in one basilica but against different walls, one to the south and the other north. In the morning the tombs were found
together, and remain so today. Therefore the inhabitants now call them the Two Lovers and venerate them with the highest honor.

## 32

**[032]** In the aforementioned city of Clermont there was also Amabilis, a priest of Riom, of admirable holiness. Excelling in great miracles, he is often said
to have commanded serpents. When Duke Victorius disdained to pray at his tomb and fixed his horse opposite, he could in no way make it move. He urged it with
whips and goads, but it stood immobile as bronze. At last, admonished by his attendants and made, so to speak, like the beast itself, the duke dismounted to
pray. After praying faithfully, he went where he wished. At his tomb I saw a possessed man cleansed and a perjurer become rigid as iron; after confessing his
crime, he was immediately released.

## 33

**[033]** A religious girl devoted to God is also said to have lived in that city. Remaining in the country, removed from the urban population, she more freely
offered worthy sacrifices of praise to God, devoting herself daily to fasting and prayer. Departing this world, she was carried to the town basilica for burial.
When they raised the bier and began carrying her body along the road, a great flock of doves began flying above her and followed by flying wherever her
relatives carried her. When she was brought into the basilica, the whole flock was seen to settle on the building’s roof. After she was buried, the doves flew
to heaven. She was therefore rightly called Georgia, having so exercised her mind with spiritual cultivation that, obtaining the sixtyfold fruit as the produce
of virginity, she was honored with heavenly funeral rites on leaving the world.

## 34

**[034]** In Saint Venerandus’s basilica, next to Saint Illidius’s, there was a vaulted cell on the west side. Many tombs carved from Pharian marble are there,
in which holy men and religious women rest. There is no doubt they were Christians, because the histories on the tombs set forth miracles of the Lord and his
apostles. At the time when George, a citizen of Le Velay, held the countship of Clermont, part of that vault, soaked by rain through long negligent disregard,
fell upon one of these coffins. Striking its cover, it shattered it. A girl appeared lying inside, so intact in every member as though recently taken from this
world. Her face, hands, and other limbs were whole, with extremely long hair; I believe she had been embalmed with spices. The garment covering her lifeless
limbs was intact and undamaged, not dissolved by rot or darkened by any blackness. What more? She appeared so intact that she seemed sleeping rather than dead.
Some of my people supposed from the whiteness of her all-silk garment that she had departed in white baptismal robes. They also said gold rings and bracelets
were found around her and secretly taken so the bishop would not learn. No age of my time has learned by report or reading her merit, family, or name. While
this little body lay uncovered for a year and no one offered the respect of humanity by covering the tomb, the aforementioned count’s wife became gravely ill
after her husband’s death. Held by prolonged illness, she was deprived of eyesight. Relieved of fever, she called physicians, tried various treatments, and
offered rewards, but could obtain no remedy until at last the Lord’s moved mercy looked upon her. A figure appeared in a night vision: “If you wish to be
restored to your former sight, go as quickly as possible, seek a clean stone, and quickly cover the resting girl’s coffin, exposed in Saint Venerandus’s
basilica. Your eyes’ sight will soon be uncovered and you will clearly see everything.” When she closed the vessel with its cover, her eyes immediately opened
and she fully received light. There is no doubt she was of noble merit who could provide such things to a sick woman.

## 35

**[035]** Many tombs in this place, as I said, are proved to belong to the faithful. A tomb adjoining this one on the left is similar in length, width, height,
and every position. On its upper face is written: OF HOLY MEMORY, GALLA. Another tomb, glorious for the merits of its carving, stands elevated between the exit
of Saint Illidius’s basilica and the entrance of blessed Venerandus’s church. A religious man named Alexander is said to be buried there. Sick people frequently
scrape dust from it, drink it diluted, and immediately obtain health. The remedy is exacted so frequently that the tomb is seen pierced through by onlookers
because of continual beneficial help. Opposite this tomb, if you enter Saint Venerandus’s basilica through the door, you will see on the right a small tomb
above ground formed of rougher stone. No one knows who rests there. What I am about to relate shows something divine is present. As I myself saw, a beggar
customarily sat upon it. I believe, as human frailty allows, he was involved in some unworthy deed. Thrown off with a great sound by the power of the one
resting there, he was cast far away, and the tomb split down the middle, as still seen. The buried man evidently considered it unworthy for someone to sit upon
his limbs. The blessed martyr Liminius is also buried in this basilica. Although the inhabitants possess the history of his contest, no worship of veneration is
paid him. As I said, men of illustrious merits are there whose names are unknown to the inhabitants but, I believe, are kept written in heaven.

## 36

**[036]** There too is the tomb of Saint Bishop Venerandus himself, from whom this building took its name, placed beneath a lectern. Whoever wishes puts his
head through a little window and prays for what necessity compels. If he asks justly, he soon obtains the result. Saint Bishop Nepotian also rests there, a man
of the highest holiness in the world, now obtaining with the Lord’s power whatever is implored from him. Prayer poured over these tombs often retains the
desired remedy for those suffering chills.

## 37

**[037]** They were great lights of the world, illuminating it with miracles as the sun does with rays. They say that in a certain monastery there was a monk
who, while devoting himself with the others to prayer and reading according to monastic rules, more secretly and specially rendered sacrifices of prayers to
Almighty God. After completing the office in the oratory, he secretly slipped from the brothers’ presence. Going among dense brambles, box trees, and holm oaks,
where he hoped to be inspected by God alone, he prostrated himself in prayer. After lying down and petitioning the Lord for a very long time, he raised himself
from the ground. With palms and eyes lifted to heaven, he silently recited a series of psalms. Intent on heaven with such compunction, rivers of tears flowed
violently from his eyes. One brother followed cautiously, observed this, and did not conceal it from the abbot. Watching for when the monk hurried to do this,
the abbot followed from afar and lay prostrate to observe what the faithful disciple practiced. Attentive from afar, he saw a great miracle. Flame proceeded
from both sides of the monk’s mouth. Gradually drawn out at length like a little cord, it ascended above him. Joining together, it formed a great lighthouse
that seemed to climb to heaven. Although its crest extended on high and grew, it did not harm his head. Astonished, the abbot restrained himself a little. When
the monk finished praying, he returned to the monastery. The abbot followed by another road. Afterward he rebuked the monk with many reproaches to restrain
vainglory, without revealing what he had seen.

## 38

**[038]** I believe this fire contains a mystical sacrament. The darkness of my understanding cannot comprehend how appearing light gives so much without
burning anyone. I know only that such things appear to or over the just. To Moses in the bush and the other fathers it appeared for a burnt offering. Bursting
from blessed Martin’s crown, it penetrated heaven’s heights. As I wrote in his Life, I often heard Abbot Brachio relate that while he kept nocturnal watch in
the aforementioned bishop’s basilica and relics brought by pilgrims lay on the altar, a globe of fire suddenly emerged from them and was seen to ascend to the
church ceiling. As he said, it was shown to few. It likewise appeared at my oratory’s dedication, as I recorded above.

## 39

**[039]** Nor is it absurd to believe that the Lord often deigns to reveal through experienced visions how saints are honored or the sick obtain remedies. I
recall that in my infancy my father suffered from gout. Weakened by burning fever and many pains, he lay in bed. I saw in a night vision a figure saying: “Have
you read the book of Joshua son of Nun?” I replied: “I know no letters beyond the alphabet, in whose study I am now constrained and afflicted. I do not know
whether such a book exists.” He said: “Go, make a little slip of wood that can receive this name, and, written in ink, place it beneath the support of your
father’s head. It will be his protection if you fulfill what I say.” In the morning I told my mother what I had seen. She ordered the vision’s commands
fulfilled. When I had done so, my father immediately recovered. After another year’s course he was again seized by this affliction. Fever kindled, his feet
swelled, and dreadful pain twisted his nerves. While he lay groaning loudly, I again saw a figure in a vision asking whether I now knew the book of Tobit. I
replied that I had not read it. He said: “Know that Tobit was blind. While his son traveled with an angel companion, he caught a fish in the river. At the
angel’s direction he removed its heart and liver and smoked his father’s eyes. The darkness was immediately put to flight and he received light. Go and do
likewise, and your father will receive relief from his pains.” Telling my mother, she immediately sent boys to the river. A fish was caught and the commanded
organs removed and placed on coals. As soon as the smoke’s odor reached my father, swelling and pain immediately departed.

## 40

**[040]** The glorious confessor Germanus died in Rome. Raised from there, after sixty days he was brought to Auxerre and committed to burial. In Queen
Theudechild’s time a tribune named Nunninus was returning from Francia to the Auvergne after rendering tribute to the queen. Solely for religion he visited
Auxerre. Prostrate at the blessed tomb and praying for a very long time, he drew a dagger from its sheath and, unseen, struck the stone over the venerable tomb.
When a small particle was knocked off, he became rigid as bronze, unable to move any member or utter a voice. His attendants saw him lying thus but did not know
what had happened. One approached and questioned him but received no answer. Rigid, he understood in his heart that he was condemned and vowed: “Most blessed
confessor, I know I was presumptuous, but devotion compelled me to presume. If you deign to release me and permit me to return home with your favor, I will
deposit these relics in a basilica and take care to celebrate your feast most devoutly every year.” Understanding his closed murmur, the holy man released him
and permitted him to depart unharmed. Coming home, he deposited the relics in a church and faithfully celebrated the saint’s feast every year. At one time I
went with Bishop Avitus to the aforementioned basilica where the relics are kept. When the holy bishop entered fasting at about the tenth hour, all of us with
him drew into my nostrils the fragrance of lilies and roses. I do not doubt this was granted through the blessed bishop’s merit. It was the ninth month. This
occurred at the village of Messigny.

## 41

**[041]** A senator named Hilary lived at the fortress of Dijon with a wife by whom he is said to have had sons. He cultivated his whole house in such chastity
and complete purity of mind and body that no one presumed to commit adultery there. What the apostle, filled with the Holy Spirit, preached was fulfilled in
this house: “Marriage is honorable and the bed undefiled.” With chastity prevailing among lords and servants, the man died. His tomb, shining carved from
Pharian marble, reveals today his worldly dignity. After his death and customary human burial, when the year’s cycle had run his wife fell ill and died and was
washed. Since the tomb was so immense that it could receive her beside her husband as he had commanded, the cover was removed. While she was being placed in the
tomb, the husband’s right hand suddenly rose and embraced his wife’s neck. Marveling, the people deposited the cover and withdrew. They recognized the chastity,
fear of God, and mutual love they had in the world, who thus embraced in the tomb.

## 42

**[042]** Saint Florida also rests in this basilica. The inhabitants say she changed her clothing and was very religious. Nearby is another basilica where Saint
Paschasia rests. She is said to have appeared to the builders of Saint Benignus the martyr’s basilica nearby, urging them to persevere in the work begun and
know they were aided by the martyr’s help. Returning to her own basilica, she appeared nowhere again.

## 43

**[043]** The blessed confessor Tranquillus also rests here, his tomb above ground. A great benefit is granted to petitioners from it. People merit remedies
from the dust collected above. I myself had a powerful experience of this. When my hands broke out in tiny pustules and I severely endured dreadful pains, I
touched them with this dust. The humor subsided and I immediately brought them back healthy.

## 44

**[044]** Bordeaux also has venerable patrons who often manifest themselves by miracles. It cultivates Saint Bishop Severinus with the highest faith in the
suburb outside its walls. Although I said in this book’s prologue that I would write only what God deigned to work after his saints’ deaths through their
intercession, I do not think it absurd to mention something from their lives where I know nothing has been written. As the faithful report of Bordeaux’s clergy
states, Saint Severinus was directed from the East to that city. While he traveled and Bishop Amandus governed Bordeaux’s church, the Lord appeared to Amandus
in a night vision: “Rise and go out to meet my servant Severinus. Honor him as Holy Scripture teaches a friend of the Divinity should be honored. He is better
than you and loftier in merits.” Bishop Amandus rose, took his staff, and went to meet him, knowing nothing of the holy man except what the Lord had revealed.
Behold, Saint Severinus came as though toward him. Approaching and greeting each other by their own names, they rushed together into embraces. Kissing and
pouring out prayer, they entered the church with loud psalm-singing. Bishop Amandus afterward loved and venerated Severinus so much that he put him in his own
place and was himself treated as the junior. A few years later most blessed Severinus died. After his burial Bishop Amandus recovered his own place, undoubtedly
returned to him through the obedience he practiced toward God’s saint. Recognizing his holiness, the inhabitants adopted him as patron. They are certain that if
disease creeps into the city, enemies besiege it, or any calamity strikes, the people immediately run to the saint’s basilica, proclaim fasts, celebrate vigils,
and most devoutly pour out prayer. They are soon saved from the impending calamity. After I wrote this, I learned that the priest Fortunatus wrote his Life.

## 45

**[045]** The holy priest Romanus is also in this territory. As the writings of his Life teach, my Martin committed him to burial. His tomb is next to the
fortress of Blaye on the bank of the Garonne. He often saves those about to perish in shipwreck by the arrival of his power when they cry amid the torrent’s
waves: “Have mercy on me, Saint Romanus, confessor of God.” The storm soon subsides and they reach the desired shores. No one who has been found worthy to
behold his basilica from midstream may perish by shipwreck. I myself experienced this in great necessity. After very frequent rain for many days had cast the
Garonne beyond its banks and wind drove it to overflow with violent waves, mighty mountains of water rose, causing no small fear to onlookers. The blessed
confessor was entreated and, as I believe, obtained by the aid of his power that the crashes were suppressed and the riverbed made level. Boarding a ship, I was
carried to the other bank without danger.

## 46

**[046]** Two priests, men of outstanding holiness as the matter itself declares, are buried in a village in the same territory. The miracle occurring there
most clearly teaches that they live after the tomb. They are buried in one basilica but against different walls, one’s tomb to the south and the other’s to the
north. When clerics begin exercising the office of psalm-singing and form choirs to sing to the Lord in melodious multitude, each man’s voice mingles with the
public psalmody. One choir gains the assistance of one voice, and the other is strengthened by the modulation of the other voice. The harmony of this sweetness
often soothes hearers’ attentive ears. Benefits are also often shown to be granted with them when faithful prayer precedes. This occurs in the village of
Bouillac.

## 47
