**[047]** Not far away is the estate of Réont, where there was a Catholic church. When the Goths arrived, they transferred it to the uncleanness of their sect.
A large house is beside it. When the Easter vigil approached, the heretical priests baptized little children in my church so that, by denying my priest access
to baptize, they might more easily entangle the people in their sect. With sagacious intention, while they were in my church, he prepared the ministry and began
baptizing in their house while they baptized in the church. Divine vengeance went before: of the infants the heretics baptized there—twenty—none reached the
close of Easter alive. Seeing this and fearing that their house would become a church, the heretics returned my church to the priest. None of those he baptized
died at that time except one whom the Lord deigned to call after a lawful age.

## 48

**[048]** Within the boundary of Bazas, in the village of Sescas, rests the holy priest Justin. Mighty in many miracles, he often cleanses the possessed who cry
out at his tomb; the blind are illuminated and paralytics made upright. Close to his merits and holiness is Similian, who held the office of the same order in
the church. He rests at the village of Targon in this territory and flourishes with similar miracles.

## 49

**[049]** Joined to these by city and territory is Saint Severus, also ordained priest and born of noble stock. On the rural estate of Sescas in his possession
he built a church. Then on another estate he built another church of God, fortifying both with saints’ relics. When Sunday came, he celebrated Mass in one place
and went to the other. The distance between the churches was about twenty miles. This was his work every Sunday. One Sunday, while traveling this route and
hastening faster, striking his horse with his heel, a branch of a medlar tree struck his head. Feeling the injury, he said: “May God, by whose will you came
from the earth, command you to dry up.” The tree immediately dried down to the very roots of its vitality. Going where he was headed and celebrating the
solemnity, he remained there three days. Returning on the fourth and seeing the dry tree, he said: “Woe to me, who cursed this tree in bitterness of heart!
Behold how it has dried!” Dismounting, he prostrated himself at its roots and said to the Lord: “Almighty God, by whose will all things are governed, by whose
command unborn things are created, created things live, and dead things are restored; holding your salutary command, I believe that through the future
resurrection I will live after this body’s death. Command this tree to grow green again and be as before.” Immediately, as though through an arrangement of
veins, moisture rose from the earth and diffused in abundant irrigation through all the spreading branches. Loosening the dry knots, it burst forth in leaves
and was marvelled at by bystanders as having revived. Great was his power and almsgiving: as said above, he made churches from his houses and distributed his
resources as food for the poor. He deposited his tomb in one of them and was buried there. He used to gather lily flowers in their season and hang them along
this building’s walls.

## 50

**[050]** What his life was in this world is thus made clear with the Lord’s cooperation and designated by evident prodigies. As time passed, the lily I said he
gathered and placed in the basilica of his tomb withered, its floral leaves loosened downward and its crest dry. It seemed so desiccated that if touched by hand
one would think it would immediately dissolve into powder. It remains in this dryness all year. On the day the confessor departed the body, it rises again in
renewed greenness. You may see the leaves gradually grow green and the flowers themselves lifted up, renewed without any moisture of water or earth into the
appearance they once had. Thus the blessed confessor brings forth new flowers from the tomb, he who flourishes like a palm in heaven with the rest of the
saints.

## 51

**[051]** Within the boundary of the village of Julien three priests are buried together. According to ancient report they are joined by no bond of
consanguinity but are companions solely in love of God and made brothers in heaven. With tombs placed side by side, they illumine the space of one place by
continual miracles. They rested in these cavities for many years. Recently the pavement, poured from lime and crushed tile like the hardest flint, split and the
top of one tomb appeared. When it rose a little, the split earth revealed another’s apex. When that emerged, a third mound followed. Since their first showing
they have gradually risen above ground. Now the first, free from earthly mass, presents itself freely to human sight. The other two still follow but advance
toward emergence every year. O wonderful mystery of the Deity, manifesting the purity of buried limbs to the world by emerging from the pavement and preparing
them for resurrection—not to be given to the undying worm, but made equal to the sun’s bright light and glorified into conformity with the Lord’s body! These
tombs are within the aforementioned boundary at the village of Ator.

## 52

**[052]** Theomastus, wonderful in holiness according to the interpretation of his name, is said to have been bishop of Momoï. Removed from that city for I know
not what reason, he sought the town of Poitiers. Persevering in good confession, he ended this present life there. His reward in heaven is shown at his tomb;
power coming from the sepulcher reveals that he inhabits paradise. What the Lord Jesus Christ says to Martha in the Gospel is truly shown in him: “He who
believes in me, though he die, lives. And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die.” His tomb above ground stands before the very forecourt of
blessed Hilary. Dust scraped from it by many and drunk so heals toothache and fevers that the drinker marvels at the effect. This blessing is so continually
sought that the stone coffin already appears pierced through in one place.

## 53

**[053]** Within the boundary of Poitiers adjoining Nantes—that is, in the village of Retz—rests Lupianus, who departed in white baptismal robes. He is said to
have received the gift of baptism from blessed Bishop Hilary but soon, as I said, departed the body. Such grace was attributed to him by God, giver of all good
things, that at his tomb the blind merit sight, the paralytic walking, and the mute speech.

## 54

**[054]** Melanius, bishop of Rennes, after innumerable signs of miracles and continually intent on heaven, shone forth from the world. Christians raised a
wonderful structure of height over his tomb. At one time, through the instigation of the malign one who always opposes good works, it caught fire. A linen cloth
covered the confessor’s holy tomb. As the mass of timbers was consumed by prevailing flame, tiles fell with fastenings and the rest of the roof apparatus. One
beam with a flaming head, propelled by the collapse’s force, fell upon the saint’s tomb. It could not only have ignited the cloth but crushed it between itself
and the tombstone. An immense multitude of coals also fell. Other veils hanging from walls or doors were burned at the first blast of flame. This cloth was not
only unburned but not even discolored at its surface by the fire. When the conflagration ended, the people entered with loud wailing and hurried to the bishop’s
tomb, to receive new joys amid weeping and tears. Removing the burning timbers above the tomb and shaking off the coals, they took hold of the tomb veil and all
marveled that it was unharmed.

## 55

**[055]** Victurius, bishop of Le Mans, often declared himself through great miracles. They say that once when the city was being consumed by fire and violent
balls of flame were driven here and there by the wind, he, like a good shepherd, could not bear the Church’s folds being devastated by Satan’s snare. He offered
himself against the whirlwind, raised his hand, and made the sign of the cross against it. The whole conflagration immediately ceased. The liberated city
thanked its shepherd for not allowing its property to be devoured by the imminent fire. The sick are also often healed at his tomb.

## 56

**[056]** Martin, abbot of Saintes and, as they say, a disciple of my Martin, rests in peace in the monastery he built after his master’s teachings in a village
of that city. A rustic brought contracted hands to his tomb and carried them back healthy. Another, unable to walk because fever had burned out the moisture of
his nerves and twisted his knees, prostrated himself at the holy tomb. Taking new strength as dryness was removed, he was raised unharmed and served there for
many years afterward. When Bishop Palladius could not move his tomb with many men, the confessor’s help assisted him. With five abbots he moved it and arranged
it as he wished.

## 57

**[057]** Bishop Bibianus also rests in a suburb of this city. The book already written about his life recounts the mass of his miracles. Now that he has been
entreated, he frequently grants health to the sick. Concerning such great miracles, I presume to relate at least one. A woman whose hands had withered and whose
wounded nails, with contracted sinews, had lost the power of work, devoutly prostrated herself at the blessed man’s tomb. After praying, with the cords of her
fingers loosened and her hands restored, she was found worthy to raise them in thanksgiving to the Lord.

## 58

**[058]** Bishop Troianus of this same city, joined to heaven, lies near his tomb. This priest is said to have possessed great power. Once, while during the
dark hours of night he was going around the holy places then surrounding the city with only one subdeacon as companion, a great globe of light appeared to him,
as though descending from heaven. When the man of God understood what was happening, he told his companion, “Do not follow at all until I call you.” The
subdeacon fell to the ground and watched from not far away to see what miracle God’s servant would perform; they were standing in a public field. As the light
approached, the bishop ran to meet it, humbled himself to the ground, and said, “Bless me, I beg you, blessed bishop.” The one who had come answered, “You bless
me, Troianus, priest of God.” They kissed, prayed, and spoke together for a very long time. The astonished subdeacon watched and saw the light that had appeared
return by the same way it had come. The bishop called the subdeacon to him and said, “Come now, so that we may complete the journey we began to visit the holy
places.” Trembling, the subdeacon said, “I beg you, lord, do not despise my lowliness, but tell me what you saw; for I perceived that something divine had
occurred.” He replied, “I will tell you, but you must tell no one. Know that on whatever day you make this public, you will depart from this world. I saw Saint
Martin of Tours, and he spoke with me. Take care, therefore, not to dare divulge God’s secrets to anyone.” In due course the bishop completed the course of this
life and died. The subdeacon, full of days and distressed that Saint Troianus’s miracle should remain hidden, summoned the bishop, clergy, and senior citizens.
He recounted in order everything he had heard from the saint and how he had seen the mystery of the light, which most clearly revealed Troianus’s faith and
Martin’s glory, concealing nothing. He added, “And so that you may know that what I say is true, when my speech ends, I will end my life.” Having said this, he
immediately closed his eyes and died, to the astonishment of those standing by. As I have said, blessed Bishop Troianus possessed great power and was honored
among all the citizens of his city. It is reported that while he lived, whenever he put on a new cloak, as was customary, before going out to tour his diocese,
different people tore away its fringes; everyone considered beneficial whatever he could snatch from him. Buried in the earth, he reveals by many miracles that
he lives in heaven. The possessed, those suffering chills, and other sick people often pray at his tomb and depart restored to health.

## 59

**[059]** Not far from this confessor’s church was a small oratory. In a corner where an arch began stood a large stone coffin, in which two people were said to
have been buried, namely a bridegroom and a bride. Clothed in white after baptism, they had departed from the world. Ancient tradition also asserted that they
were of the family of Saint Hilary of Poitiers. Situated in such a place, this tomb not only blocked the passage of those entering but also, because it stood
against the wall, prevented repairs to that wall, which had been soaked by rainwater. For this reason Bishop Palladius of the city, who was descended from the
family of the once wealthy Palladius, strove with the greatest zeal to remove it. More than three hundred men assembled; he tried to drag it with ropes and push
it with levers, and stones had already been set on which the coffin was to rest. All the strength of those pulling was exerted, but they could not move the
tomb. Every brow was drenched with sweat, yet the heavy work was not accomplished. Voices of encouragement cried, “Come on, heave, pull the rope!” but the tomb
did not move at all. Why say more? Everyone grew weary, and when night intervened, all sought rest. When the darkness of night had passed and a new morning
dawned, the bishop, anxious in thought, again asked his men to proceed to the oratory, going ahead of them all. Entering, he found the coffin resting firmly
upon the very stones he had arranged. Marveling, he glorified the Lord, who by powerful might accomplished what human hands could not. The names of these two,
however, have been revealed to no one.

## 60

**[060]** Nicetius the confessor also ended his life in the city of Lyon, a man of complete holiness, most chaste conduct, and outstanding charity. His
almsgiving and kindnesses can neither be fully discovered nor narrated by me. After he sent his blessed spirit ahead to heaven, he was placed on a bier and
carried to the basilica in which he was buried. Behold, a little boy afflicted by long-standing blindness followed among the mourners, supported by someone
helping him. As he walked, a voice came secretly into his ear, saying, “Approach the bier, and when you have gone beneath it, you will immediately receive your
sight.” He asked the person leading him who it was that spoke these words in his ears. The man denied seeing anyone speaking to him. When the voice struck his
ears a second and third time, the boy understood that something extraordinary was to occur and asked to be led to the bier. Approaching and slipping through the
crowd of white-clad deacons, he entered where he had been commanded. As soon as he began to invoke the saint’s name, his eyes were opened and he received the
light. Afterward the boy served constantly in the basilica at the saint’s tomb, lighting the lamps. But certain leading citizens oppressed and harassed him so
severely that he could not even obtain nourishment. When he repeatedly pleaded about this at the blessed tomb, the saint appeared to him in a vision and said,
“Go to King Guntram and carefully explain to him what you suffer. He will provide you with clothing and food and rescue you from the hand of your enemies.”
Strengthened by this admonition, the boy went to the king and obtained what the saint had suggested. Many miracles are still granted at the blessed confessor’s
tomb through Christ’s guidance. There the chains of the wretched are broken, the blind are illuminated, demons are put to flight, paralytics are restored to
health, and those suffering attacks of fever are freed. Miracles are shown so frequently in that place that it would take very long to write them in order.
Nevertheless, a trustworthy man told me that four blind people had been illuminated there a few days earlier, and he recently saw in good health a man whom he
had once known to be lame.

## 61

**[061]** Once, when I had walked out to meet the aforesaid bishop and was visiting the holy places around the city of Lyon, the man leading us invited us to
pray in the crypt of blessed Helius, saying, “A great bishop rests in this place.” After praying, as I admired the saint’s tomb and silently considered asking
about his merits, I saw written on the door an account of how a violator of the tomb had stripped the lifeless corpse. When I inquired whether the account
painted on the door was true, a man told me this story: “Saint Helius was bishop in this city during the time of the pagans, and when he died the faithful
buried him. On the following night a pagan came, turned back the stone covering the coffin, raised the saint’s body against himself, and tried to strip it. But
Helius extended his arms, clasped the man tightly, and held him powerfully. Until morning, while the people waited, he held the wretch in his arms as though
bound with straps. The local judge ordered the tomb violator to be pulled away and condemned to the lawful penalty, but the saint would not release him. Then
the judge understood the dead man’s will, promised to spare his life, and the man was released and restored unharmed.” O truly holy vengeance mixed with mercy!
He restrained the man to rebuke him, but did not permit the one he had already corrected to be handed over to punishment.

## 62

**[062]** When the daughter of the Roman emperor Leo was tormented by an unclean spirit and taken around the holy places, the evil spirit repeatedly cried, “I
will not leave here unless the archdeacon of Lyon comes; unless he drives me from this little vessel I have acquired, I will never depart.” Hearing this, the
emperor sent his men to Gaul. They found the archdeacon and humbly begged him to accompany them to Rome to visit the girl. He refused, protesting that he was
unworthy to be one through whom Christ would show miracles, but, advised by his bishop, he set out with the envoys. Coming to the emperor, he was received with
honor. When he heard of the girl’s affliction, he went to the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. There, continuing a three-day fast with vigils and prayers,
on the fourth day he drove the unclean spirit from the girl’s body through the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ and the standard of the cross. After she was
healed, the emperor offered him three hundred pounds of gold. But that man of loftier spirit rejected perishable riches as nothing and said, “If you wish to
enrich me with your gifts, grant what will benefit the whole city. Remit to the people the tax around the city walls at the third milestone, which is owed to
your treasury. This kindness will benefit both our souls. I have no need of your gold; distribute it to the poor for your own and your family’s good fortune.”
The emperor did not refuse: he distributed the gold to the poor and granted the city the requested tax. To this day no public taxes are paid around the walls of
that city at the third milestone. After the blessed archdeacon departed, the emperor told his men, “If this man loves God more than money, the church served by
such a minister deserves to be adorned with my gifts.” He ordered a case for enclosing the holy Gospels, a paten, and a chalice to be made of pure gold and
precious stones. When these had been completed with wonderful workmanship, he sent them to the church by a trusted man. While crossing the Alps, the messenger
carrying them stopped at a goldsmith’s house. When the craftsman asked what business he was conducting, the messenger revealed it privately and simply. The
goldsmith said, “If you follow my advice, this affair could bring us great profit.” Instigated by the devil, the messenger was seduced. As the common saying
among rustics has it, minds often unite when gold gapes before them and the deceits of trickery are introduced; he immediately agreed to the plan. The deceiver
made similar vessels of silver so that they would appear to be nothing but purest gold, and very carefully fastened with rivets the work overlaid with gems and
gold wire. He did not break up the chalice, however, because its ornaments were firmly soldered. The bearer arrived at Lyon with this fraud, presented the
gifts, and was rewarded by the bishop. Returning to his accomplice, he demanded the gold taken from the vessels. The craftsman declared that it was not yet all
ready but promised to hand it over that very night. After dinner, as they sat together in the cell where he had done the work, it was suddenly shaken by an
earthquake and collapsed upon them. The earth split beneath their feet and swallowed them together with the money; living and crying out, they descended into
hell. Thus God swiftly avenged the fraud against his church. I myself have very often seen these vessels in the church of Lyon. Let this be a lesson to the
people: let no one attempt to seize or steal church property, for he will see God’s judgment swiftly threatening him.

## 63

**[063]** In a suburb outside the walls of this city rests a woman who is said to have picked up blessed martyr Epipodius’s shoe, which fell from his foot as he
was led to martyrdom. Those suffering chills and other sick people are often healed at her tomb. They scrape dust from the tomb itself, drink it, and depart in
good health.

## 64

**[064]** They say that two people lived in this city, a man and his wife, powerful members of a senatorial family. Dying childless, they left the church as
their heir. The husband died first and was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary. His wife lived at this church for an entire year, devoting herself to constant
prayer, celebrating the solemn rites of Mass daily, and offering an oblation in memory of her husband. She did not doubt the Lord’s mercy, believing that the
dead man would have rest on the day when she offered the oblation for his soul to the Lord. She always provided a sextarius of Gaza wine in the sanctuary of the
holy basilica. But a wicked subdeacon reserved the Gaza wine for his own appetite and offered the strongest vinegar in the chalice, since the woman did not
always come forward to receive communion. When God chose to reveal this fraud, the husband appeared to his wife and said, “Alas, alas, sweetest wife, to what
has my labor in the world come, that vinegar is now offered for me?” She answered, “Truly, never forgetting your love, I have always offered the finest Gaza
wine for your rest in the sanctuary of my God.” Waking, she marveled at the vision and did not consign it to oblivion. She rose for matins as usual. When the
office was finished and Mass celebrated, she approached the saving cup. She drew such burning vinegar from the chalice that she thought her teeth would be
knocked out if she delayed swallowing the draft. Then she rebuked the subdeacon, and what had been wickedly stolen was corrected. Nor do I think this miracle
occurred without the merit of a good work.

## 65

**[065]** Bishop Memmius stands as the special patron of the city of Châlons. While still dwelling in his mortal body, he is said to have raised a dead man. At
his tomb I have often seen the broken chains and fetters of the wretched, and I myself have experienced his power. Once, while I was staying in that city, one
of my boys was seized by fever, tormented by vomiting, and unable to bear food or drink. Great anxiety consumed me because the boy’s illness would delay my
journey. Without delay I went to the saint’s basilica, prostrated myself at his tomb for the boy, and prayed with flowing tears that he who had often brought
merciful consolation to prisoners in distress by breaking their fetters would minister the cooling remedy of healing to this feverish boy. Wonderful to tell!
The sick boy was visited by the saint’s power that very night and rose from his little bed healed in the morning.

## 66

**[066]** No one is unaware that Bishop Lupus is buried in the city of Troyes in Champagne. A servant of a certain Maurus fled to his basilica after committing
an offense through negligence. His master, gnashing his teeth, pursued his tracks and entered the basilica. Without prostrating himself in prayer, he began to
pour out blasphemies against the saint, saying, “So, Lupus, will you take away my servant, and because of you will I not be allowed to exact the punishment due
him?” Laying hold of the servant, he began to drag him away, saying, “Let not this Lupus put forth his hand from the tomb today to rescue you from my hands.” As
the wretch spoke, the tongue that had poured out blasphemies against the saint was immediately bound by divine power. The man was changed and began to rave
throughout the whole church, bellowing like cattle and uttering no human speech. When this was reported to his household, they seized him and led him home. His
wife placed many gifts in the basilica, but on the third day he ended his life in severe torment. After his death the woman took back what she had given; the
servant, however, remained free.

## 67

**[067]** A certain religious man named Aventinus served this bishop. After Lupus’s death, captives fled to him for refuge. Aventinus offered their master a
price for them, but the master bound himself by an oath and said, “I will never accept it except in my own district.” He gave his right hand in pledge that if
Aventinus sent the money, he would immediately free the captives from the bond of servitude. The price was sent, but the master forgot his pledge. While he
pretended not to free the captives, he himself was bound. The tip of the finger on the hand that had given the pledge immediately began to hurt severely. Then
the pain gradually increased and spread through his hand and entire arm. Why say more? His arm was cut off at the elbow joint and fell away, and he breathed his
last. Afterward his wife wished to recall the captives to servitude, but she was struck by a pain in the head and followed her husband. Thus they remained
perpetually free without the protection of any written charter.

## 68

**[068]** The city of Embrun also has its own patron, Bishop Marcellinus, through whom Christ worked many miracles while he still dwelt in the body. He is said
to have made a font for baptism in which water springs up divinely at the Lord’s Nativity and at the Lord’s Supper. Water from it is also carried to another
font established by ancient custom for baptisms, but it does not accumulate there like the springs in Spain I described above. A lamp continually gives light at
this saint’s tomb; once kindled, it lasts through many nights without any additional oil. It often happens that when extinguished by the wind, it is divinely
kindled again. The sick often receive remedies from its oil.

## 69

**[069]** Marcellus, bishop of the city of Die, was also a man of magnificent holiness. At his tomb likewise a lamp, once kindled, usually shines for a long
time. From its oil the Lord’s power provides medicine for the sick.

## 70

**[070]** The renowned athlete Mitrias was granted to the people of Agen. According to the history of his deeds, he was a man of magnificent holiness in the
body; though a servant by condition, he was free in righteousness. As those who read the account of his contest relate, when he had completed the course of good
works, he departed from the world as a victor, often showing by manifest miracles that he dwells in heaven. Once, when Bishop Franco governed the church of this
town, Childeric, who then held first place with King Sigibert, laid claim to one of its estates, asserting that the church of Agen held it unjustly. The bishop
was quickly summoned. After giving sureties, he appeared before the king, crying out and begging the king to turn his presence away from hearing this case, lest
he be condemned by the heavenly judgment. He added, “For I know the power of the blessed man Mitrias, who swiftly inflicts vengeance upon anyone who attacks
him.” The assembled judges nevertheless heard the case. Childeric rose, heaped reproaches and accusations upon the bishop, and alleged that he wrongfully
retained fiscal property owed to the royal domains. He ordered the bishop to be forcibly removed from the judgment, and when this had been done, the estate was
taken away by the judgment of those present and the bishop was fined three hundred gold pieces. Everyone favored Childeric, and no one dared decide against his
will unless it pleased him. Condemned and despoiled, the bishop returned to the city, prostrated himself in prayer before the saint’s tomb, said the opening of
a psalm, and declared, “No light will be kindled here and no chanting of psalms sung, most glorious saint, until you first avenge your servants upon their
enemies and restore to the holy church the property violently taken from you.” Speaking through tears, he threw thorn branches with sharp prickles upon the
tomb. Leaving, he closed the doors and placed similar branches at the entrance. Without delay the despoiler was seized by fever, took to his bed, loathed food
and drink, and continually sighed in his burning distress. If thirst from the fever’s heat came upon him, he drank only water and nothing else. Why say more? He
spent an entire year in this illness, but his perverse mind was not turned. Meanwhile all his hair and beard fell out, leaving his whole head so bare that you
would think he had long been buried and recently cast from his tomb after death. Afflicted by these and similar miseries, the wretch at last reflected, “I have
sinned by despoiling God’s church and injuring the holy bishop. Go now as quickly as possible, return the estate, and place six hundred gold pieces upon the
saint’s tomb. I have hope that restoring the property will bring healing to me in my sickness.” Hearing this, his men took the money and did as commanded. They
returned the land and placed the gold pieces on the tomb of God’s servant. But as soon as they had done so, Childeric breathed his last where he lay. By
acquiring an unjust possession, he gained the loss of his soul. The bishop obtained vengeance upon the church’s enemy, as he had foretold through the power of
God’s athlete.

## 71

**[071]** Aravatius, bishop of Maastricht, is remembered from the time of the Huns when they broke forth to invade Gaul. He is said to be buried beside the
bridge on the public road. Although snow falls around his tomb, it never moistens the marble placed over it. When those places are bound by the ice of extreme
cold and snow covers the ground to a depth of three or four feet, it does not touch the tomb at all. This shows that he was a true Israelite. For the Israelites
between the walls of water, the waters were not destruction but salvation; around this righteous man’s tomb, falling snow is not a cause of dampness but of
honor. You could see snowy mountains rising all around, yet not touching the boundary of the monument. I do not marvel that the earth is covered with snow, but
that the snow has not dared touch the place of the blessed tomb. The devotion and zeal of the faithful often built an oratory of smooth wooden boards, but it
was immediately either snatched away by the wind or collapsed of itself. I believe this happened until someone came who would build a worthy structure in honor
of the glorious bishop. In the course of time Bishop Monulfus arrived in this city and constructed, arranged, and adorned a great church in Aravatius’s honor.
His body was translated there with great zeal and veneration and is now mighty in great miracles.

## 72

**[072]** The cemetery at the city of Autun is called “cemetery” in the Gallic language because the corpses of many people have been buried there. Among them
are tombs of certain faithful souls worthy of God, as the frequent mystery of hidden psalmody reveals. It often appears to many that in that very place voices
render due thanksgiving to almighty God in a chorus of praise. I heard that two inhabitants of the place, intending to go around the holy places to pray, heard
the sound of people singing psalms in the basilica of Saint Stephen adjoining this cemetery. Marveling at the sweetness of the melody, they approached the
church door, supposing that certain religious persons were celebrating vigils. Entering and remaining long in prayer, they rose and beheld the choir of psalm
singers. No lamps shone throughout the church, yet they saw everything gleaming with its own radiance; they recognized none of the persons. Astonished and
struck with stupor, they were approached by one of the singers, who said, “You have done an accursed thing by presuming to be present while I render the secret
prayers to God. Depart therefore, and do not leave your houses, or else you will quickly migrate from this world.” One of them departed and went away; the
other, who remained in the place, migrated from the world not many days later.

## 73

**[073]** In this cemetery I saw the tomb of the great priest blessed Cassianus, scraped away by so many sick people that at that time it was thought to be
almost perforated. The sick wash themselves with dust from it and immediately feel its great power. Simplicius, who they say was bishop of this same city, is
also buried there. The savage madness of the people accused him of the crime of adultery.

## 74

**[074]** Since it is helpful to say something about these men, I must first speak of Saint Riticius, because he died earlier. He was born of most noble parents
and distinguished by intellectual acuteness. After adolescence he obtained a wife renowned for similar integrity of character, with whom he was united in the
continence of spiritual love, not in lust. Almsgiving abounded, vigils were celebrated, and God’s work was performed by them without ceasing. After a long time
the woman bowed her head upon her bed and spoke her last words into the blessed man’s ears: “I beg you, most devout brother, that after my departure, when the
time of your life has run its course, you be placed in the tomb where I am laid, so that one tomb’s companionship may hold those whom the love of a single
chastity preserved in one bed.” Having spoken thus, she wept and sent forth her spirit to heaven. Riticius was then chosen by the people for the bishopric of
the city of Autun. He showed himself so religious that the goodness of his character equaled the grace of his pontificate, and at the day of his death he
arrived through the various degrees of spiritual gifts at the fullness of perfect consummation. After he was washed and placed upon the bier, the attending
servants could not move it. Fixed in astonishment, they heard from an old man that the husband had sworn to his wife that the ample space of one tomb would
receive them both. As soon as this account was finished, the bier was lifted. Brought near the tomb, the bishop recovered his spirit and addressed his
companion: “Remember, sweetest wife, what you asked of me. Now receive your long-awaited brother and join my unpolluted limbs to yours; lust did not defile us,
but true chastity cleansed us.” As he spoke, the tomb was moved in a wonderful manner and the virgin’s bones gathered into one place. The blessed bishop,
received into the sleep of peace, was covered by this tomb’s lid. Cassianus, mentioned above, succeeded him; after Cassianus, Egemonius assumed the episcopal
throne.

## 75

**[075]** When Egemonius died, blessed Simplicius was placed over that church. He came from noble stock, was exceedingly rich in worldly wealth, and was married
to a most noble wife. Their life was most chaste, concealed from the world, known to God alone but unknown to mortals. Both were righteous and most ready in
sowing alms and enduring vigils. Meanwhile, because of his worldly rank, as I have said, Simplicius was chosen by the people when Egemonius died; he was
destined by God for the glory of chastity and holiness. After receiving the episcopal office, the blessed sister, who had previously been joined to her husband
not in lust but in chastity, did not allow herself to be removed from the bishop’s bed. In the same pure chastity with which she had formerly approached the bed
of her most chaste husband, she rested secure in the conscience of a holy mind, knowing that she could not be burned by the ardor of inciting fire. But the
demon’s savage envy stirs up shameful wars against God’s saints, and what it cannot destroy by its own instigation it attempts to defame with deceitful words.
Why say more? On the day of the Lord’s Nativity the citizens were stirred to scandal and rushed to the blessed virgin, saying, “It is incredible that a woman
joined to a man cannot be polluted, nor can a man joined to a woman’s limbs abstain from intercourse. Solomon’s proverbs say that no one touching pitch can
remain clean, nor can one carrying fire in his bosom avoid being burned. Therefore I see you lying in one bed; can I suspect anything except that you have
intercourse together?” Moved by these words, the most holy virgin approached the bishop, who possessed equal chastity. Repeating before all the people what she
had heard, she called a girl who, because of the winter’s severity, was holding a small brazier full of coals, as was customary. Spreading out her cloak, she
received the burning coals and held them for nearly an hour. Then she called the bishop and said, “Receive this gentle fire, as usual; it will not harm your
garments, so that these flames may show that the flames of lust are extinguished in me.” When the bishop received them, his garment was not harmed by the fire.
By this miracle the people, who had been unbelieving, believed in God, and within seven days more than a thousand people were reborn by the renewal of sacred
baptism. Receiving them, the church rejoicingly joined these soldiers to the heavenly kingdom.

## 76

**[076]** They also say that an image of Berecynthia existed in this city, as the history of the passion of the holy martyr Symphorian declares. When the people
were carrying it on a cart for the protection of their fields and vineyards in the wretched custom of paganism, the aforesaid Bishop Simplicius was present. Not
far away he watched them singing and dancing before this image. Sending up a groan to God over the people’s foolishness, he said, “I beg you, Lord, illuminate
this people’s eyes, so that they may know that the image of Berecynthia is nothing.” Making the sign of the cross against it, the image immediately fell to the
ground, and the animals pulling the wagon on which it was carried were fixed to the soil and could not move. The innumerable crowd was stupefied, and the whole
company cried out that the goddess had been injured. Victims were sacrificed and the animals beaten, but they could not move. Then four hundred men from that
foolish multitude assembled and said to one another, “If there is any divine power in the statue, let it rise of its own accord and command the oxen fixed to
the earth to proceed. Certainly, if it cannot move, it is clear that there is no divinity in it.” Approaching and sacrificing one of the animals, when they saw
that their goddess could not move at all, they abandoned the error of paganism, sought out the local bishop, and turned to the unity of the church. Recognizing
the greatness of the true God, they were consecrated by holy baptism.

## 77

**[077]** Since I explained in the preceding chapter how chastity adorns those who love God, I remember what I heard Felix of Nantes relate while I was
discussing these matters. He said that a bishop in his own city had a wife, but when he attained the honor of the priesthood, he set apart a little bed for
himself according to Catholic discipline. His wife took this very badly. She pressed him daily to rest with her in one bed, and when the bishop would not
consent to something so improper, which the decrees of the canons did not permit, one day she was inflamed with fury and said to herself, “I do not think my
husband’s rejection of my embrace in this way is without some guilty secret. I will go and see whether another woman lies with him, for whose love he despises
me.” She immediately entered the bishop’s bedroom and found him sleeping after midday. Approaching his bed, she saw a lamb of immense radiance resting upon his
breast. Terrified, she quickly withdrew from the holy man’s bed and never again sought to learn what the man full of God did in secret. She recognized most
clearly that what the Lord himself deigned to promise his faithful was fulfilled with God’s servants: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the
world.”

## 78

**[078]** Remigius, bishop of the city of Reims, who is said to have spent seventy years or more in the episcopate and by his prayer obtained the raising of a
dead girl’s body, often extends the grace of healing to the sick and very frequently stands as an avenger against despoilers. Not far from his basilica was a
field of fertile soil—the inhabitants call such fields olcas—which had been given to the holy basilica. One of the citizens seized it, despising the man who had
conferred it upon the holy place. Although the bishop and the local abbot repeatedly summoned him to return what he had unjustly seized, he disregarded their
words and stubbornly defended his plunder. In the end, business rather than devotion brought him to the city of Reims, and he hurried to the saint’s basilica.
The abbot again challenged him about seizing the field, but he gave no reasonable answer. When his business was finished, he mounted his horse and prepared to
return home, but the injury to the bishop obstructed his effort. Stricken with a flow of blood, he fell to the ground. The tongue that had said the field should
be taken was bound, the eyes that had coveted were closed, and the hands that had seized were contracted. Stammering and scarcely able to speak, he said, “Carry
me to the saint’s basilica and throw whatever gold I have upon his tomb, for I have sinned by taking away his property.” Seeing him come with gifts, the donor
of the field said, “I beg you, saint of God, do not look upon his gifts, which you have never been accustomed to accept. Do not, I pray, assist one who,
inflamed by greed, has become a wicked possessor of your property.” The saint did not delay hearing his poor servant’s voice. Although the man gave gifts, he
lost his life while returning home, and the church recovered its property. Nor should I remain silent about what happened when the bubonic plague devastated the
people of Germania Prima. When everyone was terrified by reports of this disaster, the people of Reims assembled at the saint’s tomb to ask for a fitting
remedy. With many wax candles and lamps kindled, they kept vigil through the whole night with heavenly hymns and psalms. In the morning they examined what was
still lacking to their prayer. With God revealing it, they discovered how, after prayer, the city’s defenses might be fortified by a still greater defense. They
took a cloth from the blessed tomb and arranged it in the manner of a bier. Kindling wax candles and candlesticks upon crosses, they raised their voices in song
and went around the city and its streets. They passed no dwelling without enclosing it in this circuit. Why say more? Not many days later the plague approached
this city’s boundaries. Yet advancing only as far as the place where the blessed pledge had gone, as though it saw a boundary established, it not only did not
dare enter but, repelled by this power, also abandoned the areas it had invaded at first.

## 79

**[079]** The city of Bourges first received the word of salvation from Saint Ursinus, who was ordained bishop by the disciples of the apostles and appointed in
Gaul; he first established and governed the church at Bourges. Departing from the world, he was given a burial place in a field among the other tombs of the
people. That people did not yet understand how to venerate the Lord’s bishops or show them due reverence. Thus, as earth accumulated and a vineyard was planted
above him, all memory of the city’s first bishop was erased, and until Probianus was appointed bishop of that city no one spoke of him. There was a certain man
named Agustus from the household of the late Bishop Desideratus. His hands and feet were so contracted that if he wished to go anywhere, he could support
himself only on his knees and elbows. Inspired by God, he built an oratory with the alms of devout people at the village of Brives in honor of the holy and most
blessed Bishop Martin. When he brought Martin’s relics into it, his limbs were immediately straightened and he was healed. Gathering a few monks, he lived under
monastic rule and devoted himself constantly to prayer. Subsequently summoned by the bishop, he was ordained abbot in the basilica of Saint Symphorian, which
the bishop had built before the wall of Bourges. He did not abandon the monks he had previously gathered but appointed a superior over them and governed both
communities. While he was staying at this basilica, Saint Ursinus appeared to him in a night vision and said, “Dig into the earth and seek my little body, for I
am Ursinus, the first bishop of this city.” He asked, “Where shall I go or where shall I seek your tomb, when I do not know where you are laid?” Ursinus took
his hand, led him to the place, and said, “My body lies beneath the roots of these vines.” Waking, the abbot told this to his bishop, but the bishop thought
little of what the priest said and made no effort to search. Meanwhile blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, arrived and was received by the bishop. After dinner,
when he had given himself to sleep in the ecclesiastical house, the saint appeared in a vision to both—the bishop and the abbot—led them to the place of the
tomb, and begged them to remove him from it. They awoke and met together for vigils in the basilica of Saint Symphorian. When matins was finished, the bishop
told the abbot what he had seen, and the abbot confessed that he had seen the same. On the following night they went there with only one cleric carrying a
candle and came to the indicated place. Digging deep, they found the tomb. When it was uncovered and the lid removed, they saw the holy body like that of a
sleeping man, not dissolved by any decay. Marveling, they replaced the lid and on an appointed day told the bishop what they had seen. He summoned the abbots
and clergy, and with honor and psalmody they raised the blessed tomb. Because the poles on which it was carried were very long, when they reached the portico
they could not turn them at the entrance to approach the church door without difficulty. Blessed Germanus raised his voice and said, “Holy priest of God, if it
is your will to enter this basilica, let me feel the relief of your assistance.” Immediately the weight was lost and the coffin became so light that, leaving
the poles, a few men carried in their hands what many had borne to that place. Thus, after Mass was celebrated, he was buried beside the altar while the people
rejoiced, and he subsequently manifested himself in many miracles.

## 80

**[080]** A certain hermit named Marianus lived in that same district. His only food was wild apples, unless someone occasionally brought him honey or he found
it in the woods. Although many people often visited him, once those seeking him could not find him. The men who had come searched for him and, discovering his
tracks, found the place where he had knelt to drink water from the river. Proceeding from there, they found him lying dead beneath an apple tree. It was
commonly reported among the people that he had fallen from the tree and died, but this is not clearly known, because no one reports having seen it. The men who
had come lifted him and brought him to the village of Evaunum. After washing him and clothing him in fitting garments, they buried him in the church and
celebrated the anniversary of his death every year. The people who assembled were often healed of illnesses. One of the neighbors prepared to roast grain that
had long been soaked in water, sprouted, and fermented, making a fire beneath woven twigs to produce a drink. One of his neighbors approached and said, “Why are
you occupied with this work, man? Do you not know that it is the festival of blessed Marianus?” He angrily answered, “Do you who say this think that a man who
fell from a tree because of the cravings of his gluttony was admitted to the company of angels and ought to be adored as a saint? It is better to do necessary
work at home than to honor such a saint.” Hearing this, the other departed and went with the rest to the saint’s basilica, leaving his neighbor working at home.
Without delay the wind rose, the house caught fire, and it was entirely burned; nothing of the man’s substance remained. Then globes of flame rose above the
other little dwellings situated around, and the fire consumed this man’s threshing floor, hedges, huts for pigs or animals, and everything else belonging to
him. Nothing remained to the wretch that had not been set alight. If anyone thinks this happened by chance, let him marvel that it harmed none of the
surrounding neighbors. What are you doing now, O crude rusticity, always murmuring against God and his friends, so that you acquire loss for yourself? Another
man’s oxen had been stolen by the malice of a thief. He found their tracks but lost them among water-filled paths and deep abysses of mud, and so fled to the
saint’s tomb. After praying, as he left the basilica he noticed a man coming along the public road, driving those oxen before him and following a horse
exhausted from the journey. The thief had wandered from the way and, as though made mad, was returning with disturbed mind to the very place from which he had
set out. Recognizing the oxen he had lost, the man recovered them and allowed the thief to depart without accusation, because he knew this had been granted to
him through Saint Marianus’s power: at the very hour when, full of faith, he had approached the tomb, he recovered what was lost. After these events, the people
of Bourges began to honor God’s confessor with more diligent care.

## 81

**[081]** In this territory also lived Eusicius, a man of miracles, who as a hermit had withdrawn from human companionship amid dense thickets of thorns and
loathed the gold and riches of this world like dung. Various people came to him with various illnesses, and infants whose throats had swollen were often brought
to him. Touching them with the gentlest handling, he would say, as though delighting in a spiritual jest, “This gullet deserves to be shaken by pains, since it
will not swallow.” Then, placing the sign of the cross in the name of the Trinity, he freed the sick throats from pain and swelling. His benefit was so
immediate for those with quartan fever that he merely gave them blessed water to drink and restored them to health at once. His clerics had two containers of
honey. When one of his neighbors, tormented by the burning of quartan fever, came to him, received his customary medicine, and was restored to health, he wished
to return home but saw those containers in a tree at a distance. Immediately inflamed by greed, described as the root of all evils, he planned to steal them
secretly. Finding an accomplice like himself, he went to the tree at night. He climbed it to hand the containers down to his companion, but behold, an old man
approached from another direction! Seeing him, the accomplice on the ground fled without telling his companion what to beware. The old man stood beneath the
tree and accepted in trust one container the thief handed down. When the thief wished to remove the other, the priest said, “Let that one suffice for now, my
son; reserve the other for the man who labored over it.” Terrified by the voice, the thief threw himself down. The old man seized him, led him to his cell, and
said, “Why, my son, do you follow when the devil leads? Did you not come to me yesterday and receive the Lord’s blessing? If you desired honey, you should have
asked me, and I would have given it to you freely, without any reproach or hindrance.” Rebuking him with many other words, he gave him a honeycomb and allowed
him to depart unharmed, saying, “Take care not to do this again, for theft is Satan’s money.” King Childebert came to this old man while setting out for Spain.
When he offered him fifty gold pieces, the old man said, “Why do you offer these to me? Give them to those who distribute them to the poor; I have no need of
them. It is enough for me to be found worthy to entreat the Lord for my sins.” He added, “Go, you will obtain victory and accomplish what you wish.” The king
distributed the gold to the poor and vowed that if the Lord in his grace brought him back from that journey, he would build a basilica in honor of God at the
place where the old man’s body would rest. He later fulfilled this vow.

## 82

**[082]** Maximus, bishop and confessor of Riez, often manifests himself to the inhabitants in many miracles. At his tomb not only are the blind illuminated,
but other kinds of diseases are also driven away by his powers. I will relate recent events I have learned. There was a little boy about three years old, still
dependent upon his mother’s breasts. Seized by fever while being carried in his mother’s hands, he became so weak that he could neither suck the breast nor take
any other food. While for three days he was gravely ill and carried in the arms of those who loved him, one of the servants said, “If only this little boy were
taken to blessed Maximus’s tomb! I trust in his merits that he could restore the child to his former health.” While he was being carried in their loving hands,
the gasping child breathed his last. Seeing this, his parents wept and cried out, then laid him before the tomb of blessed Maximus the confessor. Closing the
doors, they left the lifeless body. The night passed in lamentation. When another day had dawned and the doors of the sacred building were opened, they saw the
little child standing, pulling himself along by the rails of the tomb and trying to walk; he was not yet old enough to walk properly. His parents marveled and
rejoiced. His sorrowful mother joyfully took him up and restored him healthy to their home. I myself saw this boy when he had grown up, and he told me these
things.

## 83

**[083]** The blessed confessor Valerius, first bishop of the Couserans, revealed himself in this way. An oratory had first been built over him, but it
collapsed through neglect, and the place where he rested was consigned to oblivion. The inhabitants reported only that he had been buried before the holy altar.
When Bishop Theodore arrived, he enlarged the oratory and made it into a great basilica. Then, seeking the venerable man’s holy body, he found two tombs but did
not know which of them belonged to the bishop. Summoning the clergy, he celebrated vigils throughout the night, praying that the blessed confessor would show
him where he lay. He filled two ampullae with wine, placed one upon each tomb, and said, “The one in which the Falernian wine is increased will plainly be the
burial place of Bishop Valerius.” At daylight he left the basilica, secured the doors with seals, and went to sleep. Rising at the third hour, he came with
clergy and people to the holy basilica and opened the doors. He found one ampulla containing only a little wine, while the other overflowed from its open mouth
to such an extent that it washed the entire monument of the blessed bishop. By this the bishop recognized Valerius’s tomb. Wishing to know still more clearly,
he uncovered the monument, removed the lid, and found the venerable body entirely intact. No hair or beard had fallen away, and nothing corrupt or foul appeared
on the skin. Everything was unharmed, as though recently buried, and so great a fragrance of sweetness wafted from the tomb that no one doubted God’s friend
rested there. Laurel leaves were spread beneath him. Taking some, the bishop provided medicine to many sick people. He also took relics from Valerius’s
garments, covered the tomb again, and thereafter honored the venerable bishop, subsequently witnessing many miracles through these pledges.

## 84

**[084]** The most blessed Silvester governed the church of Chalon. In the forty-second year of his priestly ministry, full of days and miracles, he migrated to
the Lord. He had a little bed woven with fine cords. When sick people suffering from quartan or various other fevers were repeatedly placed beneath it, they
were immediately healed by divinely imparted power. For this reason the little bed was carried into the church’s sanctuary and is brilliant with similar power.
Many people, as I have seen with my own eyes, cut particles from its cord and carried them far away. Placing these upon the sick, they beheld the benefit of
healing come upon them. My mother cut off a particle and had it hung around the neck of a girl feverish with chills; the disease was immediately suppressed, and
she saw the girl healthy.

## 85

**[085]** A priest named Desideratus also lived in this city. I saw him at the monastery of Gurthon, a man magnificent in holiness, who by praying often ended
chills, toothaches, and other diseases. He was not entirely enclosed—that is, he did not leave his cell, but anyone who wished could see him in the cell. As I
have said, distinguished by outstanding miracles, he shone forth from the world. Hearing this, blessed Bishop Agricola sent his archdeacon to carry the blessed
man to the city cemetery, but because the monks resisted, he did not fulfill his command. Afterward, when a suburban priest had built a hospice for lepers, the
bishop assembled the abbots and all the clergy in its basilica, translated the blessed body, and with the greatest zeal buried it in the aforementioned
basilica. Desideratus now shows by great miracles that he lives with Christ.

## 86

**[086]** Sequanus, abbot in the territory of Langres, was also a man of great power. While living he often freed people from the bond of diabolical
entanglement, and after his death he allowed those bound with prison chains to depart free through his merits at his tomb. King Guntram lost a horn that had
been stolen; by its sound he had been accustomed either to gather his Molossian hounds or to put to flight herds of horned animals in the woods. This affair
threw many into chains and deprived some of their property. Three of these men sought the aforementioned confessor’s monument. When the king learned of it, he
ordered them bound with chains and fetters, and this was done. At midnight a light brighter than human light arose in the basilica. The bolts of the iron
fetters sprang apart, the links of the chains were broken, and the prisoners were released. Hearing this, the terrified king quickly granted them the power of
free decision.

## 87

**[087]** Marcellus, bishop of the city of Paris, who once drove an immense serpent from that town, as is read in his life, now rests in a village of that same
city. Priest Ragnimod, who is now bishop of that town, came to Marcellus’s tomb with quartan fever and lay down there. He devoted the whole day to fasting and
prayer, and when evening came he fell asleep. Waking from sleep a little later, he rose from the tomb healed.

## 88

**[088]** When King Chilperic entered the city of Paris, on the day following the king’s entry a paralytic who had been sitting in the portico of the basilica
of Saint Vincent, where blessed Germanus rests in the body, was made straight. In the morning, while the people waited, he gave thanks to the blessed bishop.
There the steps of paralytics and the sight of the blind are often restored by the saint’s power, and his festival rarely arrives without his power being shown
there.

## 89

**[089]** Saint Genevieve is also buried there in the basilica of the Holy Apostles. While in the body she prevailed so greatly in power that she raised a dead
person. Petitions made at her tomb often obtain assistance, and the fevers of those suffering chills are very frequently extinguished by her power.

## 90

**[090]** Blessed Lusor, son of the late senator Leucadius, rests in the village of Déols in the territory of Bourges. He is said to have departed from the
world in white baptismal garments. Placed in a crypt above the pavement, he has a tomb wonderfully carved from marble. Once Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris,
celebrated vigils at this tomb, keeping near at hand a prayer desk on which he could bend his knees when necessity compelled. During one night of vigils, while
David’s psalms and readings were being chanted, the clergy, weary from standing, supported themselves on the saint’s tomb with their elbows fixed, as though for
some relief. The blessed confessor’s tomb immediately trembled and by this palpable vibration declared that an injury was being inflicted upon it. Bishop
Germanus, terrified, ordered the drowsy clerics removed, saying, “Stand far away from the tomb, you sluggish men, lest annoyance be inflicted upon God’s saint.”
When they were removed, the trembling ceased. Nor should I omit that this same blessed Lusor appeared in a vision to a poor man and ordered him to clean the
little room where, they say, Lusor had spent the cries of his infancy. When the poor man, though admonished twice, delayed obeying, Lusor appeared a third time
and said, “If you do what I command, you will receive one triens for your obedient service.” The man arose, swept the little room clean, washed it with water,
and sprinkled it with herbs. He stood astonished, awaiting the promised reward, until by God’s direction he noticed a triens shining on the pavement. Joyfully
gathering it, he departed.

## 91

**[091]** Saint Maximinus also dwells in a suburb of the city of Trier, a great advocate with the Lord for that people; glorious miracles are often seen at his
tomb. In the time of King Theudebert, a priest named Arboast was litigating against a certain Frank in the king’s presence. While this was happening, the king
was visiting the city’s holy places in its villages for prayer. Seeing that the priest’s prosecution was cunning, the king turned to him and said, “If what you
are pursuing is true, confirm it by an oath upon Bishop Maximinus’s tomb!” The priest answered, “I dare do what you command.” Immediately placing his hands upon
the holy tomb, he said, “May I be crushed by this saint’s power if I speak anything false in the case my prosecution maintains against this Frank.” The
barbarian raged as though furious against God’s saint, and they left the basilica. As they proceeded along the road together, the priest suddenly slipped, fell
headlong to the ground, and died. Thereafter the barbarian praised the saint’s power, which he had previously disparaged. Likewise, when the archdeacon of that
city was accused by Bishop Nicetius of adultery, he sought to clear himself by an oath at this saint’s tomb. Entering the crypt’s first threshold, he stood
still as though stupefied. Descending the steps, he came to another door. When he wished to approach the third, he was immediately seized by fever. Not daring
to take another step and placed in danger of death, he confessed the crime of which he was accused and begged the people to ask for the assistance of the holy
bishop or of his own bishop on his behalf. As soon as he confessed, he was delivered from the fever’s attack and received back into his bishop’s charity.

## 92

**[092]** Nicetius, bishop of this same city, as I said above, shone with the merit of almsgiving, charity, and complete holiness while he dwelt in the body.
Departing from the world, he was buried at the basilica of his predecessor Saint Maximinus. At his tomb the chains of prisoners are now broken; those suffering
the attack of diabolical possession are freed when demons are expelled; and the eyes of the blind are often filled with light when darkness is removed. What
shall I say about perjuries? If anyone dares utter a false oath there, he is immediately corrected by divine vengeance. Nor does anyone whose conscience
torments him and who knows himself guilty dare even to speak of presuming to discharge an oath there.

## 93

**[093]** The glorious confessor Medard rests near the city of Soissons. At his tomb I have often seen the broken fetters of the wretched. After the book of his
miracles had been written, a woman with a disabled hand devoutly sought the blessed bishop’s protection. With undivided faith she celebrated vigils with the
rest, trusting that the power that removed the chains of the unfortunate could dissolve the moisture binding her hand. While Mass was being celebrated, the dry
bonds of her sinews were loosened. Giving thanks to the confessor, she approached the holy altar and received the grace of blessing in good health. Before the
church was built, a little cell woven of small shrubs stood over the saint’s tomb; when the church was dedicated, this was removed. It is fitting to relate
something great concerning that wood’s slenderness. Small, slightly sharpened sticks often made from it brought remedies for toothache. Hearing this, Charimer,
who is now King Childebert’s referendary, sought the saint’s basilica while suffering this pain, hoping to receive medicine from the wood through the saint’s
power. Arriving, he found the door barred. Trusting that the blessed man’s power was present everywhere, he drew his knife and cut a small stick from the door.
As soon as it touched his teeth, the harmful pain departed. I also possess his staff, from which the sick have often experienced remedies.

## 94

**[094]** The confessor Albinus, whose life was recently written by the priest Fortunatus, likewise obtains the manifestation of his miracles at his tomb
through the merit imparted to him. The day of his festival had arrived. A paralytic, disabled in every limb, had been carried on a wagon and sat before the
window of the apse where the holy body is enclosed. Falling asleep, he saw a man approach and say, “How long will you sleep and not desire to be healed?” He
answered, “If only I might deserve to be healed!” The man said, “When you hear the signal sound for the office of the third hour, rise immediately and enter the
basilica to which you have come. At that very hour blessed Martin will enter the basilica with his fellow citizen Albinus so that, after praying, the man of
Tours may proceed to Martin’s festival. If you are present at that moment, you will be healed.” Without delay, when the signal sounded, the paralytic approached
the saint’s tomb. When the clergy began singing the praise of David’s song, a fragrance of sweetness entered the saint’s basilica, and the man’s feet were
straightened and he rose healed. A royal foster daughter testifies that this was seen not by a few but by many. Likewise, at the village of Crouzilles a woman
blind from birth invoked the saint’s name and was illuminated that very day.

## 95

**[095]** Hospitius, a great servant of God endowed with many miracles, lived in the region of Nice and departed from this world. When he was buried, a man
placed his hand beside the tomb, lifted a little dust, wrapped it in a coarse linen cloth, and carried it with him. Setting out the next day, he found on the
shore a ship preparing to go to Marseille, but he wished to go to the monastery of Lérins. The men who owned the ship were descended from Jewish stock. For this
reason the man did not wish to tell the sailors what he carried. After they had set out and come opposite the monastery of Lérins, the ship stopped in the
middle of the sea; although the winds blew, it did not move in any direction. While the Jews wondered what this meant, the man revealed the truth: “I have
relics of blessed Hospitius with me and now wish to go to Lérins, which I feared to tell you. Now I know that your ship is held back by his power; it cannot
move from here at all unless you consent to go where I have resolved.” Hearing this and moved with astonishment, the men changed the sails. With a favorable
wind blowing, they set the man down on the island of Lérins and freely went where they wished.

## 96

**[096]** Behold what great riches the poverty of the world gathers for its own, so that the Redeemer, who created all things from nothing, not only grants them
whatever they wish but even commands the elements themselves to serve them. I recall hearing some years ago that a certain man lived in the desert of a certain
region. When his brother came from nearby with ready devotion to seek him, he was received with full charity of spirit. They entered a very small hut, prayed,
and sat down. After speaking much about the word of God, the old man rose from his little seat, entered a small garden, and picked vegetables for food. Kindling
the hearth, he placed a wooden pot upon the fire, filled it with water and vegetables, and urged on the flames until it boiled so violently that it might have
been thought bronze. The visitor, moved with astonishment, asked what this meant. The old man answered, “I have now lived in this desert for many years and have
always prepared my food in this cauldron, at the Lord’s command, to refresh my frail little body.” When the food was cooked and due hymns rendered to God, both
were refreshed by the service of this little vessel. I heard this long ago. Recently I saw the abbot who named the man Ingenuus; he asserted that Ingenuus had
lived within the territory of Autun and that he had often eaten vegetables or meat cooked with him in this vessel. He confirmed with an oath that he had seen
the cauldron placed over the flames and boiling most vigorously, and that its bottom always remained so moist that it seemed continually wetted by someone.

## 97

**[097]** Avitus, abbot of the district of Chartres called the Perche, often foretold by the revelation of the Holy Spirit that the dissolution of his body was
imminent. Departing from the body, he was honorably buried at the city of Orléans, where faithful Christians built a church over him. After his death, when the
annual day of his assumption was being celebrated with the greatest honor, one citizen took a mattock and went to dig his vineyard while the others went to
witness the solemn rites of Mass. Rebuked by many for absenting himself from this festival, he refused to return, saying, “This man you honor was also a
laborer.” But when he entered the vineyard and opened the earth with the first stroke, his neck was immediately twisted and his face turned toward his back.
Trembling and weeping greatly while the people watched, he entered the saint’s basilica. A few days later, after praying constantly in that place, his neck was
straightened and he recovered.

## 98

**[098]** Cyprian, abbot of the town of Périgueux, was a man of magnificent holiness, through whom God deigned to work many miracles in this world. He
frequently restored disabled hands, gave walking to paralytics, restored sight to the blind, and returned three lepers anointed with oil to their former health.
Even now he often grants healing to the sick if they faithfully seek or entreat him at his tomb.

## 99

**[099]** The sick are also often healed at the tomb of Eparchius, recluse of the city of Angoulême. The fevers of those suffering chills and other afflictions
are extinguished through his merits. A blind man from the territory of Périgueux prostrated himself at that burial place and, after praying, was found worthy to
receive light. When a thief was discovered and handed over for punishment, the count of the aforementioned city of Angoulême ordered him condemned to the
gallows. Led to death, the thief began invoking this saint’s name. Brought to the post and praying upon the ground, he was left hanging from the gibbet. When
the monks learned of this, they prostrated themselves together at the saint’s tomb and prayed, “O holy confessor, if your life still remained in the world, you
could rescue this poor man from the hand of death, as you often freed those condemned to such punishment. Now I do not doubt your prayer: what you did while
living in the world, you can renew now that you are exalted in heaven.” When night came, the abbot sent a monk to the gallows. As the monk approached, the bonds
immediately broke and the man slipped to the ground. Supported by the monk, he was brought living to the monastery. After drinking a little wine, he recovered;
his life was obtained from the judge, and he departed free.

## 100

**[100]** After the passing of Felix, bishop of Bourges, a blind man received the light of his eyes at his tomb, which stood above the earth carved from Pharian
marble, and darkness was put to flight. The people recognized the friend of God whom, while he was in the body, they had not been able to know fully because
worldly darkness stood in the way. They began to frequent his threshold with constant prayers. Since, as I have said, the marble coffin was covered with a stone
of lesser value, the citizens’ discernment, and especially the bishop’s, covered the coffin with a better lid, namely Heraclean marble. When the lesser stone
was removed almost twelve years later, they found the blessed confessor’s body so unharmed that no dissolution appeared in the body and no decay in the
clothing. Everything was as intact as though it had been placed in the tomb at that very hour. Nor did the Lord’s mercy allow the rejected stone to remain
without glory. Many people scrape a little dust from it and drink it, and they are quickly freed from quartan, tertian, and daily fevers.

## 101

**[101]** Junianus was also a recluse within the territory of the city of Limoges. While living he showed many miracles to the people, and even now diseases are
often cured at his tomb. I have seen many, too numerous to count, who were brought there with blind eyes and received light, and paralytics who were made
straight. The people themselves bear witness today: when they receive healing, they immediately make themselves tributaries of that place and, as the yearly
cycle returns, pay tribute in gratitude for the health restored to them. Many of these appear to belong to the basilica of my bishop Saint Martin.

## 102

**[102]** Pelagia, mother of blessed Abbot Aredius, whom I mentioned above, was very religious. When afflicted by fevers and at the point of death, she asked
for her son and said, “I beg you, sweetest son, do not bury me before the fourth day, so that all the menservants and maidservants who come may see my little
body and none of those I most diligently nurtured may be deprived of my funeral rites.” Saying this, she breathed her last. Washed according to custom, she was
placed on a bier and carried into the church. On the fourth day, before she was buried, so great a fragrance of sweetness wafted from her body that everyone
marveled. At night a great globe of fire appeared, rising in the east and running through the circuit of heaven until it stood above the church where the dead
woman’s body lay. Sudden splendor covered the whole building so completely that they thought they were beholding midday. Immediately many possessed people cried
out, “Martin comes to Pelagia’s passing!” On the following Sunday, after she was buried, they placed a candle at her head and said, “I have little wax, and the
night is now long; when I rise for matins, then let this candle be lit.” Closing the door, they departed. When sleep was over, they entered the basilica and
found burning the candle they had left extinguished. Healings of the sick also often occur at this religious woman’s tomb.

## 103

**[103]** There was a tomb in a village of Paris, not far from the place where the church called Senior is said to stand, covered by no protective roof. On the
stone was written: HERE RESTS CRESCENTIA, A GIRL CONSECRATED TO GOD. No age could recall what merit she possessed or what she had done in the world. Recently a
cleric read this epitaph. Instigated by faith, people suspected that the virgin might have obtained some power with the divine majesty. While they remained in
this uncertainty, a man tormented by the heat of tertian fever with severe trembling scraped a little dust from the tomb and drank it. The trembling soon
subsided and he recovered. The report spread and often benefited many held by this illness. Subsequently the city watchman became gravely ill. The girl appeared
to him in a vision and said, “Go as quickly as possible and cover Crescentia the virgin’s tomb. This will help you, so that you are no longer tormented by the
disease that has seized you.” Trusting her, he sought lime, built an oratory over the tomb, and was immediately released from his illness. So that the virgin’s
power might be proclaimed with greater honors, a man from the city suffered such toothache that his jaw swelled and he could scarcely take even a little soft
food. Full of faith, he went to the tomb, sharpened a small stick at one end, as is customary for cleaning teeth, and placed it upon the young girl’s tomb. As
soon as he touched the aching tooth with it, all the pain was stupefied. Having received this proof, those tormented by such pain seek the aid of her power and
are quickly healed.

## 104

**[104]** Blessed Radegund, mentioned at the beginning of the book of martyrs, departed from this world after completing the labors of her life. Receiving news
of her passing, I went to the monastery she had established in the city of Poitiers. I found her lying on a bier, her holy face shining so that it surpassed the
beauty of lilies and roses. An immense multitude of nuns, about two hundred in number, stood around the bier. Converted by her preaching, they led holy lives;
according to worldly rank, not only did they come from senatorial families, but some from royal stock itself flourished in this form of religion. They stood
weeping and saying, “To whom will you leave me orphaned, holy mother? To whom will you commend me in my desolation? I left parents, possessions, and homeland
and followed you. To whom will you leave me except perpetual tears and never-ending grief? Until now this monastery was greater to me than the expanses of
estates or cities. Wherever I went, beholding your glorious face, there I found gold and silver; there I beheld flourishing vineyards and waving crops; there
were meadows blooming with varieties of different flowers. From you I plucked violets; you were my blushing rose and shining lily. Your words shone for me like
the sun and, like the moon, kindled the bright lamp of truth amid the darkness of my conscience. Now the whole earth is darkened for me, and the space of this
place is narrowed because I am not permitted to see your face. Alas for me, abandoned by my holy mother! Happy are those who departed from this world while you
survived! I know indeed that you are joined to the choirs of holy virgins and to God’s paradise, but although this consoles me, it is lamentable that I cannot
