Commotusque Malchus, cum stupore et lacrimis ait: 'Unum a vobis signum, si dignum ducitis, velim interrogare. Decius imperator, qui persecutus est christianos
in hac urbe, ubi est?' Marinus episcopus respondit: 'Non est in hac urbe, fili dilectissime, vir qui tempora Decii recolat; ante multos enim annos defunctus
est'.

## 9

**[009]** Haec audiens Malchus, conversus ad se, dixit episcopo: 'Putabam, me cum fratribus meis una tantum nocte dormisse; sed, ut cognosco, multorum annorum
super somnum nostrum curricula transierunt. Et nunc suscitavit me Dominus cum fratribus meis, ut cognoscat omne saeculum, quia fiet resurrectio mortuorum.
Sequimini ergo me, et ostendam vobis fratres meos, qui mecum resurrexerunt'. Tunc stupefactus episcopus, cum praefecto et omni populo sequentes Malchum,
venerunt ad speluncam. Narrante autem Malcho fratribus quae ei contigissent in urbe, ingressus episcopus, repperit scrinium duobus sigillis argenteis
praesignatum, egressusque foras, convocans multitudinem civitatis cum praefecto, aperuit sigilla et invenit duas tabulas plumbeas, in quibus scripta erat omnis
passio eorum, sicut supra retulimus, et cognoverunt, quia vera erant quae a Malcho dicebantur.

## 10

**[010]** Tone ingressi invenerunt beatos martyres in angulo speluncae sedentes, et erant facies eorum tamquam rosae florentes et sicut sol in virtute
fulgentes; nihil enim diminutum erat neque de vestimentis neque de corporibus eorum. Marinus autem episcopus cum praefecto procidit ante pedes eorum et adoravit
eos, et omnis populus glorificavit Deum, qui dignatus est tale miraculum ostendere servis suis. Sancti vero narraverunt episcopo et omni populo quae eis tempore
Decii accessissent. Episcopus vero cum praefecto miserunt nuntios ad Theodosium imperatorem, dicentes: 'Festina quantocius; potes, si vis, videre miraculum
magnum, quod manifestum est, tribuente Deo, temporibus tuis. Si enim veneris, cognosces, spem resurrectionis valde esse utilem iuxta sponsionem promissionis
euangelicae'.

## 11

**[011]** Haec audiens Theodosius imperator, surrexit cum laetitia, et extendens manum suam ad Deum, ait: 'Gratias ago tibi, domine Iesu Christe, sol iustitiae,
qui dignatus es tenebras mortalium tuae veritatis luce respergere; gratias tibi ago, qui non permisisti lucernam confessionis meae tetris assertionum
caliginibus obvelari'. Et haec dicens, ascensis equis, cum summa festinatione venit ad Ephesum. Episcopus autem cum praefecto et omni multitudine civitatis
exiit in occursum imperatoris. Ascendentibus autem illis omnibus, egressi sunt sancti martyres in obviam augusto, et factae sunt facies eorum tamquam sol in
virtute fulgentes; ceciditque augustus in terram et adoravit eos glorificans Deum. Et surgens, osculatus est eos ac flevit super collum uniuscuiusque eorum,
dicens: 'Sic video facies vestras, tamquam si videam dominum meum Iesum Christum, quando vocavit Lazarum de monumento; cui inmensas gratias· refero, quod non
fraudavit me spe resurrectionis'.

## 12

**[012]** Maximianus autem respondit: 'Scito', inquit, 'imperator, quia ad confirmandam fidem tuam nos Dominus resurgere iussit. Ergo iugiter et fidens in eum
cognosce, quia fiet resurrectio mortuorum, cum nos hodie videas poet resurrectionem tecum loqui atque enarrare magnalia Dei'. Multaque alia loquentes cum eo,
iterum prostrati in terram, obdormierunt, tradentes animas suas Regi inmortali Deoque omnipotenti. Haec audiens imperator, ruit super corpora eorum et flens
osculabatur eos, auferensque vestimenta sua, posuit super illos, mandans fieri loculos aureos, in quibus reconderentur. Sed in ea nocte apparuerunt ei sancti,
dicentes: 'Ne feceris, sed relinque nos super terram; de ea iterum suscitabit nos Dominus in die magno resurrectionis omnis carnis'. Tunc imperator fabricavit
super eos basilicam magnam et fecit ibi receptaculum pauperibus, imperans eos alere de publico. Convocatisque episcopis, celebravit festivitatem sanctorum, et
omnes glorificaverunt Deum, cui est in Trinitate perfecta honor et gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen. EXPLICIT PASSIO SANCTORUM MARTYRUM SEPTEM DORMIENTIUM
APUD EPHYSUM, TRANSLATA IN LATINUM PER GREGORIUM EPISCOPUM, INTERPRETANTE IOHANNE SYRO, QUAE OBSERVATUR 6. KAL. AUGUSTI.
# THE COURSE OF THE STARS

## SOURCE AND CONTROL

English translation prepared for this project from the Latin control text in MGH *Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum*, Volume 1, Part 2, *Miracula et opera minora*
(second edition, 1969). The full title is *De cursu stellarum ratio, qualiter ad officium implendum debeat observari*: an account of the course of the stars and
how it ought to be observed for fulfilling the office. All 47 numbered sections are included.

## SCENE AND CONTEXT

Gregory begins with the traditional seven human wonders, contrasts them with divine works in sea, soil, living things, fire, sun, moon, and stars, and then
turns from celestial observation to the practical scheduling of nocturns, cockcrow, and matins. The monthly directions occupy September through August. The
work’s stated purpose is liturgical observance, not prediction of private futures.

## KINSHIP AND SAME-NAME FENCE

The Hilary quoted on the springs of Grenoble in chapter 14 is not identified with Hilary of Poitiers solely because of the shared name. The Sigibert whose
approaching death is marked by a comet in chapter 34 is retained as the source’s King Sigibert without importing another Sigibert into the notice. Biblical,
classical, and contemporary authorities named by Gregory remain distinct voices in the text.

## RECENSION AND TEXT NOTE

The MGH control text contains 47 numbered sections. Gregory refers to painted figures for the star course, but no separate diagrams are present in this control
text; none have been invented. The compressed numerical notation of the lunar table in chapter 18 and the source’s month ordering are preserved rather than
silently modernized.

# ENGLISH TRANSLATION

## 1

**[001]** Many philosophers, devoting themselves to literary studies, wrote about seven wonders as being greater than the rest. It has pleased me to set down
some of these first and then mention others more admirable. Their forms or works are as follows.

## 2

**[002]** FIRST, therefore, I place Noah’s ark, whose construction the Lord himself commanded. Its length was three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and
its height thirty cubits. I read that the ark had two and three decks and that all its work was finished within a cubit. It had a window or door in its side.
Into it, from all the birds of heaven, beasts of the earth, and reptiles, kinds were preserved with eight human beings through the flood’s inundation for the
restoration of the world.

## 3

**[003]** SECOND I place Babylon, described by Orosius thus: visible on every side over a marvelous level plain, presenting the very pleasing appearance of a
camp, arranged in a square with equal walls. The strength and size of its walls are scarcely credible to relate: fifty cubits thick and four times as high. Its
circuit is encompassed by 470 stades. The wall is compacted of baked brick and poured bitumen. Along the wall’s face are one hundred bronze gates. At the wall’s
length along the summit of its parapets, defenders’ dwellings are equally arranged on both sides, and the space between admits four-horse chariots side by side.
Within are fourfold double houses, dwellings wonderful in their towering height. This was the first city founded after the restoration of the human race, by the
giant Nimrod.

## 4

**[004]** THIRD is Solomon’s temple, which was a wonder not so much for the magnitude of its construction as for its ornaments. He built the house’s interior
walls with cedar panels from the floor to the top of the walls and the ceiling, covered the interior with wood, and floored the house with fir boards. At the
temple’s rear he built cedar panels twenty cubits high from floor to ceiling and made the inner house of the oracle in the Holy of Holies. The temple before the
doors of the oracle was forty cubits long. The entire house was clothed within with cedar, having turned work, fashioned joints, and raised carvings. Everything
was covered with cedar boards, and no stone could appear in the wall. He made the oracle in the middle of the inner house to place the ark of the Lord’s
covenant there. The oracle was twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, and he covered and clothed it with purest gold; he also clothed the altar with cedar.
He covered the house before the altar with purest gold and fastened the plates with golden nails. Nothing in the temple was not covered with gold, and he
covered the oracle’s entire altar with gold. In the oracle he made two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high. One wing of a cherub was five cubits, so that
from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was ten cubits. The second cherub was also ten cubits, of equal measure. He placed the cherubim in the middle
of the inner temple and covered them with gold. He carved all the surrounding walls with various engravings and turning and made on them cherubim, palms, and
various figures as though projecting and emerging from the wall. He also covered the house’s floor with gold inside and outside. At the oracle’s entrance he
made small doors of olive wood, five square doorposts, and two doors of olive wood. He carved on them figures of cherubim and palms and very prominent relief
work and covered them with gold. For the temple’s entrance he made square doorposts of olive wood and two doors of fir wood on the other side. Each door was
double and closed by meeting the other. He carved cherubim, palms, and very prominent reliefs. He made many other admirable things there, which it would take
long to recount.

## 5

**[005]** FOURTH is the tomb of the Persian king, hollowed from a single amethyst stone, sculpted with wonderful workmanship and openwork, bearing on its
exterior projecting figures of human beings, beasts, and birds. It also has trees sculpted in relief with leaves and fruit.

## 6

**[006]** FIFTH is the colossal statue erected on the island of Rhodes, cast from bronze. Its height is so immense that scarcely anyone can throw a stone to its
head, and it is gilded. Many also say that a man could climb through its leg to its head if he had an opening by which to enter. They also assert that the
statue’s head can hold twenty-two measures of wheat.

## 7

**[007]** SIXTH is the theater at Heraclea made from a single mountain, so that everything is completed from one side: the exterior walls as well as the
interior arches, vaults, steps, and seats. Its entire work is completed from one stone and is clothed with Heraclean marble.

## 8

**[008]** SEVENTH is the lighthouse of Alexandria, constructed upon four crabs of marvelous magnitude. These could not have been small, since they support such
an immense weight of height and breadth. They say that if a man lay stretched out upon any one of a crab’s arms, he could not cover it. This lighthouse is
kindled at night with straw supplied at public expense, so that sailors wandering at night in wind or rain, if they cannot see the stars, may know in which
direction to steer their sails.

## 9

**[009]** Although some of these were constructed by God’s command and others by human invention, they were nevertheless founded by human beings. Some have
therefore fallen and others are near ruin. There are other things which almighty God himself renews in this world by his own work each day or displays after the
yearly cycle has passed. Some are shown in the abundance of a gift, such as the ocean’s movement and the fruits of the earth; others are produced as displays of
power, such as the sun, moon, stars, and phoenix. Some rebuke sinners and prefigure infernal fire, such as Etna and the spring of Grenoble. These are wonders
that grow old with no age, perish by no setting, and are diminished by no defect, until the Lord commands the world to be dissolved.

## 10

**[010]** FIRST of all, therefore, is the movement of the ocean sea, which daily expands so that advancing it fills the edge of the shore and receding again
provides a dry path. Then, as people walk over the dry ground, a copious multitude of fish and various shellfish is gathered. God prepared this first wonder for
the human race, both distinguished in wonder and suited to service.

## 11

**[011]** SECOND, similar to this, are grains of crops and fruits of trees. Seeds cast into the earth and covered in furrows rise to their heights when summer
comes. Adorned with foliage and ears, they are fattened within with milky substance. The Lord, the sower of spiritual teaching, changed this into a parable
about the growth of his words which he cast among the peoples, saying, “So is the word of God as when a man casts seed and rises night and day; the earth bears
fruit of itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.” The apostle Paul prefigured the resurrection by this reasoning, saying, “What
you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. So also is the resurrection of the dead: it is sown in weakness, it rises in power,” and so forth. The nature of
trees is similar and, I think, signifies the resurrection itself. In winter, stripped of leaves, they are regarded as dead; in spring they are adorned with
leaves and decorated with flowers, and in summer filled with fruit. Although this wonder employs that similitude, it nevertheless provides a present benefit to
the peoples, so that humanity may know it receives nourishment from him who created it from nothing.

## 12

**[012]** THIRD is what Lactantius relates about the phoenix. “It is,” he says, “large in body and beautiful in feathers, talons, and eyes. It is joined in
companionship with no other bird and joined in no marriage. It is clear that humans do not know its sex, whether male, female, or neither. After a thousand
years have passed, it seeks a place preeminent in height over all worldly places, where there is a place green with foliage enduring through spring and winter.
In its midst is a great spring, abundant in flow and distinguished for gentleness. On its shore a noble tree surpasses the grove’s other trees in height. At
this tree’s summit the bird constructs for itself a nest or tomb from different kinds of spices. Sitting in its midst, it draws fragrances with its mouth and
covers itself with them. Then it begins pouring out sweet songs in different melodies. Leaping from the nest, it immerses itself in the waters. After repeating
this three or four times, it climbs again upon the nest and once more draws over itself the fragrances it brought. When the sun shines, its first ray brings
fire to the bird; the nest catches and the whole bird is completely consumed. Then the burned ashes gather themselves and are formed into one mass in the
likeness of an egg. Rising again from this and resuming life, it is nourished; while featherless, no human being need feed it. Nourished only by heavenly dew,
it is recalled to its former appearance and proceeds restored in the same shape, feathers, and color as before its death.” This wonder strongly prefigures human
resurrection and shows how earthly humanity, reduced to dust, will be raised again from those very ashes when the trumpet sounds.

## 13

**[013]** FOURTH is Mount Etna on the island of Sicily, which seethes with living heat, vomits powerful flames, and terribly belches sulfur over the region.
Publius the Mantuan says of it in the third book of the Aeneid: “The harbor itself is huge and unmoved by the winds’ approach, but Etna nearby thunders with
horrid collapses, and at times bursts forth to heaven a black cloud, smoking with a pitchy whirlwind and glowing ashes; it raises globes of flame and licks the
stars.” If anything is thrown into the openings from which these flames issue, it is soon vomited out. Julius Titianus also mentions this mountain in these
words: “There are four very great mountains in Sicily: Eryx, Nebrodes, Neptunius, and Etna. Seeing Etna often roll flames from its summit, the world could
almost believe the faithful’s account. Nevertheless, when it was first reported at Rome that Etna had burned, the event was expiated among the prodigies.”

## 14

**[014]** FIFTH concerns the springs of Grenoble, from which both water and fire flow together. You may see flames flying above the waters. You draw water from
the middle of the hearth and are not burned; you drink and are not set afire; you carry it and are not seized by fire. But if you bring a wax candle or torches
near, they catch fire as soon as they touch the flames. If you put in your hand, it is not burned. A certain Hilary says of this: “If fires truly burn, why do
you live, waters? If waters truly extinguish, why do you live, fires? The enemy of waters has placed fire in their bosoms, but the high hand commands common
origins,” and so forth. O admirable mystery of divine power! One vein of the spring produces both fire and water, so that all may recognize that both the
refreshment of glorious life and the judgment of eternal death stand under his dominion. They understand that fires have not been given license to harm the
human body which, after judgment, if guilty of sin, they will perpetually burn.

## 15

**[015]** SIXTH is that which, although created by God’s work before these things, is nevertheless placed last for the purpose of this account. God, creator of
all, commanded that it be celebrated in connection with the sun’s service. It is not without great wonder that the sun itself daily casts light upon the world
as though serving it, surveys east and west, and by fertilizing the lands with its heat makes them produce crops.

## 16

**[016]** SEVENTH is the wonder of how the moon grows to fullness or diminishes to smallness in periods of fifteen days. I also marvel that stars rising in the
east depart in the west, while some appearing in the middle of heaven and some approaching the north rotate in a circuit and do not make a straight path. Some
are visible throughout the year, while others have appointed months in which they appear. If God commands, I wish to give an account of this course to those who
do not know it, insofar as I have gained experience. I set aside the names Virgil and the other poets gave them and use only the names my common rusticity
employs or those expressed by the order of the signs themselves, such as the cross, sickle, and other signs. I do not teach astrology in these matters or advise
the investigation of future events; I exhort how the course of God’s praises may reasonably be fulfilled and at what hours one who wishes to be attentive in
this office ought to rise at night or pray to the Lord.

## 17

**[017]** THIS is the reckoning of the sun: how long and for how many hours it shines in each month. Although twelve hours are always counted, their measure is
not equal; if you wish to keep equal measure, as I said, there will be fifteen hours in long days. It shines: in January, 10 hours; February, 11; March, 12;
July, 14; August, 13; September, 12; April, 13; May, 14; June, 15; October, 11; November, 10; December, 9.

## 18

**[018]** THE reckoning of the moon is this: the first shines, ς 2; 1ς 3; 2 4; 3 5; 4 6; 5 7; 5ς 23; 5ς 24; 5 25; 4 8; 6 15; 12 16; 11 9; 7ς 17; 10 10; 8 18; 9ς
11; 8ς 19; 8ς 12; 9ς 20; 8 13; 10 21; 7ς 14; 11 22; 6 26; 3 27; 2 28; 1ς 29; ς 30; it is hidden. It must be known that in summer, when nights are shorter, the
moon runs the course the sun follows in winter; in winter, during longer nights, it follows the course the sun traverses in summer.

## 19

**[019]** THE course of the stars is to be observed in this way; I have also thought it should be painted with colors in the appropriate places.

## 20

**[020]** THIS star rises in September and appears at matins; some call it robeola. It first appears at the beginning of night and then rises again in the
morning. Therefore it shines in September at the first hour, in October at the second, in November at the third, in December and January at the eighth, in
February at the eighth, in March at the seventh, in April at the sixth, in June at the fourth, in July at the third, and in August at the second. As I said, it
first rises in September. Another smaller star precedes it.

## 21

**[021]** SOME call these stars symma, that is, stefadium. When October ends, they first appear in the evening and set, but also rise in the morning, shining at
the second hour. In November they appear at the beginning of night but rise in the morning, shining at the fourth hour; in December at the sixth; January at the
ninth; February at the eighth; March at the seventh; April at the sixth; May at the fifth; June at the fourth; July at the third. In August they shine little in
the morning and more in the evening.

## 22

**[022]** I call these stars omega because they signify it. They follow the preceding stars but precede the greater cross.

## 23

**[023]** THESE stars are the greater cross, which appears lying down in the east because it lay at the world’s beginning—that is, rested after being proclaimed
among prophets and patriarchs—but appears upright in the west because it was to be erected to receive the Lord at the world’s evening time.

## 24

**[024]** SOME call these stars the lesser cross, others alpha, because they are to the left of the greater cross and because of the two smaller stars appearing
below, which the trion precedes.

## 25

**[025]** THESE stars are called the trion. The stars I said signify omega appear at the beginning of night in December, set, and rise in the morning. They
shine at the third hour; in January at the fourth; February at the fifth; March at the sixth; April at the seventh; May at the ninth; June at the tenth. In July
they first appear in the evening at about the fifth hour and shine at the fourth; in August they shine at the seventh; September at the fifth; October at the
fourth; November at the third. One is brighter than the rest, as I indicated above. The cross follows them after an interval of about one hour. Those signifying
alpha follow these after an interval of another hour; it is unnecessary to write about each separately. They follow the same path as the sun in June.

## 26

**[026]** THESE stars are called Christ’s sign because they signify it, and one is brighter. They first appear in the morning in April, shining at the second
hour; May at the third; June at the fifth; July at the sixth. In August they first appear in the evening and shine all night; in September at the seventh hour;
October at the seventh; November at the sixth; December at the fifth; January at the fourth; February at the third. From mid-March they shine at the second
hour. They follow the path of the preceding stars, but in April and May first appear in the evening, set, and rise in the morning.

## 27

**[027]** SOME call these stars the serpent. They first appear in the morning in August and shine at the first hour; September at the third; October at the
fifth; November at the sixth; December at the eighth; January at the tenth; February at the eighth; March at the seventh; April at the fifth; May at the second.
They are usually hidden in June and July.

## 28

**[028]** SOME call these stars the mass, some the Pleiades, and many butrion. They rise as June ends and shine in the morning at the first hour; July at the
third; August at the fourth; September at the sixth; October at the seventh; November at the eighth; December at the ninth; January at the eighth; February at
the seventh; March at the third; April at the first. They are hidden in May.

## 29

**[029]** SOME call these stars the bier; they follow the preceding stars. They rise in mid-July, differing from the preceding stars by only two hours, and follow the same path.

## 30

**[030]** THESE stars, which some call the sickle, first rise on the Kalends of August. They rise two hours later than the preceding stars. I have not described
their course month by month because I thought it sufficient to say they are separated from the preceding stars by an interval of two hours. It must be known
that they are hidden in May, June, and July; when risen, they follow the path the sun travels in May or August.

## 31

**[031]** THESE stars follow the sickle, differing only in following two hours behind it and holding the path of the sun in September or April. They shine first
in the evening, but faintly.

## 32

**[032]** THESE stars rise in the lowest southern region, behind the preceding stars by an interval of one hour. Some call them quinio. They follow the path the
sun holds in February.

## 33

**[033]** WHAT can I say about these stars, which rustics call the wagon, since they do not rise and set like the other stars? Nevertheless, I will not keep
silent about what I understand of them. The learned call it septentrio because of the number of stars, and some call the northern region where they are found by
their name; I call it the north. These stars are therefore always visible in the northern part. When summer nights are shorter, they are lower and at daylight
turn the wagon pole toward the west. As autumn advances and nights begin to lengthen, they occupy higher regions of heaven and continue thus until the nights
again diminish. It must be known that in winter, as daylight approaches, the wagon turns its pole toward the east. It must also be known that they appear
equally throughout all years.

## 34

**[034]** MANY learned people call this star a comet. It does not appear at all times, but especially at a king’s death or a region’s destruction. This is how
it is understood. When it appears shining with a hairy head of radiance, it announces royal death; if, bearing a sword and reddening, it scatters hairs with
blackness, it shows the homeland’s destruction. Thus it appeared before the plague in the Auvergne region, hanging over that region for an entire year.
Prudentius, wisely discussing the star of the Lord’s Nativity, says in his hymn for holy Epiphany that this star produces sorrows: “Let the sad comet depart,
and as it has offered itself a star by its vapor, let it now fall from God’s tract, to be outshone.” A hairy star also appeared to many before King Sigibert
died.

## 35

**[035]** I HAVE written about the risings, settings, and courses of the stars, setting out a few signs I thought sufficient. Now I explain how human devotion
may rise to observe God’s office. Perhaps someone objects that I did not begin in March or on the day of the Lord’s Nativity itself; let him know that the star
observed in March rises in another month.

## 36

**[036]** SEPTEMBER. In September the brilliant star I above called robeola rises, with another smaller star preceding it nearby. When it rises in September, if
the signal for matins sounds, five psalms can be sung with antiphons in God’s praise. If you wish to seek the celestial sign at midnight, observe the sickle,
and when it reaches the fifth hour of the day, rise. If you wish to celebrate a perpetual vigil and rise when the stars I above called butrion appear, you may
complete nocturns with the cockcrow and eighty psalms with antiphons before beginning matins.

## 37

**[037]** OCTOBER. In October, when the sickle rises, know that it is midnight. Then, after celebrating nocturns with the cockcrow, you may sing ninety psalms
with antiphons. Next observe robeola; when it reaches the second hour of the day, if you sound the signal for matins, you may sing ten psalms.

## 38

**[038]** NOVEMBER. In November, as nights grow longer, the sickle rises at the fifth hour of night. If you rise then, after nocturns and the cockcrow, you may
sing 110 psalms. When robeola reaches the third hour, if the signal sounds, you may likewise complete twelve psalms with antiphons at matins.

## 39

**[039]** DECEMBER. In December the sickle rises at the fourth hour of night. If you rise at that hour, after nocturnal hymns or the double cockcrow—that is,
sixty psalms in these two courses, because before the Lord’s Nativity you ought to rise earlier—you may then chant the remainder of the Psalter with antiphons.
If you sound the signal for matins when robeola rises, thirty psalms are to be chanted without delay. After it rise the stars I called sima, that is,
stephadium. Then in this month rise the stars preceding the greater cross, which I named omega. Among them is one brighter and slower than the others, which you
can observe more conveniently.

## 40

**[040]** JANUARY. In January these stars rise after nocturns. As I said above, observe the brighter one among them. When it reaches the third hour of the day,
if you begin matins, fifteen psalms may be sung.

## 41

**[041]** FEBRUARY. In February, when the star I called the brighter among the preceding stars rises, if you begin nocturns, understand that it is midnight.
When the star reaches the fourth hour of the day, if the signal for matins sounds, you may complete twelve psalms.

## 42

**[042]** MARCH. When Lent arrives in March, you ought to rise earlier. When the star is at the second hour of the day, if you rise, say nocturns and the
cockcrow doubled, as I said above—that is, sixty psalms straight through. Completing these, sing twenty psalms with antiphons, and the star reaches the fifth
hour of the day. If you thus begin matins, after thirty psalms with antiphons have been sung, dawn breaks.

## 43

**[043]** APRIL. In April, if it is still Lent, observe the same as before. If you wish to rise later, observe the star I called brighter among those forming
Christ’s sign. When it has risen, if the signal for matins sounds, you may complete eight psalms with antiphons.

## 44

**[044]** MAY. In May, when it has risen, celebrate nocturns with the cockcrow. When the other courses are completed and it reaches the third hour, if you begin
matins, you may complete seven psalms with an antiphon.

## 45

**[045]** JUNE. In June, when it rises, celebrate similarly. Beginning matins when it reaches the fourth hour, you may sing five psalms. On the eighth day
before the Kalends of July the stars I called butrion rise; you may observe them more appropriately in the following months.

## 46

**[046]** JULY. In July you may use your own moderation because the nights are shorter. If you keep vigil all night, rise at midnight. When these stars appear
and the signal sounds, complete six psalms.

## 47

**[047]** AUGUST. In August, when these stars rise, complete nocturns and the other courses. Then, when they reach the third hour of the day, if you begin
matins, complete seven psalms with antiphons. If you wish to keep vigil all night, chant the whole Psalter.

# DE CURSU STELLARUM RATIO

## 1

**[001]** Plerique philosophorum, dam studiis litterarum vacant, quasi plus ceteris septem scripsere miracula, ex quibus mihi quaedam praemittere et alia plus
admiranda libuit memorare, quorum haec habentur vel formae vel opera.

## 2

**[002]** PRIMUM ERGO miraculum ponimus Noe arcam, quae Domini ore, qualis fierit, est mandata; cuius lungitudo trecentorum, latitudo quinquagenta, altitudo
tregenta cubitorum est habita. Quam arcam bicamaratam et tricamaratam legimus, cuius omne opus in cubito consumatum est. Fenestram sive ostium a latere habuit.
In eam enim de omnibus volatilibus caeli ac besteis terrae sive reptilibus cum hominibus octo ad reparatione mundi per inluviem cataclysmi genera reservata
sunt.

## 3

**[003]** SECUNDUM ponimus Babiloniam, cuius iuxta Horosium haec est expositio: Mira campi planitie undique conspicua, laetissima castrorum faciem, moenibus
paribus per quadrum disposita; murorum eius vix credibilis relatu firmitas et magnitudo, latitudine cubitorum 50, altitudine quater tantum. Ceterum ambitus eius
470 stadiis circumvenitur; murus coctili e lapide adque infusu bitumine conpactus; a fronte murorum centum portae aereae. Ipsa autem longitudo in consumatione
pinnarum, utroque latere habitaculis defensorum aeque dispositis, media intercapidine vicinas quatrigas capit; domos intrinsecus quater geminae, habitationes
minaci proceritate mirabiles. Haec prima post humani generis reparatione a Nebroth gigante condita est.

## 4

**[004]** TERTIUM est templum Salomonis, qui non tantum in magnitudine fabricae, quantum in ornamentis miraculum fuit. Aedificavit parietis domus intrinsecus
tabolatis cedrinis a pavimento domus usque ad summitatem parietum et usque ad laquearia, operuitque lignis intrinsecus et texuit pavimentum domus tabulis
abiegnis. Aedificavitque 20 cubitorum ad posteriorem partem templi tabolata cedrina a pavimento usque ad superiora et fecit inferiorem domum oraculi in sancta
sanctorum. Porro 40 cubitorum erat ipsum templum pro foribus oraculi, et cedro omnis domus intrinsecus vestiebatur, habens tornaturas et iuncturae suas
fabricatas et celaturas eminentes; omnia cedrinis tabulis vestiebantur, nec omnino lapis apparere poterat in pariete. Oraculum autem in medio domus inferiore
fecerat, ut poneret ibi arcam federis Domini. Porro autem oraculum habebat 20 cubitos longitudinis et vigenti cubitos latitudinis, operuitque illud adque
vestivit auro purissimo; sed et altare vestivit cedro. Domum quoque ante altare operuit auro purissimo et ad fixit laminas clavis aureis. Nihilque erat in
templum quod non auro tegeretur; et totum altare oraculi texit auro. Et fecit in oraculo duo Chaerubin de lignis olivarum decem cubitorum altitudinis; quinque
cubitorum ala Chaerubin una, id est decem cubitos habentes a summitatem alae usque ad alae alterius summitate. Decim quoque cubitorum erat Chaerubin secundus
mensuram parem, posuitque Chaerubin in medio templi interioris texitque eos auro. Et omnes parietes per circuitum scalpsit et variis caelaturis et turno et
fecit in eis Chaerubin et palmas et picturas varias quasi prominentes de pariete et egredientes, sed et pavimentum domus texit auro intrinsecus et extrinsecus.
Et in ingressum oraculi fecit ostiola de lignis olivarum, postes quadrangulorum quinque et duo ostia de lignis olivarum, et sculpsit in eis pictura Chaerubin et
palmarum species et anaclifa valde prominentia et texit ea auro. Fecitque introitum templi postes de lignis olivarum quadrangulatos et duo ostia de lignis
abiegnis altrensecus; utrumque ostium duplex erat et se invicem tenens operiebatur. Et sculpsit Chaerubin et palmas et celaturas valde eminentes. Multa quidem
et alia inibi fecit admirabilia, quae prosequi longum videtur.

## 5

**[005]** QUARTUM est sepulchrum regis Persici' ex uno lapide amitisto cavato miroque opere sculptum ac interrasile et extrinsecus habens effigies hominum,
bistiarum seu avium in foris prominentes; arbores quoque sculptas habet cum foliis et pomis opere celato.

## 6

**[006]** QUINTUM est statua colossi Rodo insolae collocata ex aere fusile, cuius tam inmensa est altitudo, ut vix lapidem capiti eius aliquis possit inicere,
et deaurata est Ferunt quoque multi, per tibiam eius usque ad capud hominem posse ascendere, si aditum unde ingrederetur haberet; adserunt etiam, capud huius
statuae recipere posse tritici choros duos et viginti.

## 7

**[007]** SEXTUM est theatrum quod in Eraclea habetur ex uno monte factum, ita ut omne ex uno latere sit expletum, tam extrinsecus parietes quam intrinsecus
arcus, foveae, gradus, sedilia; et omne opus eius ex lapide uno conpletum est; est autem marmore Heracleo vestitum.

## 8

**[008]** SEPTIMUM est pharus Alexandrina, quae super quattuor mirae magnitudinis cancros constructa habetur; nec enim hi parvi esse poterant, qui tam inmensum
sustinent vel altitudinis vel latitudinis pondus. Nam ferunt, super unum quemque brachium cancri si homo extensos iaceat, eum operire non possit. Pharos autem
iste, datis de publico paleis, nocte succenditur, scilicet ut nocturno tempore errantes nautae vento vel imbre, si stellas videre non potuerint, sciant, qua
parte dirigant vela.

## 9

**[009]** Sed ista, licet quaepiam iussionem Dei, quaepiam autem adinventionem humana constructa sint, ab hominibus tamen constat esse fundata, ideoque et
quaedam deruerunt, quaedam autem ruinae sunt proxima. Nam sunt alia quae ipse omnipotens Deus noster proprio opere in hoc mundo vel per dies singulos renovat,
vel post transacto anni curriculum repraesentat, quae et in locupletatione ostenduntur muneris, ut est commotio oceani et fructus terrae; alia vero in
ostensione proferuntur virtutis, ut est sol, luna, stellae, Phinix; et quaedam ex his peccatores arguunt et ignem infernalem figurant, ut est Ethna, fons
Gratianopolitanus. Haec sunt enim miracula, quae nulla aetate seniscunt, nullo occasu occidunt, nulla labe minuuntur, nisi cum Dominus mundum dissolvi
praeciperit.

## 10

**[010]** PRIMUM est ergo omnium maris oceani commutio, in qua ita per dies singulos dilatatur, at accedens ora litoris repleat rursumque recedens siccum
praebeat iter; tunc populis per humum aridam gradientibus piscium sive diversorum liguminum maltitudo copiosa collegitur. Hoc primum miraculum Deus humano
generi praeparavit, quod et admiratione praeclarum sit et congruum servituti.

## 11

**[011]** SECUNDUM est simile huic, de granis scilicit frugum et de fructibus arborum, cum iacta terrae simina et sulcis operta, adveniente aestate eriguntur in
culmina, ornataque comis et spicis lacteo intrinsecus adipe saginantur, quae Dominus spiritalis doctrinae sator de profecto verborum suorum, quae in populos
iaciebat, parabolice commntavit, dicens: Sic est verbum Dei, quemadmodum si iactet homo semen, et exurgat nocte et diae; ultro enim terra fructificat, primum
herbam, deinde spicam, deinde plenum granum in spicam. Paulus autem apostolos de resurrectione hanc rationem figuravit, dicens: Quod seminas non vivificatur,
nisi prius moriatur. Sic est, inquit, et resurrectio mortuorum: seminatur in infirmitate, surgit in virtute, et cetera. Aequa est enim et arborum natura, quae,
ut puto, ipsam resurrectionem signat, cum in hieme nudatae foliis tamquam mortui habentur, verno vero tempore ornantur foliis, decorantur floribus, pomisque
aestate replentur. Quod miraculum quamquam hac utatur similitudinem, ad praesens tamen beneficium populis praestat, ut cognoscat homo, ab illo se accipere
victum, qui eum creavit ex nihilo.

## 12

**[012]** TERTIUM est, quod de Phinice Lactantius refert 'Magna est', ait, 'corpore et decora plumis unguibusque et oculis, quae alterius avis non est iuncta
consortio nec iuncta coniugio; nam et nescire homines manifestum est, cuius sit generis, masculus an femina sive neutrum. Haec postquam mille transierit annos,
petit locum omnibus locis mundanis celsitudinem praeminentem, in quo habetur locus viridi comam verno hibernoque perdurans, in cuius medium fons est magnus et
ubertate profluus et lenitate praeclarus. Huius in litore arbor nobilis reliquas luci arbores proceritate praecellens; in huius arboris vertice haec avis de
diversis pigmentorum generibus construit sibi seu nidum sive sepulchrum, insedensque in medio eine ore odoramenta adtrahit seque ex his tegit. Tunc diversis
modolis incipit cantos effundere suaves, ac de nido exiliens, aquarum se undis inmergit. Quod cum ter quaterque repetierit, ascendit iterum super nidum
adtrahitque denuo super se odoramenta, quae detulit. Imicante autem sole primum ei iubar inferit ignem, adprehensumque nidum, tota integre concrematur. Tunc
pulves exustus ad se collegitur et in unam massam quasi in ovi speciae conglobatur; hac exinde iterum surgens·, resumta vita, nutritur, nec cuiquam homini, dum
inplumis est, pascere cura est. Tantum caelesti rore nutrita, ad pristinam speciem revocatur et ipsius figurae, eisdem plumis eidemque colore reparata
progreditur, ut prius fuerat ante morte'. Quod miraculum resurrectionem humanam valde figurat et ostendit, qualiter homo luteus redactus in pulvere, sit iterum
de ipsis favillis tuba canente resuscitandus.

## 13

**[013]** QUARTUM est Ethna mons Siciliae insulae datus, qui vivis ardoribus exaestuat, flammasque evomens validas, ac terribiliter regione sulphor eructuat; de
quo Publeus Mantuanus in tertio Ineidum libro ita ait: Portus ab accessu ventorum inmotus et ingens Ipse, sed horrefecis iuxta tonat Ethna ruinis, Interdumque
atra prorumpit ad aethera nubem Turbine fumantem piceo et candente favilla, Adtollitque globos flammarum et sidera lambit. Sed et si qua in foraminibus, ande
haec egrediuntur flammae, iniecta fuerint, mox evomuntur. Meminet et huius montis et illo Iulius Titianus his verbis, dicens: Montes maximi in Sicilia quattuor,
Ericus, Nebrodes, Neptunius et Ethna, quem videns saepius flammas e vertice volvere, idque sentire orbis prope fide credentium, quamquam id: cum primum Romae
nuntiatum est, arsisse Ethnam, in monstris procuratum est.

## 14

**[014]** QUINTUM est de fontibus Gratianopolitanis, de quibus simul et latix manat et ignis. Namvideas limphis flammas supervolare, hauris aquam de medio foci
nec uriris, bibis nec incenderis, portas nec ab igne conprehenderis. Quod si cereum vel tedas admoveas, protinus ut flammas adtigerint, conprehenduntur; manum
quoque si inicias, non crematur. Hinc Elarius quidam ait: Si vere exurunt ignes, cur vivitis undae? Si vere extingunt undae, cur vivitis ignis? Limpharum in
gremiis inimicus condidit ignis, Communesque ortus imperat alta manus, et reliqua. O admirabile potentiae divinae misterium! Una vena fontis et ignis producit
et latices, scilicet ut cognoscant omnes dominationi eius et refrigerium gloriosae vitae et iudicium aeternae mortis adsistere, intellegantque, incendiis
licentiam esse non datam ad nocendum corpus humanum, quod post iudicium, si peccato obnoxium fuerit, accepturi erunt perpetualiter exurendum.

## 15

**[015]** SEXTUM est illud, quod licit ante ista Dei opere fuerit conditum, tamen pro ratione huius rei locatur extremum, hoc est, quod de solis officio creatur
omnium Deus praecepit caelebrari; nam non sine grande admiratione cernitur, quod ipso sol omnibus diebus quasi famulans mundo ingerit lumen, quod orientem
occidentemque perlustrat, quod calore suo terras fecundans, frugem gignere facit.

## 16

**[016]** SEPTIMUM est enim miraculum, qualiter luna in ter quinis diebus vel crescit ad integritatem vel ad exiguitate minuitur. Admiramur et illud, quod
stellae oriente ortae decedunt occidenti, et quaedam ex his in medio caeli apparentes, quaedam aquilone propinquantes, in circuitu rotentur nec rectam faciant
viam, et quaepiam toto videantur anno, quaepiam menses in quibus appareant babeant definitos. De quo cursu, si Deus iubeat, velim, de quanto experimentum
accipi, rationem nescientibus dare. Sed nomina quae his vel Maro vel reliqui indiderunt poetae postpono, tantum ea vocabula nuncupans, quae vel usitate
rusticitas nostra vocat vel ipsorum signaculorum expremit ordo, ut est crux, falcis vel reliqua signa; quia non ego in his mathesim doceo neque futura
perscrutare praemoneo, sed, qualiter cursus in Dei laudibus rationabiliter impleatur, exhortor, vel quibus horis qui in hoc officio adtente versari cupit,
debeat nocte consurgere vel Dominum deprecare.

## 17

**[017]** SOLIS AUTEM haec ratio, qualiter aut quantis horis in singulis luceat mensibus; et quamquam omni tempore horae duodicem conputentur, non tamen
aequalem habet mensuram; si vero aequalem vis tenere mensuram, erunt, ut diximus, in diebus longis horae 15. Lucit autem: mense Ianuarius hora 10. mense
Februarius hora 11. mense Martius hora 12. mense Iulius hora 14. mense Augustus hora 13. mense September hora 12. mense Aprilis hora 13. mense Maius hora 14.
mense Iunius hora 15. mense Octuber hora 11. mense November hora 10. mense December hora 9.

## 18

**[018]** LUNAE AUTEM ratio haec eat: prima lucit ς 2. 1ς 3. 2 4. 3 5. 4 6. 5 7. 5ς 23. 5ς.|24. 5.|25. 4 8. 6 15. 12 16. 11 9. 7ς 17. 10 10. 8 18. 9ς 11. 8ς 19.
8ς 12. 9ς 20. 8 13. 10 21. 7ς 14. 11 22. 6 26. 3. | 27. 2 28. 1ς 29. ς 30. latet Illud autem sciendum est, quod luna in aestate, quando noctes breviores sunt,
illum currit tramitem quem sol in hieme tenet; hieme vero in prolixioribus noctibus illum ordinem tenet quem sol in aestate percurrit.

## 19

**[019]** STELLARUM QUOQUE CURSUS hoc modo est observandus, quem etiam fucis colorum credidi pingendum in singulis locis.

## 20

**[020]** HAEC STELLA in Septembre oritur et matutino apparet, quae a quibusdam robeola vocatur, tamen prius initium apparet noctis et sic iterum oretur mane;
ergo lucit in Septembre hora 1, in Octubre hora 2, in Novembre 3, in Decembre et in Ianuario 8, in Februario 8, in Martio 7, in Aprile 6, in Iunius 4, in Iulio
3, in Augusto 2, Septembre primum, ut diximus, oritur; habet tamen alia minorem, quae praecedit

## 21

**[021]** HAEC STELLAE symma, id est stefadium, vocantur a quibusdam. Egrediente Octubre, cum primo sero appareant, occidunt, tamen et mane oriuntur, lucent
hora 2. In Novb. iam apparent in initio noctis, sed mane oriuntur, lucent hora 4. In Decemb. hora 6, in Ianuario 9, in Feb. 8, in Martio 7, in Aprile 6, in
Madium 5, in Iunio 4, in Iulio 3, in Augusto mane parum, sero plus.

## 22

**[022]** HAEC STELLAE ω vocitamus, quia eum significant; et secuntur priores, praecedunt vero crucem maiorem.

## 23

**[023]** HAEC STELLAE crux maior quae ad orientem iacens apparet, pro eo quod in primordio mundi iacuerit, id est inter prophetas patriarchasque pronuntiata
quieverit, ad occidentem vero erecta apparet, scilicet quod ad suscipiendum Dominum in occiduum mundi esset tempore erigenda.

## 24

**[024]** HAS STELLAS quidam crucem minorem dicunt, quidam autem alfam vocant, pro eo quod ad sinistram crucis maioris sunt, et propter duas minores, qui
deorsum apparent, quas praecedit trion.

## 25

**[025]** HAEC STELLAE vocantur trion. Stellae ergo, quas ω significari diximus, haec mense Decembre in initio noctis apparent, occidunt et mane oriuntur;
lucent hora 3, in Ian. hora 4, in Feb. hora 5, in Mar. 6, in Apri. 7, in Maio 9, in Iunius 10. Iam in Iulio primo sero quasi in hora 5 apparent, lucent hora 4;
in Aug. lucent 7, in Septb. 5, in Oct. 4, in Novb. 3. Habent tamen unam ceteris clariorem, sicut supra indicavimus. Crux vero istas sequitur quasi post unius
horae spacium. Illae vero quae alfam significant istas poet alterius horae spacium prosecuntur, de quibus scribere non est necesse per singula; tramitem vero
ipsum tenent quem sol mense Iunio.

## 26

**[026]** Has stellas signum Christi vocant, quia ipsum signant, sed habent unam clariorem. In Aprile mense primum apparent mane, lucent hora 2, Mai. 3, Iun. 5,
Iuli. 6. In Augusto primo sero apparent, lucent tota nocte; in Septembrio hora 7, in Octubrio 7, in Novembrio 6, in Decembrio 5, in Ian. 4, in Feb. 3. A medio
Mar. lucent hora 2, tenent tamen superiorum viam; Aprile tamen et Maio primo sero apparent, occidunt et mane oriuntur.

## 27

**[027]** HAEC STELLAE a quibusdam anguis vocantur; in Augusto primo mane apparent et lucent hora prima, in Sept hora 3, in Oct. hora 5, in Novb. 6, in Dec. 8,
in Ian. 10, in Feb. 8, in Mar. 7, in Apri. 5, in Mai. 2; in Iun. Iulioque latere solent

## 28

**[028]** HAS STELLAS quidam massam vocant, nonnulli Pliadas, plerique vero butrionem. Mense Iun. egrediente oriuntur et lucent mane hora 1, in Iul. hora 3, in
Aug. hora 4, in Sep. hora 6, in Oct. hora 7, in Nov. 8, in Decb. hora 9, in Ian. 8, in in Feb. hora 7, in Mar. hora 3, in April, hora una, in Maio latent

## 29

**[029]** HAS· STELLAS quidam arte feretrum vocant, quae superiores secuntur. Oriuntur autem mense in Iulio medio, duabus tantum horis a superioribus
discrepant; ipsum tamen viae tramitem tenent.

## 30

**[030]** HAEC STELLAE Kals. Augusti oriuntur primum, quas quidam falcem vocant. Duas hor. tardius a superioribus surgunt, quarum cursum ideo per singulos non
descripsimus menses, quia sufficere arbitrati sumus dixisse a superioribus duarum spatio horarum esse disiunctas. Sciendum tamen, quod mense Maio Iunioque et
Iulio latent et, cum ortae fuerint, ipsam viam, quam sol mense Maio vel Augusto pergit, tenent.

## 31

**[031]** ISTAE VERO stellae falce secuntur, in hoc discrepantes, quod duabus tantum horis postergum secuntur, ipsam tenentes viam, quam sol vel in Septembre
vel in Aprile. Lucent primo sero, sed parum.

## 32

**[032]** HAEC STELLAE ad imam australem plagam surgunt a tergo superiorum horae unius intervallo, quas quidam quinionem vocant, ipsam viam quam sol Februario mense tenentes.

## 33

**[033]** DE HIS STELLIS, quas rustici plaustrum vocant, quid dicere possumus, cum non ut reliquae stellae oriuntur aut occidunt? Sed tamen quantum ex ipsis
intellegimus non silemus. A sapientibus septentrio vocatur propter numero, unde et plaga illa, in qua habentur, a quibusdam ex eorum nomine vocitatur; nos vero
aqujlonem dicimus. Apparent ergo haec stellae a parte aquilonis omni tempore. Cum in aestivo noctes fuerint breviores, istae humilius habentur et ad lucem
thimonem ad occidentem faciunt; cum vero antamnum versus proficientes, noctes crescere ceperint, et haec altiora continent caeli et sic usque diminutione
reiterata nocteum faciunt. Hoc tamen sciendum, quod in hieme adpropinquante luce thimonem vertit ad orientem; noscendum etiam est et illud, quod omnibus annis
aequaliter oriuntur.

## 34

**[034]** HAEC STELLA comitis vocatur a plerisque peritis. Non omni tempore, sed maxime aut in obitu regis aut in excidio apparet regionis. Qualiter ergo
intellegatur, haec est ratio. Cum capud crinitum deadimate apparuerit fulgorans, regalem adnuntiat letum; si autem gladium ferens, rutilans, cum negrore
sparserit comas, patriae monstrat excidium. Sic enim et ante pestilentia Arvernae regionis apparuit, pendens per annum integrum super regionem illam. Quod enim
has proferat tristitias, Prudentius cum de nativitatis dominicae stella prudenter dissereret, haec in hymno sanctae Epyphaniae ait: Tristis comita intercedat,
Et sicut astrum sibi Offeruerit vapore, iam Dei Sublucendis tractu cadat. Nam et priusquam Sigibertus rex obierit, crinita multis apparuit.

## 35

**[035]** SCRIPSIMUS DE ORTIS VEL OCCASIBUS sive cursibus stellarum, pauca signa, quod arbitrati fuimus sufficere, praeponentes; nunc ea pandimus, qualiter ad
officium Dei observandum possit devotio humana consurgere. Et forsitan detrahit aliquis, cur non a mense Martio vel ab ipso nativitatis dominicae die
sumpserimus exordium; noverit, quia stella quae mense Martio observatur in alio oritur mense.

## 36

**[036]** SEPTEMBER. In mense Septembre oritur ergo stella splendide, quam supra robeola diximus, alia prope se habens minorem praecedentem. Ergo quando in
Septembre oritur, si signum moveatur ad matutinus, quinque psalmis in Dei laude concinere· in antyphanis potest. Iam vero, si ad medium noctis vis signum
caeleste requirere, falcem observa, et cum in hora diei quinta advenerit, surge. Certe si vigiliam perpetim celebrare volueris, si consurgas, cum stellae
apparent, quas butrionem superius vocitamus, explicias nocturnos cum galli cantu, octoginta psalmos in antyphanis, priusquam matutinus incipias, explicabis.

## 37

**[037]** OCTUBER. In Octubre vero falcis illa cum oritur, mediam noverit esse noctem; deinde celebratus nocturnus cum gallorum cantu, nonaginta in antiphanis
concinere poteris psalmus; deinde adtende rubeolam, quae cum hora diei venerit secunda, si signum ad matutinum moveas, decim poteris concinere psalmos.

## 38

**[038]** NOVEMBER. Mense Novembre iam prolixioribus noctibus falcis hora noctis quinta oritur. Quod si sic consurgas, celebratos nocturnos gallique cantum,
cento 10 psalmus psallere poteris. Rubeola vero cum hora tertia venerit, si signum sonit, duodecim nihilominus psalmus in antyphanis explicabis ad matutinos.

## 39

**[039]** DECEMBER. Mense Decembre falcis hora noctis oritur quarta. Si illa hora consurgas, dictis nocturnalibus hymnis vel galli cantum dupliciter, hoc est 60
in his duobus cursibus psalmis, quia ante dominicum natalem maturius consurgere debes, tunc relicum psalterium in antyphanis decantabis. Signum ad matutinus si
moveas, cum oritur rubeola, 30 psalmos expedite decantandum. Post eas oriuntur stellae, quas simam, id est stephadium, diximus. Deinde oriuntur in hoc mense
stellae illae, quae crucem maiorem praecedunt, quas ω nominavimus, in quibus est una aliarum clarior hac lentior, quam cummodius poteris observari.

## 40

**[040]** IANUARIUS. Mense Ianu. post dictos nocturnos stellae istae oriuntur, inter quas, ut superius diximus, quae est clarior, observatur; [si] ad hora die
tertia venerit, si matutinus incipias, 15 psalmos poterit psallere.

## 41

**[041]** FEBRUARIUS. Mense Februario, quando oritur stella illa quam inter stellas superiores diximus clariorem, si nocturnos incipias, mediam esse intellegas
noctem. Cum stella ad horam diei quartam advenerit, si signum ad matutinus commoveatur, 12 psalmos poteris explicare.

## 42

**[042]** MARTIUS. Mense Martio cum quadragensima advenerit, et maturius consurgere debes. Quando stella est in hor. 2. diei, si surgas, dicis nocturnus et
galli canto, quae dupliciter, ut superius diximus, hoc est in directis 60 psalmos. Quibus expeditis, psallis in antyphanis 20 psal., et stilla illa venit ad
horam 5. diei. Quod si sic inchoas matutinus, 30 decantatis cum antyphana psalmis, luciscit

## 43

**[043]** APRILIS. Mense autem Aprile, si adhuc quadragesima est, similiter observabis quae praeterita. Si tardius consurgere volueris, observabis stellam quam
inter eas, quae signum Christi faciunt diximus clariorem. Quae cum orta fuerit, si signum commoveatur ad matutinus, octo psalmos poteris in antiphanis expedire.

## 44

**[044]** MAIUS. Mense Maio cum orta fuerit, nocturnos celebrabis cum galli cantu, expeditisque et reliquis cursibus, cum ad horam tertiam venerit, ei matutinus
incipias, 7 psal. in antiphana explicabis.

## 45

**[045]** IUNIUS. Mense Iunio cum surrexerit, similiter celebrabis, et cum in hor. 4. venerit, matutinus incipiens, 5 psalmos poteris decantare. 8. autem
Kalendarum Iuliarum stellae illae quas butrionem vocitavimus oriuntur, quas in sequentibus mensibus rectius observabis.

## 46

**[046]** IULIUS. Mense vero Iulio potestatis tuae erit temperandum, quia noctes breviores habentur, si tota nocte vigilis, ei media nocte consurgas; tamen, cum
stellae istae apparent, ei signum sonet, sex psalmos expedis.

## 47

**[047]** AUGUSTUS. Mense Augusto cum haec stellae oriuntur, nocturnos reliquosque cursos adimple; dehinc cum ad hora tertia diei venerit, ei matutinus
incipias, 7 psalmos in antiphanis explicabis. Quod si nocte tota vigilare volueris, totum psalterium decantabis.
# COMMENTARY ON THE TITLES OF THE PSALMS AND TWO FRAGMENTS

## SOURCE AND CONTROL

English translation prepared for this project from the Latin control texts in MGH *Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum*, Volume 1, Part 2, *Miracula et opera
minora* (second edition, 1969). The surviving explanation of psalm titles, its 89 numbered entries, and the two fragments recovered by Mabillon are included in
printed order.

## SCENE AND CONTEXT

Gregory reads Davidic flight, persecution, temple, priestly, and royal language through Christ, the church, baptism, resurrection, judgment, and the heavenly
kingdom. He then assigns a concise Christological or ecclesial interpretation to each surviving psalm entry. The fragments address compunction, self-offering,
obedience, innocence, and the recompense of the righteous.

## KINSHIP AND SAME-NAME FENCE

David, Moses, Solomon, Cush, Absalom, Korah, and Judas retain their distinct biblical identities. The work’s Gregory is Georgius Florentius Gregorius of Tours,
named in the source title; no other Gregory is silently substituted. Christological readings are presented as the source’s interpretations rather than as
separate historical narratives about additional persons.

## RECENSION AND TEXT NOTE

The surviving commentary ends at entry 89 with the incomplete word *refu[gium]* and ellipsis points. No entries 90–150 have been reconstructed or imported.
Mabillon’s two fragments are preserved separately after the surviving sequence; their own source headings identify the lost chapters “On Compunction” and “On
the Recompense of the Righteous.”

# ENGLISH TRANSLATION

## PREFACE

**[000]** Psalms that explain David’s flight and persecution are understood to perceive the Lord’s persecution and passion. Those inscribed “Unto the end” show
the perfection of good works, because this end is unlike other ends: they have a termination, this a fulfillment. “For Christ is the end of the law,” says the
apostle, “unto righteousness for everyone who believes.” “For the winepresses” is a hymn for the fruits of eternal gifts. “For those who will inherit” teaches
the recompense of the saints or of the church, which is Christ’s body, so that they may obtain the inheritance and kingdom of heaven. “For the eighth”: some
assign this number to the Gospels because they contain eight beatitudes through which one comes to God’s kingdom, or to the eight souls of that ark. “At the
consummation” or “dedication of the tabernacle” is understood as the church’s perfection. “For those who will be changed” foresees the transformation of the
Jewish and Gentile people, or of synagogue and church. “For the hidden things” proclaims the coming of the Son of God, who was hidden from the Jews. “Song of
the resurrection” means the truth of the Lord’s resurrection itself. “Prayer of Moses, man of God” returns to God’s law because it proclaims that the law joins
me to the Redeemer’s resurrection. “Psalm for Solomon,” that is, the peaceful one, refers to Christ, who is my peace. “In confession” teaches that humanity
should continually confess God in voice and heart. Those psalms that narrate past deeds according to the letter are recognized as possessing the truth of
spiritual understanding. The psalm “for the sons of Korah” prefigured the people to be redeemed through Christ’s passion, because Korah means baldness, just as
my Lord Jesus Christ was crucified at the place of Calvary. “For the words of Cush, son of Benjamin” refers to Cush’s leaving David and going over to Absalom,
his father’s enemy, as Judas did to Christ. “At the morning assumption,” because the Lord, rising in the morning, led back the captivity he had assumed from
hell. “On the first Sabbath,” at the resurrection itself. “Before he was anointed,” before he was glorified by resurrection. “In remembrance,” certainly of
one’s own offenses. “Song of degrees” designates the heavenly ascent. The psalm in the middle of the songs of degrees is therefore placed like a most beautiful
tower. Nor do I think it without mystery that this book consists of three fifties, for this, I believe, is their rationale: the first grants remission of
crimes, the second invites me to hope for the heavenly kingdom, and the third sends me into the city of eternal blessedness. The diapsalmata, interpreted as
“always,” teach that the faithful soul’s attention should always be exercised in these things.

## 1

**[001]** The first psalm shows that he is the tree of life.

## 2

**[002]** The second, that he receives all nations from the Father as his inheritance.

## 3

**[003]** That he sleeps for me in the sleep of death and rises.

## 4

**[004]** That after the resurrection he is glorified by God the Father.

## 5

**[005]** That he is the inhabitant of the saints and the hearer of the church.

## 6

**[006]** That he is the conqueror of my enemies.

## 7

**[007]** That he is the examiner of all consciences.

## 8

**[008]** That he, the Son of Man, was made a little lower than the angels in the passion.

## 9

**[009]** That by his holy coming he will crush Antichrist.

## 10

**[010]** That he judges each one according to justice and equity.

## 11

**[011]** That he arose because of my needs and miseries.

## 12

**[012]** That he illuminates my eyes lest they sleep in eternal death.

## 13

**[013]** That he turns captivity away from his people.

## 14

**[014]** That he is the mountain on which righteous souls rest.

## 15

# TWO FRAGMENTS RECOVERED BY MABILLON

## 1

**[001]** In the chapter “On Compunction,” Gregory of Tours, in the Commentary on the Psalms: “For if the bonds of my offenses have been broken and my mind has
found delight in Christ, then I offer myself to God as a living and holy sacrifice, remaining with him in the heavenly Jerusalem.”

## 2

**[002]** In the final chapter, “On the Recompense of the Righteous,” Gregory, in the Exposition of the Psalms: “Therefore, if I do not stop my ears against
God’s commandments, if I carry out the saints’ admonitions with innocence, if I am not afflicted by the thorns of my crimes, if with the innocent I wash my
hands free of all blood, the Lord my God will honor me with worthy rewards, in which the saints rejoice perpetually with him. To him be glory with the eternal
Father and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.”

# IN PSALTERII TRACTATUM COMMENTARIUS

## PRAEFATIO

**[000]** Denique psalmi, qui fugam persecutionemque David explicant, percipiunt persecutionem passionemque dominicam. Illi autem qui In finem inscribuntur
perfectionem bonorum operum ostendunt, quia hic finis dissimilis est aliis finibus, cum illi habent terminum, hic replimentum: Finis enim legis est Christus,
ait apostolus, ad iustitiam omni credenti. Pro torcularibus pro aeternorum munerum fructibus hymnus est. Pro his qui hereditabuntur retributionem sanctorum sive
eclesiae, quae est corpus Christi, ut hereditatem capiant et regna caelorum, docent. Pro octava. Quidam honc numerum euangeliis deputant, eo quod contenentur in
his octo beatitudines, per quas venitur ad regnum Dei, sive illius arcae octo animae. In consummatione vel dedicatione tabernaculi perfectio eclesiae
intelligitur. Pro his qui commutabuntur populo Iudaico ac gentili vel synagogae et eclesiae commotationem praevidet. Pro occultis de adventu Filii Dei
pronuntiat, qui Iudaeis occultus fuit. Canticum resurrectionis, id est ipsius dominicae resurrectionis veritatis. Oratio Moysi hominis Dei ad legem Dei
revertitur, eo quod ipsa nos Redemptoris resurrectione sociare pronuntiat. Psalmus in Salomonem, id est pacificum quod est in Christo, qui est pax nostra·. In
confessione vero docet, ut iugiter homo Deum et voce fateatur et corde. IIli sane qui res gestas secundum litteram narrant veritatem spiritalis intellegentiae
cognoscuntur habere. Psalmus filiis Core per passionem Christi redemendum populum praefiguravit, quia Core interpretatur calvitium, sicut dominus noster Iesus
Christus in loco Calvariae crucifixus est. Pro verbis Chusi, fili Gemini, hoc est, quod Chusi, relicto David, ad Absalon transiit, qui erat hostis patris sui,
sicut Iudas Christi. In assumptione matutina, quia Dominus resurgens mane, assumptam reduxit captivitatem ab inferis. In prima sabbati, in ipsa resurrectione.
Priusquam lineretur, antequam resurrectione clarificaretur. In rememoratione delictorum utique suorum. Canticum graduum namque caelestem designat ascensum.
Psalmus ergo ille qui in medio canticorum graduum est tamquam turris pulcherrima ponitur. Sed nec hoc sine mysterio arbitror esse, quod hic liber in tribus
quinquagenariis constat scriptus, quorum hoc, ut opinor, ratio est: Primus enim remissionem criminum praestat, secundus ad spem nos regni caelestis invitat,
tertius nos ad regnum aeternae beatitudinis in civitatem mittit. Diapsalmae vero, quae 'semper' interpraetantur, docent, ut animac semper in his exerceatur
fidelis intentio.

# APPENDIX — THE PASSION OF SAINT JULIAN THE MARTYR

## SOURCE AND CONTROL

English translation prepared for this project from the Latin control text in MGH *Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum*, Volume 1, Part 2, *Miracula et opera minora*
(second edition, 1969), where the *Passio sancti Iuliani martyris* is printed separately. All six numbered sections are included.

## SCENE AND CONTEXT

The appendix narrative moves from persecution at Vienne to Julian’s withdrawal into the Auvergne, his voluntary surrender and beheading, burial at Brioude, and
the construction first of an oratory and later of a basilica. The released prisoner’s household and the two old men who bury Julian supply the central
posthumous testimony. The closing describes annual healings at the martyr’s feast.

## KINSHIP AND SAME-NAME FENCE

This Julian is the martyr associated with Vienne and Brioude. Ferreolus appears here as the Christian tribunician official at Vienne, not as an interchangeable
bearer of that name. The imprisoned husband’s name is not supplied by the source and has not been conjectured. This separate passion is not merged with
Gregory’s own *Passion and Virtues of Saint Julian*.

## RECENSION AND TEXT NOTE

The MGH appendix contains six numbered sections. Its Latin is visibly corrupt or damaged in places, especially in the prisoner notice of section 4 and the
transition to section 6. The English follows the transmitted sense without presenting conjectural restoration as established wording. The work remains an
appendix and does not displace Gregory’s fifty-one-segment Julian book.

# ENGLISH TRANSLATION

## 1

**[001]** The sublime and venerable passion of blessed Julian, martyr of the city of Auvergne, whose coming this people rejoices to have gained as its
patron—not because he came to this city fleeing martyrdom, but because Christ granted him as an intercessor for my sins so that this city and people might be
endowed with the protection of so great a martyr—ought now to be written for the faithful and transmitted to future times, since oblivion has not yet overtaken
his passion. And because it is most illustrious throughout the whole city to venerate God’s martyrs, Christ has deigned to grant Saint Julian the martyr to this
little people as intercessor and advocate.

## 2

**[002]** In that time persecution came upon the Christians in the city of Vienne under Crispinus, a former governor. The most holy Ferreolus, himself also
proved a martyr by God, then held tribunician power in that city. Yet he exercised his military office in such a way that he fulfilled the purpose of sacred
religion. Because Julian was a most faithful Christian, Ferreolus kept him for his own consolation. When Saint Ferreolus learned of the persecution of
Christians, he told Saint Julian, “I have learned that persecution of Christians will come to this city, and therefore I beg you to leave this place until the
persecution of Christians departs.”

## 3

**[003]** When blessed Julian heard this report, he withdrew into the territory of the city of Auvergne. Entering a certain old woman’s hut, he asked her to
hide him. This lodging was not far from where vain images were then worshiped by pagans. The persecutors immediately arrived at his hiding place and asked the
woman where the man who had taken refuge in her lodging a little earlier was staying. When she denied knowing, the holy man, unwilling to be deprived of his
crown, offered himself voluntarily to the persecutors and said, “Here is the one you seek; fulfill what your rulers commanded.” After devoting a little time to
prayer, he offered his neck to the persecutors. Without delay they drew the sword, cut off his head, and, returning, carried the holy martyr’s head with them as
an example to the others living in Vienne. He poured out a wave of his sacred blood.

## 4

**[004]** In those times vain pagan superstition was celebrated in these places. Two old men, pricked by divine power, transferred Saint Julian’s body from the
place where he had been beheaded to the village called Brioude and honorably committed it to burial. Returning from there, they felt within themselves that, as
a benefit for the burial, they had received back from God the former strength they had possessed in youth. At that time a certain wealthy man from Spain became
liable to the emperor in the city of Trier. Summoned and committed to prison for his offense, the emperor ordered him after a postponement to undergo capital
sentence. When his wife learned this, anxious and sorrowful, she hastened quickly to collect her husband’s corpse. As the matron passed the aforementioned
village, the two old men diligently inquired where she was going and why she was so sad. She explained the necessity and cause to them.

## 5

**[005]** The old men told the mistress of the household, “A little while ago a Christian was beheaded by persecutors. After burying his body with the greatest
honor, as I returned I felt that I had received back the former strength I possessed in youth.” Hearing this, the most faithful woman immediately poured out
prayer at Saint Julian the martyr’s tomb and vowed that if she saw her husband safe and he returned to her house alive, they would build a little cell in
Julian’s honor over his tomb. After praying at length, she completed her journey and came to the city. Entering, she saw that her husband had been released by
the king’s indulgence; not only did he obtain release, he also received an honor of rank. When the woman asked at what time he had obtained release, she found
that her husband had been released at the very time when she had asked blessed Julian the martyr for her husband’s safety, so that the emperor would release her
spouse. Returning to blessed Julian’s tomb and fulfilling their vows, they built the little oratory cell as the woman had promised. Thereafter, throughout all
the years of their lives, they brought immense gifts to his venerable tomb in return for such great benefits.

## 6

**[006]** After the blessed martyr’s reputation and fame had been declared everywhere and made known for celebration by all the people, such witnesses now stand
before this people that the patronage of so great a martyr does not depart from them. Therefore through many ages a basilica was built by the most faithful
Christians in honor of that most blessed man. Built, it raised a lofty summit; it now shines with an ornamented privilege in honor of his name and is filled
with the miracles of my special patron Julian the martyr. I will not keep silent about the miracle the Lord performs in praise of his name: on Julian’s natal
day the Lord works many divine benefits through the prayers and intercessions of my special patron Saint Julian the martyr. There the blind are illuminated,
demons put to flight, and all the sick healed through faith. There is praise of the Lord with all peace and joy, and there and everywhere Christ God, the Son of
God, is blessed, to whom are honor and dominion forever and ever.

# PASSIO SANCTI IULIANI MARTYRIS

## 1

**[001]** Sublimem atque venerabilem passionem Arvernae urbis beatissimi Iuliani martyris, cuius patronum sibi plebs haec venisse congaudet, – non ille
martyrium fugiens in hac urbem advenit, sed Christus pro delictis nostris intercessorem tribuens, ut urbs vel plebs haec et tanti martyris tutillam muneretur –,
quoniam passionem eius necdum intercoepit oblivio, vel nunc oportit cadem fidelibus scribi et in tempora secutura transmitti. Et quoniam in universum urbem
inlustrissimum est Dei martyres venerari, ita huic plebiculae sanctum Iulianum martyrem interccsorem vel sofregatorem praestare dignatus est Christus.

## 2

**[002]** Igitur in illo tempore in Vienensem urbem accedit persecutio christianis sub Crispino quondam praeside. Sanctissimus autem Ferreolus et ipse a Deo
martyr probatus, tunc in supradicta urbem tribuniciae gerebat potestatem. Sic tamen gerebat militiae officium, ut sacrae religionis propositum adimplerit.
Beatum autem Iulianum, quia esset fidelissimus christianus, in suo solatio detenebat. Cumque sanctus Ferreolus conperisset de christianorum persecutione, ait ad
sanctum Iulianum: 'Cognovi, persecutione christianorum ad hanc urbem esse venturam, et ideo obsecro, ut ab ista loca amoveas, quoadusque discedat persecutio
christianis'.

## 3

**[003]** Ubi hanc relationem audivit beatus Iulianus, se in territurium Arverne urbis contulit, ingressusque tugurium cuiusdam veterane, ab ea se occultare
deprecatus est. Quod hospicium non longe aberat, ubi tunc a gentilibus vana simulagra colebantur. Cuius latebram persecutores protenus adfuerunt, quam mulierem
sciscitantes, ubi mansisset ille, qui ante paulolum in suo hospicio confugisset, illaquae necante, sanctus vir nolens sibi coronam fraudari, persecutoribus se
ultro offerens, ait: 'Hic est quem queritis, implete quod vobis a principibus vestris praeceptum est'. Cumque aliquantulum oratione incubuiseet, cervices suas
persecutoribus obtullit. Ad illi nihil morati, extracto gladio capud eius amputantes atque exemplum ceterorum qui in Vienense civitate morabantur capud sancti
martyris redeuntes secum detullerunt. At ille sacri sanguinis sui unda perfudit.

## 4

**[004]** Nam illis temporibus a gentilibus vana superstitio in his locis celebrabatur. Duo tamen seneces conpuncti a divina virtute, corpus sancti Iuliani de
loco ubi decollatus est ad vicum cui nomen Brivate noncubatur transtullerunt, quem venerabiliter sepulturae tradedirunt. Inde redeuntes, pro beneficio
sepulturae sentiunt intra se a Deo quam in iuventute habuerant pristinam recipisse virtutem. In illo tempore quidam dives opibus ab Spaniam imperatorem cuidam
Trevere civitates culpabilis extitit. Quaem arcissitum et carcere mancipatum pro suo crimine iussit post comperendinatis diebus capitalem subire sententiam. Cum
haec cumperisset uxor eius, ancxia atque maesta ad cadaver mariti sui collegendum celeriter properavit. Cumque praefatum vicum matrona ipsa praetiriret,
praedicti seneces, quo tenderet vel quare [tam] tristis esset, diligentius inquiribant. At illa necessitate vel causa exposuit eis.

## 5

**[005]** Tunc dixerunt seneces matrisfamiliae: 'Ante paulolum decollatus est a persecutoribus quidam christianus, cuius corpus cum summo honore sepelientes,
inde redeuntes, quem in iuventute habuemus sensimus in nos [pristinam] recipisse virtute'. Cum haec audisset fidelissima mulier, statim ad sepulchrum sancti
Iuliani martyris orationem fudit sibique spondidit, ut, si verum suum videret incolomem et domui suae reverteretur superstitis, in illius honorem cellolam super
sepulchrum sancti Iuliani martyris aedificarent. Cumque diutissime orasset, perficiens viam quam pergebat, venit ad civitatem. Ingressaque, vidit virum suum
regis indulgentiam absolutum, et non solum absolutionem meruit, verum etiam honorem dignitatis recipit. Tempus quod absolutionem meruit interrogans cum mulier,
repperit, eo tempore virum suum fuisse absolutum, quo pro salute vire sui beatum Iulianum martyrem petiit, ut coniugem suum imperator absolveret. Quibus
remeantibus ad beati Iuliani sepulchrum, vota implentes, cellolam oratorii, sicut promiserat mulier, construxerunt, et deinceps per universos [vitae ipsorum]
annus [ingentia] munera portantes pro tantis beneficiis, ad venerabilem sepulchrum ipsius deferebant.

## 6

**[006]** Post opinionem beati martyris vel fama ubique declarata, omni populo [concelebranda innotuit, nunc vero huic] tales testis adsistat, ut plebi huic
tanti martyris patrocinia non recedant. Unde et per multa tempora a fidelissimis christianis aedificata est basilica in honore illius beatissimi viri, quae
celsum protulit aedificata fastigium, fulgit nunc in honorem nominis sui ornata privilegium, peculiaris patroni nostri Iuliani martyris referta virtutibus. Nec
silebo miraculum, quod Dominus ad laudem nominis sui facit, ut in die natalis illius multa devina beneficia orationibus vel intercessionibus sancti peculiaris
patroni nostri Iuliani martyris Dominus operatur. Caeci ibi inluminantur, daemonia effugantur, et omnes infirmi per fidem sanantur, et est ibi laus Domini cum
omni pace et gaudio, et benedicitur ibi et ubique Christus deus, Dei filius, cut est honor et imperium in saecula saeculorum.

# MGH EDITORIAL APPARATUS REGISTER

The critical apparatus belongs to the MGH editors, not to Gregory’s transmitted works. It is therefore registered separately rather than silently incorporated
into the bilingual text. Page references below are to the printed control editions used for this volume.

## MGH *Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum* 1,1 — *Libri historiarum X*

Bruno Krusch and Wilhelm Levison, second edition, 1951.

- Title pages and contents: preliminary pages I–VII.
- *Praefatio*: IX–XXXVIII.
- *Literaturverzeichnis*: XXXIX–XLII.
- *Gregorii episcopi Turonensis libri historiarum X*: 1–537.
- *Addenda et emendanda*: 538.
- *Corrigenda*: 539.
- *Index*: 540–566.
- *Lexica et grammatica*: 567–641.

The English and Latin Histories above follow this edition’s work order and text. Editorial preface, bibliography, manuscript discussion, addenda, corrigenda,
indices, and grammatical-lexical collections remain identifiable as MGH editorial matter rather than Gregory’s narrative.

## MGH *Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum* 1,2 — *Miracula et opera minora*

Bruno Krusch, second edition, 1969.

- Title pages and contents: preliminary pages III–VI.
- *Gregorii episcopi Turonensis libri octo Miraculorum*: 1–370, including *In gloria martyrum*, *De passione et virtutibus sancti Iuliani martyris*, *De
  virtutibus sancti Martini*, *Liber vitae patrum*, and *In gloria confessorum*.
- *Liber de miraculis beati Andreae apostoli*: 371–396.
- *Passio sanctorum septem dormientium apud Ephesum*: 397–403.
- *De cursu stellarum ratio*: 404–422.
- *In psalterii tractatum commentarius*: 423–427.
- Appendix, *Passio sancti Iuliani martyris*: 428–431.
- *Addenda et emendanda*: 432.
- *Index*: 433–446.
- *Lexica et grammatica*: 447–456.

The English and Latin works above follow this edition’s printed sequence. The addenda, indices, and grammatical-lexical collections remain MGH editorial matter.
Source lacunae, incomplete transmitted endings, capitula without corresponding narrative chapters, recension distinctions, and damaged appendix readings are
noted at the works to which they belong.
